column15: The City of Atlanta (CoA) utilizes a resilience framework through the Mayor's Office of Sustainability and Resilience (MOSR) to provide oversight on climate-related issues. The City Resilience Framework (CRF) is a unique framework developed by Arup with support from the Rockefeller Foundation, based on extensive research in cities. It provides a lens to understand the complexity of cities and the drivers that contribute to their resilience. Looking at these drivers can help cities to assess the extent of their resilience, identify critical areas of weakness, and identify actions and programs to improve the city's resilience. This CRF lens also provides a common language that enables cities to share knowledge and experiences. CRF is built on four essential dimensions of urban resilience: • Health & Wellbeing: of everyone living and working in the city • Economy & Society: the social and financial systems that enable urban populations to live peacefully and act collectively • Infrastructure & Environment: the way in which man-made and natural infrastructure provides critical services and protects urban citizens • Leadership & Strategy: effective leadership, empowered stakeholders, and integrated planning. Climate-related issues are incorporated within this framework along with issues such as disaster risk reduction, and emergency response through coordination. https://issuu.com/resilientatlanta/docs/100rc_strategydocument_withcover. Additionally, we report quarterly to the City Utilities Committee for Atlanta City Council to report on programmatic actions for sustainability and resiliency efforts.

Currently, “Plan A,” the City of Atlanta's Comprehensive Development Plan, is a community vision for the next 5, 10, and 15 years and more. The Department of City Planning led an 18th month planning process to update the current Vision and Goals, Needs and Opportunities, and Policies and Actions for every element in Plan A. This included 18 community workshops and 12 community open houses, as well as pop-ups throughout this community engagement process. The 2025 January community meeting focused on Climate Resilience and hosted a panel to highlight needs, opportunities, and actions proposed in Plan A and how to protect the environment and build capacity to face how to prepare, adapt, and respond to the effects of climate change. 

For the first time, climate resilience is a priority in the plan and is represented in the Climate Resilience + Natural Systems chapter. This chapter identifies how the natural environment and climate resilience factors into future planning. The goals revolve: climate resilience, tree canopy, watersheds, parks and trails, food systems, and environmental justice and critical partners.
Draft of the Plan (Ready for Adoption): file:///C:/Users/mmidanier/Downloads/Plan%20A%20_All%20Chapters_FinalDraft%205_July%202025%20(1).pdf.
column17: The CoA is continually including budgeting to tap into climate and community-related issues including: economic inequality, housing insecurity, energy burden, environmental stresses, infrastructure deficiencies, and mobility/transit. For municipal-owned buildings, energy savings performance contracts and the Sustainable Buildings Ordinance (>5k sq ft need to reach LEED Silver Certification) are included in budgeting to reduce energy and GHG emissions usage for our building stock. CoA has had several green programs related to climate-related issues. Examples have been included below that involve mitigating climate change effects through financial planning: -Green Infrastructure Design Challenge = $1,727,639-Green Infrastructure = $627,731-\'The GI Design Challenge was created to spark interest in developing creative solutions to some of the City's water quality and infrastructure challenges in a friendly and competitive manner. The difference with this Challenge is that the winning teams get to take their concept visions all the way through final design. \'-Greenway Acquisition Project (600430): = $5,419-Edgewood Greenspace Acquisition (600432): = $101,724- 34 Energy Saving Project Roof Repair 2020 CDBG (300264): = $100,000-Lakewood Park Project Partnership Agreement (PPA) with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE): = $15,000,000-Department of Parks and Recreation for improvements to four City of Atlanta parks: $2,032,301.70. MOVING ATLANTA FORWARD: 2024 INFRASTRUCTURE PACKAGE Atlanta voters approved three ballot measures on May 24, 2022, that will make significant investments in the city's infrastructure and economy. The measures — two bonds and the renewal of a special sales tax — will put $750M toward vital transportation, recreation, public safety and arts projects across the city for the next five years. The City of Atlanta has identified major infrastructure needs across streets, sidewalks, parks, and more. $190M bond will address horizontal infrastructure including transportation and parks. These two bonds are general obligation (GO) bonds which have long been a primary source of funding for capital investments to replace and expand city climate-supporting infrastructure. The third measure is a renewal of the TSPLOST (Transportation Special Purpose Local Option Sales Tax) program which will generate $350M for transportation projects. Our office and our sustainability and climate resilience plans are the basis of the ESG strategy and Social Bond Framework for the program. Additionally, in 2024, a reallocation of funds went into an Atlanta Community Energy Trust Fund of $500,000. This fund will be utilized to support clean energy projects and programs and a mechanism for generated revenue from the sale of renewable energy credits and federal funding opportunities.
column18: High Population Growth: According to the Atlanta Regional Commission, from 2020 - 2050, metro Atlanta is predicted to add 2.9 million residents. From 2015 -2019 Atlanta increased its population size by 10%. As a center for innovation and business, Atlanta will continue to have new businesses move to its city center. This population rise will increase demand in items such as water, food, and energy often stemming from carbon-intensive industries. For example, 97% of Atlantans consume a meat-heavy diet, with an average 1.56 mt annually (University of Oxford), implying that Atlanta diets produce about 723,309.60 metric tons annually of CO2e using the 2020 population count of 478,000. This number is likely to drastically increase. Additionally with a business as usual framework, car dependency will not decrease as from 2015 -2019 there was a 700,000 metric ton increase in greenhouse gases due to transportation. This increase in population will also increase traffic congestion. https://www.100atl.com/https://atlantaregional.org/atlanta-region/population-employment-forecasts/#:~:text=Forecast%20Highlights,over%20the%20next%2030%20years. Business Investment and Buy-in: Investors and businesses must undergo new regulatory institutions and legislation to slowly make the transition to a low-carbon economy. Investment companies, energy producers from fossil fuel sources, and large energy users will suffer the harshest short-term losses. At this moment the majority of corporations and businesses transitioning to the low-carbon industry are primarily voluntary, meaning that hitting a community-wide goal of 100% renewable energy in 2035 may be difficult. Sustainability must be a central pillar to business strategy. According to the U.N, a major challenge to achieve a \'just transition\' will be relocating jobs from traditional fossil fuel industries to renewable energy industries. Georgia Power is planning to shift away from coal-fired plants by 2035 state-wide will fuel this challenge. An inclusive sustainable growth model will be vital for managing market changes. In Atlanta, aligning with a just green/sustainable job market transition will heavily rely on collaboration/partnerships across the utility, energy companies, municipalities, possibly the green jobs alliance, and other relevant NGO's; this will assist in expanding renewables in the mix which will not only reduce risk in the energy space but also help meet the clean energy target. Furthermore, for Atlanta, carbon offset programs may have to be reserved for industries that have historically been difficult to decarbonize such as agriculture and transportation. https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/content/documents/22101ijtguidanceforinvestors23november1118_541095.pdf Centering Equity: Low-income and marginalized communities are starting to receive benefits from local government and regional projects, but on a low scale. Gentrification is a major issue within the City of Atlanta as the creation of greenspaces such as the Beltline have increased property values and overall cost of living. This has caused local and native residents to relocate to non-sustainable communities after being long-time residents. The Mayor's Office under Andre Dickens has worked to provide affordable housing and sustainable building practices to combat gentrification and inequities. https://www.urbandisplacement.org/maps/atlanta-gentrification-and-displacement/#:~:text=When%20UDP%20met%20with%20stakeholders,and%20other%20urban%20greening%20projects.https://www.11alive.com/article/money/mayor-andre-dickens-587-million-housing-affordable-housing-strike-force/85-88cae0a7-5f61-4df3-81ce-64f548d8ae62. Additionally, under the current Mayoral term, there is a Neighborhood Transformation Initiative where Mayor Dickens is uniting public, private, and philanthropic actors with residents in transforming disinvested neighborhoods. This applies the “Purpose Built Communities,” model of place-based change to these areas, with government leading and ensuring resident voices are centered. These neighborhoods in SW Atlanta have been chosen due to histories of disinvestment, shared poor outcomes, and available assets.

City Council adopted the Austin Climate Equity Plan in September of 2021 as well as a resolution directing City departments to report on ongoing climate action, including items in their budgets that fund climate-related work. The Office of Climate Action & Resilience and relevant City departments report verbally and in writing to City Management, City Council, and boards and commissions, on regular intervals. Currently, the One Austin Resilience Plan is also under development.

Recently, the Office of Climate Action & Resilience developed a Climate Implementation Plan with support from other departmental partners to focus on the most urgent actions to be taken every two years. This plan includes foundational climate actions that are essential to unlock potential GHG emission reduction opportunities as well as actions that will actually reduce emissions when implemented, the cost of implementation, and cost per ton of GHG emission. It also includes other quantitative and qualitative co-benefits (equity, just transition, accessibility, etc.) for each action.

A subcommittee of elected City Council Members meet monthly to hear from staff a out updates, progress, and issues related to climate, environment, water, and parks.
column16: Austin Climate Equity Plan is designed to be integrated and complementary to the City's other master plans including- Austin Energy Resource, Generation and Climate Protection Plan; Project Connect; Austin Resource Recovery Zero Waste Plan; Austin Strategic Mobility Plan; Austin Strategic Housing Blueprint; Water Forward, One Austin, and the City-wide Strategic Plan.
column17: City Council and the Budget Office have requested relevant City departments to highlight ongoing climate-action that is currently funded and intend to collect information on unmet climate-related needs within departments. The City of Austin Office of Climate Action & Resilience has also led city-wide efforts to pursue federal funding opportunities stemming from the Inflation Reduction Act and the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. Currently, the Office is also leading the effort in installing solar on municipal facilities, as well as supporting foundational support to develop a regional rail system to reduce GHG emissions due to regional traffic congestion on I-35.

column15: A permanent commission has been set up that will integrate climate and economic policies and an executive commission to coordinate the monitoring of the Climate Mission (Government Measure Climate Plan). • Permanent committee: Chaired by the mayor and made up cross-sectionally by the most relevant political and managerial positions in the City Council. The mayor may delegate the presidency to a deputy mayor. Specific functions: set the strategic lines, carry out operational monitoring of the mission, endorse the City Council's plans from a climate perspective, raise specific proposals and initiatives, identify and unblock bottlenecks and coordinate climate activity with the aim of strengthening the Administration and speeding up its activity. • Executive committee: Chaired by a person delegated by the municipal manager, and composed of people from the most involved areas of the City Council. Monthly frequency (at least). Space open to innovative proposals to achieve decarbonisation. Specific functions: coordinate the monitoring of the Mission and its corresponding reports and dashboard, incorporate transversal perspectives into climate action, promote collaboration between departments, coordinate working groups on adaptation, mitigation and of multilevel governance to generate and consider public policies, and to develop internal training at the City Council and deploy the Program for a carbon-neutral City Council.
column16: The new Government Measure Climate Plan is a transversal plan that incorporates objectives and actions from all areas of the City Council involved (Water Cycle; Waste Prevention and Management; Green and Biodiversity; Energy and Public Space; Public Health Agency; Digital Transition and Sports). 6 subplans deliver all these policies: Energy Transition Plan, Mobility Plan, Heat Plan, Neighborhood Climate Plan, Resilience Plan and \'Let's change for the climate\' plan.\nIn addition to the Climate Change and Sustainability Office, the Barcelona Energy Agency, the Department of Resilience, the Barcelona Public Health Agency, the Social Rights Area and the Food Policy are the driving force behind this plan. All this work is also present in the Climate City Contract within the framework of the 100 Climate Neutral and Intelligent Cities Mission, as the Climate Plan Government Measure is the tool to deliver it.
column17: One of the commitments included in the new Climate Plan is the evaluation and publication of the effect of the City Council's main investment items and current spending in terms of reducing GHG emissions. This will feed a new Climate Budget. \nA basic tool to carry out this environmental policy is the municipal budget and its distribution. For the preparation of the annual budget project, priority is given to assigning resources to one or another municipal action by virtue of government decisions. The detailed study of what municipal spending is intended for and its evolution over time is also a thermometer of how municipal policies are developed. This evaluation is possible thanks to the program budget methodology. \nIn the case of the climate budget, in general, the concepts with a clear impact on greenhouse gas emissions in the city and the possible improvements in this regard have been considered, compiling the following lines of action:- Neighborhood plan.- Promotion and management of public housing.- Environmental education.- Waste management, collection and treatment.- Public lighting management.- Green spaces and biodiversity.- Management and promotion of energy resources, water cycle, public space and mobility.

column15: Our environment and net zero work is supported and overseen by a cabinet member for the environment and transport, Cllr Majid Mahmood. A team is in place which is monitoring and supporting active projects underway to decarbonise council activity. This team reports quarterly on these projects to our climate change, nature and net zero programme board and provides oversight to the Cabinet member of the council. Over the last year, the team has continued to deliver 'Carbon Literacy Training for Local Authority Officers' to over 100 council staff, who have become accredited though the Carbon Literacy Trust. The team also continues to publish a bi-monthly newsletter which updates readers on our progress on Net Zero, shared with an audience of 2,500+ stakeholders, including residents and city-based organisations. The team has also implemented an environment and sustainability assessment process, in place since 2022, that requires all decisions going to cabinet to identify and mitigate negative environmental impacts, and highlight positive outcomes. Authors must complete an Environmental and Sustainability Assessment (ESA), which is then reviewed by the R20 team and appended to any cabinet decision report. These reports are published via the Council's CMIS system. Over 190 ESAs have been completed since they were introduced in 2022 (correct as of August 2025). We are currently refining and refreshing our ESA process and accompanying guidance to increase their rigour and impact. The Route to Net Zero team has worked with the councils Insight, Policy & Strategy team to produce a climate change briefing book in 2024, making data on Birmingham city's emissions (and other metrics) more open, accessible & engaging. Work was undertaken in 24/25 to update the briefing book. The briefing book is interactive and dynamic and accessible to all and can be viewed here: https://app.powerbi.com/view?r=eyJrIjoiNGY3MDliMmItMTI3Ny00Y2ExLWI4MGQtMDFmNjRiM2I5OGQ3IiwidCI6IjY5OWFjZTY3LWQyZTQtNGJjZC1iMzAzLWQyYmJlMmI5YmJmMSJ9&pageName=ReportSectiond03e1ded3dfd38e985cf . This data is available to all, citizens and businesses.\nThe Council has recently adopted a new Corporate Risk Management Policy and Strategy which seeks to review and mitigate principal and corporate level risks. Climate resilience and Corporate Net Zero delivery are two risks currently being reviewed for inclusion in this new corporate level risk management approach and will lead to regular assessment and action on an organisational wide basis. \n
column16: We are in the process of reviewing the Birmingham Development Plan, the statutory planning framework which guides all decisions on development and regeneration activity until 2031. This review includes an in depth update of the city's sustainability and energy policies and targets, making the net zero ambition compatible with new planning frameworks for developments in the city. This has involved gathering an evidence base on climate change that has helped inform the proposed policies as part of the issues and options consultation - this was completed in January 2024 and can be found here: https://www.birmingham.gov.uk/downloads/download/6619/low_carbon . The revised plan will address all climate related issues (Flooding, overheating, fuel poverty resulting from colder winters) and the proposed changes to the Birmingham Development Plan have been submitted to account for each of these. The Issues and options document undertook consultation at the end of 2023. The plan has now moved to the preferred options phase and was published for public consultation July-Aug 2024. We are currently refining the planning policies based on this consultation and will be publishing a cabinet report in Autumn 2025 outlining the proposed changes. Alongside the Birmingham Development Plan, the Our City Future 2040 Framework (OFC), sets out a long term development vision, seeks to continue Birmingham's development whilst accounting for climate related issues and articulates the city's net zero ambition. The 2040 goals set out in the plan are to:- Establish Central Birmingham as an integrated collection of vibrant, distinct and liveable neighbourhoods with services and amenities to ensure that residents can meet their daily needs within walking and cycling distances to increase sustainable transport links. OFCP also aims to: Support residential development at densities that make local services and public transport viable, Promote mixed use developments providing employment, open spaces, leisure and social infrastructure within walking, cycling and public transport environments, Ensure that communities have the resources, skills and support to build resilience within their areas. Together, the two plans demonstrate how climate related issues are considered by the jurisdiction at both the current implementation level of planning and the future strategic vision.
column17:
The priority that 'Birmingham is a city that takes a leading role in tackling climate change' was subsequently added as a 6th priority in the City Council's Budget and Plan in 2019. Our most recent financial plan 2023-2027 embeds climate change into its key principles: “Principle 2 - Increasing the pace and scale of growth, for those that need it the most, while delivering our climate change objectives”. The council is currently operating under a section 114 notice. To support cost savings, the council has published an improvement and recovery plan (IRP). The IRP includes net zero as a cross-cutting IRP corporate priority, committing the council to “working in a way which embeds climate action at the heart of the future Council and Council decision-making, ensuring that all directorates make the necessary changes to deliver these outcomes”. In 2024/25 the Route to Net Zero team has been working across the council to drive the delivery of savings where they align with and support the council's net zero commitments, including: 
Corporate Landlord programme to establishing an energy management function, deliver savings and reduce council GHG emissions. This is now operational and is working to cleanse our energy data and identify discrepancies between billed and actual usage.
Highways to develop business cases and pathways to continue the conversion of the city's existing (~50,000) sodium streetlights to LEDs. 
Procurement to improve their undertaking of our supply chain impacts and inform decisions re opportunities to make GHG and cost savings. We plan to write a net zero procurement strategy.
Waste Service Transformation Strategy, and decisions regarding the transition of waste collection vehicles (supported by our newly set up vehicle management service) and waste strategy review. 
Strategic Housing and Housing Asset Management to attract greater investment through a scaled-up delivery of ECO-funded housing retrofit with the potential to also create significant savings to the HRA.
Our newly established vehicle management system service - the centralised management of the council's vehicle fleet will support the council's longer-term decarbonisation activities and other priorities through, for example, the centralised management of infrastructure development (e.g., charging infrastructure for electric vehicles), ensuring fleet replacement responds to council needs - informed by comprehensive knowledge of the council's fleet makeup and its utilisation, and through consolidating purchasing and leasing arrangement to deliver value for money.
column18:
The City's 2019 Cabinet report on a 'just transition' sets out that measures taken to achieve the net zero ambition need to ensure that deprived communities who are most at risk and least able to defend themselves against climate-related issues (extreme heat, extreme cold, flooding). If measures do not prioritise these communities then they will continue to be more at risk despite the transition to a low-carbon economy. As mentioned, the City of Nature Plan seeks to put the green infrastructure in place to make these communities more resilient to environmental risks, whilst the long term retrofit ambition will also bring benefits to disadvantaged communities by improving home insulation and ventilation (helping alleviate fuel poverty and excess winter deaths). Similarly, the transport plan also seeks to address the risk of an unjust or unequal transition by prioritising affordable modes of transport, such as walking, cycling, and public transport. The emerging Birmingham Local Plan also incorporates consideration of climate risks and vulnerabilities, including overheating and flooding, into the core policies. Work is underway as of July 2025 to consider how our climate risks and vulnerabilities, combined with the impacts of climate change, are likely to impact upon both the council and our delivery of services to citizens, but also wider impacts on the city. Once agreed, these risks will be included in our corporate risk register.

The Birmingham Transport Plan 2031 sets out a bold approach to reducing transport emissions by reallocating road space, transforming the city centre, promoting active travel, and managing demand through parking. The Birmingham Clean Air Strategy sets out a series of pledges as to how the council and others in the city can support the journey towards cleaner air, including creating a Clean Air Zone which has now been introduced and resulted in reduced emissions in the city. The 2021 City of Nature plan sets out a 25 year plan to dramatically increase the number and quality of green spaces available to residents, prioritising the most disadvantaged areas first whilst also focussing on children, housing, health, wellbeing, jobs, and skills. This is a hugely ambitious plan which will have dramatic climate mitigation and resilience effects for residents, creating opportunities to not only provide all the benefits of quality green spaces and community groups (mental health, wellbeing, skills, etc.) but also increase drainage and tree canopy which will make areas more resilient to heating and flooding. Our Future City Central Birmingham Framework to 2040 sets out a planning vision for how Birmingham will look and feel to live in the future. Quality of life considerations and acting to limit climate-related issues are at the core of this document which provides a guide to future development plans, identifying the opportunities which come with a green focused development approach. - We are in the process of reviewing the Birmingham Development Plan, which will include an in depth review and update of the city's sustainability and energy policies and targets. As of July 2024 we are currently out for public consultation on a new suite of policies which include a number of ambitious measures including requirements for the consideration of embodied carbon and whole life cycle carbon.

column15: Cambridgeshire County Council does not have complete oversight of climate relates issues. While we are able to set our own strategy and policy, and undertake actions, these are only those within our remit as an upper tier authority. Operating across the region we also have a variety of other public sector organisations who all, largely independently, have their own political positions and policies on the environment. These include: Fenland District Council, Huntingdonshire District Council, Cambridge City Council, South Cambridgeshire District Council, East Cambridgeshire District Council, Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority, Police Service, Fire Service and the NHS amongst others. While we coordinate action where possible, we have little influence over the decisions and actions taken by these organisations, and cannot speak to functions that are their responsibility to deliver. For example, Government (DEFRA) places responsibly for air quality with the district councils. We can report some of that information here, but ultimately they have the statutory responsibility on this topic and therefore the actions are primarily developed, delivered and monitored by them.

column15:
The City of Chicago employs several oversight methods to address climate-related issues. Effective in 2024, the City reinstated the Department of Environment (DOE The department is led by a Commissioner and the Mayor's Office retained the Chief Sustainability Officer (CSO) role to ensure coordination at the highest level of municipal management. The Chief Sustainability Officer of Chicago is responsible for developing the city's strategic environmental vision, hiring a team of experts to create policy, spearheading innovative climate mitigation and adaptation projects, and providing guidance to departments and the Mayor. The DOE will become the city's central driver of environment and sustainability policy and programming while supporting department level initiatives and implementation. 

The City of Chicago's 2022 Climate Action Plan (CAP) establishes a robust and ambitious framework for climate action throughout city government. The CAP contains specific information regarding the implementation of projects that achieve Chicago's climate goals, which explicitly calls for the consideration of equitable climate principles in planning, policy development, and budgeting. The CSO works directly with Chicago's departmental leadership and City Council to align budgets and policies with the city's Climate Action Plan goals. 

Additionally, CSO and DOE staff are invited to support any department in the development of their respective strategic plans and commitments to ensure alignment with the 2022 CAP's targets. Chicago's City Council, specifically the Committee on Environmental Protection and Energy, holds regular and as-needed hearings and meetings to discuss climate and environmental issues, including but not limited to utility affordability, energy policy, environmental regulations, and environmental justice. The committee serves as a public-facing entity responsible for addressing constituent needs, holding the city accountable, and considering environmental legislation and resolutions. Relevant departments, committees, and/or subcommittees are informed about climate-related issues by Committee management.
column16: Chicago faces the dual challenge of supporting economic activity while ensuring sustainable, climate-conscious, and equitable development. Like many urban centers, Chicago is experiencing the growing impacts of climate change—such as extreme heat, more frequent and intense storms, urban flooding, and shoreline erosion—which place both chronic and acute stress on communities. The city has adopted an all-of-government approach to climate action. The city's Climate Action Plan (CAP) identifies specific, department-level actions to help the city reach its 62% emissions reduction target by 2040. As climate-related events become more frequent and severe, the plan embeds both mitigation and adaptation strategies throughout the city's governance. The planning process included meaningful collaboration across agencies, ensuring that even departments not directly involved in climate initiatives understand their potential roles in future efforts. A central principle of the CAP is equity. The plan emphasizes the need to address historical harms and reduce ongoing impacts in communities most affected by environmental and economic burdens. It also seeks to prioritize the equitable distribution of climate benefits to those same communities. Additionally, the city has integrated climate considerations into its hazard identification and mitigation planning—not as an isolated threat but as a factor influencing a wide range of hazards. This approach extends to collaboration with regional partners at the county level, reinforcing climate resilience across jurisdictions By working closely with community organizations, residents, city departments, and sister agencies, Chicago is taking a comprehensive, inclusive, and forward-looking approach to addressing climate change—ensuring that progress is not only sustainable but equitable for all. \n\n
column17: Climate change has significantly impacted the City of Chicago's financial planning, forcing the city to rethink how it allocates resources, raises revenue, and funds infrastructure. These impacts are being felt in both short-term budget decisions and long-term investment strategies. clean energy initiatives are embedded into departmental budgets (e.g., Transportation, Public Buildings, Planning) and long-range capital plans. However, Chicago continues to leverage state and local investments to meet its environmental and social equity commitments. In 2022, the City of Chicago entered into a five-year retail electricity contract to purchase renewable energy. In 2025, Chicago began supplying 100% renewable energy to city-owned buildings including its two airports. Chicago is investing heavily in green stormwater infrastructure (GSI) to combat flooding, especially in neighborhoods experiencing repeat urban flooding. Early projects included schoolyard transformations, green complete streets, bioswales, and permeable pavements. These 39 projects were backed by $6.1 million city funding and leveraged nearly $18 million from partners like Chicago Public Schools, Chicago Department of Transporation, and the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District (MWRD). In October 2024, Chicago issued an RFP for a new, equity-focused GSI Strategy, which aims to enhance permeable surfaces, green roofs, bioswales, and integrate equity and community engagement into planning. The City launched its Climate Infrastructure Fund, distributing around $5 million to environmental justice nonprofits to support green infrastructure, EV transitions, as well as community-driven climate efforts. From infrastructure upgrades to emergency response, from equity-centered investments to bond markets, nearly every facet of the city's financial planning is climate-impacted. \n\n
column18: As Chicago accelerates efforts to meet its climate and emissions reduction goals, including targets outlined in the 2022 Climate Action Plan, it must address the complex risks that arise from transitioning to a low-carbon economy. In Chicago, transitional risks span economic, infrastructural, social, and regulatory domains—and if unaddressed, could hinder progress toward equitable decarbonization. Economic and labor market disruptions are a key risk that the city has to consider as it shifts towards a low-carbon economy. Job losses and economic dislocation in carbon-intensive sectors will have disproportionate effect on historically underinvested communities and unionized workforces. Being one of the oldest cities in the country, the city's aging infrastructure is a major risk that the city faces. To mitigate aging infrastructure would require costly overhauls, and due to the lack of federal support toward infrastructure this is going to continue to be an issue fo rthe city. Electrification and retrofitting homes and buildings will increase short-term cost, which will place a financial burden on low-income residents and renters. The increase demand for data centers, cities like Chicago which is home to more that 160 data centers will continue to face an increase demand for electricity. This type of demand will cause major outages and grid stress especially during peak hours, as well as exceed the current grid capacity. Revenue and budgetary risk could arise from the decrease in fossil-fuel-related taxes and revenue. Governance and policy alignment could present a major challenge for the City of Chicago and its residents. Mismatches in climate policies between the federal, state and local governments can create compliance and implementation delay, inefficiencies and stalled progress on climate goals. Due to extreme weather events, the City is constantly looking for innovative strategies to mitigate climate and environmental risk. Without sufficient green space and cooling strategies, vulnerable neighborhoods may suffer from intensified heat, undermining Chicago's Department of Public Health (CDPH) public health goals.

column16: The City's long term strategic plan is required by local law to identify and analyze long-term planning issues associated with climate change and resiliency, and critical infrastructure and built environment. The strategic plan, along with the 10-year capital plan and other planning processes, inform the city's comprehensive planning efforts. The City publishes Climate Resiliency Design Guidelines, which incorporate forward-looking climate change data in the design of City capital projects.
column17: To ensure that we remain focused on prioritizing climate change and environmental justice in our investments and decision-making, New York City is one of the first global cities, and the first major city in America, to launch a Climate Budgeting initiative in 2024. Climate budgeting is a process that incorporates science-based climate and sustainability considerations into the City's budget decision-making process by evaluating how actions and spending today contribute to meeting longer-term climate targets. The process will allow our City to understand the climate impact of the dollars we spend, identify where more investment is needed, and champion forward-looking investments. For example, while switching buildings to efficient electric heating may have a higher cost than replacing fossil fuel equipment today, electrification reduces GHG emissions and improves local air quality over its lifetime. Similarly, while protecting vulnerable communities from heat waves will require significant investments, taking these steps will mitigate medical costs associated with increasingly intense heat while saving lives. The New York City Mayor's Office of Management and Budget's (OMB) newly established Environmental Sustainability & Resiliency Task Force, a group that coordinates and guides smart sustainability and investments, leads this initiative in partnership with the Mayor's Office of Climate & Environmental Justice (MOCEJ). Climate budgeting will be continuous and include an annual publication that will be part of the City's Executive Budget. This climate budget publication will highlight the City's new and ongoing investments and provide a snapshot of the projected impacts of our collective actions on the path toward meeting long term climate goals. Monitoring and reporting on progress will ensure transparency and accountability and will help guide the City's continued work. The first Climate Budget publication through City's Fiscal Year 2025 Executive Budget was released in April 2024.
column18: New York City Panel on Climate Change (NPCC) provides scientific projections and identifies climate risks for New York City, which include intense rainfall events, coastal flooding, extreme cold and heat events, and poor air quality for residents. Without climate mitigation and adaptation, by 2050 more New Yorkers will die each summer from intense heat. Greater dependence on air conditioning will increase demand on the electrical grid, increasing the chances of rolling brownouts or blackouts, leading to infrastructure outages and spoiled food and medicine stocks. It will also impact our ability to meet renewable energy targets. New York City's economy is one of the largest in the United States and the world. It is critical that climate legislation in NYC lowers the city's overall emissions while bolstering a vital global economy at the same time.

column15: The Mayor has set a target for London to be a net zero carbon city by 2030. The Mayor has a duty to address climate change (mitigation and adaptation) under the Greater London Authority (GLA) Act 1999. The Mayor can: implement policies to mitigate emissions, particularly through the Mayor's Transport Strategy, the London Environment Strategy, London Plan and London Economic Development Strategy. Under the GLA Act, the provision of London's Environment Strategy dealing with adapting to climate change shall contain; assessment of the consequences of climate change for Greater London; proposals and policies for mitigation and adaptation to climate change relating to Greater London. In 2001 the GLA, the Environment Agency, the UK Climate Impacts Programme, and other partners set up the London Climate Change Partnership (LCCP) to be the centre of expertise on climate change adaptation and resilience to extreme weather in London. LCCP's (renamed as the London Climate Ready Partnership - LCRP) mission is to coordinate public, private, and community sector organisations to prepare London for extreme weather today and climate change into the future by collecting and sharing high quality research and evidence, informing policy and supporting champions within partner organisations who drive forward action. London Resilience coordinates institutions and communities to prevent, handle, recover and learn from disruption, and adapt to change. They work on behalf of the Mayor, the GLA, local authorities and London Fire Brigade to support the work of the London Resilience Partnership, which brings together more than 170 organisations (fire, police, local authorities, utilities etc.) with responsibilities for preparing for, and responding to, emergencies. This is achieved by assessing risks, working to reduce the likelihood or impact of those risks, and, where risk can't be eliminated, preparing arrangements to respond, recover, and learn from emergencies. London Resilience has prepared the London Risk Register, designed to provide a summary of the main risks affecting Greater London, including climate-related risks. Following increasing severity and frequency of climate impacts, including the flash floods in 2021 and the 40-degree heatwave in 2022, the Mayor commissioned an independent London Climate Resilience Review, chaired by Emma Howard Boyd, to take stock and make recommendations to guide London's preparations for more extreme weather. The Review published in July 2024 provides an assessment of London's climate resilience and makes 50 recommendations for action to guide London's preparations for more frequent and intense climate impacts. It gathered evidence from individuals, communities and organisations including the National Health Service, Transport for London, London Fire Brigade, the Metropolitan Police, Borough Councils, the GLA, UK Government, NGOs, the financial services sector, sports and cultural institutions. The Mayor has allocated additional funds over the next 3 years and set out his priorities for a Greener & More Climate Resilient London in his delivery plan (MD3384 Delivery Plan - Delivering a Greener, More Climate-Resilient London | London City Hall ) www.london.gov.uk/programmes-strategies/environment-and-climate-change/climate-change/climate-adaptation/london-climate-resilience-review Departments and teams across the GLA are supported to embed best practise on climate in all projects and programmes. The Climate and Equalities Tool (the C&E Tool) has been developed by GLA staff with the University of Manchester Tyndall Centre's Centre for Climate Change and Social Transformations. The C&E Tool is a simple excel tool that staff are encouraged to use at the start of a new project to assess the potential climate and equalities impacts of their work, and help strengthen these or avoid unintended negative consequences during project development. The C&E Tool is applicable to all types and scales of projects, including regulatory, strategic and capital programmes. The Climate and Equalities teams also provide support, guidance and review to users across the GLA. There is a public version of the C&E Tool for boroughs and partners: data.london.gov.uk/dataset/climate---equalities-tool. To further embed climate into all projects and programmes, the GLA is rolling out Climate Literacy Training which will be available to all staff members. The full day in-person course has been accredited by the Carbon Literacy Project and will ensure that GLA staff understand the science behind climate change, the impact it is already having globally and locally, the role the GLA has in tackling it and increase staff competence and confidence in talking about climate change. It requires staff to commit to 3 action-based pledges setting out what they will do in their role at the GLA to reduce carbon emissions as well as help London adapt and prepare for the impacts. Over 300 staff have now undertaken the training.
column16: Climate is taken into consideration through the London Plan, which has policies designed to drive down greenhouse gas emissions from new buildings, both in terms of construction materials and when the buildings are in use, and for adapting to climate change e.g. managing overheating risk. The London Plan is delivering carbon reductions far in excess of those required by national building regulations in England. The London Plan also takes consideration of climate in terms of ensuring new developments are well served by public transport, and it commits the Mayor to working with the Environment Agency and relevant local authorities including outside London to safeguard locations for a new Thames Barrier in the future (which is likely to be needed to protect the city from future climate related flood events). A Sustainability Statement has been made available that outlines and describes the environmental and sustainability considerations and the views of consultees that have been integrated into the London Plan 2021: https://www.london.gov.uk/sites/default/files/london_plan_2021_sustainability_statement.pdf Along with other evidence, the London Climate Resilience Review will inform development of the next London Plan. The GLA is investigating ways to enhance climate adaptation measures through the new London Plan.
column17: The Mayor has declared a climate emergency and committed London to be net zero by 2030. As part of that commitment the Mayor is working with the functional bodies (GLA Group) to develop Net Zero 2030 strategies for their own emissions. The functional bodies of the GLA are the Metropolitan Police, London Fire Brigade, Transport for London, the London Legacy Development Corporation and Old Oak and Park Royal Development Corporation. Since the 2023-24 budget, each Functional Body of the GLA Group has prepared a climate budget, which sits alongside the GLA group financial budget. The climate budget outlines what each Functional Body will be spending in the coming years to reduce emissions over the next three financial years and the estimated carbon savings this will deliver and encompasses both mitigation and adaptation measures. This climate budget also estimates the scale of further funding required to deliver Net Zero by 2030 for our estate and fleets and programmes that contribute to lowering London-wide emissions. Having a climate budget has put climate at the front and centre of the budget process. It has ensured that responsibility is being taken across the organisation to demonstrate that our net zero target is being taken seriously and that budget is being made available to tackle our emissions. The climate budget itself has highlighted clearly the investments we're making across our estate and fleet to reduce emissions, such as upgrading to more energy efficient lighting, introducing fleet telematics and EV charge points, installing heat pumps and solar arrays, buying electric buses and progressing the Transport for London Power Purchase Agreement. We are working towards widening the climate budget to include scope 3 emissions. In his 2021 manifesto, the Mayor committed to developing a green financing facility for London, with the aim to support the acceleration of private sector finance and the development of robust business models for environmental priorities. In June 2023, he launched the London Climate Finance Facility (LCFF), which aims to unlock billions of long-term, flexible, private finance to support the decarbonisation of London's buildings, energy and transport systems, thereby tackling the triple dangers of toxic air pollution, climate change and congestion; to accelerate significantly the development and delivery of climate and environmental projects, working with strategic partners; and to build on and work with London's existing financing sector's capabilities to secure investment for London from both private and public sector sources and strengthen its competitiveness as a sector. As part of the LCFF, the Mayor also launched at LCAW 2023, the Green Finance Fund (GFF) to support the GLA's goals of accelerating delivery of public sector net zero projects, establish maintain credibility and begin building a track record of successful investment. The GFF is will lending up to £500m to projects working towards London's net zero ambitions. The aim is to accelerate decarbonisation in London by lowering the cost and simplifying the conditions of borrowing for eligible organisations, and so provide flexible loans to support partners to accelerate towards net zero 2030. The Mayor has also announced (December 2023) the LCCF's first partnership with a private investor Sustainable Development Capital LLP (SDCL), establishing the London EDGE Fund. The Mayor has committed 50m, which has been matched by SDCL to make it initially a £100m fund capable of providing an off-balance sheet financing solution for organisations where energy can be delivered as a service. Discussions are already underway with other investors to increase this. In total since 2018, the Mayor's green financing programmes have made available a total of £1.1 billion of investment to decarbonisation projects in London. The GLA is currently exploring further options to secure greater levels of private sector finance and has announced a Green Finance Taskforce to identify measures and support that the Mayor can put in place to accelerate private sector investment into London projects.
column18:
The Mayor, through the Green New Deal mission (part of London's Recovery programme) has set the goal of doubling London's green economy by 2030. This is equivalent to growing green businesses to around £100 billion in sales by 2030, bringing with it more jobs and support to the London economy. London uses the value of sales in London's Low Carbon and Environmental Goods and Services (LCEGS) sector as a proxy for measuring the size of the green economy. The latest figures (GLA, forthcoming) show that the green economy sector in London was worth £54.9bn in 2023/24. This value was generated by over 20,000 businesses that employed over 341,100 people in the sector in 2023/24. London's LCEGS employment annual growth rate was 9.5% from 2022/23 to 2023/24; which is stronger than the UK growth of 7.9% from 2022/23 to 2023/24. London's LCEGS sector exports have a value of £3.8bn in 2023/24, accounting for 23% of the UK's LCEGS exports. In 2023/24 London's Low Carbon and Environmental Goods and Services sector was made up of the following proportions: Low Carbon 60%, Renewable Energy 30% and Environmental 10%, which have remained at similar proportions in recent years. Under these three sectors the research identifies 24 sub-sectors. Overall, the five largest sub-sectors in the LCEGS sector by sales make up 72% of London's total sales. They are carbon finance, wind, geothermal, building technologies and alternative fuels. All these sub-sectors have grown in terms of sales, employees and companies since 2020-21, and demonstrate London's relative strength in these areas.

The London Growth Plan includes Green Growth Ambition and activity to support the just transition to a low carbon circular economy. It sets out to accelerate London's transition to net-zero by integrating low-carbon priorities into economic recovery and growth strategies. The London Growth Plan specifically commits to:
Mobilise institutional investment into zero-carbon infrastructure and sustainable real estate, aiming to scale up critical green infrastructure; Support businesses in their decarbonisation and climate adaptation efforts, helping them align with broader net-zero objectives; and Invest in net-zero infrastructure, under the housing, infrastructure, and green skills pillars—ensuring sustainable development and workforce readiness.

The GLA has undertaken research to understand which sectors are most at risk from the transition. This revealed that the most impacted sectors are manufacturing, energy, transport and storage, electricity, gas and manufacturing. High emitting industry groups such as these are relatively small with London's economy mainly reliant on tertiary services. However these sectors typically have a strong spatial concentration in London, in some cases a high proportion of Black, Asian and Minority Ethnic employees and in some cases low levels of pay. The transition to a low carbon economy will require a substantial shift in gear, meaning supply chains will need the workforce and skills to meet the required need. Further work is underway to understand what skills will be needed and how these can be matched to the existing workforce and at risk sectors. The Mayor is investing in green training opportunities to ensure London has the skills needed to transition to a low-carbon economy. The Mayor is investing in the equipment needed for training in low carbon technologies so that adult education providers can deliver the training employers need. The Mayor is funding green skills programmes, building partnerships of employer and training providers to ensure Londoners get the skills they need to be able to access green job opportunities and to support a just and fair energy the transition. This includes the Green Skills Academy, part of the Mayor's £44million Skills Academies (MSA) Programme which focuses on areas where there is high or growing demand for skills and jobs. As of March 2024, the Green Skills Academy has supported over 6,570 Londoners on to new green skills training and 3,640 into a good job, apprenticeship, or paid work placement. Most training through the MSA is at Level 3 or below and work continues with for example a Youth Board established in February 2025, which is a student-led advisory group formed to shape green skills programming, starting with a 'Women in STEM' event. The Mayor's Skills Bootcamps for programme is providing opportunities for Londoners who are unemployed or in work, including self-employment, to train in higher level green skills. This includes retrofit assessor and energy efficiency skills. The Mayor's Adult Education Budget (AEB) funds a range of green skills. The GLA estimates approximately 10 per cent of the £320 million AEBs annual budget funds green skills training - from horticulture and recycling, through to construction and engineering skills important for retrofitting and low carbon transport. The Mayor has made additional green qualifications eligible for adult skills funding

column18: There are risks with a rapid transformation, such as protests against sharp measures for instance increases in prices, bans, etc. Higher prices can lead to reduced availability and higher housing costs. Socially paid transports can be more expensive (transport service, school transport, waste management) which burdens public finances. Lack of electrical power threatens electrification and can lead to the use of fossil reserve power. Dependence on biofuels can affect shortage situations and increase costs. There are many important aspects to consider in the governance of a city; in some cases the climate work can conflict with other important goals. In procurement, there is a risk that finances always outweigh the climate effect, a risk of receiving too few tenders and making a bad deal. The Local Government Act's requirements for financial management, profitability in municipal incorporated companies in municipalities and the EU's state aid rules can limit the possibility of taking the lead and require collaboration with private actors. Densification of buildings can reduce the opportunities for green spaces locally, which can increase problems with heat islands and biodiversity. A fast transition e.g., digitalization can lead to an increased vulnerability , exclusion due to rapid digitization, e.g., older people.

column15: Essex County Council (ECC) established the Essex Climate Action Commission (ECAC), an independent body which advises on Essex's approach to climate action, setting out strategic direction and approach to action plans. The Commission advises ECC on direction of travel of its own plans. • Responsibility for the climate agenda is held by the Leader of the Council, who has appointed the Cabinet Member for Environment, Waste Reduction and Recycling to lead the programme of work and represent him. • ECC makes representations on the climate agenda to central government, including working with our local MPs to lobby on climate related issues and representing local government at committee hearings in Parliament. • Climate related issues are considered in all decisions across the whole of the Council's operations via the Equalities Comprehensive Impact assessment which must be completed before any decision can be made by the Council. • ECC recognises the alignment between Climate Action and Levelling Up. Whilst in the broadest sense all Essex residents are affected by climate change, it is people living in places with the highest levels of deprivation who experience the impacts of climate change most acutely; have fewer resources to respond to, and recover from, extreme weather events such as flooding; and are therefore less resilient. • In 2024, ECC developed a Climate Adaptation Plan Framework called 'Essex Strengthening Adaptation & Resilience to Climate Change' which outlines the immediate and long-term priorities and strategies for climate adaptation in Essex, including climate risks to Essex communities, businesses, and services. It describes Essex County Council and community actions to build resilience and adapt to the effects of the climate challenge.\n
column16: • A dedicated Climate Action Planning Team of specialists/experts within Planning has been established to drive the implementation of the built environment ECAC recommendations. They advise and support district officers, as well as developers, with new build housing and commercial standards, to deliver net zero, climate resilient and nature friendly planning policies. They also support with advice on planning applications (including on overheating, sustainable drainage and green infrastructure as well as carbon reduction) and support the performance of building post-development. This team also helps deliver on net zero carbon housing demonstrator/pilot projects in each district. This capacity and specialist knowledge enables ECC to work with District, Borough & City Councils to provide good design, appropriate challenge, and support so that new build and development proposals positively contribute to meeting our climate change targets.(https://www.essex.gov.uk/news/2024/new-team-working-towards-net-zero-housing#::textNew%20homes%20in%20Essex%20will,Carbon%20in%20New%20Homes%20category.) (https://www.essexclimate.org.uk/news/award-winning-team-exemplifies-essex%E2%80%99s-commitment-net-zero-housing) ECC has produced a suite of resources to support net zero and climate resilient housing development, published on the Essex Design Guide. (https://www.essexdesignguide.co.uk/climate-change/) • ECC collaborates with the local planning authorities in Essex and responds to development proposals and local plans to achieve high standards in climate change mitigation and adaptation. District Councils are now adopting net zero as a requirement in their local plans, leading to significantly more new homes across Essex being built to net zero standards. As of September 2025, the adoption of net zero policies in local plans will lead to 85,000 out of the 283,000 new homes to be built by 2050 being net zero in operation. 61,000 of these will also have lower embodied carbon.
column17:
• Climate related issues are considered in all decisions across the whole of the Council's operations through the Equalities Comprehensive Impact Assessment which must be completed before any decision can be made by the Council. • In November 2021, Essex County Council (ECC) endorsed in full the recommendations made in the Essex Climate Action Commission's report 'Net Zero: Making Essex Carbon Neutral' in July 2021. To support delivery of these recommendations, a four-year Climate Action Plan was developed, with a budget of 200 million allocated over four years. The first Climate Action Plan was published in November 2021 and was updated in July 2023, when the budget was increased to £250 million. Due to impending devolution and local government reorganisation, elections in Essex have been delayed and the administration extended for two years. The Climate Action Plan is currently being updated to cover this additional two year period and it will be published later in 2025, with a budget of circa 117 million for the period 2025-2027/28.. • The Council has revised its Treasury strategy to prohibit investment in fossil fuels and other environmental harmful activities. The Treasury Strategy can be found at the 'Essex County Council Everyone's Essex Annual Plan and budget 2025/26' (p95) and it includes a commitment that: 'The Council will not knowingly invest directly with counterparties whose activities and practices pose a risk of serious harm to individuals or groups, or whose activities are inconsistent with the Council's values. This would include, inter alia, avoiding direct 
investment in institutions with material links to:
• human rights abuse (such as child labour and political oppression)
• environmentally harmful activities (for example, pollutants, destruction of habitat and fossil fuels)
• socially harmful activities (such as tobacco and gambling)' (p115). (https://www.essex.gov.uk/sites/default/files/2025-03/Essex%20County%20Council%20Annual%20Plan%202025%20to%202026.pdf)'
column18: \'The transition of the economy of Essex to a low-carbon economy will require new employees entering the workforce with educational backgrounds and training in green skills. It will also require re-skilling and upskilling for existing members of the workforce. Following a recommendation from the Essex Climate Action Commission (ECAC), Essex County Council (ECC) commissioned Mace to undertake a review of green skills and related infrastructure in the county (March 2022). Gaps and challenges were identified such as: (i) limited availability of data for both supply and demand; (ii) shortage of teaching staff; (iii) lack of carbon literacy; (iv) disconnection of educators with industry and business needs. (https://www.essex.gov.uk/sites/default/files/migration_data/files/assets.ctfassets.net/knkzaf64jx5x/2boS3yEpHGwgLnZMXqRFfp/1918c6857a4f61ed7a73a1b100c730aa/Essex-Green-Skills-Infrastructure-review-2022.pdf) Building on this, ECC's Local Skills Improvement Plan (2024) sets out how to close the identified skills gap. (https://www.essexlsip.co.uk/issue30/home.htm) Significant skills and business challenges exist in reaching net zero, particularly across industry. ECC's sector development strategy highlights five key sectors with the highest growth, each requiring a transition to greener processes and practices. Essex County Council is supporting the golden thread of climate, ESG, and resilience across these business sectors and more generally through a number of initiatives, including Great Start and Essex Construction and Manufacturing Alliances. Great Start is an example of providing access to simple, accessible, and non-technical information, advice, and guidance that is available on demand and self-serve, supporting businesses on their first tangible steps to more sustainable processes and practices. This imperative was reiterated at our Green Summit in May 2025, with 100 business leaders in attendance.\n\nSome risks related to the transition to a low-carbon economy are addressed by the Essex Sector Development Strategy, which defines priorities for a stronger, more sustainable economy and reflects the system and culture changes required of businesses and local communities in order to thrive in a low-carbon, energy-efficient economic system. ECC engages directly with business leaders - for example through an energy roundtable in July 2025 with a further summit planed in the autumn - to identify and work together to address risks arising from the transition to net zero energy. Clean energy is a key priority identified by the newly established Greater Essex Business Board.

column16: The City of Las Vegas 2050 Master Plan contains comprehensive implementation strategies that can be acted upon by City departments set by Council resolution or ordinance or in, covering Land Use & Environment, Economy & Workforce, Systems & Services. Associated and related goals and outcomes of the master plan include:-Master & Development Plans: There are 16 areas of the City. There is baseline data already for each area, with goals listed in the Master Plan to improve the area. Each area will have work done to revitalize the neighborhood and considers climate and resilience in decision making. Currently, a special area plan has been adopted for Downtown Las Vegas and East Las Vegas, with plans for La Madre Foothills, Rancho, and Charleston commencing 2022-23. -Urban Forestry: Plant and maintain 60,000 diverse and high quality native and adaptive trees on public and private property by 2050. The City's tree canopy increases to 20% by 2035 and 25% by 2050 utilizing native and adaptive drought tolerant tree species. 85% of the City's population lives within a 1/3 mile from green infrastructure features that provide localized cooling through park space, tree canopy cover, or vegetative surfaces.- Environmental Justice: Achieve attainment or maintenance status for all measured criteria pollutant. For any non-attainment pollutants, a decrease in the annual concentration. By 2050, no brownfields are found within the City. The annual number of days in which the Air Quality Index (AQI) exceeds 100 decreases over time. For each identified planning area, priority environmental justice conditions, risks, and exposure are reduced.- GHG Emissions: Achieve carbon neutrality by 2050.-Water Conservation Goals: Community water consumption will be reduced to 105 GPCD by 2035 and 90 GPCD by 2050, consistent with SNWA's Water Resource Plan. The City municipal operations shall reduce total water consumption 2% annually, covering the sectors of buildings and facilities, park and landscaping, and wastewater treatment.-Energy Conservation Goals: 80% of region's energy consumption at residential and commercial buildings is reduced through energy efficiency measures by 2050. 50% of both municipal and community energy supply is from renewable sources by 2030, consistent with the Nevada RPS (Renewable Portfolio Standard); and 100% by 2050. Municipal operations shall reduce total energy consumption 2% annually, covering the sectors of buildings and facilities, streetlighting, and wastewater treatment.-Waste Conservation Goals: 80% of the region's waste disposed of by landfill is reduced by 2050 and a recycling rate of at least 40% is achieved. Eliminate landfill-based emissions by 2050. CLV municipal operations shall reduce waste stream 2% annually.

column15: The City of Los Angeles is a Mayor-Council-Commission form of government. A Mayor, City Controller, and City Attorney are elected by city residents every four years for a maximum of two terms. Fifteen City Council members representing fifteen districts are elected by the people for four-year terms (for a maximum of three terms) by individual geographic districts of about equal sizes in population. Members of Boards & Commissions are generally appointed by the Mayor, subject to the approval of the City Council. As the Chief Executive Officer, the Mayor supervises the administrative process of the City and works with the City Council on matters relating to legislation, budget, and finance. The Mayor recommends and submits the annual budget to the Council. As it relates to general governance structure, the Mayor brought climate consideration into the mainstream of governance structures with the release of the 2015 Sustainable City pLAn by adding Chief Sustainability Officers to key departments throughout the city. These officers report to the General Manager of their respective departments, but also have a direct connection to the Chief Sustainability Officer of the City. This provides that sustainability goals are coordinated across the City and throughout departments, and that leadership from all City departments are focused on sustainability goals. The Mayor's Office of Energy and Sustainability (MOES) is the central body in the City charged with climate policy and leads the implementation of L.A.'s Green New Deal (GND 2019), an expanded vision of the Sustainable City pLAn (2015). L.A.'s GND elaborates in even more detail L.A.'s vision for a sustainable future and provides an action plan that tackles the climate emergency with accelerated targets and new aggressive goals. MOES liaises with a network of 30 Departmental Chief Sustainability Officers who serve as the sustainability leads in each of their respective departments and also works with critical partner organizations and stakeholders to implement L.A.'s GND initiatives. Additionally, City Council also has the authority to legislate climate policy. Los Angeles established the Climate Emergency Mobilization Office within the Department of Public Works. The office, guided by the principles of environmental justice, coordinates with the Mayor and City Council, and collaborates with City departments through engagement with frontline leaders and their communities. The activation of a community-led Climate Emergency Commission (CEC), ongoing community assemblies and virtual events, and broad public mobilization will be key to the effective implementation of equitable and just climate policies and execution of LA's Green New Deal. The City Council is the governing body of the City, except as otherwise provided in the Charter, and enacts ordinances subject to the approval or veto of the Mayor and may override the veto of the Mayor by a two-thirds vote. As required by the City Charter and established by Resolution, the Council is organized into committees to facilitate adequate consideration of matters subject to its attention. All members are appointed by the President of the City Council. Each Council Member is the Chair of one committee and a member of two others. One of the current council committees is the Energy and Environment committee which discusses matters related to climate change and environmental issues. Through reports and hearings, Committees obtain information on matters under consideration and make recommendations to the Council in the form of signed written reports which are summarized on an Agenda by the City Clerk for the information of individual Council Members, City departments, and the public.
column16: The City of Los Angeles General Plan is the City's blueprint to guide development decisions. It contains 11 Citywide Elements and a Land Use Element comprising 35 Community Plans. State law details mandatory topics that must be addressed in a General Plan but affords local jurisdictions latitude in creating a structure for their document. Each General Plan Element includes goals and policies, which speak to the position and priorities of the local jurisdiction and must be referenced as findings in major development decisions. Most elements also include a list of programs, which captures a broad range of work efforts that are envisioned to advance such goals and policies. The City of Los Angeles General Plan is a strategy for sustainable and resilient long-term growth of the City. Various elements of the General Plan - including the Health and Wellness Element, Safety Element, Housing Element, Mobility Element, Open Space Element, and Conservation Element - all include policies, objectives, and implementation programs to advance the sustainability and resiliency of the City. Additionally, the State requires General Plans to include certain topics and information regarding sustainability and resiliency, including identification of potential hazards, and approaches to climate adaptation and resilience. Strategies in the City's General Plan to advance sustainability and climate resiliency include directing future jobs and housing growth to transit-served areas to reduce greenhouse gas emissions; supporting a mix of uses and walkability in neighborhoods; encouraging multimodal transportation options and access for users of all ages and abilities; promoting water conservation, food sustainability, and the use of clean energy; implementing various efforts to reduce vehicle miles traveled such as mobility hubs, transportation demand management, and technology improvements; improving air quality and reducing urban heat island effects by planting, preserving, and protecting the urban forest; and implementing green infrastructure and green streets by using sustainable materials and green building techniques. The City's General Plan was updated in 2021 to reflect additional opportunities to incorporate strategies around climate adaptation, hazard mitigation, and recovery as well as efforts to increase equity to respond to the most vulnerable communities. The updated General Plan more clearly address environmental justice and underlying social vulnerabilities that compound communities' hazard exposure, as well as incorporates more recent Citywide plans, policies, goals, and programs including Los Angeles' Green New Deal (2019) and the Resilient Los Angeles Plan (2018), as well as operational plans such as the Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (2018), Emergency Operations Plan, Floodplain Management Plan, and Floodplain Management Ordinance. The City is currently embarking on a Climate Vulnerability Assessment to guide priorities in climate adaptation, emergency and safety preparedness, risk management, and community resilience. The City of Los Angeles completed the 2024 Hazard Mitigation Plan (HMP) to lessen the vulnerability to disasters, and demonstrate the City's commitment to reducing risks from natural hazards. An HMP serves as a guide for decision makers as they commit City resources to minimize the effects of natural hazards. The HMP is intended to integrate with existing planning mechanisms such as building and zoning regulations, long-range planning mechanisms, and environmental planning. The planning process includes conducting a thorough hazard vulnerability analysis, creating community disaster mitigation priorities, and developing subsequent mitigation strategies and projects. For the first time, the 2018 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan considered and profiled the impacts of climate change on the natural hazards of concern.
column17: The City's concept of the budget includes the traditional orientation of budgeting as a plan of financial operations, providing an estimate of proposed expenditures for a given period of time or purpose, and the proposed means of financing them. Therefore, budgeting consists of a management program, a decision-making program, and a financial program. Although climate-related issues and considerations are not yet intimately integrated into the City's financial planning, the Mayor's Office of Budget, Finance, and Innovation is a participant in the C40 Climate Budgeting pilot network to design and develop a multi-year implementation plan for mainstreaming climate considerations into the City's annual budgeting process.
column18: A rapid transition to a low-carbon economy without just-transition policies may result in inequitable impacts on Los Angeles. Without a strong decarbonized workforce pipeline, many legacy workers may become displaced as green jobs overtake carbon-intensive careers. It is critical to establish training and pipeline programs so that the green economy is available to both local Angelenos and to displaced fossil fuel sector workers. In addition, a decarbonized economy should strategically transition sectors simultaneously. For example, transportation must decarbonize alongside the electric grid. If the grid electrifies before rapid renewable integration, homes and vehicles will be powered by the grid run predominantly by natural gas. This presents the danger of offsetting the air quality benefits of electric vehicles by increasing pollution emitted from power plants. Also, if the grid decarbonizes without commensurate transition by the building and transportation sector, electricity costs may dramatically increase. By electrifying all sectors, and increasing overall electricity sales, average electricity rates can stay low and affordable.

Manchester's climate-related oversight is anchored by the Manchester Climate Change Framework 2020-2025, endorsed by the Leader of Manchester City Council (MCC), updated in 2022 and fully aligned with the city regions (Greater Manchester Combined Authority) 5 year Environment Plan https://www.greatermanchester-ca.gov.uk/media/alnl0fsy/gmca_5-year-plan_final_digital_v3-ua.pdf . The Manchester Climate Change Partnership (MCCP), comprising key sectors like the local authority, universities, and energy providers, is responsible for delivering the Framework. Membership can be found here: https://www.manchesterclimate.com/MCCP. The Council plays a key role, with its Deputy Chief Executive and Executive Member for Environment on the Partnership board. The Manchester Climate Change Agency (MCCA), established by the Council in 2015, is an independent body that supports the Partnership and reports to the Council's Environment and Climate Change Scrutiny Committee. Manchester City Council has its own Climate Change Action Plan 2020-2025, coordinated by the Zero Carbon Coordination Group, chaired by the city's Director of Planning and Place. This group, alongside five key workstreams, meets regularly to drive climate action. Governance is reinforced by regular meetings of the MCCP board and task groups addressing specific climate challenges. This integrated approach ensures climate oversight across all sectors, advancing Manchester's net-zero goal by 2038. Please note- at the time of writing the City and City Council are updating their Climate Change Plans to cover 2025-30 see here https://democracy.manchester.gov.uk/ieListDocuments.aspx?CId=358&MId=4922&Ver=4

Both the Manchester Climate Change Framework and the Manchester City Council's Climate Change Action Plan are being updated for the period 2025-2030 and will be published in October 2025. 
Please see these links for further information:
https://democracy.manchester.gov.uk/documents/s56554/Manchester%20Climate%20Change%20Framework%20and%20Adaptation%20Plan.pdf
and
