column16:
The 2025-35 Our Manchester Strategy (OMS) sets the city's overarching priorities for the next ten years, created through consultation with over 10,000 residents. One of 12 priorities for the city over the next ten years is to adapt to a changing climate and rapidly reduce carbon emissions, acknowledging that climate change is one of the most urgent challenges facing Manchester. The Council's Climate Change Action Plan sets out the specific actions it will take in responding to this priority by 2030, and ensuring it is on track to deliver its Zero Carbon 2038 target. The priorities of the OMS are not intended to be addressed in isolation and the approach for zero carbon work is no different. Adapting to a changing climate and reducing carbon emissions can also support delivery of other priorities in the plan including building good-quality, genuinely affordable homes, developing good-quality green spaces, a growing economy that provides jobs and equal opportunities for everyone, and reliable transport. 

All other strategic documents are aligned with this climate agenda, ensuring a city-wide, cohesive approach to climate action. Key plans and strategies include: 

•	Economic Recovery Plan: This plan (Powering Recovery) incorporates climate resilience as a fundamental pillar, ensuring that the post-pandemic recovery is underpinned by sustainable investments and low-carbon economic growth. 

•	Green and Blue Infrastructure Strategy: This strategy integrates natural ecosystems into urban planning, contributing to climate mitigation and adaptation while enhancing biodiversity and public health. 

•	Digital Strategy (2021-2026): Sustainable resilience is a key theme, ensuring that Manchester's digital innovation aligns with climate goals and builds a resilient, low-carbon digital infrastructure. 

•	Housing Strategy: By 2025, 50% of new homes will be low or zero carbon, and by 2032, at least one-third of Manchester's 70,000 social homes will be retrofitted to low-carbon standards. A broader retrofit programme for the city's housing stock is also underway. 

•	Local Area Energy Plan (LAEP): The LAEP sets out a roadmap for transitioning to a sustainable energy system across Manchester. It outlines how the city will decarbonise its energy supply, invest in renewable energy infrastructure, and enhance energy efficiency to support the city's net-zero targets. 

•	City Centre Transport Strategy (Transport for Greater Manchester): This strategy defines how Manchester will achieve a sustainable modal mix, with clear targets for walking, cycling, and public transport, alongside the necessary investments to support the shift away from car dependency. It plays a critical role in reducing transport-related emissions and improving air quality in the city. 

•	Regeneration Plans: All regeneration initiatives now include specific targets to achieve zero carbon through investment in sustainable infrastructure, buildings, and energy systems. 

•	Integrated Water Management Plan: In collaboration with the Environment Agency, Manchester City Council, and water companies, this plan ensures alignment of water resource management priorities with climate resilience goals. It addresses flood risk, water conservation, and the long-term sustainability of Manchester's water infrastructure. 

•	GM Strategic Infrastructure Board: This board brings together all critical infrastructure providers to enable more integrated investment and long-term planning. By coordinating efforts across transport, energy, water, and digital infrastructure, the board ensures that the city's climate ambitions are supported through cohesive, cross-sector planning. 

•	Local Plan Refresh: The draft of Manchester's refreshed Local Plan - Places for Everyone (PfE) - was adopted by Manchester City Council in 2024. It is designed to balance the city's growth with the goal of achieving zero carbon by 2038 or sooner. PfE includes a suite of policies designed to guide future development decisions, with a strong emphasis on sustainability, energy efficiency, and climate resilience. 


Additionally, climate change actions are systematically integrated into Manchester City Council's service planning. Departments are required to report on climate-related initiatives, providing a comprehensive view of progress toward the city's zero-carbon goals.
column17:
As part of our response to the declared climate emergency, we have integrated climate-related considerations across all aspects of our financial planning and decision-making. This includes embedding green finance capacity within the City Council and conducting a comprehensive review of the climate risks associated with our financial expenditures, such as increased energy costs, infrastructure resilience, and the need for adaptation measures. This risk assessment will be reviewed periodically. It was used as the basis of an exploratory exercise involving senior Finance, Development and Risk colleagues within the City Council. This exercise undertook to explore the extent to which the Council could align with the Taskforce for Climate Related Disclosure outcomes.
Finance is aligning our approach with the Council's zero-carbon ambitions and the development of the new Climate Change Action Plan (2025-2030). We are
also exploring innovative financing mechanisms to support the net-zero transition, particularly in
geographic areas across Manchester, leveraging DESNZ funding for this purpose. Our financial
planning actively supports our zero-carbon journey by aligning both our revenue and capital budgets with climate goals. 
We use our 500 million annual spending power to prioritise sustainability, with a 10% weighting in all procurement decisions favouring companies committed to achieving zero carbon and contributing to local community resilience. In addition, a 20% social value weighting incentivises contractors to invest in local environmental schemes, education, skills development, and training for our communities. 
We recognise the direct impact of climate change on our revenue budgets, particularly with the increasing cost of energy. While these costs are anticipated to rise, we are redirecting these resources toward enhanced energy efficiency and transitioning to low-carbon delivery mechanisms, such as electrifying heating systems and vehicle fleets. To further ensure
sustainability, all our budgetary processes include environmental impact assessments and a focus on decarbonisation opportunities. In terms of capital planning, every investment decision incorporates environmental weightings and zero-carbon considerations. We prioritise high energy efficiency and sustainable building methods for all capital projects and are actively transitioning our vehicle fleet toward electrification, including the promotion of e-bikes. Additionally, specific environmental
initiatives such as tree planting and park development are integrated into our capital programme. Our financing structures include 'invest-to-save' funding, allowing for long payback periods and enabling the feasibility of sustainability-focused programmes. Capital prioritisation also encourages the exploration of external funding sources, including capital grants and matched funding opportunities, to accelerate our progress toward net-zero targets.
As part of the CCAP structure, a Finance and Investment subgroup exists, chaired by the Head of Capital Finance, and attended by senior stakeholders from across Council Directorates. The group provides financial oversight of the decarbonisation programme, as well as supporting services to identify and deliver low carbon funding schemes.
MCC have carried out initial assessment of climate related risks aligned to TCFD and are currently producing a Green Finance Strategy due to be published in 2026
column18:
Manchester recognises that transitioning to a low-carbon economy is essential but brings several risks that must be carefully managed to ensure a fair and inclusive transition.
A key risk is workforce disruption and skills gaps. Jobs in carbon-intensive sectors such as construction, manufacturing, and logistics may decline, while demand for new skills in retrofit, renewable energy, and digital systems grows rapidly. Without targeted reskilling, sections of the workforce could be left behind.
Supply chain constraints also present challenges. The rapid pace of transition may outstrip the availability of sustainable materials, renewable energy infrastructure, and low-carbon technologies. This could lead to project delays and rising costs, particularly in retrofitting programmes and large-scale energy projects.
There is also a risk of rising costs and widening inequalities. Higher upfront costs for low-carbon technologies, alongside fluctuating energy prices, could increase financial pressure on both households and businesses. Low-income groups are especially vulnerable, raising the risk of deepening social and economic inequalities if these impacts are not managed.
Finally, policy and regulatory uncertainty could deter investment and slow innovation. Businesses and investors may hesitate to commit resources without clear and consistent frameworks to guide long-term decision-making.
Together, these risks highlight the importance of coordinated action across skills, supply chains, affordability, and policy certainty at a national, regional and local level to ensure Manchester's transition to a low-carbon economy is both successful and equitable.

The City has assorted powers over many aspects of city life in which climate action can happen. In some instances the Mayor has stronger powers, such as over the City budget or infrastructure, and in other cases City Council has stronger powers, such as over the energy supply and regulating utility providers such as Entergy New Orleans, Delta Services Utilities, and Sewerage and Water Board of New Orleans;, and in many cases they must work jointly together. 

A few key areas for local climate action are not directly controlled, led, or regulated by the City and the Mayor and City Council must work from positions of influence to advance the City's goals and vision. These include regional transportation planning and transit led by the Regional Planning Commission and Regional Transit Authority;, water, wastewater, and drainage infrastructure under management at Sewerage and Water Board (SWBNO), and waste management and recycling for businesses and large buildings. 

On the energy side, City Council regulates Entergy New Orleans, which continues to be a major point of leverage for the City's clean energy goals. The Council passed an energy benchmarking ordinance in July 2025 that will require large commercial and multifamily buildings to measure and report their energy use, creating transparency and driving energy efficiency upgrades citywide. At the same time, the broader energy landscape is shifting: Delta Utilities recently purchased Entergy's natural gas portfolio in New Orleans, introducing a new player into the energy system whose decisions will directly impact the City's climate action efforts.

The City's abilities on climate actions are also dependent on leadership and funding from both Federal and state government. While the City is making good headway in reducing our greenhouse gas emissions, we've had significant barriers with the state. In 2020, the Louisiana state legislature passed a bill that prohibits any parish or municipality from restricting use of natural gas to support its climate goals or any other reason. Due to this restriction, the City cannot take any regulatory action to reduce use of natural gas and its related emissions. However, in 2022 Louisiana also adopted a climate action plan for the first time, becoming the first state in the gulf south to do so. Like the city's plan, it calls for the state to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2050.

This work is unfolding in a new political context. At the state level, leadership changes have created more uncertainty about whether Louisiana will continue to actively pursue its climate plan, especially around renewable energy and electrification. At the federal level, shifts in administration and Congress bring both opportunities and risks: while major laws like the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law and Inflation Reduction Act continue to deliver unprecedented resources for climate action, their long-term durability and implementation are increasingly subject to political debate. This means that while New Orleans is making measurable progress, sustaining and scaling that progress will depend on navigating these evolving state and federal realities.
column16:
Chapter 12 of the City's Master Plan relates to adapting to Climate Change. The City's Master Plan regular 5 year update was completed and adopted at the end of 2023. The current Master Plan can be found here: https://www.nola.gov/city-planning/plan-for-the-21st-century/. Chapter 12 of the Master Plan includes a variety of goals, each with a number of strategies to carry these out. The goals include:- A healthy functioning coast that sustains communities, industries, and ecosystems while providing critical flood protection as part of a multiple lines of defense strategy.- A New Orleans that embodies the principles of 'living with water', managing urban stormwater and groundwater carefully to align with natural processes and support economic growth.- A population that has the ability and capacity to adapt to a changing environment and future threats- A new Orleans that is prepared for future disasters and ready to carry out an efficient, comprehensive, and equitable recovery - Improved environmental quality, increased resource efficiency, and economic growth through the mitigation of our climate impact- Environmental quality and justice through targeted investments in natural resources and improved ecosystem services- Global leadership in urban resilience and sustainability with the facilities and resources to share our experiences while continuing to learn from the daily realities of a complex urban condition. 

The City of New Orleans City Planning Commission and New Orleans Office of Resilience and Sustainability developed a Transit Oriented Communities plan, which prioritizes walkable neighborhoods with equitable housing options that will be connected to effective and convenient transit options. The TOC study was presented and unanimously adopted in October 2023: https://nola.gov/next/city-planning/topics/major-studies-projects/transit-oriented-communities/

The City Planning Commission also conducted a Tree Preservation Study in 2020, found here: https://www.nola.gov/city-planning/major-studies-and-projects/tree-preservation-study/ Based on the City's Master Plan, the following goals have been developed:
-Promote and expand New Orleans' urban forest to reach 50% tree canopy by 2030. Promote tree preservation and planting on private property.
-Establish criteria for “heritage trees” to inform future development; identify heritage trees as those trees of native species, significant caliper (top 20%), located along public corridors. Use additional criteria as appropriate. Consider additional protections for qualifying trees and appropriate incentives for their retention. Explore regulatory options for the retention, replacement and enhancement of the landscaping and live oak canopies characteristic of New Orleans, providing for complete protection of trees and landscaping during private and public construction, and power line maintenance and construction work by public utilities.
-Promote a diversity of tree planting species and speeds of growth. Additionally, the City worked with New Orleans community group Sustaining Our Urban Landscape (SOUL) to develop a reforestation plan. 

The New Orleans Reforestation Plan was completed in December 2022. It was recognized through a City Council Resolution on January 19, 2023. The plan includes recommendations for future canopy growth and outlines neighborhood level projects in underserved areas of the city to reach more equitable canopy coverage. You can find the complete plan at https://soulnola.org/reforestationplan/
column17:
The City's financial planning has also been directly shaped by external shocks. The historic snowstorm of 2025 significantly strained the City's budget, as emergency response and recovery costs diverted resources away from long-term priorities. This event contributed to the City's current deficit, underscoring the urgent need to strengthen financial resilience through diversified funding sources, innovative financing strategies, and climate-informed fiscal planning.

In September 2020, Mayor Cantrell coordinated with C40 Cities and twelve other mayors from cities around the world including New York, London, Cape Town, Pittsburgh, Seattle, and Milan to declare a commitment to divest from fossil fuels and invest in a sustainable future. With this commitment to leverage the City's financial resources for a more equitable and sustainable economy, the City will prioritize investments in clean energy and other climate solutions and coordinate with the New Orleans Municipal Employees' Retirement System to put in place an update to NOMERS Investment Policy Statement with a goal of full divestiture. The City presented divestment and investment policy recommendations to the New Orleans Municipal Employee's Retirement System board in 2023 and continues to work to bring those recommendations to a formal board vote. However, given the current state and federal political landscape, and Louisiana's role as one of the nation's largest exporters of liquefied natural gas (LNG), progress toward full divestment has become increasingly challenging.

As part of its effort to grow the local climate action economy, the City is also pursuing new financing pathways. In 2025, New Orleans placed a municipal bond proposition before voters, designed to generate significant local capital for infrastructure, resilience, and neighborhood improvement projects on the November 2025 ballot. At the same time, the City and its partners are developing a Municipal Investment Fund (MIF) that would create a dedicated financing vehicle for clean energy, resilience, and climate-related projects. These tools are essential as the scale of climate action requires billions in investment, and federal and state grants alone are insufficient to meet local needs.
column18:
Louisiana, including the City of New Orleans, has traditionally been an “oil state,” since the early 20th century. Louisiana currently is in the top five states in natural gas production and accounted for 9% of U.S. total marketed gas production in 2020. The state's 17 oil refineries account for nearly 20% of the nation's refining capacity. Due to this economic system, Louisiana has been disproportionally affected by the “boom and bust” energy cycles historically. 

The coming 'energy transition' could mean more economic hardships, including major layoffs and unemployment, if no major action is taken by the city and state to ensure that the workforce is ready for 21st century 'green' jobs. These risks are compounded by a shifting political environment at both the state and federal levels. The repeal of clean energy tax credits and the elimination of programs such as Solar for All threaten to undermine emerging markets for renewable energy and make it more difficult for local governments to deliver affordable, community-based clean energy solutions. At the same time, efforts by the Trump Administration to roll back federal climate and infrastructure grants jeopardize one of the few reliable funding streams available for cities like New Orleans to pursue resilience, decarbonization, and workforce development initiatives.

Together, these changes heighten the risks of an uneven or stalled transition. Without consistent federal and state support, New Orleans faces the dual challenge of protecting its economy from the volatility of fossil fuel dependency while also trying to build a low-carbon future with fewer resources and more uncertainty.

There are several mechanisms through which Newcastle City Council considers climate-related issues. These are outlined below:
-	Climate Change Committee: This cross party non-executive committee made up of councillors meets quarterly to discuss the progress towards Newcastle City Councils' Net Zero 2030 Action Plan. This involves highlighting climate-related issues as part of our adaptation and carbon sequestration thematic area.
-	Climate Change Team: The Council has a dedicated Climate Change Team which focuses on delivering the Net Zero 2030 Action Plan. A key responsibility of the team is tracking the impact of climate-related issues and working with the broader business to respond to these.
-	Net Zero Board: This officer focused board meets quarterly and tracks progress against the Net Zero 2030 Action Plan. Officers responsible for each thematic area raise climate related issues including those related to flooding and extreme weather events (heating and cooling).
-	Marmot champions officer group: Newcastle is a Marmot City. As part of this programme Marmot champions meet quarterly to discuss progress against the eight principles, one of which is ensuring Newcastle is a sustainable city. As part of this principle climate related issues and their impacts on city resident health are considered.
-	Delegated decisions process: As part of the Council's delegated decisions process every decision considers both the impact of climate related issues on them and also their impact on climate related issues.
-	Business continuity planning: As part of business continuity the Council considers the impact of climate related issues on the functioning of the broader business
-	Climate Change Forum: This is targeted at our residents and engages them on climate related issues including how these impact on them and how we as a Council are responding to them. This also includes providing guidance on how they can respond to climate related issues.
-	Youth Council: The Council engages with the city's younger residents via the Youth Council and raises how climate related issues impact on them.
-	Net Zero North East England: Newcastle City Council is a member of this group comprised of the seven North East local authorities. The group meets monthly and considers, among other things, the impact of climate related issues.
column16: Newcastle City Council's master/development planning is governed by the Council's planning department. The impact of climate related issues (primarily flooding and microclimate) on master/development planning is captured in a number of key documents governing our planning and development activities:\n-\tNewcastle's Core Strategy (Policy CS1, Policy CS16, Policy CS17): Policy CS1 (Spatial Strategy for Sustainable Growth) requires all development to be designed to reduce carbon emissions and adapted to the effects of climate change. Policy CS16 (Climate Change) requires development to be sustainable, able to function effectively in a changing climate and address the impacts of climate change emissions. There are six criteria that all new residential, non-residential and mixed-use developments must meet to conform with Policy CS16 (Climate Change) of the Core Strategy and Urban Core Plan (CSUCP): (1). A good standard of building fabric, passive design and landscape measures to minimise energy demand (2) Flexible design to allow for adaptation to alternative uses. (3) A good level of sustainability through the applicant demonstrating best practice project and site management, site water use, site transport, waste reuse and recycling, the sustainable use of materials and construction techniques. (4) Minimise a developments contribution to, and provide resilience from, the on-going and predicted impacts of climate change. (5) A reduction in whole-life CO2 equivalent emissions impact (6) Optimise the use of local renewable or low carbon energy in accordance with a hierarchy, prioritising decentralised energy schemes, followed by other renewable energy solutions and finally other lower carbon energy solutions. Where no decentralised energy scheme exists, strategic and other large-scale developments must evaluate the feasibility of providing a decentralised energy system and, where feasible implement such schemes. Policy CS17 (Flood Risk and Water Management) ensures Development will avoid and manage flood risk from all sources, taking into account the impact of climate change over its lifetime. Development will (1) Avoid and manage flood risk to people and property by: (i). Locating new development in areas with the lowest risk where appropriate by applying the Sequential Test (ii). Managing flood risk from development to ensure that the risk is not increased on site and/or elsewhere, where appropriate by applying the Exception Test, (iii). Ensuring opportunities for development to contribute to the mitigation of flooding elsewhere are taken,(iv). Prioritise the use of Sustainable Drainage Systems (SuDS), given the multifunctional benefits to water quality, green space and habitat enhancement, (v). Ensuring development is in accordance with the Council's Strategic Flood Risk Assessment, and (vi). Requiring a Flood Risk Assessment for sites over 0.5ha in Critical Drainage Areas as identified in the Council's Strategic Flood Risk Assessments. (2). Ensure water supply and foul and surface water infrastructure are provided with adequate capacity. (3). Not adversely affect water quality and where possible seek to improve water quality. (4). Separate, minimise and control surface water runoff, discharging in order of priority to: (i). Infiltration based Sustainable Drainage Systems, (ii). A watercourse, (iii). A surface water sewer, and (iv). A combined sewer.\n-\tDevelopment and allocation plan: One of the key strategic objectives of the plan (SO11) focuses on reducing CO2 emission from development and future growth while adapting to the issues, mitigating adverse impacts and taking advantage of the opportunities presented by climate change. Policy DM20 - Design states that development will be required to deliver high quality and sustainable design by building in 12 key aspects including incorporating measures to address the impacts of climate change and adverse microclimatic conditions. Policy DM26 - Flood Risk and Water Management ensures that developments will be required to manage and reduce flood risk and that developments will be required to demonstrate that its surface water drainage strategy, site layout and design will prevent properties from flooding from surface water, including an allowance for climate change and urban creep; not increase the risk of flooding elsewhere and that exceedance flows will be managed; ensure run-off from development is constrained to greenfield rates, or as close to greenfield rates as possible; for brownfield sites, up to a minimum 50% reduction; manage surface water as close to source as possible using source control measures; follow the SuDS management approach, to manage water quantity and quality throughout the site; provide the most sustainable SuDS techniques from the SuDS Hierarchy; where feasible and appropriate, integrate SuDS into public open space and connect to adjacent watercourses or wetlands; and demonstrate the life-time maintenance and management of the SuDS

Newcastle City Council produces annual accounts which provides a summary of the Council's financial performance and its future financial prospects. The Council also conducts forward looking annual financial projections in the form the Medium-Term Financial Plan (MTFP). Both the annual accounts and MTFP reflect where climate related issues have impacted our Council's financial planning. Key examples include:
-	The requirement to provide a Climate Change Team to deliver the Net Zero 2030 Action Plan: This is a cost to the Council and comes out if the Council's revenue budget. This cost could be allocated to front line services if the team was not required to deliver the action plan.
-	The need to fund flood alleviation projects: As stated in our CDP submission one of the key climate related issues is flooding. The Council is the Lead Local Flood Authority and in this capacity delivers multi-million pound flood alleviation schemes (examples include Kenton Bar and Denton). The costs attached to these schemes is capital expenditure which could be allocated elsewhere if the Council was not required to respond to these climate related issues.
-	The need to fund business continuity planning: Newcastle City Council is required to provide business continuity plans in response to risks which impact the provision of Council Services. A number of risks highlighted in the continuity plans related to climate (e.g. flooding, extreme temperature events). The business continuity plan requires that the Council responds to these risks. Risk mitigation involves financial planning, both to fund interventions that mitigate risks (e.g. flood alleviation) and set aside potential funds in the reserve to respond to major incidents (of which climate change has the potential to cause.
-	Costs related to public health aspects of climate change: The vast majority of costs related to the impact of climate change on health fall on the National Health Service in terms of dealing with climate caused acute care illnesses (e.g. heat stroke from extreme weather events). The provision of public health climate focused interventions to prevent these are costs met by the Councils. Examples include public health funding to tackle poor air quality and funding to improve the quality of homes. Both are costs which could be avoided if climate related issues did not exist (in this instance, poor air quality resulting from vehicle emissions which have significant health impacts, and poorly insulated homes which respond poorly to extreme weather events and impact on the health of our residents).
A more detailed summary of the financial implications of Net Zero can be found in a report prepared for the City Council's Finance and Budget Monitoring Scrutiny Committee: https://democracy.newcastle.gov.uk/documents/s207626/7.%20Financial%20Implications%20of%20Net%20Zero.pdf
column18:
The key risks related to transitioning to a low-carbon economy are outlined below:
-	Funding the investment: Our experience from the Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme (where over £27 million has been invested in low carbon technologies in Newcastle) is that where this is not 100% grant funded the borrowing costs to deliver the project need to be balanced against the ongoing revenue costs of delivering day to day council services. The risk is that unless a robust business case is developed which considers borrowing costs, balanced against cost savings based on reduced energy bills and income from installed solar, this results in increased day to day costs. The outcome could be a service failing (for example a swimming pool or leisure centre) or a resident getting in to debt.
-	Maintaining ongoing support for low carbon investment: In the United Kingdom there is a growing backlash to Net Zero and climate change. There is the risk this results in a reversal in terms of the transition as decision makers elected by a small albeit influential (and likely to vote) sceptic population cancels decarbonisation projects. The main party taking this approach is Reform who have successfully gained control of several local authorities and will seeking to win Newcastle City Council's local elections in 2026. Putting aside the political angle there is also the risk that lack of support from the general public means that we are unable to rollout solutions in social houses as residents refuse to move in or deliberately tamper with the solutions to break them.
-	Supporting the most vulnerable who may see slight increases in their energy bills: As stated above there is the risk that some low carbon technologies (heat pumps for example) result in small increases in energy bills due to the cost of electricity verses gas. For those who are financially vulnerable even this small increase may force them into fuel poverty, and for those already in fuel poverty, this may make their situation worse.
-	Upskilling city residents to deliver green growth: To successfully transition to a low carbon economy this requires a skilled workforce who are able to carry out the various jobs which must be completed, ranging from solar panel and heat pump installers all the way through to specialists in offering green insurance products. There is the risk that to there are not the necessary skills available in the populace to continue to decarbonise at pace.
-	The transition is not just: Installing low carbon technologies and adoption low carbon solutions (like EVs) is expensive, involving an initial outlay. The UK Government continues to support this transition through various grants and subsidies, however these are targeted primarily at those who are more affluent and are able to 'top up' these grants with additional capital of their own. Once these technologies or solutions are in place residents tend to see benefits in terms of lower energy costs or transport fuel costs. There is the risk that those from less affluent backgrounds are unable to make the initial capital outlay, meaning they get left behind in the green transition.

The corporate plan 2023 - 2026 outlines Northumberland County Council's key priorities and goals. Three priority areas are identified; Achieving Value for Money, Tackling Inequalities, Driving Economic Growth. Priorities for Net Zero, Sustainability and Climate Change are included across all three areas with actions and progress indicators identified. The corporate plan can be accessed here - https://www.northumberland.gov.uk/NorthumberlandCountyCouncil/media/About-the-Council/Policy%20and%20priorities/CORPORATE-PLAN-2023-26.pdf.
The Council has a dedicated team working towards set climate change targets. The team works with partners across the organisation, the wider county, and the region to implement a range of projects to reduce emissions, improve sustainability, protect the environment, reduce inequalities and drive green economic growth. 
The most recent climate change action plan has been developed and published covering the years 2024 - 2026. This plan sets out targets and communicates the successes and challenges from the previous action plan timeframe (2021 - 2023). The action plan is available for download using the following link - https://www.northumberland.gov.uk/Climate-Change/Climate-Change.aspx. The action plan sets out updated targets, pledging to make Northumberland carbon neutral by 2030 and achieve net zero for all greenhouse gases for the county of Northumberland by 2040. Northumberland County Council also aims to become a carbon neutral organisation by 2030. 
The council has recently introduced Integrated Impact Assessments which consolidate approaches from Equality Impact Assessment and Carbon Impact Assessment processes. Integrated Impact Assessments are a crucial part of the council's decision making process and allows for actions being deliberated by the council to be considered against NCC net zero, environment, and equity, targets so that informed and just decisions are made.
column16:
Northumberland's Local Plan 2016 - 2036 (Adoption date 2022) sets the strategic planning policies of the council and aims to address climate change by promoting strategies for mitigation and adaptation. The full plan can be accessed at this link - https://www.northumberland.gov.uk/NorthumberlandCountyCouncil/media/Planning-and-Building/planning%20policy/Local%20Plan/Northumberland-Local-Plan-Adopted-March-2022.pdf. Policy STP 4 focuses specifically on climate change mitigation and adaptation. 
Policy STP4 states that development proposals should mitigate climate change and contribute to greenhouse gas emission reduction targets. STP 4 further states that support will be given to development proposals that help to mitigate climate change with consideration to how proposals reduce the need for travel and encourage sustainable transport, reduce energy consumption, incorporate decentralised renewable and low carbon energy, include reuse of existing buildings and materials, incorporate green infrastructure, protect and enhance habitats providing carbon sinks and incorporate EV charging facilities. 
Policy STP 4 addresses adaptation stating that support will be given to development proposals that help to provide future resilience to climate change with consideration on how proposals incorporate design features to ensure they provide resilience to climate change, reduce demand on water resources, take into account risk of flooding and coastal change, incorporate use of sustainable drainage systems and incorporate green infrastructure. 

Northumberland County Council's (NCCs) vision is to make sure Northumberland is, and remains, 'a land of great opportunities' for all our residents. Public health and wellbeing and reducing inequalities, climate change mitigation& adaptation; and the protection, repair, and enhancement of the environment, are all critical to the realisation of this long-term vision for Northumberland, and are all deeply interconnected. In addition, Policy QOP5 covers sustainable design and construction and Policy REN 1 covers Renewable and low carbon energy and associated energy storage. 
Environmental protection and enhancement: 
NCCs Environmental Policy Statement recognises the interwoven issues and need for holistic action across both the natural environment and climate change targets, this statement provides details of the work that NCC does to conserve and enhance the environment. In July 2023 NCC officially recognised the ongoing ecosystem and biodiversity crisis facing the county by declaring an ecological emergency. This emergency is deeply interlinked with the climate emergency, which NCC declared in 2019. 

NCC also uses long term planning powers to protect and enhance the environment. The Northumberland Local Plan - forms part of the statutory development plan for Northumberland, alongside the Neighbourhood plans. It guides the type and location for new developments and is used when making decisions on planning applications. Local plan policies must, when taken as a whole, contribute to the mitigation of, and adaptation to, climate change. 
The Northumberland Local Plan takes a proactive approach to mitigating and adapting to climate change, considering the long-term implications for flood risk, coastal change, water supply, biodiversity and landscapes, and the risk of overheating from rising temperatures. There are many policies within the plan that support the future resilience of communities and infrastructure, such as: 
•	The Location of new development and transport 
•	Sustainable design and construction of new buildings 
•	Renewable energy 
•	Protection of carbon sinks 
•	Building resilience and adapting to climate change 

Neighbourhood plans - allow Parish and Town councils to produce neighbourhood plans for their areas. Where the Local Plan covers Northumberland, Neighbourhood Plans focus on the specific needs of a specific area and allow the local community to specify what they expect from development in their area. These plans may deal with a wide range of social, economic, and environmental issues (e.g. housing, employment, design, heritage, transport, environment, renewable energy sites), or focus on one or two issues only. 
 
Health, wellbeing and Inequalities: 
NCC has adopted the One Health approach, One Health recognises that human, animal, and ecosystem health are closely interlinked, so there needs to be cross-sector approaches to these fields. All the climate change mitigation and adaptation projects and actions outlined in the climate change action plan 2024-2026, complement the themes and action areas within the Northumberland Joint Health and Wellbeing Strategy 2018-2028 and provide one-or-more more co-benefits for human and environment health.

The Council's Climate Change Action Plan (CCAP) 2024-2026 was approved by Cabinet in June 2024 and contains our overarching Net Zero targets.  The CCAP is aligned with the Council's Corporate Strategy 2023-2026 which outlines the vision, strategic aims and policy priorities of the Council - achieving value for money, tacking inequalities, and driving economic growth. Climate change and the environment are explicitly embedded within the corporate priorities detailed in the Corporate Strategy and the Council's Environmental Policy Statement.


NCC's Corporate Strategy directly influences how delivery of services and functions are shaped and sets the context for budgeting and financial planning processes to ensure spending aligns with corporate priorities. This ensures that climate issues are considered in financial planning and budgeting. Responding to climate hazards (eg planning for and responding to extreme weather events and flooding) are statutory functions resourced separately to decarbonisation activities as they affect the council's ability to deliver services to residents and maintain business continuity.


Specific allocations detailed below relate to decarbonisation allocations specifically managed through the Climate Change Team for Financial 2024/2025 onwards, so exclude significant levels of funding for projects that are not directly managed by the Climate Change Team.


Northumberland County Council allocated £1.15m in revenue funding (of which £704,703 was grant funding) to support the delivery of the CCAP. This covered staff costs for 25.6 Full Time Equivalent (FTE) posts and £50,000 in grant funding that local community groups can apply for through our 'Climate and Environment Fund' scheme that aims to encourage and support environmental and climate change projects and initiatives. Northumberland County Council allocated £6,042,853 in capital funding. This includes a £3,039,324 allocation of funding for climate change capital projects in the Council's Medium Term Financial Plan used for projects such as replacing end of life boilers with low carbon heating systems and installing photo-voltaic panels to generate solar electricity and funding to improve both public and NCC fleet EV infrastructure that contributes to economic growth and greening our fleet. This allocation includes £3,003,529 co-funding from the Housing Revenue Account Major Repairs Reserve to co-fund energy efficiency upgrades to council houses through the Warm Homes: Social Housing Fund. In total the council was allocated £13,363,411 in grant funding for schemes to support residents to keep warm, reduce bills and carbon emissions, and have a healthier living environment due to improved ventilation that reduces damp and mould risks to health.


The figures provided above also exclude private sector funding allocated to improving the energy efficiency of council homes through the Energy Company Obligation (ECO) and Great British Insulation Scheme (GBIS). During the period between 1st July 2024 to 31st March 2025 a total of £6,590 of council funding was spent on this project. To date, the value of private sector funded works on council homes undertaken under the ECO and GBIS project was reported to the council as £1,240,797.


These figures exclude significant grant funding and Northumberland County Council co-funding for projects and programmes that are not delivered by the Climate Change and Warmer Homes teams. However, many projects and programmes significantly contribute to the objectives and targets in the Northumberland County Council Climate Change Action Plan and Northumberland County Council Corporate Plan that reduce energy costs, increase energy efficiency, improve technological efficiencies, encourage public and active travel, and improve the environment of Northumberland. Some of these projects reduce the amounts of greenhouse gases being produced (as well as reducing bills or fuel costs), or they increase the amount of greenhouse gases being absorbed/used by natural process (e.g. plants and soils absorbing or storing carbon dioxide through natural processes).  Some of these projects also reduce our vulnerability to severe weather hazards including flooding and storms. These projects include but are not limited to:

• The Northumberland Line (rail expansion)

• Public EV infrastructure

• Bus Service Improvements

• Local Cycling and Walking Infrastructure Plans

• Active Travel and Bikeability training for school children

• Great Northumberland Forest

• Local Nature Recovery Strategy

• Rural Asset Multiplier Programme

• Local Investment in Natural Capital Project

• Flood and Coastal Erosion Risk Management projects

• Local Resilience Forum

• Waste and Recycling initiatives

• Energy Central Campus

• James Calvert Spence College in Amble - a net zero carbon in operation school
column18:
The transition to a low carbon economy poses risks to Northumberland as this shift will require significant investment into green technologies. This may disproportionately affect areas with higher levels of deprivation, low-income households, and residents who may already be affected by fuel poverty. Carbon pricing on energy generation from fossil fuels may cause further negative effects on low-income households and those already living in energy poverty. Northumberland's economy may also be impacted due to job losses in sectors such as those relying on fossil fuel-based energy. Additionally, small and medium sized businesses may not be able manage the costs of adapting to new technologies alongside pressures from the cost-of-living crisis. This could lead to further job losses and losses of local businesses. Committing to ambitious targets relating to the low carbon transition brings reputational risk, if these targets are missed, this could cause reputational damage.


However, the council recognises the significant opportunities associated with the transition to a low-carbon economy in our Corporate Strategy. The first offshore wind turbines in the UK were installed in Blyth, Northumberland, and we are home to the Offshore Renewable Energy Catapult (OREC) which is the UK's leading technology innovation and research centre for offshore renewable energy. OREC was established in 2013 by the UK Government and plays a key role in delivering the UK's Net Zero targets by accelerating the creation and growth of UK companies in the offshore renewable energy sector. Their mission is to deliver the UK's largest clean growth opportunity by accelerating the creation and growth of UK companies in offshore renewable energy. The landmark Energy Central Learning Hub in Blyth was officially opened by Secretary of State for Education, Bridget Phillipson MP in June 2025. The £15m, four storey development - the first of its kind in the country - offers sector specific training to young people entering the industry as school leavers and those looking to retrain from other industries such as oil and gas. A visitors' centre with stunning views of the nearby Blyth Offshore Demonstrator Wind Farm will provide an immersive, educational experience for school children and the public wanting to learn more about offshore wind and the race towards Net Zero. Energy Central Campus is a unique skills partnership between the Port of Blyth, Northumberland County Council, and the Offshore Renewable Energy (ORE) Catapult, with a mission to create the pipeline of talent required for the expanding clean energy sector, as well as inspiring, training, and delivering pathways to employment for the local community.


In addition, there is a brand-new Welding and Fabrication Technical Training Centre at the Port of Blyth which is a dedicated facility with state-of-the-art equipment to support skills development in the growing sectors of advanced manufacturing, welding and fabrication.

The oversight of climate-related issues within our jurisdiction is managed through a structured governance framework, ensuring accountability and alignment with our climate goals. 

Operational decisions are overseen by the Council's CN28 & Air Quality Strategy Board, which consists of senior managers, each responsible for leading a specific theme from our climate action plan. These themes cover various areas of our climate strategy, ensuring a focused approach across different sectors. 

To monitor progress, detailed reports on the achievement of delivery targets are submitted to the CN28 & Air Quality Strategy Board on a rolling basis. This board is chaired by the Lead Councillor for Climate Change, who plays a pivotal role in providing direction and ensuring that climate targets are met. The councillor then reports to the Council's Executive Board, which is the highest decision-making authority within the Council, ensuring alignment between climate initiatives and the Council's broader strategic goals. 

In addition, city-wide delivery efforts, beyond the Council's direct remit, are managed by the Nottingham Green Partnership. This partnership brings together key stakeholders from across the city, including universities, the local Hospital Trust, as well as businesses and other partner organisations. 

This collaborative approach enables the jurisdiction to effectively mobilise resources, engage with diverse sectors, and ensure that all areas of the city contribute to climate resilience and sustainability initiatives. 

This governance structure fosters a collaborative and transparent approach to achieving our climate objectives, ensuring that both internal and external partners are engaged in driving progress toward our environmental goals.
column16:
Climate-related issues have significantly influenced our jurisdiction's master and development planning, positioning sustainability at the core of our strategic decision-making. Achieving carbon neutrality by 2028 is a top policy priority for the City Council, and this target has reshaped the approach to urban planning, infrastructure development, and resource management. 

In 2024, the Council adopted a new Strategic Council Plan, elevating carbon neutrality as one of the top priorities to be delivered over the next three years. This priority is embedded across all facets of the Council's decision-making processes, ensuring that climate resilience and sustainability are integral considerations in development projects and planning frameworks. 

A dedicated division within the Council is tasked with managing and coordinating efforts toward this goal. This division works to ensure that all development activities—from new housing projects to transportation and public infrastructure—align with the city's climate objectives. It actively integrates green building standards, sustainable transport systems, renewable energy initiatives, and climate resilience measures into the master planning process. 

As a result, every significant development decision made by the Council is guided by a commitment to reducing emissions, improving energy efficiency, and enhancing climate resilience. This proactive approach ensures that our jurisdiction not only meets its carbon neutrality goals but also fosters sustainable urban growth that benefits both current and future generations.
column17:
Climate-related issues have had a profound impact on our jurisdiction's financial planning, ensuring that sustainability is fully integrated into our budgeting and resource allocation processes. The Council has made it a standard requirement that all actions aimed at reducing carbon emissions are incorporated into the financial planning of each service area. 

This means that every service delivery plan across the Council must evaluate and include the costs associated with lowering emissions, improving energy efficiency, and adopting sustainable practices. These climate-focused activities are not treated as separate or optional but are built into the core budgeting requirements of each department. 

As a result, sustainability considerations are reflected in the financial framework, guiding long-term fiscal decisions. This approach ensures that our financial planning is aligned with our carbon neutrality goals, allowing for strategic investment in green infrastructure, renewable energy, and other climate resilience projects. Moreover, by embedding these climate-related costs into the annual budget cycle, we can anticipate future financial needs and allocate resources efficiently, avoiding reactive or ad-hoc spending. 

This alignment between financial planning and climate goals promotes a proactive, fiscally responsible approach to addressing climate change while ensuring that we meet our sustainability targets in a financially sustainable manner.
column18:
The transition to a low-carbon economy presents both opportunities and risks for our jurisdiction, and these are carefully managed to ensure a smooth and effective shift. To address the risks associated with this transition, the Council maintains a high-level risk register, specifically designed to align with the delivery of the CN28 action plan. 

This risk register outlines 12 key risks that are actively managed by the CN28 & Air Quality Strategy Board. These risks range from operational challenges, such as funding gaps or delays in project implementation, to broader concerns, such as technological adaptation and stakeholder engagement. The most critical risk—the potential of not achieving the CN28 carbon neutrality target by 2028—is also included in the Corporate Risk Register, ensuring that it is continuously monitored and managed by the Corporate Risk Management group. 

By integrating these risks into our broader risk management framework, the Council ensures that any potential barriers to achieving carbon neutrality are identified early and mitigated effectively. This approach allows for the proactive management of financial, operational, and reputational risks, safeguarding the jurisdiction's ability to transition to a low-carbon economy while maintaining financial stability and public trust. 

Ultimately, this risk management strategy enables us to remain resilient in the face of challenges, ensuring that our jurisdiction can successfully navigate the complexities of this transition while delivering on our climate commitments.

column16: The most important action Oslo has initiated is the stormwater strategy and action plan. The action plan contains 18 different actions where the most important are creating a thematic map for stormwater and urban flooding and linking itto the land-use element of the municipal master plan and clarify routes and zones requiring special consideration. The second is producing a plan for, and construction of the main floodway and retention network. Both actions are in progress.
column17: In 2017 Oslo launched its climate budget and the city began tracking its carbon emissions alongside its finances. Oslo's Climate Budget is believed to be the first of its kind. It is a pioneering approach to mainstreaming climate into decision-making processes, which the city considers to be its most important tool for achieving its climate targets. The climate budget is a fully integrated part of the regular financial budgeting system and ensures that climate measures and financing are decided in the same process. See attached climate budget in section 7 on planning.
column18: Oslo is on many aspects a leading city on climate action. However this also comes with a transition risk. For example being the first city with Carbon capture and storage technology on a waste incineration facility comes at the risk of unforseen costs or technology lock-in effects. The same is true for many of Oslos other initiatives for example in clean construction. The fast transition can also be challenging for businesses in Oslo. The Norwegian Agency for Local Governments has made an overview of climate risk for the different municipalities. For Oslo they highlight the industries: retail trade, land and pipeline transport, warehouse and support activities for transportation, and manufacture of food products as sectors that are particularly vulnerable to transition risk and employ a large number of people within the municipality. Common for these sectors is that they have transition risk associated with increasing regulatorly pressure on the transport sector and possible changes in consumer habits related to food.

column15: The City's Chief Sustainability Officer keeps Council, City management/leadership, and climate practitioners across the City informed of Climate-related issues. The Bureau of Planning and Sustainability reports annually to City Council on climate-related issues, as directed through Portland's Climate Emergency Declaration. The Sustainability and Climate Commission to advise all city bureau and make recommendations to Council on sustainability and climate related issues and development of the City's next climate plan. Other departments like Transportation, Parks, Environmental Services have other advisory boards that may make climate related recommendations in their content areas. The Portland Clean Energy Community Benefits fund has an advisory committee that approves a 5-year Climate Investment Plan to prioritize where the city invests and how dollars are delivered to community for climate related projects. In addition, city departments are required to look at the social costs of carbon and lifecycle assessment when considering alternatives for capital expenditures.
column16: Portland has long history of leadership on master/development planning and integrated climate and environmental goals into planning and urban form. Both the City's comprehensive plan and Portland Plan include a strong focus on climate change. Our historic planning for urban form have significantly impacted development in Portland, contributing to denser and more walkable neighborhoods, helping to keep local carbon emissions down. In fact, in 2023, Portland Metropolitan area's daily on-highway vehicle miles travelled were 28% lower than the national average, a result of local urban and transportation planning.
column17: Portland City Council adopted an internal cost of carbon policy requiring lifecycle assessment and a shadow cost of carbon for all major building and infrastructure investments. Staff are currently applying the carbon shadow price on various city projects. Ultimately staff are working to integrate carbon assessment and shadow price to the annual capital budgeting process in order to generate decision-useful information on the financial opportunities and barriers to decarbonizing citywide infrastructure systems. Staff are also partnering with capital asset managers to integrate carbon management and asset management best practices in order to institutionalize cost-effective decarbonization strategies in capital improvement planning and asset management processes. In addition, all legislation, including financial planning, before council must include an impact statement that discusses how the action contributes to the City's goal of meeting 100 percent of community-wide energy needs with renewable energy by 2050.
column18: Higher energy prices, housing affordability, job losses in fossil fuel industry, risk of loss of industrial jobs, and risk of emission leakage from stronger local regulations compared to other neighboring communities, which compounds perceived higher costs of doing business in Portland.

column15: The City of Seattle is deeply involved in the oversight, planning, management, and implementation of climate-related issues both within municipal operations as well as for the city's residents and businesses. In Seattle, like in most cities, those who shape and benefit from environmental policies and outcomes are primarily white, upper-income communities despite the fact that people of color, immigrants, refugees, and people with low incomes often bear a disproportionate burden of environmental impacts. The Office of Sustainability & Environment (OSE) partners with the community to create strategies to help us achieve shared environmental goals and we coordinate among City departments, the Mayor's Office, and City Council to ensure successful implementation these strategies. We integrate equity by elevating opportunities to increase racial, social, and environmental justice throughout Seattle's environmental work. Climate-related issues are strongly considered in everything from capital projects to the development of new programs and policies across multiple sectors.
column16: The Comprehensive Plan is a 20 year vision and roadmap for Seattle's future. Our plan guides City decisions on where to build new jobs and houses, how to improve our transportation system, and where to make capital investments such as utilities, sidewalks, and libraries. Our Comprehensive Plan is the framework for most of Seattle's big-picture decisions on how to grow while preserving and improving our neighborhoods. Climate-related issues are one of four core values being considered during the process of updating the Comprehensive Plan in 2022. The four core values of Seattle's Comprehensive Plan are:Community - developing strong connections between a diverse range of people and placesEnvironmental Stewardship - protect and improve the quality of our global and local natural environmentEconomic Opportunity and Security - a strong economy and a pathway to employment is fundamental to maintaining our quality of lifeRace and Social Equity - limited resources and opportunities must be shared; and the inclusion of under-represented communities in decision-making processes is necessaryhttps://www.seattle.gov/opcd/ongoing-initiatives/seattle-2035-comprehensive-planAdditionally, Seattle has a dedicated series of Climate Action Plans that focuses on city actions that reduce greenhouse emissions and also support vibrant neighborhoods, economic prosperity, and social equity. These plans can be found here: https://www.seattle.gov/environment/climate-change/climate-planning/climate-action-plan
column17: All departments across City government strongly consider climate-related issues in capital and financial planning decisions. Here are a few examples: The City of Seattle Green New Deal Oversight Board was established by City Council (Ordinance 125926) to provide proposals for the design of new policies, programs, and projects and for modifications to existing policies, programs and projects to the Mayor, City Council, and City departments to advance a Green New Deal for Seattle. Key among these proposals is a commitment to make budget recommendations to the City for the allocation of revenue from the Payroll Expense Tax prioritizing investments that address environmental injustice. https://www.seattle.gov/green-new-deal-oversight-board/about-the-board, https://www.seattle.gov/documents/Departments/GreenNewDealBoard/Board%20Documents/GNDOB_22-23_Budget_Recommendations.pdfThe City has a Sustainable Buildings & Sites Policy for municipal facilities aims to maximize the environmental quality, economic vitality, and social health of our city through the design, construction, operation, maintenance, renovation, and decommissioning of City-owned buildings and sites. https://www.seattle.gov/environment/climate-change/buildings-and-energy/city-facilities/sustainable-buildings-and-sites. Seattle City Light has conducted an assessment that will help City Light better understand the energy needed for the electrification of buildings, transportation, and commercial and industrial applications within City Light's service territory. It also provides insight into the available capacity on our existing distribution grid. https://powerlines.seattle.gov/2022/01/20/planning-for-an-electrified-future/
column18: The primary risk associated with a transition to a low-carbon economy is one of grid resilience. The City of Seattle has made significant commitments to address the climate crisis through decarbonization, and the key means of achieving those goals is electrification—the transition from other forms of energy to electricity for various end uses. Recent pivotal technological advances around electric vehicles in all sectors and the development of efficient cold climate heat pumps have been gamechangers that set the stage for electrification at scale. These advancements will bring many customer benefits and improve local air quality. And thanks to Seattle City Light's carbon-free generation resources, electrification will be a major contributor to regional decarbonization. Seattle needs to therefore ensure that our grid infrastructure is sufficient to carry this anticipated extra load over the next few decades. It is also imperative that the City considered the risk of stranded assets pertaining to gas infrastructure. As more customers switch to electric heating and cooling, and EVs, the customers least likely to be able to afford to switch will be the ones left to bear the burden of supporting gas infrastructure costs through increasing use fees.

column15: The Climate and Ecological Emergency (CEE) was declared on the 26 June 2019 following the May 2019 local elections. A Climate and Ecological Emergency Action Plan was adopted by Cabinet on 22 April 2020 and approved by Council in October 2020. The Council undertook a carbon audit in 2024 and in March 2025 a revised Climate and Ecological Emergency Action Plan was adopted. This can be found here. This set out new net-zero targets and identifies the required interventions and measures necessary to ensure both the council and jurisdiction can be net-zero by 2045. The plan also identifies key focus areas: Council operations, air quality and sustainable transport, low carbon business and industry, low carbon buildings and energy efficiency, waste and resource consumption, biodiversity net gain and ecology, and resilient communities and engagement. \nThe CEE is embedded as a corporate priority of the borough council, including in the corporate plan. The department is situated within the portfolio of the Head of Environment and Leisure, reporting to the Director of Regeneration & Neighbourhoods. Work completed by the Climate Change Officer, Climate and Ecological Emergency Projects Officer, Active Travel Officer reports to the Environmental Services and Climate Change Committee as well as a member/officer Climate and Ecological Steering Group. \n
column16: Climate and Ecological Emergency is embedded in corporate planning e.g all reports must include climate implications. CEE projects and action plan reported to senior management every 6 months. Another area in which there has been significant influence is the Local Plan Review process. Swale has recognised the importance of climate change and biodiversity in planning, and is going above and beyond standards set by the NPPF to pursue net zero developments. Swale Borough Council recognises that there are cross-cutting actions needed to underpin the specific actions targeted at the particular causes of carbon emissions. The strategy set out in the Action Plan is based on an approach to Lead, Show, Support. LEAD: We will lead by taking actions to reduce carbon emissions from the Council's own operations and to enhance biodiversity in the management of the Council's own estate. SHOW: Use the council's improved operations and estate as beacon of good practice on the road to net zero. SUPPORT: Assist businesses, organisations and residents to take their own actions and to build the capacity to move towards a low carbon economy in Swale.
column17: Special projects funding allocated to CEE work, however yet to be included formally in annual budget. Climate implications now included in procurement processes. Special projects fund has been used to finance the Carbon Trust report of our estate, employment of the Climate and Ecological Emergency Project Officer and Fuel and Water Home Adviser, as well as projects such as LED lighting, tree planting, a car club, EV charging points and air quality measures. Due to this, external funding sources are paramount to financial planning in this area.
column18: Significant industrial sector - due to the nature of businesses in Swale, the district has always had high energy consumption and emissions compared with other Kent districts - the 2017 total of 648.4kt CO2 comprises 55% of the districts total CO2 emissions. Despite an overall downward trend in emissions they are not falling quickly enough to achieve our borough wide target of net zero carbon by 2030. Swale's domestic emissions (2019 figures) are the 4th highest in the County, with 67% resulting from domestic gas emissions, for which Swale also ranks 4th. A major risk to the Swale area is the number of residents classified in the highest Indices of Multiple Deprivation. The SBC Climate and Ecological Emergency Declaration 2019 set out that \'In meeting this pledge, the Council will take steps to avoid any adverse impacts on our most vulnerable residents\'. The risk that residents will be 'left behind' or unable to access climate friendly initiatives is at the forefront of all decision making. Overall, one of the largest risks to Swale is the urgency at which this issue must be tackled. As a coastal borough, including the Isle of Sheppey, the district is at high risk of sea level rise and coastal flooding. The UK Climate Impacts Programme (UKCIP) 2018 projections for Swale state that we are likely to have: Hotter summers with an increase in average summer temperature of 2-3°C by 2040 and 5-6°C by 2080. Warmer winters with an increase in average winter temperature of 1-2°C by 2040 and 3-4°C by 2080. Drier summers with a reduction in average precipitation of 20-30% by 2040 and 30-50% by 2080. Wetter winters with an increase in average precipitation of 10-20% by 2040 and 20-30% by 2080. Sea level is projected to rise by up to 0.3m by 2040 and 0.8m by 2080.These in turn present a number of risks, including: Risks to health, wellbeing, productivity and infrastructure from high temperatures. Flooding and coastal change risks to communities, businesses and infrastructure. Risk of storm events / intense rainfall impacting productivity and transport infrastructure. Risks of shortages in the public water supply and for agriculture, energy generation and industry. Overheating, flooding, drought and coastal change risks for natural capital. Soil erosion and slope destabilisation as a result of flooding and drought, impacting infrastructure, natural environment andproductivity. Risk of new and emerging pests and diseases and invasive non-native species affecting people and biodiversity, and likely toaffect Kent (first in the UK) in the future.

column15: As alterações climáticas são uma realidade com impacte ao nível ambiental, social e económico. Neste contexto, reduzir significativamente as emissões de Gases com Efeito de Estufa (GEE) através da construção de uma economia de baixo carbono é uma prioridade para evitar que o aquecimento global atinja níveis indesejáveis nas próximas décadas. Uma aposta em inovação e no investimento em tecnologias verdes permitirá alcançar uma sociedade de baixas emissões e, simultaneamente, impulsionar a economia, criar empregos e reforçar a competitividade do Município.O Município de Torres Vedras tem vindo a desenvolver vários projetos no sentido de alcançar uma maior sustentabilidade energética e ambiental. Em dezembro de 2010, o Município de Torres Vedras aderiu ao Pacto de Autarcas, assumindo o compromisso de reduzir as emissões de CO2 no seu território em, pelo menos, 20% até 2020. Em 2021, o Município atualizou este compromisso, adotando uma abordagem integrada à atenuação e adaptação às alterações climáticas através de uma transição justa, assumindo o objetivo de ultrapassar a meta de redução de 55% de emissões de CO2 até 2030, a redução da pobreza energética e a criação de uma visão a longo prazo para alcançar a neutralidade climática até 2050, através de uma transição justa. Em termos de planeamento, o Município de Torres Vedras iniciou em 2020 a elaboração de dois importantes instrumentos da sua política climática: o Plano de Ação para a Energia Sustentável e o Clima, com enfoque na mitigação das alterações climáticas, redução da pobreza energética e promoção de uma transição justa e o Plano Municipal de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas de Torres Vedras, com enfoque na redução da vulnerabilidade aos efeitos negativos das alterações climáticas. Munida da informação recolhida no âmbito destes processos e tendo por base as melhores práticas de planeamento, a Câmara Municipal de Torres Vedras procedeu à elaboração de um único de instrumento de planeamento e ação climática municipal, compreendo simultaneamente as componentes de mitigação e adaptação: Plano Municipal de Ação Climática de Torres Vedras (PMAC), aprovado em fevereiro de 2024.
column16: O Plano Diretor Municipal está a ser revisto integrando as orientações emanadas por estes planos, em especial pelo PMAC, cujas medidas de adaptação têm tradução indireta no modelo territorial e nas intervenções.
column17: O planeamento financeiro das ações, em especifico a inscrição orçamental das medidas previstas nos planos é integrada todos os anos no orçamento municipal, dependendo das orientações e capacidade financeira global do Município.
column18: Em relação à jurisdição do Município na transição para uma economia de baixo carbono, reconhecendo a extraordinária importância de envolvimento da comunidade e dos atores locais e regionais relevantes para o processo de ação climática, o Executivo Municipal determinou a necessidade de constituição de um Conselho Municipal de Ação Climática, adiante designado por CMAC, como uma instância de consulta e concertação relativa à política de ação climática do Município de Torres Vedras.A elaboração do Regulamento do CMAC, iniciado em 2022, passou por um processo de consulta pública, após o qual, sob proposta da Câmara Municipal e aprovado pela Assembleia Municipal de Torres Vedras, foi publicado no Edital n.º 913/2023, de 1 de junho de 2023, do Diário da República n.º 106, 2.ª série, Parte H (ver anexo).O CMAC pretende assumir-se como um órgão consultivo, com sede no Município, que procura articular a intervenção dos agentes e forças vivas do território bem como a participação das entidades ligadas, direta ou indiretamente, ao ambiente e alterações climáticas. O novo órgão visa a análise e acompanhamento da política municipal climática, fomentando a identificação de novas medidas e ações para a adaptação às alterações climáticas e a descarbonização do território de Torres Vedras, em linha com a Agenda 2030 da ONU e indispensáveis ao cumprimento das metas previstas nos Objetivos de Desenvolvimento Sustentável (ODS), em particular o ODS 13 “Ação Climática”.
