column15: The City's main climate mitigation plan is the Climate Emergency Action Plan (CEAP). CEAP governance: The Climate Emergency Directors Forum provides oversight at a working level, while the Climate Emergency Steering Committee provides oversight at a program level. The Sustainability Group tracks progress and reports to Council annually. Executive reports are also prepared as required. The CEAP includes an indicators framework and an annual report, more details of which are available here: https://vancouver.ca/files/cov/ceap-2025-annual-report-dashboard.pdf. \nThe City's main climate adaptation plan is the Climate Change Adaptation Strategy (CCAS). CCAS governance: The Adaptation Steering Committee provides oversight to implementation. This committee is comprised of senior managers, many of whom are also in the Corporate Leadership Team. The Sustainability Group tracks progress and reports to Council annually. Executive reports are also prepared as required. The review cycle for the Climate Change Risk assessment will be aligned with the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) five-year reporting process. Climate projections from the IPCC report are downscaled to address the City of Vancouver context. As new information becomes available the City reviews and updates our Adaptation Strategy. The City aims for a five-year review cycle of the Adaptation Strategy, which includes updating climate information and reviewing the status of adaptation actions. The City will complete a risk and vulnerability assessment every 10-15 years, to capture any changes. and support action plan updates.
column16: Vancouver was one of the first cities in the world to recognize the significance of climate change. In 1990, the groundbreaking Clouds of Change Task Force recommended that Vancouver begin to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions. The City of Vancouver is committed to taking action to mitigate and adapt to the emerging and anticipated impacts of climate change. This commitment began with the adoption of our Greenest City Action Plan in 2011, followed by our Climate Change Adaptation Strategy (CCAS) in 2012 and 2018 and more recently the Climate Emergency Action Plan in 2020 (CEAP).The February, 2022 Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) report identifies with very high confidence that the magnitude and rate of climate change and associated risks depend strongly on near-term mitigation and adaptation actions, and projected adverse impacts and related losses and damages escalate with every increment of global warming. The City is addressing both carbon emissions that cause climate change (through CEAP) and enhancing resilience to climate-related shocks and stresses (through CCAS). In addition, the Vancouver Plan 2050 includes a Climate section. The vision is for Vancouver to produce zero greenhouse gas emissions, while improving our resilience to the changing climate, capturing carbon, and promoting sustainable consumption.
column17: The City's current capital planning framework includes sustainability and resilience benefits as considerations to guide capital investments and assist with prioritization. However, the advent of TCFD disclosure has brought greater institutional awareness to the need for more formalized, overarching frameworks for incorporating climate mitigation and adaptation priorities into capital planning and asset management systems. Work is underway within the Finance and Sustainability departments to create and integrate these frameworks. This work will continue over several years, and will help inform the preparation of the upcoming Capital Plan and future Annual Capital Budget allocations. MITIGATION: At the programmatic level, the Climate Emergency Action Plan (CEAP) includes a financial framework that acts as a roadmap, projecting capital and operating funding requirements for new and existing CEAP initiatives. Estimates are periodically refined based on project reprioritization, improved costing estimates and emerging timeline challenges or implementation opportunities. ADAPTATION: Adaptation work at the City has relied primarily on existing departmental budgets and grants from other levels of government in matching funds. Work is underway to better incorporate climate-related risks into the Enterprise Risk Management System, which will help identify funding needs where the risk is highest. The City is improving its tracking of climate-related capital and operating budgets; we also need to begin monitoring the impact of climate change on available capital and operational budgets themselves.
column18: Risk analysis at the City has focused on physical risks to date. More work is required to better identify and quantify transition risks. However, reductions in the City's corporate GHG emissions (mainly from the City's buildings and vehicle fleet) help to illustrate commensurate reductions in corporate exposure to transition risk. For example, the City has an ongoing priority of zero-emissions capital replacement of heating and hot water systems in City-owned facilities. Likewise, fleet fuel purchases are also shifting to renewable natural gas (RNG) and renewable diesel (R100). In 2021, 50% of the fuel used by the City was either RNG, R100, or Electricity. Declines in corporate GHGs from these and other initiatives shows a reduction in exposure to commodity and carbon tax fluctuations. TCFD recommends disclosure of the amount or percentage of assets and service delivery vulnerable to physical and transition risks. The City does not have these figures at this time. Generally, the City's climate metrics have tended to be descriptive and contextual, and do not include a risk dimension or analysis (e.g., total community GHGs without commentary on risk-exposure profile that this figure represents). Similar to many organizations, the City has physical risks well identified and assessed but more work is required to better identify and quantify transition risks.

column15: At a national level Glasgow City Council has a statutory requirement via Scotland's Climate Change Duties of Public Bodies Reporting Requirements to submit our progress in tackling climate change on an annual basis. This involves reporting on our emissions reductions alongside our climate targets and projects relating to climate change via a centralised process to Scottish Government. In addition, the Sustainable Glasgow Partnership has been established to bring together major stakeholders in the city to work across the challenge of making the city Net Zero Carbon by 2030 and pulling the collective intellect and power of these major stakeholders including stakeholders such as the council, universities, housing organisations, regeneration companies, the Distribution Network Operator, national government agencies, and the National Health Service (NHS). This Partnership is crucial in coordinating action and progress at a city level and ensure there is communication and oversight of projects across the city The partnership is led by Glasgow City Council and chaired by the Leader of the Council and collects an annual membership fee from its Board members to support resource and action in support of its Net Zero Carbon target. The Partnership is supported by four thematic hubs (covering the themes of Heating & Housing, Green Infrastructure and Transport, Green Economy & Private Sector, and Greening the City) where action is discussed with a view to accelerating progress towards climate resilience and net zero. At local level policy any project development relating to climate change needs to pass through Council Committees to ensure political oversight of direction. These policies and projects go through our Net Zero and Climate Progress Monitoring City Policy Committee, before being formally approved at the City Administration Committee. At Corporate Management Team level, the Executive Director of Neighbourhoods Regeneration and Sustainability (NRS) has responsibility as the Corporate Champion for net zero targets and climate resilience championing and providing leadership in these areas. This is delivered through a Climate and Sustainability Board which includes directors from each of the Council services and is supported by the Sustainability Team. This board governs the Climate and Sustainability work plan managing project issues by exception and providing resolutions to issues. The Board also evaluates and onboards new projects onto the programme that support the goal of being Net Zero Carbon by 2030. Feeding into the Board is the Climate and Sustainability Scoping Group chaired by the Head of Sustainability. This Scoping Group screens new projects and decides whether these need board approval to be brought onto the programme. The Scoping Group has authority to onboard projects up to a certain scale without board approval. The Board and Scoping Group ensure visibility and management of the Climate programme across the Council as a corporate entity. Within the Sustainability Team there is an established Project Management Office (PMO) that coordinates the programme of works emanating from our Climate Plan. The PMO consists of 4 officers who monitor project progress and provide assistance to project owners in resolving issues arising within projects across a range of specialisms
column16:
• Two of the four key challenges identified as part of Council's Strategic Plan 2022-2027 (agreed at Full Council on the 27th October 2022) are Grand Challenge 2 'Increase Opportunity and Prosperity for All Our Citizens' and Grand Challenge 3 'Fight the climate emergency in a just transition to a net zero Glasgow'. Grand Challenge 2, Mission 1 aims to support Glasgow residents into sustainable and fair work, and develop skills for a just transition into low carbon industries. Mission 2 aims to support the growth of an innovative, resilient, and net zero carbon economy. Grand Challenge 3, Mission 1 aims to deliver sustainable transport and travel aligned with the city region, and Mission 2 is to become a net zero carbon city by 2030. To achieve Glasgow's vision of becoming a just, net zero carbon, and climate resilient city by 2030, it is essential that we work in collaboration with our communities and institutions; the Strategic Plan ensures that Glasgow embeds all 17 of the UN Sustainable Development Goals into all of its policy and strategy decision making (https://tinyurl.com/5e3wdfda). 
• The National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4) is the national spatial strategy for Scotland; it sets out regional priorities, national developments, and national planning policy and sits alongside our City Development Plan (https://www.gov.scot/publications/national-planning-framework-4/). 
• Glasgow's over-arching Climate Plan outlines how the city aims to achieve net zero carbon by 2030, 15 years ahead of the national target; it was created after the declaration of a state of climate and ecological emergency in 2019 by GCC following review and appreciation of the escalating impact of climate change on Glasgow and the world. 
• Glasgow's Adaptation Plan contains action to consider climate change risks to the city such as: increased rainfall, increased temperatures, warmer and wetter winters with more rain and less snow, high summer temperatures with increased rainfall, sea level rise. 
• Our Net Zero Route Map (https://app.climateview.global/v4/public/board/3e7cb896-9a30-4aad-9590-aab0349ac538) has reviewed our current trajectory to 2030 (based on existing policies and strategies) and has provided us with a clear Route Map to take us from where we are now (baseline) to where we hope to be in 2030, our net zero target. In an ongoing manner, this will also be used to identify areas where additional actions could be implemented to further support our net zero goal. The prioritised actions within the Route Map are science and data driven and through the use of the Climate View tool, will enable Glasgow to be agile and receptive to real life changes as we move forwards. The tool is built on a data inventory which can be used to influence wider master planning for the city as we move towards 2030. 
• Our Open Space Strategy and City Development Plan have policies that are aimed at reducing risk from flooding, reducing emissions and improving local climate resilience.
• Glasgow's Liveable Neighbourhoods Plan (noted at the Environment, Sustainability and Carbon Reduction City Policy Committee on the 8th June 2021) and our City Centre Transformation Plan (approved at the City Administration Committee on 1st December 2022) both include acknowledgement of the risks around climate change, particularly flooding and increased temperatures.
• Glasgow's Transport Strategy includes assessment of increased risk of flooding and heating and how this could impact on transport networks.
• Glasgow's Low Emissions Zone (LEZ) is now fully implemented. Glasgow's LEZ considers the impacts of climate change and air quality and is part of Glasgow's Climate Plan
• Our Avenues Programme (transformation of 21 city centre locations to be more pedestrian and cyclist friendly) acknowledges and factors in both flood risk management and emissions reduction and will include: green/blue infrastructure (such as street trees, planting, and rain gardens), enhanced and widened footways, and segregated cycle lanes. This will reduce risks from flooding and heat, as well as increasing and supporting biodiversity. 
• One of the five priorities identified in our Local Housing Strategy (LHS) 2023-2028 is 'Improving the energy efficiency of Glasgow's homes, reducing fuel poverty and supporting a Just Transition to Net Zero through decarbonising domestic heating and energy'. It also identifies flooding and impacts relating to this from a housing perspective and considers how to integrate expected temperature increases with retrofitting programmes. 
• Glasgow's Local Heat and Energy Efficiency Strategy (LHEES) includes a delivery plan to advance deployment of district heating across the city as a means of significantly reducing heating-based emissions. It also sets out a pathway to significantly increasing the energy efficiency of building stock in the city and includes potential heat networks, heat pumps, and fabric improvements to upgrade existing housing stock.
column17:
• Significant capital funding under the Climate Emergency Fund has been allocated for financial year 2025/26 with £4M for energy efficiency and retrofit of the Council estate. A further £1M is expected to be raised through community municipal investments to supplement the existing funding for the continued rollout of PV solar on the estate. Use of income from the Glasgow Low Emission Zone has also been directed to fund community led climate projects with £0.75M distributed by end of 2025.
• Glasgow has embarked on a process to establish the correct Model for Climate Investment to formulate a route for delivery and to create a method to allow the private sector to invest in climate related projects, supporting the ambitions to become a net zero city. To address the barriers and understand the best model for Glasgow, the City Administration Committee approved (21st March 2024) a project budget of £4m to be spent on creating an internal team and supplementing the knowledge and experience with external specialists to establish Glasgow's own Model for Climate Investment. Glasgow is specifically focusing on two workstreams that are separate but intrinsically linked:
> The delivery vehicle: With a focus on council owned assets, and building on Glasgow's Local Heat and Energy Efficiency Strategy (LHEES) which provides a clear direction for decarbonising heat and improving building efficiency in the city, a public private partnership or concession agreement will be explored. This could see investment in areas such as low/zero-carbon heat networks, renewable energy from wind and solar, energy efficiency, and smart energy systems but can be extended to other energy related project. A critical part of the project scope will be consideration of additional social value, community involvement and ensuring a Just Transition. The full scope will be determined through competitive dialogue with the market to ascertain the most commercially viable offer for the Council.
> The climate investment vehicle: The creation of an investment vehicle for the city/city region would unlock access to capital from the private sector, as well as long-term patient capital from other sectors, such as Pension Funds. The fund would help to address the funding gap as well as providing city partners with the opportunity to progress projects that otherwise may not be able to be delivered. In addition, further mechanisms for appointing institutional investors will be assessed to allow for a more streamlined approach to mobilising investment opportunities.
• To help optimise the Council's own resources a two-stage approach is being developed. GCC is developing a Climate Change Impact Assessment which, once finalised, will need to be completed by all projects and policies that go through our Committee approval process. Secondly as part of our budgeting process each year a carbon impact assessment is undertaken on all budget proposals to ensure that the impact of any budget allocation is understood prior to final budget decisions being made.
• In June 2023, the Scottish and UK Governments announced that the Glasgow City Region would be one of two areas to host the first Investment Zones in Scotland. The Glasgow City Region Investment Zone will support climate-resilient economic development and a just transition. The Glasgow City Region Investment Zone will draw on existing partnerships and a strong sense of where successful clusters of priority sectors can be amplified, and will benefit from £160 million of government support over the next decade through a mix of tax and spend incentives. Once bids have been reviewed and assessed the final phase of the Investment Zone process will involve the collation of the city regions formal proposal including the package of projects for consideration and approval by the UK and Scottish Governments.

The potential risks which Glasgow may encounter on its journey towards its ambition of achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2030: 
• A change in political direction by UK or Scottish Government (e.g. a change in administration at local government level, changes in climate-related national legislation, UK general election) 
• Changes to climate-related public sector policies 
• Reduction or changes to public sector financial budgets which may impact the ability to fund climate-related projects
• Market policy and landscape decisions and a change of direction (e.g. hydrogen EV delay in phasing out new diesel and petrol vehicles) 
• Unforeseen impacts on society such as economic inflation and changes in interest rates 
• Exacerbation of existing social and health inequalities 
• Public perception of the importance of climate change and 'competing' issues such as the Cost of Living Crisis 

In common with other cities, Glasgow is affected by energy costs significantly elevated from those observed at the start of the decade. These lie outside of local government control or influence but have been offset to some degree by central government action in relation to energy price caps for domestic users. However, the impact of increased energy prices remains significant.

column15: The District's Department of Energy and Environment (DOEE) leads the city's climate action planning and reporting efforts, including by developing the Clean Energy DC plan (the District's roadmap to halving citywide emissions by 2032), the Climate Ready DC plan (climate adaptation plan) and Sustainable DC 2.0 (the District's 20-year sustainability plan, led in partnership with the DC Office of Planning). Implementation of these plans is shared across numerous District Government agencies, many of whom have integrated climate actions and goals into their own guiding documents and workplans. For example, the Department of Parks and Recreation's Ready2Play master plan incorporates climate projections in its plans to expand and enhance the District's park system, and specifically calls for adopting resilient hub standards for the design and retrofit of recreation centers. DOEE reports annually on the District's progress toward actions identified in these core planning documents, as well as on citywide greenhouse gas emissions, tracking trends in overall progress toward our climate action goals. These metrics are also part of the agency's annual key performance indicators. The DC Council's Transportation and Environment Committee provides performance and budget oversight over DOEE and key implementation agencies, and is active in advancing legislation related to climate action. For example, the Clean Energy DC Omnibus Amendment Act codified key actions named in the District's Clean Energy DC plan, including establishing the nation's first building energy performance standards, and increasing the District's renewable portfolio standard to reach 100% by 2032. The District also has an independent Commission on Climate Change and Resiliency, composed of 16 members, half appointed by the Mayor and half by the Council. Members are appointed to thematic seats, including energy, emergency preparedness, environmental science, public health, transportation, natural resources, environmental justice, and insurance, and are tasked with making recommendations to Council and the Mayor for increasing the District's ability to mitigate and adapt to climate change, including preparing, planning, absorbing, and recovering from adverse events.
column16: The District has incorporated climate change across its long-term planning documents to ensure climate adaptation and mitigation are addressed holistically. Building on the District's sustainability and climate planning efforts, the 2020 update to the Comprehensive Plan for the District of Columbia includes several goals around climate mitigation and resilience and policies to support resilience to sudden shocks, such as flooding and extreme weather, as well as to chronic stressors, such as urban heat. Additionally, as part of the 100 Resilient Cities initiative, the District released Resilient DC in 2019, which identifies climate change as a major stressor and reasserts the District's commitment to action. Together these plans reflect the District's climate commitments under the Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate & Energy, and Mayor Bowser's commitments to the Paris Climate Accord and to making the District carbon neutral. Examples of how these issues are reflected in the Comprehensive Plan include: 1. Energy Efficiency: The plan includes several goals around efficiency, from an overarching goal to \'promote the efficient use of energy, additional use of renewable energy, and a reduction of unnecessary energy expenses. The overarching objective is to achieve reductions in per capita energy consumption \' through policies and goals around energy efficient building and site planning, energy efficiency at major employment centers, energy consumption for residential heating and cooling, consumer education, and removing potential barriers in existing laws and codes to efficiency. It also echoes the Sustainable DC plan and Clean Energy DC quantitative targets to reduce per capita energy use 50% by 2032.2. Renewable Energy: The Comprehensive Plan for the District includes several goals around renewable energy throughout its chapters on infrastructure, housing and environmental protection. Examples include referencing the District's Renewable Portfolio Standard (RPS), to promoting the use of renewable energy, and procuring green power for District operations. The DC Office of Planning's 2020 amendments to the Comprehensive Plan reflect the District's commitment to renewable energy and the strengthening of the District's RPS, which was most recently revised in March 2019 to require 100% renewable electricity by 2032. 3. Emissions Reductions: The 2020 Comprehensive Plan acknowledges the need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and adapt to climate change as a critical environmental issue facing the District and references the District's climate commitments under the Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate & Energy, and Mayor Bowser's commitments to the Paris Climate Accord and to making the District carbon neutral. The proposed amendments to the Comprehensive Plan are also aligned with the interim goals and targets around greenhouse gas reduction in Sustainable DC and Clean Energy DC (i.e. 50% below 2006 levels by 2032).4. Adaptation and Resilience: In the 2020 amendments to the Comprehensive Plan, the DC Office of Planning included new \'policies and actions to advance the concept of resiliency in the District as it impacts land use and community quality of life.\' In addition, the new content developed for the Comp Plan is aligned with the District's other resilience-related efforts, including Resilient DC, the District's comprehensive resilience strategy developed as part of 100 Resilient Cities. (see https://plandc.dc.gov/page/resilience). In 2025, the Office of Planning began the first full rewrite of the District's Comprehensive Plan in nearly 20 years. The Comprehensive Plan rewrite process will identify the challenges and opportunities the District faces to make sure that our city grows equitably, with vibrant and resilient neighborhoods. This is a once-in-a generation opportunity to collectively imagine a future that reflects our values and the DC Office of Planning is working in close collaboration with DOEE to carry forward more resiliency and clean energy strategies. Finally, the District of Columbia Department of Energy and Environment (DOEE) published its revised \'Flood Hazard Rules,\' also known as the \'Floodplain Regulations,\' on June 20, 2025, in the DC Register. column17: The District is committed to climate action and building resilience, which is also being increasingly incorporated into credit and bond ratings from external parties. column18: The District is committed to centering equity in its transition to a carbon neutral and climate resilient city. Implementing large-scale action both to mitigate and adapt to climate change must be rooted in community needs in order to advance opportunity for the District's residents of color and other residents most vulnerable to the impacts of climate change, and must seek to reduce both the legacy and current disproportionate impacts faced by these communities. Failure to do so risks continuing to exacerbate the impacts on residents of color and low-income residents, risking increasing inequity in the city. The District's Resilient DC plan highlighted equity in governance as a key priority for the District in combatting racial inequality that impacts the health, housing, opportunity, and prosperity of its residents. In passing the Racial Equity Achieves Results (REACH Act), the District has made a commitment to developing the infrastructure to ensure policy decisions and District programs are evaluated through a racial equity lens. The District's Chief Equity Officer and the Council Office of Racial Equity are working to guide agencies to evaluate existing programs and new policies and legislation for their impact on racial equity.

City of Melbourne is taking a leadership role in addressing climate change by setting ambitious goals and driving climate action across our municipality. We are taking action to achieve our climate-related ambitions by using our own direct powers, empowering our community, collaborating with others and advocating for policy change from other levels of government.

The City of Melbourne declared a climate and biodiversity emergency in 2019, recognising the need to take more urgent climate action. This declaration was accompanied by a Climate Change and Biodiversity Emergency response plan that accelerated our ambitions and included a commitment to reaching our zero emissions target for the municipality by 2040, ten years earlier than previously planned. This plan identified ten priorities for accelerated action, based on our greatest opportunities to have impact, including accelerating the uptake of renewable energy, supporting zero emissions transport, facilitating the transition to zero emissions buildings and precincts, and stimulating the circular economy. 

Our Climate Change Adaptation Strategy (refreshed in 2017) highlights the key priority areas for action based on an in-depth risk assessment. These actions include enhancing the natural environment and green spaces, shaping our built form to withstand future climate change impacts, strengthening the resilience of our culturally diverse community, protecting and enhancing our economy and building the City of Melbourne's adaptation capabilities and expertise. 

The risks, opportunities and priority actions identified in the Climate Change Adaptation Strategy and Climate Change and Biodiversity Emergency Response plan have informed the development and delivery of the Council Plan 2021-2025 which prioritised the climate change and biodiversity emergency as one of six strategic objectives for the municipality. Climate and Environment has also been a key them in the development of Council's draft Council Plan 2025-2029, M2050 vision and 2025-26 Council Plan and Budget, and is strongly reflected in the vision and actions set out by these documents,

City of Melbourne is demonstrating leadership in our actions to reduce our operational emissions and prepare our city for the impacts of climate change. We have been a certified carbon neutral organisation since 2012. Our Emissions Reduction Plan for Council Operations 2021-26 sets out a comprehensive plan of actions that Council is delivering for its own operations to keep the organisation on course for net zero by 2040 and includes 72 actions across 8 priority areas. We are well on track to achieving these goals, including reaching our 100% renewable electricity target for council operations in 2019. 

City of Melbourne is set to experience significant financial impacts to our assets due to climate change and extreme weather events. Recent modelling of climate change hazards on City of Melbourne's assets found that found damage is expected to increase by 1,200 per cent in the next 75 years under a 'Do Nothing' scenario. This represents average annual damages costs of between $22 million and $37 million. Embedding environmental sustainability and climate resilience into our asset planning and operations helps Council determine the risk and susceptibility of assets to climate impacts and to put in place appropriate mitigation measures. Our draft 10 year Asset Plan for Council proposes to embed climate resilience and sustainability in life-cycle management. Two examples include 1) planning and design life-cycle stage: 'assets are designed with these considerations in mind: current and future affordability, accessibility, equity, maintainability, environmental sustainability and climate resilience' and 2) renewal phase: 'council optimises the timing of renewal or replacement, so that assets remain safe, functional and resilient to climate change effects, with timely investments, to save money in the long term

At the time of publishing, the City of Melbourne's Council Plan 2025-2029 is in draft and out for final consultation before the final version being endorsed by Council in October 2025. 
The Council Plan is one of the City of Melbourne's key strategic documents. Developed alongside the M2050 Vision, these documents describe the community and Council's vision for the future of Melbourne and the steps we will take over the coming years to get there
These documents have been developed in collaboration with Melbourne's diverse communities, including residents, businesses, workers, students and visitors. Across a range of engagement activities, these communities have shared their aspirations and ideas for the future, and what they want us to prioritise now to get there.
To help frame the conversation Council chose six interrelated themes to guide the conversation, including 'Climate and Environment'. Over 130 unique ideas emerged during the Melbourne 2050 Summit event that specifically related to climate and the future of Melbourne's environment. An open-ended survey saw 49% of respondents prioritise a green, environmentally friendly city, with references to actions to support greening and open space, circular economy, renewable technology, and climate change action. A People's Panel (48 everyday citizens) spent 35 hours deliberating and developed 8 principles to guide council decision making, including principles such as future-focused resource stewardship, deepening connection to Country and climate action as a collective responsibility. Insights and ideas gleaned from the Community engagement has informed the draft Council Plan 2025-2029 strategic priorities and outcomes. 
The draft Council Plan 2025-2029 continues Council's commitment to 1) United Nations Sustainable Development Goals and Targets, 2) health and wellbeing priorities of climate resilience and natural and built form resilience and 3) a 'living sustainably' strategic priority. Climate action considerations are also woven through other strategic priorities including 'governing for our future,' 'healthy, safe, clean and connected communities,' 'leveraging our economic strengths and building a city for people'. 
The draft Melbourne 2050 Vision also supports our climate ambitions, with principles such as 
•	Grounded in First Nations knowledge and culture: Our future city honours and empowers First Peoples self-determination, guided by their knowledge, culture, and enduring connection to Country, working together to care for and shape Melbourne for generations to come. 
•	Green and alive with experiences: Our green spaces are connected across every neighbourhood, street and building. We create vibrant places and experiences, celebrating culture and design. 
•	Driven by regeneration: Our systems are circular. We restore, renew and replenish our natural environment and biodiversity.

The Council Plan 2021-25 reflects Council's strong climate ambition and identified climate change and biodiversity emergency as one of six strategic objectives within the plan. This ensured that Council's four year workplan prioritised the environment and ensure urgent action was taken to reduce emissions to protect public health, strengthen the economy and create a city that mitigates and adapts to climate change. During that time, Council measured progress against ten key climate-related indicators that include greenhouse gas emissions, waste, water and biodiversity metrics.

Global Frameworks
An overarching framework to the previous and now draft Council Plan is Council's ongoing commitment to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) as our framework for action towards sustainable development. The City of Melbourne undertook a Voluntary Local Review (VLR) in 2022 to develop city-relevant targets, identify progress and where we need to prioritise our effort. The VLR provides a baseline for ongoing monitoring, evaluation and focused action for Council, our stakeholders and community. Council shares this progress report publicly via our open data platform and Participate Melbourne website . SDG targets and associated data helps Council prioritise investments and helps create the business case for climate related programs and services. For example: SDG Target 7.1 Promote universal access to affordable, reliable and modern energy services has led to building up an Energy Hardship Initiative and research project to help understand how Council can support the energy needs of our most vulnerable. SDG Target 7.3 By 2030, substantially improve the energy efficiency of infrastructure and buildings across the municipality has resulted in Retrofit Melbourne Plan and an approved annual budget for FY25/26 activity to deliver the Retrofit Melbourne Plan including exploring repurposing of vacant office buildings. 
Website: United Nations Sustainable Development Goals

Council Plan 2021-2025 :
Our previous four-year Council Plan (valid up to Jun 2025) prioritised the Climate and Biodiversity Emergency as one of six strategic objectives and included eight Major Initiatives that are directly related to climate change. The elevation of these actions in the 2021-2025 Council Plan meant that they were specifically identified in each Annual Budget and ensured that funding was prioritised for the delivery of these initiatives. The establishment of related progress indicators in the Council Plan enabled measurement, accountability and incentives for Council to prioritise investment in climate-related actions. 

Climate and Sustainable Development Goal Budgeting: Our Climate Change and City Resilience team has been working with City Finance since to 2023 to trial an SDG investment analysis approach. This 'SDG Budget' project is drawing upon global best practice, including from Strasbourg, France; Barcelona, Spain; and Jakarta, Indonesia. SDG budget analysis has provided insights into: Strategic emphasis - which Goals/targets the organisation is focusing on within the four-year term (this excludes business as usual programs and services); approximate budget investment for each goal (combined capital and operational expenditure); and Gaps in funding for any specific SDG targets. Initial analysis of major initiative investment (2023-2024) shows that Goal 7 (affordable and clean energy), Goal 11 (sustainable cities and communities), Goal 13 (climate action), goal 14 (life below water) has received approximately 44% of total investment. The project is continuing for 2024-2025 and includes the trial of new methodologies and with an expanded scope to incorporate all Council programs and services budget line items including labour spend. This work will reveal our best approximation of climate related investment across the organisation and help identify areas for further investment and performance improvement. 

The draft Council Plan 2025-2029 includes a key deliverable for 2026-2029 financial years to 'introduce and develop climate budgeting'. This will support Council's continuing commitment to C40 leadership standards as well as future-proofing Council climate investments.

Asset Plan: Climate change is identified as a key consideration in our draft Asset Plan, which provides a strategic overview of how we will sustainably manage our community's assets over the next 10 years to support our community vision. It outlines how we will ensure our assets continue to support the delivery of services into the future, including their resilience to climate impacts.

Annual Plan and Budget for FY25/26:
The approved Annual Plan and Budget for FY25/26 includes significant climate related investments, particularly in urban greening and gas free council operations. These commitments will result in $44.3 million investment in the next 12 months to shape a greener future and support the physical and mental wellbeing of Melbourne's growing population. The investment will deliver 6 new green open spaces—including pocket and linear parks—while advancing designs for 10 additional sites and continuing to renew existing parks. Key projects include completing phase 1 of the Greenline project with 450 metres of new boardwalks, promenades and greening, boosting the Urban Forest Fund by $400,000 for private realm greening, and planting 3,000 trees across the municipality. 
Council is continuing its transition away from fossil gas to achieve its commitment to be gas-free for all municipal buildings by 2030. A consolidated program of eleven sites will begin their electrification works in 2026, including the iconic Melbourne Town Hall and the innovative Library at the Dock at a cost of $5.3M 
 
Following the opening of the City's first all-electric recreation centre in Kensington, a further two aquatic centres; Carlton Baths and North Melbourne Recreation Centre, will be electrified in 2027. All sites will join the existing portfolio of City buildings being powered by 100% renewable electricity under the City's Melbourne Renewable Energy Project (MREP), Australia's first renewable power purchase agreement consisting of group of local governments, cultural institutions, universities and corporations collectively purchasing renewable energy from a newly built facility. 
The consolidated electrification program of eleven City assets will reduce the City of Melbourne's carbon footprint by 565 tonnes of CO2-e per annum and eliminate 10,967GJ of natural gas.
The annual plan also includes a $250k investment for a new pilot program offering a suite of services to support apartment residents and businesses with energy costs, efficiency, renewables, electrification, resilience and net zero goals, in close collaboration with Owners Corporation committees. As well as a $250k to deliver the Retrofit Melbourne Plan including exploring repurposing of vacant office buildings.
column18: We have identified climate change as one of 11 strategic risks facing our organisation and formally report on our risk management responses to City of Melbourne's Audit and Risk Committee. Our climate change risk assessment was updated in 2024 to include the most up-to-date climate change projections and community vulnerability data. In this assessment we have provided spatial information and neighbourhood risk profiles to enable climate change risk to prioritised in decision making. The assessment includes liability and physical risks and focuses on how climate change interacts with City of Melbourne's operations, assets and communities. Transition risk will be integrated into future iterations as part of an adaptive management approach and a Climate Change Transition Risk Assessment is being undertaken in 2025 to update our understanding of transition risk in our jurisdiction. \n\nA failure to adequately address climate change will have significant impacts on our community and economy. Modelling previously undertaken to inform our Climate Change Mitigation Strategy indicates that the impacts of climate change and missed economic opportunities of transitioning to a low carbon economy will cost AU$12.6 billion to the municipality's economy by 2050 under a business as usual scenario. As Australia's second largest city and an important centre for finance, professional services and the knowledge economy in the Asia-Pacific region, Melbourne is well placed to benefit from the transition to a low carbon economy. However, the transition presents both opportunities and risks. Council has an important role to play to ensure that the benefits of the transition to a low carbon economy are shared equitably. This is demonstrated by the transition of the energy sector, for example. National rises in energy prices are increasingly impacting on households in our city. For example, the results of our annual 2024 Community Social Indicator Survey showed that over 50% of residents were experiencing some kind of energy hardship such as energy rationing, difficulty paying energy bills or inability to afford other essentials as a consequence of energy costs. These impacts are disproportionately felt by vulnerable groups including multicultural communities, renters and people with a disability. This is evidenced by City of Melbourne's recent study into energy hardship, funded by the Climate Neutral Cities Alliance. The transition to renewable energy technologies like rooftop solar PV present opportunities to reduce energy costs. However, approximately 83% of residents in the City of Melbourne are renters or apartment-dwellers. This means most residents are locked out of the financial benefits of rooftop solar or home batteries. Our Power Melbourne community battery project is an example of the action we are taking to provide more residents and businesses with access to the benefits of the energy transition. Our recently completed Climate Justice Project, undertaken with the support of the Climate Neutral Cities Alliances, has provided the opportunity to engage more deeply with Community Sector Organisations to enhance their work, gain insights into community vulnerability and identify opportunities to better support vulnerable communities. The project has established climate justice principles that will be embedded into our work, including the Inclusive Melbourne Strategy, Food Policy, Municipal Public Health and Wellbeing Plan and Urban Forest Strategy.

column15: In 2023, the net greenhouse gas emissions in Kaohsiung City were 49.52 million metric tons, taking one-fifth of the national total. In 2022, there was already a 25.1% reduction (base year:2005), approx. 16.62 million tons of CO2e reduced. The emissions breakdown by sector reveals that the industrial sector accounted for the largest portion of 81%, the residential and commercial sector accounted for 10.4%, the transportation sector accounted for 7.8%, the environmental and agricultural sector accounted for 0.8%, and the carbon sink sector accounted for -2.3%. Therefore, how to respond to domestic and international net-zero regulatory requirements such as CBAM, CCA, or energy transition-related legal measures, and assist industry in reducing carbon emissions has also become a challenge for Kaohsiung City. \nVia the SBTi methodology, the city's carbon reduction target for 2030 is expected to be 30% compared to the baseline year. On the regulation side, Kaohsiung City has formulated the \'Kaohsiung City Net-Zero Urban Development and Self Government Ordinance\'. The regulation aims to strengthen government governance for achieving net-zero, provide guidance for carbon reduction in industries, promote public participation, and ensure a just transition. This regulation will serve as a foundation for climate legislation and strengthen the legal framework for climate action in Kaohsiung City. \nThe Kaohsiung City government has established the \'Kaohsiung City Sustainable Development and Climate Change Response Promotion Commission\' in 2023 to oversee 161 sustainable development indicators, review major net-zero related policies such as the carbon budget, “Net-Zero Policy White Paper,” “Net-Zero Sustainability Report,”(temporary translation) and emission reduction and adaptation implementation plans, and set the \'Climate Change Response Section\' and the \'Green Energy Promotion Task Force\' under the Environmental Protection Bureau. These entities have developed the \'Second Phase (2021-2025) Greenhouse Gas Reduction Implementation Plan,\' the \'Renewable Energy Six-Year Plan (2021-2026) 1250MW,\' and First-phase (2025-2026) Carbon Budget(Approved version), which are regularly monitored and reviewed.
column16: Based on the emission structure of Kaohsiung City, where industry has accounted for the largest share at 80%-82%, with industrial emissions mainly from the steel industry (accounting for 40.9% of the city's total), the petrochemical industry (29.4%), and the electronics industry (2.5%), Kaohsiung City has formulated a climate governance framework that includes nine major aspects and five foundations. Strategies have been developed respectively for energy, industry, residential and commercial sectors, transport, environment, agriculture, net-zero green lifestyle, carbon sinks, and just transition. Specifically for the industrial sector, the main strategies include transitioning away from fossil fuels, building low-carbon industrial chains, and converting waste into energy resources. \nWithin Kaohsiung City, there are three Taiwan Power Company(Taipower) thermal power plants: Hsinta, Dalin, and Nanpu. These plants have a total installed capacity of 6,878 MW. In addition, Kaohsiung City, as an industrial city, has 17 cogeneration plants and 35 boilers, primarily fueled with coal and natural gas, with a total installed capacity of 1,275 MW. It plays a vital role in Taiwan's energy supply. To reduce GHG emissions from energy generation, efforts are made to gradually increase the proportion of natural gas in power generation and request all cogeneration plants to phase out coals by 2025. Furthermore, the evaluation and gradual adoption of low-carbon fuels such as hydrogen and solid recovered fuel (SRF) are being considered. To accelerate the energy transition, Kaohsiung City established the \'Green Energy Promotion Task Force\' at the municipal level in 2020. Vice Mayor Charles Lin has served as the convener, with the support of the Economic Development Bureau and Public Works Bureau. Various city government departments, including the Environmental Protection Bureau, Water Resources Bureau, Education Bureau, Civil Affairs Bureau, Police Department, Agriculture Bureau, Marine Bureau, and Urban Development Bureau, were working together to further promote the goals. The task force has set a target of 1.25GW of renewable energy capacity from 2021 to 2026, focusing on three aspects: \'energy-creating,\' \'energy-saving,\' and \'energy-storing.\' Due to sufficient sunlight, Kaohsiung City actively develops solar energy and has reached an installed capacity of 1.279 GW as of July 2024, ranking fifth in Taiwan. The city also continues to develop biogas power generation from landfill and livestock waste. As industrial emissions account for more than 80% of the total emissions in Kaohsiung City, a \'Net-Zero Industry Alliance\' has been established with companies with major emission sources. Through industry leaders leading the way and state-owned enterprises setting an example, the alliance aims to share carbon reduction technologies, promote cross-industry collaboration, and require industries to set short, medium, and long-term reduction goals and plans to achieve carbon reduction.\n
column17:
In 2022, Kaohsiung City proposed its 2050 net-zero emissions target and strategies. Based on the “Kaohsiung City Net-Zero Urban Development and Self Government Ordinance,” various agencies have formulated relevant reduction measures. In 2024, departments allocated approximately NT$22.17 billion for net-zero-related budgets, expected to increase to NT$28.5 billion in 2025 (including aspects like energy transition, energy efficiency improvement, and net-zero transport). Budget for transport accounts for the largest portion, including MRT projects and vehicle electrification, followed by resource recycling and zero waste initiatives, bottom ash treatment, and sewage connections. Additionally, efforts are being made in green lifestyle, carbon sinks, and agricultural net-zero practices. 
Regarding the industrial sector, which accounts for the largest share of emissions in the city, according to the 2024 Net-Zero Industrial Alliance questionnaire results, enterprises have allocated budgets for relevant measures to achieve net-zero transition by investing at least NT$3 billion in 2022 and at least NT$13 billion in 2023.
As of March 2024, Kaohsiung Bank has provided NT$8.4 billion in green financing and NT$24.2 billion in green loans. At the end of 2023, the Finance Bureau and the Mass Rapid Transit Bureau collaborated to apply and obtain permission from the Taipei Exchange to issue government green bonds, creating the first case nationwide of a government unit issuing green bonds. The total amount is 2 billion NTD, used for loans for the MRT Red and Orange Line project.
column18: The industrial sector is the main source of emissions in Kaohsiung City, and achieving the net-zero emissions target by 2050 poses challenges given the existing industrial technologies. Continuous support is needed to assist businesses in developing and implementing short, medium, and long-term emission reduction plans, as well as promoting low-carbon and zero-carbon innovation. The majority of businesses in the city are small and medium-sized traditional industries, which face challenges due to international supply chain decarbonization requirements, the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), and domestic carbon costs. Investing in innovative technologies requires substantial manpower and funding. Therefore, self-investment in technology development is challenging. Local governments rely on funding support and, through the \' Kaohsiung City Net-Zero Urban Development and Self Government Ordinance” encourage enterprises to reduce emissions; by establishing “Net-zero Industrial Alliance” the larger companies can support smaller ones, creating opportunities for collaborative emission reduction efforts.

We avoid investments that are harmful to the environment and work with financial institutions and investment advisors to investigate suitable products that support positive environmental performance and meet our financial risk and return outcomes. Following market feedback, including from the City of Sydney, Westpac developed a new sustainable investment product known as a Green Tailored Deposit. The City was the first council to invest in Green Tailored Deposits, in late 2018. These deposits are associated with a defined pool of eligible assets which meet the Climate Bond Standard criteria including renewable energy, low carbon transport, low carbon intensity emitting buildings, waste and water products and are independently certified annually. The Commonwealth Bank subsequently launched a similar product, with the City placing its first investment in early 2020.

As at June 2025 the City held $55 million across eleven tranches with Westpac's Green Tailored deposit. 
The City also held $5.0M in a sustainability bond/FRN with Bank Australia due to mature on 24 November 2025 and an additional $4.5M, invested in February 2023 due to mature on 22 February 2027.

This is based on an investment framework that is in line with the 2021 versions of the ICMA Green Bond Principles (GBP), Social Bond Principles (SBP) and Sustainability Bond Guidelines (SBG). This Socially Responsible investment opportunity meets both the credit risk and maturity profile requirements of the City.

Integration into the City's Governance Framework:
•	The CAP has been integrated into the City's Integrated Development Plan (IDP) — the statutory five-year strategic plan in terms of the Municipal Systems Act — and is updated annually. The 2024/25 IDP explicitly recognises the CAP as the overarching city-wide climate plan and embeds its ten thematic priorities addressing both mitigation and adaptation.
•	The IDP cascades into the Service Delivery and Budget Implementation Plans (SDBIPs), which allocates annual budgets and project deliverables, including those for climate-related initiatives.
Oversight and Decision-Making Structures:
•	The Environment & Infrastructure Services Department (EISD), as the CAP lead agency, submits biannual progress reports to the Mayoral Committee, chaired by the Executive Mayor, ensuring high-level political oversight.
•	Prior to Mayoral Committee review, reports are assessed by four cross-sectoral technical clusters of municipal departments and entities, comprising middle-to-senior level officials, which ensures technical validation, mainstreaming, and early problem resolution.
•	Quarterly Climate Action Forum (CAF) meetings, convened by EISD since 2018, bring together all city departments and entities to coordinate action, share progress, and align implementation. The 23rd CAF was held in June 2025 and the 24th is planned for October 2025.
Mainstreaming and Risk Management:
•	Since CAP approval, multiple departments and municipal entities have integrated climate risk considerations into their business plans.
•	As of 2024, climate change screening criteria have been formally included in the City's Infrastructure Planning System, ensuring all infrastructure projects are assessed for climate resilience and alignment with CAP objectives. This requirement is now formally included in the annual Infrastructure Planning System of the City.
Continuous Improvement and National Alignment:
•	The City's climate governance now incorporates requirements from the South African Climate Change Act (2024), ensuring alignment with national climate targets, carbon budgets, and resilience planning obligations.
•	A CAP Tracking Dashboard, under development with Sustainable Energy Africa, will provide real-time progress monitoring and public transparency, further strengthening oversight.

Climate-related issues — particularly the vulnerability of South Africa's coal-dependent energy system and the growing pressures on water resources — have significantly influenced Johannesburg's master and development planning. The national energy crisis, driven by overreliance on coal, aging infrastructure, and climate-related risks to both energy and water systems, directly impacts economic productivity, service delivery, and resilience in the city.
Integration into Strategic Planning Frameworks:
•	The City has embedded energy security, water resilience, decarbonisation, and climate adaptation as core priorities in its Integrated Development Plan (IDP) and Climate Action Plan (CAP).
•	The updated City Energy Plan 2025 outlines the pathway to diversify energy sources, scale renewable generation, improve efficiency, and promote demand-side management.
•	The Net-Zero Carbon by 2050 Policy commits the City to achieving carbon neutrality in the building, transport, and energy sectors, with interim milestones monitored through the CAP Tracking Dashboard.
•	The Water Security Strategy (2022) ensures that water demand management, climate-resilient infrastructure, and sustainable catchment management are embedded into spatial and infrastructure planning to safeguard water resources against climate risks such as droughts and heatwaves.
•	The City's Infrastructure Planning System now applies climate change screening criteria to all new projects, ensuring alignment with CAP objectives, net-zero goals, and water security priorities.
Strategic Response - Energy and Water Transition Initiatives:
•	In May 2022, Johannesburg hosted an Energy Summit, bringing together public, private, and academic stakeholders to accelerate the shift to renewable and distributed energy generation.
•	A political resolution followed to integrate Independent Power Producers (IPPs) into the city's supply mix, diversify energy sources, and reduce reliance on Eskom.
•	A benchmarking delegation to the City of Cape Town informed Johannesburg's IPP engagement framework and procurement processes.
•	By 2024, the City has advanced IPP procurement frameworks and identified projects for solar PV, waste-to-energy, and battery storage, directly supporting the Energy Plan's 2030 renewable targets.
•	In parallel, the City has commenced the roll-out of solar mini-grids in informal settlements, improving access to affordable, clean, and reliable electricity, enhancing resilience in underserved areas, and reducing dependence on diesel generators.
Policy Implementation and Compliance:
•	The City is implementing Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) compliance for all qualifying municipal-owned buildings, informing retrofit priorities and operational efficiency improvements.
•	Energy efficiency programmes and EPC compliance are tied directly to the Net-Zero Policy's interim milestones.
•	The Water Security Strategy is operationalised through projects such as non-revenue water reduction, water reuse pilots, and the integration of climate-resilient water supply systems into new developments.
Impact and Just Transition Considerations:
•	Planned renewable and distributed energy projects, including mini-grids, are expected to contribute hundreds of megawatts to the city's supply, avoid thousands of tonnes of CO₂e annually, and create green jobs.
•	Mini-grids and water resilience measures address both climate equity and basic service access, reducing vulnerabilities in informal settlements and low-income communities.
•	The City's Just Transition approach ensures that both energy and water interventions are inclusive, economically empowering, and socially equitable.

While the Covid-19 pandemic has posed significant financial challenges for Johannesburg, the City recognizes that climate-related risks and opportunities are increasingly integral to its financial planning and investment strategies.
Current Financial Impacts and Risk Awareness:
•	A significant portion of the City's revenue is generated from rates and taxes paid by residents. Although direct climate-related impacts on revenue streams are still emerging, Johannesburg is proactively assessing how climate risks—such as infrastructure damage from extreme weather events, energy supply disruptions, and water scarcity—may affect fiscal stability and future budgets.
•	International credit rating agencies, including Moody's, have heightened their focus on environmental and climate stewardship in municipal credit evaluations. This has heightened awareness within Johannesburg's finance teams to integrate climate considerations into comprehensive financial planning and budgeting processes.
Climate Finance and Investment Opportunities:
•	In 2024, Johannesburg partnered with the International Finance Corporation (IFC) to conduct a comprehensive Climate Investment Opportunities Diagnostic (CIOD). This diagnostic identifies priority sectors and projects where climate finance can be mobilized to accelerate the city's transition to a low-carbon and climate-resilient economy.
•	The CIOD highlights opportunities across renewable energy, energy efficiency, sustainable transport, water management, and green infrastructure. It also outlines pathways to attract private sector investment, leverage public funds, and access international climate finance instruments, including green bonds and concessional financing.
•	The City is integrating CIOD recommendations into its Climate Action Plan (CAP) financial strategies, ensuring alignment with national policies and international funding programmes such as UK PACT.
Environmental and Social Governance through ESMS:
•	To ensure responsible investment and project implementation, Johannesburg has established an Environmental and Social Management System (ESMS). The ESMS provides a framework for assessing, managing, and monitoring environmental and social risks associated with climate-related projects and investments.
•	The ESMS integrates environmental and social safeguards into the City's project appraisal and financial decision-making processes, enhancing transparency, stakeholder engagement, and compliance with national and international standards.
•	This system supports the City's commitment to a Just Transition, ensuring that climate investments promote social equity, protect vulnerable communities, and minimize adverse impacts.
Financial Planning and Risk Management Integration:
•	Climate-related financial risks are increasingly embedded within Johannesburg's risk management frameworks, guiding capital expenditure prioritization and asset management decisions to safeguard fiscal resilience.
•	The City is developing analytical tools to model potential fiscal impacts from climate hazards, enabling evidence-based budgeting and long-term risk mitigation.

The City of Johannesburg recognizes that the transition to a low-carbon economy presents both significant risks and opportunities, with certain economic sectors facing potential disruptions.
Key Transition Risks Identified:
•	A recent city-led study on the low-carbon transition highlighted that specific economic value chains may experience job losses, particularly in sectors reliant on fossil fuels and traditional manufacturing processes.
•	The shift from petroleum-based fuels to green alternatives, such as electric vehicles (EVs), poses a risk of downstream job losses linked to reduced demand for internal combustion engine (ICE) components. The automotive sector, a critical part of Johannesburg's industrial base, may experience decreased manufacturing activity for parts and components related to ICEs.
•	Beyond automotive, sectors such as fossil fuel supply chains, traditional energy generation, and certain heavy industries may face employment risks due to decarbonisation and technological change.
Managing Transition Risks through a Just Transition Framework:
•	The City has embedded a Just Transition approach within its Climate Action Plan and economic development strategies, focusing on minimizing adverse social impacts and supporting workers and communities affected by structural shifts.
•	Initiatives include targeted skills development and retraining programmes, fostering emerging green industries, and supporting economic diversification to create new employment opportunities in renewable energy, energy efficiency, and sustainable transport sectors.
•	Social protection measures and stakeholder engagement ensure vulnerable groups are involved in decision-making and benefit from the transition.
Strategic Alignment and Future Outlook:
•	Transition risks are continuously assessed and integrated into the City's broader economic planning and resilience frameworks, guided by national policies such as the South African Climate Change Act (2024) and aligned with international commitments under the Just Transition imperatives.
•	The City's proactive stance on managing these risks supports a socially equitable and economically sustainable low-carbon future, maintaining community resilience and economic vitality throughout the transition process.

column15: Toronto City Council adopted the Net Zero Strategy (NZS) in December 2021 which includes a target of net zero by 2040 and presents a set of 2030 interim targets for community-wide emissions as well as City of Toronto corporate targets to demonstrate leadership by example. These targets are designed to reduce emissions by 6.8Mt CO2e in the next eight years. The NZS establishes interim goals for 2030 across the sectors of homes & buildings, energy, transportation, waste, and corporate goals. The NZS presents short-term implementation actions for 2022-2025 in order to put us on track to meet our interim and net zero emissions targets. The short-term implementation plan actions guide decisions, strategy, and action on climate-related issues across many corporate divisions. Many short-term implementation actions are assigned to City divisions with scheduled deliverables and reports back to City Council on progress. More details on the NZS and associated progress/reporting requirements can be found: http://app.toronto.ca/tmmis/viewAgendaItemHistory.do?item=2021.IE26.16https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/water-environment/environmentally-friendly-city-initiatives/transformto/City staff have developed a Climate Lens program to provide staff with the resources, tools and support to integrate climate mitigation and adaptation/resilience considerations into their initiatives (projects, programs and policies). The Climate Lens program consists of several parts that serve the capacity-building mandate: an internal website called 'Climate Hub' (launched on January 31st 2023) that includes climate-related resources and information, and tools and data to assist staff in applying a climate lens; an internal \'Climate 101\' Learning Program to introduce any/all City staff to concepts of climate change and the City's plans to combat climate change; and climate investment tracking and analysis in the City's annual budget process. Capital and operating budget process use a set of \'Climate Lens\' questions to determine whether budget projects contribute to the City's goals of reducing GHGs and increasing climate resilience and to prompt staff to provide further information where available. As of 2022, this is now a mandatory requirement for all new and existing budget projects. Since 2022, and as part of the short-term implementation actions, Toronto developed a carbon accountability framework (carbon budget) and associated key performance metrics that will ensure emissions impacts associated with major decisions are estimated and factor into decision-making: http://insideto.toronto.ca/climate-hub/index.htmlApproved on May 10, 2023, City Council adopted the Carbon Accountability Governance System Report, which addresses the first of the five critical steps the City is taking to steer community-wide emissions and emissions from the City's own operations towards net zero. The report outlines a process to establish multi-year emission budgets for the City's own corporate and community-wide emissions, enacted as part of Chapter 669 (Climate Change Goals and Governance) of the Toronto Municipal Code. An annual Carbon Budget process will link City decision-making on policies, programs and projects in the annual financial budget to their expected GHG reduction impact from now until net zero is achieved by 2040. The Carbon Accountability Report also establishes a science-based corporate policy on offset credits aligned with net zero governance best practice, which will continue Toronto's leadership in this rapidly developing space. The first pilot carbon budget report will be released in January 2024, as part of the 2024 Capital and Operating Budget: https://secure.toronto.ca/council/agenda-item.do?item=2023.IE3.4https://www.toronto.ca/legdocs/mmis/2021/ie/bgrd/backgroundfile-173757.pdfhttps://www.toronto.ca/news/toronto-city-council-advances-torontos-climate-leadership/\n\nCity Council approved an Accountability and Management Framework for the TransformTO NZS in May 2022. This framework initiates the creation of advisory groups and management processes that will guide the City's accountable and inclusive implementation of the NZS. These groups include:1. Climate Advisory Group (CAG) made up of community members; 2. Joint TransformTO Implementation Committee (JTIC) made up of City staff and labour union organizations; and3. TransformTO Climate Leadership Table (TCLT) made up of internal, inter-divisional City senior management staff. Details on the framework and oversight groups can be found here: http://app.toronto.ca/tmmis/viewAgendaItemHistory.do?item=2022.IE29.10Toronto produces a publicly-available annual territorial GHG inventory report and reports progress against our interim and net zero emissions targets. Toronto's latest territorial GHG inventory can be found here: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/water-environment/environmentally-friendly-city-initiatives/transformto/
column16: Climate-related issues are a critical component of Toronto's Official Plan (OP) and updates to the OP. In 2022, the city is undergoing a Municipal Comprehensive Review (MCR) to update the current Official Plan, as dictated by the province of Ontario's statutory requirement. As part of this MCR and OP update and against the backdrop of Toronto's 2019 declaration of a climate emergency and efforts to accelerate climate mitigation and adaptation action, such as through the NZS, Toronto will review our land use policies in the context of the health of our people, the environment, water, parks and open spaces, natural areas and air quality. The time horizon considered through the MCR process extends to 2051 and is dictated by the province, the level of government above the municipality. More information on the MCR and OP update can be found here: https://www.toronto.ca/city-government/planning-development/official-plan-guidelines/official-plan/official-plan-review/
column17: As part of the NZS short-term implementation actions for 2022-2025, Toronto's Chief Financial Officer (CFO) will report on all major climate risks associated with existing programs, services and assets, identified via the climate lens program, to City Council by 2024, and Council will direct the appropriate Divisions/Agencies to address risks in future capital planning. The CFO will also provide ongoing annual updates on the City's climate risks as part of its annual consolidated financial statements. Identifying and disclosing climate-related risks to assets enables the City to minimize risk, inform more efficient, long-term decision-making and enhance accountability to meeting targets. 2026 -2023 Action plan will be presenting to City council in Fall 2026. https://www.toronto.ca/legdocs/mmis/2021/ie/bgrd/backgroundfile-173757.pdf\n\nIn 2022, the City of Toronto began a process to understand how climate change could affect the delivery of the City's core services as part of a larger financial planning process. We know that climate change will impose additional costs related to upgrading and adapting physical infrastructure to withstand extreme weather events. Major infrastructure assets such as roads, bridges, water drainage and buildings will unquestionably require a higher level of investment in future due to increased frequency and intensity of such events. Aside from physical assets, City operations and therefore, City service delivery will also be affected. To start to quantitatively measure this impact, the City initiated focused work at the end of 2022 looking at operational impacts of heatwaves and flooding within the City's boundary. This work is ongoing and will help inform future financial planning processes.
column18: Transition risks for Toronto's transition to a low-carbon economy include challenges identified through the NZS. This includes the following risks in the \'market,\' \'current & emerging regulation,\' \'technology,\' and \'reputation\' categories:1. Action must begin now and must focus on equity: Achieving the 2030 GHG target requires that all existing climate actions continue and for additional bold action to begin as soon as possible. A focus on equity in program and policy design and delivery will maximize participation of all Toronto residents so that benefits can be realized sooner and last longer. 2. Action from all levels of government will also need to align and accelerate: Provincial and federal policy and resources are required to enable Toronto's ability to realize a net zero future. Aligned action will also amplify local efforts so that financial returns are realized sooner and GHG emissions reductions start earlier.3. The electricity system needs to be carbon free: The emissions intensity (amount of GHG emitted per unit electricity) of Ontario's electricity grid is projected to increase. For Toronto to get to net zero, the grid needs to be carbon free. Failing this, the city can only rely on the “net” part of the target and will need to purchase carbon offsets or renewable energy certificates, both of which add significant cost to becoming net zero. Ensuring that electricity generation does not produce carbon pollution also addresses the scale of the global challenge. At a local level, the electricity system needs to be able to adapt to new demands as heating and transportation are electrified. Focusing on conservation first can reduce electricity consumption and is the most inexpensive way to provide additional electricity capacity; however, additional work will be necessary to fully understand how to enable large-scale electrification of transportation and buildings and manage peaks in electricity demand.4. The labour market must shift and local supply chains must be developed: The labour market must shift and new critical supply chains need to be developed to bring down costs. The skills mix and capacity of the labour force will need to scale up rapidly and new robust supply chains for new technologies, such as heat pumps and electric vehicles, will need to be in place in order to deliver the actions required to achieve net zero.5. Innovative and adaptive delivery mechanisms must be adopted to scale up: Although all actions presented in the Strategy are technologically feasible, conventional delivery mechanisms are likely too slow and costly to deliver the rapid transformation envisioned to achieve the 2030 target. City processes will need to be nimble, as already demonstrated in the quick implementation of new programs in response to the COVID-19 pandemic. ActiveTO is one of those programs where dedicated road space facilitated active transportation for essential trips and physical activity keeping residents safe and healthy during the pandemic in 2020. ActiveTO demonstrated a quick response to support a crisis by \'instituting priority bus lanes, improved cycling infrastructure, expansion of bike share and weekend recreational street closures, among others.\'Similarly, quick action will need to be applied to the volume of building retrofits needed to reach Toronto's proposed targets. A bulk retrofit program where many houses are improved at once must be instated. To do this, municipal processes and programs will need to adapt and be aligned in order to address barriers that households might face. For instance, a household wishing to undertake a retrofit or use an electric vehicle should not face any barriers in terms of information or action that might result from conflicting municipal, provincial or utility policies.6. Impacts on material and land resources should be accounted for: The economy will need to produce large numbers of electric vehicles and deliver building retrofits and renewable energy in short order. Supplying or manufacturing these resources creates demand for concrete, wood, insulation, batteries, and land. The environmental, social, and economic implications will need to be carefully considered to ensure this does not result in additional GHG emissions and negative impacts to the environment. Indigenous worldviews and circular economy principles are required to minimize impacts on resources and ensure principles of global sustainability are maintained.
