column15: The City of Adelaide endorsed a new Integrated Climate Strategy 2030 on 11 June 2024. As part of this work Council has developed a new reporting and implementation framework that includes comprehensive oversight, responsibility and accountability of climate related issues throughout the organisation. A new cross-organisational ICS Steering Group has been established, and they review progress against targets and existing and emerging climate risks. The Steering Group reports progress to the Council's Executive and Strategic Risk and Internal Audit Committee, who will report to the Council's Audit and Risk Committee, who will advise Council as required. As part of this responsibility, an external review of the old risk and opportunity register is being undertaken. This review is consolidating and simplifying risks and opportunities and better align them with the Strategic Risk Register and the Integrated Climate Strategy 2030. The Integrated Climate Strategy 2030 includes as one of its fifteen priorities that climate change and sustainability are integrated into how we do business. Part of the risk review project are three staff workshops for Managers and Team leaders, who will help to incorporate and mitigate climate risk thorough the organisation. These workshops are themed around (i) green and grey assets, (ii) people, economy and culture, (iii) and the corporation. \n\n
column16: The City of Adelaide's 2024 - 2028 Strategic Plan is structured to focus on five aspirations, one of which is Our Environment. This aspiration includes the objectives of being climate conscious and resilient, and prioritising sustainability in our decisions for the future. This aspiration also includes outcomes to lead as a low carbon emissions city and be a sustainable city where climate resilience is embedded in all that we do. The Strategic Plan guides all of the City's planning and activities. \n\nThe City of Adelaide has finalised its City Plan 2036, an urban design framework to guide planning within the City of Adelaide, working towards Council's target population of 50,000 residents by 2036. One of the four priorities of the Plan is a Greener and Cooler City, with a focus on increasing green spaces and streets throughout the city and the Adelaide Park Lands. It also includes the priority of Transit Diversity, with a focus on mode shift to active transport and transit diversity for less carbon-intensive movement around the city.
column17: The implementation plan for the new Integrated Climate Strategy 2030 (ICS) includes a multi-criteria assessment tool to inform the prioritisation of climate-related projects in the annual business plan and budget process. The ICS Steering Group meets annually to rate and rank the budget bids relating to the ICS. This ranking is informed by the climate risk and opportunity register and its ranking of risks, and is used as a factor to determine which budget bids are successful. As the Associate Director of Finance and Procurement as well as the Associate Director from Governance and Strategy are part of the ICS Steering Committee, climate risks are considered in annual budget allocations.
column18: The City of Adelaide is well position to transition to a low carbon economy, and identified the importance and opportunities that come from this transition in its former Carbon Neutral Strategy 2015-2025. The Strategy included a priority to “create and foster opportunities for partnerships and businesses to grow and prosper from the low carbon economy”, and lead to the creation of a Carbon Neutral Adelaide partnership program to support local businesses in the transition. The importance of this transition has continued to be reflected as one of the five goals of the Integrated Climate Strategy 2030 of “Transition to a decarbonised economy”. The Strategy has a priority to grow circular economy industries in the city, focused on the six key areas of food, fashion, furniture, fix it (repair), fit outs and festivals. \n\nCouncil will also use its supply chain to drive change, with another strategic priority of making procurement decisions that localise supply, priorities reuse, and drive green industries. The City of Adelaide's 2024 - 2028 Strategic Plan also includes, under its outcome of leading as a low carbon emissions city, an action to “generate, lead and support new circular economy activities to support sustainability and economic outcomes.” Despite this support for the transition to a local carbon economy, the City of Adelaide does face risks. One of the key risks is the impact that an uptake in active and public transport would have on Council's off-street car parking business UPark, and on-street car parking revenue.

column15: Climate action is tied to many of Boston's wider social, environmental and economic goals, and is embedded in many citywide and neighborhood plans, including capital investment plans. Boston has set citywide performance metrics and targets across a range of issues, including climate, that are integrated into and considered during the annual budget review and reporting process. For metrics reported by the City of Boston Environment Department on climate mitigation and adaptation and resilience related projects, see page 356 of the FY24 budget: https://content.boston.gov/sites/default/files/file/2024/09/V2%2010-%2025%20A%20Environment-Energy-and-Open-Space-Cabinet.pdf
column16: Imagine Boston 2030, the City of Boston's master plan, tracks 14 quantitative metrics, including 5 metrics related to climate action. These goals are implemented through a variety of related City planning initiatives, including the 2030 Climate Action Plan, Climate Ready Boston, the Open Space and Recreation Plan, and Go Boston 2030. The City's budget makes critical investments in every Boston neighborhood, guided by Imagine Boston 2030 and the schools, streets, arts, climate and resilience plans under its umbrella. Taken together, these initiatives support Boston's dynamic economy and improve quality of life for residents by encouraging affordability, increasing access to opportunity, promoting a healthy environment, and guiding investment in the public realm. The City's emissions reduction target, codified in Imagine Boston 2030, is to become carbon neutral by 2050, with an interim goal of reducing emissions by half by 2030. The City released its updated Climate Action Plan in October 2019, accelerating key actions to decarbonize Boston's building and transportation sectors, building on the results of the Carbon Free Boston analysis. Imagine Boston 2030 also set adaptation targets, namely to reduce economic loss and the number of people exposed to climate-related flooding. These goals are to be attained through the Climate Ready Boston strategy. Under Climate Ready Boston, the City is developing district scale approaches for each of Boston's coastal neighborhoods to plan, design and invest in nature-based and hard-engineered flood protection, develop and implement climate-ready zoning, and facilitate district energy planning in Boston's neighborhoods. Together with the upcoming Climate Action Plan 2025 update, the City will work to support “carbon-neutral climate-ready” neighborhoods for climate preparedness and adaptation. Imagine Boston 2030 includes transportation-related goals. First, Boston commits to increasing the number of Bostonians who walk, bike and take public transit to work. Second, regarding walkability, the City will increase the Walk Score of City neighborhoods and reduce the number of households classified as car dependent by half. To do so, the City has developed a comprehensive transportation plan, Go Boston 2030, to improve the accessibility, safety, and reliability of our transportation network. The Imagine Boston 2030 goal for quality of life and open spaces is to increase the number of parks in excellent condition and parks with at least one active recreation feature. The Parks Department's 2015-2021 Open Space and Recreation Plan contributes to this goal, including by connecting the final section of the Emerald Necklace, a corridor of continuous greenspace, to Boston's waterfront, investing in Franklin Park (the City's largest park), restoring the Boston Common, creating a new generation of parks along Boston's waterfront, and investing in new open spaces and maintaining existing open spaces in the commercial core and in both new and existing neighborhoods. The City's zero waste planning process was detailed in Imagine Boston 2030 (p. 344 - https://www.boston.gov/sites/default/files/imce-uploads/2018-06/imagine20boston202030_pages2.pdf ). In 2018, the City of Boston launched the Zero Waste Boston initiative, and released a plan in June 2019. By implementing 30 near- and long-term strategies over the next 30 years, the City will increase its overall recycling rate from 25% to 80% or more. https://www.boston.gov/departments/environment/zero-waste-boston
column17: The City of Boston is required to meet its long-term financial commitments, such as pensions and debt service. Boston has been preparing for climate change by investing at least 10% of all new capital funding to open space, infrastructure, and facilities projects that are climate resilient or contribute to making the City more environmentally friendly since its FY20-24 Capital Plan (reflected through current proposed FY23-27 Capital Plan). https://www.boston.gov/news/278-billion-be-invested-boston-neighborhoods-through-fy20-24-capital-budget https://www.boston.gov/sites/default/files/file/2022/04/1A-Volume%201%20-%20Executive%20Summary.pdf \nS&P Global Ratings has assigned a AAA rating to the City of Boston, based in part on Boston's proactive approach to addressing risks like weather- and climate-related events. https://www.boston.gov/news/city-boston-achieves-aaa-bond-ratings-eighth-consecutive-year
column18: Transition risks include:- Jurisdiction: Massachusetts is a home rule state, whereby the City of Boston does not have jurisdiction over the building code or the ability to adopt new taxes without seeking permission from the state legislature. There is also a statewide prohibition on rent control. The City submitted a home rule petition to address this to the state legislature in 2023. Furthermore, our public transit system is operated by a regional public agency, and the airport and harbor are operated by an independent public authority.- Technology: Decarbonization of district energy systems is critical to support the decarbonization of our medical and hospital sector, including vital life support systems. Decarbonizing our transportation sector requires electrification of a large component of our transportation sector, which, combined with building sector electrification, could add pressure to the electric grid and exacerbate peak demand if not appropriately coupled with sufficient energy use reduction measures.- Market: Massachusetts has some of the highest electricity rates in the country, as well as a legacy natural gas system. We will also need to grow the green labor workforce in order to support the transition towards a decarbonized building sector.

column15:
The city of Zurich has a well-defined, multi-level process for oversight and governance of climate-related issues, focusing on transparency, progress tracking, and democratic involvement, see the two documents for more information:
- Climate Action Plan 2024 (https://www.stadt-zuerich.ch/content/dam/web/de/aktuell/publikationen/2024/klimaschutz/climate-action-plan-2024.pdf) 
- Net Zero Progress Report 2024 (https://www.stadt-zuerich.ch/content/dam/web/de/aktuell/publikationen/2024/klimaschutz/net-zero-progress-report-2024.pdf)

# Core Governance Structure
- City Council and Departments: The Zurich City Council, along with its various departments and committees, holds principal responsibility for planning, implementing, assessing, and adapting measures to reach climate goals. Each department annually reviews progress using key indicators and a city-wide greenhouse gas (GHG) inventory, in collaboration with the Environmental and Health Protection Service Zurich (UGZ) and the net zero project team.

- Annual Audit and Reporting: Progress is analyzed and documented in the Net Zero Progress Report. When measures fall short, the responsible departments decide how to accelerate, adapt, or supplement them. The UGZ prepares an overall assessment and highlights gaps in existing strategies.

- Legally Anchored Targets: Climate actions are bound by municipal regulations (Municipal Code Article 152, para. 3) and specific ordinances such as the Heat Supply Ordinance, which requires buildings to be heated with fossil-free energy sources by 2040.

- Targets and Packages of Measures: Targets are set for sectors like buildings, mobility, and procurement, based on municipal strategies, expert assessments, and resolutions. Each target is tied to measurable indicators, and progress is tracked annually in the city's “net zero cockpit”.

# Oversight Mechanisms
- Cross-Sector Steering: Sector-specific committees and service departments develop, implement, and oversee climate measures. Additionally, there are cross-sectoral initiatives to coordinate on issues like circular economy, sustainable procurement, and awareness campaigns. (https://circularcitiesdeclaration.eu/cities/zurich)

- Stakeholder Engagement: Zurich forms partnerships across levels (municipal, cantonal, federal) and with other cities internationally, as well as with companies and citizens. The city participates in legislative consultations and external committees to influence basic policy conditions conducive to climate action. The city engages in dialog with companies and citizens to fürther climate action. (https://ec.europa.eu/research/participants/documents/downloadPublic?documentIds=080166e51a6fe5f3&appId=PPGMS)

- Public Participation and Transparency: Citizen referenda play a crucial role; Zurich's ambitious net-zero targets are the outcome of direct public voting. Progress and inventories are publicly reported. (https://www.hfp.tum.de/fileadmin/w00cjd/environmentalpolicy/_my_direct_uploads/MS1_Part_2__Report_1.2_-_Analysis_of_climate_governance_structures_in_pilot_cities_-_Dias_Carneiro__Dolan__Isidoro_Losada__Schreurs__June_2022_.pdf)

- External Review: Zurich cooperates with transnational networks (e.g., ICLEI, C40 Cities) for benchmarking, learning, and additional oversight. (https://ec.europa.eu/research/participants/documents/downloadPublic?documentIds=080166e51a6fe5f3&appId=PPGMS)
column16:
Zurich's electorate approved the city's 2022 climate protection targets with a clear majority of 75 percent. 
Four climate protection targets were set, 2 for the city of Zurich with its inhabitants and 2 for the city administration.
See the details here in the Climate Action Plan 2024 (https://www.stadt-zuerich.ch/content/dam/web/de/aktuell/publikationen/2024/klimaschutz/climate-action-plan-2024.pdf).

The city of Zurich takes responsibility for climate protection and aims to become climate neutral by 2040. 
1) The city of Zurich is taking its responsibility for climate protection seriously and aims to achieve net zero direct emissions in the city by 2040. 
2) Indirect emissions target released outside of the city perimeter but are also caused by Zurich residents, are minus 30 percent of emissions reduction of the 1990 levels until 2040 per resident (relative number). 

The city administration is aiming for net zero by 2035, and Zurich is also pursuing a reduction target for greenhouse gas emissions that are emitted outside the city limits.
3) The city administration aims to implement all measures for reducing greenhouse gas emissions within its own sphere of influence for the direct emissions to net zero by 2035. The exception is the area of heat supply, for which the target year 2040 applies. 
4) The indirect emissions are to be reduced in absolute terms to minus 30 percent of the 1990 emission level by 2035.

Integration of Climate Targets: Zurich's urban planning is aligned with its net-zero emissions target, set by city government and binding in municipal regulations. Every sector (buildings, mobility, public spaces) must revise strategies and measures to meet these climate objectives, with progress tracked using indicators like direct and indirect greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Non-exhaustive list of relevant master / development planning impacted by the climate protection targets: 
1) Signing of the Circular City Charta (https://circularcitiesdeclaration.eu/current-signatories) and endorsement of the circular economy strategy 'Circular Zurich'(https://www.stadt-zuerich.ch/de/umwelt-und-energie/klima/kreislaufwirtschaft/massnahmen.html) 
2) Creating and signing of the Charta for climate-friendly menues in gastronomy (https://www.stadt-zuerich.ch/de/aktuell/medienmitteilungen/2023/03/230320a.html); 
3) Developed a Strategy for Urban Space and Mobility (https://www.stadt-zuerich.ch/de/politik-und-verwaltung/politik-und-recht/strategie-politikfelder/stadtraum-mobilitaet-2040.html).
4) Urban Microclimate Design: Projects such as the HB/Central 2050 masterplan integrate microclimatic strategies into urban design. For example, sunny locations are chosen for transport stops in winter, while shaded walkways are prioritized in summer to improve thermal comfort and address heat stress. Indoor and outdoor climates are considered as an interconnected system for future development. (https://www.stadt-zuerich.ch/content/dam/web/de/aktuell/publikationen/2024/strategies-2040-summary-en.pdf)
5) Resilience and Adaptation Measures: Zurich has launched programs to build climate resilience, preparing the city for flooding, heatwaves, and other weather extremes. The Urban Climate Resilience Program, supported by the Zurich Flood Resilience Alliance and city networks, identifies vulnerable areas, analyzes risks, and implements targeted adaptation solutions. (https://roesler.arc.usi.ch/praxis/masterplan-hb-central-2050-zuerich)
6) Legal Framework and Planning Instruments: The city's building sector must transition to fossil-free heating by 2040, dictated by municipal ordinances. Energy planning and mobility upgrades are scheduled with clear deadlines and reviewed annually. The Strategies Zurich 2040 plan harnesses business and scientific innovation for transformation toward climate neutrality, including evaluating options for negative emissions. (https://www.stadt-zuerich.ch/content/dam/web/de/aktuell/publikationen/2024/strategies-2040-summary-en.pdf)
7) Monitoring and Public Engagement: Strategy updates and climate measures are disclosed regularly, involving public participation and coordination across departments. Annual progress on climate targets is documented, and residential sectors are required to adapt according to evolving climate scenarios. (https://www.stadt-zuerich.ch/content/dam/web/de/aktuell/publikationen/2024/strategies-2040-summary-en.pdf) (https://www.stadt-zuerich.ch/content/dam/web/de/aktuell/publikationen/2024/klimaschutz/climate-action-plan-2024.pdf)
column17:
Climate-related issues have increasingly influenced the financial planning of the City of Zurich in the following ways:
The city expects to invest around half a billion CHF a year to achieve its climate and energy targets. This will be funded by businesses, private individuals and the public sector. At the same time, local businesses will benefit from investments in efficiency measures in buildings, charging stations and the expansion of renewable energies. Current model calculations give confidence that by 2040, the energy cost savings will surpass the expenses for infrastructure expansion and building renovations. Additionally, the quality of life will increase due to cleaner air, quieter surroundings, and more green spaces in the city.

The city of Zurich has been proactive in addressing climate-related issues (https://www.stadt-zuerich.ch/content/dam/web/de/aktuell/publikationen/2024/klimaschutz/climate-action-plan-2024.pdf):
1. The city prioritizes sustainable urban planning, integrating green spaces, pedestrian-friendly zones, and an extensive public transportation network. These initiatives help reduce the city's carbon footprint and improve resilience against climate-related risks.
2. Budgeting for Climate Action and investment in Reslilience: The city integrates climate objectives into its budget and medium-term financial planning. The Administration ensures financial transparency and allocates funds toward projects that mitigate climate risks, invests in urban climate resilience programs targeting increased heat, floods, and other climate impacts, as well as reduce greenhouse gas emissions across the municipal portfolio. (https://www.stadt-zuerich.ch/site/umweltbericht/de/index.html)
3. Policy Alignment and Incentives: Municipal financial planning supports legal mandates such as the Heat Supply Ordinance, which requires fossil-free heating by 2040. Incentives and support programs for building owners encourage faster adoption of renewable energy heating systems. Financial strategies include facilitating district heating expansion and renewable energy purchases.
4. Green Bond Issuance: In July 2023, Zurich issued its first green bond worth CHF 300 million with a 21-year maturity. The proceeds are earmarked to (re-)finance environmentally friendly buildings and climate protection measures, especially in the building sector (e.g., heating system replacement, support programs). This financing mechanism supports the city's goal to achieve net-zero emissions by 2040. (https://www.ifbc.ch/en/latest-thinking/supporting-the-city-of-zurich-with-its-first-green-bond)
column18:
1) Technological and Infrastructure Transformation: Achieving net-zero by 2040 for the city of Zurich and the administration of the City requires extensive changes in electricity supply, heating systems, and mobility infrastructure. This involves replacing fossil fuels with renewable energy and implementing new technologies like heat pumps, photovoltaics, and electric vehicle charging networks. These transitions require significant investments and coordination as well sufficient supply of renewable technologies and materials, foreshadowing supply chain challenges.
2) Societal Acceptance and Behavioral Change: The shift demands significant behavioral changes from citizens, such as adopting new heating methods or switching to electric vehicles. Gaining public support and acceptance poses challenges, especially when changes affect daily habits or incur upfront costs. 
3) Regulatory and Political Complexity: There is broad consensus on the goal but less agreement on the path forward. Expanding renewable infrastructure faces local opposition, regulatory hurdles, and coordination issues across municipal and cantonal levels.
4) Financial and Risk Management: Transitioning involves managing financial risks and uncertainties, including upfront costs, stranded assets, and investment in resilient infrastructure. The city must balance short-term expenses with long-term benefits while maintaining fiscal responsibility.
5) Integration across Sectors: The low-carbon transition spans multiple sectors—energy, transport, buildings, industry—requiring coordinated planning and policy integration across departments and external stakeholders.
6) Innovation and Skills Development: The complexity of new technologies necessitates training for specialists, managers, and citizens to ensure effective adoption and risk management. 
7) Overarching legal frameworks that could change are also a risk factor, over which we have no direct influence (e.g. building program).

Climate-related issues and risks are evaluated at multiple organizational levels, including at the corporate strategic level (City Council), Executive Leadership Team (administrative senior management), and by individual City services. City Council receives regular reporting from administration regarding The City's corporate climate performance, progress on climate goals, and climate-related risks including climate impacts (to people, infrastructure, and the environment) and financial risks. 

The City's Sustainable City Principal Corporate Risk is overseen by the General Manager of Planning & Development Services. It is currently undergoing a review to update this risk to be more specific to climate and environment related risk. Additionally, there are three relevant Corporate Operating Risks, including Climate Risk, GHG Risk, and Environment Risk which are identified and evaluated by all business units as part of service risk assessment. 

The Climate & Environment business unit provides the leadership, expertise, and support required for integrating climate considerations into key decision-making processes. 

The City's Climate Strategy and Climate Implementation Plan identify the climate-related principles, goals, targets, pathways and key actions that guide the development of other City policy, plans, actions, priorities, and budgets. 

The Climate Advisory Committee of Council provides external oversight on climate-related City programs and evaluates The City's governance model and climate performance, providing recommendations directly to Council. 

Climate considerations have been made in developing statutory and non-statutory plans and are considered when setting key performance measures for city services. 

Climate change has been used as a criteria to assess projects seeking funding as well as a criteria to help prioritize capital investments.
column16: Climate considerations have informed land use and development plans that incorporate climate mitigation and adaptation best practices. This includes local area plans, parks master plans (e.g. Parks Open Space Plan which is currently being updated), and The City's Municipal Development Plan which is currently being updated (i.e. the Calgary Plan). \n\nThese plans have guided climate adaptation improvements in planning applications by requiring climate risk and resilience assessments and recommending enhancements to reduce climate risk. These plans have also guided climate mitigation improvements in projects through the incorporation of renewable energy generation, and other best practices for greenhouse gas reduction.
column17:
The City's climate goals (reducing GHG emissions and climate-resilient city building) are key considerations in The City's 4-year Service Plans and Budgets planning process. Demonstrating a climate-related benefit is a requirement for some capital project funding streams such as the Centralized Climate Fund. 

The City has investigated the economic costs of climate change to justify investment into climate adaptation work. 

The City of Calgary evaluates climate-related financial risks which are reported in the Annual Financial Report through the unaudited Climate-Related Financial Disclosure. 

The City currently quantifies and tracks its Primary Climate Investments which are financial investments made in direct response to the Climate Emergency Declaration. 

The City is working to develop tools, systems, and processes to enable the identification, quantification, and tracking of secondary climate-based expenditure (investments that are aligned to The City's climate goals but are considered business as usual) for more informed decision-making processes in the future.
column18: The City has identified several risks related to the transition to a low carbon economy in The City's latest Climate Related Financial Disclosure in the unaudited section of the 2024 Annual Financial Report. These include policy and legislation changes from other orders of government, changes in technology and energy systems, changes in the legal landscape related to climate and the low-carbon economy, changes in financial market trends, and reputational risks.

column16: Os problemas relacionados ao clima têm exercido uma influência significativa no Plano Diretor de Belo Horizonte, levando a diversas adaptações e estratégias voltadas para a sustentabilidade e resiliência urbana. A preservação e criação de espaços verdes tornaram-se essenciais para melhorar a qualidade do ar e mitigar o calor urbano, influenciando diretamente a destinação de áreas no planejamento.\nA participação da comunidade também foi fundamental, com consultas públicas que permitiram que as demandas da população fossem incluídas no planejamento. Por fim, estudos sobre os impactos das mudanças climáticas foram considerados na elaboração do Plano Diretor, possibilitando uma análise mais aprofundada das vulnerabilidades enfrentadas por diferentes regiões da cidade. Essas adaptações refletem um compromisso com a sustentabilidade, buscando não apenas mitigar os problemas climáticos, mas também promover um desenvolvimento mais equilibrado e resiliente em Belo Horizonte.\n
column17:
Os problemas relacionados ao clima tiveram um impacto significativo no planejamento financeiro do município de Belo Horizonte, exigindo uma reavaliação das prioridades orçamentárias e a alocação de recursos para enfrentar os desafios ambientais. Com o aumento da frequência e intensidade de eventos climáticos extremos, como exemplo o aumento das ondas de calor, o município precisou investir em infraestrutura resiliente, como os Refúgios Climáticos. 
Além disso, a necessidade de promover práticas sustentáveis de mitigação e adaptação dos impactos das mudanças climáticas levou à criação de novos programas e iniciativas, exigindo recursos adicionais. Esses investimentos, embora essenciais, demandaram um redirecionamento de verbas que poderiam ser aplicadas em outras áreas também necessárias. Projetos voltados para a preservação de áreas verdes e recuperação de ecossistemas foram incorporados ao orçamento, refletindo a urgência de enfrentar os desafios climáticos.
Em resumo, os desafios climáticos impactaram profundamente o planejamento financeiro de Belo Horizonte, forçando o município a reavaliar suas prioridades, redirecionar recursos e buscar novas fontes de financiamento para garantir um desenvolvimento urbano mais sustentável e resiliente.
column18:
A transição para uma economia de baixo carbono em Belo Horizonte traz consigo diversos riscos que o município vem considerando cuidadosamente. Um dos principais desafios é o impacto econômico, pois a mudança exige investimentos significativos em novas tecnologias e infraestrutura, sobrecarregando o orçamento municipal. 
Outro risco relevante é a resistência tanto da população quanto de setores produtivos tradicionais. Essa resistência pode dificultar a implementação de políticas públicas e a adoção de práticas sustentáveis. A desigualdade socioeconômica também é uma preocupação, uma vez que as comunidades mais vulneráveis tendem a ser as mais afetadas pelas mudanças, aumentando a desigualdade e potencialmente gerando conflitos.
Embora a transição vise mitigar os impactos das mudanças climáticas, ela também expõem o município a novos riscos se não for planejada adequadamente. Investimentos em infraestruturas que não considerem a resiliência climática, por exemplo, podem se tornar obsoletos rapidamente. Por fim, a captação de recursos financeiros para implementar essas mudanças pode ser desafiadora, especialmente em um contexto de restrições orçamentárias, o que gera dependência de financiamentos externos e instabilidade nas iniciativas.

column15:
Ankara Metropolitan Municipality has established a comprehensive oversight structure to ensure that climate-related issues are addressed at every level of governance, from strategic planning to day-to-day operations. Oversight is coordinated by the Mayor's Office and the Municipal Council, which receive regular updates from specialized departments and affiliated organizations. The Department of Climate Change and Zero Waste and the Department of Environmental Protection and Control act as the central coordinators, ensuring that the city's policies are consistent with both national targets and international commitments such as the Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy.

Climate oversight extends across multiple executive departments. The Department of Public Works and Urban Planning integrates climate resilience and energy efficiency into building codes and development approvals. The Department of Transportation Planning and Rail Systems collaborates with the General Directorate of Electricity, Gas and Bus Operations (GDEGBO) to reduce transport emissions through metro expansion, electric bus deployment, and park-and-ride systems. The Department of Health Affairs incorporates climate-linked health impacts such as air pollution, extreme heat, and disease outbreaks into health planning. The Department of Disaster Affairs addresses flooding, droughts, and storms, aligning urban systems with national disaster management frameworks. The Department of Strategy Development ensures climate goals are built into the municipal budget and tracked annually.

Affiliated organizations play critical roles. The General Directorate of Water and Sewerage Administration (GDWSA) manages Ankara's reservoirs, monitors water security, and implements wastewater treatment and conservation programs. Waste subsidiaries promote recycling and prepare for the closure of the Mamak Solid Waste Facility by 2025, while new facilities are developed to support a circular economy.

Oversight is institutionalized in planning documents including the Ankara Climate Change Action Plan (ACCAP), Local Climate Change Action Plan (LCCAP), and Green City Action Plan (GCAP). These set measurable targets for emissions, adaptation, and resilience. Monitoring is conducted annually, covering renewable energy uptake, water efficiency, waste diversion, and per-capita green space. Reports are made public to ensure transparency.

Equity is a core principle. Oversight includes stakeholder consultations and participatory workshops to integrate the perspectives of vulnerable groups such as low-income households, rural residents, the elderly, and women. Adaptation and resilience projects are prioritized for at-risk districts, ensuring that climate action delivers social as well as environmental benefits.

Through this integrated, multi-level oversight structure, Ankara Metropolitan Municipality institutionalizes climate governance across departments, affiliated organizations, and the Council. By embedding accountability into planning, budgeting, and monitoring, the city ensures climate issues are treated as central to its long-term social, environmental, and economic development.
column16:
Climate-related issues now define Ankara's master and development planning. Strategic documents such as the Strategic Development Plan, Master Development Plan, and Transportation Master Plan embed climate priorities from the Ankara Climate Change Action Plan (ACCAP), the Local Climate Change Action Plan (LCCAP), and the Green City Action Plan (GCAP). Urban planning emphasizes resilience by avoiding flood-prone areas, promoting green corridors, and requiring energy-efficient infrastructure.

Water scarcity is a critical driver of planning. The General Directorate of Water and Sewerage Administration (GDWSA) incorporates drought projections into planning for dams and reservoirs. Development plans now include rainwater harvesting, greywater reuse, and advanced wastewater treatment, with public campaigns promoting conservation. These measures protect both urban and rural populations.

Transport planning has been reshaped by climate concerns. The General Directorate of Electricity, Gas and Bus Operations (GDEGBO) is transitioning to electric bus fleets, expanding the metro system, and promoting cycling infrastructure. Park-and-ride facilities reduce reliance on private cars, lowering greenhouse gas emissions and improving air quality. Land-use planning supports transit-oriented development, integrating climate and accessibility.

Waste policies reflect climate priorities. The decision to close the Mamak Solid Waste Facility by 2025 is integrated into spatial planning, requiring construction of new recycling and waste-to-energy plants. This ensures waste facilities are distributed more equitably, reducing environmental burdens while cutting methane emissions. Circular economy principles, including sustainable construction waste management, are built into development frameworks.

Green infrastructure is prioritized. Parks, trees, and ecological corridors mitigate the urban heat island effect, improve biodiversity, and absorb stormwater. In rural districts, the Department of Agriculture and Rural Services integrates climate-smart farming and soil conservation, supporting resilience in agriculture.

Health and disaster resilience are embedded into planning. The Department of Health Affairs promotes heat-resilient urban design, while the Department of Disaster Affairs aligns new infrastructure with flood risk and early warning systems.

All measures are data-driven. Emission inventories, projections, and vulnerability assessments provide the basis for climate-informed planning. District-level data identifies vulnerable communities, ensuring development prioritizes equity.

Overall, climate change has shifted Ankara's planning paradigm. Development no longer focuses solely on economic expansion but balances growth with resilience, inclusiveness, and sustainability, ensuring the city can thrive under future climate pressures.
column17:
Financial planning in Ankara is strongly influenced by climate issues. The Department of Strategy Development ensures that climate priorities are integrated into the municipal budget and capital investment framework, aligning allocations with the ACCAP, LCCAP, and GCAP. Budgeting processes prioritize projects that reduce emissions, increase resilience, and promote equity.

Water security is central to financial planning. The General Directorate of Water and Sewerage Administration (GDWSA) invests in dam monitoring, wastewater treatment, rainwater harvesting, and leakage reduction. These expenditures prevent long-term service disruptions and reduce costs from drought emergencies.

Transport financing is shaped by mitigation goals. The General Directorate of Electricity, Gas and Bus Operations (GDEGBO) receives capital allocations for electric bus procurement, metro expansion, and park-and-ride systems. These investments lower dependence on fossil fuels, reduce long-term operational costs, and provide affordable mobility for vulnerable residents.

Waste sector funding is redirected from landfilling to recycling and energy recovery. The closure of the Mamak facility by 2025 drives investment in new waste-to-energy and recycling plants. This reduces methane emissions, spreads facilities more evenly, and creates green employment.

Financial risk management incorporates climate hazards. Floods, droughts, and heatwaves are factored into fiscal forecasts. Emergency reserves are maintained, while health budgets cover preventive infrastructure against climate-related illness and heat stress.

The municipality also seeks external climate finance. Participation in programs such as the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development's Green Cities Program expands access to concessional loans and grants. Alignment with international frameworks, including the Global Covenant of Mayors, supports additional funding and technical assistance.

Performance metrics track climate finance effectiveness. Indicators include emissions reduced per unit of investment, renewable energy installed, waste diverted, and hectares of new green space. Results are published annually to maintain transparency.

In this way, Ankara's financial planning reflects a shift from reactive spending to proactive climate investment. By aligning budgets with mitigation, adaptation, and equity, the municipality ensures resilience and fiscal sustainability while advancing a fair transition to a low-carbon economy.
column18:
Transitioning to a low-carbon economy introduces risks across finance, infrastructure, social equity, and governance. The Department of Strategy Development faces fiscal pressures as significant upfront capital is required for renewable energy, electric transport, waste-to-energy plants, and green infrastructure. While these investments yield long-term benefits, they risk diverting funds from immediate social needs.

Water management faces transition risks. The General Directorate of Water and Sewerage Administration (GDWSA) must finance advanced treatment and efficiency upgrades. Delays or underfunding could exacerbate water scarcity, raising costs and reducing service reliability.

Transport faces risks tied to electrification. The General Directorate of Electricity, Gas and Bus Operations (GDEGBO) requires large investments in electric buses, charging stations, and technology upgrades. Dependence on imported technology creates exposure to supply chain disruptions and exchange rate volatility.

Waste sector risks include the 2025 closure of the Mamak facility. If replacement plants are delayed, Ankara risks waste management shortfalls, public dissatisfaction, and reputational harm. Transitioning to circular economy systems also requires behavior change and private sector participation, which may advance unevenly.

Social risks are significant. Workers in fossil-fuel-intensive and traditional waste sectors may face job losses unless retraining programs succeed. Low-income households could struggle with affordability of sustainable technologies, creating inequality. To manage these, the municipality integrates just transition principles into planning, but inadequate support could worsen disparities.

Institutional risks include capacity constraints. Managing cross-sectoral transitions requires expertise, coordination, and adaptation to evolving regulations. Limited capacity may slow progress. Regulatory changes at national or international levels could also impose compliance costs.

Reputational risks arise if Ankara fails to meet climate commitments under the ACCAP, LCCAP, and Global Covenant of Mayors. Missing targets could reduce public trust and international finance opportunities.

By embedding risk analysis into planning and finance, Ankara seeks to mitigate these threats. Proactive measures—capacity building, external finance, stakeholder engagement, and social safeguards—support a transition that is both environmentally sustainable and socially fair.

column15:
Mayor Brandon Scott established a 1st Term Action Plan which identifies goals and actions to be achieved under his administration and identifies primary agencies for implementing the goals and actions under each of the plan's pillars. A few of the climate-related actions include the following: 1. increase outreach and education efforts to encourage transit use and carpooling, 2. conduct an internal review on the City's sustainability footprint, focused on carbon, energy usage, single use plastics, and construction waste, 3. improve community resiliency to support communities through extreme natural and manmade events resulting from climate change, 4. deploy new extreme heat mitigation and management options for residents, and 5. evaluate potential code improvements to increase overall energy efficiency and resiliency. Mayor Brandon Scott also established a Sustainability and Resiliency Subcabinet to improve the long-term sustainability, preparedness, and environmental practices of the city, and facilitate interagency collaboration to support the implementation of sustainability and climate-related actions identified in the Mayor's Action Plan and Sustainability Plan. 

Baltimore has a 21-member Commission on Sustainability, consisting of one City Council representative and 20 members appointed by the Mayor. The Commission has duties defined in the City Code that include: 1. preparing and amending a comprehensive Sustainability Plan, 2. monitoring the Office of Sustainability and the implementation of the Sustainability Plan, and 3. reporting to the City Council annually. The Baltimore Office of Sustainability is the office charged with a mission to develop and advocate for programs, policies, and actions by government, citizens, and businesses that lead to sustainable communities in the City. 

The Director of the Office of Sustainability is a management-level position who leads office and inter-agency staff in efforts that include: 1.working with the Commission on Sustainability to develop and implement the Sustainability Plan, 2. developing, implementing, and coordinating City policies that make all City operations achieve mid- and long-term GHG emissions targets, 3. developing or coordinating policies and programs to improve environmental performance in City operations, 4. facilitating compliance with federal, state, and local environmental regulations, 5. integrating sustainability and climate priorities into City plans, programs, and policies, including the City's Climate Action Plan, Disaster Preparedness Plan, environmental and development-related codes, and 6. setting other climate-related targets and objectives for the City. The Office of Sustainability Director and staff are assigned duties that include: 1. considering sustainability and climate-related issues in development reviews and approvals, 2. making recommendations to the City Council on climate-related codes, policies, and programs, 3. reporting to the Mayor and City Council on the performance in meeting sustainability and climate-related targets and objectives of each agency and the City overall, and 4. serving as the City's representatives to boards, commissions, and organizations engaged in issues relating to sustainability and climate-related issues. 

The City's fiscal budgeting efforts recognize that investments in projects that improve energy efficiency support the City's emissions reduction targets while also delivering savings in operating costs. Recent City budgets include funds to support climate-related efforts such as the purchase of a new energy software system to monitor energy usage data for City-owned buildings and identify savings opportunities, energy efficiency measures installed under energy performance contracts, and grant-funded projects from the Maryland Energy Administration and U.S. Department of Energy. Previous budgets included funds to support the update of the City's Climate Action Plan, which will identify new strategies and set sector targets to meet the City's zero-emissions target. As part of the annual fiscal budget performance measure reporting, the Office of Sustainability reports on the percentage of Climate Action Plan recommendations implemented or completed and the Department of General Services reports on energy use and projected savings resulting from implementation of energy-efficiency improvements. 

The evaluation criteria for ranking projects to be funded through the City's Capital Improvement Program incorporates the evaluation of the environmental impact of projects. The scoring guide for projects awards projects that will result in significant, measurable improvements to air or water quality or measurable reductions in greenhouse gas emissions three points (out of 18 possible points).
column16:
Baltimore's Capital Improvement Program, which is developed in 6-year increments, integrates climate and resilience considerations for capital projects through guidelines, training, and climate and resilience-related questions that must be answered as part of the submission process. In addition, agency staff are invited to meet with the Baltimore Office of Sustainability team members to discuss their projects and identify how they can address current and future hazard conditions. The evaluation criteria for ranking projects to be funded through the City's Capital Improvement Program incorporate the evaluation of the environmental impact of projects. The scoring guide for projects awards projects that will result in significant, measurable improvements to air or water quality or measurable reductions in greenhouse gas emissions three points (out of 18 possible points). 

In recent years, Baltimore has developed plans and updated development codes and related environmental mapping to better incorporate climate and resilience science and considerations into development planning. These updates have included work to specifically integrate hazards and climate adaptation efforts into planning processes. Strengthened and updated the Forest Conservation, Critical Area Management Program, and Floodplain Management Program code. A Nuisance Flood Plan was developed to better track, understand, and manage nuisance flooding along the waterfront in the city emphasis on heat. Community Wildfire Protection Plans have been established for the City-owned portions of the Liberty, Prettyboy and Loch Raven watersheds. The 2020 Less Waste, Better Baltimore Plan incorporated hazard planning to suggest increased capacity for the landfill in case of disaster. Enhanced and strengthened waterfront zoning and permitting. The latest Solid Waste Management Plan, adopted in 2023, includes a zero-waste section that includes ambitious goals to reduce waste and promote a circular economy. The Complete Streets Manual was adopted to encourage safer, greener streets for pedestrians, cyclists and other transportation modalities. The City's current DP3, the City's All Hazards Mitigation Plan, is also an adaptation plan. As noted previously, the City updated the ten-year Climate Action Plan that outlines its greenhouse gas emission strategy in early 2024. 
In 2025, the City's Comprehensive Master Plan was updated. It included significant consideration of work that will enhance climate related action.
column17:
In 2021, a law was enacted that gives Baltimore's three employee retirement systems five years to divest from fossil fuel companies listed on The Carbon Underground 200, an environmental organization that identifies the top 100 coal and the top 100 oil and gas publicly traded reserve holders globally. 

Baltimore's Capital Improvement Program integrates climate and resilience considerations for capital projects through climate and resilience-related questions that must be answered. The evaluation criteria for ranking projects to be funded through the City's Capital Improvement Program incorporate the evaluation of the environmental impact of projects. The scoring guide for projects awards projects that will result in significant, measurable improvements to air or water quality or measurable reductions in greenhouse gas emissions three points (out of 18 possible points).

The City's fiscal budgeting efforts recognize that investments in projects that improve energy efficiency support the City's emissions reduction targets while also delivering savings in operating costs. Recent and current budgets includes funds to support climate-related efforts such as the purchase of a new energy software system to monitor energy usage data for City-owned buildings and identify savings opportunities, energy efficiency measures installed under energy performance contracts, and grant-funded projects from the Maryland Energy Administration and U.S. Department of Energy. 

The City's Climate Action Plan (CAP) includes a financial analysis of ten municipal goals contained in the plan to estimate investment needed to achieve the goals. 

The City's finance department has considered allocating more funds to the City's 'rainy day' account to respond to increased frequency of climate disaster events. Finally, in 2024, City Council passed a bill calling for a recommendation to establish a resiliency authority. This year, a study is being conducted to evaluate the feasibility of resiliency authority or other entity to help finance or fund resiliency projects.
column18:
As part of the City's CAP Update, the City hired team of consultants to help develop the city-wide climate action strategy, as well as a municipal inventory and carbon neutrality roadmap. This includes a fiscal impact assessment to identify costs to city of implementing City-wide and government carbon neutrality. This assessment will help us better understand financial impacts and related risks of the transition to a low-carbon economy. 

A risk identified relates to the lack of local government level control of the regional public transportation system. This limits our ability to reduce reliance on fossil-fuel based transportation within our jurisdiction because we do not have the ability to manage the pace of increasing the availability of transit access compared to the demand for expansion. 

Another risk our jurisdiction faces relates to how to finance the costs of the transition and ensure equitable distribution of cost impacts. Baltimore has a high tax rate compared to neighboring jurisdictions and a high percentage of low-income residents. It will be a challenge to balance the need for funding the transition to a low-carbon economy, maintaining current levels of City services, and ensuring that our City remains affordable for low-income residents. 

Another risk relates to capacity. As more people transition to solar energy, addition strain will be placed on the electric grid. The CAP calls for the City to work with the local utility provider, BGE, to address the issue however expansion to support increased could be costly which could further raise energy rates for residents and businesses that have recently increased dramatically and has proven to be very burdensome to residents.

column15:
지역 기후위기 대응을 위해 국가의 “기후위기 대응을 위한 탄소중립 녹색성장 기본법”에 근거한 “부산광역시 기후위기 대응을 위한 탄소중립 녹색성장 기본조례”를 2022년 7월부터 시행하고 있다. 이 조례에는 경제, 사회, 교육, 문화 등 모든 분야에서 기후위기 대응을 위한 부산시의 책무를 규정하고 온실가스 감축과 기후변화 적응 시책을 추진하도록 규정하고 있다.
 이 조례를 근거로 부산시는 다음과 같이 기후문제 완화를 위한 업무를 추진하고 있다.
 
1. 지역의 온실가스 감축목표를 2030년까지 2018년 온실가스 배출량 대비 45%를 감축하고 2050년까지 탄소중립을 실현하는 목표를 설정하여 대·내외에 알리고 단계적 시행계획을 수립하여 이행하고 있다.

2. 제1차 국가 탄소중립녹색성장 기본계획(2023년 4월)과 연계하여 제1차 부산광역시 탄소중립녹색성장 기본계획을 수립(2024.4.)하고, 16개 기초지방 자치단체에서도 제 1차 탄소중립녹색성장 기본계획을 2025년 4월까지 수립 완료하도록 지원하였다.

3. 2022년부터 공무원과 학자, 기업인, 시민단체 대표자 등 50명 이상으로 구성된 부산광역시 2050 탄소중립 녹색성장위원회를 구성하여 운영 중이고, 이 위원회는 6개 분과(에너지산업, 건물, 수송, 폐기물·흡수원, 기후위기적응, 시민실천협력) 위원회로 구성되어 있으며, 탄소중립 사회 이행과 녹색성장의 추진을 위한 주요 정책 및 계획과 그 시행에 관한 사항을 심의 의결하고 의견을 제시하는 기능을 수행하고 있다.

4. 온실가스 감축 및 기후위기 적응 시책 등을 마련하였다. 소속된 66개 공공기관을 대상으로 온실가스 목표 관리제를 시행하여 특히, 건물 수송 부문에서 발생하는 온실가스를 2050년까지 2018년 온실가스 배출량에 근거하여 설정한 기준배출량 대비 50% 이상을 감축하도록 목표를 설정하였다. 이를 위해 해마다 별도의 감축목표를 정해서 이행점검을 병행하고 있다. 공공기관별로 자체적으로 예산을 확보하여 신재생 에너지 시설 설치, 전기차, 수소 전기차 등의 전환, 에너지 효율화를 통한 이행을 추진하도록 유도하고 있다.

5. 건축물 신축 하는 자와 기존 건축물을 소유자에게 녹색건물 설치 기준과 절차를 준수하는 경우 행정적, 기준적, 기술적 지원을 하고 있으며, 수송부문에서의 온실가스 감축을 위해 대중교통을 이용하는 시민에게 교통비의 일부를 보조하는 동백페이 사업 추진과 전기차, 수소차 등의 친환경 자동차 보급을 위한 충전 인프라 확충 지원과, 친환경 자동차 구매자에게 구매 비용을 직접 지원하는 사업을 적극 추진하고 있다.

6. 탄소 흡수원 확대를 위해 과거 생활쓰레기 매립장으로 활용한 곳에 해운대 수목원, 낙동강 하구 생태공원 등의 녹지대를 복원 조성하여 탄소 흡수원으로 활용하고 시민들에게 힐링 할 수 있는 공간을 제공하고 있으며, 도시숲 조성, 가로수 조성, 나대지, 공·폐가 등 도심지 버리진 땅에 작은 도심공원을 조성하는 사업을 추진하고 있다. 개발 사업 등으로 불가피하게 산림을 훼손하는 경우에는 예상되는 온실가스 배출량을 상쇄하기 위한 대체 조림을 조성하도록 하고 있다.

7. 해마다 심화되고 있는 도시열섬 현상에 채계적으로 대응하기 위해 2016년부터 16개 지점에 기온 측정 장비를 설치하여 시민이 느끼는 체감 기온(지면에서 약 2m 위에서 측정하므로 기상 관측상의 기온보다 약 2~3℃ 정도 높게 측정 됨) 측정 자료를 분석하여 기온예측 결과를 사전에 시민들에게 공개하여 폭염, 한파 등에 대응하도록 안내하고 있다. 또한 이 구축 자료는 도시열섬 대응을 위한 지붕 차열 페인트 시공, 사람들이 다닌 길에 차열페인트를 시공하는 쿨 페이브먼트 시공 등의 사업을 할 수 있는 기본 자료로 활용되고 있다.

8. 국가의 기후위기 적응대책에 연계하는 부산광역시 기후위기 적응대책을 5년마다 연동 수립하고 있다. 지역의 기후 리스크를 분석하여 지역 기후변화로 인한 부정적 영향을 최소화하고 긍정적인 사항을 극대화하는 시업을 추진하도록 하고 있으며, 해마다 8개 부문(물 관리, 생태계, 국토 연안, 농수산, 건강, 산업 에너지, 기후감시 예측, 적응 주류화) 73개 사업에 대해 목표 달성률과 예산 집행 정도를 점검하고 있다. 이 과정에서 지역의 현황을 잘 알고 있는 전문가 시민 참여단을 구성 운영 하여 시민들의 의견도 반영하고 있다.

9. 지역의 기후위기에 취약한 계층을 대상으로 지붕 쿨루프 시공, 재래시장 등 취약 계층 밀집 이용시설 등에 쿨링포그 설치, 그늘막 설치, 무더위 쉼터 조성 등을 추진하고 있으며, 도로변 가로수 조성, 도로 살수 차량 운영 등을 통해 도시의 폭염 피해를 낮추기 위한 사업을 지속적으로 추진하고 있다. 
 폭우, 태풍 등의 기상재해와 하천 범람 등의 기후재난 문제를 예방하기 위해 연안 방파제 보강 등의 재해예방 사업을 단계적으로 추진하고 있으며, 재해예방 시스템 구축을 통해, 하천범람, 산사태, 산불 등의 피해에 대비한 시민의 위치 주변 상황과 대피 경로 안내 등을 온라인 플랫폼을 구축하여 실시간 제공하고 있다.

10. 탄소중립과 녹색성장을 위해 지역에 소재한 중소기업이 온실가스 배출량을 저감하는 제품을 생산하여 판매하는 경우 제품 생산에 필요한 대출 자금의 발생이자와 탄소가치 평가료, 자본대출 보증료를 전액 지원하는 탄소저감 기술기업 금융비용 전부 지원 사업을 2024년 7월부터 2027년까지 추진하고 있으며, 이 사업은 지역 은행과 부산광역시, 공공기관 등이 업무 협약을 맺어 40여개의 중소기업을 지원함으로써 녹색기술을 보유한 기업의 녹색산업으로의 안정적인 전환을 유도하고자 한다.

11. 시민들의 기후위기 대응과 탄소중립 생활실천을 유도하기 위해 탄소중립 마을을 선정하여 1년에서 최대 3년까지 생활실천 교육을 추진하고 있으며, 생활 속 우수한 사례를 가진 단체, 기업 등을 발굴하고 격려하는 탄소중립 생활실천 경진대회를 2022년부터 해마다 개최하여 우수한 사례를 전파 확산하고 있다.

12. 지자체 재정사업이 온실가스 감축에 미칠 영향을 분석하여 그 결과를 예산 편성에 반영하고 결산 시 적정 집행되었는지를 평가하여 환류하는 제도인 온실가스 감축인지 예산을 시범 운영하고 있으며, 이를 통해 사업 시행 방안을 온실가스 감축을 유도하거나, 유도할 수 있는 사업을 수행하도록 하고 있다.

13. 2025.1.1.부터 “부산광역시 기후대응 기금 설치 및 운용 조례”를 제정하고 이 기금을 활용하여 지역 온실가스 감축 및 기후적응 시책사업 추진, 기후위기 대응 관련 조사, 연구 또는 기술개발, 설비 투자 등에 필요한 재정지원, 기후위기 대응을 위한 융자, 투자 등의 금융 지원, 교육, 인력양성 국제 협력 등을 추진하고 있다. 

14. 부산광역시 탄소중립녹색성장 지원센터를 2022년부터 구성 운영하여 지역의 기후대응과 탄소중립 이행로드맵 및 각종 계획 수립과 이행을 지원하고 있으며, 시민들이 보다 쉽게 탄소중립의 개념을 이해할 수 있도록 콘텐츠 제작 홍보, 지역 이슈에 대한 전문가 포럼, 세미나를 개최하여 문제 해결 방안을 제시하는 사다리 역할과 시민들의 의견을 수렴하는 역할을 수행하도록 하고 있다.

15. 지역의 고위 공무원을 탄소중립정책 이행책임관으로 지정하여 기후위기 대응 및 탄소중립 실현을 위한 시책 및 사업 추진의 구심점 역할을 수행하도록 함으로써 지역 사회의 탄소중립 실현을 위해 적극 노력하도록 하고 있다.
column16:
부산광역시는 50여개의 중형 및 대형 하천이 존재하고 이 하천들이 연안으로 연결되어 있어 폭우와 만조가 겹치면 침수 피해가 항상 발생하고 있으며, 바다와 접한 해안선이 404㎞에 달하고 있고 인공 해안이 발달되어 있어 연안 재해에 항상 노출되어 있다.

기습 폭우 시 하천 및 바다로 배수되지 못한 빗물 등으로 인해 하천 범람이 발생하여 주택 상가 등의 침수피해가 발생하고, 폭풍, 월파 등으로 인한 연안에 위치한 도로나 방파제 등이 크게 훼손되는 사고가 발생하고 있다.

부산시는 홍수, 호우 등으로부터 재해를 예방하기 위하여 처리가능한 시간당 및 연속강우량 목표를 정하여 방재시설 설계 시 적용하여 기후 회복력을 키우기 위한 적응전략과 협력 방안을 마련하였다.
방재시설은 하수도 시설, 배수펌프장, 빗물펌프장, 하수저류시설, 우수유출 저감시설, 배수로, 길도랑, 설치예정 배수로 등으로 홍수, 강우로 인해 영향을 받는 일체의 시설을 말한다.

이에 따라 2017년에 정한 방재시설이 기후변화로 인해 계속 증가하고 있는 강우를 감당 할 수 없다고 판단하여 2023년부터 상향된 설계기준을 만들어 반영하도록 하였다. 도시에 설치된 방재시설을 보수하는 경우와 신규 설치나 새로이 설치 계획하는 방재시설은 상향된 방재성능 기준을 준수하여야 한다.

가령 2017년도에는 방재시설 성능 목표가 1시간 105㎜, 2시간 145㎜, 3시간 175㎜였으나 2023년 새로이 규정한 방재성능 목표는 1시간 114㎜, 2시간 160㎜, 3시간 190㎜로 상향하였다.

 추가적으로 기습 폭우 시 하천 친수공간에서 하천 범람으로 인한 인명 피해 사고와 지하차도에서 사망사고가 최근 발생함에 따라 일정 강우 시 하천 및 지하차도로의 진입을 전면 금지하고 관련 개발 사업 시 비상대피로, 사다리, 유도선 등의 비상대피시설을 설치와 대피로 안내 등을 의무화 하고 있다.

연안관련 사업 추진 시에는 연안재해위험 평가를 통해 각종 연안개발 기본 계획, 종합계획 수립에 반영하고 정비사업 수립, 시설물 유지관리 위험지구 지정 등에 활용하도록 하고 있다. 국가 및 지방 정부 차원의 연안 침식 실태조사, 해안침수예상도 제작, 연안재해 취약성 평가체계 구축, 실시간 고조 정보 서비스 제공, 기후변화 해수면 변동 분석, 지진해일대응 시스템 등을 구축하여 활용 중이다. 

과거 피해 발생한 이력 지구, 정비계획만 있고 실제 정비가 이행되지 않은 연안, 연안 지형적 민감도, 파랑 위험, 해일 위험 재난 경보 시스템 4~5등급 지역 등은 자연재해 위험지구예비 후보지로 지정하여 해안 재해로부터 보호방안을 실행하도록 하고 있다.

또한 대규모 주택 단지 등을 조성하는 경우에는 저 영향 개발기법을 반영하고 바람길을 조성하도록 하여 도시열섬을 최대한 완화시키고 있으며, 일정 규모 이상의 탄소흡수원이 되는 자연녹지 등을 훼손하는 개발 사업을 시행하는 경우에는 완충지를 의무설치하고, 사업자에 대해 부담금을 부과 징수하여 훼손된 면적에 상응하는 대체 녹지 등을 조성할 수 있는 방안을 강구하고 있다.
column17:
폭염에 따른 온열질환자 발생자 증가 등으로 폭염 한파를 자연재난으로 규정하고 재해예방과 재난 발생 시 복구를 위해 편성하는 재난 기금에 2023년부터 여름 겨울철 자연재난 관리 용도의 예산을 반영하여 오고 있다.
2023년에는 9천7백만원의 예산을 편성하였고, 2024년에는 26억원, 2025년에는 약 10억원의 예산을 편성중이며, 향후 당해 예산의 증액은 불가피 할 것으로 예상된다.

연안을 관리하는 부서에서는 별도로 연안의 자연재해 복구와 예방하기 위한 연안정비 사업을 매년 예산 반영하여 추진 중이고, 수산업 관련 부서에서는 해수온 상승과 해양 산성화에 따라 바다 생물들의 먹이 공급과 회피 장소를 마련하기 위해 바다에 해초 숲을 조성하는 사업을 단계적으로 조성하여 관리하고 있다. 
또한 기후변화에 취약한 토종 어종에 대해 치어(어린물고기) 방생을 추진하고 특히, 하절기에는 수산업 보호를 위해 양식장의 용존산소 농도 유지 장비를 지원하고 있다.

기후변화로 인한 대응과 탄소중립 실현의 중요성이 부각됨에 따라 이를 위한 재원으로 기후대응 기금을 2025.1.1.부터 조성하여 운용 중이다.

부산광역시 환경기본조례에 의거 환경보전 시책을 원활하게 추진하기 위해 부산광역시 환경보전기금을 조성하여 운용 중이었으나, 부산광역시 환경보전기금을 2025.1.1.부터 기후대응기금으로 전환하여 운영하고 있으며. 지역 온실가스 감축 및 기후적응 시책사업 추진, 기후위기 대응 관련 조사, 연구 또는 기술개발, 설비 투자 등에 필요한 재정지원, 기후위기 대응을 위한 융자, 투자 등의 금융 지원, 교육, 인력양성 국제 협력 등을 추진하고 있다.

또한 지자체 재정사업은 온실가스 감축에 미칠 영향을 분석하여 그 결과를 예산 편성에 반영하고 결산 시 적정 집행되었는지를 평가하여 환류하는 제도인 온실가스 감축인지예산제도를 시범 운영하고 있으며, 이를 통해 사업 시행 방안을 온실가스 감축을 유도하거나, 유도할 수 있는 사업을 수행하도록 하고 있다.
column18:
부산광역시는 2019년 산업별 총 생산량 순위를 살펴보면 제조업이 18%, 운수 및 창고업 8%, 건설업 6% 등으로 재조업 비중이 높아 저탄소 경제로의 급격한 전환 시 경제적 타격이 매우 클 것으로 예상되고 있다.

제조업 중 온실가스 배출현황을 보면 금속제조 53%, 전기·전자·정밀기계, 석유화학, 운송 기타 기계, 음식 담배, 섬유 의복, 목재 펄프 인쇄 순으로 나타나고 있고 
금속 제조업의 경우 탄소 집약도가 높고 2018년 온실가스 배출량에 비해 2019년도에 소폭 증가하였다.

2004년부터 2019년 7개 제조업종(1 금속제조 2 전기·전자·정밀기계, 3 석유화학, 4 운송 기타 기계, 5 음식·담배, 6 섬유·의복, 7 목재·펄프·인쇄)은 공통적으로 화석연료비중 효과 개선(화석연료 사용 감축)으로 CO2 배출 감축을 이룬 반면 연료전환 효과(전기·열 사용 증가)로 인해 CO2 배출이 증가하였다.
부산지역의 번영과 발전을 위해 경제활동과 고용효과로 인한 배출증가는 반드시 필요한 사항이므로 연료전환, 화석연료 비중, 에너지집약도 효과 개선을 통한 배출감축을 도모해야 한다.
2019년 기준 부산지역 다배출 제조업종을 보면 금속제조(1,240천t CO2), 전기·전자·정밀기계(330천t CO2), 석유화학(231천t CO2), 운송기타기계(218천t CO2) 순으로 나타났다.
금속제조는 다른 6개 업종 배출량 총합(1,106천t CO2)보다 압도적으로 높기 때문에 절대적 감축이 필요한 업종이고 연료전환 및 에너지집약도 효과가 온실가스 배출에 크게 기여하였기에 에너지 관련 조치가 시급하다.
석유화학과 전기·전자·정밀기계는 부산 경제발전과 고용에 크게 기여하는 만큼 배출요인이 높은 수준으로 나타난다. 석유화학은 화석연료의 비중이 크고, 전기·전자·정밀기계는 연료전환 효과가 CO2 배출에 큰 요인으로 작용하여 대처가 필요하다.
2030년 제조업 CO2 배출 전망을 보면 이전부터 CO2 배출 감축을 위한 노력보다 더욱 적극적인 조치를 취하지 않으면 더 많은 배출량을 보일 것이다.
지속적 경제성장과 배출량 감소라는 과제는 모든 업종에 해당되지만 한정된 자원과 인력으로 최대의 효과를 보기 위해서는 선택과 집중이 필요할 것으로 생각됨으로 온실가스 배출 제조 업종에 대한 선제적 조치가 필요하다.

column15: Cincinnati remains a leader among cities in the United States for its sustainability, equity, and resilience efforts. The Climate, Environment & Infrastructure Committee is focused exclusively on climate issues. In addition, the Committee played an important role in the development of the City's 2023 Green Cincinnati Plan (“GCP”) and has also played a critical role in the implementation of the GCP. First introduced in 2008, the GCP has been updated every five years since. The GCP guides the City and partners to create a more sustainable, equitable and resilient community for all that call this area home. The GCP process was guided by a Steering Committee appointed by the Mayor and comprised of government, corporate, academic, non-profit, faith, and community organization representatives. The City's Office of Environment and Sustainability (“OES”) coordinates development of the plan. OES guides the GCP update process with an emphasis on equity-based community engagement, data-driven decisions, and collaborative negotiations with residents and partners. The City Council approved the creation of an Environmental Advisory Board in 2023 to help guide sustainability policy efforts moving forward.
column16: The City of Cincinnati's comprehensive plan, Plan Cincinnati, was adopted by City Council in 2012. It is the official document guiding future planning and development in the City. A portion of the document focuses on sustainability with the goal of reducing energy usage, improving air and water quality, and reducing sewer overflows. These goals, along with the Green Cincinnati Plan, have played a critical role in aligning City efforts to address climate impacts through planning. The impacts of climate-related issues have also impacted planning in other ways. Repeated flooding in neighborhoods along two waterways due to intense precipitation events led the City to purchase properties in the area. In the case of the Lick Run, the City developed a greenway that assists with storm water management by collecting over 800 million gallons of rainwater from the watershed annually. The City has also experienced an increase in landslides on its hills due to intense precipitation events. The City has a Hillside Overlay District that establishes standards to guide development of land and structures in hillside areas. These standards along with hillside stabilization projects have helped to reduce the impacts of climate-related landslides.
column17: At this time, the City does not have a fund specifically reserved for climate-related issues. Recently, this resulted in the shifting of funds originally identified for other projects to address climate-related issues. The City has faced a growing number of landslides on its hills as the number of intense precipitation events increases. To stabilize these areas, the City was forced to redirect funds in its general fund intended to support other priorities and use them for the hillside projects. Climate-related issues are beginning to play a more important role in the City's financial planning. In recent budget cycles, the City and Mayor Aftab Pureval dedicated $9 million towards funding climate action efforts in the City. While not relevant to financial planning, per se, this is the most significant climate investment in the City's history. These funds are being utilized for fleet electrification, a revolving loan fund, and more. In addition, the City is investing in green infrastructure, increasing its use of renewable energy through on-site solar installations, and completed an assessment if its tree canopy to ensure that its tree planting efforts are directed to areas with a lower-than-average tree canopy.
column18: The City has made a commitment to transition to a low-carbon economy, but it faces unique challenges at the state level. The Ohio legislature has passed a number of bills in recent years that impact the City's ability to meet its carbon goals. Laws are currently in place that limit wind turbine installations, make it increasingly difficult to site new utility scale solar installations, decrease renewable energy portfolio standards and eliminate energy efficiency programs for investor-owned utilities. In addition, building codes are set at the state level which means the City must search for innovative ways to encourage developers to increase the efficiency of their projects. Despite these headwinds, the City continues to explore creative solutions and to use the policy tools at its disposal to work toward its carbon goals. \n\nThe largest financial risk to a low carbon shift in the near-term in Cincinnati relates to the low cost of natural gas as compared to electricity. Ohio is a natural gas producing state. While natural gas faces resource limitations causing the cost to undoubtedly rise in coming years, its production is heavily subsidized and supported. Until solar can be installed at great scale and electricity prices can descend, shifting to a low-carbon economy is tricky.
