Guiding strategy: In May 2021, the City of Cape Town Council adopted its latest Climate Change Strategy. The Strategy is accompanied by a Climate Change Action Plan that was approved in August 2021 at City Manager level and which provides detailed information on programme and project level actions that are allocated to Departments to implement in order to achieve the vision of the strategy. Various City sector specific strategies have also been informed by the Climate Change Strategy and Action Plan (e.g. the Energy Strategy 2023 and Waste Strategy 2025). The City's policy process now also incorporates the consideration of climate change and sustainability objectives in the development of all new relevant strategies, policies and by-laws. 

Governance: The monitoring, evaluation and reporting of the Climate Change Strategy and Action Plan is coordinated by the City's Climate Change Planning team in the Risk and Resilience Department, under a transversally functioning Directorate called the Future Planning and Resilience (FPR) Directorate. The Risk and Resilience department was formed during 2022/23, when the City's Integrated Risk Management and Business Continuity Management functions joined merged with the Resilience Department to form an updated Risk and Resilience Department. The merge of these functions means that there will be increased opportunities for mainstreaming of climate risk considerations into the City's integrated risk management processes. 

The FPR Directorate reports directly to the mayor at political level and consist of departments focused on the short, medium and long-term future planning of the city. The climate change planning and monitoring function therefore sits alongside impactful transversal functions for the whole organisation, including corporate programme, project and portfolio management, communications, policy and strategy, organisational performance management and organisational effectiveness and innovation. The location of the climate change planning function in this Directorate therefore provides a greater opportunity to mainstream and prioritise climate change as part of the overall resilience function of the City. This was a notable development of the current political administration and positions climate change in an increasingly transformative position. The Future Planning and Resilience Portfolio Committee (a type of sub-committee of Council made up of councillors) plays an additional political oversight for this function. 

Additionally, in November 2024 the City established a transversal Climate Change Response Forum, comprising of representatives across 20 departments. The Forum serves to enhance the coordination of climate change response activities, monitoring, reporting and knowledge sharing across the organisation, considering the cross-cutting nature of climate change response. It will also serve as a platform to facilitate inputs into CCAP planning and review processes. The Forum is managed and chaired by the Risk and Resilience Department and meets twice a year. The most recent meeting took place in June 2025.

Overseeing progress: The Climate Change Strategy and Action Plan is reviewed on an annual basis. Three review reports have been produced and published to date (2021/22, 2022/23 and 2023/24). Prior to being published online, these are submitted to various committees, including the FPR Portfolio Committee (referred to above), the Risk Committee and the Executive Management Team (comprising all the Executive Directors of Directorates) and the Mayoral Committee to inform leadership on progress and key issues. The development of these annual progress review reports is embedded in the annual FPR Directorate scorecard (i.e. the City's Directorate's performance management system called the Service Delivery Budget Implementation Plans (SDBIPs).

Please see the latest implementation review report here: https://resource.capetown.gov.za/documentcentre/Documents/City%20research%20reports%20and%20review/ClimateChangeStrategyandActionPlanAnnualImplementationReport2023-24.pdf
column16:
Over recent terms of office, climate change response has increasingly been integrated into the City's overall five-year master plan, the Integrated Development Plan (IDP). The current IDP (2022-2027) was approved by Council in May 2022 and includes a dedicated programme on 'Climate Change Planning and Monitoring' under 1 of 3 foundational priorities, called “A Resilient City”. Programmes that contribute to climate change response have been tagged within the IDP and their link to the City's Climate Change Action Plan actions identified. 

Furthermore, the current IDP has prioritized various projects related to energy security (including cleaner energy and energy efficiency), new water programmes, public transport and improved waste management as one of its top three tier priorities (i.e. excellence in basic services). The new 16 IDP objectives are aligned with relevant SDGs and will ultimately see the municipality enact or implement the SDGs locally. The IDP document also illustrates programme-level SDG alignment through the use of relevant SDG icons. The City's Risk and Resilience Department is continuously exploring how to further integrate climate change response into the IDP reporting process, building on the institutional progress achieved in previous years. For more on the City's IDP please see here: https://www.capetown.gov.za/Family%20and%20home/Meet-the-City/our-vision-for-the-city/the-citys-idp-2022-2027. The most recent progress report of the IDP can be found here: https://resource.capetown.gov.za/documentcentre/Documents/City%20research%20reports%20and%20review/CCT_Integrated_Annual_Report_2023-24.pdf 

A few examples of key City sector strategies and plans that have been informed and driven in part by climate related issues include the City's Energy Strategy (2023) which includes the longer term goal of carbon neutrality, the Water Strategy (2019) which was a direct response to build Cape Town's water resilience following a multi-year drought and the new Waste Strategy (2025) which has a strong emphasis on waste diversion and circularity. The City's Comprehensive Integrated Transport Plan (2023-2028) also includes key references to climate goals and actions.

Furthermore, as an integral component of the City's IDP, the City's Municipal Spatial Development Framework (MSDF) translates the vision and strategy of the IDP into a desired spatial vision for the municipality. The MSDF is a long-term (20-years+) plan to guide and manage current and future growth of the City, as informed by various sector-specific strategies and guided by the vision of the City. It recognises that the City's climate change response goals can only be reached through significant transitions in urban form, energy sources, transportation and resource efficiency, such as building an effective public transport system, cleaning up our sources of electricity, and making the built environment more efficient. Climate risk considerations have been integrated into the MSDF, particularly in regards to limiting development in high-risk areas such as floodplains and the coastal zone. See the MSDF here: https://resource.capetown.gov.za/documentcentre/Documents/City%20strategies%2C%20plans%20and%20frameworks/MSDF_Vol_I_Ch1-6_Tech_Suppl_A.pdf 

Additionally, in 2024/25 work took place towards integrating climate risk response considerations into the City's infrastructure sector plans through the development of a tool and methodology for assessing and updating these. This tool will enable increased integration of climate risk considerations into the Sector Plans in the future.
column17:
The City's Integrated Development Plan (IDP - overall master plan) informs the City's budgetary framework. As noted in the previous question (1.3.3), the current IDP (2022-2027) has prioritised various projects related to energy security (including cleaner energy and energy efficiency), new water programmes, public transport and improved waste management. Based on these priorities, as an example, the City of Cape Town's 2025/26 capital budget of more than R1.3 bn for the Energy Directorate, includes allocations, to develop the City's small-scale embedded generation (rooftop PV) market, to develop City owned solar plants, invest in battery storage technology and for rolling out a LED streetlight replacement programme. The longer term (three year) budget includes significant allocations to bring on board (cleaner) independent generation and procurement. These programmes aim to build energy resilience, reduce load-shedding over time and contribute to meeting Cape Town's climate mitigation targets. In addition, the Water and Sanitation sector received the largest capital budget allocation for the financial year 2025/26 of over R5 bn, which represents approximately 40% of the City's total capital budget. This capital budget will contribute to major projects to enhance Cape Town's water resilience, focussing on the implementation of the City's New Water Programme as outlined in the Water Strategy; Catchment, Stormwater and River Management; Flood Alleviation; and both water supply and Wastewater Treatment infrastructure upgrades. 

In February 2023, the City launched its R120 billion infrastructure portfolio - which sets the foundation for economic growth in the city over 10 years, to be funded by a blended finance model leveraging the City's own balance sheet, as well as finance from local and international markets. R55,5 billion, or 40%, of this 10-year pipeline, aims to contribute to strengthening the Cape Town's climate change resilience against drought, fires, heat, flooding and storm surges. 

The challenges that the portfolio aims to address include: 
•Upgrade wastewater works and sewer to reduce spills and ensure a healthy and dignified environment 
•Deliver 300 million litres from new water sources daily - to address Cape Town's water security and protect the city from future droughts, Cape Town is investing around R5 billion to introduce 300 Mega-Litres per day of new water by 2030 
•End load shedding over time - between now and 2028, Cape Town will spend approximately R1 billion a year on electricity infrastructure to prepare for a dynamic, decentralised energy future 
•The new Khayelitsha-Claremont bus route and fixing passenger rail once control is devolved to the City with over R6.28 billion over the next three years going to the MyCiti (BRT) south-east expansion. 
•Expanded waste collection, drop-off sites and landfill - the City is also allocating a significant 21% of planned spending over ten years to landfill infrastructure 
•Land release and bulk services for more affordable housing 

Please see the Infrastructure reports here: 
2022: https://resource.capetown.gov.za/documentcentre/Documents/City research reports and review/CCT_Mayors_Infrastructure_Report_2022.pdf 
2023: https://resource.capetown.gov.za/documentcentre/Documents/City%20research%20reports%20and%20review/CCT_Mayors_Infrastructure_Report_2023.pdf 

Over the past 2-3 years, a number of steps have also been taken to integrate climate risk into the City's project management process, including an assessment of both the three-year and ten-year capital projects portfolio. The assessment identified various areas where the City is currently investing in climate change response - most notably water resilience - and also highlighted some gaps where additional investment is required. As a result, a guidebook was developed to help project managers consider climate resilience in the project management process. 

A climate budget tagging process was also carried out for the three-year capital budget (2025/26 - 2027/28). This process used a simple methodology in which projects were tagged in terms of whether or not they contributed to climate change response, whether this contribution was as a primary goal of the project or as a co-benefit, and whether those projects contributed to climate change adaptation and resilience, climate change mitigation, or both. This analysis showed that, for the three-year 2025/26 - 2027/28 capital budget, approximately R4.24 billion has been allocated to programmes or projects which respond to climate change as a primary goal while approximately R22.91 billion will be going toward projects that have a climate change co-benefit

Together, these processes and resources aim to support the stronger integration of climate change response into future service delivery programmes and projects.
column18:
The City of Cape Town, as South Africa's second-largest metro and the economic engine of the Western Cape, recognises both the opportunities and risks posed by the transition to a low-carbon economy. Municipalities play a critical role in enabling this transition, but they also bear exposure to risks associated with demographic change, regulatory uncertainty, financial sustainability and infrastructure readiness. 

The following are key risk considerations for Cape Town within the energy sector: 
•The transition to a low-carbon economy places increasing pressure on the City's financial framework. Rising input costs—including Eskom bulk electricity purchases, infrastructure maintenance, and investments in embedded generation and load-shedding mitigation—are escalating operational expenditure. These pressures are further compounded by theft, vandalism of infrastructure, shrinking grant allocations, and growing service demand due to rapid population growth, informality, and rising indigent support needs. As more consumers adopt alternative energy solutions and shift consumption patterns, the City's traditional revenue model—historically reliant on electricity sales—is being challenged. This creates financial sustainability risks for trading services and may reduce the ability to cross-subsidise vulnerable households. In response, the City is working towards modernising its revenue model to reflect the realities of decentralised generation, energy efficiency, and changing customer behaviour. 
•The evolving national energy landscape presents both opportunities and constraints for Cape Town's energy transition. While reforms such as the Electricity Regulation Amendment Act and the upcoming South African Wholesale Electricity Market create new avenues for municipal power procurement, it is important for financially stable and capable municipalities to be able to participate. This will require the City to not only undertake its own internal reform processes, including tariff restructuring, utility modernisation, and institutional capacity-building, but also ensure alignment with broader national reforms to avoid policy conflict, or misalignment with evolving market structures.
•Significant upgrades are needed to accommodate variable and distributed energy sources, including developing a smart grid and maintaining readiness for high renewable energy penetration. These grid modernisation investments to enable the energy transition will be crucial, particularly regarding maintaining the stability and integrity of the grid.
•Ensuring equity is crucial, particularly for low-income households. Policy adjustments for energy subsidies and alternative sources of energy are needed to address energy poverty and ensure the equitable distribution of the transition. 
•Managing the transition to a low-carbon energy system requires specialised technical and operational skills. As municipalities expand their role in energy planning, procurement and grid management, the City must strengthen institutional capacity to support this shift. Specialised skills in big data, GIS, and business process analysis, as well as customer-centred skills are needed. Succession planning and attracting skilled workers will be challenging. Capacity building for municipalities to play an increased facilitation role in a more liberalised energy generation market will also be crucial, particularly around contract negotiation and contract management for IPPs and wheeling. 
•To support accurate emissions reporting, climate planning, and a credible transition to a low-carbon economy, there is a growing need to enhance inter-governmental data practices through more open, standardised, and high-quality data sharing. 
•Cape Town and South Africa will likely remain in a position where it must accept the prevailing market price of most zero-carbon technology in an economy with substantial social burdens. It is therefore likely that it will not be possible or practical to significantly subsidise mitigation actions, but the City can be proactive where technology is viable so that Cape Town becomes an active participant in a global green economy - taking up niches where we can be competitive. South Africa's high carbon intensity and low effective carbon price expose it to economic shocks from carbon border adjustment mechanisms and shifting consumer preferences. While short-term impacts on Cape Town's energy system are minimal, these may increase in the medium-to-long term. 
•Businesses bear the primary burden of preserving livelihoods and the trauma of business closure in the face of transitions or shocks which may impact workers, owners and management. 
•The reality of vulnerability and threatened interests can negatively inform the response of the City's critical rates paying citizens when they are tasked with being more resource efficient, welcoming of inclusive land-use planning and development decisions, lifestyle changes and cross-subsidisation mechanisms.

column15: Climate action within the City of Cleveland has been largely overseen by the Mayor's Office of Sustainability, with the Director of Sustainability serving on the Mayor's cabinet and sustainability staff members representing and pushing for climate action in various inter-departmental initiatives (such as pushing for a more sustainable building policy, electric vehicle purchasing goals, and more). Larger, budget-related issues relating to climate action are also approved through a Development, Planning, & Sustainability committee within City Council. The City recently lunched a Climate Action Working Group (CAWG), which meets on a monthly basis to coordinate on joint sustainability projects and guide the implementation of the updated Municipal Action Plan (MAP), which is the roadmap to achieve net zero emissions from City operations.
column16: The City's Climate Action Plan is utilized and referenced in the annual City Plan. City Planning is updating the Citywide Mater Plan and coordinating with Sustainability staff to align this plan with the Climate Action Plan and incorporate both adaptation and mitigation planning. Sustainability staff have been involved in updating City plans for parks and transportation/mobility.
column17: The City has had additional focus on more equitable community funding, especially during and after the COVID pandemic. Though not directly impacted by climate-related issues, these initiatives are closely tied with climate priorities. The City has also instituted a Residential Green Building tax abatement that has been a direct product of climate planning. As part of its updated Municipal Action Plan, the City has called for incorporating carbon budgeting and life cycle analyses (LCA) into its capital investment planning processes.
column18: Much of Cleveland's economy has been built around a traditional, high emissions manufacturing industry, which may suffer impacts in the transition to a low-carbon economy if it does not have reliable access to affordable alternative energy and natural resources. In particular, the region's steel industry is heavily dependent upon metallurgical steel and access to abundant, affordable gas. The transition to green steel production has been hampered by a lack of availability to affordable green hydrogen and abundant clean energy. Without finding ways to utilize existing manufacturing infrastructure for lower carbon production, Cleveland could take an economic hit in this transition. The recent changes in policy at the federal level present significant challenges, as grants and tax credits that the City was depending on, such as Solar For All and the Investment Tax Credit (ITC), are being eliminated or are threatened.

column15: Climate oversight in the City of Dallas is guided by the Comprehensive Environmental & Climate Action Plan (CECAP). Adopted in 2020, this plan established a framework for addressing climate policy, planning, and management for the City including adaptation, mitigation and environmental quality measures implemented through an analyses of equity. The purpose of the CECAP is to improve our natural environment, economy, housing, and transportation while reducing greenhouse gas emissions to targets set by the Paris Agreement, and achieving carbon neutrality by 2050. The City has an oversight committee made up of City Council members that track and address climate issues through monthly meetings. This committee is supported by a commission made up of residents, with environmental and social advocacy as well as public health backgrounds that also include technical experts that provide input on climate and health related issues. There are 97 actions in the CECAP that are set forward to reach 8 different sector goals. These actions are implemented by 17-20 different City departments, and are budgeted, and tracked under an annual Implementation Work Plan that is reported through the City Manager's Office. The director of the Office of Environmental Quality and Sustainability assigns responsibilities for climate actions and reviews results. City departments are responsible for specific climate actions that impact their departments. Each department assigns managers to manage climate actions in their department. Climate-specific actions are also address as a part of the budget priorities.
column16: Climate related issues are identified as one of the primary corner stones in most of the City's current and ongoing planning efforts:- Connect Dallas Mobility Plan (2021) included CECAP Transportation goals towards, sidewalks, transit, mobility, and micro-mobility options in addition to goals set for reducing parking, and implementing more transit-oriented development- The Dallas Urban Forest Plan (2021) was developed as one of the goals of the CECAP Urban Green Spaces Sector, and focusses on expanding green space and urban forest canopy, reducing heat island impacts, developing a tree inventory and other canopy management goals.- The Comprehensive Urban Agriculture Plan (2022) provides the detailed actions towards the climate related agriculture and food access goals set forward in the CECAP, focusing on increasing local food production and providing equitable access to healthy, locally grown foods. - The Hensley Field Redevelopment Plan (2022) is the redevelopment of a 700 acre former airfield into a multi-use development on a lake, and is being developed under the direction of \'piloting concepts from the CECAP\' including green infrastructure, tree canopy expansion, walkable, bikeable mixed use, urban agriculture, renewable energy generation/micro grid, and mixed income housing, along with commercial, and educational anchor institutions. Net Zero Carbon goals are being included into the design parameters for the site.- Economic Development Plan (2022) also included CECAP measures supporting sustainable development.- The Comprehensive Land Use Plan includes the CECAP as one of the primary guiding principles, and incorporates GIS mapping of sites with potential for pollutant sources, for implementing urban agriculture, along with habitat, heat island areas, and optimal locations for implementing green infrastructure, in addition to typical social, and economic considerations.- Staff worked with the Environmental Commission, and experts from the US Green Building Council (LEED), Architecture 2030, National Academy of Sciences, Carbon Leadership Forum, International Living Future Institute, Institute for Sustainable Infrastructure (Envision), Smart Surfaces Coalition and others to recommend technical specifications to be used for all horizontal (Infrastructure) and vertical construction (Buildings) in the 2024 Municipal Capital Bond Program to ensure net zero carbon-compliant construction per CECAP goals for 2030.Lastly, the Racial Equity Plan (2022) was revised at City Council direction because it did not include any actions to address environmental justice: new metrics were added to the plan based on relevant CECAP actions including neighborhood air quality programs, heat island mitigation, food access and brownfields remediation. Climate awareness and responsibility are clearly seen in the actions of managers and employees throughout the City. For example, the managers of the City's fleet are implementing the recommendations of the study that provided the road map to electrifying of all City non-emergency vehicles (however, leadership in first-responder departments are also independently discussing how they can transition as well). The City's energy manager has recently completed projects that have doubled the City's capacity to produce electricity from PV, and is actively implementing energy efficiency measures based on energy audits. These are two examples of a trend to better awareness of how City actions can impact the climate.
column17: Cost considerations for environmental and climate actions are now considered in all financial planning for planned City projects. In a recent community survey of City priorities to be considered for the FY 24 budget, Environment & Sustainability was listed as the top concern in one survey, and 3rd of 10 in another. The City Manager is shaping the city budget accordingly, and a process for implementing budgeting for climate is underway to shape the FY 24-25 budget process.
column18: The risks associated with the transition to a low-carbon economy have been very low to date and are not expected to be significant in the future. There is consensus that there are greater risks associated with the failure to implement this transition on a meaningful timeframe. Texas is estimated to have the highest increase in electricity demand due to climate change by mid-century; heat-related labor productivity will decline across all sectors in Texas and will likely cost the economy up to $12.5 billion statewide each year, with a 1-in-20 likelihood of costing more than $19.6 billion annually. Transition is imperative for Dallas' economy.

column15: eThekwini Municipality oversees climate-related issues through the Durban Climate Change Strategy (DCCS), Climate Action Plan (CAP), and the Climate Change Implementation Framework, supported by a governance structure that includes the forthcoming eThekwini Municipal Forum for Climate Change Committee and the Technical Task Team with its subcommittees. Progress on the Implementation Plan is monitored and reported every six months to ensure accountability. Oversight also extends to health, with alignment to South Africa's National Climate Change and Health Adaptation Plan, which addresses climate-related health risks through stronger surveillance, early warning systems, and knowledge sharing.\n\n
column16:
Climate-related events such as the April 2022 and April 2019 floods and the 2007 storm surge have underscored eThekwini's vulnerability to flooding, sea level rise, and extreme heat, driving the integration of climate resilience into master and development planning. Climate change is now embedded in Plan One of the Integrated Development Plan (IDP), with initiatives such as the Transformative Riverine Management Programme (TRMP) and community-based Flood Early Warning Systems enhancing catchment management and preparedness. To strengthen accountability, the City is developing Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) for programme owners under the Durban Climate Change Implementation Plan.

The Municipal Spatial Development Framework (SDF), reviewed annually under the Security and Emergency Services Portfolio Committee, now incorporates climate change, disaster risk reduction, and urban planning to ensure legislative compliance and risk-informed development. Sectoral integration has also advanced, with the Health Unit embedding climate resilience into water quality, food safety, pollution control, and disease surveillance.
column17:
Climate-related disasters, particularly the April 2022 flood, have placed severe strain on eThekwini's financial planning, forcing significant capital budget reallocations from long-term housing and service backlog reduction programmes to immediate disaster recovery. Funding has been redirected to provide temporary rental accommodation, permanent housing for storm victims, and to repair damaged water, sanitation, and electrification infrastructure.

Operational expenditure has also shifted toward resilience-building, including allocations to the TRMP Palmiet project and the Global Environmental Change research programme to strengthen evidence-based planning. The Health Unit's Vector Control Section is recapitalising its laboratory to improve vector identification capacity, while in the waste sector, reprioritisation of capital works and operational efficiencies are being pursued to stabilise systems within fixed fiscal reserves, balancing urgent recovery with long-term resilience.

column15: The City of Ekurhuleni (CoE) has recently revised the 2017 Climate Change Response Strategy/Climate Action Plan in 2025 to align with the City's commitment to the Paris Agreement, South Africa's Climate Change Act and the C40 Leadership Standards as part of the membership status. In addition, incorporate adaptation targets and actions which were missing in the 2017 version. This strategy has been approved by the Mayoral committee and details the climate risks and vulnerabilities that the City is faced with along with 2030 and 2050 targets to build climate resilience in the City. These targets are further supported by response plans (mitigation and adaptation) that have been signed by departments on various measures to be implemented to build resilience in the City. These response plans have been integrated into various Departmental business plans to ensure implementation. The CoE is committed to being a carbon-neutral city by 2050. Building on its Climate Change Response Strategy, and in collaboration with International Finance Corporation (IFC), the CoE developed a Green City Action Plan (GCAP) in 2022. This Green City Action Plan sets out actions that can help CoE meet its climate mitigation and sustainability targets. The plan has focused on four main sectors: energy, wastewater & water, transport and waste. The GCAP prioritizes implementation of 20 solutions, which are expected to support reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 of over 20%. In addition, the plan targets a 25% reduction in fossil fuel energy use, 20% reduction in private fossil fuel vehicle travel, 50% reduction in waste sent to landfill, and 20% improvement in water security. The City's Resilience and Just Transition Forum has become the coordinating body for all climate and resilience related actions across the various Departments. Moreover, the Forum also serves as a platform to track Departmental progress against the measures in the Green City Action Plan, Climate Change Response Plan and the Just Transition.
column16: The City has started ensuring that climate change risks and disaster risks are included in the screening of the City's Capital Investment Projects. This has been through the inclusion of climate change risks into the risk screening tool that is used by City Planning to screen and approve projects. The high priority climate hazards that could be included when looking at the settlement vulnerabilities within the city include floods, fires and strong winds (informed by disaster management). These form part of the adaptation criteria as secondary indicators (Risk indicators) as the Ekurhuleni 2030 targets would be the primary indicators. Maps of the floods and fires are available to within the City's GIS climate change database and in the 2025 Climate Change Response Strategy, with 2050 predictions also available. Examples of how the screening could be done has been provided of a few projects with the primary and secondary indicator as well as how these could be scored, they could have positive, negative or no alignment. The indicators will be used by climate change and disaster management department of the City to screen projects. The evaluation of the various CAPEX projects are done in such a manner that the scoring is fixed for the Climate change adaptation criteria with primary and secondary indicators, this is used for all the projects in the various categories. Each project is scored against both primary and secondary indicators with positive or negative impacts, those with no alignment are scored as such. In addition, the City has revised its Disaster Management Plan for the environment and climate change (2023/24 FY).
column17: The City has begun looking at the extent that climate risk and disaster risk can impact its capital investment project. This is through pre-feasibility screening of projects through the CAPEX Screening process which allows early consideration of these risks. Furthermore, the City with assistance from the National Treasury and World Bank are currently reviewing some Capital Infrastructure projects to look at to what extent climate change and disaster risk has been considered. This project is also proposing detailed financial implication of not considering climate risk in project planning. This project which is near completion will be used to drive the point for the need for early consideration of climate risks in projects. This project is spearheaded by the City's Climate Change division alongside the Enterprise Project management office as the implications are going to be policy wide needing to be implemented institutionally. The City is also looking at including climate change in the City-wide risk register, this would mean that all Departments need to account for it in their business plans.
column18: The City of Ekurhuleni Metropolitan Municipality is home to an estimated 4, 006,691 people and is an important industrial and logistics hub in Gauteng Province, South Africa. Through implementation of the Growth and Development Strategy 2055 (GDS 2055), the City aims to become a “delivering, capable, sustainable” city by 2055. The City has prioritised responding to climate change through various initiatives, including the implementation of its Green City Action Plan. The plan identifies actions including city-level policies, investments, and planning strategies that can help the City meet its climate mitigation and sustainability targets. Specific targets pursued in the Green City Action Plan, which are aligned with the City's existing Ekurhuleni+ Challenge 2030 targets, are as follows:-25% reduction in fossil fuel energy use -20% reduction in private fossil fuel vehicle kilometres travelled-50% reduction in waste sent to landfill -20% improvement in water security -20% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions. The Green City Action Plan will be implemented within the context of a national and global transition towards a low-carbon, sustainable and resilient economy and society. As the national and local economy transitions away from fossil fuels, jobs within carbon intensive sectors may be deprioritised as new jobs are created in the green economy. Some carbon intensive value chains in Ekurhuleni remain at risk and will need to be substituted to achieve the City's goal to be carbon neutral by 2050. These will include: •Coal to electricity: Coal-powered electricity prices to increase, as renewable energy becomes more affordable.•Crude oil to petrol: Job losses at refineries due to lower fuel demand as alternatives become more accessible and affordable. •Combustion engine vehicles: job losses at manufacturing and assembly plants; and decreased demand for some raw inputs into combustion engine vehicles. The City of Ekurhuleni labour market currently faces the following structural challenges such as: -Already high levels of unemployment and economic inactivity. -Worsening youth participation in economic activity. -Relatively high salaries in carbon-intensive sectors; and -Decline in representation of previously disadvantaged individuals in the workforce. Therefore, it is imperative that the City ensures that the move towards a low-carbon economy is just and fair its most vulnerable population. The Green City Action Plan is supported by the 2025 Climate Change Response Strategy which extends targets to 2050 and incorporates adaptation. The City acknowledges that the transition must be well-managed and must be informed by an inclusive stakeholder consultation which takes multiple perspectives into account and aims to leave no one behind. To facilitate inclusion, the City integrated the existing Resilience Forum with the Just Transition initiative which represented a key step towards planning and implementing an inclusive, sustainable transition in the City of Ekurhuleni and ensuring climate resilience. The forum will seeks to feed into provincial and national just transition dialogues and planning and consider climate change in all city level projects. This will ensure that those processes are more inclusive and take the local context into account. To date, the City hosts quarterly Resilience and Just Transition forum.

Desde 2013, Fortaleza vem trilhando um percurso consistente em direção à resiliência climática, por meio de acordos, projetos e políticas que reforçam os compromissos de mitigação e adaptação e contribuem para o alcance das Contribuições Nacionalmente Determinadas (NDCs) no âmbito do Acordo de Paris, além de alinhar-se à Política Nacional sobre Mudança do Clima. Nesse período, a cidade aderiu a compromissos internacionais como o Pacto Global de Prefeitos pelo Clima e a Energia (GCoM); a campanha Race to Zero, promovida pela ONU, que estabelece a meta de emissões líquidas zero até 2050; a iniciativa Construindo Cidades Resilientes (MCR 2030), voltada a tornar as cidades inclusivas, seguras e resilientes; e associações estratégicas como a rede ICLEI - Governos Locais pela Sustentabilidade, com participação em projetos como Urban-LEDS I e II, SD Labs, além do Fórum de Secretários de Meio Ambiente das Capitais Brasileiras (CB27). Em 2024, Fortaleza foi oficialmente reconhecida como cidade-membro da rede C40, consolidando sua posição de liderança no cenário climático global.
No campo do planejamento, Fortaleza elaborou em 2020 seu Plano Local de Ação Climática (PLAC), estruturando metas e ações integradas para mitigação e adaptação. Em 2025, esse instrumento está passando por atualização e passará a ser denominado Plano de Ação Climática (PAC), reforçando seu caráter institucional e abrangente. A atualização está sendo subsidiada por dados oriundos de diferentes instâncias participativas ocorridas ao longo de 2025 — como a 1ª Conferência Municipal de Meio Ambiente de Fortaleza, a Conferência das Cidades e os Fóruns Territoriais — cujas proposições foram sistematizadas e priorizadas no âmbito do Fórum Climático de Fortaleza (FORCLIMA).
Outro marco importante é a elaboração e envio à Câmara Municipal da Política Municipal sobre Mudança do Clima (PMMC), que estabelece princípios, diretrizes e instrumentos para o enfrentamento das mudanças climáticas. Essa política propõe mecanismos de planejamento, monitoramento e financiamento climático; define uma estratégia integrada para ações de mitigação e adaptação; institui a elaboração de planos setoriais (como o Plano Municipal de Contingência para Desastres Climáticos - PMCDC, em construção pela Defesa Civil com apoio do Governo Federal e entrega prevista para 2026); e estabelece periodicidade para acompanhamento e atualização dos documentos.
O Índice de Vulnerabilidade Climática de Fortaleza (IVCC), elaborado em 2020, também está sendo atualizado de forma integrada. Parte de suas análises estão sendo incorporadas à Análise de Riscos e Vulnerabilidades Climáticas (ARVC) que integra o novo PAC, enquanto outra parte se desdobrará no Plano Setorial de Riscos elaborado pela Defesa Civil, fortalecendo o planejamento preventivo frente a desastres. Essa atualização é apoiada por relatórios técnicos recentes de áreas de risco, que revisaram poligonais e graus de risco de alagamentos, inundações e movimentos de massa em diferentes regionais da cidade, incluindo vistorias de campo e participação comunitária.
A supervisão das ações climáticas ocorre de forma coordenada pelo Gabinete de Governança Climática (GGC), criado por decreto em 2022 e fortalecido em 2025 como espaço de decisão intersetorial. O GGC reúne gestores de múltiplas secretarias e órgãos municipais e funciona como secretariado deliberativo, garantindo a transversalidade da pauta climática e a execução dos compromissos assumidos. O Observatório Climático, lançado em 2025, complementa essa estrutura, atuando como ferramenta de transparência e centralização de dados para monitoramento contínuo e apoio à tomada de decisão. O Comitê Climático, previsto na minuta da PMMC, será incorporado como instância técnico-executiva de acompanhamento.
O engajamento e a transparência política também foram fortalecidos. O FORCLIMA consolidou-se como instância permanente de participação social consultiva, com três edições realizadas em 2025, das quais duas dedicadas à minuta da PMMC e à priorização de propostas coletadas em espaços participativos. Essa articulação social garante maior legitimidade às decisões e contribui para a integração entre poder público, sociedade civil, academia e setor privado.
Dessa forma, Fortaleza conta hoje com um arcabouço de supervisão climática que combina compromissos internacionais, instrumentos locais robustos (PAC, PMMC, IVCC/ARVC, PMCDC), órgãos de governança intersetorial (GGC e Comitê Climático), mecanismos de monitoramento e transparência (Observatório Climático) e instâncias participativas (FORCLIMA). Esse arranjo fortalece a capacidade adaptativa da cidade, garante alinhamento entre planos e políticas e assegura acompanhamento contínuo das metas, mas também evidencia a necessidade de manter a atualização periódica das bases de dados, de consolidar os planos setoriais e de assegurar recursos financeiros estáveis para a execução das ações previstas.
column16:
O processo de revisão do Plano Diretor Participativo e Sustentável de Fortaleza (PDPS) foi diretamente impactado pelos desafios climáticos enfrentados pelo município, incorporando de forma mais robusta premissas e diretrizes relacionadas à adaptação, mitigação e resiliência urbana. Atualmente em fase de audiências públicas e sistematização para minuta de lei, o Plano Diretor integra a agenda climática a partir de suas políticas setoriais, notadamente no Política de Meio Ambiente e Resiliência Urbana, que organiza de maneira transversal as ações e instrumentos em cinco sub-políticas: Biodiversidade (Paisagem e Áreas Protegidas, Fauna e Flora), Mudanças Climáticas (Adaptação e Resiliência Climática), Capital Natural e Serviços Ecossistêmicos, Águas Urbanas e Resíduos Sólidos (Saneamento Ambiental e Recursos Hídricos).
Essa reestruturação foi impulsionada por problemas concretos enfrentados pela cidade, como inundações urbanas recorrentes, ondas de calor, perda de cobertura vegetal e pressão sobre mananciais e ecossistemas frágeis, que evidenciam a urgência de um modelo de desenvolvimento urbano adaptado às mudanças climáticas. Dessa forma, o tratamento aos sistemas ambientais passou a ocupar posição relevante na dimensão espacial do planejamento, reconhecendo que o equilíbrio entre expansão urbana, preservação dos recursos naturais e promoção da resiliência é condição necessária para garantir qualidade de vida e sustentabilidade a longo prazo.
Para assegurar a efetividade das ações previstas, o Plano Diretor prevê que suas diretrizes sejam regulamentadas por legislações urbanísticas complementares — como a Lei de Parcelamento, Uso e Ocupação do Solo (LPUOS) e o Código da Cidade — além de planos setoriais conduzidos pelas secretarias finalísticas. Com isso, os problemas relacionados ao clima não apenas influenciaram o conteúdo do Plano Diretor, mas redefiniram sua lógica de desenvolvimento urbano, orientando políticas públicas para uma cidade mais justa, sustentável e preparada para enfrentar os riscos climáticos. Mais informações podem ser obtidas no site: https://planodiretor.fortaleza.ce.gov.br/
column17:
A emergência climática vem sendo crescentemente abordada no planejamento financeiro de Fortaleza, exigindo que o município estruture investimentos de forma transversal, integrando ações de mitigação, adaptação e resiliência ao orçamento público. Entre 2021 e 2024, foram mobilizados aproximadamente R$ 1,7 bilhão em iniciativas voltadas a energia, saneamento, mobilidade e resiliência climática, com destaque para o Programa de Infraestrutura em Educação e Saneamento (PROINFRA), responsável pelas maiores obras de drenagem e pavimentação permeável, fundamentais para a adaptação em áreas vulneráveis. A gestão, requalificação e recuperação de áreas verdes concentraram mais de 11% desse montante, reforçando a integração entre preservação ambiental e infraestrutura urbana.

Outros investimentos estratégicos incluem o Monitoramento da Qualidade do Ar, desenvolvido em parceria com a Universidade Federal do Ceará, com a instalação de uma Estação Móvel (EMQAR) e uma rede de 25 monitores de baixo custo, além da realização de estudos técnicos como a atualização dos inventários de emissões de GEE, que já somam mais de R$ 2 milhões nesse período. Esses recursos demonstram que o enfrentamento dos impactos climáticos vem orientando a priorização orçamentária do município.

A minuta da Política Municipal sobre Mudança do Clima (PMMC), elaborada intersetorialmente por grupo técnico vinculado ao Gabinete de Governança Climática e aprovada por esse secretariado, traz avanços importantes ao prever o uso de fundos municipais já existentes, como o FUNDEMA (Fundo de Defesa do Meio Ambiente) e o FUNDURB (Fundo de Desenvolvimento Urbano), para financiar ações climáticas. Essa integração reconhece que o enfrentamento da crise climática envolve tanto preservação ambiental quanto investimentos em infraestrutura, mobilidade e saneamento, criando novas possibilidades de financiamento cruzado e assegurando maior estabilidade para a execução das ações.

Dessa forma, o planejamento financeiro de Fortaleza passou a ser diretamente impactado pela pauta climática, não apenas pela necessidade de ampliar investimentos em resiliência e adaptação, mas também pela criação de mecanismos institucionais de financiamento climático. Apesar dos desafios, a cidade tem avançado na consolidação de um modelo de desenvolvimento urbano mais sustentável, resiliente e inclusivo.
column18:
O estabelecimento de mecanismos eficazes para transformar o processo de descarbonização em crescimento e desenvolvimento sustentável é um desafio para Fortaleza, trazendo riscos significativos no curto e médio prazo. Esses riscos se concentram principalmente nos setores de serviços públicos concedidos — como transporte, energia e saneamento —, em que a necessidade de adaptação tecnológica e de redução de emissões pode pressionar o equilíbrio econômico-financeiro dos contratos vigentes e dificultar a manutenção da qualidade dos serviços. Um exemplo concreto é a descarbonização do transporte público, que demanda investimentos elevados em eletrificação da frota e infraestrutura de recarga, ao mesmo tempo em que deve assegurar tarifas acessíveis e sustentabilidade operacional.

Outro risco relevante está na viabilidade financeira da transição, que depende da mobilização de recursos estáveis e da integração de fundos municipais já existentes (como FUNDEMA e FUNDURB) com operações de crédito voltadas a investimentos de impacto sustentável. Caso esses instrumentos não sejam devidamente regulamentados e articulados, há o risco de fragilidade no financiamento das ações de mitigação e adaptação. Também se destaca a necessidade de fortalecer mecanismos de regulação e análise de risco climático, garantindo segurança jurídica e previsibilidade para investidores e concessionárias.

Além disso, a transição para uma economia de baixo carbono pode gerar desafios sociais se não for acompanhada de estratégias inclusivas, como programas de capacitação profissional, incentivos à economia verde local e apoio às populações mais vulneráveis. A governança já estruturada pelo Gabinete de Governança Climática, o Observatório Climático e o FORCLIMA mitiga parte desses riscos ao assegurar maior transparência, participação social e acompanhamento intersetorial. Apesar dos desafios, Fortaleza tem construído bases sólidas para transformar esses riscos em oportunidades, consolidando um ambiente favorável à inovação, à atração de investimentos verdes e ao fortalecimento de uma cidade mais resiliente, inclusiva e sustentável.

column15: El Área Metropolitana de Guadalajara (AMG) es la única metrópoli en México que cuenta con un mecanismo de gobernanza y coordinación que integra a los tres órdenes de gobierno (municipal, estatal y federal) y representantes ciudadanos, con el fin de planear, gestionar y administrar políticas públicas metropolitanas. Comprendiendo cuatro componentes esenciales (político, técnico, ciudadano y de gestión) que promueven mecanismos de participación y toma de decisiones, facilitan una mayor previsibilidad y coherencia con los instrumentos de planeación y desarrollo metropolitanos. - El componente político está representado por la Junta de Coordinación Metropolitana (JCM).- El componente técnico es el Instituto Metropolitano de Planeación y Gestión del Desarrollo del Área Metropolitana de Guadalajara (IMEPLAN).- El componente ciudadano está representado por el Consejo Ciudadano Metropolitano (CCM).- Componente de gestión está compuesto por las agencias metropolitanas (Agencia Metropolitana de Bosques Urbanos y la Agencia Metropolitana de Infraestructura para la Movilidad y en proceso de planificación la Agencia Metropolitana de Residuos). Dentro de este modelo de gobernanza, el IMEPLAN se instituye como el órgano técnico articulador del sector metropolitano y coordinador de las Instancias de Coordinación Metropolitana, entre ellas, las mesas metropolitanas como mecanismos de trabajo donde participan funcionarios(as) de distintas áreas para construir de manera colectiva las políticas públicas y proyectos de escala metropolitana cuya aprobación depende en gran medida de la JCM. Un hito fundamental en cuanto a la supervisión de asuntos relacionados con la metrópoli fue el lanzamiento del Plan de Acción Climática del AMG (PACmetro) en 2020, pues a partir del mismo se ha fortalecido la gobernanza climática del AMG, ya que fue aceptado por los plenos de los nueve Ayuntamientos que conforman el AMG, con los que se da inicio a los procesos formales de integración con los instrumentos municipales de planeación y gestión existentes. Posteriormente, fue instalada la Mesa Metropolitana de Acción Climática y Energía (inicialmente Mesa Metropolitana de Gestión del Plan de Acción Climática del Área Metropolitana de Guadalajara - PACmetro) como un órgano que ha dado seguimiento a los avances de los compromisos climáticos de la metrópoli, siendo de gran relevancia, pues constituye el espacio de donde derivan otros esfuerzos para transversalizar la acción climática e integrarla en políticas y proyectos de diversas escalas y niveles de gobierno que inciden en la metrópoli. Para el monitoreo, evaluación y reporte de la acción climática, en específico sobre los riesgos climáticos, cuenta con la plataforma web denominada Sistema Informático para el Monitoreo la Evaluación y Reporte (SIMER) donde los líderes municipales, estatales y metropolitanos que están vinculados con la adaptación ante el riesgo climático, reportan los avances en la materia (http://simer.imeplan.mx/index.php).\nAsí mismo, la agenda climática metropolitana se ve robustecida a través de la asistencia técnica por parte de Imeplan en conjunto con el Grupo de Liderazgo Climático C40 al municipio de Guadalajara, para la implementación de dos acciones de alto impacto (Zonas Bajas en Emisiones y Eficiencia Energética en Edificaciones) 2022-2025.
column16: El proceso de desarrollo y apropiación del Plan de Acción Climática del AMG (PACmetro) por parte de los 9 municipios que conforman la metrópoli (El Salto, Guadalajara, Ixtlahuacán de los Membrillos, Juanacatlán, San Pedro Tlaquepaque, Tlajomulco de Zúñiga, Tonalá, Zapopan y Zapotlanejo), implica que se internalicen los asuntos climáticos y puedan incorporarlos en la actualización de sus propios instrumento de planeación (tales como los Planes Municipales de Desarrollo y Gobernanza, los Programas de Ordenamiento Ecológico Local, o los Programas Municipales de Cambio Climático, entre otros). Así, de conformidad con el marco normativo aplicable a nivel estatal, la transversalización de cambio climático se lleva a cabo mediante la incorporación de políticas y estrategias en materia de cambio climático dentro de sus planes municipales de desarrollo, para el caso de los municipios metropolitanos, lo hacen en línea con lo que establece la ruta climática metropolitana, por lo que una vez publicados reflejarán dichos asuntos. Asimismo, el IMEPLAN publicó en 2024 la actualización del PLAN de Movilidad Urbana Sustentable (PIMUS) y el Programa de Desarrollo Metropolitano (PDM)/Plan de Ordenamiento Territorial Metropolitano del Área Metropolitana de Guadalajara (POTmet), instrumento de planeación que busca orientar el rumbo y evolución de la metrópoli. Cabe resaltar que dichos instrumentos clave, incorporan ya el componente climático, alineados a criterios de la hoja de ruta climática representada por el PACmetro.
column17:
La acción climática ha cobrado gran importancia en la planificación financiera del estado de Jalisco, en el que se inscribe el Área Metropolitana de Guadalajara (AMG), lo que explica el creciente presupuesto que ha sido destinado al Anexo Transversal de Cambio Climático dentro del presupuesto de egresos del estado, pasando de $3179022520 (MXN) en 2019 a $6117091875 en el ejercicio fiscal 2024 y $6506853699 para 2025. En el Anexo Transversal del Presupuesto de Egresos del Estado de Jalisco es donde concurren Programas Presupuestarios, Componentes de estos y/o Unidades Responsables, cuyos recursos son destinados a obras, acciones y servicios vinculados a la atención del cambio climáticos, que en parte abonan a la implementación de acción climática en el AMG.

Enlace al Anexo transversal de cambio climático: https://presupuestociudadano.jalisco.gob.mx/web/content/support.material.line/1554/document/V.%20e.%20Anexo%20Transversal%20_%20Cambio%20clim%C3%A1tico.pdf 

En la metrópoli, demostrar el compromiso multisectorial y multiescala de diversos actores con metas climáticas, ha favorecido sustentar y formular proyectos para acceder a financiamiento y apoyo en el ámbito metropolitano a través de IMEPLAN. A finales del 2021 se asignó una subvención por parte de la Unión Europea al AMG, para el desarrollo de la acción Metro Resilience Guadalajara, la cual comprende, entre otros, la creación de la Estrategia de Resiliencia Metropolitana y el pilotaje de una acción climática en materia de residuos sólidos para implementar centros de acopio y promover los principios de economía circular mediante la instalación de 9 Puntos Verdes Metropolitanos (1 en cada municipio de la metrópoli), concluyendo en 2025. 

En 2022 la agenda climática metropolitana por sus avances y liderazgo, se ve seleccionada como una de las ciudades acreedoras de la asistencia técnica financiada por la Embajada Británica e implementada por el Grupo de Liderazgo Climático C40, para apoyar al municipio de Guadalajara y a Imeplan en la implementación de dos acciones de alto impacto (Zonas Bajas en Emisiones y Eficiencia Energética en Edificaciones) 2022-2025, que a la fecha se ha traducido en un apoyo de $430,752.55 dolares.

Con base en esta experiencia, y mediante el fortalecimiento de la gobernanza climática en la metrópoli será posible identificar con mayor precisión el impacto que tiene dar seguimiento a la agenda climática en términos financieros, a partir de la estructuración y proyectos presupuestales, los esfuerzos para la procuración de recursos y la gestión para obtener acceso a capital. A escala local, el municipio de Guadalajara dio a conocer en 2023 su “Compromiso Verde”, un conjunto de acciones públicas y privadas —derivadas del PACmetro— que impulsa la sustentabilidad y busca detonar la competitividad económica, así como garantizar el desarrollo social incluyente y respetuoso con el medio ambiente. En él se contemplan más de 40 acciones que impactan de manera positiva a la capital de Jalisco y está ligado a un presupuesto verde que para 2023 consistió en 434 millones de pesos mexicanos.

El uso de combustibles fósiles se ha asociado con numerosas problemáticas en México, mismas que se reflejan en diferentes escalas, como la metropolitana. Al respecto de las mismas, GreenPeace reporta daños a la salud, ausentismo laboral y efectos desiguales en la población. https://www.greenpeace.org/mexico/blog/9853/como-afectan-los-combustibles-fosiles-a-la-salud-humana/
Por su parte, el Instituto Mexicano para la Competitividad A.C. elaboró el reporte: ¿Cuánto nos cuesta la contaminación del aire en México? (2013) En el que se estiman los impactos en salud y en productividad para 34 ciudades mexicanas, entre ellas Guadalajara. https://imco.org.mx/wp-content/uploads/2013/09/Anexo-Metodol%C3%B3gico-24Sep13.pdf 

Así mismo, en la realización de las consultorías para la implementación de las dos Acciones Seleccionadas de Alto Impacto (SHIA, por sus siglas en inglés), en la ciudad de Guadalajara y con escalamiento planeado para toda la metrópoli con acompañamiento de C40 de 2022-2025, se han solicitado análisis de impactos/riesgos y sus alternativas de mitigación para dos acciones climáticas (Zonas de Bajas Emisiones y Eficiencia Energética en Edificaciones Públicas).

column15: The City of Miami's Office of Resilience and Sustainability (ORS) exists as an independent office within the City of Miami. The Chief Resilience Officer reports directly to the City Manager's Office. ORS is responsible for providing expertise on climate, resilience, and environmental best-practices to City leadership and departments, leading City-wide strategy on climate adaptation and carbon mitigation through the implementation of the Resilient305, Miami Forever Carbon Neutral, and Miami Forever Climate Ready plans. The Chief Resilience Officer chairs a monthly Resilience Action Group (RAG) convening Directors from multiple City departments to collaborate on resilience initiatives. ORS is responsible for conducting biannual greenhouse gas inventories, both community wide and government operations and quarterly tracking of the 180+ resilience actions included in the City's resilience strategies. In relation to sea level rise and flooding, the Department of Resilience and Public Works manages the City's stormwater system and oversees the implementation of the City's updated Stormwater Master Plan (2021) that factors sea level rise into capital projects and level of service. The Building Department oversees floodplain management and the City's participation in the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Community Rating Score (CRS) Program. In 2023, the Planning Department led an Evaluation & Appraisal Review (EAR) of the Miami Comprehensive Neighborhood Plan, setting a vision for Miami through 2035, which integrated additional long-term climate considerations. This is a process that the City conducts every seven years, as required by State Statute. The Miami Comprehensive Neighborhood Plan includes policies adopted by Miami City Commission related to addressing sea-level rising and flooding. In relation to tropical cyclones and extreme heat, the Fire Department Division of Emergency Management leads the City's preparedness, response, and recovery. The Emergency Manager leads the Emergency Operations Center (EOC) during natural disasters when activated and, with the City Manager, directs internal and external stakeholders. In 2019, the City of Miami consolidated the Sea Level Rise Committee and Waterfront Advisory Board into the Climate Resilience Committee. The charge of the committee has expanded to include recommending, to the Commission, changes to City Code and policy that will help the City thrive in the face of all climate change threats and providing input on City-owned waterfront land use issues when tasked. The Committee meets monthly.
column16: The City of Miami recognizes the threat posed by climate change and strives to consider the anticipated impacts into all planning activities. In 2019, City of Miami declared a state of \'Climate Emergency\' and strives to incorporate climate considerations into all elements of planning. The City of Miami has acknowledged flooding, sea level rise, extreme heat, and intensifying storms as its main climate threats. The City of Miami has developed climate action plans to address adaptation and mitigation to reduce greenhouse gases and increase energy efficiency. These are the Miami Forever Climate Ready Plan, the Miami Forever Carbon Neutral Plan, and the Miami Forever Climate Ready: Extreme Heat Plan. City of Miami updated our Stormwater Master Plan to integrate sea level rise projections and advise on infrastructure needed to manage flooding. The adopted Miami21 form-based zoning code takes climate-related issues into consideration. Waterfront design guidelines for Miami's most climate-vulnerable infrastructure is subject to advisory by the Climate Resilience Committee. The Climate Resilience Committee also provides additional climate mitigation and adaptation advisory to City leadership. The Miami Comprehensive Neighborhood Plan (MCNP) contains goals, objectives, and policies directing the City to pursue planning, redevelopment, design, and management practices which take resilience and mitigation of projected climate impacts into consideration. In January 2023, the City Commission adopted Ordinance 14135 updating the Miami Comprehensive Neighborhood Plan (MCNP) to include development principles that address the “Peril of Flood.” The state of Florida requires that all coastal communities provide development and redevelopment principles, strategies, and engineering solutions that reduce the flood risk in coastal areas that result from high-tide events, storm surge, flash floods, stormwater runoff, and the related impacts of sea-level rise in their comprehensive plans. Under Florida Statute, the City of Miami is obligated to conduct an Evaluation and Appraisal Review (EAR), led by the Planning Department, to determine whether the need exists to amend the comprehensive plan to reflect changes in state requirements and community conditions every 7 years. The City updated the MCNP to include climate considerations and it came into effect in May 2024. In 2022, the City Commission adopted updated policies on addressing sea-level rising and resiliency concerns throughout the City of Miami, Florida Statute requires the designation of a “Coastal High Hazard Area” subject to additional protections and policies meant to preserve safety and mitigate disaster impact. The MCNP's Coastal Management Element addresses the additional restrictions, requirements, and designations for properties and projects within the CHHA. The Streetscape Master Plan includes the mitigation of climate impacts as a guiding purpose. Specifically, the Streetscape master plan aims to address extreme heat impacts and promote multi-modal transportation. City of Miami capital projects consider the Southeast Florida Regional Climate Change Compact's Unified Sea Level Rise standards. In addition, City of Miami passed a resolution (R-22-0419) directing that the City Manager adopts a policy to require that City of Miami capital projects that address stormwater management or flood mitigation take into consideration and address (as appropriate and feasible) heat mitigation, heat and stormwater monitoring, greenhouse gas reduction, and non-carbon-emitting mobility. The City developed procurement guidance and an internal policy to implement this directive.
column17: The City of Miami passed a $400 million General Obligation Bond in 2017 to fund climate-resilient infrastructure projects. The intent of Miami Forever Bond is to build a stronger, more resilient future for Miami, alleviating existing and future risks to residents, the economy, tourism, and the city's legacy. The Bond is funding a series of projects dedicated to climate mitigation and adaptation across five categories: Sea-Level Rise and Flood Prevention, Roadways, Parks and Cultural Facilities, Public Safety and Affordable Housing. In FY 22-23, Bond funding was allocated to a total of 33 capital projects. The City actively seeks grant funding to leverage these funds and multiply their impact. According to the City's 2021 updated Stormwater Master Plan, the City has $3.5-5 billion in needs for stormwater infrastructure alone to update the current system to be responsive to sea level rise and increased levels of service. In addition, City of Miami incorporates climate planning into its budgeting consideration through input provided by the City of Miami's Chief Resilience Officer to City leadership during the annual budget planning process. City of Miami has been asked during credit rating evaluations by agencies such as Fitch Ratings and S&P Global Ratings to disclose its policies and programs related to climate resilience and emergency preparedness to exemplify strong social and financial management.
column18: Reputation: Miami is globally one of the most vulnerable cities to climate change impacts. As such, the City of Miami has an implicit call to response and leadership on climate issues including the transition to a low-carbon economy. Failure to meet goals related to resilience and sustainability may be more likely to draw significant negative attention from media and the public and have an outsized impact on reputation. Market: The real estate industry is a significant sector of Miami's economy, and the City possesses a high concentration of flood vulnerable real estate. Unless adaptation and mitigation goals are met, one of the City's most prominent sectors could suffer adverse impacts which may threaten future investments. Considering the prominence of this sector, the City of Miami has a uniquely strong opportunity to provide significant mitigation through development of more sustainable building construction and operation practices. Net-zero buildings and low-embodied carbon are crucial for Miami to have a successful low-carbon economy. Market: Rising insurance rates are already beginning to impact City of Miami residents. The City of Miami improved its FEMA CRS score to a Class 6 in 2022, thus securing lower flood insurance rates for residents. Home insurance, flood insurance, and other costs to protect against the increased impacts of flooding and storm surge events are generally rising. Current and emerging regulations: State of Florida legislation has both aided and constrained City of Miami's climate resilience efforts. In 2021, SB1954/HB7019 was passed establishing the Resilient Florida program to “enhance [Stat]e efforts to protect [Florida's] inland waterways, coastlines, shores and coral reefs, which serve as invaluable natural defenses against sea level rise.” Since its establishment in 2021, the State of Florida has invested a total of $1.8 billion “to ensure state and local communities are prepared to deal with the impacts of sea level rise, intensified storms, and flooding.” The State of Florida is supportive of adaptation efforts but has passed several laws preempting sustainability and carbon mitigation action. In 2008, the State of Florida pre-empted local governments from regulating plastic bags. Since then, an amendment to also limit regulation on plastic straws was passed by both the State House (HB771) and Senate but then was vetoed by the Governor (2019), and attempts were made in the 2023 and 2024 legislative sessions to reintroduce legislation to preempt municipalities from passing plastic straw bans but both ultimately failed. In 2021, SB1128/HB919 “Preemption Over Restriction of Utility Services” was passed prohibiting municipalities from “restricting or prohibiting the types or fuel sources of energy production used, delivered, converted, or supplied by certain entities to customers.” This legislation prevents municipalities from adopting electrification policies. In 2024, SB1084 was passed “Preempting the regulation of electric vehicle charging stations to the state; prohibiting local governmental entities from enacting or enforcing such regulations.” As a result of the rulemaking process completed in May 2025, this preemption extends to the regulation of supporting infrastructure thus nullifying the City's EV Capability Ordinance. In 2024, there was an attempt to pass legislation to preempt local regulations on gas-powered leaf blowers. The proposal moved forward as a one-year moratorium and companion study funded by the State but was ultimately vetoed by the Governor. Technology: In 2023 the US Economic Development Administration designated Miami-Dade County as the South Florida ClimateReady Tech Hub, now known as South Florida's Risk and Resilience Tech Hub. In 2024 they recommended $19 million of funding for the region to further invest in flood and coastal protection projects made with clean concrete, development of workforce development programs, and fostering a market for private investment in climate technology. Safety: Increased incidence of extreme heat makes ensuring reliable energy access for all residents a critical safety need as we transition our energy economy. Local temperature and weather conditions as well as infrastructure limitations through the surrounding metro area facilitate single-use vehicle transportation. As such, efforts to reduce urban heat island effect and mitigate extreme heat are vital to the achievement of both adaptation and mitigation goals. Energy Security: City of Miami is subject to extreme storms and storm surge. As Miamians transition to electric vehicles and electrified appliances, we need to ensure our energy resources grow and develop in concert with that transition and that carbon-free energy sources are prioritized. Disposal of batteries will also need to be considered.

A través del eje rector de Ciudad Sostenible, descrito en el Plan Municipal de Desarrollo 2024-2027 (PMD) de Monterrey se busca la implementación de programas incluyentes y efectivos que respondan a la problemática actual de la degradación ambiental. 

Dichos proyectos, se encuentran alineados a los Objetivos de Desarrollo Sostenible y a la Agenda 2030, con el fin de construir una ciudad más resiliente, sostenible, y regenerativa. 

El municipio de Monterrey cuenta con una Secretaría de Desarrollo Urbano Sostenible (SEDUSO), que alberga a la Dirección para un Desarrollo Verde, entidad encargada de liderar estrategias locales para la adaptación y mitigación del cambio climático. 

Bajo este esquema y para poder ejecutar sus labores, la Dirección para un Desarrollo Verde colabora con otras Direcciones y Secretarías del municipio, para integrar acciones en ejes transversales como: infraestructura urbana, servicios públicos, educación, salud pública, inclusión y protección de comunidades vulnerables ante el cambio climático, entre otros. 

Como parte de la estrategia local, se ha trabajado en la integración de las perspectivas y propuestas de la ciudadanía, academia, sector privado, y organizaciones de la sociedad civil en los proyectos de política climática desarrollados e implementados a nivel subnacional.
column16:
Temas relacionados con el cambio climático han impactado de manera significativa diversas áreas de planeación e implementación del gobierno municipal, por lo que se busca constantemente tener más y mejor comunicación con otras Secretarías y organismos. 

Dicha comunicación permite coordinar programas que incluyen desde su planeación, consideraciones en torno a la crisis climática que vivimos y cómo afecta de manera desproporcionada a las poblaciones más vulnerables de nuestra ciudad. 

La política pública estatal, como el Programa Estatal de Cambio Climático del Estado de Nuevo León y Zona Metropolitana de Monterrey (PECC NL y ZMM) y el Plan Integral para la Gestión Estratégica de la Calidad del Aire (PIGECA) están reflejados directamente en la política municipal como en el PMD.
column17:
En aras de abarcar las problemáticas ambientales originadas ante la crisis climática actual, la Secretaría de Desarrollo Urbano Sostenible (SEDUSO) tiene un centro de costos específico para la Dirección para la Atención del Cambio Climático. De este presupuesto es donde se trabaja para las actividades diarias, los programas y los eventos relacionados a la acción climática y su planeación. 

Además, se busca constantemente canalizar fondos nacionales e internacionales por medio de convocatorias. 

Aunado a lo anterior, en el Reglamento de Cambio Climático del Municipio de Monterrey se establece la creación del 'Fondo Municipal para el Cambio Climático', el cuál designará recursos de manera exclusiva para la implementación de acciones de mitigación y adaptación para enfrentar los efectos adversos del cambio climático, con especial énfasis en comunidades vulnerables.
column18:
La transición hacia una economía de bajo carbono sigue siendo un reto a nivel local. Sin embargo, para alcanzar la descarbonización, es necesario contar con ciertas condiciones habilitadoras, tales como: 

1. Gobernanza climática colaborativa, eficaz y de largo plazo. 
2. Un sistema de financiamiento consolidado.
3. Desarrollo, innovación y adopción tecnológica.
4. Aumento de capacidades institucionales.
5. Marco regulatorio robusto a nivel nacional, estatal y local. 

Al tratarse de grandes cambios estructurales y sistémicos, la ruta de descarbonización debe ser liderada por la iniciativa pública y debe estar acompañada constantemente por la iniciativa privada y el sector social.

column16: O Plano Diretor do Recife inaugurou a Política de Resiliência e Adaptação Climática estruturada a partir do diagnóstico das vulnerabilidades do território e da necessidade de mitigar riscos associados a chuvas intensas, ilhas de calor e elevação do nível do mar. A partir desse direcionamento, o Plano Diretor subdivide a cidade em Macrozona do Ambiente Natural e Cultural (MANC) e Macrozona do Ambiente Construído (MAC). Essa divisão orienta o ordenamento territorial com base em critérios ambientais e de resiliência climática. A MAC promove intensificação da ocupação, uma vez que possui maior capacidade de absorver o adensamento urbano sustentável, enquanto a MANC assume função de proteção, recuperação e integração dos sistemas naturais e culturais, exigindo maior controle sobre os impactos das novas ocupações.\nA nova lei de parcelamento, uso e ocupação do solo (LPUOS) operacionaliza essa política ao estabelecer parâmetros urbanísticos e ambientais mais restritivos para a MANC. Também institui a Taxa de Contribuição Ambiental (TCA), mecanismo associado à Taxa de Solo Natural (TSN) que promove a utilização de Soluções Baseadas na Natureza, exigindo a implantação de medidas de desempenho ambiental no lote, como pisos permeáveis, telhados e fachadas verdes, preservação e plantio de árvores, arborização em faixas de rolamento e volumes adicionais de reservatórios de retardo, ampliando a capacidade de retenção e infiltração das águas pluviais, em alguns casos abastecendo diretamente o lençol freático.\nEsses instrumentos consolidam a incorporação das variáveis climáticas ao planejamento urbano e reforçam a adaptação, a resiliência e a infraestrutura verde como bases estruturadoras do desenvolvimento urbano do Recife.
