El Consejo Ambiental del Medellín, adoptado por Acuerdo municipal 067 de 2017, representa el máximo órgano del Sistema de Gestión Ambiental de Medellín y se establece como un espacio de concertación y coordinación en el cual se discuten las políticas ambientales. Este escenario de deliberación es presidido por el alcalde o su delegado y cuenta con representación de los departamentos y secretarías con funciones ambientales, la academia, el sector empresarial y comunitario. El Consejo Ambiental de Medellín está definido como instancia del nivel de coordinación administrativa para la implementación del Plan de Acción Climática a través del cual se asumen compromisos institucionales en diferentes niveles de gobierno.El Comité temático interinstitucional de Cambio Climático es una instancia conformada por profesionales y técnicos delegados de los departamentos y secretarías con funciones asociadas a la gestión de emisiones y la adaptación en la ciudad. Tiene como función fomentar la articulación técnica en la formulación y seguimiento de políticas, programas y proyectos enfocados en Cambio Climático, este grupo técnico promueve la articulación técnica. El Decreto Municipal 1240 de 2018 “establece el Sistema Municipal de Gestión del Riesgo de Desastres” y crea el Consejo Municipal de Gestión del Riesgo de Desastres, presidido por el alcalde, como la instancia superior de coordinación, asesoría, planeación y seguimiento para la reducción del riesgo y el manejo de desastres, y emergencias. Además, establece el Comité municipal para el conocimiento y la reducción del riesgo de desastres con la función de, entre otras cosas, orientar y articular las políticas y acciones de gestión ambiental, ordenamiento territorial, planificación del desarrollo y adaptación al cambio climático que contribuyan al conocimiento y reducción del riesgo de desastres. Medellín asigna responsabilidades en la gestión del cambio climático. El acto que establece el funcionamiento de la estructura administrativa de Medellín define que el Departamento administrativo de gestión del riesgo de desastres -DAGRD- tiene, entre otras, la función de liderar y coordinar el desarrollo de planes, programas y proyectos requeridos para la Gestión del Riesgo de Desastres y la adaptación al cambio climático, de acuerdo con las políticas y directrices municipales e institucionales. La Secretaría de Medio Ambiente tiene como responsabilidad hacer seguimiento al Plan de Acción Climática de Medellín. 

El Concejo Distrital realiza seguimiento político a las acciones emprendidas por la administración en materia de cambio climático. En este sentido, esta corporación ha generado espacios seguimiento y control a la administración, se destacan la comisión accidental CA-56 de Noviembre de 2020 ESTUDIO, SOCIALIZACIÓN E IMPLEMENTACIÓN DEL PLAN DE ADAPTACIÓN Y MITIGACIÓN AL CAMBIO CLIMÁTICO EN MEDELLÍN y la Comisión Accidental CA-329 SEGUIMIENTO A LAS MEDIDAS ENMARCADAS EN LA EMERGENCIA CLIMÁTICA MEDELLÍN de mayo de 2022. Del mismo modo, la Contraloría General de Medellín, entidad de control fiscal, ha adelantado actuacion especial de vigilancia al desempeño administrativo en materia de implementación del Plan de Acción Climática de Medellín. 

Los Nodos Regionales de Cambio Climático son un mecanismo de gobernanza regional clave para la aplicación de la Política Nacional de Cambio Climático, integrando diferentes niveles de gobierno. Son responsables de promover, acompañar y apoyar la implementación de las políticas, estrategias, planes, programas, proyectos y acciones en materia de cambio climático en las regiones de acuerdo con la política nacional de Cambio Climático. Medellín hace parte del Nodo Regional de Cambio Climático de Antioquia en donde se promueve la implementación de los lineamientos de política nacional, regional y municipal y su inclusión en la formulación de planes, programas y proyectos.

El Consejo Ambiental Metropolitano es el escenario de discusión de asuntos ambientales a escala supramunicipal a través del cual se discute y orienta la toma decisiones en materia ambiental a escala local.
column16: El Plan de Ordenamiento Territorial, adoptado por Acuerdo Municipal 048 de 2014, es el instrumento que orienta el desarrollo físico, ambiental y urbano de la jurisdicción de Medellín. Este instrumento estratégico es un determinante normativo para la formulación de políticas, programas y proyectos que, además, define como parte del modelo de desarrollo el “sistema ambiental, de gestión del riesgo y cambio climático” y el subsistema de adaptación al cambio climático. A través de este mecanismo se fijan lineamientos en materia de adaptación y mitigación al cambio climático que deben ser adoptados en el desarrollo de intervenciones físicas y que obligan a la formulación de un plan para la gestión del cambio climático. El Plan de Acción Climática retoma y desarrolla estos lineamientos definiendo una línea base en carbono y orientaciones para la construcción de programas de mediano y largo plazo. El Plan de Acción Climática y el decreto que lo adoptan asegura la convergencia entre este y los instrumentos maestros de planeación a nivel local. A nivel regional, tanto el Plan de Ordenamiento Territorial como el Plan de Acción Climática responden a las orientaciones dadas por las autoridades correspondientes en materia ambiental y de gestión de riesgo y emisiones. En tal sentido, se asegura una correspondencia entre los Planes de Desarrollo Municipal, formulados por los respectivos gobiernos electos y los instrumentos maestros de planeación de nivel local y regional, Incluidos aquellos en materia de Gestión del Cambio Climático. El Departamento Administrativo de Planeación, responsable de la planificación del desarrollo social y económico de la ciudad, incorpora la articulación con el Plan de Acción Climática como parte del procedimiento de formulación del Plan de Desarrollo Distrital, el cual, es el instrumento que ordena la inversión en corto plazo. El Plan de Desarrollo 2024-2027 incorpora el Sello Distrito Verde y el anexo de relacionamiento con el Plan de Acción Climática para señalar aquellos programas y metas de gobierno que contribuyen al logro de las metas climáticas de la ciudad.\n\nLa formulación de nuevas políticas y instrumentos incorporan el cambio climático como un asunto transversal en sus dimensiones; por ejemplo, la Política Pública de Economía Circular, la Política pública de ciencia, tecnología, innovación y sostenibilidad , la Estrategia de implementación de la Política Pública Territorial de Gestión del Riesgo de Desastres de Medellín y el Plan integral de movilidad sostenible de Medellín. Otras iniciativas de la ciudad han virado hacia la inclusión de in enfoque de climático en su desarrollo.
column17:
Los asuntos relacionados con el clima inciden en la planeación del financiamiento de Medellín a través del diseño de programas de corto, mediano y largo plazo que requiere la asignación y compromiso de recursos y el diseño de instrumentos tributarios que permitan en el involucramiento de actores. Se destaca: El Acuerdo distrital 093 de 2023, que adopta el estatuto tributario local contempla un listado taxativo de los tributos territoriales (impuestos, tasas y contribuciones) que pueden ser cobrados en el Distrito de Medellín. Dentro del listado taxativo del artículo 7 del citado acuerdo, se establecieron beneficios que incentivan la protección del Medio Ambiente o compensan las cargas soportadas por los contribuyentes con ocasión de las medidas de protección que asumen en razón de predios con características especiales, entre otros se definen exenciones por reforestación, beneficio por sustitución de combustibles, beneficios por reducción de emisiones y beneficios por construcción sostenible. Estos beneficios y exenciones se han considera a razón de su impacto en los ingresos de Medellín. 

Bajo colaboración del Ministerio de Hacienda de gobierno nacional, Medellín formuló una Estrategia de Protección Financiera del Riesgo de Desastres con Enfoque en Cambio Climático y Variabilidad Climática en la cual se hace hincapié en la consideración de los impactos del clima sobre la gestión del riesgo financiero de la ciudad. 

Medellín destinará un estimado 1.082.099 Millones de COP a lo largo de quince años para la ejecución del Tren Ligero de la 80, principal proyecto de movilidad limpia de la ciudad y clave en el proceso de expansión del sistema de transporte público masivo. Esto, implica el compromiso de gastos futuros que quedan comprometidos para el pago de deuda. Además, anualmente, Medellín destina 63.295 Millones de COP de recursos propios como parte del pago de deuda del sistema Metro. La principal apuesta de Medellín para enfrentar el cambio climático es la transición energética en el sector transporte con una ampliación y fortalecimiento del sistema de transporte masivo. 

Durante el período 2024-2027 se estima una inversión aproximada de $ 5.420.173
Millones de COP en iniciativas enfocadas en mejoramiento de infraestructura, gestión ambiental, promoción de movilidad activa, mejoramiento de vivienda, gestión del riesgo de desastres y generación del espacio público, entre otro tipo de proyectos vinculados al plan de acción climática. 

Mediante el uso de la herramienta de Prácticas Avanzadas para la Excelencia Ambiental en las Ciudades (APEX), una innovación de la Corporación Financiera Internacional (IFC), con el apoyo de la Cooperación Económica y Desarrollo de Suiza (SECO) como donante del proyecto, se formuló el Diagnóstico de oportunidades de inversión climática (CIOD) de Medellín. La herramienta informática en línea APEX ayuda a cuantificar y priorizar las soluciones política e inversiones de las ciudades en los sectores del entorno construido, la energía, el transporte, los residuos sólidos, y el abastecimiento de agua y tratamiento de las aguas residuales. Ese documento aporta un portafolio de medidas y estrategias de financiación para el desarrollo de proyectos climáticos que sirve de base para procesos de planificación del financiamiento.

Según disposición de la Superintendencia Financiera de Colombia, Medellín reporta trimestralmente cambios en materialidad de asuntos sociales y ambientales, incluyendo asuntos climáticos, y se prepara para aplicar los estándares TFCD y SASBI en sus reportes.

Normas actuales y emergentes: Existe gran dependencia de las disposiciones nacionales para acelerar la transición en materia energética y de transporte. A pesar de los esfuerzos institucionales para acelerar el tránsito a tecnologías limpias en el sector transporte, en Medellín el 98,5 % de los vehículos tipo automóvil, camioneta y motocicletas registradas se impulsan mediante combustibles fósiles. Del mismo modo, el 99% de los buses de servicios público y el 99,7% de los camiones se movilizan por combustibles fósiles. 

El desarrollo de estrategias más ambiciosas de renovación de flota es posible con la concurrencia de actores privados y el gobierno nacional. Sin embargo, un proceso no planificado de transición puede detonar riesgos de conflictos económicos y sociales por los cambios requeridos en cadenas de suministro, financiación e infraestructura y los eventuales incrementos en costos iniciales para las cadenas logísticas y empresas de transporte, especialmente, que podrían trasladarse al consumidor final.


Tecnología: Impacto de la reducción de lluvias en fase cálida del ENSO sobre la disponibilidad de agua para la generación energética, lo que pueda llevar a la necesidad de aumentar la participación de fuentes no renovables en la matriz energética nacional. En consecuencia, se podría dar un incremento en el valor del área construida para los usuarios finales.

column15: The implementation of Phoenix's climate action plan requires the city to work with partners across multiple sectors. The City lacks certain authorities to completely implement all actions in the 2021 Climate Action Plan. The city must rely on the electric utility companies to reduce the GHG emissions from the electric grid. Phoenix implements clean energy and energy efficiency improvement projects, such as behind-the-meter solar projects on city properties and LED streetlighting. In the Transportation Sector, motor vehicle emissions are regulated at the federal level, while regional transportation planning falls under the Maricopa Association of Governments (MAG), and the Valley Metro Transit System, the organization responsible for public transit in the greater Phoenix metro area. Phoenix coordinates with these partners to support ways for residents to reduce single occupancy car use and use alternative transportation instead, such as the light rail, bus, bike, walk, or other micromobility. The region has a half-cent dedicated sales tax for transportation infrastructure projects, like funding public transit routes, light rail investments, and major freeway construction. The Phoenix Mayor worked with MAG, other municipalities' elected leadership, and stakeholders like the business sector, on an effort to extend the half-cent sales tax that was set to expire in 2025. The extension of this tax, Proposition 479 on the Maricopa County ballot, was passed on November 5, 2024, and is set to expire in 2045. Funding from this tax will directly help support city goals with increased transit-oriented development, active transportation infrastructure, including protected bike lanes. Other projects include transition to electric vehicles with investments in electric vehicle infrastructure and community education and outreach, as articulated in the City of Phoenix Transportation Electrification Action Plan. Phoenix's Zero Emission Bus Plan aims to have a low and zero-emission bus fleet by 2040. Phoenix does have with issues of preemption at the state level. Energy benchmarking is preempted. Phoenix is preempted by state law from banning single-use plastic bags. The city can only offer recycling to single-family households per city ordinance. Multi-family complexes and businesses must receive trash and recycling services from a private hauler. The city does have a zero waste team. This team creates opportunities to reduce waste further, such as the new Master Recycler program (https://www.phoenix.gov/administration/departments/publicworks/education-programs/zero-waste-team.html ). A Circular Economy Microfactory Manufacturing facility opened in Phoenix at the Phoenix Goodwill Center on February 6, 2024. This effort is a new plastics recycling and remanufacturing “microfactory” converting waste material into new products, creating green skilled job opportunities, and creating a cooperative business model in the City of Phoenix (https://www.axios.com/local/phoenix/2024/02/07/microfactory-phx-plastic-recycling). This facility consists of partnerships between Goodwill of Central and Northern Arizona, Hustle PHX, Arizona State University, and the City of Phoenix and has won the Award of Distinction at the 2025 Arizona Forward Environmental Excellence Awards (https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/public-works-news/environmental-excellence-awards--phoenix-circular-plastics-micro.html) in 2025. The facility is anticipated to save as much as 550 tons of plastic from the landfill per year. This project recycles plastic that would have otherwise been landfilled. This project also creates opportunities for underserved and BIPOC communities to participate in circular economic development opportunities. Additionally, Arizona has self-imposed constraints limiting the state's authority to regulate beyond the scope of Federal authority. For Arizona, rules must be examined to ensure that they are “...consistent with and no more stringent than the corresponding federal law that addresses the same subject matter.” (ARS 49-104(A)(17)).
column16: Phoenix's GHG emissions from transportation are increasing as the population grows. Transportation emissions are also a continuing issue since the city is over 530 square miles and is considerably less dense than our counter parts. According to Phoenix's 2022 GHG community inventory, transportation was the largest emission sector, with 36% of all GHG emissions in Phoenix coming from the use of gasoline fuel in passenger vehicles. The Complete Streets concept, Transit Oriented Development (TOD) Districts, and Village Cores are tools Phoenix uses to reduce GHG emissions and to promote accommodation of safe and accessible multimodal travel, like walking, bicycling, and other micromobility. The Phoenix City Council adopted the South Central TOD Community Plan in March 2022. This plan attracts, guides, and prioritizes strategic investments to make South Central Phoenix a world-class destination where residents share the prosperity of a walkable and transit-oriented community. Phoenix has many initiatives and plans addressing residents' transportation needs like the Comprehensive Bicycle Master Plan and the Active Transportation Plan. Phoenix is also working to make our city's canals multi-use. Our goal is by 2050, over 90% of these canals will feature paved paths and have connections with crossings at major streets. In March 2025, Phoenix completed the Grand Canalscape Phase 3 with a new pedestrian bridge connecting recreation paths totaling 16 miles (https://www.abc15.com/news/operation-safe-roads/maryvale-community-city-leaders-celebrate-grand-canalscape-as-new-path-forward). These improvements add connectivity for commuting and recreational use while creating a safe corridor for residents traveling by foot or on a bike. Multi-use path projects that are part of the T-2050 Mobility Program will connect South Phoenix to downtown, pedestrians/bicyclists from downtown and South Phoenix, and regionally to Tempe and Mesa. The Walkable Urban Code provides guidelines that include requirements for 75% shade that supports TOD. This code promotes walking, bicycling, other micromobility, and transit use by emphasizing increased density and decreased automobile reliance while creating active and welcoming street/sidewalk environments near transit. These efforts, and others, are being aligned within PlanPHX, the city's General Plan. The General Plan is updated every 10 years and guides the city's development and how to shape its natural and built environment. The General Plan's goals and strategies are aligned with the Transportation 2050 Plan, Reimagine PHX, 2050 Sustainability Goals, Housing Plan, Arts and Culture initiatives, Food Action Plan, Historic Preservation initiatives, Climate Action Plan, Transit-Oriented Communities, Road Safety Action Plan, and others. Voters approved an update to the Phoenix General Plan 2025 in November 2024. The Office of Heat Response and Mitigation staff updated the 2010 Tree and Shade Master Plan to the Shade Phoenix Plan adopted by the Phoenix City Council in November 2024. The Shade Phoenix Plan includes trees and engineered shade to support a cooler city with goals of planting 27,000 trees and building 550 shade structures by 2030 (https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/mayors-office-news/3278.html). Green stormwater infrastructure (GSI) is also included in the plan to support water conservation by directing stormwater runoff to vegetation. Prolonged drought is a major issue impacting Phoenix. Phoenix planned and built the Drought Pipeline (completed in 2023) that brings water to North Phoenix from the south side. (https://www.phoenix.gov/administration/departments/waterservices/development-infrastructure/our-infrastructure/drought-pipeline-project.html). This project moves Salt and Verde River water supplies to areas of the city that are currently entirely dependent on Colorado River water. The city is also planning on building direct potable reuse plants. The Phoenix City Council approved the rehabilitation of the Cave Creek Water Reclamation Plant (CCWRP) in October 2023. The CCWRP will use advanced water purification technologies for wastewater treatment to potable standards, and is expected to be operational by 2030 (https://www.phoenix.gov/administration/departments/waterservices/development-infrastructure/cave-creek-plant.html).
column17: Many climate actions require significant funding to implement, including increased public transit, renewable energy generation, and water conservation. Funding for Transportation 2050 will increase public transit options and has an estimated $31.5 billion in funding over 35 years. This funding is through a combination of a specific sales tax, Proposition 479, with federal and local funding (https://www.phoenix.gov/administration/departments/publictransit/about-us/transportation-2050/funding-tax-revenue-distribution.html). This significant funding source for transportation projects across the region also impacts light rail construction and local public transit routes. The Phoenix City Council adopted a goal to see 280,000 electric vehicles in the City by 2030. The city is installing publicly available electric vehicle charging stations on city-owned properties to support this transition. Over 350 EV charging stations for the public, employees, and city fleet have been installed as of 2024, with the goal of having 500 stations by 2030 (https://cmpr-dashboard-phoenix.hub.arcgis.com/pages/oos). Phoenix also prioritizes financial resources to transition its fleet to low or zero-emission vehicles. The Public Transit Department had an initial contract of $230 million approved by the Phoenix City Council to begin the transition of the bus fleet to low or no-emission buses. The city is also planning its first Bus Rapid Transit corridor. Phoenix continually investigates different financial tools to implement sustainability projects. Phoenix has developed one of the nation's first Sustainability Bond Frameworks (https://www.phoenix.gov/content/dam/phoenix/oepsite/documents/climate/cdp/06-30-2024%20Sustainability%20Bonds.pdf?appId=aemshell) to attract new investors interested in supporting sustainable infrastructure. These bonds were used for the city's water infrastructure. Additionally, Phoenix is planning on building a multibillion-dollar direct potable reuse project; the Cave Creek Water Reclamation Plant (CCWRP) . CCWRP will use advanced water purification technologies for wastewater treatment to potable standards. The Phoenix City Council approved a construction contract up to $300 million for rehabilitation of the CCWRP in February 2024 (https://www.12news.com/article/news/local/water-wars/phoenix-moves-forward-reopening-water-plant-recycle-wastewater-drought-colorado-river/75-4846a080-ec09-4b9f-add8-73c6bfc126d9#::textA%20%24300%2Dmillion%20construction%20contract,water%20resource%20by%20purifying%20wastewater ). Effective October 2023, the city increased its water and wastewater rates, using an approach that incentivizes residential and commercial water conservation measures. Phoenix adopted a Green Stormwater Infrastructure (GSI) Handbook in 2024 that includes design details, landscape recommendations, and typical maintenance practices, making it easier for residents and businesses to obtain city approval to incorporate GSI into projects (https://www.phoenix.gov/content/dam/phoenix/pddsite/documents/residential-building/green-stormwater-infrastructure-handbook.pdf ). The city continues to invest in its municipal operations, including energy and water conservation projects, installation of solar on city properties, and electric vehicle charging stations. Phoenix will finance some of these projects through General Obligation Bonds (GO). These bonds allow the City to pay for major capital public improvements, such as energy and water efficiency improvements, public safety facilities, parks, libraries and community centers, arts and cultural facilities, street and storm drainage improvements, and affordable housing. Voters approved the GO Bond Program at a Special Bond Election on November 7, 2023. Mayor and Council directed all Bond-funded buildings to achieve LEED Silver certification, and all projects to integrate heat mitigation and energy and water efficiency to the ma ximum extent possible. Additionally, a one-million dollar revolving fund was established in the FY2025-26 budget to accelerate energy efficiency projects in municipal operations.
column18: The transition to renewables is highly dependent on the capability of the electric utilities to execute their sustainability plans. Arizona's 2006 Renewable Energy Standard and Tariff required that 15% of electricity come from renewables by 2025, but this was repealed in 2024 by the Arizona Corporation Commission and had no replacement. All proposed renewable requirements and standards have been rejected. For transportation infrastructure, the region relies heavily on a half-cent sales tax for funding. Since the inception of this tax, 280 corridor miles of freeway, 140 miles of street projects and millions of bus service miles have been implemented as of November 2023 (https://www.azauditor.gov/sites/default/files/2023-11/21-107_Highlights.pdf ). The City of Phoenix Mayor worked with the Maricopa Association of Governments, other municipalities' elected leadership, stakeholders like the business sector, and state leadership to continue this transportation funding. An extension of the original tax Proposition 400, was approved by Maricopa County voters in November 2024 as Proposition 479. These types of transportation investments would not be possible if voters had not approved the extension of the tax, and would have resulted in the reduction of more than half the funds available for this kind of work. Current state regulation prohibits state employees or agencies from adopting or enforcing a state or regional program to regulate the emission of greenhouse gases for the purposes of addressing changes in atmospheric temperature without express state legislative authorization. Additionally, Arizona passed a prohibition on banning vehicles based on their energy source in August 2023. Arizona has self-imposed constraints limiting the state's authority to regulate beyond the scope of Federal authority. Practical and technological barriers exist in the implementation of public transit options, electric vehicle deployment, and renewable energy generation. Transportation options are difficult to implement in a city as widespread as Phoenix. Phoenix is over 530 square miles in size. Electric vehicle deployment requires significant infrastructure upgrades for residents and businesses. Electric vehicle options for medium- and heavy-duty vehicles are limited at this time. Hybrid electric buses being deployed initially in Phoenix have shown significant limitations; mainly because battery electric buses used in Phoenix for public transit have increased energy requirements for air conditioning. Hydrogen as a fuel has been considered but current federal policy has made this option less likely. Transitioning our electricity grid to renewable, low carbon or zero emission energy will require storage options that are currently unavailable or not practicable. Phoenix is exploring the feasibly and availability of low-carbon materials needed for construction projects that may reduce emissions. Maintaining low electricity costs or reducing electricity costs so that residents can afford energy costs associated with cooling indoor spaces during the heat season, while transitioning to low-carbon and/or renewable sources of energy, is extremely important. In addition, regional collaboration is necessary to accomplish transportation and air quality goals, since these activities are planned and regulated at the regional level. Actions within the Climate Action Plan include advocating for policies at the municipal, state, and federal levels to accomplish these goals.

column15:
The Department of City Planning is a convener of residents, communities, civic organizations, commissions, and public entities, and works with these partners to plan and deliver a vision for the City's future grounded in a Just Transition. The Department works at the intersection of climate change, racial justice, and social equity to ensure healthy, safe and vibrant neighborhoods for all residents. Because the built environment plays a vital role in the lives of Pittsburgh residents, City Planning incorporates policies and activities that promote sustainability, climate resilience, design justice, arts and culture, housing affordability and economic opportunity in the development and implementation of the City's Comprehensive Plan, neighborhood plans, land use policies, zoning regulations, approval of development projects, and coordination of community development programs and partnerships. The Department is committed to focusing core planning activities to prioritize neighborhoods that have been harmed by past planning policies and practices which have contributed to existing racial and economic inequities throughout the city. This effort requires deeper engagement and additional resources in the development of plans and policies, working to remove barriers to the Department's services, and by recognizing a more holistic set of metrics to advance the wellbeing of our diverse communities. The Department of City Planning recognizes the power of residents to transform their neighborhoods and calls on us to use that power to shape the future of Pittsburgh. 

 
Sustainability and Resilience advances Pittsburgh's vision for environmental protection, climate change mitigation, adaptation, and strategies to address the impacts of climate hazards on vulnerable residents and communities. The Sustainability and Resilience division leads interdepartmental coordination and implementation of the City's Climate Action Plan. The division oversees relevant compliance with climate and environmental regulation and codes, including developing and maintaining performance standards. Sustainability and Resilience partners with other public entities to incorporate high performance standards for City operations. The division also collaborates with residents to inform about innovative climate investments across energy, waste, stormwater, and parks and open space that are incorporated into neighborhood plans and the City's Comprehensive Plan. Sustainability and Resilience supports the capacity of community-based organizations in Pittsburgh's environmental justice communities to advance climate goals, access historic federal climate investments, steer the equitable distribution of vital infrastructure improvements, and minimize unwanted burdens in those communities.
column16: The Pittsburgh Climate Action Plan was adopted by both the Planning Commission and City Council to be enacted as a guiding document. The Planning Commission oversees all master plans, neighborhood plans, and development plans throughout Pittsburgh. Because Planning Commission has adopted the Climate Action Plan, all plans and developments that are approved by the Commission must incorporate the goals and actions established in the Climate Action Plan. The Sustainability and Resilience Division oversees implementation of the Climate Action Plan and is integrated into the Department of City Planning. The City of Pittsburgh is also developing a Citywide Comprehensive Plan in 2024 and will be integrating climate action planning into long range goals.
column17: The City of Pittsburgh has been working with ResourceX and Priority Based Budgeting tools to create a more data-driven view of their budget to clarify how city funds were being spent and empower decision-makers with more information, specifically information driving two initiatives important to their leadership and community: Equity and Climate Action. Priority Based Budgeting allowed the Sustainability and Resilience Team to begin to fuse the conversation of what they were trying to achieve with the Climate Action and Resilience Plans and where it actually intersected with the Budget Cycle. Utilizing Priority Based Budgeting, we are able to ensure that the City's budget aligns with our long term climate, equity, and resiliency goals. https://www.resourcex.net/blog/pittsburgh-climate-action-plan-budgeting-alignment
column18: Pennsylvania, especially the Southwestern PA region where Pittsburgh is located, is heavily dependent on fossil fuels both from an energy standpoint and an economic standpoint. Fossil fuel industries contribute jobs and economic activity to the region. As Pittsburgh transitions to a low-carbon economy, we must ensure that there is a focus on local job creation and economic development in order to mitigate loss of fossil fuel driven economic activity.

The Sacramento City Council regularly engages with climate-related issues, both formally (through adoption of climate-related ordinances, resolutions, and plans) and informally (through regular updates from staff).

In 2019, the City Council declared a climate emergency and committed to achieving carbon neutrality by 2045 (Resolution No. 2019-0465). This declaration built on the City's first climate action plans and 2035 General Plan. Specifically, the Resolution committed to advance feasible efforts to implement carbon reductions as much as possible by 2030. The Resolution also committed to present the City's plan to “achieve carbon neutrality by 2045 and emergency actions needed towards emissions elimination by 2030.” 

The 2040 General Plan (Resolution No. 2024-0066) and Climate Action & Adaptation Plan (Resolution No. 2024-0067) were adopted in 2024 and include strategies to reach carbon neutrality by 2045.

Located in the Department of Public Works, Mobility and Sustainability Division, the Office of Climate Action & Sustainability (OCAS) supports City Council's engagement with climate-related issues. OCAS leads the City's efforts to address climate change and accelerate City actions to achieve a resilient, carbon zero future. Formed in 2021, OCAS works closely with City Council (e.g., through annual updates) and departments (e.g., to plan and operationalize urgent climate initiatives). OCAS supports a 'Green Team' which is a group of employees spread across departments who communicate sustainability and climate initiatives in their departments. These team members also help spread news back to their departments and build sustainability culture in the City Staff.
column16:
The City of Sacramento has a long-standing commitment to both reducing GHG emissions and adapting to the impacts of climate change, as reflected in several key plans. In 2012, the City adopted its first community-wide Climate Action Plan and targeted reducing community GHG emissions to 15% below 2005 levels by 2020. With the adoption of the 2035 General Plan in 2015, the City incorporated an updated community Climate Action Plan into the General Plan.

The Climate Action Plan was recently updated as a standalone Clime Action & Adaption Plan with an Adaptation Chapter added, and adopted by City Council in February 2024 in conjunction with the adoption of Sacramento's 2040 General Plan. The Climate Action & Adaptation Plan includes strategies to achieve carbon neutrality by 2045, including updated GHG emission goals and emissions reduction actions. Climate Action & Adaptation Plan measures include a variety of actions to mitigate GHG emissions such as planning for mixed use development, encouraging walking, biking and use of public transit, and accelerating building decarbonization. The Climate Action & Adaptation Plan also contains a range of adaptation goals and implementing actions such as creating built environments that reduce exposure to extreme heat and mitigate urban heat island effect, reduce the risk of damage to life, infrastructure, and property due to flooding, address the adverse health effects of air pollution, increase government preparedness and community resilience to prepare for climate impacts, and enhance water management and conservation to build resilience to the effects of climate change. The 2040 General Plan contains applicable regulatory and supporting policies. As part of this process, the City completed a Community-wide GHG Inventory and a Municipal GHG Inventory for 2016 and will complete a subsequent inventory prior to the next update of the Climate Action & Adaptation Plan, tentatively scheduled for 2027.
column17:
The City's Climate Action & Adaptation Plan (CAAP), adopted in 2024, outlines a funding and financing plan to implement GHG reduction measures that discusses the costs to individuals and the City, up-front vs lifecycle costs, and incremental costs. Complete implementation of the CAAP GHG reduction measures is estimated at a minimum of $3.2 billion in direct City investments. Investments from private citizens, businesses, and other agencies will also be needed, as well as a substantial commitment of staff time. Though many of these investments will provide substantial savings to Sacramento over time by mitigating the financial impacts of climate change, full implementation will require the City to identify funding for up-front investment.

In 2021, prior to finalization of the CAAP, City Council allocated $4.4 million for accelerated implementation of priority CAAP actions. Although there is no citywide climate finance policy, climate-related issues inform City procurement and budgeting. For example, the Fleet Sustainability Policy outlines processes for purchasing zero-emission vehicles first, as available. The Sustainable Procurement Policy sets requirements for purchasing recycled and otherwise sustainable materials, in compliance with California Senate Bill 1383.
column18: Ensuring a just transition to a low-carbon economy is a key concern for the City. As Sacramento pursues building decarbonization, for example, potential job losses for gas plumbers and pipefitters are a concern. The City passed an Alternative Water Reuse Ordinance to help provide jobs to gas pipefitters who might see a decrease in jobs from decarbonization efforts. Further challenges include avoiding burdening locally owned small businesses with the costs of transition, protecting residents from rising natural gas prices, preventing displacement, and ensuring equitable distribution of benefits.

column15: The City of Tampa has had a Sustainability and Resilience Officer (SRO) leading sustainability, climate action, resilience, and renewable energy transition since May 2020. This work has been at the senior level, requiring collaboration and support in various city departments, often including solid waste, water, wastewater, mobility, and parks and recreation. The SRO reports to the Chief of Staff who reports to the Mayor and is a peer to city administrators responsible for multiple departments. In April 2023, the sustainability team added a full-time coordinator to support efforts throughout the city. The city also is currently accepting applications for an energy manager and carbon analyst that will be working under the SRO to increase energy efficiency and transition city staff and citizens to renewable and carbon-free energy sources.
column16: Climate change is the focus of the City of Tampa's Climate Action & Equity Plan (CAEP) which was released in June 2023. This plan has 143 initiatives over ten categories including energy, water and wastewater, stormwater, waste management, and transportation and land use. The plan will be consulted by departments to guide projects, policy changes, and adapt infrastructure using climate adaptation and mitigation strategies. One key component of the plan is to engage residents and communities as the city creates these changes. Accompanying the CAEP, Executive Order 2023 was signed by Mayor Castor to ensure that the CAEP was consulted in the planning phase of city capital improvement projects. The verbiage in the executive order is the following: “When developing a capital improvement project, the sponsoring city department shall review the Tampa Climate Action & Equity Plan to determine if there are opportunities for energy efficiency, renewable energy, resilient infrastructure, or risk reduction measures related to forecasted climate impacts. In May of 2023, the City of Tampa's Parks & Recreation Master Plan was released with perspectives such as climate change, climate shocks and stressors, vulnerabilities, resiliency, adaptation, climate hazards, and green infrastructure being weaved throughout. The City of Tampa has a sustainability ordinance in the city code with various requirements and incentives. Requirements include that \'All new construction of municipal buildings, regardless of the source of the funds, in excess of five thousand (5,000) square feet of air-conditioned space, shall be built to satisfy, at a minimum, the most current USGBC LEED Silver standard. This ordinance was used when the newest municipal building was being constructed and is expected to open at the end of the summer of 2023 with the silver LEED facility rating. The City Center at Hannah Avenue building included a $1,000,000 investment in solar panels and electric charging stations that will cover approximately 55 percent of the overall annual energy requirements.
column17: On June 14, 2023, Mayor Castor signed an executive order that will require city departments to review the City of Tampa Climate Action & Equity Plan to determine if there are opportunities for energy efficiency, renewable energy, resilient infrastructure, or risk reduction measures related to forecasted climate impacts. Combined, City departments consumed 176,380,772 KWHs of electricity in 2019. In fiscal year 2022, the combined electric bill was approximately $25,000,000. Using funding to transition to renewable energy will help save the city money while lowering the greenhouse gas emissions emitted by municipal operations. A contributor to the funding of renewable energy projects will be the new ability for municipalities to receive direct pay from the Department of Treasury through the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). Grant funding made available through historic federal legislation, such as the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law and IRA, will further incentivize the adoption of lower-emissions technologies through consumer tax credits for energy-efficient and clean energy solutions such as heat pumps, solar panels, and electric vehicles.
column18: Total emissions from government operations are 234,084 mtCO2e, which is less than one percent of total city-wide emissions according to the greenhouse gas inventory completed in 2021. Energy production by the local utility and transportation systems make up 47% and 46.3% of greenhouse gas emissions respectively. In the overall carbon emission profile, local government operations are directly responsible for a relatively small percentage. In 2021, the Florida Legislature passed Section 366.032, Florida Statutes, which prohibits local governments from restricting the types of fuels and energy sources that utilities may offer their customers, including policies such as building electrification mandates. Given this broad preemption, the City of Tampa is not considering any actions as part of this plan that would have the effect of restricting the energy options available to the City's residents and businesses

column15: The Climate Smart division in the Environmental Services Department leads the City's climate action work. It is supported by an interdepartmental Steering Committee (composed of relevant department directors) and a Technical Working Group (composed of staff below the director level). The Climate Smart division reports at least twice a year to City Council and the Transportation and Environment committee. In 2024, a Climate Advisory Commission composed of San Jose residents was established to advise City Council and staff on all aspects of the City's climate action work, serving as a community voice. Climate strategies are woven into the City's General Plan and transportation plans. The Department of Transportation and the Community Energy Department (which runs the City's Community Choice Aggregation program, San Jose Clean Energy, and supplies electricity to most customers in the City) also play a key role in implementing climate strategies.
column16: Sustainability has become a normal consideration in San Jose's master/development planning and associated activities. The need to reduce transportation-related GHG emissions has influenced the City General Plan's emphasis on densification and transit-oriented development. In 2019 and 2020, to reduce emissions from the built environment, the City Council adopted and then expanded a reach code and ban on natural gas infrastructure in new buildings, such that all new buildings (with few exceptions) constructed in San José must now be all-electric. In June 2022, City Council approved removing parking minimums for new development citywide, in order to support increased densification and reduced transportation emissions as well as providing businesses more location flexibility and supporting housing affordability. In January 2024, City Council approved an update to the electric vehicle charging infrastructure requirements in the City's reach code, which will apply to all new multifamily construction beginning July 1 2024. The update requires 100% of parking spaces for residents to be electric vehicle ready.

column16: Climate action and associated state legislation has resulted in stand-alone changes to municipal code, amendments to the general plan, climate-focused community plan updates, a municipal energy strategy, a community choice aggregation program to purchase cleaner energy, a climate adaptation and resilience plan, a CEQA qualified Climate Action Plan and multiple new development regulations. column17: The City is is responsible for implementing and updating the CAP, transitioning all city facilities to zero-emissions, and encouraging City-wide mode shift to more sustainable forms of transportation. Tel Aviv-Yafo's Climate Action Plan is a two-pronged strategy, consisting of an Adaptation Plan and a Mitigation Plan. The Adaptation Plan was published in 2020 and is currently being updated for the next five years, the Mitigation Plan was finalized and released in 2024. These plans are integral components of the city's overall strategy, seamlessly integrated into the municipal agenda and translated into actionable work plans across relevant departments. With the completion of the two foundational pillars of the climate plan—adaptation and mitigation, the Integrated Climate Action Plan was drafted. The plan outlines broad climate missions that include both adaptation and emission reduction activities with goals for 2030. The Integrated plan includes an update of the climate analysis of 2020. and aligns the two strategies together. The Climate Action Plan sets to mainstream and institutionalize climate action across municipal departments. This approach ensures that climate considerations are integrated into all relevant policies and decision-making processes, promoting a more holistic and effective response to climate change. To ensure effective oversight and accountability, the plan incorporates the following mechanisms: •Institutionalization: Climate-related responsibilities are assigned to specific departments, such as the City Architect Office, Infrastructure Division, and Transportation Authority. This helps to ensure that climate action is a priority within the municipal government. •	Mainstreaming: The plan is being integrated into existing policy frameworks, promoting resource efficiency and fostering collaboration across sectors. •	Advisory committee: An expert advisory committee provides guidance and support to the planning process, helping to identify gaps and refine the plan. •	Monitoring and evaluation: Regular monitoring and evaluation of the plan's progress will help to identify areas for improvement and ensure that climate actions are on track. The plan's implementation is overseen by the Deputy CEO of the Municipality, supported by a dedicated Steering Committee. The Environment and Sustainability Authority provides overall supervision through the Municipal Climate Focal Point. Given the plan's comprehensive nature and its implementation across numerous departments, key departments have been assigned focal points for both adaptation and mitigation activities: •	City Architect Office: Sustainable Planning, Green Buildings, and Building Codes •	Infrastructure Division: Water Management •	Transportation Authority: City Sustainable Mobility Masterplan (Mitigation), Reversing the Mobility Pyramid •	City Beautification Department: Urban Forest and Shade (Adaptation), Nature-Based Solutions •	Municipal Corporations: Atarim (City Coastline), Ganei Yehoshua (City Parks) To strengthen the plan's effectiveness, an advisory committee of experts was established. This committee plays a crucial role in identifying gaps, refining the plan, and ensuring the maximum impact of planned actions. By institutionalizing climate action, Tel Aviv-Yafo demonstrates its commitment to addressing climate change effectively and sustainably, which will build resilience, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and improve the quality of life for residents.
Recently, Tel Aviv-Yafo's published it's first Voluntary Local Review (VLR) for 2025, the first local report for Israel. The report outlines the city's commitment to implementing the SDGs at a local level. The report aligns the city's strategic goals with the SDGs, with a focus on creating a metropolitan center, a city for all residents, a dynamic municipality, and a sustainable urban environment. The report's key areas of focus include:
•	Climate Action (SDG 13): Tel Aviv-Yafo published its climate adaptation plan in 2020 and its Mitigation and Green Growth Plan in 2024. The plans set targets to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 50% by 2030 and achieve net-zero emissions by 2050. The city's strategy focuses on cooling the city through nature-based solutions and on shifting from top-down regulation to community-driven initiatives. It is also addressing energy poverty by establishing a Climate Risk Coordinator role to prepare vulnerable populations for extreme weather.

During Israel's second Voluntary National Review (VNR) at the High-level Political Forum, of the UN, Tel Aviv-Yafo's Strategic Planning Unit presented the city's VLR. The presentation detailed the city's climate actions and its local implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The Israeli delegation, which included representatives from the Ministry of Environmental Protection and the Ministry of Construction and Housing, highlighted Tel Aviv's initiatives at a special conference focused on implementing SDG 13. This positioned Tel Aviv-Yafo as an example of a city demonstrating civic resilience, sustainable urban development, and environmental innovation, even amidst national challenges.

The Tel Aviv Yafo Master Plan has been updated, from the previous version of 2016. The 2022 update created an opportunity to establish the existing practices into clear and meticulous policy tools that define, for the first time, the environment, infrastructure, and preparedness for climate change as urban focuses. The plan defined a series of changes in planning processes to address the following: 
Key Policy Changes:
•	Sustainable Planning Framework: The plan introduced a new section dedicated to sustainable planning, outlining specific guidelines for future development.
•	Climate Change Adaptation: The plan emphasized the importance of urban preparedness for climate change, including strategies to mitigate heatwaves, promote green infrastructure, and protect against extreme weather events.
•	Carbon Neutrality: The plan set ambitious targets for reducing carbon emissions, including requiring carbon neutrality for large-scale projects and promoting energy efficiency in buildings.
•	Water Management: The plan highlighted the need for improved stormwater management, particularly in vulnerable areas. It also promoted the use of underground and above-ground water storage.
•	Energy Efficiency: The plan encouraged the integration of renewable energy generation and storage into new developments and promoted energy efficiency standards for buildings.
•	Ecological Framework: The plan expanded the city's ecological framework, emphasizing the importance of green spaces and biodiversity.
Implementation and Enforcement: To ensure the effective implementation of these policies, the city has adopted a number of measures, including:
•	Policy Document: The city council approved a comprehensive policy document on sustainable planning in March 2023.
•	Performance Standards: The city has established new performance standards for buildings, including energy efficiency requirements and mandatory green roofs.
•	Procedural Requirements: The city has introduced new procedural requirements for development projects, such as the submission of climate impact assessments. 
Binding Directives: The plan includes a range of binding directives related to climate issues, such as:
Green Building Standards: The city has implemented new green building standards for both residential and commercial buildings, requiring a minimum of 3 stars for buildings between 2 and 15 floors and for public buildings over 1,000 square meters.
Urban Greening: New construction projects are now required to include at least one tree for every 50 square meters of land.
Sustainable Transportation: The city has mandated electric vehicle charging stations for 15% of all parking spaces and parking spaces for two bikes per apartment.
Innovative Glare Reduction Measures:
Tel Aviv-Yafo has pioneered a new approach to reducing glare from glass towers, requiring developers to conduct a comprehensive survey to identify potential reflection hotspots and implement mitigation measures.
By implementing these comprehensive measures, Tel Aviv-Yafo is demonstrating its commitment to addressing climate change and building a more sustainable and resilient city. These efforts contribute to reducing greenhouse gas emissions, improving air quality, and enhancing the overall quality of life for residents.
Overall, the updated master plan positions Tel Aviv-Yafo as a leader in sustainable urban development. By integrating climate considerations into all aspects of urban planning, the city is building a more resilient and sustainable future.
column17:
Tel Aviv, as a major metropolitan city, is uniquely exposed to the economic impacts of climate change. The increasing frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, such as heatwaves, floods, and coastal erosion, are expected to incur significant costs to the city. 
Tel Aviv Yafo's financial planning is increasingly incorporating climate considerations to mitigate risks and expand economic benefits. The city is beginning to incorporate climate risk assessments to identify potential vulnerabilities and develop strategies to minimize economic losses from climate-related events like heatwaves, floods, and sea-level rise. By investing in climate-resilient infrastructure, promoting sustainable development, and adopting green technologies, Tel Aviv Yafo aims to reduce its exposure to climate risks and create new economic opportunities. Additionally, the city is begining to integrate climate considerations into its financial decision-making processes, such as evaluating the long-term financial implications of infrastructure projects and considering climate risks when assessing investment opportunities. This proactive approach to climate-conscious financial planning is crucial for ensuring Tel Aviv Yafo's economic resilience and sustainability in the face of a changing climate.
Proactive Risk Assessment
To address these economic impacts, Tel Aviv Yafo is compiling risk assessments that analyze climate-related risks in terms of economic impacts, specifically:
o	Coastal Flooding and Storm wave impact: Threatening coastal infrastructure and properties.
o	Heatwaves: Increasing energy consumption, reducing productivity, and impacting public health and the urban space.
The first climate risk study was conducted in 2023, addressing the economic impacts of urban warming on Tel Aviv-Yafo by 2050. While short-term changes may still be minor, the study emphasizes that current trends significantly influence the situation until mid-century. The study analyzes two potential warming scenarios: RCP4.5 and RCP8.5, which are commonly used in climate projections. The economic quantification is based on macroeconomic parameters and 2021 price levels, with adjustments for projected population growth. The analysis perdicts that the cost of damage in Tel Aviv-Yafo due to climate warming in 2050, is 2 billion NIS per year under RCP4.5 to 4 billion NIS per year under RCP8.5. 
The new study improves the city's financila planning by providing concrete, quantitative estimates of the economic costs associated with urban heat in Tel Aviv-Yafo. It can be integrated into the city's plans by enhancing policy recommendations informing the development of more targeted and effective climate policies, such as those related to urban planning, energy efficiency, and public health.
Beyond Risk Reduction: Seizing Opportunities While climate change presents significant challenges, it also offers opportunities for economic growth and innovation. Tel Aviv Yafo, with its strong entrepreneurial spirit and technological capabilities, is well-positioned to capitalize on these opportunities. By investing in climate-friendly technologies and businesses, the city can create new jobs, attract investment, and enhance its reputation as a global leader in sustainability.
Key considerations for Tel Aviv Yafo:
•	Coastal protection: Developing and implementing comprehensive coastal protection measures.
•	Urban greening: Increasing green spaces to mitigate urban heat island effects.
•	Sustainable infrastructure: Investing in resilient infrastructure, such as stormwater management systems and renewable energy.
•	Climate-friendly businesses: Supporting the growth of climate-friendly businesses and industries.
By proactively addressing the economic impacts of climate change, the city will be able to improve it's financial resiliency.

A transition to a low-carbon economy could bring several economic and technical challenges. The cost of living and energy services may increase due to carbon taxes. Waste treatment costs could also rise from higher dumping taxes. For lower-income families, carbon taxes might make mobility more challenging. Building costs could also rise due to new low-carbon restrictions.

From a technical standpoint, new plans and areas are required to accommodate energy storage within the city. Low-carbon energy supply may not be enough to provide the necessary cooling energy in a hot climate. Furthermore, since water and sewage systems are energy-based, their transition to a low-carbon economy may lead to higher costs or new technical barriers.

War's Impact on Tel Aviv's Low-Carbon Transition
The current war's effects on Israel's low-carbon transition are particularly acute in Tel Aviv, given the city's role as a dense economic and cultural hub. National challenges are often amplified by the city's unique urban context.

The national shift in government spending toward defense and recovery directly impacts Tel Aviv's ability to fund its climate initiatives, which often depend on national subsidies and a stable regulatory environment to attract private investment. This political instability can disrupt long-term strategic projects that require consistent policy and multi-year funding. The city's prominent tech sector, a key driver of green innovation, may also see its funding and focus diverted to security and defense applications.

Social and Urban Development Complications
The war can deepen social inequalities and complicate urban development goals within Tel Aviv. Economic strain may lead to cuts in public green initiatives like improved public transportation or energy efficiency programs for low-income residents. The high cost of living in Tel Aviv means that green technologies like home solar panels or electric vehicles are often only accessible to the wealthy. A slow transition could worsen these divides, as lower-income communities in the south of the city are left with less efficient and more expensive energy options.

Additionally, urban planning in the city must now balance competing demands for scarce public land. The need to build new bomb shelters, security infrastructure, and social services may come at the expense of crucial climate adaptation projects, such as urban green spaces and coastal resilience initiatives.

column15: The Municipality of Turin is aware that sustainability will be the main challenge of the upcoming years and it will be fundamental in order to design the city of the future and lead the community to a new phase of growth.Thus a new department responsible for ecological and digital transition, environment, mobility and transport has been set up recently with the election of the new mayor.The strategic objectives of this department are the production of energy from renewable sources, the creation of energy communities, the energy efficiency of public and private buildings, waste sorting and the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions. The main concrete actions to achieve these objectives include:❖ Implementing the door-to-door waste collection system in order to increase the percentage of waste sorting in the city. Implementing initiatives aiming at preventing waste production, recovering unsold food and durable goods through social economy initiatives❖ Promoting the spread of electric mobility, through efficient and widespread recharging systems ❖ Enhancing car sharing by encouraging the achievement of suburban areas as well❖ Supporting and accompanying innovation and experimentation by companies, universities and research centers towards new and more sustainable modes of urban height transport enabled by new technologies ❖ Implementing interventions to improve the energy efficiency of public spaces❖ Implementing actions to fight emissions to improve air quality. Turin aims to approach climate neutrality across its municipal territory by 2030, throughout any area of the city or sector of the economy. In order to tackle this challenge, Turin intends to exert a positive influence on decision-making processes through the implementation of a structured approach. This approach is characterized by its integration across various levels, acknowledging the interconnectedness of different areas involved and relying on scientific foundations, utilizing measurements, mathematical models and analytical tools to assess potential impacts of strategic choices. It is dynamic, identifying trajectories and adapting political decisions throughout their evolution. Achieving such a medium-to-long-term goal requires the implementation of multiple interconnected actions that align with the overarching vision of climate neutrality. This endeavor is made possible through the collaborative efforts of the Administration and organizations that have committed to share this objective with the city. To structure this process effectively, Turin has established a Mission Team comprising two working groups: the Transition team within the City Administration, and the technical working group established at the Energy Security and Transition EST@EnergyCenterLab of the Politecnico di Torino. This team has played a pivotal role in guiding the co-design of the climate action with various city stakeholders.
column16: Turin has been one of the first large Italian cities to join the Covenant of Mayors, a voluntary European initiative that aimed at reducing the CO2 emissions by at least 20% by 2020. Turin joined the Covenant of Mayors in 2009 and in September of the following year the City Council approved TAPE (Turin Action Plan for Energy), drawn up with the scientific support of Politecnico di Torino: the emission reduction target was set at 30% with respect to 1991. This plan has been periodically monitored in order to update the progress of the actions and monitor the emission reduction trend. Three Monitoring Reports have been prepared and the latest showed an overall reduction of CO2 emissions of 51% compared to 1991, getting very close to what the European Union sets as a binding target for 2030 (55%) and clearly exceeding the 30% target that the City had set itself. Turin has been chosen for the UE call “100 climate neutral and smart cities by 2030” aiming at delivering 100 European cities reaching the goal of climate neutrality to 2030, set as binding by the European Union on 2050. In order to meet this target five main pillars of action have been identified. First of all, efficient energy management, obtained with building redevelopment and efficiency-oriented public lighting. The second pillar is the role of digitization and intelligent management, through continuous monitoring and data collection towards an “Urban data platform” in support of data-based sectoral policies. The third is the adoption of circular economy business models. The fourth is the active involvement of citizens as central actors in the decision-making process, promoting their role as prosumer and fostering the growth of energy communities as one of the strategic objectives of the next “Policy Lab”. The fifth pillar is urban regeneration oriented towards “proximity”, pushing towards a strong modal shift towards urban mobility. In the period 2021-2027, around 200 million euros have already been allocated for sectoral interventions in the area of slow / smart mobility, energy efficiency, urban forestry and \'walkable neighborhoods\', ensuring that people live close to the things of they need.It should be noted that the City has adopted the Climate Resilience Plan, approved by the City Council in November 2020, following a period of public consultation. The Plan has identified a total of 80 actions to adapt the urban area to the new climatic conditions, improve the quality of life and maximize the well-being of all. On the one hand, the actions are aimed at creating a resilient administration, which manages emergencies, which communicates and raises awareness among its citizens, on the other hand they are aimed at reducing the occurrence of a phenomenon and addressing critical issues. Among the actions, the implementation of nature-based solutions (the so-called NBS) both to mitigate the heat island effect and to manage rainwater, especially in the event of intense precipitation events, play a predominant role; the actions of information and awareness of citizens are also very important, but also those of training municipal technicians to promote the resilient design of public spaces. The Administration is acutely aware that the climate emergency stands as one of the foremost challenges of our time. It acknowledges the significance of this emergency in both present and future social, economic, and spatial transformations, and deems it imperative to take prompt measures to mitigate its impacts. In this regard, the urban environment assumes a critical role as it accommodates a large population and serves as the primary location for the production and provision of essential community services. Therefore, Torino has decided to participate in the Mission “100 Climate Neutral and Smart Cities by 2030” to bolster and expedite a process that has been ongoing for years. This commitment involves various initiatives, projects, and investments aimed at combating climate change, encompassing both mitigation and adaptation policies. More broadly, it aims to create a sustainable, livable, resilient, and circular city. This participation represents an opportunity to streamline the objectives and impacts of policies affecting different areas of the city. The ultimate goal is to achieve climate neutrality by 2030, leveraging the synergy of efforts and commitments from both the Administration and the network of stakeholders involved in the process.
column17: The City has decided to direct a large part of the funding allocated for the recovery (REACT-EU and PNRR funds) to the design and implementation of interventions aimed at combating climate change, both in terms of reducing greenhouse gas emissions and in terms of adaptation in order to make the city territory able to respond to local impacts caused by climate change
column18: The Municipality of Turin has identified the following generic project-level risks as having the potential of affecting the results of the climate neutrality activities: • Economic. risks regarding the improper calculation and management of costs and benefits of the projects, both in terms of CAPEX and OPEX. • Financial: risks concerned with the investment factors: rising costs, unrealistic budget, additional labour-resources, failure in securing funding, fluctuations in credit rates, inflation, etc. • Legislative and administrative: risks linked to issues with the public authorities in terms of changing law, regulations, etc., or of deficiencies in the management of administrative matters. • Engagement of citizens: risks related to failures in the links with citizens, and their acceptance and commitment to the actions anticipated. • Political changes: risks related to the potential variations in political priorities and sensibility following political elections in the city, and changes of policies at the regional, national and European levels. • Project results: risks related to the operation and maintenance of the solutions put in place by the project, and in particular related to the performance of technologies, the capacity to operate them, the integration and interoperability among systems, etc. The City of Turin faces as well the risk that the transition to a low-carbon economy could damage the automotive sector that is very important for the territory of the city.

Hyderabad, like many other rapidly growing cities, is increasingly exposed to climate-related risks due to urbanization and population growth. To address these challenges, the city has implemented several targeted initiatives. Notably, the Strategic Nala Development Programme (SNDP) is focused on enhancing the stormwater drain infrastructure to mitigate flooding, while the Strategic Road Development Programme (SRDP) addresses road construction and repairs to improve urban resilience.
Hyderabad also participates in broader national climate and environmental initiatives, such as the National Clean Air Program (NCAP), which aims to reduce air pollution through improved monitoring and control of pollutants, and the Swachh Bharat Mission, which enhances solid waste management systems.
In addition, Hyderabad is actively working on climate adaptation strategies, including the development of an early rainfall warning system, which will enable timely public notifications and preparedness measures to mitigate the impact of extreme weather events.
These initiatives are part of Hyderabad's broader strategy to enhance climate resilience and mitigate the environmental impacts of rapid urbanization.
column16: The Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation (GHMC) is developing a Climate Action Plan to evaluate current vulnerabilities, anticipate future climate impacts, and take proactive steps to mitigate the effects of climate change on urban infrastructure and services. At the same time, the Hyderabad Metropolitan Development Authority (HMDA) is revising its Master Plan for 2041, which includes various sustainable urban development strategies such as the integration of Blue-Green Infrastructure (BGI), promotion of transit-oriented development (TOD), updating the Comprehensive Mobility Plan, enhancing land use efficiency, and others. These initiatives are aimed at managing future urban growth, regulating density, and optimizing land use across the metropolitan area. Together, these efforts aim to improve urban services, conserve natural resources, enhance energy efficiency, and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. The Master Plan also emphasizes the development of lakes and the conservation and management of open and green spaces, ensuring the preservation of the city's natural ecosystems while promoting sustainable urban growth.
column17: The Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation currently does not have specific budget allocations dedicated solely to climate change mitigation or adaptation in its financial planning. However, provisions for such allocations are expected to be considered during future financial planning, basis the upcoming Climate Action Plan. In the meantime, special initiatives that are tackling climate change impacts like the Strategic Nala Development Program and Strategic Road Development Program are receiving state grants, supplemented by the GHMC budget supported through bank guarantees. Additionally, Hyderabad benefits from national grants for implementing broader national schemes.\n\nThe Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board (HMWSSB) manages water supply and wastewater services with its own financial resources, which include state budget grants and national funding for infrastructure development.

NCCS is part of the Strategy Group, which supports the Prime Minister and his Cabinet to establish priorities and strengthen strategic alignment across Government. Established in 2007, the IMCCC is chaired by Mr Gan Kim Yong, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry.
column16: Climate-related issues have impacted Singapore's master/development planning and required us to enhance resilience and sustainability. As a low-lying island, Singapore is particularly vulnerable to sea level rise. The government has implemented coastal protection measures on at least 70% of its coastal areas and raised minimum land reclamation levels for new developments to mitigate this risks. For example, the minimum land reclamation level in Singapore was raised from 3m to 4m above the Singapore Height Datum in 2011. This level is adequate in addressing projected sea level rise under the Second National Climate Change Study. Government agencies will continue to review the minimum reclamation levels with information from new studies available. \n\nUrban heat and flood management has also been accounted for as Singapore faces projections of rising temperatures and increased rainfall. This includes developing green buildings and enhancing natural ventilation systems to reduce reliance on air conditioning.
