Santiago de Cali a través de su Secretaría de gestión del riesgo gestiona e invierte en el territorio para la mitigación de los riesgos asociados al cambio climático. Además dentro de el departamento administrativo gestión del medio ambiente existe el grupo de gestión del riesgo y cambio climático a través del cual se le hace seguimiento a el cumplimiento de las metas del plan integral de gestión de cambio climático y se hace cumplimiento de las metas del plan de desarrollo asociado al riesgo. El 'Comité de Gestión del Riesgo' en Cali se refiere a la estructura organizativa de la Alcaldía de Santiago de Cali, liderada por la Secretaría de Gestión del Riesgo de Emergencias y Desastres, encargada de planificar, coordinar y ejecutar acciones para prevenir, preparar, responder y recuperar ante desastres naturales o de otro tipo. Este sistema busca proteger a la ciudadanía y sus bienes, y es fundamental para la implementación del Plan Distrital de Gestión del Riesgo. 

Tambien a través de decreto municipal 20 39 del 2020 se crea el comité directivo de cambio climático de Santiago de Cali donde se gestione el cumplimiento de las metas y la articulación con entidades locales regionales y nacionales para la gestión del cambio climático de Santiago de Cali
column16: En Santiago de Cali, los asuntos climáticos transformaron la planificación urbana y sectorial, integrando criterios de riesgo, mitigación y resiliencia en el POT y en los planes maestros. El inventario de GEI (2010) reportó 4,17 millones tCO₂e, de las cuales el 71% proviene del sector energía, lo que impulsó metas de eficiencia energética, movilidad eléctrica y economía circular. La microzonificación climática mostró aumentos de hasta 1,5 °C en tres décadas y proyecciones de +2,3 °C hacia 2071-2100 en la zona oriental, junto a un incremento de eventos extremos; más de 250.000 habitantes viven hoy en áreas de amenaza alta por inundaciones y movimientos en masa. Estos datos reconfiguraron la planeación: se electrificó parte de la flota del MIO (60 buses eléctricos en 2022, reducción potencial de 4.000 tCO₂e/año), se avanza en restauración de nacimientos de agua y en ecoparques metropolitanos como el Corazón de Pance (inversión inicial de 37.816 millones COP), y se ampliaron los sistemas de monitoreo ambiental. Entre 2019 y 2024 se restauraron más de 150 hectáreas de ecosistemas urbanos, se fortaleció el Observatorio Ambiental y se consolidaron proyectos de cooperación internacional en economía circular, empleabilidad verde y atención a población migrante. Con la Estrategia Municipal Bajo en Carbono y la alineación con la hoja de ruta nacional de descarbonización, Cali proyecta reducir entre 20-25% sus emisiones a 2030, apostando por infraestructura verde, movilidad sostenible y alianzas globales como motores de desarrollo resiliente y bajo en carbono.
column17: En Santiago de Cali, los asuntos climáticos han influido de manera directa en la planificación financiera. En costos operativos, la gestión de riesgos por inundaciones y deslizamientos obliga a destinar anualmente recursos de contingencia y a fortalecer el sistema de alerta temprana, mientras que la operación del Sistema de Vigilancia de Calidad del Aire y del Observatorio Ambiental demanda inversiones sostenidas en monitoreo y personal técnico. En gastos de capital, la ciudad priorizó grandes proyectos verdes como el Ecoparque Corazón de Pance (37.816 millones COP en su primera fase), restauración de cuencas y arborización urbana, además de la incorporación de 60 buses eléctricos al MIO en 2022, con financiamiento mixto y beneficios estimados de reducción de 4.000 tCO₂e/año. En asignación de capital, los riesgos climáticos identificados en la microzonificación y el Plan Integral de Cambio Climático reorientaron inversiones hacia infraestructura resiliente (drenaje urbano, protección de laderas, reubicación de viviendas en riesgo) y hacia programas de eficiencia energética. En cuanto al acceso al capital, la ciudad gestiona cooperación internacional (GIZ, Swisscontact, ONU) y mecanismos de financiamiento climático para escalar proyectos de movilidad sostenible, economía circular y restauración ecosistémica, lo que amplía su capacidad de apalancar recursos externos. Así, la variable climática no solo condiciona el gasto, sino que define la estructura de inversión y abre oportunidades de financiamiento verde a futuro.
column18:
Normas actuales y emergentes. La alineación con la Estrategia Nacional de Carbono Neutralidad 2050 y el Plan Integral de Cambio Climático de Cali exige cumplir con estándares de reducción de emisiones. Esto implica reconversión de flotas y edificaciones que pueden aumentar los costos iniciales de inversión. Por ejemplo, la electrificación de 60 buses del MIO en 2022 costó un 30% más que unidades diésel convencionales, aunque con beneficios ambientales y operativos a largo plazo. El cumplimiento de futuras regulaciones de calidad del aire y eficiencia energética puede generar presiones adicionales sobre el presupuesto municipal y los operadores privados.

Tecnología. La transición requiere adoptar nuevas tecnologías (electromovilidad, energías renovables, gestión de residuos con biogás). Los altos costos de infraestructura —como cargadores eléctricos y redes inteligentes— y la falta de proveedores locales son riesgos de implementación. La ciudad estima que la migración completa a buses eléctricos en el SITM-MIO costaría más de 1,2 billones COP en la próxima década, lo que supera la capacidad financiera actual del municipio sin apoyo externo.

Legal. Existen riesgos de litigios por incumplimiento de compromisos climáticos o por afectación de comunidades en zonas de riesgo. En 2020-2023 se registraron demandas ciudadanas por calidad del aire en sectores industriales, que presionan al municipio a acelerar medidas de control. Esto puede generar costos legales y de compensación si no se cumplen estándares nacionales e internacionales.

Mercado. La transición genera cambios en la demanda y oferta. El consumo energético de la ciudad depende en más del 60% de combustibles fósiles, y la gradual reducción de subsidios nacionales al diésel y la gasolina puede incrementar los costos de transporte público y privado, con riesgo de afectar la competitividad. En residuos, el aumento de exigencias para reducción de metano obliga a inversiones en tecnologías de captura y aprovechamiento, cuyo costo supera los 100.000 millones COP en escenarios de modernización del relleno sanitario.

Reputación. La falta de avances visibles en proyectos de descarbonización genera riesgos de pérdida de confianza de la ciudadanía y de la cooperación internacional. Cali emite alrededor de 4,17 millones tCO₂e (inventario 2010), y si no demuestra reducciones alineadas con la meta nacional (-51% a 2030), puede perder acceso a financiamiento climático. Al contrario, mostrar lentitud frente a otras ciudades del país debilitaría su reputación como ciudad sostenible y afectaría la atracción de inversión internacional.

En conclusión, los principales riesgos de transición para Cali se concentran en el alto costo de nuevas tecnologías (≥1,2 billones COP en transporte eléctrico), la presión normativa creciente, los posibles litigios por calidad del aire, y el riesgo reputacional frente a la cooperación internacional. Estos factores exigen una planeación financiera sólida, esquemas de cofinanciación y alianzas estratégicas que mitiguen las brechas de capacidad local.

La supervisión climática en el cantón Guayaquil se ha consolidado de manera progresiva mediante la creación de unidades técnicas especializadas dentro de la Municipalidad, como SEGURA EP, PARQUES EP, la Dirección General de Ambiente, y la Coordinación General de Proyectos con Financiamiento Externo. Estas instancias lideran la incorporación de la variable climática en la planificación del desarrollo, el ordenamiento territorial y la gestión de riesgos, en concordancia con el COOTAD y las directrices de la Secretaría Nacional de Planificación.
Un hito clave fue el Proyecto Huella de Ciudades (2015-2016), que permitió calcular por primera vez la huella de carbono e hídrica a nivel institucional y territorial, establecer indicadores y un plan de acción, así como transferir metodologías y capacidades técnicas que hoy posibilitan una gestión autónoma de dichas huellas. En paralelo, se desarrolló un índice de vulnerabilidad parroquial que mide sensibilidad (pobreza, densidad, acceso a servicios), exposición (inundaciones, aumento del nivel del mar, fenómenos extremos) y capacidad adaptativa (conocimiento, inversión social). Este sistema identificó “hot spots” de alto riesgo en parroquias como Tarqui, Pascuales, Letamendi y Monte Sinaí.
La supervisión se expresa también en medidas comunitarias y proyectos piloto: brigadas barriales, jardines de lluvia, techos verdes, restauración de bosques protectores y experiencias de conservación. A nivel presupuestario, se fortaleció la capacidad adaptativa mediante incrementos significativos en salud (+25%), educación (+55%) y gestión de riesgos (USD 2.53 millones en 2015).
En el ámbito normativo y de planificación, la actualización del Plan de Desarrollo y Ordenamiento Territorial (PDOT) y el Plan de Uso y Gestión del Suelo (PUGS) 2023-2027 han integrado el cambio climático como eje estructurante, delimitando áreas no aptas para la expansión urbana, condicionando o restringiendo usos del suelo en zonas de amenaza y definiendo parámetros urbanísticos orientados a la resiliencia. Estas disposiciones se traducen en acciones técnicas como diagnósticos de vulnerabilidad frente a inundaciones, erosión costera, incremento del nivel del mar y olas de calor urbano; implementación de soluciones basadas en la naturaleza (parques inundables, corredores verdes, reforestación urbana, zonas de amortiguamiento hídrico); y priorización de infraestructura resiliente, desde sistemas pluviales y sanitarios reforzados hasta corredores ecológicos y movilidad sostenible.
La supervisión también ha incorporado la dimensión social, contemplando la regularización condicionada, el reasentamiento y el mejoramiento integral de barrios en asentamientos informales expuestos a riesgos climáticos, lo que otorga a la acción climática un enfoque de equidad territorial y justicia social.
Finalmente, Guayaquil articula sus acciones con marcos nacionales e internacionales como la Estrategia Nacional de Cambio Climático (2012-2025), el Plan Nacional de Desarrollo y la Agenda 2030, además de participar en espacios globales como Hábitat III y la CMNUCC. Esta articulación se complementa con cooperación de organismos multilaterales y con iniciativas de gobernanza climática que fortalecen la proyección internacional del cantón.
En síntesis, la supervisión climática en Guayaquil es integral, normativa y técnica: abarca desde la planificación territorial y la gestión del riesgo hasta la inclusión social y la cooperación interinstitucional, con el objetivo de construir un cantón más resiliente, justo y sostenible.
column16:
El cambio climático ha tenido un impacto estructural en la planificación urbana y de desarrollo de Guayaquil, transformando la manera en que se conciben el crecimiento territorial y las decisiones de ordenamiento. La ciudad presenta una alta exposición a inundaciones, deslizamientos y aumento del nivel del mar, condiciones que han obligado a replantear sus instrumentos rectores de planificación. El análisis de vulnerabilidad realizado por CAF identificó parroquias críticas como Tarqui, Pascuales, Letamendi y Monte Sinaí, lo que evidenció la necesidad de priorizar intervenciones diferenciadas en estas zonas.
En respuesta, la Municipalidad ha incorporado criterios de resiliencia y sostenibilidad en la actualización del Plan de Desarrollo y Ordenamiento Territorial (PDOT) y en el Plan de Uso y Gestión del Suelo (PUGS), convirtiendo la variable climática en un eje fundamental de la planificación, en concordancia con el COOTAD y las directrices nacionales. El PDOT 2023-2027 integra diagnósticos de vulnerabilidad frente a riesgos como inundaciones, erosión costera, aumento del nivel del mar y olas de calor urbano. A partir de esta información, se han delimitado áreas no aptas para expansión urbana, se ha priorizado la conservación de ecosistemas estratégicos —como esteros y zonas de amortiguamiento hídrico— y se han definido lineamientos de resiliencia en proyectos urbanos y rurales.
El PUGS traduce estas orientaciones en normativa específica de uso de suelo, estableciendo usos condicionados o restringidos en sectores expuestos a amenazas climáticas y fijando parámetros urbanísticos que promueven la infraestructura resiliente. Asimismo, se refuerzan los sistemas de drenaje pluvial y sanitario para enfrentar eventos extremos, complementándolos con soluciones basadas en la naturaleza como parques inundables, corredores verdes, reforestación urbana, jardines de lluvia y techos verdes. De manera paralela, también se promueve infraestructura híbrida y gris —muros de contención, sistemas de drenaje reforzados— que actúa como complemento en la reducción de riesgos.
La planificación maestra también contempla la gestión de riesgos en equipamientos estratégicos, priorizando la protección de zonas industriales, centros de salud, complejos educativos y comerciales ubicados en áreas inundables, con el fin de reducir impactos sociales y económicos. En este sentido, el Proyecto Huella de Ciudades (2015-2016) aportó un plan de acción con proyectos de mitigación y adaptación que orientan el crecimiento urbano hacia modelos de menor huella de carbono y mayor eficiencia hídrica, fortaleciendo la visión de sostenibilidad a largo plazo.
El impacto climático ha exigido además la incorporación de la dimensión social en la planificación territorial. Tanto el PDOT como el PUGS incluyen estrategias de regularización condicionada, reasentamiento y mejoramiento integral de barrios en asentamientos informales situados en zonas bajas o ribereñas. Estas medidas buscan reducir la vulnerabilidad de la población más expuesta y garantizar el acceso a servicios básicos, vivienda segura y equipamientos resilientes, bajo un enfoque de equidad territorial y justicia social.
Asimismo, proyectos estratégicos en movilidad, vivienda y regeneración urbana se han reorientado bajo criterios de adaptación climática. Se prioriza un modelo de ciudad compacta, con densificación de áreas consolidadas, incremento de áreas verdes y movilidad sostenible, medidas que contribuyen tanto a la reducción de emisiones como a la generación de entornos urbanos más saludables y seguros.
En síntesis, los asuntos climáticos han redefinido la planificación territorial de Guayaquil, dotándola de un carácter integral que articula gestión de riesgos, sostenibilidad ambiental y justicia social. El PDOT y el PUGS han dejado de tratar el cambio climático como un tema transversal para convertirlo en un eje estructurante del desarrollo territorial. De esta forma, la ciudad busca consolidar un modelo de crecimiento resiliente, equitativo y sostenible, en coherencia con la normativa nacional y los compromisos internacionales asumidos.
column17:
El cambio climático ha transformado profundamente la planificación financiera del Municipio de Guayaquil, obligándolo a replantear prioridades y reforzar presupuestos en sectores clave para la resiliencia social y económica.
Entre 2010 y 2015, se destinaron crecientes recursos hacia salud y educación como parte de una estrategia para fortalecer la capacidad adaptativa de la población. En ese período, el gasto en educación aumentó en un 55% y el de salud en un 25%. Paralelamente, las unidades técnicas relacionadas con cambio climático y riesgos experimentaron incrementos sostenidos en su financiamiento: la Dirección de Gestión de Riesgos alcanzó USD 2.53 millones en 2015, mientras que la Dirección General de Ambiente pasó de USD 1.0 millón en 2010 a USD 1.38 millones en 2015.
La presión sobre las finanzas municipales también responde a los altos costos asociados a eventos climáticos extremos. Estudios internacionales ubican a Guayaquil entre las cuatro ciudades costeras del mundo con mayores pérdidas económicas previstas por inundaciones. Entre 2012 y 2015 se registraron 79 inundaciones y 28 deslizamientos de tierra, con consecuencias humanas y materiales significativas. Esta evidencia obligó a establecer provisiones presupuestarias permanentes para atender emergencias y contingencias, reconociendo que la prevención resulta menos costosa que la inacción frente a los desastres.
Además, el Municipio ha innovado en la incorporación de un portafolio de proyectos de inversión climática dentro de su programación presupuestaria. Con el apoyo del Proyecto Huella de Ciudades, se impulsaron acciones orientadas a reducir la huella de carbono e hídrica, que hoy forman parte de la planificación financiera municipal. Estas incluyen inversiones en transporte sostenible, eficiencia energética, tratamiento de aguas residuales, infraestructura verde y restauración de ecosistemas, con un doble objetivo: mitigar emisiones y reducir vulnerabilidades.
En síntesis, el impacto del cambio climático en la planificación financiera de Guayaquil puede sintetizarse en tres dimensiones principales: 1) Reasignación de recursos sociales y técnicos hacia salud, educación y gestión de riesgos como pilares de la capacidad adaptativa. 2) Incorporación de provisiones permanentes para atender desastres naturales, mitigando las elevadas pérdidas económicas y sociales que generan inundaciones y deslizamientos. 3) Integración de proyectos de inversión climática en el presupuesto municipal, asegurando que la mitigación y la adaptación sean parte estructural del desarrollo urbano.
Finalmente, esta estrategia se articula con el Plan Nacional de Desarrollo, la Agenda 2030 y las políticas de adaptación climática, lo que no solo garantiza coherencia con los marcos normativos, sino que también abre oportunidades de financiamiento a través de la cooperación internacional y de fondos climáticos. De este modo, Guayaquil avanza hacia un modelo de planificación financiera resiliente, consciente de que invertir hoy en adaptación y mitigación reduce los costos humanos, sociales y económicos del mañana.
column18:
La transición hacia una economía baja en carbono en Guayaquil representa una oportunidad histórica, pero también conlleva riesgos significativos de carácter económico, financiero, social e institucional que podrían comprometer el ritmo y la equidad del proceso.
En el ámbito económico y productivo, la ciudad mantiene una alta dependencia de sectores intensivos en energía y emisiones: el comercio al por mayor y menor representa el 46,7 % del ingreso total, mientras que las industrias manufactureras aportan el 26,2 %. La descarbonización de estas actividades implica un desafío complejo: reconvertir procesos y tecnologías podría generar pérdidas de competitividad, elevados costos de adecuación y afectaciones al empleo en el corto plazo. Estos riesgos no solo amenazan el crecimiento económico inmediato, sino que también pueden generar resistencia de actores productivos tradicionales, requiriendo políticas de apoyo y estímulos para la innovación.
En el ámbito financiero, la transición demanda inversiones de gran magnitud en infraestructura y servicios urbanos. Proyectos como sistemas resilientes de aguas urbanas, infraestructura híbrida contra inundaciones y programas de movilidad sostenible requieren recursos sostenidos que podrían tensionar las finanzas municipales. Sin acceso oportuno a mecanismos de cooperación internacional y fondos climáticos, los costos de la transición podrían superar la capacidad presupuestaria local, comprometiendo la sostenibilidad fiscal y la continuidad de servicios esenciales.
En el ámbito social, los riesgos se relacionan con la equidad y la inclusión. Zonas vulnerables como Pascuales, Febres Cordero y Monte Sinaí, caracterizadas por altos niveles de pobreza y déficit en servicios básicos, enfrentan una mayor probabilidad de quedar marginadas si no se diseñan políticas específicas de apoyo. La falta de programas de reconversión laboral, subsidios a la transición energética y medidas de protección social podría traducirse en una ampliación de las brechas sociales y en una percepción de injusticia climática, debilitando el respaldo ciudadano al proceso de descarbonización.
En el ámbito institucional y de gobernanza, la transición a una economía baja en carbono exige coordinación interinstitucional, continuidad política y fortalecimiento técnico en el nivel municipal. La falta de articulación entre los diferentes niveles de gobierno, o la ausencia de capacitación en herramientas como financiamiento verde, monitoreo de emisiones y mecanismos de participación ciudadana, podría fragmentar los avances logrados. Asimismo, la falta de estabilidad política en torno a la agenda climática podría poner en riesgo la sostenibilidad de los compromisos asumidos.
En conjunto, los principales riesgos para Guayaquil frente a la transición se concentran en cuatro dimensiones interrelacionadas: 1) Económica: costos de reconversión productiva que pueden afectar competitividad y empleo. 2) Financiera: presión fiscal derivada de las altas inversiones en infraestructura y servicios resilientes. 3) Social: posible marginación de los sectores más vulnerables si no se aplican políticas inclusivas. 4) Institucional: limitaciones de coordinación y capacidades técnicas para sostener el proceso en el tiempo. Superar estos riesgos requiere de una planificación integral, apoyo financiero externo y políticas públicas inclusivas que aseguren que la transición hacia una economía baja en carbono sea entendida no solo como una obligación ambiental, sino como una oportunidad de transformación estructural hacia un modelo de desarrollo más justo, competitivo y sostenible para Guayaquil.

column15: The Department of Urban Sustainability and Energy Efficiency is in charge of coordination and monitoring of the city's SECAP implementation. The City Government reviews the measures and actions under Climate-neutral Tallinn and their relevance every two years and, if necessary, \namends or supplements them. Every four years, a full inventory report is conducted to monitor energy consumption and CO2 emissions data, assessing the achievement of the goals set in the plan Climate-neutral Tallinn and in particular the reduction of CO2 emissions. In addition, an indicator dashboard will be launched in the fall of 2025, which supports data-driven decision making in the city government as well as informs the public on how the city is progressing toward its goal of climate neutrality by 2050.
column16: Climate-Neutral Tallinn has been prepared based on the goals of the development strategy Tallinn 2035, especially the goal of the green transformation. The strategy sets clear objectives to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to climate neutrality by the middle of the century and to adapt to climate change. Environmental protection, mobility, preservation and development of city property and urban planning all contribute to achieving the goal of reaching climate neutrality. Making buildings energy efficient, making urban transport emissions-free and the transport infrastructure climate-resistant, increasing the share of renewable energy in energy consumption, activities for mitigating flood risks and heat islands and ensuring the climate-resistance of vital services all contribute to the achievement of climate goals. Raising the awareness of the population is also essential from the viewpoint of coping with climate change and more resource-efficient living. Sectorial development plans all contribute to the development plan Tallinn 2035 and Tallinn's SECAP: Climate-Neutral Tallinn.
column17: The financial resources necessary for the implementation of Climate-Neutral Tallinn are planned according to the city's budget possibilities in the budget strategy and the city budget, specific activities along with the budget are specified in the implementation plan of Climate-Neutral Tallinn approved by the city government annually after adopting the budget.

column16: Climate and microclimate - Municipal Urban Plan:http://puc.comune.genova.it/03_11_2014/DEF/1_DF/1_01_doc.pdf \nGenoa's path for the future is based on clear steps: learning from the past, studying the future scenarios and prepare, anticipate, prevent, transform challenge into opportunities. Our vision to 2030 and 2050 foster a deeply interconnected city, renewed and robust in relations and solutions that target sustainability as a cultural, infrastructural and economic transformation. This is the reason that move the city to foster new model of sustainable development, through an innovative initiative investing in smarter resilient future under the paradigm of the green, just and productive city according to the main principle of the new Leipzig Charter to which the city contribute as part of the coordinators of the partnerships of the Urban Agenda for the EU Mechanism. In the main planning document of the city such as the Urban Municipality Plan, Sustainable Urban Mobility Plan at metropolitan level, SEAP now SECAP, the Lighthouse City Strategy on resilience and sustainable development there are suggestions that facilitate the transition to an urban regenerated territory. Both mitigation to adaptation measure are foreseen also to face climate change effects and improve people wellbeing complying the new path of development of a holistic resilience and environmental friendly strategy of the city.As well as many other medium-sized European cities, the territory of Municipality of Genoa is affected by different natural and anthropogenic phenomena caused by orographic features, chaoticurban development and climate change that expose the territory and the population to serious risks. In particular, the urban environment of the city, mainly situated along the coast (see above), is extremely vulnerable to storms, violent rainfall, flash-floods, heat waves, coastal erosion and other extreme weather events (storms surge, winds) that occur with increasing intensity and frequency.On the “climate related” perspective this simple diagram shows the climate-related risk effects analysed and the projections in terms of likelihood and possible damages. The meteo-hydrogeological risk that threatens the city of Genoa can be identified both in the dense natural hydrographic network which innervates the urban area (65 river basin) to the needs of urban settlements developed near the coast. Furthermore, the city of Genoa is heavily exposed to the increase in temperature and consequent extreme weather events that cause a reduction in the quality of life in urban areas (eg: heat islands, reduction in quality and availability of water, drought, etc.); damages and economic losses; impact on human health, especially for the most vulnerable groups of the population. The socio economic tissue of the city is fairly complex, one hand it counts on several Hi-tech excellences, blue economy sector representatives and some industrial reality at international level; on the other hand a capillary and fragmented micro enterprises and handcraft to sustain in their effort to maintain their cultural identity and prosperity. The Municipality risk assessment recognizes the following main negative climate change impacts combined with the effects of anthropogenic stress on natural resources: - change on the hydro-geological regime with potentially increased risk of flash-flood in several medium and small basins, and widespread risk of landslides in the slope areas; - Increased risk of forest fires and wildland-urban interface fires in the most critical areas of urban boundaries. In the Municipality planning documents there are effort to increase detailed analysis referred to the following impacts: - effects on human health that could increase mortality and morbidity related to heat waves and warm spells stress, diseases and mortality from air pollution, allergic disorders, diseases related in change of vector-borne, water-borne and food-borne spreading; - reduction in water availability and quality due to protracted stress on water resources; - increased occurrence of extreme weather events combined with sea level rise, and related risk of coastal flooding and coastal erosion; - losses in key economic sectors, such as energy; tourism; declining productivity in fishery and agriculture; infrastructure, transport and human activities; human settlements and the entire socio-economic activity.

column16:
Palermo has joined the Covenant of Mayors: the SECAP roadmap sets a goal of reducing CO₂ emissions by at least 40% by 2030, with a trajectory toward neutrality by 2050; it also includes adaptation measures (heat waves, floods, etc.) and participatory processes.

- The municipal SUMP was adopted in 2019 and developed with updated technical documentation (2024 Environmental Report), which integrates congestion/emissions assessments and guides decisions regarding public transport, the tram network, cycling, and limited traffic zones (ZTL) as climate mitigation levers. Metropolitan City then adopted its own SUMP in 2024.

- In 2025, Palermo began the participation phase for its PUG (General Urban Plan), a key tool for integrating environmental protection, landscape, and natural resources into urban transformation. This provided an opportunity to structurally incorporate climate resilience criteria (greenery, permeability, ecological corridors, vulnerability to risks).
column17:
- The SECAP's actions include interventions on energy efficiency of public/private assets and increased renewables (e.g., photovoltaics), with regional indicators and guidelines to support municipal planning. These interventions can also be implemented thanks to financial incentives offered by the national government. Energy efficiency improvements to public buildings (LED lighting, photovoltaic panels, thermal insulation) reduce the municipality's current energy costs.

- Climate choices consistent with EU strategies have allowed the Municipality to intercept hundreds of millions of euros in structural funds, PNRR and Horizon 2020 programmes.

- Interventions on drainage and areas at risk of flooding can also reduce extraordinary costs for repairs and compensation.

- The limited traffic zones generate revenues which, at least in part, are reinvested in mobility and the environment.

- Regenerated neighborhoods with greenery and soft mobility tend to increase property value and tourist attractiveness, with implications for municipal taxes (IMU, tourist tax).

Once the ongoing interventions are completed, the investments will bear fruit thanks to energy savings, reduced damage from extreme events, and greater economic attractiveness.

Sustainable mobility, energy efficiency, renaturalization, and green infrastructure projects require significant capital. If European or national funding is reduced, the municipality risks having to cover more expenses with its own resources, putting pressure on the budget. Furthermore, the deadlines required for European funding are often not met due to Italy's significant bureaucracy, which means there is a risk of losing funding already allocated.

- The EU and Italy are raising standards for emissions, energy efficiency, and waste management. If Palermo doesn't comply within the expected timeframe (due to technical, bureaucratic, or financial constraints), it risks fines, loss of funding, and a loss of reputation.

- Policies such as expanding traffic-restricted zones (TZLs), restrictions on polluting vehicles, or increasing energy costs for certain buildings can burden low-income residents, creating social tensions if not accompanied by compensatory measures.

- Activities related to fossil fuels, traditional transportation, or inefficient construction could suffer repercussions, with job losses and the need for professional retraining.

- Managing complex decarbonization projects requires specialized skills (energy, sustainable mobility, EU fund management) that the Municipality must strengthen to avoid errors, delays, or extra costs.

- Green infrastructure, electric vehicles, and renewable energy systems require scheduled maintenance: if the budget doesn't cover it, degradation reduces the environmental and economic benefits.

column15:
O compromisso de Salvador com o enfrentamento das mudanças do clima teve início em 2015, quando passou a integrar a C40, uma rede que reúne as principais cidades do mundo comprometidas com a redução de emissões de GEE e a mitigação dos impactos climáticos. No mesmo ano, foi instituída a Política Municipal de Meio Ambiente, marco na consolidação da legislação ambiental local, reunindo em um único instrumento as diretrizes para a gestão ambiental da cidade.
Em 2017, o então prefeito de Salvador assinou o Compromisso 2020, assumindo a meta de elaborar um plano climático até o final daquele ano. Esse compromisso foi reforçado em 2019 com o lançamento da Estratégia de Resiliência, que consolidou a agenda climática como prioridade da gestão municipal. Em 2020, foi publicado o Plano de Mitigação e Adaptação às Mudanças Climáticas (PMAMC), que estabelece diretrizes, metas e ações para alcançar a neutralidade de carbono até 2049. O plano posiciona Salvador na vanguarda da ação climática ao propor estratégias voltadas à redução de emissões, promoção do desenvolvimento sustentável e justiça climática. Sua elaboração foi fundamentada em uma base científica e técnica robusta, com ampla participação social.
O PMAMC foi concebido como um instrumento técnico essencial para o planejamento urbano, promovendo a integração de políticas públicas setoriais orientadas por saberes científicos e tradicionais. Seu objetivo é enfrentar os desafios impostos pela intensificação dos eventos climáticos extremos, promovendo uma atuação coordenada e estruturada do poder público.
As ações climáticas também foram incorporadas ao Plano Estratégico de Salvador (2021-2024), que atua como uma bússola para tornar a cidade mais sustentável, inclusiva e resiliente. O novo ciclo do Plano Estratégico (2025-2028), atualmente em elaboração, seguirá a mesma linha, estabelecendo metas e estratégias fundamentadas em planos setoriais já executados, como o Plano Diretor de Desenvolvimento Urbano (PDDU), a Estratégia de Resiliência e o próprio PMAMC.
Inspirado no Painel Intergovernamental sobre Mudanças Climáticas (IPCC) e reconhecendo o papel das cidades na mitigação e adaptação às mudanças climáticas, Salvador instituiu, em 2019, durante a Climate Week, o Painel Salvador de Mudanças Climáticas. Essa iniciativa, prevista na Estratégia de Resiliência, constitui uma rede de conhecimento técnico e científico voltada para a crise climática, com o objetivo de observar, sistematizar e comunicar de forma acessível soluções de mitigação e adaptação aplicáveis à cidade. O Painel promove a intersetorialidade e a transdisciplinaridade fundamentais à formulação de políticas públicas e à tomada de decisões estratégicas.
No âmbito da gestão de riscos e desastres, a Defesa Civil desempenha papel central na prevenção, preparação e resposta a eventos climáticos extremos. Entre suas principais iniciativas, destaca-se a criação do Centro de Monitoramento e Alerta da Defesa Civil (CEMADEC), que realiza o acompanhamento contínuo de sistemas meteorológicos com o uso de imagens de radar e satélite. Além disso, a Fundação Mário Leal Ferreira (FMLF) contribui com projetos urbanísticos que incorporam a perspectiva climática e priorizam soluções baseadas na natureza para adaptação.
Outro reconhecimento importante foi a nomeação de Salvador, em fevereiro de 2023, como Hub de Resiliência pela UNDRR. Esse título é conferido a governos locais com reconhecida liderança em redução de riscos de desastres e compromisso com o apoio a outras cidades no âmbito da iniciativa Making Cities Resilient 2030 (MCR2030).
Além disso, destaca-se a atualização do Inventário de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (IEGEE) de Salvador, que abrangeu a série histórica de 2019 a 2022. Esta edição incorporou análises pós-pandemia, os dados populacionais do Censo de 2022 e refletiu os efeitos de ações estratégicas como a eletrificação do transporte público e a modernização da iluminação com tecnologia LED. O inventário também avaliou os impactos da implementação do PMAMC sobre as emissões no período. Para 2025, estão em curso a revisão do PMAMC e a elaboração de um novo IEGEE, abrangendo os dados referentes aos anos de 2023 e 2024.
Como parte do fortalecimento da governança climática no município, foram instituídos o GT de Emergência Climática e o Comitê de Promoção à Sustentabilidade e Resiliência. O GT deve promover estudos e levantamentos técnicos para a formalização de diagnóstico e viabilização de ações efetivas de adaptação às mudanças do clima, em alinhamento com o PMAMC. Já o Comitê, deve propor diretrizes sistêmicas e setoriais para a mitigação de impactos ambientais, promover estudos voltados às rotinas administrativas com as melhores práticas de sustentabilidade e fomentar, no âmbito dos órgãos e entidades da Prefeitura, uma cultura organizacional pautada na preservação ambiental e na conscientização sobre as relações de causa e efeito associadas às ações humanas e suas implicações no meio ambiente.
column16:
As medidas de mitigação e adaptação às mudanças climáticas em Salvador se materializam por meio de atividades, políticas e programas setoriais voltados à adequação da infraestrutura urbana, ao gerenciamento de transportes, à saúde, à assistência social, à conservação ambiental, à habitação, à gestão de riscos e desastres, entre outras áreas. A integração entre esses diversos setores representa um desafio, ao incluir aspectos técnicos, institucionais e financeiros, especialmente no momento da execução.
Apesar dos desafios existentes, a convergência entre planos e programas nos âmbitos municipal, estadual, federal e internacional que apresentem sinergia com a agenda climática é fundamental para viabilizar ações ambiciosas voltadas à preservação do clima e à prevenção de desastres. Nesse cenário, destaca-se a importância de estimular o engajamento de outros municípios baianos, especialmente aqueles pertencentes à Região Metropolitana de Salvador, promovendo articulações e parcerias que assegurem a efetividade e a sustentabilidade das iniciativas climáticas.
A Política Municipal de Meio Ambiente e Desenvolvimento Sustentável orienta essa atuação cooperativa ao reconhecer, entre seus princípios, a “cooperação entre municípios, estados e países, considerando a abrangência e interdependência das questões ambientais, em especial as mudanças climáticas globais”. Além disso, estabelece como objetivos a “transversalidade da questão ambiental na formulação e implantação das políticas públicas” e a “articulação e compatibilização com as políticas de gestão e proteção ambiental nos âmbitos federal e estadual”.
Em alinhamento, a Política Nacional sobre Mudança do Clima define como diretriz a integração das estratégias de mitigação e adaptação nos níveis local, regional e nacional. Complementarmente, o Plano Nacional de Adaptação (BRASIL/MMA, 2016) destaca que os planos e políticas públicas setoriais e temáticos devem incorporar a gestão dos riscos associados à mudança do clima como parte estruturante de seus objetivos e ações.
De acordo com o Painel Brasileiro de Mudanças Climáticas (PBMC), dois critérios fundamentais para a avaliação de políticas climáticas são a eficácia, isto é, o grau em que a política atinge os objetivos de mitigação ou adaptação propostos, e a viabilidade institucional, que diz respeito à capacidade de governança e implementação. Nesse sentido, as diretrizes do PMAMC contribuem significativamente para aumentar a efetividade das ações e fortalecer a capacidade institucional da Prefeitura, permitindo avanços concretos na implementação de medidas cada vez mais ousadas.
As reuniões realizadas com secretarias, órgãos da administração municipal e subprefeituras vêm fortalecendo a atuação integrada da gestão e estimulando a incorporação da lente climática nas atividades e planejamentos dos diversos setores da Prefeitura. Essa diretriz tem como objetivo articular o Plano de Mitigação e Adaptação às Mudanças Climáticas (PMAMC) com outras políticas, planos e instrumentos em vigor, como o Plano Diretor de Desenvolvimento Urbano (PDDU), o Plano de Mobilidade Urbana, a Estratégia de Resiliência, entre outros. Também orienta a inclusão da variável climática em processos futuros de revisão, atualização ou elaboração de novos marcos de planejamento urbano e setorial.
O PDDU atualmente em vigor, instituído em 2016, foi concebido em um momento em que as discussões sobre mudanças climáticas ainda estavam em fase inicial no município. Por isso, sua abordagem ao tema é limitada. Está prevista para 2025 a atualização do PDDU, que representará uma oportunidade estratégica para consolidar e integrar de forma clara, objetiva e transversal as questões climáticas no ordenamento territorial e no desenvolvimento urbano de Salvador, alinhando-o às metas de mitigação, adaptação e resiliência definidas no PMAMC.
Com isso, evidencia-se que a emergência climática vem sendo considerada de forma crescente e transversal não apenas no PMAMC e na construção do novo Plano Estratégico de Salvador (2025-2028), como também em diversos outros instrumentos de planejamento e gestão municipais. As ações previstas no PMAMC não se limitam ao enfrentamento das mudanças do clima, mas também contribuem de forma estruturada para o desenvolvimento ambiental, social e econômico da cidade, de maneira integrada com outras políticas públicas existentes.
column17:
Os custos financeiros para a implementação de muitas medidas de prevenção e adaptação às mudanças climáticas ainda representam um desafio significativo para a administração pública. No entanto, os custos relacionados aos impactos adversos das mudanças do clima, como perdas humanas, danos à infraestrutura, à saúde pública e ao meio ambiente, são substancialmente maiores. Isso reforça a premissa destacada por Stern (2007), de que investir em desenvolvimento sustentável e em resiliência é mais viável economicamente do que não agir. 
Em Salvador, os investimentos contínuos na estruturação e modernização da Defesa Civil Municipal têm desempenhado um papel fundamental na redução de riscos e na proteção da vida da população, especialmente diante da intensificação dos eventos climáticos extremos. A criação do Centro de Monitoramento e Alerta da Defesa Civil (CEMADEC), a ampliação dos sistemas de alerta precoce, o mapeamento de áreas de risco e a implementação de ações preventivas em comunidades vulneráveis têm fortalecido significativamente a capacidade de resposta da cidade. Como resultado direto dessas medidas, mesmo com a ocorrência de fortes chuvas, deslizamentos e outras situações de emergência, não houve registro de perda de vidas humanas durante anos, o que evidencia a efetividade dos investimentos em prevenção, planejamento e gestão de risco. São 75 pluviômetros automáticos, 2 estações hidrológicas, 12 estações meteorológicas com 147 sensores monitorados e 14 sistemas de alerta e alarme, todos operando a partir do CEMADEC. No entanto, o aumento da frequência e da intensidade das chuvas, associado às mudanças climáticas, impõe a necessidade de constante evolução tecnológica, garantindo maior precisão, agilidade e cobertura territorial no monitoramento. 
Além disso, para que Salvador alcance a meta de neutralidade de emissões até 2049, é necessário enfrentar e superar diversas barreiras, especialmente de natureza financeira e econômica. Entre elas, destacam-se a insuficiência de recursos disponíveis, a existência de subsídios que ainda favorecem combustíveis fósseis e as restrições legais ou institucionais quanto à alocação de receitas públicas para ações climáticas. Além disso, tecnologias sustentáveis, como energias renováveis e geração distribuída, embora mais acessíveis do que no passado, ainda representam um custo elevado de implementação para grande parte da população, constituindo uma barreira econômica importante.
Nesse contexto, mesmo com obstáculos e limitações, a Prefeitura tem adotado medidas concretas, como o decreto municipal que determina a substituição gradativa do combustível da frota de veículos da administração pública, priorizando o uso de etanol em substituição aos combustíveis fósseis mais poluentes. Essa transição tem ocorrido de forma gradual, justamente em razão de limitações financeiras e orçamentárias, que exigem planejamento e execução escalonada. Ainda assim, a iniciativa representa um passo importante na transição energética do setor público.
Outro desafio relevante é a eletrificação da frota de transporte, tanto pública quanto privada. Apesar de representar uma solução estratégica para a descarbonização, os altos custos de aquisição de veículos elétricos e a infraestrutura ainda incipiente de recarga dificultam sua adoção em larga escala. No entanto, Salvador já vem avançando nesse caminho, pois conta com uma frota de veículos 100% elétricos no sistema BRT, além de uma estação de recarga instalada para abastecimento dos ônibus.
Nesse contexto, o planejamento público de médio e longo prazo torna-se fundamental para garantir que os recursos disponíveis sejam direcionados de forma estratégica. Salvador conta com o Plano Plurianual (PPA), elaborado a cada quatro anos, sempre no primeiro ano de gestão, que estabelece diretrizes, objetivos e metas da administração municipal em diversas áreas. O PPA dialoga diretamente com outros instrumentos de planejamento, como o Plano Estratégico e o Plano Diretor de Desenvolvimento Urbano (PDDU), promovendo uma visão integrada e alinhada com os compromissos climáticos.
Atualmente, estão em processo de elaboração o Plano Plurianual 2026-2029 e o Plano Estratégico 2025-2028, que definirão o orçamento e as prioridades da gestão para os próximos anos. Ambos incorporarão as dimensões da sustentabilidade, resiliência, inovação e mudanças climáticas, assegurando que os compromissos assumidos pelo município estejam refletidos nas ações concretas e na alocação de recursos em todo o âmbito da administração pública.
column18:
A transição para uma economia de baixo carbono exige uma redução significativa das emissões de gases de efeito estufa, o que implica a adoção de políticas públicas integradas, focadas em ação climática, inovação tecnológica e mudanças nos padrões de produção e consumo da sociedade. Trata-se de um processo que, se conduzido de forma abrupta, pode gerar impactos em diversos setores econômicos e sociais. Por isso, é essencial que o setor público exerça um papel firme, coordenador e estratégico, promovendo essa transição de maneira gradual, porém determinada e consistente.
Definir como Salvador conduzirá sua trajetória rumo à neutralidade de carbono, promovendo a resiliência climática e incentivando um desenvolvimento econômico inclusivo, será determinante para que a sociedade compreenda as sinergias e transversalidades envolvidas. A liderança local nessa agenda é uma oportunidade para integrar diferentes setores em torno de soluções sustentáveis e inovadoras.
Os riscos da transição para uma economia de baixo carbono envolvem o desafio de manter e modernizar os setores produtivos, garantindo que a redução das emissões ocorra sem comprometer a atividade econômica nem os empregos existentes. Ao mesmo tempo, essa transição traz a oportunidade de incorporar a lógica da descarbonização em futuros planos e políticas, priorizando a eficiência no uso de recursos, a ampliação de fontes renováveis de energia, o desenvolvimento tecnológico, e a criação de novos modelos de negócios sustentáveis.
Além disso, Salvador tem o desafio de incorporar em futuros planos e ações a perspectiva da redução e neutralização de emissões como forma de garantir o fim de uma economia carbonizada, prevendo a eficiência no uso de recursos, a promoção de fontes renováveis de energia e inovação tecnológica, buscando a criação de novos modelos de negócios e postos de trabalho verdes e justos.

column16: El Plan Metropolitano de Ordenamiento Territorial (PMDOT) y el Plan de Uso y Gestión de Suelo (PUGS), son los dos principales instrumentos de carácter vinculante en materia de política pública y planificación urbana en la ciudad de Quito. column15: The Office of Sustainability is tasked with the implementation of Thrive Indianapolis, the City's first sustainability and resiliency plan. column16: Resolution 2019-CPS-R-001, amends a segment of the Comprehensive or Master plan of Marion County, Indiana, by the adoption of Thrive Indianapolis.
column17: The City of Indianapolis received its first 'green bond' designation by independent reviewer Kestrel Verifiers in a 2022 bond sale for a $50 million investment in stormwater infrastructure. This designation was celebrated, and greater attention is being placed on sustainability reporting as it relates to our financial planning and opportunities. \n\nIn 2025, the City of Indianapolis began participating in a cohort of cities hosted by Climate Solutions International focused on climate-ready capital budgeting. Project managers and finance officers from various city departments are piloting a proprietary software platform to begin visualizing how municipal capital projects that incorporate decarbonization, resilience, and equity considerations can impact the long-term operating costs and ROI over the lifetime of the project. Marion County is served by an investor-owned electric utility, AES Indiana. The City of Indianapolis does regularly engage and intervene in the Integrated Resource Plan, offering recommendations that the administration would like to see the utility take. In 2022, AES Indiana did respond to the City's recommendations, citing that their newest energy mix projection values will achieve a 69% reduction in CO2 by 2030 compared to 2018 levels, aligning with our 2030 Science Based Target we set in 2022.

As of September 2025, the City of Indianapolis is participating in AES Indiana's current IRP process.

AES Indiana has an outstanding rate increase request submitted to the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission for review; the utility is largely citing rising costs associated with wind and solar developments as a driving factor for the 13.5% rate increase request. According to the utility, it seems investing in renewable energy is resulting in increased energy burden for Indianapolis ratepayers. City of Indianapolis counsel is participating in conversations with the utility regarding this rate case.

A handful of major employers in the Indianapolis area have supply chains tied to carbon-intensive manufacturing and/or activities, including Rolls-Royce, Allison Transmission, Cummins, Roche, the Indianapolis Motor Speedway, and potentially Eli Lilly as well. A transition to a low-carbon economy could affect their operations or employment practices.

Finally, the Indianapolis International Airport is the 46th busiest airport in the U.S. and the busiest in Indiana. Low-carbon economy transitions that affect air travel and airlines would affect the airport's operations.

column15: The Environmental Collaboration Office, which is part of the Department of Administration, is the primary city agency responsible for climate-related issues. The City's Environmental Sustainability Director leads that office and currently has a staff of nine people, including the Director. An official joint City-County Taskforce on Climate and Economic Equity was created in 2019, and was comprised of 13 members. That Task Force met for 4 years developing recommendations to fight climate change while also fighting economic and racial inequity. The Task Force developed 9 work groups to work on substantive issues from \'greening\' the grid (adding more renewables), to electrifying transportation and increasing energy efficiency, among other substantive topics. Upon completion and adoption of the City of Milwaukee's Climate and Equity Plan on June 20th, 2023, the Task Force transformed into an Accountability Committee to monitor and inform on implementation of the Climate and Equity Plan's 10 Big Ideas (See here: https://city.milwaukee.gov/climate/Climate-Plan). The committee will meet annually to review progress on implementation of the Climate and Equity Plan, which will mostly be comprised of reviewing an implementation report from ECO and asking questions on that annual report. ECO hit an important milestone in September 2024, having secured funding to support and implement each of the 10 Big Ideas.\n
column16: The City of Milwaukee Climate and Equity Plan was approved by the City of Milwaukee Planning Commission on June 5th, 2023 as an amendment to the City of Milwaukee's Citywide Policy Plan. This means that further City or neighborhood plans will need to follow the recommendations in the Climate and Equity Plan. This is particularly relevant regarding a component of Big Idea 5, to prioritize transit-oriented development in the City's zoning code as a means to reduce vehicle miles traveled. Beyond implementing this component of the Climate and Equity Plan, prioritizing transit-oriented development helps to implement the City of Milwaukee Department of City Development's \'Equitable Growth through Transit-Oriented Development Plan.\'
column17: Beginning with City of Milwaukee Department Capital Budget Allocations, all departments must explain how their capital budget requests are helping to advance the City's Climate and Equity Plan goals. Funding requests that support the Climate and Equity Plan are given higher priority for funding. ECO hit an important milestone in September 2024, having secured funding to support and implement each of the 10 Big Ideas in the Climate and Equity Plan. Receiving significant levels of funding, mostly from the federal Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act and the Inflation Reduction Act, has allowed ECO's staff to grow from six in 2023 to nine in 2024 continues with a staff of nine in 2025. Looking back a few years, the City of Milwaukee Common Council allocated limited American Rescue Plan Act funds to help implement two projects recommendations in the Climate and Equity Plan: (1) $15 Million to renovate City-owned homes to make them extremely energy efficient, including installing high-efficiency appliances and electric stoves; (2) $2 million to ensure that when homes are abated of lead hazards, energy efficient upgrades are added, as well. In addition, in early 2023, the City of Milwaukee Common Council allocated an excess $200,000 (accumulated from vacant positions in the City's Department of Administration) to the City of Milwaukee's Environmental Collaboration Office (ECO) to hire consultants and grantwriters to help apply for the dozens of grant opportunities now available through the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, and the Inflation Reduction Act. This additional allocation of funds helped ECO win significant funding to advance the 10 Big Ideas in the Climate and Equity Plan.

column15: The city launched the Green Works Orlando initiative in 2007 to demonstrate its commitment to sustainability and its goals to enhance the quality of life and well-being, generate diverse economic growth, and create equitable access to resources and services for the entire Orlando community. The mayor assembled the city's first Office of Sustainability & Resilience to implement the Green Works Orlando initiative by coordinating with city departments and community stakeholders to ensure the effectiveness of immediate and long-term sustainability planning efforts.
column16: The Office of Sustainability and Resilience was established in 2007 as a small team and has since expanded to include between 16 and 20 members. Recently, it was rebranded as the Office of Sustainability, Resilience, and Future-Ready, reflecting the city's recognition of the need for future planning in light of the significant impacts of climate change. The city has dedicated substantial resources to this office, enabling it to lead initiatives in decarbonization and connect residents with essential resources. \n\nMoreover, this office plays a vital role in informing and advising the local government, ensuring that policy decisions take into account sustainability. The Director and Assistant Director of the office report directly to the city's executive team, which includes key decision-makers involved in development planning. This structure guarantees that climate-related issues are integrated into the city's master and development planning processes.
column17: The Office of Sustainability, Resilience, and Future-Ready has grown to include between 16 and 20 members with an increasing annual budget allocated by the city. This growth reflects the city's commitment to addressing climate-related challenges. Leadership within this office collaborates closely with the city's Chief Financial Officer (CFO) to integrate climate considerations into financial planning. This includes allocating funds for sustainability initiatives, resilience projects, and climate adaptation strategies. The financial planning process also involves assessing potential climate risks and incorporating them into budgetary decisions to ensure that resources are effectively utilized to mitigate and adapt to the impacts of climate change. By embedding climate-related issues into the financial planning framework, the City of Orlando aims to ensure long-term financial resilience and sustainability.
column18:
There is a risk that marginalized communities may not fully benefit from the transition to a low-carbon economy. The city recognizes barriers to community access to resources, funding, and programs crucial to this transition. There is also a historical lack of trust between these communities and the local government due to past failures that excluded many low-income residents and people of color from decision-making and potential benefits. Thus, a level of trust must be built authentically to work with all communities in planning for the future. 

There is also a risk that the transition may be too slow. While the city has outlined several sustainability strategies and goals, including reducing GHG emissions by 90% by 2040 and transitioning to 100% renewable energy by 2050, these commitments may still be insufficient to address the scale and urgency of climate change. There is also a potential risk that the city, along with other cities around the world, might not meet its targets and, as a result, continue to release more carbon into the atmosphere.

Moreover, there has been pushback from the state regarding local policies that support the low-carbon transition. Specifically, local policies that set efficiency standards have been overturned by more conservative state legislation. This political friction can hinder the implementation of effective measures at the local level, slowing progress toward our sustainability goals. 

To mitigate these risks, the City of Orlando is focused on inclusive engagement strategies to ensure all communities benefit from the transition, accelerating efforts to meet ambitious emissions targets, and advocating for supportive policies at the state and national levels.

column15: The City of Columbus is leading on sustainability and climate action on behalf of the Columbus community and Central Ohio through the Columbus Climate Action Plan. The City operates as a strong-Mayor system and has authority to implement policies and programs that support waste reduction, building efficiency, transitioning to clean energy, preservation of green space and tree canopy, transportation infrastructure that supports micromobility and increased public transit. The City has direct operational control over residential waste removal services, all water utility services including water reuse and a compost facility, a small Division of Power (does not cover the entire community), streetlighting, zoning and building permits, health department and inspections and first-responders. The City does not have jurisdiction over the local transportation system (COTA - Central Ohio Transit Authority) but is a chief partner in providing shared infrastructure and planning for our community.
column16: The City of Columbus does not have a singular master plan or document guiding planning and development. Rather individual Departments or organizations are responsible with strong guidance on direction from the Mayor's Office which has laid out the Opportunity Rising framework as a guide. Release of the city's inaugural Climate Action Plan (CAP) in 2021 has strengthened inter-departmental planning and operations within the City of Columbus, as well as enhanced partnership and collaboration with external organizations. It has truly aligned our entire community behind a specific goal and prioritized our community's sustainability efforts. An example of that is how the Central Ohio Transit Authority (COTA) utilized the CAP to create and align their own sustainability plans and efforts to help meet our larger community goals. Columbus' CAP goals represent a substantial transition for departments spanning the entire City of Columbus because it necessitates new ways of executing responsibilities for existing staff, new collaborations, and the creation of new duties, including additional specialized sustainability staff. Sustainable Columbus has established 5 Working Groups based on the 5 sections of the CAP composed of lead agencies, City Departments, and external organizations. These work groups meet regularly to track goals, prioritize projects, budget, and report on CAP implementation progress. For example, to execute the City's municipal Comprehensive Energy Management Plan (CEMP), three departmental teams meet quarterly to manage the vast array of energy audits and the resulting upgrades outlined in the CEMP. This work ties directly to the targets outlined in the (CAP Action 8.1 (improve municipal building energy efficiency 25% by 2030) and is supported through the internal/external agency CAP Buildings Working Group. The CAP elevated the need for City of Columbus' transportation infrastructure master planning and provided the City of Columbus, Department of Public Service with a means to generate discussion regarding carbon-free vehicles, equitable mode shift, and the implementation of a comprehensive multi-modal network to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050. Reducing single occupant vehicle miles traveled and increasing the use of public and mass transit are other top transportation priorities at the City. To support the increased use of electric vehicles and thereby reduce emissions from transportation, the City passed its Equitable EV Readiness Ordinance in the July 2022. This ordinance requires additional EV-charging infrastructure for both commercial and residential new development, as well as in cases of major renovations. Climate goals and strategies are also central to the City's LinkUS initiative - a growth and mobility effort to better connect our community and businesses through the creation of bus rapid transit (BRT) corridors throughout Columbus. This integrated mobility system will make it easier to walk, bike or take public transit in our region's busiest areas. The initiative is a partnership between the City of Columbus, Franklin County, Central Ohio Transit System (COTA), and the Mid-Ohio Regional Planning Commission (MORPC). As part of our Climate Action Plan commitments and Mayor Ginther's Equity Agenda, the City is working to bolster the sustainability of its neighborhoods while imparting environmental justice. This means ensuring climate-related policies and actions benefit our most climate-vulnerable residents, primarily our communities-of-color and lower-income neighborhoods. In order to impart environmental justice while realizing our emissions goals, we recognize the need to co-create more policy and programs with community members who are most affected. Due to increased staffing within our Sustainable Columbus office, sustainability and climate is able to be represented in critical planning spaces such as the City's newly established Citywide Equity Team or the Bike Plus planning process. This ensures sustainability and climate goals are included and complementary to high priority efforts led by other City Departments. We know to further our climate-related equity goals, we must support healthy and resilient communities by establishing a coordinated network of “resilience hubs” and bolster regional emergency alert systems to include climate hazard notifications. It also means implementing land use planning strategies for healthy ecosystems by increasing development density, upgrading to LED streetlights, increasing equitable access to green space, and implementing water adaptation strategies. Finally, the City must support residents in preparing for warmer and wetter seasons. This entails protecting vulnerable assets from the impacts of climate change, reducing urban heat island effects through increased tree canopy cover, and evaluating microgrid and storage projects for sites that could serve as community shelters in the event of a natural or other disaster.
column17: To achieve our Columbus Climate Action Plan's (CAP) goal of reducing our community-wide greenhouse gas emissions 45% by 2030, the City recognizes that the benefits to this work outweigh the costs of implementation. The CAP has assigned Lead Agencies as well as Implementing Partners for each of the 13 strategies of action. The implementing agencies are responsible for helping to fund initiatives that support the implementation of the CAP from their department's or organization's annual budget. This budgeting process at the City takes place on an annual basis and funding levels do depend on income tax collections, the primary source of City funding. Cost/benefit and lifecycle cost analyses are important aspects to planning and budgeting for all projects, climate-related and otherwise, around the City. It is up to each individual department to submit priorities for project requests. Departments do frequently prioritize projects for CAP implementation, but to assume the CAP will be fully funded on the City's budget alone is not a feasible, long-term strategy for the plan's success. One specific example of an estimate for the work outlined by the CAP concerns Action 8.1, work supporting the City's Comprehensive Energy Management Plan (CEMP). This work is anticipated to cost between $14 - 20 million. However, because the costs for capital and operating projects all generate gas, electric, and water savings, all of the items will pay for themselves over time, in addition to reducing pollution and greenhouse gas emissions.. The Sustainable Columbus team now regularly meets with all City Department leadership to help guide fiscal conversations to incorporate the full cost of the CAP's implementation directly into each Department's annual budget considerations. The City's Auditor Office has recognized and noted the increasing importance of ESG factors to rating agencies and banking institutions when considering municipal governments. The City of Columbus is proud to maintain a AAA bond rating, which is crucial to financing our capital improvements -- many of which have direct connection to climate-related issues and policy. The City of Columbus issues bonds to finance its capital projects, including its park improvements, road work, sidewalks, streetlights, fire stations, safety equipment, and other public improvements. These bonds are repaid with income-tax money that's set aside for major public works. Maintaining a AAA bond rating saves the City and our residents millions of dollars due to providing lower interest rates. In order to continue demonstrating the City's strong fiscal management, the Auditor has begun reporting disclosure (to be included in the City's bond issuance documents) regarding the City's efforts to combat environmental risk. Another impact the Climate Action Plan and expansion of the sustainability office has had, is the need to think through how sustainability funding is tracked and monitored. This will assist in understanding how much the City is investing as a whole in its climate and sustainability efforts, while improving the ability to plan for the future. These conversations are ongoing with the Department of Finance and the Mayor's Office to determine how the current financial planning systems can be improved or changed to better support our sustainability work. This further underscores the importance of the Columbus Climate Action Plan and how climate related issues are impacting financial planning in the City of Columbus.
column18: The primary risk related to City of Columbus' transition to a low-carbon economy will be changes to energy generation and clean energy policies and practices that may occur at the state, county, and/or federal level and are beyond the direct control of the City. These changes will have a broad impact across the Central Ohio region and may inhibit ability to achieve climate goals. Central Ohio is also one of the nation's largest and fastest growing data center hubs, which will drive major increases in energy and water consumption. This is a major point of conversation amongst leadership in Central Ohio currently, as there is projected to be an energy shortfall in the next few years due to energy generation not keeping pace with demand. This has already resulted in State and Federal policy makers pushing to use fossil fuel sources as the solution. Another risk in our jurisdiction's transition to a low-carbon economy concerns the massive electrification effort for buildings and transportation. The conversion of natural gas heating equipment to all-electric facilities can be costly and difficult, particularly as electricity costs are rising at rates of nearly 20-30%. Sustainable Columbus staff are working to help grow City staff knowledgeable on new, energy-efficient systems and technology in order to ensure proper operation and maintenance. Additional staff training will be necessary to support the operation of new types of technology that will be employed. Furthermore, the City operates many critical water, wastewater, and safety (police and fire) sites that must maintain 24/7,365-day operation. Making sure these and other community sites are adequately heated through winter and cooled in summer is integral to the City's operation. Bolstering grid resiliency, including battery storage and microgrid deployment are other critical components of this electrification transition. Proper training for staff will also be needed for these projects to ensure maximum benefits are obtained.

The City's current climate change governance structure includes:

- City Council: Responsible for assessing and managing climate-related risks and opportunities as part of their decision making, and to consider climate-related issues as part of its review of the City's strategy, budget, and capital planning.
-Environment and Climate Change Committee: is a subcommittee of City Council made up of Members of Council responsible for making recommendations to Council on environmental initiatives, such as waste management, water quality, climate change, natural systems, green space, urban forest, etc. 

- Strategic Initiatives Department and Climate Change and Resiliency Services: Responsible for responding to climate change issues and driving positive environmental results for the City by focusing efforts to advance key strategies, including the Climate Change Master Plan, Energy Evolution Strategy, Climate Resiliency Strategy, Urban Forest Management Plan and associated priorities, programs, projects and policies. This includes coordinating and supporting climate considerations embedded across the organization.

- Climate Change Council Sponsors Group: Members include Council representatives from key Committees including Environment and Climate Change, Transportation, Transit, Financial and Corporate Services, Planning, and Ottawa Board of Health, as well as support from both the Mayor and City Manager's offices. The responsibilities of the group is to advise on how climate change issues will intersect with Committee and departmental priorities and considerations and provide advice to staff regarding specific policies, projects or Master Plan reviews that support achieving the City's climate change goals.

- Climate Change Executive Steering Committee: Members consist of the City Manager's office, all department General Managers, the Chief Financial Officer, and the Medical Officer of Health. The responsibilities of the group are to champion policies, programs, and projects related to climate change within their own departments with Committees and Council and to be kept informed by all relevant departments about key climate-related risks, opportunities, impacts and city initiatives. 

- Climate Change Key Advisors: Members consist of departmental representative largely at the Director and Manager level. The responsibilities of the group as to provide feedback and strategic advice on cross cutting corporate projects and Climate Change Master Plan priorities, advise on how climate change considerations will be embedded and prioritized into City business, and champion projects to their senior management.

The Official Plan (OP) provides a vision for the future growth of the city and a policy framework to guide the city's physical development. The plan's vision is for Ottawa to grow to be the most liveable mid-sized city in North America. To achieve this vision, Ottawa must be an energy conscious city where people can live, work, and play in all future climate conditions. The Official Plan is an essential tool to meet climate change objectives through land use planning, urban design, regulatory practice, building design and environmental protection. The new Official Plan took an innovative approach by translating health, inclusivity and sustainability into growth planning and land use policy. Strategic Directions specific to “Healthy and Inclusive Communities” and “Energy and Climate Change” were woven into the new OP as cross cutting issues, which are essential to the achievement of a sustainable and resilient city. Eight strategic goals were identified to support climate change mitigation and/or adaptation. Updates to the Transportation Master Plan (TMP), Infrastructure Master Plan (IMP), Greenspace and Urban Forest Master Plan (GUFMP), Parks and Recreation Facilities Master Plan, Solid Waste Master Plan (SWMP), the new comprehensive Zoning By-Law, and the Development Charges By-law will also consider alignment with the policy directions set out in the new Official Plan and Council's greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets. 

To find out more about the Official Plan and the climate change policies that were embedded, visit: https://ottawa.ca/en/planning-development-and-construction/official-plan-and-master-plans/official-plan#section-9190f110-4c31-467a-ba8c-927bb0a0a51d

The Comprehensive Asset Management (CAM) program guides the management of the City's assets. Risk management and asset resiliency are already core principles of assetmanagement. Further integrating climate considerations into CAM enables climate change to be considered alongside additional challenges such as aging infrastructure, growth, and limited resources. This involves embedding climate change considerations into the management of existing assets, the design of new capital projects, and City asset management policies and practices. It supports the City to meet provincial regulation (O. Reg 588/17) which requires municipalities to commit to considering climate change in asset management planning, and better positions the City to respond to external funding opportunities and integrate these considerations into municipal budgets and long-range financial plans processes. 

To find out more, visit: https://ottawa.ca/en/city-hall/budget-finance-and-corporate-planning/corporate-planning/comprehensive-asset-management#section-6f0364fc-56f5-4bdc-9a1f-b8f8c3a44dcc
column17:
For Budget 2024 and Budget 2025, the City of Ottawa applied a climate lens to its capital budget requests with the purpose to better understand how the City is investing to implement the Climate Change Master Plan, reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and increase Ottawa's resilience to current and future impacts of climate change. This is the first step towards building a climate change accounting framework to support decision makers. Future budgets will build upon this exercise, including establishing a carbon budget. 

In this exercise, capital budget requests were rated on a qualitative scale of no contribution to minor, moderate or major contribution to reducing GHG emissions or building climate resiliency. Investments were rated as making:-
 A minor contribution if they were considered in line with Energy Evolution's business-as-planned scenario or the project had been modified to consider climate impacts.
- A moderate contribution if they were considered to go beyond business-as-planned to reducing GHG emissions or directly addressed a climate risk.
- A major contribution if they were considered in line with Energy Evolution's 100 per cent scenario or significantly addressed a climate risk. 

Overall, 155 capital budget requests were rated as having a climate contribution in Budget 2024. Of these, 24 were identified as going beyond business-as-planned or business-as-usual and were rated as having a moderate or major contribution, totalling more than $278 million of new investments ($188M for capital investments that reduce emissions and $86M for capital investments that build climate resiliency). More projects with moderate or major contributions are expected in future years as climate considerations are embedded more fully in projects, policies, and master plans, and the Climate Resiliency Strategy is completed. 

More information on Budget 2024 and how a climate lens was applied can be found here: https://pub-ottawa.escribemeetings.com/filestream.ashx?DocumentId=165537
