It is recognized that the municipality alone will not be able to accomplish the scale of investment required. Future year funding commitments by the municipality, combined with revenue streams, private capital sources, and funding from senior levels of government will ultimately influence the municipality's success in achieving emission reductions.

- Governance: Collective action is required from all levels of government, utilities, businesses, organizations, and individuals is required to change things at a system level. It is estimated that the majority of emissions within Ottawa are attributable to activities outside the direct control of the municipality; however, research shows that municipalities can influence over half of emission reductions in cities.

- Policy and Regulatory Requirements: Provincial and federal government policies, regulations, standards, and authorities can have significant impacts on the collective ability to accelerate action. They can either support achieving the transition to a low-carbon economy, or they can hinder, delay, or outright cancel the ability to take action. 

- Data: Access to timely and reliable data is a challenge and impacts the ability to support decision makers and track progress.- Staffing: Accelerated action requires accelerated training and scaling up of the workforce to plan, design, implement, operate and maintain, and monitor each action.

- Supply chain issues: Current and continued supply chain issues, compounded by rising interest rates and inflation, will impact the collective ability to accelerate action and investment.

- Emerging technologies: Some projects are reliant on new and emerging technologies, which come with additional financial and operational risks.

column15: City Council unanimously adopted the Strategic Energy Action Plan in December of 2018. Since then, the City has been working diligently to reduce carbon emission and mitigate the effects of climate change. Tackling carbon reduction goals takes teamwork, accountability, and collaboration. The SEAP Operations Team has been a standing internal leadership group since early 2019 and is comprised of representatives of more than 20 city departments who meet regularly throughout the year to connect on goals and initiatives for a low-carbon Charlotte. This group provides a critical perspective to advance the SEAP by providing department-specific input on climate issues. This team also ensures that climate-related issues are considered in multiple City processes from budget to building infrastructure to water. The CharlotteFuture 2040 Comprehensive Plan and implementation framework, such as Community Area Planning, provide additional mechanisms, including a dashboard with cross organizational and cross sectoral reporting and oversight. In 2024, The City has consultants complete a Climate Risk Assessment as part of our SEAP Update. While the update was officially adopted in spring 2025, the Climate Risk Assessment was completed in 2024 and shared in public meetings toward the larger effort. As part of this assessment, the climate risks reviewed are: Severe thunderstorms, hurricanes/tropical cyclones, urban flooding and wildfire acute risks as well as extreme heat, drought, water stress, and precipitation for chronic risks. The highest risk for Charlotte is Extreme Heat, as we've seen a 300% increase in extreme heat days since our baseline average (1960-1990). This information has helped highlight areas to address in the updated SEAP+ and the city is working to address.
column16: The SEAP calls for city planning processes to incorporate the mission of becoming a low-carbon city. The Charlotte Future 2040 Comprehensive Plan is a shared, comprehensive vision to guide the Queen City's growth over the next 20 years. The Plan is the foundation for strategic policy, equitable investment in infrastructure, and regulatory tools such as the Unified Development Ordinance Charlotte's UDO simplifies, consolidates, and updates the regulations that guide Charlotte's development into a single document. In addition, the UDO aligns these standards with the vision of the Charlotte Future 2040 Comprehensive Plan and other adopted city policies, like the SEAP. Some examples of concepts embedded in Charlotte Future 2040 Comprehensive Plan and the subsequent UDO include (1) requiring electric vehicle charging infrastructure for off-street vehicle parking and added height bonus for exceeding required electric vehicle charging infrastructure, (2) added height bonus menu options for High Performance Construction to increase energy efficient buildings and renewable energy, (3) added bonus menu options for additional EV charging infrastructure above what is now required, (4) added height bonus menu option for Affordable Housing Equitable Energy Efficient Home Rehab Projects, (5) Fee Program to drive low-carbon investments in affordable housing, (6) enhanced safety and accessibility of transit, bike lanes, and sidewalks to promote micromobility, and (7) implementing Resilient Innovation District (RID) programs throughout the city that are responsive to different Place Types and contexts, and promote net-zero development and carbon neutrality. When the SEAP was developed, the idea of having Resilient Innovation Districts (RIDs) resonated with staff to support implementation work. City staff worked to formalize the concept and ensure that the Charlotte Future 2040 Plan supported the integration of these districts formally within the city's growth management plans. However, in 2020, the Charlotte City Council formally started the Corridors of Opportunity program, a program to foster thriving communities for residents and businesses, build lasting legacies, and grow communities equitably in six underinvested areas in Charlotte. With the creation of these investment priority corridors, the Office of Sustainability staff has transitioned away from creating criteria to establish additional investment areas specifically for sustainability and resiliency innovation and has instead adopted the six corridor geographies as resilient innovation districts. \nIn addition, throughout 2024, the Office of Sustainability and Resilience worked with the Charlotte-Mecklenburg Planning Department, by attending all Community Area Planning (CAP) meetings to represent sustainability initiatives throughout the city. This coordination allowed planning and sustainability staff to highlight connections and create language that will live in the SEAP+ (2025 adoption) as well as the CAPs (adoption forthcoming). \n

As a local administration, Sofia Municipality does not hold legislative power at the national level, but it plays a critical role in climate governance through strategic planning, policy implementation, and service delivery. While national frameworks set the overall regulatory context, the municipality has significant levers to influence local development, particularly in sectors such as transport, energy efficiency, air quality, waste management, and land use.
Oversight of climate-related issues is ensured through several mechanisms:
The Municipal Council and its permanent committees (e.g. Environment, Transport, Infrastructure) regularly review and approve climate-related policies, strategies, and investment programs.
The Mayor and Deputy Mayors oversee the integration of climate considerations into municipal operations, with relevant directorates reporting progress and proposing measures.
Interdepartmental working groups have been established to coordinate the implementation of the Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP 2021-2030), the Integrated Development Plan, and the Green City Plan.
Sofia Municipality also participates in the EU Mission for 100 Climate-Neutral Cities, having signed a Climate City Contract (CCC) that aligns municipal actions with EU climate neutrality targets.
Through this governance structure, climate-related issues are systematically embedded into strategic and financial planning, ensuring policy coherence with national authorities and leveraging EU funding to deliver adaptation and mitigation initiatives at the local level.
column16:
Climate-related issues are systematically integrated into both sectoral and long-term strategic documents of Sofia Municipality, including the Integrated Development Plan (Vision for Sofia 2050), the Spatial Development Plan, and the Green City Plan. The Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP) 2021-2030 serves as the municipality's leading climate framework, ensuring that mitigation and adaptation measures are embedded across sectors. To guarantee coherence, an interdepartmental coordination mechanism was established to align these strategies and mainstream climate considerations into land use, energy, mobility, and health planning.

Detailed sectoral analyses of risks such as heatwaves, flooding, air quality deterioration, and biodiversity loss inform zoning decisions, infrastructure investments, and public health preparedness. These assessments provide the evidence base for future-oriented planning and resilience-building.

Innovative tools also support climate-sensitive planning. The DS4PED initiative applies a digital twin approach to deliver climate and meteorological data services, strengthening risk prevention, disaster resilience, and district-level adaptation planning, with potential for scaling city-wide.

In recognition of this structured and forward-looking approach, Sofia received the EU Mission Label (May 2025) after developing and signing its Climate City Contract (CCC) under the EU Mission for 100 Climate-Neutral and Smart Cities. This high-level recognition validates the robustness of Sofia's planning framework and improves access to EU and private financing for the delivery of climate measures.
Collectively, these initiatives ensure that climate considerations are not only included in planning documents, but are also embedded into Sofia's long-term development trajectory—transforming policy commitments into measurable action.
column17:
Based on the strategic documents adopted by the Municipal Council, including the Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP 2021-2030), the Integrated Development Plan, and more recently the Climate City Contract (CCC) under the EU Mission for 100 Climate-Neutral and Smart Cities, funds are allocated annually in Sofia Municipality's budget for both climate change adaptation and mitigation.
In response to the increasing manifestation of climate risks, the municipality has steadily increased its climate-related expenditures over the past four years. Budget lines now regularly include measures such as the prevention of vector-borne infections, summer surface cooling through water sprinkling in public areas, the creation of shaded and “cooled” urban spaces, and enhanced maintenance of green infrastructure. Significant resources are also allocated to the rehabilitation of deteriorated residential areas, replacing outdated pavement surfaces that accumulate heat and dust with environmentally friendly materials.

Climate considerations are integrated into capital investment planning, particularly in sectors such as sustainable transport, renewable energy deployment, energy efficiency of municipal buildings, and air quality improvement. Through the CCC and its EU Mission Label, Sofia Municipality also leverages EU funds and private investment to co-finance major climate initiatives, ensuring that climate action is embedded into the long-term financial framework of the city.
This consistent prioritization of climate issues in the municipal budget illustrates how climate risks and opportunities are shaping financial planning, enabling both immediate adaptation responses and long-term pathways towards climate neutrality.
column18:
The transition to a low-carbon economy presents a number of strategic risks for Sofia Municipality:

Regulatory risks - Uncertainty related to evolving EU and national frameworks (e.g. building renovation requirements, carbon pricing in transport and heating, and clean air directives) may create challenges for long-term planning and investment. Legal and political disputes around climate measures could also slow down implementation.

Financial risks - Achieving climate neutrality requires significant upfront investment in energy efficiency, renewable energy, sustainable mobility, and resilient infrastructure. Insufficient or delayed access to EU and national funding, combined with pressure on the municipal budget, could limit the pace of decarbonisation.

Energy system risks - Sofia's energy transition depends on reducing reliance on fossil fuels, especially in heating. Slow progress in diversifying energy sources or modernising infrastructure could expose the city to energy price volatility and undermine emission reduction efforts.

Social and equity risks - Measures such as stricter building standards, low-emission mobility, and phasing out of polluting heating systems may disproportionately impact low-income and vulnerable groups if not paired with targeted support and financial assistance. This could lead to public resistance and affect social acceptance of climate policies.
Institutional and capacity risks - Delivering climate neutrality requires enhanced administrative capacity, data availability, and inter-departmental coordination. Limited capacity could delay implementation and monitoring of transition measures.
Sofia Municipality is addressing these risks through phased implementation of policies, stakeholder engagement, integration of climate action into long-term financial planning, and alignment with the Climate City Contract (CCC) under the EU Mission for 100 Climate-Neutral Cities, which strengthens access to technical and financial support.

The City of Ljubljana ensures strong oversight of climate-related issues through its governance system, which includes the City Council, the Municipal Administration, public companies owned by the city, and district communities. Decisions are led by the Mayor together with five deputy mayors, one of whom is specifically responsible for environmental protection, climate change, and spatial planning. The Environmental Protection Department responsible for climate related issues reports directly to this deputy mayor, ensuring clear accountability and vertical integration of responsibilities.

Climate-related issues are regularly reviewed in committee meetings, where heads of municipal departments and public companies (e.g., Public Holding Ljubljana) provide updates on progress, identified risks, and policy adjustments. City established as well a Climate Change Council, that brings together representatives of public institutions, the private sector, academia, and residents, that enables inclusive governance. The City Transition Team (CTT)- public administration department representatives and representatives of public companies and the Core City Team (CCT)- public administration representatives further coordinate climate measures across departments and public companies, ensuring coherence in governance processes.

Processes and frequency of oversight are formalized: operational updates are prepared quarterly at committee level, and annual reports to the City Council include a review of implemented measures and the Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Inventory. Dedicated Specialized Focus Teams (SFTs) monitor key areas such as mobility, waste management, and energy efficiency, preparing detailed analyses that feed into decision-making. Based on these reviews, strategies and action plans are regularly updated, ensuring that climate-related goals remain relevant, achievable, and aligned with both local needs and set targets.

Climate related targets are fully embedded in strategic and spatial planning and are integrated across key documents such as the Local energy concept (LEK), SECAP, the Sustainable urban mobility plan, the Strategy for circular potentials, the Environmental protection programme, Urban forest development strategy. 

As the capital, Ljubljana also has special legal responsibilities under the Law on the Capital of the Republic of Slovenia, mandating cooperation with national authorities on environmental protection, climate, and spatial planning.

Oversight extends to budgeting and financial planning, where climate priorities are systematically included in annual budgets and capital investment plans. Participation in EU projects further strengthens monitoring since it requires structured reporting at city, national or European level.

Finally, oversight involves as well strong community participation. Namely, Ljubljana's 17 district communities provide platforms for regular public debates and workshops, ensuring two-way communication between residents and decision-makers. This participatory approach guarantees that climate projects are not only technically sound but also socially accepted and aligned with citizens' needs, reinforcing the robustness of Ljubljana's governance model.
column16:
Climate-related issues have had a profound impact on the City of Ljubljana's master and development planning, influencing both long-term visions and operational decisions. 

The city first outlined its sustainability roadmap in Ljubljana Vision 2025, which set the goal of becoming carbon-neutral by 2050. This ambition was strengthened in Ljubljana Vision 2045, advancing the target to 2040. These documents establish the long-term (up to 2045 and beyond) horizon, while the Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP) provided a medium-term framework of 40% reduction till 2030. Together, they provide a multi-layered planning structure that systematically integrates climate risks and opportunities.

Adaptation activities are a core part of development planning. An initial cross-sectoral vulnerability and risk analysis was conducted in the SECAP. In 2025 Ljubljana launched a more detailed assessment in line with the EU Mission on Adaptation and the IPCC AR5 methodology, including climate projections and scenario-based modelling. This analysis supports targeted actions such as:
(i) Revitalisation of the Gradaščica and Mali Graben rivers with nature-based solutions (widened riverbeds, side channels, vegetated banks, hydro-morphological monitoring) to improve flood resilience.

(ii) Expansion of green areas and projects like the Dynamic UHI Atlas and installation of meteorological sensors to monitor and mitigate urban heat islands.

(iii)Upgrades of water management systems to cope with heavier rainfall events.

(iv)Integration of adaptation measures into sectoral strategies such as Rural development, agriculture, and the urban forest development strategy.

Mitigation activities are equally embedded into planning. Ljubljana has:

(i) Adopted strict building codes to enhance energy efficiency in line with PURES.

(ii) Carried out the Energy Renovation of Ljubljana Public Buildings (EOL) project, retrofitting over 80 public facilities, with support from EU cohesion funds and private partners.

(iii)Installed solar power plants on 51 public buildings under a Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) scheme.

(iv)Invested in sustainable transport, including cycling infrastructure and the BicikeLJ bike-sharing system.

(v) Prioritised district heating decarbonisation, energy retrofitting, and expansion of renewable energy as key long-term measures.

Strategic decisions influenced by climate risks and opportunities include the adoption of the City Climate Contract (CCC) under the EU Mission 100, which commits Ljubljana to achieving climate neutrality by 2030, supported by a detailed financial and action plan. The award of the European Green Capital title in 2016 was also a turning point, catalysing over 2,400 projects that transformed Ljubljana into a more liveable, sustainable city.

Linkages with national and European frameworks further reinforce these efforts. Ljubljana's CAP contributes directly to Slovenia's National Energy and Climate Plan (NEPN) and National Adaptation Plan (NAP), while aligning with EU policies such as the Green Deal and Fit for 55. The city also participates in the Covenant of Mayors and Mission 100 NZC ensuring consistency with higher-level strategies.

By combining short-term actions, medium-term strategies, and long-term visions, Ljubljana ensures that both adaptation and mitigation are embedded in development planning. This systemic approach enhances resilience, accelerates the path to climate neutrality, and secures broad stakeholder support, making climate-related risks and opportunities a central driver of the city's sustainable future.
column17:
Climate-related issues have significantly influenced the City of Ljubljana's financial planning and budgeting processes across multiple areas, shaping both operational and capital allocations as well as strategic financial initiatives. Below is a detailed analysis of how these influences manifest:

 Operating Costs and Revenues: Climate-related issues have led to an increased focus on funding for initiatives that mitigate and adapt to climate change. The city has incorporated climate actions across various departments and sectors rather than allocating a dedicated climate investment budget. This strategic integration has increased operational costs related to climate initiatives such as waste management, energy efficiency programs, and flood protection. Revenues from fees, taxes, and government subsidies also partially support these initiatives, with tax revenues constituting around 2/3 of the city's general revenues. Non-tax revenues, including subsidies and public-private partnerships (PPPs), provide essential support for the increased operational focus on climate resilience and sustainable development.

Capital Expenditures and Capital Allocation: The city's climate-related investments have shown a consistent upward trend, with the total funds for climate actions rising from EUR 120 million to EUR 260 million between 2020 and 2024. The share of these funds in the overall budget has also increased from 21% to 42%. Investments are targeted towards priority areas like waste management, energy systems, built environment, and transportation, demonstrating the city's commitment to climate action. Major projects include the decarbonisation of district heating, energy retrofitting of buildings, and investments in green infrastructure and sustainable transport. This significant capital allocation underscores Ljubljana's determination to meet its climate neutrality targets by 2030.

Access to Capital: Climate-related opportunities and risks have necessitated the exploration of diverse funding sources to ensure sufficient financial capacity for executing large-scale projects. The total estimated CAPEX (capital expenditure) for climate-related investments by 2030 is around EUR 7.8 billion, with mobility and transport being the largest share. The city's share of these investments is estimated at EUR 387 million, representing 5% of the total, supplemented by EUR 838 million (11%) from municipal utilities. Additionally, the city relies on a mix of external sources including EU and national subsidies, loans from institutions like the EIB (European Investment Bank), and private sector involvement through PPPs and other financial instruments. This mix helps the city diversify its capital sources, reduce financial risks, and leverage innovative funding opportunities like green bonds and blended finance.

Impact on Long-Term Financial Planning: The city's climate neutrality goal by 2030 has influenced the development of a structured investment plan, prioritizing sectors such as mobility, building retrofits, energy systems, and waste management. Ljubljana's financial planning includes measures like the phased allocation of EUR 55 million annually until 2030 for climate-related investments, indicating the city's preparedness to handle necessary expenditures within its budget constraints. Moreover, private sector contributions and citizen involvement are critical components in covering the remaining costs, highlighting the participatory nature of Ljubljana's financial approach.

Public-private partnership (PPP) projects in Ljubljana represent an important model of cooperation between the public and private sectors aimed at developing, financing and implementing infrastructure and other important projects in the city. 
Examples of such projects are:
1. energy refurbishment of public buildings (EOL project): This extensive project involved the energy refurbishment of over 80 public buildings such as kindergartens, primary schools, sports facilities, city's administration buildings and cultural facilities. The project focussed on improving energy efficiency and integrating renewable energy sources. The project involved an investment of around €60 million, the majority of which was provided by the private partner, supplemented by EU cohesion funds and funds from the City of Ljubljana. The project received international recognition and was highly praised at the United Nations Global Forum.
2. solar power plant project: In the context of this project, we would like to emphasise that the project is implemented through a power purchase agreement (PPA). This project involved the construction of a community of solar power plants covering 51 public buildings. column18:
The City of Ljubljana has embarked on an ambitious journey towards climate neutrality, outlined in its CCC, SECAP and LEK. This transition requires systemic shifts across energy, buildings, mobility, waste, and other sectors. Risks are acknowledged within the CCC and are managed through proactive governance and planning.

(1) Skill shortages. A key barrier is the scarcity of skilled professionals both within the municipal administration and the wider labour market. There is a limited pool of experts with the knowledge required to implement energy retrofits, advanced mobility systems, renewable energy solutions, and climate-smart urban planning. In addition, there is insufficient understanding of the interdependence between different fields of action, which limits systemic responses. This could slow the implementation of projects and reduce their effectiveness.

(2) Institutional barriers. Existing organisational structures are not always designed to support interdisciplinary collaboration. Cooperation with national-level institutions is sometimes weak, which hampers alignment of policies and investments. Knowledge gaps in certain specialised areas of climate action may further delay implementation.

(3) Regulatory barriers. The transition depends on regulatory changes at both national and EU level. Slow acceptance of new construction materials and technologies, the absence of harmonised regulation, lengthy procedures, and bureaucratic hurdles can delay projects and increase costs. Complex permitting processes, for example in energy retrofitting or infrastructure upgrades, pose a particular risk.

(4) Digitalisation challenges. ICT systems in the city are still partly siloed, limiting data interoperability and effective monitoring. A digital divide persists among certain population groups, which can slow the uptake of smart solutions. Risks also include cybersecurity threats, data quality issues, and high costs of integration across platforms.

(5) Financial barriers. Climate neutrality requires large capital expenditures. Limited municipal budgets, complex approval procedures, and long project implementation periods increase financial risk. High upfront investment costs (e.g. energy retrofits, district heating decarbonisation, large-scale renewable systems) and long payback periods make projects less attractive to investors. Fluctuations in energy and material prices, inflation, and interest rates further raise costs. Engagement from private investors, EU funds, and national programmes is essential, yet often constrained by knowledge gaps and limited awareness.

(6) Stakeholder involvement challenges. Behavioural patterns and a lack of awareness among citizens can hinder the adoption of energy-efficient solutions, low-carbon mobility, and waste reduction. Public acceptance of new technologies and infrastructure projects is not guaranteed, particularly if perceived as costly or disruptive. Ensuring synergy between local actions and national strategies is also challenging.

(7) Dependence on technology. The city increasingly relies on innovative technologies in energy, waste, and mobility. While these solutions are essential, they carry residual risks of technological failure, malfunction, or obsolescence, which could lead to higher lifecycle costs and missed climate targets.

(8) Community resistance. Public opposition to certain projects, especially large infrastructure developments or behavioural measures, could delay implementation. If citizens perceive measures as inequitable the support for the transition may weaken.

(9) Economic and market risks. Volatility in markets, disrupted supply chains, and limited availability of key equipment or skilled labour can affect timelines and budgets. The construction and energy sectors are particularly exposed, leading to delays in tenders or increased costs for essential materials.

(10) Legal risks. Climate-related litigation is a growing concern. Potential lawsuits could arise from non-compliance with EU air quality and emission standards, environmental due diligence failures, or insufficient delivery of PPP/PPA contracts. Non-achievement of statutory or EU climate targets could expose the city to legal liability, penalties, or forced remedial investments.

(11) Reputation risks. Ljubljana's strong climate commitments raise expectations. Any delay in meeting neutrality milestones, or failure to ensure a socially fair transition, could undermine public trust, reduce investor confidence, and weaken partnerships.

column15: (1) Auckland Council voted unanimously to declare a Climate Emergency in 2019 signalling councillors' commitment to putting climate change at the front of our decision making. (2) Councillors also unanimously adopted Te Tāruke-ā-Tāwhiri: Auckland's Climate Plan in 2020 reaffirming our commitment to halving Auckland's total emissions by 2030 and reducing transport emissions by 64 per cent over the same period. (3) In August 2022 Auckland Council endorsed the Transport Emissions Reduction Pathway TERP. The TERP plan developed by Auckland Council and Auckland Transport sets out a pathway to reduce transport emissions by 64 per cent by 2030 as directed by Te Tāruke-ā-Tāwhiri. TERP describes how the transport system must transform in eight years if Auckland is to drastically cut its transport emissions and realise the benefits of a much more sustainable, safer and healthier transport system. (4) We are required under legislation to manage our climate risks and are currently in a multiyear process to understand our organisational risks prioritise them and develop a risk management framework to manage them. (5) In April 2021 the Government introduced the Financial Sector Climate related Disclosures and Other Matters Amendment Bill. The Act requires reporting entities to prepare climate elated disclosures compliant with reporting standards based on the Taskforce for Climate Related Disclosure TCFD framework. As an issuer of bonds on the NZX New Zealand's Stock Exchange and other exchanges, Auckland Council is captured within the mandatory disclosure regime and because it is the parent entity of a group, it must prepare climate standards for the entire group. Auckland Council is required to prepare a compliant climate elated disclosure for the financial year commencing on 1 July 2023. Due to investor demand, the group started voluntarily preparing climate disclosures aligned to the TCFD in 2019. Under the new legislation the group must report climate related risks and opportunities over the short medium and long term and how both transitional and physical risks are identified and integrated into group risk management processes. (6) Work has so far been undertaken to identify and prioritise key risks for the group. The climate risks are included in the groups Climate Disclosure from FY23. (7) Auckland Council released the latest State of the Environment report in September 2025, providing a snapshot of the health of Tāmaki Makaurau's air, land, freshwater and marine ecosystems. The report produced every few years highlights encouraging progress in some areas since the last assessment in 2021, alongside persistent pressures driven by population growth, urban development and climate change.
column16:
(1) The Auckland Plan 2050 adopted in 2018 is our long-term spatial plan to ensure Auckland grows in a way that will meet the opportunities and challenges of the future. It is required by legislation to contribute to Auckland's social, economic, environmental and cultural wellbeing. The plan outlines the big issues facing Auckland and recommends the way in which Aucklanders and others involved in the future of Auckland can best respond to them. The Development Strategy and six outcomes set Auckland's strategy to 2050. They consider how we will address the key challenges of high population growth and environmental degradation and how we can ensure shared prosperity for all Aucklanders. Within the Auckland Plan 2050, climate change is one of the three key challenges facing Auckland. Further detail is provided in the Environment and Cultural Heritage Outcome. It is clear however that action on the priorities detailed within Te Tāruke-ā-Tāwhiri: Auckland's Climate Plan adopted in 2020 will deliver opportunities and benefits across each of the Auckland Plan 2050 outcomes, not just Environment and Cultural Heritage. Action within the Transport priority, for example, supports the directions and focus areas outlined in the Transport and Access outcome of the Auckland Plan 2050, whilst the Built Environment priority has strong links to both the Homes and Places outcome and the broader Development Strategy.
(2) In response to the extreme weather events of 2023, including Cyclone Gabrielle, Auckland Council is advancing a dedicated Resilient Tāmaki Makaurau work programme. Now in its second year, this initiative has expanded from water-focused response to a comprehensive, hazard-inclusive community adaptation planning programme. It is guiding long-term, transformational decision-making to help existing communities across Tāmaki Makaurau adapt, thrive, and prosper amid increasing climate disruption (https://infocouncil.aucklandcouncil.govt.nz/Open/2025/04/20250410_PEPCC_AGN_11327_WEB.htm)
(3) Auckland Council is undertaking a regional climate change risk and impact assessment to build a consistent evidence base that will inform council policy, strategy, and operations. This work will support the effective prioritisation of investment in adaptation planning for communities, infrastructure, and ecosystems, while also identifying regional climate-related risks, impacts, and opportunities. (https://www.gets.govt.nz/AC/ExternalTenderDetails.htm?id=31072605).
(4) Transition planning arises from the Aotearoa Climate Standards (NZ CS1), which require Auckland Council Group to disclose in its annual climate statement how business models and strategies may change to address climate-related risks and opportunities. Its intention is to support a low-emissions, climate-resilient future by ensuring long-term resilience of key assets and services. To date, the Council has delivered an integrated climate transition plan that connects work across the organisation, developed climate scenarios to test possible futures, and applied dynamic adaptive planning to priority assets and services.' Here is the link of our FY24 climate statement which also mentions transition planning - https://new.aucklandcouncil.govt.nz/en/plans-policies-bylaws-reports-projects/our-annual-reports.html
column17: (1) Te Tāruke-ā-Tāwhiri: Auckland's Climate Plan is a long-term approach to climate action for the Auckland region. It outlines eight priority action areas designed to deliver our goals to reducing emissions and adapting to the impacts of climate change. (2) The council also has obligations under the Financial Markets Conducts Act which requires it to make annual climate statements which comply with the climate-related disclosure framework as set out in the Aotearoa Climate Standards from 30 June 2024. The aim of the standards is to support the allocation of capital towards activities that are consistent with a transition to a low-emissions, climate-resilient future. (3) Auckland Council long-term Plan 2024-2034 (10-year Budget) (adopted on 27 June 2024) makes investment to address climate-relates issues. The Investment Impact Assessment for the long-term plan identifies investment that provides value relating to reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Approximately $4.8b (around 13 per cent) of the council's 10-year capex on infrastructure investment was identified as delivering investment that is in line with the emissions reduction goals under Te Tāruke-ā-Tāwhiri: Auckland's Climate Plan and avoiding or minimising embodied and operational emissions as much as practicable. The Investment Impact Assessment for the long-term plan identifies investment that is highly aligned to climate resilience and adaptation goals in Te Tāruke-ā-Tāwhiri: Auckland's Climate Plan. Approximately $14.1 billion (around 38 per cent) of the council's 10-year capex on infrastructure investment was identified as increasing the resilience of the surrounding existing community and/or ecosystems to natural hazards and climate change in the long-term (30+ years). (4) Auckland Council adopted its Annual Plan 2025-2206 in June 2025 to continue with Long-term Plan priorities and action 21 local board agreements. It continues to invest in our priority (seven areas of investment: transport, water, the built environment, the natural environment, community, economic and cultural development, and well-managed local government) with a significant level of investment in critical infrastructure. Over the next 12 months, $4.3 billion will be invested in roads, pipes and transport infrastructure to further improve services to Aucklanders and build a more resilient region, for example, 1 delivering key infrastructure including renewing assets such as footpaths, roads, bridges, decarbonising ferries and road safety, 2 stormwater investment for flood resilience and recovery work, and increasing capacity to meet the region's growing needs. (5) The Group Strategic Framework (GSF) was adopted in August 2025. The GSF is Auckland Council's new system for connecting what the community wants to what we actually deliver. It creates a clear, reliable pathway from what matters most to people through to the council's decisions, budgets, and day-to-day actions.
column18: There is a need to accelerate the delivery of climate action to meet our climate goals. Te Tāruke-ā-Tāwhiri: Auckland's Climate Plan 2022 Progress Report identifies that there are currently more actions underway and less actions not in progress compared to the previous progress report 2021. This represents positive progress but significant additional action and commitment is required by a range of stakeholders. With staff now recruited for key positions at Auckland Council facilitating the accelerated delivery of Te Tāruke-ā-Tāwhiri will be an important focus for the years ahead. This will require collaborative working with a range of stakeholders and partners. Engagement with mana whenua to better understand how implementation of Te Tāruke-ā-Tāwhiri can be taken forward in partnership with mana whenua is a priority for the years ahead. There is a need to build capacity and capability within the Auckland Council Group to enable and support delivery that upholds the partnership approach outlined through Te Tāruke-ā-Tāwhiri. A Regional Leadership Group sets out to accelerate the implementation of Te Tāruke-ā-Tāwhiri through cross sectoral partnerships and climate action. The Regional Leadership Group includes leaders from the Auckland Council Group, mana whenua, central government, business community, district health boards and youth. Climate Connect Aotearoa, an innovation hub to support collaborative climate action and drive transformation towards a climate resilient and low carbon Tāmaki Makaurau Auckland was launched in 2022. Delivery of the 152m climate investment package in the 10-year Budget 2021-2031 is ongoing with key deliverables outlined in this report. A number of programmes are established or implemented further in 2022/23 with monitoring and control processes more closely monitoring the performance and delivery of the package. Governance and delivery plans were established for programmes funded by the Climate Action Targeted Rate CATR. All programmes across Auckland Transport and Auckland Council progress design and procurement phases. To achieve our climate goals climate action needs to be embedded across all our planning investment and decision making. A Climate Impact Assessment Tool to enable the effective integration of climate change considerations in Auckland Councils decision making processes were rolled out in 2022/23. The Transport Emissions Reduction Pathway TERP has outlined the transformational change required to reduce transport emissions by 64 per cent by 2030. Auckland Council and Auckland Transport need to embed implementation of the TERP through all of their activities, including future updates to key transport planning and funding processes, such as the Auckland Transport Alignment Project and the Regional Land Transport Plan and land use policy, such as the Future Development Strategy and the Auckland Unitary Plan.

WCC has well-established climate governance structures comprised of political oversight committees made up of elected members that are supported by the executive leadership team led by the council's Chief Executive officer. WCC has three committees that it leverages to provide oversight of climate related risks and opportunities: 
• the Environment and Infrastructure Committee (Committee of the Whole): Provides oversight of the operationalising of emission reduction, climate risk management and resilience. This committee holds the official council delegation for climate change oversight.
• the Audit and Risk Committee: Charged with providing assurance that the processes and controls for identifying capturing and reporting climate related risks are robust and fit for purpose; 
• the Long-term Plan, Finance and Performance Committee (Committee of the Whole): Provides oversight of the strategic management of risk and opportunities being adequately reflected in financial strategy and budget.
column16:
Wellington's hazard maps are an important tool for empowering Wellingtonians to make land use decisions based on the most granular information available. These physical risks are considered and applied to our spatial planning and growth projections for the city. 

The 2021 Spatial Plan identifies resilience and adapting to climate change as one of seven key influences on how we plan for future growth. 
 
The 2024 District Plan takes a risk-based approach to managing development across the city based on natural hazard and climate change risks. Some of the climate hazards considered in the district plan are inland flooding, coastal inundation and sea level rise.

The District Plan also has a strategic objective for the City's built environment to support achieving net zero emissions by 2050 through energy efficiency, renewable energy, healthy ecosystems and low carbon transport options.
column17:
Climate change is identified in WCC's financial strategy as one of the key challenges increasing both infrastructure demand and the balance sheet resilience required to respond to natural disasters, whilst also increasing insurance costs for Council and our community.

The WCC infrastructure strategy has two approaches for addressing the challenges of climate change:
- Targeting emissions reductions for the greatest gains and operational efficiency.
- Growing our understanding of climate impacts and adaptation costs.
In addition a disaster resilience fund is being capitalised using the proceeds from sales of selected ground leases and the capital program has been reduced to create borrowing capacity for unforeseen events. This compliments WCC's insurance coverage and provides flexibility to balance financial risk mitigation with operating costs as insurance premiums increase.

•Difficulty in sourcing finance, or increased cost of finance
•Restrictions on the availability of adequate insurance for Councils and/or their constituents (both catastrophe-based and financial lines such as public liability et cetera);
•Ultimately Council may have 'stranded' assets, materially devalued prior to the planned end of their useful lives
•Wellington Council is particularly exposed to litigation arising from the risks of climate change should its climate interventions fail to appropriately or adequately address climate-related impacts
•Possible decline in revenue as traditional sectors go through disruptive phases with possible declines in revenue

•Lack of appropriate skills and experienced personnel needed to manage and upscale the transition particularly in technical fields

The climate agenda is split into two main axes: adaptation and mitigation. 

Historically, climate change adaptation was under the Dubai Municipality Environment Department. Climate mitigation was under the Dubai Supreme Council of Energy (DSCE) which is the regulatory entity responsible for water and energy. It was also responsible for setting the carbon abatement strategy of the Emirate. It is worth noting the DSCE Board includes the Directors General of all the key entities overseeing the sectors responsible for emissions in the Emirate (buildings, waste, energy and water, transportation, industry as well as oil and gas activities). 

In 2024, Dubai's Ruler, HH Sheikh Mohammad bin Rashid Al Maktoum announced the launch of the Dubai Environment and Climate Change Authority which is responsible for both climate change mitigation and adaptation overarching strategies for the Emirate. DECCA will build on the Municipality's and DSCE's cross-governmental coordination in taking climate action forward, and continues close coordination with the main stakeholders in the Emirate including (but not limited to) the Road and Transport Authority, the Dubai Electricity and Water Authority, the Dubai Economic and Tourism Department, Dubai Health Authority, Dubai Airports as well as the Dubai Municipality and key industry players in the Emirate.
DECCA is in its first year of operations. It will therefore gradually establish the necessary committees to oversee the climate change adaptation strategy and will lean on the Dubai Supreme Council of Energy's leadership and strong governance model in this intermediary phase for matters related to the carbon abatement strategy which will remain heavily involved going forward.

Ecosystems resilience: the environmental protected areas framework includes measures to mitigate desertification. There is a city-wide demand side management programme as well as sectoral plans to improve efficiency and reduce demand from all high-emitting sectors including energy, water and waste. \nThe carbon abatement strategy also identifies the sector specific carbon reduction targets which have been set together with the lead authorities or entities responsible for the respective sectors.

El Distrito elaboró el Plan de Gestión Integral del Cambio Climático PIGCC y actualmente se encuentra en etapa de revisión por parte del Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible en espera de su aprobación, este plan será un insumo valioso que dictará las directrices especificas relacionadas con el cambio climático que se constituyen en una determinante de superior jerarquía al plan de ordenamiento territorial.
Con relación a riesgos en el 2023 a través de la Agencia Francesa de Desarrollo en Colombia (AFD )y Ecoversa se realizó una consultoría de escenario de riesgos climáticos. 
Además, se elaboraron estudios detallados de riesgo para fenómenos de movimientos en masa, y los estudios básicos de amenaza por fenómenos de inundación y avenidas torrenciales, en las áreas de la ladera occidental del distrito estos resultados también son un insumo fundamental en el planificación territorial del distrito.
column17:
La planificación financiera del distrito destina recursos a proyectos de infraestructura y programas que tienen un impacto directo en la adaptación al clima. Algunos de los proyectos clave incluyen:
Canalización de arroyos: La ciudad ha invertido en la canalización de sus arroyos para reducir los riesgos de inundaciones durante las temporadas de lluvias intensas. Estos proyectos no solo protegen a la población, sino que también evitan daños a la infraestructura pública y privada, lo que reduce los costos de reparación y recuperación post-desastre.
Recuperación y revitalización de ecosistemas: Se destinan fondos a la restauración de la Ciénaga de Mallorquín y otros ecosistemas de humedal. Esto no solo mejora la biodiversidad, sino que también fortalece la capacidad de la ciudad para gestionar los efectos del cambio climático, como la erosión costera y las inundaciones.
Infraestructura verde: La administración distrital ha promovido la inversión en proyectos de infraestructura verde, como la arborización, el paisajismo y huertas urbanas. Estos no solo mejoran la calidad del aire y la vida urbana, sino que también contribuyen a la reducción de las temperaturas extremas.
El Plan Plurianual de Inversiones que forma parte del Plan de Desarrollo Distrital 2024-2027, se presenta la estimación de los recursos de inversión para atender la ejecución de los programas y proyectos identificados. Allí se destina un porcentaje de 1.646.727 millones de pesos a la Línea Estratégica Ciudad Ambiental y Sostenible, que incluye el componente de 'Medio Ambiente y Adaptación al Cambio Climático' que representan el 8.5% del presupuesto total.
La financiación de estos proyectos climáticos se realiza mediante una combinación de presupuesto distrital, recursos de cofinanciación nacional y préstamos de organismos multilaterales de desarrollo, lo que refleja una estrategia diversificada para asegurar la sostenibilidad financiera de las iniciativas de adaptación al clima.

1. Climate Information Collection
 - Regularly and as needed, Daegu receives climate information from the IPCC, Korea Meteorological Administration, universities/research institutes, and private companies.

2. Incorporation into Planning
 - Climate change is considered not just as a response, but as an essential factor for sustainable development.

3. Basic Plan Establishment
 - In line with the Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth Act, a 10-year plan is established every 5 years.
 - The 1st Basic Plan was established in April 2024 with GHG reduction targets: 45% by 2030, 70% by 2040, 100% by 2050.
 - Sectoral reduction plans include buildings, transport, agriculture/livestock, waste, and sinks.

4. Performance Review and Reporting
 - Annual review and reporting of progress.
 - Reports are deliberated by the Daegu Committee, submitted to the Ministry of Environment, and reported to the national committee.
 - The national committee may provide recommendations, which Daegu must reflect in policies.

5. Review of Ordinances and Plans
 - Any ordinance or administrative plan affecting the Basic Plan must be reviewed by the Daegu Committee before enactment or amendment.

 - Rising disaster recovery costs due to more frequent extreme weather, reducing resources for other projects
 - Expanded infrastructure investment (e.g., disaster prevention, roads, water systems) increases long-term financial burden
 - Declining tax revenue from industrial shifts and population decrease, making it harder to secure climate response funds

column15: - 광주광역시는 2008년부터 현재까지 매년 기후변화대응 관련 사업에 대한 자체적인 평가를 진행하고 있음. '제1차 탄소중립 녹색성장 기본계획 수립', '광주광역시 기후변화대응 기본계획', '기후위기 적응대책 세부시행계획'을 수립하고, 해당 사업들에 대한 이행평가를 추진함. 평가 항목에는 사업의 성과 목표 대비 달성도, 온실가스 감축량, 예산집행률 등이 포함됨.\n\n- 2022년부터 전국 지자체 중 최초로 '출연기관 온실가스 에너지 목표관리제'를 추진하여 공공기관에서의 에너지 사용량 및 온실가스 배출량 감축을 목표로 하고 있음. 공공기관에서는 매년 감축 이행계획을 수립 하고 이행 결과보고서를 제출함. 그리고 이 결과를 기관 경영평가 지표에 포함하여 실질적인 온실가스 감축이 이루어지도록 함
column16: - 2023년 5월부터 '광주광역시 기후위기대응 기본조례'에 따라 '기후위기대응 사전검토제'를 추진함. 시의 탄소중립 비전에 영향을 미치는 행정계획의 수립 시 기후영향 검토, 정책의 일관성, 기후영향 최소화 등 관련 내용에 대한 관련 전문가 검토 후 광주광역시 기후위기대응 위원회의 심의를 받도록 하고 있음\n\n- 폭염 그리고 열섬현상은 도시의 열환경을 악화하는 대표적인 현상으로서 결국 시민들의 삶에 불편을 가중하고 심한 경우 인명상의 피해, 농축산의 피해 등 다양한 형태의 피해를 입히고 있음. 광주광역시는 2020년 폭염 및 도시열섬현상 대응조례에 기반을 둔 기본계획을 수립하여 폭염 및 도시열섬현상과 관련한 지역경제피해를 최소화하고 체계적인 정책 수행 기반을 마련하고자 함.
column17: '온실가스 감축 인지예결산제도'는 예산과 기금이 기후변화에 미치는 영향을 분석하고, 이를 국가와 지방자치단체의 재정운용에 반영하는 제도임. 광주광역시는 2023년부터 온실가스감축인지 예산제 도입을 추진 중임. 2024년부터 본예산 예산서를 바탕으로 모든 실국의 세부사업에 대해 사업 유형을 간접감축/직접감축/배출/잠재적영향/중립으로 분류하고, 중립사업을 제외한 사업들에 대해 온실가스감축 인지예결산서를 작성토록 하여 '2024년, 2025년 온실가스감축인지 예산서'와 '2024년 온실가스감축인지 결산서'를 발간함. 이 예결산제도를 통해 사업담당자 및 해당 부서에게 온실가스 감축사업은 추가적으로 감축량을 증대시키는 방법을 고민하도록하고, 배출 및 잠재적 영향 사업은 온실가스 배출을 최소화하고, 온실가스 감축 수단을 추가 도입하는 사업방향을 유도함
column18: 광주광역시 온실가스 배출량의 대부분이 건물과 수송 부문에서 배출되고 있음. 따라서 온실가스 배출량 감축을 위해서는 그린리모델링과 친환경차(전기, 수소 등)로의 전환 등이 필수적인데, 이를 위해 막대한 재정적 지원이 필요함. 또한 지방정부의 노력만으로는 한계가 있어 무엇보다 시민들의 적극적이 참여가 요구됨.

column15: 기후관련 계획 수립 시 위원회를 개최하여 의견 수렴하는 과정을 거치며, 탄소중립 녹색성장 관련 분야교수, 연구원, 기관, 시민단체 및 공무원으로 구성된 탄소중립 정책 컨트롤 타워이다. 태양광 보급, 그린리모델링 등의 수원시의 사업을 공유하고 자문을 받으며 정책 계획의 이행현황을 보고하고 평가받고 피드백하는 체계를 정립하여 운영한다.
column16: 국제사회는 탄소중립 사회로 전환을 가속화하고 새로운 경제질서를 형성했다. 유럽, 미국 등 주요국들은 탄소중립을 선언하고 추진전략을 수립했다. EU가 탄소국경세에 도입('26) 하며 글로벌기업 중심의 RE100과 ESG경영이 확산될 예정이다. 우리나라도 탄소중립 선언('20.10)을 하고 기본계획을 수립했으며 법적 추진체계를 정비했다. 탄소중립 시나리오('21.10)를 작성하여 국가 탄소중립녹색성장 기본계획('23.3)을 발표하고 「탄소중립 기본법」 시행('22.3.)하였으며 대통령 직속 2050 탄소중립위원회 재정비('22. )를 하였다. 현재까지 국가 탄소중립녹색성장 기본계획('23.), 경기도 탄소중립녹색성장 기본계획('24.)이 수립되었으며, 2025년 4월, 수원시 탄소중립녹색성장 기본계획이 수립되고, 환경부와 경기도의 승인까지 받았다. 현재 해당 기본계획 내 온실가스 감축사업이 진행 중이다.
column17: 기후변화로 인한 가뭄, 폭염과 여름철 폭우, 집중호우와 겨울철 폭설 같은 재난발생 빈도 증가가 우려됨에 따라 시설정비 비용의 예산을 확충해야 하며, 예산 성립 시 이 부분을 반영해야한다.
column18: 저탄소 경제로의 전환과 관련하여, 지자체에서는 기후변화 적응, 대응을 위한 다양한 사업을 추진해야 하며 그에 따른 예산확보는 필수적인 사항임. 또한 지자체에서 시행하는 기후변화 완화 정책과 관련 하여 시민들이 쉽게 체감할 수 있어야 하는데, 시민들이 받아들이지 못한다면 정책 시행의 의미와 방향성을 잃을 수 있어 시민 의식 개선을 통한 저탄소 생활 관행 확대 등 다양한 대 시민적 홍보가 필요하다. 최근 저탄소로의 경제 전환으로 고탄소 업종이 위협받고 있는데, 이는 인공지능(AI)이 산업 전반에 확산된 결과이기도 하다. 수원시는 지식정보 산업이 발달하여 전통적인 고탄소 업종의 비중이 낮으나, 정의로운 전환을 위하여 이들에 대한 녹색 일자리 안내, 녹색산업 공정 전환 등의 필요성이 커지고 있다. 이는 제1차 탄소중립 녹색성장 기본계획 보고서 내 기후위기 대응기반 강화 중 정의로운 전환 부문에 명시하였다.

column15:
Goyang City has a plan titled the '2035 Goyang City Basic Plan' to guide its development. This plan not only focuses on the city's growth but also considers climate change. In addition, the city has established the 2030 Greenhouse Gas Reduction Implementation Plan (Goyang City's environmental policy to implement the Paris Agreement), which sets greenhouse gas reduction targets and detailed implementation plans for each year, and conducts annual performance evaluations for each project. 
One of the key concepts of the plan is a 'Low Carbon Green City.' This concept envisions a city that minimizes environmental pollution and greenhouse gas emissions while enhancing urban competitiveness through eco-friendly industrial development. It combines the principles of a 'low carbon city' with 'green growth.'
A low carbon green city incorporates various energy-saving strategies and innovative structures, including compact and mixed-use planning, securing wind paths, and energy efficient spatial designs through green networks. It also emphasizes public transportation, bicycle and pedestrian-friendly green transport systems, the use of new and renewable energy sources such as solar power, and energy-saving buildings. These strategies aim to reduce environmental pollution, greenhouse gas emissions, and carbon output by implementing green city planning techniques.
Several key principles guide the establishment of a low carbon green city. First, to address climate change and reduce greenhouse gases, a systematic and comprehensive approach must be taken in urban planning sectors such as transportation, environmental conservation and management, energy, and green spaces. Second, to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and promote resource-saving development and management, the plan must aim to minimize the consumption of resources like land and fossil fuels, while ensuring their efficient use. Third, the potential for securing renewable energy sources such as solar and wind power should be analyzed and incorporated into the plan, alongside measures to promote the use of environmentally friendly energy, including new and renewable energy sources. Lastly, the plan should be tailored to mitigate and adapt to climate change by reflecting the region's geographic and socio-economic characteristics
column16:
To implement the Paris Agreement Goyang City established environmental policies in 2019 that comply with its provisions. It includes 2030 greenhouse gas emission projections, reduction targets, and annual implementation plans. We decided to reduce GHG emissions by 32.8% below the business-as-usual (BAU) level by 2030, established 6 tasks by area, and continued to implement related projects under the GHG reduction plan. To strengthen the implementation and reach the targets, Goyang city will readjust intermediated goals every 5 years.
Furthermore, in 2022, we enacted the ordinance on carbon neutrality to lay the institutional foundation so that our efforts are not limited to establishing a GHG reduction plan and can be implemented in practice including tracking the progress of the implementation plan each year. 
In addition, in 2020, the city promoted the Goyang-type Carbon Reduction Clean Complex development project. This includes developing the Goyang Biomass Carbon Reduction Methodology, which is related to a patent application for a blockchain-based integrated energy management system. The city also promoted pilot projects for carbon reduction technology in public housing complexes. 
Events such as field trips, local forums, and policy forums, film festivals were held to realize a sustainable city and to explore ways for Goyang City to respond to climate change. These events included discussions with the UNFCCC working group. We
column17: Goyang City's climate change response plan for 2023 is composed of 55 detailed projects across six sectors: buildings, transportation, waste, agriculture/fisheries, land use, and response infrastructure.\nThe planned budget was 141,113.6 million KRW, of which 104,671.5 million KRW was executed, resulting in a 74.17% execution rate, with 36,442.1 million KRW (25.83%) remaining unspent.\nThrough these initiatives, 96,169 tCO2eq of greenhouse gases were successfully reduced, achieving 83.50% of the target reduction of 115,166.1 tCO2eq.
column18: The transition to a low-carbon economy entails a fundamental change in the economic structure, which also requires significant changes in our way of life. The current economic structure is built on fossil fuels, meaning that all economic activities involving fossil fuels must be transformed into activities that do not emit greenhouse gases. This change needs to span across all areas of production and consumption, including power generation, agriculture, fisheries, manufacturing, heating & cooling, and transportation. Therefore, it is essential to encourage the participation of all economic actors, and meticulous strategies that align with these goals, along with policies to implement them, are necessary.\nGoyang City is a large city with a population of one million, but it has very few industrial facilities or businesses, making it a typical bedroom community. As mentioned in the inventory section below, Goyang City's greenhouse gas emissions primarily came from the transportation and building sectors. Thus, to transition to a low-carbon economy, efforts should be concentrated on these sectors. However, there are challenges, as the national reduction measures are not yet concrete, the reduction efficiency is low, and significant long-term budget investment is required. To achieve '2050 carbon neutrality', as declared by the national and local governments, and to facilitate a rapid transition to a low-carbon economy, continued systematic government support is essential.

기후변화와 관련된 문제에 대해 정부 정책을 지역차원에서 실행하고, 지역 고유의 여건을 반영한 자체 정책과 감독 기능을 수행
□ 안산시의 기후관련 문제에 대한 감독 기능 및 내용
1. 정책수립 및 감독 권한
- 지역 기후·에너지 계획 수립
- 온실가스 배출 관리
- 기후 리스크 관리 및 적응

2. 안산시 감독 및 집행체계
- 환경정책과 : 기후정책 총괄, 환경계획 수립, 온실가스 감축관리
- 자원순환과 : 폐기물 감축 및 재활용 정책 시행
- 에너지정책과 : 신재생에너지 보급 확대, 에너지 절약 캠페인 운영 등
column16: 1. 도시 비전 및 정책방향 전환\n- 기존 : 산업중심, 인구유입 및 개발중심의 도시계획\n- 현재 : 탄소중립·녹색도시 지향, 지속가능성 및 기후 회복력을 핵심가치로 설정
column17:
○ 기후대응 예산의 구조화 및 확대
- 환경, 에너지, 도시계획, 교통 등 다양한 부서의 기후관련 예산을 통합 관리
- 기후위기대응 특별회계 또는 기후예산제 도입
- 연차별 탄소중립 예산 투자계획 수립

○ ESG 및 탄소중립 연계 원칙을 반영
- 예산투자 심의 시 기후영향평가 또는 ESG 영향분석 결과를 반영함
- 탄소저감 효과가 높은 사업에 우선 예산을 배분
- 기후 리스크가 높은 시설 투자에 대한 조정 및 위험 회피 전략을 수림
예시) 노후 공공시설 리모델링 시, 단순보수 → 제로에너지 건축으로 전환, 교통인프라 확장보다 대중교통 및 친환경 교통 예산 우선투자
○ 중앙정부 및 외부 재정자원의 적극 확보
- 기후관련 공모사업 적극참여, 환경부·산업부의 국고보조사업 매칭 비율을 반영한 재정계획 수립
○ 공공투자의 녹색 전환
- 도로확장 중심 → 친환경교통, 전기버스, 자전거 도로 중심
- 일반설비 개선 → 고효율 에너지설비 및 스마트시스템 도입
- 단순 공원 조성 → 기후적응형 도시숲, 빗물정원 조성 등으로 전환
○ 기후리스크에 따른 재정 리스크 관리체계 도입 등
- 자연재해 복구 예산의 사전확보
- 재난관리기금의 기후재해 대응비중 증가
column18:
1. 정책 및 규제 위험

규제 변화 불확실성: 정부가 저탄소 목표를 달성하기 위해 새로운 환경 규제나 탄소세를 도입할 경우, 해당 규제에 적응하지 못하는 기업이나 산업은 큰 타격을 받을 수 있음.

지역별 정책 차이: 국가나 지방정부마다 저탄소 정책의 강도와 방향이 다르므로, 국제 비즈니스나 다국적 기업은 각 관할구역별 규제 준수 부담이 증가.

2. 경제 및 산업 구조 위험

화석연료 의존도: 석탄, 석유, 가스 등 화석연료에 크게 의존하는 지역은 저탄소 경제 전환 시 경제적 타격과 일자리 감소 위험이 큼.

산업 구조의 취약성: 저탄소 기술로의 전환이 어려운 전통 제조업 중심 지역은 경쟁력 저하 위험.

3. 금융 위험

자산 가치 하락: 화석연료 관련 자산(광산, 발전소 등)의 가치가 급격히 하락하거나 '좌초자산(stranded assets)'이 될 위험.

투자 불확실성: 저탄소 전환 기술에 대한 투자 결정이 불확실해지면서 금융 시장의 변동성 증가.

4. 사회적·정치적 위험

일자리 전환 문제: 저탄소 경제로의 전환 과정에서 기존 산업 노동자들의 실업과 사회 불안 발생 가능성.

지역 간 불균형 심화: 저탄소 전환이 잘 이루어지는 지역과 그렇지 않은 지역 간 경제적, 사회적 격차가 커질 위험.

5. 기술적 위험

기술 수용 및 인프라: 일부 관할구역은 저탄소 기술 도입을 위한 인프라가 부족하거나, 기술 확산이 더딜 수 있음.

기술 혁신 속도: 기술 발전이 느리거나, 예상보다 비용이 많이 드는 경우 전환 비용 상승.

column15:
Jeonju City has established a formal oversight structure for climate-related issues through the Jeonju Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth Committee, which was launched in June 2023. The committee comprises representatives from relevant municipal departments, public research institutes, civil society, academia, and industry, enabling cross-sectoral coordination and inclusive governance.

In April 2025, the Committee officially approved the 1st Jeonju Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth Master Plan (2025-2034), and has since actively taken on the role of supervising the city's implementation of its climate targets—namely, a 30% reduction in greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by 2030 and a 34% reduction by 2034 compared to 2018 levels.

Climate change issues are embedded into the city's strategic, sectoral, and development planning processes. The Committee receives regular updates and briefings on the implementation status of major strategies, such as the Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth Master Plan and the 3rd Jeonju Climate Change Adaptation Plan (2025-2029). Jeonju City conducts annual implementation evaluations for both plans and reports the results to the city's Committee. And also these evaluation outcomes are submitted annually to the national Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth Committee through the Ministry of Environment.

These evaluation results are submitted annually through the Ministry of Environment to the National Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth Commission. 

The National Carbon Neutral and Green Growth Commission is giving feedback on the entire Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth Master Plan, including reviewing evaluation results submitted by the state and local governments and calling for revisions and supplementation if necessary.
column16:
Since July 2014, Jeonju City has integrated climate-related impact assessments into its master and development planning processes. Urban management plans, district unit plans, and major development projects—particularly those involving land areas of 10,000㎡ or more—are required to undergo urban heat island impact assessments that specifically examine climate-related risks such as urban heat island effects, wind path disruption, and local microclimate changes.

In recent years, the influence of climate change has led to significant updates in Jeonju's strategic planning framework. The city's 1st Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth Master Plan (2025-2034) and 3rd Climate Change Adaptation Plan (2025-2029) have institutionalised the integration of mitigation and adaptation considerations into all new development plans, including land use, transport, housing, and industrial infrastructure.

Climate-related issues have also influenced long-term planning horizons. While traditional development plans covered 10-15 years, the 2025 Carbon Neutrality Master Plan aligns with a 2030 and 2050 vision to ensure consistency with Korea's national mid-term targets and global climate agreements.

Overall, climate risk and opportunity assessments now play a central role in shaping Jeonju's spatial development decisions, investment priorities, and regulatory updates.
column17:
Climate-related considerations are increasingly integrated into Jeonju City's financial planning processes. Since 2013, climate-related budget items have gradually expanded within the city's general budget. Since 2017, Jeonju has operated a dedicated Energy Fund, allocating approximately KRW 4 to 5 billion annually to support renewable energy projects, energy efficiency improvements, and climate adaptation measures.

In April 2023, Jeonju City participated in a pilot program initiated by the Ministry of Environment to implement a Greenhouse Gas Reduction Cognitive Budget System. Through this program, the city conducted a comprehensive analysis of its 2023 budget to identify the scale of investments related to GHG reduction and climate resilience.

Building on this initiative, Jeonju has been actively analyzing the 2024 and 2025 budgets to assess the climate impact of each department's programs. The aim is to institutionalize a climate-responsive budgeting system that links financial decisions directly to emission reduction outcomes and adaptation benefits.

Our city is currently developing methodologies to:
 - Categorize climate-relevant budget items based on mitigation/adaptation impact.
 - Quantify GHG reduction outcomes of public investments.
 - Use climate budget analysis results to inform budget allocation priorities during the annual budget cycle.

These efforts are part of Jeonju's broader strategy to align fiscal policy with its long-term climate goals under the 1st Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth Master Plan (2025-2034). In the near future, Jeonju aims to formally adopt a climate-informed budgeting framework to evaluate the effectiveness and sufficiency of climate-related financial flows across all sectors.

column15:
Ahmedabad Climate Resilient City Action Plan (Towards A Net Zero Future by 2070) is prepared through intense stakeholder consultation and launched by the city in June 2023. This action plan includes GPC compliant GHG emissions inventory, ward and area level vulnerability and risk assessment, scenario planning based on various National and State Government targets. City is considering sector wise climate change mitigation and adaptation interventions/ actions/ projects during Annual Municipal Budget Planning every year, which is being approved by city council (Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation General Board). City has constituted Climate Core Team, chaired by Municipal Commissioner and includes head of various departments. Climate Core Team meets every quarter to discuss climate resilient interventions and monitoring implementation status. Information and updates from Climate Core Team is being used for Annual Municipal Budget planning every year. 

Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation has established a 'Net-zero, Environment and Climate Resilient Cell', chaired by Municipal Commissioner and lead by Deputy Municipal Commissioner. All departmental heads are part of the cell. The Cell is responsible for coordinating climate-related efforts across various departments, institutions, and stakeholders, both internally and externally. Operating under the 'Analyse,
Act, and Accelerate' approach, the cell is working towards a sustainable future by conducting research, engaging and collaborating with stakeholders, conducting climate readiness reviews, exploring innovative finance options, and integrating climate actions into regular planning processes amongst others. Additionally, the cell supports all departments in
prioritising sectoral climate actions, creating a data bank for data-driven monitoring and
evaluation, and promoting liveable and sustainable urban planning practices.

Please refer below sections from Ahmedabad Climate Resilient City Action Plan (Towards A Net Zero Future).1) Annexure 1.1 Formation of Stakeholder Committee and Climate Core Team and Annexure 1.2 Stakeholder Engagement (Page A3 to A8); 2) Chapter 3 (section 3.1.5, 3.2.7, 3.3.2, 3.4.10, 3.5.6, 3.6.2) for information on sector wise budgetary planning for climate actions in FY 2023-24.

Please refer the AMC notification number 243, dated 15/03/2024 for 'Net-zero, Environment and Climate Resilient Cell'.
column16: Ahmedabad Development Plan for 2031(prepared in 2021) is emphasizing on 1) densification of existing areas for optimum resource utilization, 2) enhance the skyline through additional FSIs in central business districts, 3) densification along transit corridors through transit-oriented zone (200m on both sides of metro and BRTS transit corridor, eastern high-density corridor between Narol-Naroda highway (NH8) and 132 feet road on eastern side of the city), 5) development of growth centres around the city and providing logistic zones etc. This planning will help Ahmedabad to manage future growth, regulate density and organize land use within the urban area, which will not only help to provide effective and efficient urban services but also conserve natural resources, save energy, and mitigate GHG emissions. Ahmedabad Development Plan for 2031 also emphasizes on blue green infrastructure management and planning, including lake development, open/ green space conservation and management. Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation is following Town Planning Scheme (local area planning concept), which is micro level implementation of larger Development Plan. \n\nPlease refer below sections from Ahmedabad Climate Resilient City Action Plan (Towards A Net Zero Future).1) Chapter 2 (Section 2.6 - from page number 19 to 22) for land use and development planning
column17: Based on Ahmedabad Climate Resilient City Action Plan (Towards A Net Zero Future by 2070) and climate related issues, city has proposed various climate resilient interventions, which has increased capital allocation of Annual Municipal Budget (i.e., lake interlinking, replacing old water supply and sewerage network, 7MW of RE plants, developing urban forests to increase in green cover, biomining of legacy waste etc.). By implementing climate resilient interventions (i.e., 21MW of RE installed for municipal facilities, replacement of streetlights with EE LED lights) has reduced the operating costs and increased revenue. Also, city has proposed some of the projects based on PPP model for accessing climate finance (i.e., 2000 TPD waste to energy plant, 500 TPD waste to bio-CNG plant etc.). City is in progress for releasing Green Bonds under Government of India's AMRUT 2.0 Scheme. City is also part of Gujarat Resilient Cities Program (GRCP), where city is receiving INR 30,000 million from the World Bank for climate resilient infrastructure for wastewater sector. Please refer below sections from Ahmedabad Climate Resilient City Action Plan (Towards A Net Zero Future).1) Chapter 3 (section 3.1.5, 3.2.7, 3.3.2, 3.4.11, 3.5.6, 3.6.2) for information on sector wise budgetary planning for climate actions in FY 2023-24.
