column15: Se ha creado un Comité de Sostenibilidad Energética (CSE), compuesto por los responsables políticos de los departamentos municipales implicados en la toma de decisiones de carácter energético y climático, que afectan a los servicios de rehabilitación y mantenimiento de edificios municipales, al parque móvil, al transporte público urbano, a la gestión del agua, a la rehabilitación del parque edificado, al espacio público y el alumbrado público, y a la instalación de energías renovables. A este comité, le asiste técnicamente un grupo de trabajo técnico, formado por jefes de servicio y técnicos de los ámbitos anteriores, que tiene entre otras responsabilidades la elaboración de la planificación general energética del ayuntamiento y el seguimiento de los avances en materia de los objetivos energéticos legalmente vinculantes y los aprobados en la planificación local.
column16: El nuevo Plan General de Ordenación Urbana de Vitoria-Gasteiz (PGOU), aprobado inicialmente en 2023, se ha elaborado teniendo en cuenta una serie objetivos estratégicos ambientales, económicos y sociales, que se recogen en el documento \'Criterios y objetivos que servirán de base para la elaboración del PGOU\'. \nhttps://blogs.vitoria-gasteiz.org/medios/files/2021/06/Criterios-y-Objetivos-PGOU.pdf\nEn este documento se señala que “todos estos objetivos urbanísticos (preservación y protección del medio natural, preservación del suelo no urbanizado, regeneración urbana y rehabilitación del patrimonio edificado, etc.) deben ir orientados a tener en cuenta la vulnerabilidad climática de la ciudad y establecerán criterios de planificación que den respuesta a las consecuencias de las alteraciones climáticas”. Los objetivos estratégicos sobre los que se han fijado los criterios de base para la redacción del PGOU, alineados con las metas establecidas para los 17 ODS y la Agenda 2030 son los siguientes: 1. Una ciudad compacta, compleja y cohesionada, que facilita la movilidad sostenible y la reducción de emisiones2. Impulso y protección del medio rural y los pueblos3. Puesta en valor del patrimonio natural, cultural y paisajístico, para mantener y reforzar la consideración del medio físico como soporte vital y de mejora de la calidad ambiental ante los retos del futuro, especialmente ante el equilibrio sostenible del territorio y la adaptación al cambio climático.4. Un territorio sostenible y energéticamente eficiente (horizonte de ciudad neutra en CO2.), integrando los criterios derivados de las medidas de mitigación y adaptación del Plan de Acción para el Clima y la Energía Sostenible (PACES) que tengan impacto urbanístico como, entre otras, las orientadas a mitigar el efecto isla de calor: la plantación de arbolado autóctono, la creación de sombras, la permeabilidad del pavimento, la orientación respecto a las corrientes de aire y ventilación son las claves que se deben tener en cuenta a la hora de actuar a este respecto. La tipología de las viviendas así como los materiales empleados en su construcción también deben analizarse en base a los incrementos de temperatura esperados en los diferentes escenarios climáticos contemplados. 5. Equilibrio económico del territorio6. Vitoria-Gasteiz, de y para todas las personas (objetivo estratégico transversal a todos los anteriores).
column17: En los últimos años, y en buena parte ligados al Plan de Recuperación, Transformación y Resiliencia (PRTR), estrategia española para canalizar los fondos destinados por la Unión Europa a reparar los daños provocados por la crisis del COVID-19 y, a través de reformas e inversiones, construir un futuro más sostenible, se han accedido a fondos económicos para llevar a cabo proyectos con una clara incidencia en la transición energética y el clima. Los 4 ejes transversales del PRTR (transición ecológica, transformación digital, cohesión social y territorial e igualdad de género), se proyectan en 10 políticas palanca, que recogen 30 componentes. Entre las 10 palancas destacan al menso dos de ellas con una implicación directa en materia de clima, como son las de Transición energética justa e inclusiva, con la componente de despliegue e integración de las energías renovables, y la de Infraestructuras y ecosistemas resilientes, con las componentes de conservación y restauración de los ecosistemas y de la movilidad sostenible, segura y conectada. Gracias a estos programas, y otros de carácter regional, se ha conseguido incorporar a los presupuestos municipales recursos para la instalación de energía fotovoltaica en edificios municipales, o la revitalización de determinadas áreas degradas, a través de la rehabilitación energética de viviendas, y la regeneración del espacio público, a través del desarrollo de proyectos de infraestructura verde urbana.
column18: Se han detectado una serie de riesgos sistémicos transversales, relacionadas con la insuficiencia de capacidades, los procesos y/o procedimientos ineficientes, la falta de infraestructuras o de fondos económicos, o la necesidad de colaboración entre agentes públicos, privados o entre ambos, que pudieran dificultar la transición hacia una economía baja en carbono y el avance hacia la neutralidad climática:• Insuficiente capacidad administrativa y/u operativa. Por un lado, por falta de personal y por la dificultad existente para la incorporación de personal adicional a integrar en la plantilla, incluso personal temporal. Por otro lado, se detecta la necesidad de personal técnico especializado, que se ajuste a nuevos perfiles profesionales, y que incorpore una visión transversal de la administración y de las políticas públicas, y trabaje con mentalidad de proyectos.• Burocracia regulatoria. Por un lado, se detecta una proliferación regulatoria y normativa, por otro lado, procedimientos demasiado farragosos y garantistas, que no facilitan la eficiencia y la respuesta en tiempo que los problemas y las demandas que los distintos agentes requerirían. Necesidad de búsqueda de un equilibrio entre seguridad/eficiencia y transparencia.• Falta de procedimientos consolidados y unificados de seguimiento y verificación• Escasa digitalización, lo que impide o retrasa la transformación digital. Resistencia al cambio. Coste. Falta de competencias. Ausencia de oferta adaptada al mercado (infraestructura, dispositivos y soluciones...). Seguridad. Incertidumbre jurídica. Nulo compromiso en la gestión. En muchas organizaciones, la mayor barrera para la transformación digital es el pensamiento heredado, junto con la falta de voluntad por parte de los departamentos de TI que ya están agotados para un cambio radical.• Fragmentación de responsabilidades: Funcionamiento en silo entre los distintos departamentos o entre las distintas instituciones. Los problemas multidimensionales/sistémicos y complejos requieren modelos de gobernanza innovadores, que faciliten las relaciones multinivel, la integración de políticas, y el trabajo por proyectos, más allá de la estructura departamental actual. • Dificultades en la construcción de la colaboración público-privada. Falta de confianza. Se necesita un marco legal bien establecido e innovador. Perspectiva diferente de las expectativas. Son necesarias nuevas ideas, cláusulas innovadoras, así como la superación del concepto tradicional de “público”. Dificultad para la búsqueda del equilibrio entre lo público y lo privado.• Falta de financiación /esquemas de financiación: insuficiencia financiera para realizar las inversiones a largo plazo; necesidad de una nueva forma de pensar más allá de las subvenciones.• Falta de alineamiento entre las necesidades locales y los programas europeos o nacionales• Costes de inversión prohibitivos: nuevas tecnologías, nuevas soluciones para acciones climáticas requieren unos costes muy elevados, que a veces resultan prohibitivos.• Dificultad de acceso a conocimientos especializados.

The Vice-Mayor of the Municipality of Porto is also the City Councilor responsible for the portfolios of Environment, Climate, Innovation and Digital Transition portfolios, highlighting the city's strong commitment to addressing climate change, particularly in reducing emissions, transitioning to clean energy sources, and adapting to the impacts of climate with a strong climate adaptation strategy. Under the Vice-Mayor's leadership, there is the coordination of several entities and municipal departments responsible for, among others, the skills related to climate change response, such as the Municipal Department of Environmental Planning and Management (focused on environmental planning and management), the Municipal Department of Green Infrastructure (focused on operational activities in green spaces and tree management), the Porto Energy Agency (an organization with 10 municipalities that is focused on energy transition and sustainability), the Municipal Water and Energy Company of Porto (A 100% municipally-owned company that manages the entire water cycle in the city, focused on water distribution and sanitation and energy related issues, like energy purchase, public lighting management, and installation and management of clean energy production for self-consumption), the Municipal Environment Company Porto Ambiente (a 100% municipally-owned company that manages waste collection and city cleaning) and the Porto Digital Association (an association focused on promoting digital transformation and technological innovation in the city). In addition, a specific department within Porto Ambiente — the Carbon Neutrality Department — is dedicated to organizing and advancing the city's climate action to carbon neutrality, ensuring its strategic alignment and coordination with several internal departments and mainly external entities. Among them, it is also worth highlighting the role of LIPOR — an association that manages waste treatment for Porto and seven neighboring municipalities. LIPOR also falls under the political oversight of the Vice-Mayor of Porto. 

In close partnership, these organizations recently integrated all the planned city's climate strategies and action plans into the Municipal Climate Action Plan 2030, to be soon approved in Municipal Assembly. This document outlines a pathway for climate change mitigation, aiming for carbon neutrality by 2030. 

Therefore, the Municipality has placed climate-related issues at the top of its agenda and employs a wide range of resources in its planning and management by integrating the themes of environment, water, energy, innovation, and waste under the responsibility of the Vice-Mayor of the city. There is also significant collaboration in the areas of mobility, transportation, and buildings, even though these are not directly within the Vice-Mayor's portfolio. It is evident that these themes are cross-sectoral and require continuous coordination, which is present both at the political level and in technical work. 

Given the diversity of entities that somehow manage climate-related issues in the city, a cross-cutting in-house Climate Mission Structure for carbon neutrality has been set up with elements of these units, which meets regularly to discuss strategy and action. The launch of the Porto Climate Pact, with the commitment to achieve climate neutrality by 2030 among public and private entities, and the selection of Porto by the European Commission as one of the 100 cities of the EU Mission on Carbon Neutral and Intelligent Cities, benefited from the creation of this structure, which assumed the coordination these municipal initiatives and all the municipal climate action. 

The Municipality of Porto also has a Municipal Environment Council, since 2003, that acts as an advisory forum that allows to give voice and opportunity to participate to the civil society and other environmental organizations of the city. It includes the academic community, policy makers, representatives of civil society, among others, and discusses the greatest environmental and climate issues in the city.
column16:
The Municipality of Porto approved its Municipal Master Plan (MMP) in 2021.This plan reflects the city's major concerns and ambitions for the future presenting a new approach to the issues of sustainability, the quality of the urban environment for citizens as well as the resilience and adaptation of the territory to the challenges of climate change. The Municipal Ecological Structure is acknowledged as a fundamental element of the Urban Planning that establishes a new paradigm of ecological structure of the city, and places it as one of the priorities in the territory management, committing to double the existing green area until 2030.The Municipal Ecological Structure aims to promote the continuity of natural and cultural systems, the sustainability of the territory, the increase of biodiversity and the safeguarding of the natural and landscape heritage. One of its main goals (among others) is to provide the city with a green infrastructure that promotes the resilience of the municipal territory to climate change, as well as preserving the wet system. On the other hand, the MMP penalizes the waterproofing of public places, identifies with protection status all reserve spaces for installation and protection of retention basins (which have a fundamental role in minimizing surface flows in extreme events) and creates regulations to protect and condition the occupation in aquifer recharge zones or contamination of groundwater levels. In 2022, the Municipal Plan for Water Lines Enhancement and Rehabilitation (PVRLA) was presented, indicating which rivers and streams are most vulnerable to the effects of climate change. The creation of retention basins, increasing the permeability of the territory and the renaturalization of piped sections are the main solutions indicated. In the same direction, the Porto + Permeável project introduced innovative solutions to increase the permeability of the territory, promoting the reduction of the impact of rainwater in the municipality. 

Another innovation brought by the MMP is the establishment of the Environmental Index (EI) (under public consultation until November 2025). The EI of the Municipality of Porto was created from scratch, adapted to the environmental needs of the city, and its major goal is to promote the best practices in construction that contribute to the city's four major environmental objectives: 1) decarbonisation of the energy system through efficiency and self-production; 2) preservation and improvement of biodiversity and ecosystem services; 3) increased permeability and sustainable management of rainwater drainage; 4) circular economy and sustainable construction. This implementation of this new regulation is based on a calculator with four dimensions: Energy; Green infrastructures; Blue infrastructures; Circular construction. Each dimension includes several required measures and each of the implemented measures scores. In the end, a system of equivalence is applied to correspond the final value of the EI and the reduction in urban taxes. For instance, mantaining the pre-existing tress in the construction plot is scored, as well as creating natural stormwater drainage and infiltration systems to mitigate storm and flooding impacts. 

Porto also launched a program, in 2023, to encourage the use of soft modes and the conditioning of the use of vehicles in certain areas of the city, entitled Rede 20. The first phase of implementation of the program was deployed in the Historic Center, with the implementation of specific signage and traffic calming measures, in a concept of sharing public space where people can move around with greater freedom and convenience. This network currently counts with about 100 streets already intervened and more will be intervened by the end of the project. This program received a distinction under the spanish prize 'Cidades que caminham'. The MMP also strengthens the definition of a structuring network consisting of high-quality bus corridors, circular routes, and radial axes. Additionally, the MMP envisions the expansion of soft mobility, including the increase of the cycling network and other more sustainable options, based on the establishment of a fundamental circulation network structure aimed at promoting soft modes. This includes the creation of pedestrian zones in the Historic Centre of Porto, contributing to the reduction of vehicle use for short distances.
column17:
To comply with the Municipal Master Plan (MMP) more than 3200 M€ is planned until 2030, 80% of which will be invested in decarbonization and emission reduction measures (improvement and expansion of the public transport network, the renovation of buildings and the decarbonization of energy system) and 20% in adaptation to climate change (permeability efforts, green areas, restoring watercourses, among others). Given the relevance and magnitude of the amount, different sources of funding are foreseen, most of which are guaranteed by the municipality's own revenues and resources. However, it is crucial to use funds from national programmes, and partnerships with other regional and local public and/or private entities, as well as access to other European and international operational and strategic financing programmes. In order to complement access to financial resources, the Municipality created the Municipal Fund for Environmental and Urban Sustainability (Fundo Municipal de Sustentabilidade Ambiental e Urbanística - FMSAU), as an exceptional form of revenue and with the foundation of contributing to support projects and investments for the operationalization of capital gains redistribution processes according to the principles of equity and justice, provided for in the MMP, in particular for land and financial support for the implementation of the MMP's actions, including environmental and/or urban safeguarding and recovery operations and to ensure the provision of land for public infrastructure, equipment and green spaces, among others. 

The use of natural, innovative and sustainable solutions is recurrent in the MMP, so the Municipality of Porto is also adopting these solutions in its urban operations, reinforcing the investment of the Municipality in adapting the building and public space to climate issues. Proof of this investment are some developed infrastructures like the Intermodal Terminal of Campanhã (which includes 4 hectares of green roofs and an integrated energy efficiency system), the Central Asprela Park (it is a sponge park, able to retain 10000 cubic meters of water in heavy rain episodes), My Building is Green (co-financed by the LIFE Program and which seeks to create, develop and produce natural and innovative solutions for the adaptation of school buildings in the city), URBiNAT (co-financed by H2020, aims the creation of participatory healthy corridors though a diverse set of nature based solutions), the Asprela + Sustainable Project (co-financed by the European Environmental Grants, it seeks to create the first renewable energy community in Porto based on local photovoltaic production, and will allow self-consumption and storage of surpluses in second life storage systems), NBRACER project (co-financed by H2020, Quinta de Salgueiros restoration in order to create and implement a BioLab - a space where universities, citizens and policy-makers can learn and research about urban ecology and climate change, by conducting experiments and testing new NBS), Lapa Urban Park (the result of a partnership between the Municipality and Mercan Properties with 1,7 ha that includes the planting of several trees species, the Ribeira do Vilar renaturalization and walkways creation). In addition to the strong investment envisaged for combating and adapting to climate change, the city's effort is visible, not only in financial availability and investment capacity, but also through the incessant demand for the most diversified sources of financing so as not to compromise the path and strategies outlined and the economic sustainability of the plans. 

Porto has already some experience in climate investment, with a focus on mitigation actions, demonstrated through initiatives like the Sustainable Energy Action Plan and the European City Facility-approved Investment Concept, particularly the Porto Energy (R)Evolution. Porto developed a Climate Neutrality Investment Plan. This project significantly enhanced the understanding of sustainable investments among municipal staff and supporting actors. Therefore, the Municipality conducted consultations with municipal entities and Porto Climate Pact subscribers, aligning investments with city decarbonization goals. Porto estimated climate implementation costs. The cost projections for achieving climate neutrality in Porto amount to over 1775 M€ (CAPEX) with an additional 396 M€ in operating costs (OPEX) until 2030. Mobility & Transport investments constitute the majority at 65%, emphasizing fleet electrification and transport infrastructure, followed by Built Environment improvements at 22% of the total investment. This Plan requires 2171 M€ of a mix of funding sources. Of the total required amount, approximately 19% (423 M€) has already been invested both from the Municipality and other stakeholders with a significant investment gap of over 1747 M€ remaining as of January 2024.
column18: The main risks are those directly related to investment capacity and access to resources capable of complying with the plans. The access to sources of funding and the availability of these funds is crucial for the operationalization of mitigation and adaptation measures. The unpredictability of markets and the volatility of prices and construction costs may negatively affect the compliance of many planned projects and measures, making them more expensive and requiring greater effort on the part of the Municipality and other public and / or private partners. Another critical aspect is investment generation, i.e., how to leverage private investment. How can alternative and innovative financing mechanisms be developed that do not rely on subsidies and public funding? - so that access to finance is not too dependent on public capital, but also becomes attractive to the private sector, while being desirable and sustainable. Another risk may relate to the partners' ability to engage, in particular in terms of the capacity to build partnerships or collaborations with private sector organizations and entities, which are essential to leveraging a low-carbon economy, given the importance of the private sector for creating green, fair, low-carbon jobs. The fact that most of the main sectors with influence, such as transport and construction are outside the control of the municipality, reinforces the importance of involvement and participation of private individuals in the transition. To minimize and control this risk Porto launched the Porto Climate Pact, aiming to enroll all organizations - public, private and the citizens - working in and for the city, for the climate transition. The Porto Climate Pact is a collaborative network where all its subscribers are committed to contributing to the construction of a carbon-neutral, resilient, competitive, fair and participatory city. However, we are aware that this process of involvement of the various private sectors will be a demanding and difficult process, but equally challenging and divided, in which everyone is called to contribute.

column15: In 2015, The Office of Sustainability & Resiliency (OSR) was created. OSR works with other executive offices, the City Council Health, Energy, Resiliency and Sustainability (HERS) Committee, City departments, businesses, and the community to develop innovative environmental solutions that foster equity, vibrant communities and shared prosperity. The HERS Committee deliberates and makes recommendations on policies relating to St. Petersburg's sustainability initiatives including energy efficiency, recycling, green infrastructure, alternative energy sources, climate, and environmental protections. In 2018, St. Pete joined the Tampa Bay Regional Resiliency Coalition. At least 24 jurisdictions in the Tampa Bay area formed the coalition to coordinate climate adaptation and mitigation activities across county lines, and to advance local and regional responses to and preparations for economic and social disruption due to the climate crisis. In 2020, City Council approved a full time Urban Forester Position responsible for conducting a city wide tree canopy analysis to assess the age, location, and health of St. Petersburg tree canopy, setting a tree canopy goal, and initiating strategies to strategically increase the city's canopy cover. In 2022, the City adopted a 30% tree canopy goal (by area) as a means to improve public health, increase energy efficiency, and foster community resilience.
column16: The City of St. Petersburg recognizes that integrating sustainability into decision-making will enhance its equity, livability, and resilience, and it will promote future growth that addresses environmental, economic, and social equity challenges. column16: En 2021, la Ville de Québec s'est dotée d'une stratégie de développement durable, de laquelle découle le Plan de transition et d'action climatique 2021-2025 (PTAC). Il s'agit d'un plan comprenant 21 chantiers prioritaires, regroupant chacun plusieurs projets. Par sa vocation structurante, le Plan de transition et d'action climatique de la Ville regroupe plusieurs autres documents de planification: le plan d'action en agriculture urbaine 2020-2025, la Vision de la mobilité active, la Vision de l'arbre, le Plan d'action solidaire 2021-2025, le Plan régional des milieux humides et hydriques (PRMHH), le Plan de mise en valeur des rivières et la Vision 2018-2028 pour une saine gestion des matières résiduelles, pour en nommer quelques uns. En tant que premier plan climat officiellement adopté par la Ville, le PTAC a pour objectif implicite de jeter les bases d'une nouvelle structure de gouvernance. Cela implique: l'élaboration et la mise en oeuvre d'un processus de suivi et de reddition de compte de l'action climatique, un changement de pratiques interne, la prise en compte des changements climatiques dans les documents de planification existants et la création de nouveaux documents de planification adressant la lutte aux changements climatiques.
column17: Dans le cadre de son Plan d'action et de transition climatique, la Ville de Québec prévoit investir 100 M$ en argent neuf d'ici 2025, s'ajoutant aux sommes déjà investies par la Ville. En 2022, c'est un total de plus de 77 M$ qui a été investi dans la mise en œuvre du Plan, ce qui exclut quelques projets majeurs, tel que la planification et la construction du nouveau service de tramway de la Ville, de même que la construction et la mise en service de la nouvelle usine de biométhanisation municipale.
column18: La transition climatique a le potentiel d'entraîner la hausse du coût de certains biens, dont la production est plus émissives de gaz à effet de serre. Vu le contexte inflationniste auquel la Ville et les citoyens font face, cela peut freiner l'acceptabilité sociale liée au déploiement des politiques climatiques. La perspective de modifier les pratiques d'aménagement du territoire, de même que le mode de vie des citoyens pourrait également entraîner un certain nombre de contestations. À ce titre, la pédagogie et la vulgarisation des ambitions climatiques de la Ville auprès de sa population sont primordiales. C'est pourquoi la Ville mise sur la concertation avec les citoyens et les acteurs du milieu, notamment dans le cadre du chantier sur la mobilisation collective du PTAC.

column15: Kansas City is a Mayor/Council form of government. The City Council formally adopts resolutions or ordinances to deal with climate related issues. These resolutions or ordinances are informed by staff, subject matter experts, the public, and our environmental committee. The city's internal operations are led by the City Manager who is responsible for creating Administrative Regulations that direct staff to act on various initiatives. The Environmental Management Commission, appointed by the Mayor, is tasked with overarching environmental issues including environmental protection and environmental compliance. The commission has been active since 2007. The City adopted the Climate Protection and Resiliency Plan (CPRP) in August 2022, which informs sustainability and plans for future climate-related issues. The city's Office of Environmental Quality, led by the Chief Environmental Officer, is directly tasked with both compliance and sustainability efforts.
column16: In 2020, the current City Council adopted Resolution 200005, which reaffirmed that climate protection and greenhouse gas reduction should be key factors in all decisions and actions by the City. Kansas City has worked since 2021 to update the existing Climate Plan to include resiliency, adaptation and sequestration efforts. At the same time, the City worked to update the citywide Comprehensive Plan which is called the KC Spirit Playbook. Staff from the Office of Environmental Quality and the Planning and Development department used community and staff feedback to help draft both plans and regularly sat in on public meetings and strategy prioritization sessions together. The Climate Protection and Resiliency Plan (CPRP) was just finalized and adopted by City Council in 2022. The KC Playbook (comprehensive plan) was adopted in 2023. The KC Spirit Playbook lists 15 vision statements, one of which directly addresses Environmental Systems: \'Healthy Environmental Systems: We will promote and value the health of our environmental and natural systems and protect them from degradation.\' https://playbook.kcmo.gov/what-are-the-big-ideasThe adopted 2024-28 Citywide Business Plan includes sustainability as one of our core values: \' We pursue policies and practices that allow our City to support sustainability, which we define as making decisions and taking actions that simultaneously promote economic vitality, social equity, energy conservation, environmentally responsible transportation and land use policies, and strategies to mitigate the serious effects of climate change.\' KC Water, the local water utility that is a enterprise department of the city, joined the Race to Zero in 2021. They are working with a consultant to evaluate their current greenhouse gas emissions and electricity use and advise them on climate related mitigation and adaptation strategies and technologies to increase efficiency. This consultant will help them draft a climate adaptation plan that supports the City's plan so they can determine how they will approach risk management for various climate scenarios in the future.
column17: The Office of Environmental Quality's (OEQ) budget was increased to fund two new FTE positions to jumpstart implementation of the Climate Plan in 2023. The City was invited to join Bloomberg American Sustainable Cities (BASC) to support climate action, economic development and the development of Black wealth. This project is in progress and will fund two new staff members for two years. In partnership with Cultivate KC, Kansas City plans to hire a Food Systems Coordinator in January 2025. The position is funded for 5 years through a USDA grant. Additional grant writing staff were brought on board to assist with acquiring federal grants. The MidAmerica Regional Council (MARC) provided just over $50,000 to Kansas City through the solid waste management grant. This grant will jumpstart the City's Event Waste Diversion Pilot. The City was awarded $5 million through the American Rescue Plan Act to restore vital riparian corridor along Kansas City's Blue River. The City also secured a $12 million grant from the United States Department of Agriculture's Forest Service to fund tree care programs, tree supplies, and personnel to carry out tree care programs throughout the City. In 2024 the City began distribution of $5 million dollars in Rebuild KC grant funding, which goes to departments and the public to implement various neighborhood improvements including those related to energy efficiency and neighborhood resiliency programs. The City budgeted $12 million in FY 23-24 for street light conversion, which is now in progress, and will save an estimated $3.5 million on both energy and maintenance costs. The City applied for the Energy Efficiency and Conservation Block Grant with the US Department of Energy, and was awarded $477,000. The money was spent in 2024 to fund a Benchmarking Help Desk with the Metropolitan Energy Center and the Energy Savers Program with Bridging the Gap. From FY 24-26, $1 M per year has been budgeted to plant 10,000 trees through Kansas City's Neighborhoods Department.
column18: Financial risk to the city and residents: In the last 70 years, the physical size of Kansas City has quadrupled while the population has remained relatively stable. (Put another way, every resident of Kansas City is on the hook for maintaining four times as much of the city as his or her predecessors. The Kansas City Metro has an average 6.7 roadway miles for every 1,000 persons, one of the highest ratios in the US). Kansas City's large land area (315 sq miles) is problematic to our transition in several ways. 1) We have a small tax base to fund needed climate related infrastructure transitions over a large area and the transition to a low-carbon economy over requires massive infrastructure investment by the city and our utilities (and in turn, our tax and ratepayers). 2) Our sprawling city makes it difficult to make decarbonized public transportation accessible to all and presents challenges to decarbonizing our large city fleet vehicles 3) The development community has quite a bit of political sway because new development can easily go into adjacent cities in Kansas to avoid strict climate regulations. 4) Supply chain issues, increased construction costs and lead times are causing the cost of infrastructure to rise already which makes it even more difficult to afford to adopt newer, and often more expensive technologies. All of this creates barriers to the strong level of action needed to reduce our carbon footprint. Legislative risks: The state of Missouri has a proven record of creating preemption laws when cities try to legislate environmental issues, such as the plastic bag ban and the natural gas preemption. Strong climate action comes with the risk of state authorities overriding and stalling the work we are doing and makes it difficult to create climate policies that work for our city. Risk to climate vulnerable communities: The weather in Kansas City is highly variable. Our summers are extremely hot and humid, and our winters can get very cold. Many homes currently rely on natural gas for winter heat and backup generators that burn fossil fuels. column15: Metro Nashville/Davidson County has several mechanisms that provide consideration of climate-related issues. A statutory 15-member Sustainability Advisory Committee -- a multidisciplinary group of stakeholders across the community -- advise the Mayor on environmental, sustainability, and resilience-related issues, including climate-related issues. Statute (https://www.nashville.gov/departments/mayor/boards/sustainability-advisory-committee). A previous instantiation of this group created Nashville's Climate Action Plan (https://www.nashville.gov/departments/mayor/sustainability-resilience-environment/climate-adaptation-and-resilience-plan) which includes a number of actions identified for maximizing carbon reductions. The city has finalized its first climate adaptation and resilience plan. Draft CARP at (https://www.nashville.gov/sites/default/files/2023-09/Climate-Adaptation-and-Resilience-Action-Plan-Review-Version-230919.pdf?ct=1695145988). The plan spans across Metro departments and lays the groundwork for high-priority and high-impact adaptation actions that will build resilience. The adaptation plan is complemented by a sustainability and resilience toolkit, which includes a number of primers, templates, and analytical tools designed to meet city departments where they are in their sustainability and resilience journeys. The toolkit is based on adaptation best practices pursued by other cities, and Metro departments, through a series of workshops, that allow them to identify the greatest opportunity areas for this work. A Climate Working Group, comprised of representatives from various city departments, meets monthly to implement the toolkit's action steps. Finally, Metro Nashville departments often independently consider climate-related issues as they relate to significant projects. For example, Nashville is planning for redevelopment of 300+ acres along its East Bank riverfront and flood management strategies are intentionally being incorporated into intended use of that space. Nashville has also begun deployment of a resilience hub network, a mechanism for allowing neighborhoods across the city to rapidly evolve into emergency response and recovery centers that are tailored to the unique needs of its diverse neighborhoods. For example, select libraries display emergency services information and have developed Hazard Vulnerability Assessments to prioritize climate risks and begin working on preparedness actions. City departments have utilized available federal funding for sustainability and climate related purposes. For example, Energy Efficiency and Conservation Block Grant funds allowed upgrades to lighting and building envelope in the city's Historic Courthouse; $13M from Safe Streets and Roads for All grant will modernize transit along a major traffic corridor; $4.7 from the Charging and Fueling Infrastructure grant will modernize city-supported EV charging infrastructure as well expand the public-facing network. These are just a few of many examples of how departments are working to incorporate climate mitigation and adaptation into their work.
column16: Extreme heat and flooding are two of the most significant climate-related events facing Nashville. The city is taking intentional steps to better plan for stormwater management and flooding events, given anticipated increase in rain events. This is demonstrated through our current engagement in a comprehensive stormwater management study and our consideration of appropriate land use and design elements associated with our 300-acre East Bank area along the Cumberland River. We are in the process of using the results of our urban heat mapping exercise held in 2022 to identify locations for cool pavement installations. While this work will occur on a small scale at 5 specific stretches of road, there are plans for expansion once we are able to document impact. The city's planning department has also recently formed a natural resources focused group, the Ecological Design Studio, which will provide increased focus on natural resources and how our land use decisions interact with those natural resources. The Mayor's Office has launched a resilience planning framework and toolkit, and this includes recommendations for building resilience into city planning processes and also decision support tools that can lead to more data-informed decisions that can help the city mitigate and adapt to climate change.

Oversight of climate-related issues is accomplished through the efforts of several City departments and includes the creation of planning strategies, capital expenditures in infrastructure rehabilitation and upgrades, routine infrastructure maintenance, public safety and cleanup response for large storms, pursuit of grant funding, improvements to City facilities and operations, and education and collaboration opportunities with community organizations and residents. The City expands its jurisdiction and efforts through collaborative partnerships with the Lehigh Valley Planning Commission, Lehigh County Conservation District, Allentown Environmental Advisory Council (EAC), Lehigh County Authority, and Lehigh and Northampton Transportation Authority (LANTA).

 In 2024, City Council budgeted for a new 'Sustainability Coordinator' position to be added to the Parks and Recreation Budget. That position was filled in March 2024 and the Sustainability Coordinator is responsible for general climate issues and GHG emission reduction. GHG reduction initiatives focused on in 2024 include applying for grant funding for an EV fleet pilot program, collaborating with a local CBO to apply for a home repair and workforce development project focused on energy efficiency, weatherization and electrification of low-income housing. Funding was allocated in the 2025 budget to complete a climate action plan to formally identify strategies for the sustainability program going forward. The CAP will include recommended strategies for both municipal operations, policies, and community partnerships to reduce GHG in the City overall.

The EAC started reviewing large land development projects and providing specific recommendations for consideration by the Planning Commission. One of the EAC members is also the Chair of the Planning Commission and serves as the EAC/Planning Commission liason.
column16: Climate-related issues were woven throughout the City's 2030 Comprehensive Plan, particularly in its Living Systems section which outlines the City's principals to 1) plan for a sustainable and resilient Allentown, 2) improve community health outcomes, 3) increase environmental stewardship, and 4) create productive and connected urban landscapes. The plan includes energy efficiency programs and policies including for municipal buildings. The plan recommends review of zoning ordinance to incorporate high-performance building policies and reduce impervious surfaces by changing parking lot regulations. The plan also includes safe and efficient transportation, enabling alternative mobility choices, and developing climate action and resilience plans that integrate with regional plans. It mirrors Lehigh Valley Planning Commission's climate goal “to create a land use pattern that helps to mitigate climate change impacts through a compact urban development area, mixed land uses, higher densities in urban areas and through preserving land for agriculture and environmental purposes”. \n\nZONEAllentown is a project that will result in a comprehensive update of the City of Allentown's Zoning Ordinance as well as strategic revisions to the Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance (SALDO). Over the past several months, staff have closely considered all public comments submitted during the project's public review period through Summer 2024. Community concerns, priorities, and suggestions have been considered through proposed revisions, where staff have addressed feedback while remaining consistent with ZONE Allentown's core goals. The City of Allentown requested feedback on these public review documents by March 21, 2025. All comments will be considered for inclusion in the Final Adoption Draft, which will be presented to City Council later this year. The promotion of Low impact development (LID) practices, water treatment and volume control in streetscape design, and use of the City's Green Stormwater Infrastructure Credit Program are included in the new SALDO. In conjunction with the SALDO update, the City's Stormwater Management Ordinance is being revised in coordination with Lehigh Valley Planning Commission's Act 167 update. Changes include updated design specifications for rate control and provisions for water quality treatment facilities. In addition, the Stormwater Bureau is undertaking a Watershed Restoration Strategy to address stream impairments resulting in conceptual and capital planning which support climate action and sustainability goals. Goals are met by first understanding the amount of pollutant loading carried within each watershed, its sources and impacts. Target reductions are calculated through installation of engineered stormwater management facilities to include green infrastructure. The nearest target goal is to conduct and complete analyses on the most impaired waterway, the Little Cedar Creek. The engineering report was submitted to PA Department of Environmental Protection. In addition to addressing water quality of stormwater runoff, the City is undertaking an investment strategy that will build off of a long range subbasin Hydrologic and Hydraulic (H&H) modeling program. Stormwater Bureau staff collected field data throughout 2024 and 2025 for a flow and capacity study of the system within a large sewershed of Trout Creek impacted by flooding. The modeling study will gauge the impact on the stormwater infrastructure during 2-year, 5-year, 10-year, 25-year, and 100-year storm events. In addition, the City's Parks master planning process includes significant measures to address stormwater reduction, enhance tree canopies, and plant native vegetation, while aligning efforts to reduce maintenance requirements as a means to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Such efforts are exemplified in completion of the City's Percy Ruhe Park Development Plan.
column17:
The City's financial planning has been impacted primarily in fleet, facilities, and streets. In anticipation of carbon neutrality requirements in the coming years, the City must look to gradually transition its vehicles and equipment towards lower carbon emitting options. The City received funding from Federal and State sources to conduct an electric vehicle fleet pilot, purchasing 8 EVs and installing at least 8 charging stations to serve these vehicles. The City purchased its first EV in February 2024 and is on track to purchase the remaining seven vehicles in September 2025. The fueling and maintenance costs will be tracked and used to inform the future fleet plan. The City will use that document to plan how to continue to incorporate EVs, Hybrid Vehicles, and other alternative fuel source vehicles over the next 5 years.

 Furthermore, the City will look to modernize its aging facilities with the aim of reducing emissions, while also maintaining a comfortable work environment amidst rising temperatures. Both of the aforementioned are substantial capital acquisition and improvement burdens, which, nevertheless, must be planned for. Additionally, if, as we anticipate, our reliance on liquid fuels excise taxes, which funds streets maintenance and snow removal, is undercut by a transition away from fossil fuels, the City anticipates the need to plan for alternative financial planning to cover these costs.

In 2018, the City created an enterprise fund through implementation of a Stormwater Utility fee which established an adequate, sustainable, and dedicated revenue source to fund operating costs and infrastructure capital planning. Annual Stormwater Bureau budgeting includes monies for water quality modeling and hydraulic engineering studies.

 In late 2024, new imagery and lidar data were collected through a flyover of the City. An updated impervious area layer will be processed in 2025. Updated and accurate impervious data may be used in capital planning of projects to treat existing untreated surface for quality and volume.

Public opposition also presents a potential risk to the City's climate transition. This may stem from limited public awareness of the benefits of transitioning to a low-carbon economy and the possible negative perceptions of certain initiatives, such as shifting away from fossil fuel energy.

The plan includes targets, actions, monitoring, and reporting requirements. column16: Much of Omaha's current Master Plan is guided by a strong awareness of climate-related risks and opportunities. The plan was partly informed by Omaha's first GHG emissions inventory conducted in 2011. Climate issues have influenced Omaha's zoning codes since 1980. Zoning regulations include the North Hills Environmental Resources Overlay District, Cunningham Lake Water Quality Environmental Overlay District, Floodplain Development Standards, the Stormwater Management Ordinance, Accessory Dwelling Units, Planned Unit Redevelopment Districts, Development Reserve Districts, Transit Oriented Development Districts, and Urban Agriculture. These regulations protect natural and open spaces, tree canopy, soil, air, and water resources, and strengthen Omaha's flood protection, food security, and resilience. The Environment Element of the Master Plan also includes guidelines under which all new development in Omaha's jurisdiction is reviewed, protecting natural features, such as tree canopy, prairie, streams, and wetlands. In addition, the Master Plan guides Omaha's expanding transit, bicycle, and pedestrian infrastructure. Combined with the zoning code's design standards, landscaping, and streetscaping regulations, along with tax increment financing, they support denser, greener development and redevelopment within the urban core and cleaner mobility options. When we completed our climate action plan in 2024, we noted that many actions were already well underway thanks to our Master Plan. Current and new climate actions will be incorporated into our new Comprehensive Plan, which is currently being developed.
column17: Omaha's Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) primarily reflects climate-related concerns through environmental and transportation expenditures. The 2023-2028 CIP totals about $2.79 billion in capital improvements over six years, an increase from last year's $2.27 billion. Environmental expenditures historically tend to be in the 20-30% range of the six-year total of the overall CIP instead of the current 49%. Transportation accounts for 30% of the budget, public facilities 17%, parks and recreation 3%, and public safety 1%. Higher percentages within the Environment section are attributable mainly to the CSO Control Implementation Program, the Combined Sewer Renovation Program, and the Capital Asset Replacement Program. The Sewer Revenue Improvement fund makes up 47% of the revenue sources in the 6-year CIP, much of which will go toward funding the Combined Sewer Overflow (CSO) Control Implementation program. City-related sources (Bond Issues, Other City, & Sewer Revenue) and outside sources (Special Assessments, Federal, and Other Local) equate to the entire sources of revenue. Like many other U.S. cities, combined sewer and stormwater systems serve older parts of Omaha. The CSO Control Implementation Program minimizes the impact of combined sewer and stormwater overflows during wet weather, allowing the city to meet federal water quality standards. Additional benefits include street improvements, improved stormwater management, enhanced vegetation in city parks and streetscapes, cleaner waterways, and infrastructure that encourages redevelopment in the city core. The Combined Sewer Renovation Program separates sanitary and storm sewers in areas impacted by combined sewers. The program identifies areas for combined sewer rehabilitation, service level improvements, and basement backup prevention. The Capital Asset Replacement Program replaces, upgrades, and improves existing water resource recovery and collection system facilities. Improvements include energy conservation, biogas recovery and conversion to renewable natural gas, and electrical improvements, including new cogeneration equipment. In addition to these projects, the CIP includes Missouri River flood levee maintenance and repairs, creek channel rehabilitation and flood mitigation programs, sewer rehabilitation, and erosion/storm sewer repair programs.

column16: The City has a Macro Spatial Development Framework (MSDF), which is legislative planning document that was approved by the City Council in 2021. The principles underpinning the MSDF are spatial transformation to allow for spatial compaction and densification. The spatial form of the City bears the scars of Apartheid planning which ensured that people resided in particular areas on the basis of race and ethnicity. Due to the economic impact of separate development, this has translated into the creation of class-based residential patterns whereby it is financially prohibitive for people to live closer to the areas with greater economic opportunity, infrastructure and resources. Therefore the process of reconfiguring the spatial form of the City to achieve greater equity has positive implications for the transport-related emissions as these will reduce as the need to commute long distances from home and work will be minimised. The MSDF is also informed by the Open Space Development Framework which guides the protection and preservation of open spaces. This is important for controlling the formation of the Urban Heat Island effect as well offering a buffer against flooding as the risk of flooding has intensified in those parts of the City where permeable surfaces have been replaced with impermeable surfaces.
column17: Climate related issues has had a positive impact on the City's financial planning. It has ignited conscious and innovative financial and budgeting considerations. This has raised climate change consciousness in the overall city financial and strategic planning. Although the financial allocation may have not drastically improved, the capacity of the City's financial practitioners and project managers has improved about climate related issues. The city is continuing with the Climate Budget piloting program which started in 2021 with the intention of piloting a climate budget in future. Introducing the Climate Budget program to the city operations has been delayed and affected by the local dynamics relating to the political and administration instability. The departure of the Chief Financial Officer as the key driver of the program and the appointment of the new administrative head - the City Manager has created significant delays. The former Executive Mayor of City of Tshwane publicly announced during the C40 Mayoral Summit 2022 that the city intends to introduce the Climate Budget considering local resources and dynamics. The processes were further affected by the change in the political heads which was finalized recently. However, because the conceptualization of the program was already at an advances stage - the activities were resuscitated immediately when the municipal operations with the new political head resumed. The Climate budget will be introduced in phases. Currently the city is undertaking an internal stakeholder engagement through various platforms like one-on-one departmental engagements, individual engagements etc. The Climate Budget program leaders have also attempted to develop a draft Climate Budget which is still under wraps for consultation purposes. The City is still attending to the global climate budget engagement activities of the pilot cities until the end of the year. The city has also accepted the invitation to become a member of the City Advisory Group which is the ongoing project on \'Advancing GHG Quantification and Analysis for Climate Budgeting”. We believe the city will significantly contribute to the overall Climate Budget and further this will enhance the capacity building element in relation to the need to quantification.
column18: The City of Tshwane is one of the largest municipalities in South Africa, which brings an array of other conflicting service delivery priorities which needs to be attended to. This poses a risk to low carbon development as service delivery or other service delivery tasks are prioritised without mainstreaming low carbon development / low carbon service delivery. Another risk is the myth around sustainability or climate responsiveness being expensive, which brings implementations risks that comes with lack of financial allocation to sustainable development. Political buy-in where there is no action-oriented commitment or buy-in is another risk that will derail low carbon economy transition as there is or will be a lack of focused priority towards sustainable development. The risk of Communities not buying into the low carbon economy is feasible as members of the community will want to understand what it is in for them and what value they are getting in within the transition. That is why it is important to make reference to just transition in low carbon economies to ensure no one is left behind both from knowledge and economic perspective. Similar with businesses that are more concerned with the bottom line and profits, there is a risk that if the message is not conveyed correctly there might be challenges from the private sector in assisting the city within their operations to be low carbon, especially if the city is unable to provide the necessary incentives towards low carbon developments.

column15: The Local Government Act from 2022 provides the legal framework within which the council operates. For the city, apart from the 2022 Local Government Act, the Transform Freetown Agenda18 is the backbone of Freetown's climate work and guides the structure of this first strategy. The Transform Freetown Agenda is the first of its kind for Freetown and a reflection of a mindset to inspire change. The eleven Transform Freetown priority sectors are grouped within four clusters - Resilience, Human Development, Healthy City and Urban Mobility - and respond to the challenges of climate change across all aspects of urban life.
column16: Floods regularly affect Freetown during the rainy season due to heavy precipitation and from storm surges along the coast of the city. These events take a toll on agricultural production, infrastructure, people's homes, public health and biodiversity along the coastal area. A challenging climate impacts human health and the environment and this create a room for development planning of the city. The GHG inventory, as well as the Climate Risk Assessment that were conducted as part of Freetown's Climate Action Planning process are a key component informing the Transform Freetown Agenda, Freetown's strategic planning document. Further, the Freetown Structure Plan is currently under revision and equally benefits from the outcome of the Climate Risk Assessment, as well as further studies undertaken to identify areas in Freetown that are subject to climate risks and hazards.
column17: The development of Freetown's Climate Action Plan also brought about changes in the institutional set up of the council. The council has established a climate action and disaster risk management unit within its administrative arm and a corresponding council committee. The formation of these governance structures have implications for the council's budget. As part of the Transform Freetown Agenda, FCC has widened access to own-source and external financial resources through an innovative property rate reform, private sector partnerships, targeted development partner funding, building city-to-city networks and tapping into funding from philanthropists and the diaspora. Further, as part of our #FreetownTheTreeTown campaign FCC is showcasing its ambition to tap into yet uncovered resources by developing an impact investment scheme. The city offers the opportunity for corporate and institutional partners to donate to and invest in a socially and environmentally impactful initiative, focusing on climate resilience in Freetown. We are digitally tracking the growth of our trees using a customised tree tracker app and will create impact tokens based on the tree growing progress and success. Other financing options that we are also exploring 51 are the creation of municipal bonds, diaspora bonds as well as results-based financing schemes, that could further boost the city's revenues over the long-term, supporting the implementation of the Transform Freetown Agenda and the fight against climate change.Projects and programs addressing climate-related issues are, where possible, prioritised and funding is allocated accordingly.
column18: In Freetown where everyone is often preoccupied with putting out fires (literally and figuratively) and generally responding to short term crises of one form or another, every bit of effort that goes towards long-term planning is incredibly valuable. However, transition to a low-carbon economy might not be perceived as the most important objective and the council risks support from stakeholders. Hence, while this transition might seem or could almost be considered luxury and it allows Freetownians to keep an eye trained on the end goal - a climate safe future for all.

column16: At the level of Turku urban region (consisting of 13 municipalities of the Turku urban region commuter area), sustainable development of community structure is steered and advanced through the regional structural model (the Structural Model 2035 for the Turku Urban Region) and the MAL agreement (Agreement on land-use, housing and transport between the city / region and the state, including an investment programme). The MAL agreement and related collaboration is a significant tool for Turku in consolidating development that supports carbon neutrality. Greenhouse gases in the urban region are an indicator of the MAL agreement. The Turku Master Plan 2029 goals have been set by city council. Climate and sustainability targets have been integrated in the process from the beginning. Community decentralization in the Turku region will be hindered by planning the population growth in proximity to existing infrastructure and main public transport lines and by enabling light rail transport in the near future. The master plan for the city has been based on this model aiming at 66 % share of walking, cycling and public transport. Climate Impact Assessment was carried out twice during the process: quantitative analysis in the first phase and qualitative reflection in the final phase. Based on GI analysis on mobility, services and density of housing conducted in the Urban Zone I - III research projects the plan aims at optimizing locations of housing, services and public transportation nearby and accessibility for the majority of the city's inhabitants - with a lot of green areas between as well. The Turku Master Plan 2029 outlines objectives significantly supporting reaching carbon neutrality in the Turku area and also preparing for climate change. Water bodies and green areas form a solid ecological network. Sustainable management of water is analysed and shown very systematically as one of the main themes of the Turku Master Plan 2029. The regulations cover storm water management, sea flood risk areas, protection of natural waters and groundwaters.
column17: Turku has been developing climate budgeting as a concrete tool for preparation, steering and monitoring green investments and making them a natural part of the financial planning and annual management of cities and urban companies. Over the years 2025 - 2030, Turku's climate investments will be EUR 1.7 billion €. In climate budgeting, the EU taxonomy classification of sustainable funding has been used as the framework for assessing the climate impacts of investments, which enables a multidimensional examination of environmental objectives and, for example, the utilization of green funding.
column18: Subsequent to approval of the Turku Climate Plan, a workshop was arranged to assess the risks involved in the implementation of its main entities. Also mitigation strategies were considered. Afterwards, the relevant working groups dealt with the results and expanded on them. Current and emerging regulation was considered important especially for the energy sector requiring continuous awareness and dialogue. Also technological risks which are related e.g. to the uncertainties, trade-offs, and mainstreaming of the new solutions are relevant in energy and construction. Promoting innovations, working closely with R&D organizations, and carrying out demonstration projects have been considered as key solutions. In addition to financial issues, inadequate human resources or lack of knowledge and skills of personnel have been linked to many actions. As a solution we have been focusing on staff training and enhancing climate expertise at all levels of education. Finally, improving community perception is crucial to be able to mobilize citizens, communities, businesses, stakeholders, development partners and universities - the entire civil society - to join the work of creating climate actions and implementing a carbon-neutral Turku. This requires clear and transparent communication as well as constant development of attractive opportunities to participate.

Monitoring and Enforcement of Climate-Related Issues in Gaziantep

Gaziantep Metropolitan Municipality carries out a range of monitoring and enforcement activities related to climate change, particularly in the areas of air quality, energy use, solid fuels, and urban infrastructure. Below is a summary of these efforts based on up-to-date and verifiable sources:

1. Air Quality and Fuel Monitoring

Air Quality Measurements: The Environmental Protection and Control Department of the Gaziantep Metropolitan Municipality conducts passive air sampling at 30 different locations throughout the city during winter. These samples are analyzed and reported annually.

Transition to Cleaner Fuels: In 23 neighborhoods, 72% of buildings have switched to natural gas, while 28% continue using solid fuels. Out of 23,889 buildings, 11,888 transitioned to gas, covering 69,952 of 97,834 housing units. This transition was supported by financing campaigns from institutions like Şekerbank and GAZDAŞ, offering low-interest and installment options.
Poor-Quality Coal Monitoring: The Municipality, in coordination with the Chamber of Coal Traders and the Provincial Directorate of Environment, actively monitors and prevents the entry of low-quality or illegal coal into the city.
Urban Planning and Gas Infrastructure: In newly zoned and planned development areas, the rate of natural gas usage has reached 95%. This success is largely due to coordinated inspections and institutional collaboration.
2. Institutional Structures and Strategic Monitoring Commitments

The Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP) and Climate Change Action Plan have laid the foundation for Gaziantep's climate-related governance since 2011. These plans allow for long-term, measurable, and accountable implementation and monitoring.

In 2017, Gaziantep signed the Covenant of Mayors (CoM), committing to reducing GHG emissions by 40%. This commitment includes both implementation and periodic monitoring/reporting.

3. Awareness, Education, and Monitoring Tools
The city's Environmental Directorate has been strengthened since 2011, carrying out public education on air, soil, and water pollution alongside ongoing environmental measurements.

In neighborhoods with high pollution levels, public awareness campaigns have been implemented, and over 60,000 students have received environmental education in schools.
As part of the “Strengthening Climate Change Adaptation in Turkey” project, local governance capacity has been improved in key areas such as infrastructure, financing, and environmental governance.
column16:
The Impact of Climate-Related Issues on Gaziantep's Master and Development Planning - With Reference to the Climate Change Adaptation Action Plan

Gaziantep Metropolitan Municipality completed its Climate Change Adaptation Action Plan (CCAAP) in 2023. This strategic document aims to reduce the city's vulnerability to future climate-related risks and to implement adaptation-focused actions that promote environmental sustainability and urban resilience. The action plan significantly informs and shapes Gaziantep's master and development planning processes.

Key Components of Gaziantep's Climate Change Adaptation Action Plan

The plan, prepared as part of Gaziantep's commitment to climate resilience, focuses on the following thematic areas 
Renewable Energy Investments: Emphasis on solar power plants, biogas, and clean energy infrastructure.

Waste Management and Recycling: Strategies for waste reduction, reuse, and circular economy.

Water and Wastewater Management: Efficient use of water resources and improved treatment systems.

Sustainable Green Transportation: Promotion of low-emission transport systems and infrastructure.

Climate-Friendly Urban Development: Nature-based and climate-compatible city planning.

Air Quality Improvement: Measures to reduce pollution and improve public health.

Energy Efficiency (Buildings & Industry): Reducing energy use and emissions in all sectors.

Energy Management: Systematic approaches to optimize energy consumption across the city.

This roadmap aims to guide Gaziantep toward a net-zero carbon future and sustainable urban transformation.

Integration of the Adaptation Action Plan into Urban and Master Planning

Gaziantep's planning framework is being restructured in alignment with the CCAAP's objectives, with a clear focus on resilience and sustainability.

1. Water Resources and Urban Growth

Water and wastewater strategies prioritize water-efficient land use planning for residential, industrial, and agricultural zones. This supports the development of water-resilient urban spaces.

2. Energy Use and Infrastructure

Investments in renewable energy, such as city-wide solar systems, are directly integrated into energy infrastructure planning.

Energy efficiency standards in buildings and industry are increasingly embedded in urban development plans as either mandatory or incentivized practices.

3. Transportation and Mobility

Sustainable transportation models reshape road networks and new urban development areas to encourage low-emission, eco-friendly transport.

4. Green Areas and Urban Fabric

The plan supports the creation of green infrastructure to lower urban heat and enhance biodiversity. Green belts, parks, and water elements are prioritized in spatial planning to improve urban livability.

5. Air Quality and Healthy City Design

Air quality improvement goals influence traffic planning (e.g., low-emission zones) and industrial zoning decisions.

6. Resilience and Disaster Risk Management

The plan introduces a risk-based approach to climate threats such as droughts, heatwaves, and floods, guiding infrastructure and building codes for more resilient urban growth.

Conclusion

Gaziantep's master and development plans are increasingly aligned with the city's Climate Change Adaptation Action Plan, bringing climate considerations to the forefront of urban strategy.

Core principles now shaping the city's planning include:

Water efficiency,

Use of renewable energy,

Low-carbon and green mobility,

Air quality improvement,

Climate-smart construction and infrastructure.

Through these initiatives, Gaziantep is actively building a future that is sustainable, resilient to climate change, and consistent with national and global climate action goals.
column17:
How Climate-Related Plans Affect Gaziantep's Financial Planning

Gaziantep's strategies to combat and adapt to climate change not only address environmental concerns but also directly impact the city's financial planning. To achieve its sustainability goals, the city has had to restructure its budget allocations and seek out new funding sources.

Below is a detailed explanation of how climate-related plans influence Gaziantep's financial policies and budgeting:
1. Green Infrastructure and Energy Investments: New Budget Items

Projects such as solar power plants (SPPs), energy efficiency programs, and sustainable transportation have introduced new investment categories into the local budget.

The municipality has allocated significant funds from its own budget for initiatives like renewable energy, bike paths, and energy-efficient public buildings.

While these investments pose a short-term financial burden, they offer long-term benefits such as reduced energy costs and access to carbon markets.
 2. Climate Resilient Infrastructure Expenditures

In response to increasing risks such as drought and flash floods, Gaziantep has included rainwater harvesting systems, greywater infrastructure, and flood control projects in its financial planning.

These projects have created a dedicated area within the city's infrastructure budget for climate risk adaptation.
 3. Project Financing and External Funding Sources

To fund its climate plans, Gaziantep has turned to EU funds, World Bank loans, UNDP grants, and other international climate finance tools.

For example, projects under the Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP) have received financial support through the European “Covenant of Mayors” network.

In its financial planning, the municipality has established dedicated units for international fund management and coordination.
4. Climate-Sensitive Budgeting

In recent years, Gaziantep has begun adopting the approach of “climate-sensitive budgeting”, which integrates the climate impact of each investment into the financial evaluation.

For example, when planning a road project, the city considers not just the cost, but also factors like greenhouse gas emissions, green space loss, and the urban heat island effect.
5. Urban Renewal and Financial Incentives for Energy-Efficient Buildings

To promote the construction of energy-efficient buildings, the municipality has introduced:

Fee exemptions,

Facilitated credit access, and

Fast-tracked permitting for eco-friendly structures.

These incentives may lead to temporary reductions in municipal revenue, but they contribute to long-term energy savings and environmental benefits.
6. Education and Awareness Spending

Activities related to climate change awareness, education, and capacity building are also covered by the city's budget.

Special budget lines have been allocated for environmental education programs, particularly targeting children and youth.
column18:
Risks of Transitioning to a Low-Carbon Economy in Gaziantep

Gaziantep's transition toward a low-carbon economy presents significant environmental and economic opportunities, but it also brings a range of risks that must be addressed. These include both short-term and long-term threats that can impact the local economy, workforce, and social dynamics.

Below are the major risks associated with the transition to a low-carbon economy in Gaziantep:
1. Transformation Risk in an Industry-Based Economy

Gaziantep is a production- and export-oriented industrial city, and the shift to a low-carbon economy places substantial transformation pressure on certain sectors.

Energy-intensive sectors (textiles, plastics, food processing, etc.) are high in carbon emissions and may:

Struggle to comply with new environmental regulations,

Face negative impacts from carbon taxes and border carbon adjustment mechanisms (CBAM) in international trade.

The technological upgrades required for transformation can be financially burdensome, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).
 2. Employment Risk and Sectoral Shifts

Workers in carbon-intensive sectors are at risk of job loss due to reduced production or sectoral transformation.

The development of new green sectors (e.g., renewable energy, energy efficiency, recycling) will take time, potentially leading to employment gaps during the transition.

Without sufficient education and re-skilling programs, this may worsen socio-economic inequalities.
 3. Financing and Adaptation Costs

Transitioning to low-carbon technologies imposes high investment costs on both the private sector and local governments.

Implementing infrastructure and systems for energy efficiency, emission reduction, and clean production requires long-term financing.

Small-scale businesses may struggle to access the necessary financial resources to keep up with this transition.
 4. Energy Supply and Transition Period Security

As fossil fuels are phased out, ensuring a stable and sufficient supply of renewable energy becomes critical.

During infrastructure transformation, fast-growing cities like Gaziantep may face risks to energy supply security.
5. Competitiveness Loss Risk

Firms that are slow to adopt low-carbon production techniques may lose ground in domestic and international markets.

Especially in exports to the EU, companies producing high carbon footprint products may face customs duties or trade restrictions under new carbon regulations.
 6. Social Acceptance and Behavioral Resistance

Public awareness of climate change and carbon emissions is still developing.

As a result:
There may be resistance to behavioral changes (e.g., switching from private cars to public transport),

Backlash against green taxes and fees,

Lack of interest in energy-saving practices, which may hinder the success of policies.
