The City of Aspen's Climate Action Office (formerly the Canary Initiative) strives to promote environmental stewardship and lead climate action efforts throughout the Roaring Fork Valley in partnership with leaders across the state of Colorado and around the world. The Climate Action Office has published several Climate Action Plans (CAP). In February 2023, the Aspen Sustainability Action Plan (ASAP) was adopted by City Council and was updated in 2024. The ASAP outlines GHG emissions across 5 key sectors and offers a path for Aspen to reach its climate goals.

Aspen's City Council identified 'Climate Action and Resource Conservation' as 1/13 priorities in their 2024 Policy Agenda. Other priorities include: water availability & conservation, river health, renewable energy, and public lands. 

More detail is found on page 13 of the policy agenda document: https://www.aspen.gov/DocumentCenter/View/12158/2024-PolicyAgenda
column16:
Aspen is particularly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change: the increased frequency and magnitude of extreme weather events including from drought, wildfire, landslide, and flood have already caused harm to local environment, property and community health and safety.

These impacts directly impact master planning in many ways. One example is the in 'Castle Creek Bridge' project has been identified as important in part because: 

'In the event of a wildfire, mudslide, or other natural disasters, an evacuation of Aspen could be necessary. Currently, the primary evacuation route is the old Castle Creek Bridge. Adding a new bridge would double the number of evacuation routes for automobiles and triple the number of lanes available for evacuation.'

The effects of warming are also apparent in a snowy climate. Earlier loss of snow (and/or later arriving snow) mean a shorter season for skiing; changes in the timing of peak runoff from streams and rivers, and the potential for a longer fire season. 

A key indicator of local climate change is represented in the number of consecutive frost-free days. Since 1940, the number of frost-free days has increased by forty-six days, and by thirty days since 1980 (AGCI). This is the equivalent of losing a month of winter in less than a lifetime. 

Aspen's local emissions and growing population of full-time and part-time residents, visitors, and commuters are contributing to the global climate emergency. 

Aspen has adopted the following goals and plans:
•Aspen Sustainability Action Plan (ASAP) (2023): Council approved the ASAP as the City's new roadmap of objectives and action items to reach our climate goals. 
•Organics Waste Diversion and Compost Collection (2023): Council updated the Municipal Code to prohibit organic material, such as food, from being thrown away as landfill trash. 
•Building Code Adoption (2023): Council adopted updated building codes, which align with science-based targets, energy efficiency, electrification, and wildfire resilience.
•Council's Carbon Goal (2021-2025): Council adopted a carbon reduction goal via Resolution #76_Series 2021, which directs staff to reduce Aspen's greenhouse gas emissions by taking meaningful action and providing leadership in the following categories: low and zero emissions transportation, waste reduction, energy reduction in buildings, and advocating for state and federal regulations that support GHG emissions reductions. (reapproved in 2023)
•Building IQ (2022): Council adopted the Building IQ ordinance to address emissions from existing buildings in Aspen. Building IQ is a phased, two-part program: benchmarking and developing building performance standards. 
•GoEV City (2022): Aspen signed on to become the eleventh GoEV City in Colorado and to transition the municipal fleet to 100% electric and zero emission vehicles by 2050. 
•Fleet Zero Emissions Roadmap (FZER) (2022): Council approved the FZER, which supports department decisions to purchase electric and zero emission options on a timeline specified by Aspen's climate goals while also ensuring that city operational needs are met.
•Race to Zero (2021): Council signed on to Race to Zero, committing Aspen to work towards a zero carbon, resilient future.

column15: Climate oversight in Kingston is embedded at both the Council and staff levels. Council declared a climate emergency in 2019 and directed staff to integrate climate considerations across planning and budgeting. The City created a Climate Leadership Division within the Chief Administrative Office to coordinate corporate and community action. Climate-related matters are reported through Council and standing committees, with annual updates on emissions and program implementation. Departments integrate climate considerations into major capital projects, and financial incentives such as the Green Standard CIP are overseen by Council to ensure alignment with climate goals.
column16: Climate priorities have been embedded into Kingston's land use and development planning. The Climate Leadership Plan (2021) sets a pathway to community carbon neutrality by 2040, influencing zoning, development standards, and incentive programs such as the Green Standard CIP. Tree canopy targets, floodplain management, and active transportation strategies are also incorporated into the City's Official Plan and Transportation Master Plan, ensuring climate mitigation and adaptation guide long-term growth.
column17: Climate-related issues are reflected in both capital and operating budgets. Examples include dedicated funding for Better Homes Kingston, investments in electric transit vehicles, and annual funding allocations for tree planting and afforestation. Financial planning processes also assess long-term climate risk, such as flood-related infrastructure upgrades and stormwater system investments, which are considered essential to avoid higher future costs. Climate considerations are embedded in capital project business cases, ensuring Council decisions factor in both mitigation and adaptation outcomes.
column18: Key transition risks for Kingston include the high upfront costs of low-carbon infrastructure (e.g., electric transit fleet, building retrofits), the availability of skilled labour and contractors to deliver energy efficiency projects, and supply constraints for electric vehicles and buses. There are also risks associated with energy affordability during the transition, particularly for lower-income households. These risks are being addressed through financing programs like Better Homes Kingston, partnerships with post-secondary institutions to grow the local green workforce, and staged procurement of electric transit vehicles aligned with funding availability.

The City of Tempe is deeply committed to being an inclusive, transparent, and high-performing organization. This commitment is reflected in the City's Strategic Plan, which outlines the Council's priorities and direction in a clear, measurable, and publicly accessible way. Link (https://performance.tempe.gov/).

The Strategic Plan is built around five core priorities:

- Safe and Secure Communities - Ensuring safety and justice through a strong commitment to public safety services.

- Strong Community Connections - Building and maintaining strong relationships with residents by promoting open government, excellent customer service, and clear communication.

- Quality of Life - Enhancing the well-being of all who live and work in Tempe through investments in neighborhoods, parks, the arts, human services, and community amenities, with a focus on equity and diversity.

- Sustainable Growth and Development - Advancing sustainable practices to improve environmental outcomes, community health, and economic opportunity. Tempe aims to make long-term, generational investments in infrastructure, technology, and public transit to create a safe, clean, and equitable city.

- Financial Stability and Vitality - Securing Tempe's financial future by supporting economic development, business retention, and job creation to strengthen the local economy.

Each strategic priority includes a set of performance measures the City uses to track progress and evaluate results. For example, under the Sustainable Growth and Development priority, there are 12 performance measures ranging from carbon emissions and water efficiency to solid waste diversion. Link (https://sustainable-growth-and-development-tempegov.hub.arcgis.com/). These performance indicators are audited annually to ensure accountability and continuous improvement.

Additionally, departments within the City of Tempe frequently collaborate on projects, recognizing the interconnected nature of their work. Because sustainability touches many areas, the Transportation and Sustainability Department partners with:

- Economic Development to support small businesses and entrepreneurship opportunities,

- Public Works to improve the energy efficiency of city facilities,

- Community Services to plant trees and support community gardens, and

- Community Development to strengthen the sustainability of building codes and standards.

Department directors also meet twice a week to share updates and coordinate across teams.

The City also encourages resident involvement through various boards and commissions that provide opportunities for community input and help shape city projects. Some of the most relevant groups include the Sustainability and Resilience Commission, the Transportation Commission, and the Climate Justice Advisory Group.

On heat related issues, Tempe recently adopted a new heat safety ordinance to protect outdoor workers. This ordinance is a response to the increasing severity of summer heat in the area and aims to prevent heat-related illnesses and deaths among workers. 

Key Provisions of the Tempe Heat Ordinance:

- Written Heat Safety Plans: Employers must develop and implement comprehensive heat safety plans. 

- Access to Water and Shade: Workers must have access to potable water and shaded areas within 0.25 miles of their work location. 

- Rest Breaks: During heat advisories, workers are entitled to 10-minute rest breaks every two hours. 

- Heat Safety Training: Annual training on heat-related illness prevention and emergency protocols is required. 

- Acclimatization: New employees must undergo acclimatization procedures to adapt to the heat. 

- Bilingual Signage: Signage outlining worker protections, first aid, and reporting mechanisms must be provided in both English and Spanish. 

- Whistleblower Protection: The ordinance includes provisions to protect employees who report violations.

The general plan is the overarching policy document for the City of Tempe. It reflects the community's vision for the future, and is an expression of how the community wants to grow and change over the next 30 years. Link: https://www.tempe.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/101702/638817062863000000

The plan guides how Tempe plans for development, land use, transportation, mass transit, economic development, historic preservation, neighborhood enhancement, public art, cultural amenities, human services, recreation, and open space. It also guides the City of Tempe in planning for sustainability, climate change, environmental improvements, and in achieving a good quality of life and community well-being.

These plans are created in concert with residents, area businesses and other interested people. The General Plan 2050 that was adopted by the Tempe City Council on August 24, 2023. 

Tempe's General Plan 2050 includes sustainability initiatives aimed at achieving carbon neutrality by 2050 and prioritizing renewable energy sources. The plan focuses on reducing greenhouse gas emissions, promoting compact growth patterns, and enhancing transportation options, all while addressing environmental sustainability and climate change impacts. 

Key Sustainability Aspects of General Plan 2050:

- Carbon Neutrality: Tempe has set a goal to become carbon neutral by 2050

- Land Use and Development: Promotes compact growth patterns, increased housing density near transit lines and open spaces, and mixed-use developments to create more sustainable and walkable neighborhoods. 

- Transportation: Aims to improve transportation options, including public transit, cycling, and walking, to reduce reliance on single-occupancy vehicles. 

- Environment: Adapting to a warming Tempe by increasing tree and shade canopy across the city while only planting drought tolerant vegetation.
column17:
Climate-related issues have become an increasingly important consideration in the City of Tempe's financial planning. As part of the process of preparing to issue bonds to raise money for city projects, the City has sought to get credit ratings from financial agencies to assess how financially stable and trustworthy the city is for potential investors. As part of this process, the rating agencies ask questions about various risks that could affect the city's ability to repay its debt. While Tempe has not experienced significant direct disruptions to its finances due to climate impacts, the City proactively integrates climate resilience into its long-term planning and investment strategies to mitigate potential risks, mainly around water security, heat resilience and infrastructure, and climate justice efforts. 

The Municipal Budget Office is responsible for preparation of budget documents, long-range financial capacity study, revenue forecasting, capital improvements program, benchmarking, budget monitoring, forecasting, and fiscal impact analyses. The annual budget process is linked to the city's strategic priorities and performance measures, ensuring alignment with community goals. The budget process covers both the operating budget (day-to-day expenses) and the capital budget (major infrastructure projects). The process kicks off in November with the development of the proposed budgets and concludes with final adoption and property tax levy in June. The city actively solicits public input through various channels, including online surveys, public meetings, and City Council sessions. 

Each year, departments are allocated funding to cover programming, infrastructure and personnel costs. Through special revenue funds, the Transportation and Sustainability Department receiving funding for bus, light rail, streetcar and other public transit services, maintains streets and sidewalks. Through Capital Project Funds, the Transportation and Sustainability Department receives funding for traffic calming infrastructure improvements. Link 1: (https://www.tempe.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/109500/638606108445030000). Link 2: (https://www.tempe.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/113593/638865497007870000).

Each year, based on public input, the City Council selects five performance measures to prioritize and accelerate. These accelerated performance measures receive focused attention through strategies such as cross-department collaboration, resource realignment, and additional budget support.

For two consecutive years, the Community Carbon Neutrality performance measure was selected as a top priority. More recently, the Tree and Shade Canopy performance measure has been identified for acceleration, reflecting the City's continued focus on climate action and urban cooling.

Risks associated with transitioning to a low-carbon economy in Arizona include extreme heat and rising energy consumption. Extreme heat puts significant strain on the electric grid, often leading to system overloads, equipment failures, and ultimately power outages, especially during the summer months. At the same time, Arizona's growing population and expanding economy are increasing energy demand, particularly in the Phoenix metropolitan area.

While Arizona has strong potential to be a leader in solar energy, the current political climate, especially within the Arizona Corporation Commission, is not supportive of renewable energy development. This poses a challenge to progress. Both utilities serving Tempe have set net-zero carbon emissions goals for 2050, but they face an uphill battle in reaching them.

As of 2023, Arizona's electricity generation relied primarily on natural gas (46%), followed by nuclear power (27%), coal (10%), solar (10%), hydroelectric (5%), and wind (1%). The state's continued dependence on natural gas means a full transition to clean energy will take time and sustained effort.

Transportation presents its own set of challenges. Building a regional public transit system that can fairly compete with single-occupancy gas-powered vehicles is difficult, especially when not all cities in the metro area value or prioritize transit investments to the same degree that Tempe does. There's also significant opportunity for a shift to electric vehicles (EVs), but the region's spread-out, car-centric development pattern creates range anxiety for potential EV users. Without a robust charging infrastructure in place, many residents, especially those without access to home chargers, feel hesitant or inconvenienced about making the switch.

In summary, Tempe faces these key risks in its transition to a low-carbon economy:

- Grid Vulnerability: Increasing extreme heat and population growth are driving up energy demand, straining the electric grid and raising the risk of power outages.

- Energy System Dependence: The state remains heavily reliant on natural gas, making it challenging for utilities to meet long-term clean energy goals.

- Political and Regulatory Barriers: A lack of policy support from state-level leadership slows progress on renewable energy deployment.

- Preference for low-density urban development: EV adoption is slowed by range anxiety, limited charging infrastructure, and the metro area's sprawling layout, which requires long-distance travel.

column15: The City of Alexandria's governance and oversight of climate-related issues is handled in multiple ways: 1) the City Council's strategic plan and priority areas include climate-related issues as a core focus, in addition to equity and environmental/climate justice; 2) climate-related issues and targets/goals are further set forth in the City's Environmental Action Plan 2040, and other integrated plans, including, but not limited to, the Alexandria Mobility Plan (i.e. transportation master plan), Small Area Plans (neighborhood-level development plans incorporated into the City's Comprehensive Master Plan), Hazard Mitigation and Emergency Management Plan, Stormwater Master Plan, Housing Master Plan, and many others; 3) the City's citizen-led Environmental Policy Commission, Transportation Commission, and Planning Commission also have climate-related oversight, including policy and program recommendations; 4) specific climate-related programs oversight is handled by coordination and collaboration of relevant departments and agencies; 5) climate-related issues are included in the City's budget at a programmatic level and where certain departments or agencies have climate-specific program implementation responsibilities; 6) The City has established a centralized Office of Climate Action within the City Manager's Office.The City recently completed its Energy and Climate Change Action Plan (ECCAP) and the newly formed Office of Climate Action is designing and implementing programs that advance the objectives of that plan.
column16: The City of Alexandria's master/development planning has been impacted by climate-related issues to date in 5 ways:1) Since mid-2000s the City's standard development policy has been centered around transit-oriented development and low-impact development principles. These policies are due, in part, to climate-related issues and minimizing greenhouse gas emissions.2) Since ~2010, stormwater management and development limitations in flood zones has been implemented to manage impacts of increasing stormwater penetration from increasing precipitation as a result of a changing climate.3) A green building policy was instituted in 2009 to introduce a comprehensive approach to sustainable design in new development, including focus on energy reduction, stormwater reduction, reducing transportation reliance, enhancing open space and tree canopy, and minimizing waste.4) Small Area Plans (neighborhood-level master planning chapters) have included sustainability and climate action recommendations since ~2010 to include reduction of greenhouse gas emissions from operational carbon and to minimize climate-related risks such as flooding and increased heat/urban heat island effects.5) Starting in 2020, three specific development projects were required to file comprehensive sustainability plans to include climate-action measures, and two of these were required to file full carbon neutrality plans to achieve carbon neutrality in the new developments over time by 2040 consistent with the City's carbon reduction goals.

column18: One of the greatest risks to the City of Naperville's transition to a low-carbon economy is the City's membership and energy contract with the Illinois Municipal Electric Agency (IMEA). On June 1, 2011, the City of Naperville began purchasing electric power for its municipal Electric Utility with the IMEA. While this contract has provided citizens with low-cost, reliable energy for over 10 years, a significant source of that energy comes from coal-fired power plants. This contract is set to end in 2035. The current generation mix is 78% coal, 11% renewables, 11% market purchases, and <1% member generation. Alternative transportation, EV infrastructure, and building & development policies are also top challenges to the transition to a low-carbon economy. As a result of the pandemic, transit ridership has declined. The primary public transportation option, Metra, provides residents with access to Chicago and the suburbs in between Chicago and Naperville. However, there are limited bus routes and no light rail to connect other parts of the community. There is also the challenge of balancing economic development and placing additional requirements on developers. In order to understand challenges and opportunities with sustainable building & development policies like EV charging requirements, stretch codes, benchmarking, and building performance standards, staff have participated in high level conversations and attended educational programs about these topics. City staff has also been in conversations with NEST to develop a series of stakeholder meetings with the aim of collecting feedback from developers regarding a proposed ordinance that would require a certain level of EV-capable parking spaces to be incorporated into new commercial developments. If enacted, such an ordinance would complement newly-passed EV charging legislation at the state level requiring a certain level of EV capability for newly-constructed residential properties.

Policy Direction and Strategic Integration

The Fayetteville City Council provides top-level oversight of climate-related issues. It adopted the Energy Action Plan in 2018 and expanded it into the Climate Action Plan (CAP) in 2024, embedding climate considerations into citywide strategic guidance, master plans, and development frameworks.

Climate-related issues are integrated into City Plan 2040, the Mobility Plan, the Parks Master Plan, the Recycling and Trash Master Plan, the Urban Forestry Master Plan, and the Active Transportation Plan, ensuring that land use, transportation, and sustainability priorities are coordinated.

Administrative Oversight

The Sustainability and Resilience Department leads day-to-day management, coordinating with divisions including Utilities, Public Works, Transportation, Fleet Operations, Parks, Urban Forestry, Recycling & Trash, and Communications.

Cross-departmental collaboration ensures climate issues are addressed holistically across infrastructure, natural systems, energy, waste, and transportation.

Stakeholder and Advisory Processes

Oversight is supported by advisory boards and commissions such as the Environmental Action Committee, Active Transportation Committee, Urban Forestry Advisory Board, and Parks & Recreation Advisory Board.

These groups meet monthly to review projects, provide guidance, and advise Council and staff on climate-related decisions.

Partnerships with nonprofits, utilities, watershed groups, and community stakeholders further inform priorities and implementation.

Reporting and Review Frequency

Monthly Reports to Council: The City Council receives monthly energy and financial performance reports, keeping elected officials informed about cost savings, efficiency gains, and sustainability investments.

Annual Reporting: An Annual Sustainability Report consolidates greenhouse gas (GHG) inventories, project updates, and key performance indicators, providing accountability to both Council and the public.

Annual GHG Inventories: Fayetteville conducts annual inventories of both municipal operations and community-wide emissions, using ICLEI's ClearPath platform.

Five-Year CAP Updates: The Climate Action Plan is formally updated every five years, with Council review and public engagement to refine targets and strategies.

Oversight of Goals and Targets

Council and staff monitor progress toward goals including:

100% clean energy for City operations by 2030

Net-zero community emissions by 2050

40% waste diversion rate by 2030

5% per-capita water use reduction by 2030

These targets are tracked through monthly reports, annual sustainability reporting, performance contracts, and sector-specific KPIs (e.g., energy use, diversion rates, water consumption, fleet electrification).
column16:
Climate-Related Impacts on Master and Development Planning - City of Fayetteville

Integration of Climate in Long-Term Planning

Fayetteville's master planning framework—including City Plan 2040, the Mobility Plan, the Parks Master Plan, the Recycling and Trash Master Plan, the Urban Forestry Master Plan, and the Active Transportation Plan—has been explicitly aligned with the Climate Action Plan (CAP, adopted June 2024).

These plans cover near-term (5-10 years), medium-term (10-20 years), and long-term (20+ years) horizons, with climate risks and opportunities embedded across transportation, utilities, land use, parks, and conservation planning.

Adaptation Activities

Climate-related risks of flooding, heat waves, and drought have reshaped land use and infrastructure planning. The City has adopted nature-based solutions, such as restoring riparian corridors, creating conservation and climate-focused zoning districts, expanding tree canopy ordinances, and converting flood-prone land into parks.

The Emergency Management Plan has been updated to incorporate climate risks, leading to the development of resilience hubs, cooling centers, and stormwater infrastructure investments.

Mitigation Activities

Master and development planning now prioritizes compact, connected development to reduce vehicle miles traveled and support low-carbon mobility. This is reinforced through investments in active transportation infrastructure and transit access.

Water utility and wastewater planning incorporate conservation and efficiency, with smart retrofits and incentive-based rate structures that reduce per-capita consumption.

The CAP also commits the City to 100% clean energy for government operations by 2030 and net-zero community emissions by 2050, shaping all facility planning, fleet procurement, and capital investments.

Substantial Strategic Decisions Influenced by Climate Risks and Opportunities

Entering into an Energy Savings Performance Contract (ESPC) with Johnson Controls in 2023, allowing $4.45 million in upgrades across 47 facilities, paid for entirely through guaranteed future energy savings. This decision addressed both financial risks of rising energy costs and mitigation goals.

Establishing a stormwater utility to finance flood mitigation, conservation land acquisition, and resilient infrastructure.

Incorporating ecosystem services and carbon sequestration as formal planning priorities, a first for Fayetteville, ensuring that conservation and land management serve both adaptation and emissions-reduction functions.
column17:
Climate-Related Impacts on Financial Planning and Budgeting - City of Fayetteville

Operating Costs and Revenues

Rising infrastructure repair and maintenance costs are anticipated from more frequent floods, storms, and extreme weather.

Insurance premiums for both municipal assets and residents have increased due to higher climate risk exposure.

Public health expenditures are expected to grow from climate-driven impacts such as heat stress, poor air quality, and disease vectors.

Property values in flood-prone areas may decline, putting pressure on property tax revenues.

At the same time, energy performance contracting and efficiency retrofits are reducing utility costs, creating long-term operating savings that can be reinvested.

The City also dedicates $100,000 annually to Climate Action Plan implementation, a recurring operating expense that institutionalizes climate response.

Capital Expenditures and Allocation

Fayetteville is implementing a Stormwater Utility to fund capital projects in flood mitigation, resilient infrastructure, and conservation land acquisition.

Major capital retrofits (e.g., through the Johnson Controls Energy Savings Performance Contract) are financed by future energy savings rather than new debt, protecting financial stability.

Climate priorities influence capital allocation by embedding resilience and carbon reduction into decisions on fleet procurement (electrification), facility upgrades, and park development.

The City is also exploring bond financing and development impact fees to support land preservation, stormwater management, and resilience-focused park investments.

Access to Capital

Climate-related goals enhance Fayetteville's eligibility for federal and state grants, public-private partnerships, and utility rebate programs, many of which are directed toward energy efficiency, electrification, and equity-focused investments.

Establishing dedicated revenue streams (stormwater utility, bond measures, and performance contracting) strengthens the City's fiscal capacity to attract outside investment.

In 2021, Fayetteville established a Climate Refugee Resettlement Fund through a resident donation. This trust serves as a pass-through vehicle for refugee resettlement services, administered by the City. It expands Fayetteville's financial preparedness to meet future humanitarian needs while aligning with its designation as a Welcoming City.
column18:
Transition Risks - City of Fayetteville

According to the June 2024 Fayetteville Climate Action Plan, the transition to a low-carbon economy presents several risks for the community, even though the local economy is not heavily tied to fossil fuel industries. Economic shifts may create challenges around energy costs, infrastructure demands, insurance premiums, and adaptation requirements. The transportation and natural gas sectors are particularly identified as ongoing sources of emissions, requiring substantial change in energy systems and consumer behavior.

Two of Fayetteville's largest economic drivers—the University of Arkansas and a regional hospital system—face transition risks as they adjust facilities, operations, and workforce needs in line with low-carbon requirements. Both sectors must contend with rising energy efficiency standards, potential retrofitting costs, and the challenge of maintaining affordable service while decarbonizing operations.

At the same time, Fayetteville's limited reliance on fossil-fuel-led industries lessens the severity of transition risks compared to many other jurisdictions. The City's high concentration of educational services and knowledge-based employment is expected to help cushion the transition, providing opportunities for reskilling and specialization in emerging low-carbon sectors.

Transition Risks by Category (TCFD Framework)

Regulatory Risks: Recent state legislation in Arkansas has constrained local authority in several areas:

Solar: Net-metering caps and reduced reimbursement rates weaken the financial viability of solar adoption for households, businesses, and municipal facilities.

Waste: State law limits regulation of plastics and styrofoam, hindering Fayetteville's ability to meet its 40% diversion goal.

EVs: New requirements for battery supply chain attestations increase procurement complexity and costs for electrifying the municipal fleet.

Technology Risks: Constraints on renewable energy adoption and recycling system upgrades delay deployment of clean technologies. High upfront costs for building retrofits and low-carbon infrastructure also pose barriers.

Legal Risks: Preemption laws at the state level may create legal challenges if Fayetteville attempts to pursue stricter climate measures. Broader climate-related litigation remains a potential risk for municipalities.

Market Risks:

Volatility in energy supply and demand during the transition to electrification.

Community rejection of cart-based recycling threatens the City's ability to meet waste diversion goals and align with recycling market standards.

Rising costs of low-carbon goods and services, including clean energy and EVs, may impact budgets and procurement.

Reputation Risks: Failure to meet stated climate and diversion targets—due to state-level restrictions or community pushback—could undermine Fayetteville's reputation as a leader in sustainability. Conversely, demonstrating innovation and resilience despite these barriers is critical to maintaining credibility and public trust.

column16:
Following the declaration of a climate emergency in 2019, the City Council directed staff to develop comprehensive Climate Change Adaptation and Mitigation and Energy Transition Plans. These overarching plans serve as a foundational framework, informing and shaping all of the City's other master and development plans.

The recommendations from these climate plans have been systematically integrated into various municipal strategies and frameworks. This integration ensures that all planning documents, including the City's Active Transportation Plan, Bike Master Plan, Healthy City Strategy, Development Design Manual, Accessibility Plan, Water Master Plan, Urban Forest Plan, and several neighborhood level plans are aligned with the City's climate change objectives.

By embedding climate considerations into these plans, the City ensures a cohesive and unified approach to addressing climate-related challenges, enhancing resilience, and promoting sustainability across all aspects of urban development and infrastructure planning.
column17: Climate-related issues have significantly shaped the City of St. John's financial planning. Following the development of the Climate Change Adaptation and Mitigation and Energy Transition Plans, these frameworks have informed and guided all subsequent master and development plans. As a result, the City's financial plans are closely aligned with these overarching climate strategies. Recommendations from the climate plans are seamlessly integrated into the financial planning process, ensuring that resources are allocated to actions that support the City's climate priorities.\n\nThis alignment means that the City's budget reflects and prioritizes investments in climate-resilient infrastructure, sustainable development, and other climate-related initiatives. In the coming years, the City plans to undertake a study to evaluate the feasibility of a carbon budget. This study will focus specifically on financial strategies needed to achieve the City's climate targets. The insights gained will be incorporated into the City's financial planning, further ensuring that financial resources are effectively directed toward meeting climate goals and supporting long-term sustainability.
column18:
The transition to a low-carbon economy presents several risks to the City of St. John's, which need to be carefully managed:

Financial Risks: The shift towards low-carbon technologies and infrastructure can require significant upfront investment. There is a risk that the financial burden may exceed initial projections, impacting the City's budget and financial stability. Additionally, the transition may involve unforeseen costs related to retrofitting existing systems or developing new technologies.

Technical and Operational Risks: Implementing new technologies and systems can pose technical challenges. There may be operational disruptions or inefficiencies as new systems are implemented and older systems are phased out.

Regulatory and Policy Risks: Changes in regulations and policies at the provincial or federal levels can impact the feasibility and cost-effectiveness of the City's low-carbon initiatives. Uncertainty or shifts in policy direction could affect project timelines and funding.

Stakeholder and Community Risks: Engaging stakeholders and the community in the transition process is crucial. There is a risk that insufficient consultation or resistance from community members and businesses could hinder the implementation of low-carbon projects. Ensuring broad support and addressing concerns is essential for successful transition efforts.

Supply Chain Risks: The transition to a low-carbon economy may involve reliance on new materials, technologies, or expertise that could be subject to supply chain disruptions. Ensuring a stable supply of necessary components and services is critical for maintaining project timelines and budgets.

column15: The City of Little Rock's oversight lives between the Mayor's Office/Office of Executive Administration and the City's Sustainability Office. The Sustainability Office was created in 2008. Within the scope of the Sustainability Office is interfacing with the Sustainability Commission, made up of 15 residents who are appointed to advise the City on sustainability-related issues across City Government. Since being elected in 2018, Mayor Scott has made Sustainability a priority. As the Mayor often notes, Little Rock has seen the impact of climate change through historic floods in 2019, historic snowfall events in 2021/2022, a high-end EF-3 tornado in 2023, and record heat. Little Rock's temperature hit 107° in 2023 - the highest temperature on record since 2012. Much like equity issues, the current administration views sustainability as something that is only successful when it is integrated across the City government, not just within the Sustainability Office. As such, the Mayor's Team has kept a liaison between the Mayor's Office and the Sustainability Office, meeting monthly since 2019. This liaison role helps to keep the administration appraised of opportunities within Sustainability. Because of this close collaboration, Sustainability has been featured prominently in the Mayor's goals as outlined in the State of the City (SOTC) addresses in 2021, 2022, and 2023. In 2021, the SOTC outlined the creation of an energy reduction plan and an EV fleet and accompanying infrastructure by 2030. In 2022, the SOTC doubled down on its energy goals, committing to powering city operations with 100 percent clean energy by 2030. The 2022 SOTC also included increasing recycling by 10 percent across the City and within the City organization by the end of 2023. Finally, in the 2023 SOTC, the Mayor committed to completing a greenhouse gas inventory and formally adopting a Sustainability Action Plan by the end of the year.

column15: Our City Commission crafted a resolution declaring climate change a crisis in September 2021 and is provided briefings on the status of climate work . In 2022 the City Manager adopted (and City Commission affirmed) community-wide science-based targets - 62.8% per capita GHG reduction communitywide by 2030 from 2019 emissions, and 100% per capita GHG reduction by 2050 from 2019 emissions. In 2021 the Mayor's Energy Advisory Committee worked toward creating a data-based target for municipal carbon emissions reduction goals, which the City Manager adopted (and City Commission affirmed) - a goal of 85% reduction by 2030 and 100% (carbon neutral) by 2040. Our commitment to addressing climate change is most prominently displayed within the Strategic Plan. The desired outcome of this priority is that the health of all people and the environment are advocated for, protected and enhanced. The first objective under this priority is to reduce carbon emissions, support climate adaptation and increase climate resiliency. Strategies within this objective include: Increase the knowledge, awareness and understanding of climate change among staff, partners, community stakeholders and residents; enhance collaboration with partners on strategies and actions to address climate change; reduce carbon/greenhouse gas emissions from City operations (buildings, utilities and fleet); create and support programs and policies to reduce carbon/greenhouse gas emissions from the building, transportation and other key sectors throughout the community; and create and begin implementing a Climate Action and Adaptation Plan (CAAP) in partnership with the community that works in parallel with and compliments the new Community Master Plan. column16:
The City of Grand Rapids adopted a Community Master Plan in November 2024. A Community Master Plan Steering Committee was established and included local climate justice advocates. The second round of community engagement (Summer 2023) focused on feedback sessions on both environmental justice and climate change. 
The 2024 Community Master Plan identified Sustainability as one of the City's six core values. As written in the plan, it is stated that The climate change crisis is one of the City's top concerns. While the City of Grand Rapids has been a leader in environmental sustainability, the impacts of climate change are being felt in Grand Rapids. To avoid the worst impacts, it's necessary to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and plan for known changes and increased extreme weather
The following chapters, with corresponding objectives and recommendations, are included in the 2024 Community Master Plan:
•	Design and maintain streets that are safe for all road users; Support viable transportation options that are affordable and accessible; Coordinate land use and transportation decisions.
•	Ensure an equitable distribution of public parks and recreational facilities.
•	Accommodate natural parks or park-like settings and preserve identified open space land and uses from development pressures, including the Grand River and other environmental areas.
•	Consider modes of travel other than cars in the development review and approval process.
•	Ensure new developments maintain walkable and bikeable roadway networks with appropriate access to transit.
•	Support programs and funding sources that promote the use of green infrastructure. Expand public education on the benefits of rain gardens, native plants, infiltration basins, rain barrels, and vegetation for stormwater management.
•	Promote native plant use in home landscapes. Consider adoption of a Landscape Manual, referenced within the Zoning Ordinance, to capture evolving best practices and provide guidance for projects subject to landscaping standards. Evaluate recommended plantings and include plants that are suited for warmer climates, to account for the changing climate. Identify opportunities to promote technical assistance.
•	Support implementation of the Climate Action and Adaptation Plan (CAAP). Participate fully in the actions recommended by the Climate Action and Adaptation Plan, including the subsequent implementation plan. Use the science based targets established when evaluating updates to the CMP.
•	Continue to work towards the City's 40% tree canopy goal. Trees help to offset the impact of greenhouse gases, provide shade, minimize the urban heat island effect, and contribute to a more comfortable walking environment.
•	Support facilities that locally generate and distribute energy. Support a distributed model for renewable energy production and distribution. Work with utility providers to address the need for and inclusion of on-site solar and wind production, bio-digestion, microgrid and neighborhood-based storage and distribution, electric vehicle charging stations (public and privately located), and similar measures as the renewable energy landscape continues to evolve.
•	Improve accessibility to fresh foods throughout the community, with a focus on food deserts and economically challenged neighborhoods. Promote full-service grocery stores that will increase access to fresh and affordable food in neighborhoods with less access. The zoning code should be reviewed, and amendments considered, that reduce upfront development costs and encourage local neighborhood-based businesses that can address food desert needs.
•	Continue to support community gardens and promote an edible landscape. The Energy & Sustainability Framework is Regina's plan to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions and sourcing net-zero energy from renewable sources for the community of Regina by 2050. This mitigation plan was approved by City Council in March of 2022. Following the adoption of the Framework, Administration moved from a planning and development phase to an implementation phase. The Sustainable Energy & Adaptation (SE&A) department was created in October 2022 to advance this work for the City and the community. This new department provides leadership and support all areas within the organization. SE&A tailors its approach based on what is required by each service area.In service areas where programs and policies don't exist, the SE&A team leads the development of policies and programs. Examples of work that the group is leading includes the idle reduction program, the development of the Energy & GHG Inventory and in the development of a Green Building policy.Some service areas have more mature policies and programs related to sustainability and GHG reduction. For these groups SE&A provides a support role by conducting reviews for best practices, calculating GHG emissions and coordinating work as required. Examples of this work include review of climate lens assessments for grant applications and participating in building designs for City facilities.

Oversight also extends to climate adaptation through Regina's Corporate Climate Adaptation Strategy (2025), which identifies the City's exposure to climate-related risks such as extreme heat, severe storms, flooding, drought, and wildfire. This Strategy provides a structured risk assessment process and prioritizes actions to ensure City services and infrastructure remain resilient to changing climate conditions. Climate adaptation has influenced planning by embedding climate risk considerations into corporate decision-making, asset management, and long-term service delivery planning.

By integrating both mitigation and adaptation into oversight, the City ensures that climate-related risks and opportunities are systematically considered in corporate planning, policy development, and capital investment decisions. This dual focus supports Regina's broader goal of building a climate-resilient and net-zero community.

column15: City Council set its first emissions goals in 2008 (renewed in 2019), adopted its first Energy & Sustainability Work Plan in 2011, and formed an Office of Sustainability in 2012. Today, the Director and Office of Sustainability manages climate-related programs across the City, including data and reporting, stakeholder engagement and priority-setting, and capital projects related to climate change mitigation and adaptation. The most recent Energy & Sustainability Work Plan (2021) was informed by input from the Mayor's Climate Council and guides citywide activities to lower emissions and combat climate change based on our GHG emission inventories and community priorities. The Office of Sustainability directly oversees multiple activities to reduce the City's operational footprint, while also exploring opportunities to influence reductions across the community.
column16:
Planning efforts for the City are led by the joint Knoxville-Knox County Planning agency and directed by a Metropolitan Planning Commission. The City and Knox Planning have partnered closely to administer Knoxville's Climate Pollution Reduction Grant, which is the first-ever climate action planning process undertaken for the 9-county MSA. 

The City adopted its most recent master plan (Knoxville-Knox County General Plan 2033) in 2003 as the official 30-year comprehensive plan for the City and County. While the Plan does not specifically address climate change, it does address many related causes and outcomes: reducing traffic congestion, prioritizing compact development, increasing use of public transit and alternate transportation, promoting alternative fuels, preserving natural landscapes, requiring development to minimize water runoff/pollution, etc. Action proposals include expanding a 'Smart Trips' program to reduce traffic congestion and improve air quality; incorporating multimodal design and mixed-use development in major corridors; conserving natural areas to preserve environmental quality; and connecting greenway trails. 

The 2033 General Plan is complemented by specialized plans addressing localized areas and sectors (for example, a Long Range Regional Mobility Plan, Tree Plan, and One Year Development Plan) as well as a Multi-Jurisdiction Hazard Mitigation Plan.
column17: The City has incorporated climate mitigation into limited elements of internal financial planning. For example, the City created a Sustainable Innovation Fund in 2020 to fund capital solutions that reduce energy consumption across municipal operations, which allows departments to consider efficiency in addition to cost when planning equipment replacement and facility upgrades.
column18:
The City has made several major commitments to reducing the climate impact of our own operations, including setting emission reductions goals, joining programs like the Department of Energy's Better Buildings Challenge and Better Climate Challenge, funding energy-efficiency and lower-carbon upgrades on municipal facilities, and expanding fleet and transit EVs. 

Decarbonizing the wider community remains a significant challenge. Mitigation strategies such as natural gas disincentives, stretch building codes, and EV- or solar-ready ordinances have been made difficult by legislative pre-emption and public opposition. The monopoly of public power utilities and relatively low cost of fossil fuels has also limited grid decarbonization, although TVA's Valley Pathways Study of 2023 developed a roadmap to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050. 

However, the Knoxville region is home to some of the country's climate leaders, which represents a significant economic opportunity. Tennessee Valley Authority, the largest public energy provider in the U.S., is headquartered in Knoxville. Oak Ridge National Lab leads global research on clean energy, building science, advanced manufacturing, and more. The University of Tennessee is home to several initiatives related to climate, and is the largest university in the state.
Organizations such as the Tennessee Advanced Energy Business Council have formed to take advantage of this economic cluster.

column15: Greater Sudbury's Community Energy and Emissions Plan (CEEP) was developed to respond to City Council's 2019 Climate Emergency declaration. The program uses energy, emissions, land-use, and financial modelling to determine the community-wide efforts required to meet a 2050 net-zero emissions target (a reduction of 1.6 million tonnes of emissions by 2050). CEEP was designed according to 3 key concepts: the reduce-improve-switch paradigm, community energy planning prioritization, and infrastructure, mechanical, and energy systems turnover. The CEEP has been informed by a collection of past City efforts and policy documents, helping to establish goals and objectives for Greater Sudbury's environmental and sustainability performance: Strategic documents (Community Economic Development Strategic Plan; Downtown Community Improvement Plan)- Ecosystems and Sustainability Focus ( EarthCare Sudbury Local Action Plan (2010); Greater Sudbury Biodiversity Action Plan (2009) )- Transportation Focus (Transportation Master Plan (2016); Transportation Demand Management Plan (2018); Complete Streets Policy (2018); Transit Action Plan (2019) )- Water, Wastewater, and Waste Focus ( Facilities Master Plan; Water and Wastewater Master Plan)- Energy and Emissions Focus ( Strategic Energy Plan (1995); Partners in Climate Protection Program (1995); Efficient Sudbury campaign (2006); Community energy plan discussions led by Greater Sudbury Utilities (2013-2015) )) *****The Greater Sudbury Community Climate Change Adaptation Plan (CCCAP) aims to provide guidance and recommendations for the City, homeowners, property owners, businesses and the entire community. It is a comprehensive, long-term plan to improve resiliency and growth in the community. By planning for climate change, Greater Sudbury can better adapt and bounce back after a crisis or disaster. This Plan took a community-engaged approach, guided by municipal administration. Climate actions presented in this plan were co-developed using the knowledge and experience of multiple municipal staff, residents, community groups and organizations. The intent of this plan is to help organizations, institutions, businesses, vulnerable populations, and individuals of all ages adapt to current and future climate-related risks and opportunities. Although the City of Greater Sudbury administration is the lead actor for many actions outlined in the Plan, numerous climate-related risks extend beyond municipal jurisdiction, requiring the collaboration of important community service providers, local partnerships and other levels of government*****The City of Greater Sudbury completes studies to assess the health and make recommendations for the care of several area watersheds with financial support through the Ontario Ministry of Environment and Climate Change. The studies seek feedback from local residents on findings and proposed mitigation strategies. All public comments will be compiled and considered to develop recommendations for best management practices to reduce erosion, prevent flooding and improve water quality. The Stormwater Master Plan, including several sub-watershed studies, also demonstrates how climate change affects the future planning of the community. *****The City of Greater Sudbury participated in ICLEI Canada's Train-the-Trainer Initiative of the Great Lakes Climate Change Adaptation Project and performed a risk and vulnerability assessment in 2017 to determine and prioritize climate impacts. City staff developed a large list of impact statement which are concise sentences that outline locally relevant climatic changes expected to occur, and how they will affect the municipality. This initial list of over 80 impact statements was presented to several municipal departments as well as staff at Conservation Sudbury and Public Health Sudbury & District. Based on responses, City staff reduced the list to under 40 impact statements to be presented for a public Risk and Vulnerability Assessment workshop, with the intention to prioritize climate change adaptation efforts\nSince the completion of the CEEP, CCCAP, and Risk and Vulnerability Assessment, the City has completed a Sustainable Waste Strategy and an Urban Tree Master Plan. Additionally, in November 2024, City Council directed staff to provide a) a report itemizing the current City fleet of low-emissions vehicles, and outlining multiple scenarios for increasing the number of low-emissions vehicles over the next 10 years, with short-, medium-, and long-term goals, anticipated investments, cost efficiencies, and payback periods; and b) recommendations for the development of an agreement with reputable third-party providers to increase the number of pay-to-use public EV chargers at City-owned parking facilities, at little to no additional cost to the City.
column16: The City of Greater Sudbury has passed a resolution that all reports presented to Council or Committees of Council include content which describes how the recommendation or information aligns with the climate goals and where appropriate the impact on greenhouse gas emissions. The City of Greater Sudbury Official Plan helps guide Greater Sudbury's development and land use. The Official Plan introduces a watershed-based approach to planning. It provides land use policies which protect our natural resources to support long-term economic growth, including mining, aggregate and agricultural lands. The Plan also recognizes and includes policies that support climate change mitigation and adaptation.
column17: The City has a climate lens for all reports going to Council for decision that shows alignment of the project to climate change. The City has a scoring system for the capital budget that includes a section for climate change. The City is in the initial phases of planning the creation of a Sustainable Procurement Working group that will look at environmental, economic, and social considerations for purchasing.
column18:
There has been a noticeable shift in climate change awareness and in the sense of urgency for action over the course of CEEP's project engagement events, as evidenced by a citizens' petition to declare a municipal climate emergency, and the adoption of that declaration by council. Engagement of various groups and individuals over the course of the project has shown that there are legitimate concerns in how policy and action will be successfully implemented given a range of challenges. Potential concerns outlined by stakeholders include : concerns around the transition to personal electric vehicles such as potential regulations and a lack of charging infrastructure; funding for infrastructure maintenance without the gas tax; political priorities; Manufacturing retooling; battery technology; disinformation campaigns' grid capacity - transformer upgrades required in areas that add EVS; the need for commercial building retrofits and recommissioning; capital costs associated with the transition; an aging grid / system constraints, capacity of the grid; making maintenance a priority; the effect on taxes; poor building codes; a lack of local training opportunities for industries like engineering; successfully implementing changes to leased buildings because you need landlord and tenants to cooperate; the allocation of funding (i.e. the City takes money out of dense areas making it hard to upgrade centers for walking); snow and active transportation route accessibility; needing time to build new infrastructure; not having enough renewable energy storage;; aging infrastructure on roofs; a building code that supports renewable energy projects like solar; snow on solar panels; getting buy-in from the community to invest in and accept new technology; potential conditions or competing interests that might interfere with implementing this action.

Key economic sectors in the City of Greater Sudbury are Mining Supply and Services and Manufacturing and Industry. The City of Greater Sudbury is home to the largest integrated mining complex in the world. This industry employs 14,000 people and generates approximately $4 billion in annual exports. The manufacturing sector in Greater Sudbury has mostly grown out of the mining supply and service sector. Many manufacturers supply equipment, machinery and other machined industrial components to mining and supply service companies. There are more than 250 manufacturing companies in Greater Sudbury, that provide services and products globally. While a market shift towards renewable technology is increasing demand for minerals and metals, the climate transition risks include the implementation of climate policy and regulations, increasing costs of materials, and shifts in the types and availability of jobs in certain industries and markets. While the industrial sector continues to invest in renewable energy and technologies, they remain one of our largest emitters.

Other risks to the jurisdiction include not having the infrastructure to support a renewable energy transition and the costs associated with the transition to low-carbon technology. Additionally, as the impacts of climate change worsen the litigation risk and reputational risk associated with not meeting our climate goals is also increasing.

The City of Sunnyvale has multiple ongoing, completed, or planned projects with the goal of mitigating and adapting the community to the changing climate. Climate-related issues are taken seriously and are a core part of many of Sunnyvale's planning and development efforts. The City has published the Climate Action Playbook (CAP), which establishes measurable target goals, such as reducing communitywide emissions 56 percent below 1990 levels by 2030, and reports progress transparently through the public-facing Climate Action Scoreboard.

Adaptation initiatives are also central to Sunnyvale's approach. For example, Play 6.3 strengthens community resilience by updating emergency preparedness and response plans to address climate-related events such as heat waves, air quality episodes, and flooding. Similarly, Play 4.2 focuses on setting water reduction targets and ensuring the long-term resilience of Sunnyvale's water supply. The CAP also includes multiple measures to update and implement building codes to encourage all-electric new construction, support electrification of existing buildings, and reduce overall energy consumption.

Sunnyvale's adaptation and mitigation work is supported by the City's broader planning framework. The General Plan - Environmental Management Chapter establishes policies to protect natural resources, reduce pollution, and improve resilience to climate impacts, providing a comprehensive long-term foundation for sustainability across the community. In addition, the City's Area Specific Plans, including the El Camino Real Precise Plan, the Moffett Park Specific Plan, and the Village Centers Plan, embed climate-smart design, sustainable mobility, and green infrastructure into neighborhood-level development, ensuring that growth and redevelopment contribute to climate resilience.

The City of Peterborough added a full-time permanent Climate Change Coordinator position in January 2021. The coordinator's responsibilities include advancing climate action objectives outlined in the 2016 Climate Change Action Plan, conducting GHG accounting for community and corporate sources, and communicating climate change actions to the senior leadership team, committees, and City Council. The Climate Change Coordinator resides in the Asset Management & Capital Planning division, which oversees a wider portfolio of staff responsibilities that target adaptation, such as stormwater sewer resilience, community flooding adaptation measures and planning, asset management, and sustainable transportation. In 2024, a new position, the Climate Change Project Manager, was created that is dedicated to overseeing community and corporate climate action projects. 

The City currently considers the implications of adaptation and mitigation during new construction and existing building renovations. This has manifested in the construction of a net-zero fire station built from reclaimed wood, with mitigation features like solar PV and ground source heat pumps and adaptation features like bioswales. The City completed an extensive decarbonization study of the top nine energy consuming facilities to determine the pathway to decrease emissions that will be considered during annual budgets at end of life of equipment. Lastly, to further support climate-related issues being elevated across the corporation, a climate lens has been incorporated into the first stage of the corporate procurement process to flag opportunities or climate risks for projects early on in bid & tender development. 

The City also reports monthly to the Peterborough Environmental Advisory Committee (PEAC) comprised of community members with environmental expertise, with City Council representation. The PEAC receives monthly climate initiatives update reports chronicling the advancement of community and corporate climate action projects instigated by the City. The committee also receives presentations of projects from city staff who are seeking input from committee members to inform their bodies of work. Finally, staff write reports to Council that include annual corporate and community GHG reporting and the impacts of climate action projects to date. column16: The City of Boulder continuously works to provide service excellence for an inspired future through the city's guiding document, the Sustainability, Equity, and Resilience (SER) Framework, which guides budgeting and planning processes for the Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan, City Strategic Plan and for all city departmental strategic plans. The framework outlines seven overarching goals and 36 specific objectives that advance these goals. The framework provides consistent goals necessary to achieve Boulder's vision of a great community and the actions required to achieve them, including goals specific to climate change, as referenced in the Environmentally Sustainable section. These goals are further defined in the city's Comprehensive Plan in Section 3 and Section 4. The goals and targets are further integrated into all other city-wide-master plans and subcommunity plans. A staff representative from the city's Climate Initiatives Department serves on the city's Strategic Planning Coordination Committee. The City of Boulder has taken steps to shift from a traditional emergency management preparation and recovery posture to one of prevention, resilience and sustainability. This shift builds upon lessons learned during and after the 2013 floods, seeks systemic change to foundational processes of government, and complements other city initiatives—including open data and performance measurement—that are focused on high-performance government, data-informed decision-making, and operational effectiveness and efficiency. As part of the 100 Resilient Cities network, Boulder released a comprehensive citywide resilience strategy in April 2016. Since then, Boulder has been aiming to institutionalize resilience, including identifying budgeting for resilience as one of its core 'frontier' areas of action. In 2017, Boulder hosted two workshops—Realizing the Resilience Dividend: Budgeting for Resilience and Innovative Finance for Resilience—and participated in the inaugural global cohort of cities deploying the City Resilience Index. 

In 2022, the City of Boulder updated its Sustainability and Resilience Framework to include Equity, which positions the city to support its communities to rebound from, positively adapt to, and thrive amidst changing conditions. The framework is intended to guide budgeting and planning processes by outlining several outcomes necessary for Boulder's vision of a great community. The city is using the Sustainability, Equity, and Resilience (SER) Framework as a key planning and budgeting tool to provide consistent, shared goals that help the city achieve Boulder's vision of building a more resilient and equitable community. Since 2022, the city worked to implement an enhanced budgeting approach using outcomes and performance measures to guide budget development, called Budgeting for Resilience and Equity (BRE). As part of this new budgeting approach, BRE identifies and incorporates performance measures to program outcomes, heightens strategic and data-informed decision-making, and increases the transparency of the development of the annual budget and investments as they align with community goals. In addition, the recently adopted Citywide Strategic Plan was developed to align with the SER Framework goals. The Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan, Department Strategic Plans, and Subcommunity or Area Plans are also developed to align with and support the achievement of the outcomes of the SER Framework.

The City of Boulder has included climate and sustainability issues in its budgeting for years. Boulder's original 2006 Climate Action Plan (CAP) Tax was the nation's first voter-approved tax dedicated to addressing climate change. In November of 2022, voters approved the most recent update to the CAP tax that provides long-term climate and resilience funding for the community. The updated tax is in effect until 2040 and funds ongoing programs and new projects that confront the climate crisis and strengthen the wellbeing of everyone in our community. The Climate Tax, which is collected on customer electricity and natural gas bills, funds city-level climate resilience efforts that center equity and work toward systems change in and beyond Boulder. Boulder voters have also given the city authority to borrow against the Climate Tax. This option, called “bonding authority,” will allow the city to accelerate investment in climate action and wildfire resilience by issuing debt that would be repaid with future Climate Tax revenues. Boulder's zero waste efforts are funded by a separate 1994 voter-approved ballot initiative that charges a tax on residential and commercial waste. The trash tax is an occupation tax on trash haulers serving customers within the city limits and helps fund waste reduction in Boulder. Over the years, the trash tax has funded a variety of waste reduction activities including: curbside compost collection; the switch to single-stream recycling; a portion of the new Hazardous Materials Management Facility; and the purchase of land and buildings at 6400 Arapahoe Avenue to house Eco-Cycle offices, the Center for Hard-to-Recycle Materials (CHaRM), and the Center for ReSource Conservation used building materials donation and sales yard.

Our jurisdiction has formally adopted goals to achieve carbon neutrality by 2035. Types of risk associated with this transition include financial, land use, equity, local economy, supply chain, and local control. 
•	Financial: Regionally and locally, extensive investment has been made in legacy infrastructure. There will likely be a range of stranded assets and challenges associated with retrofitting buildings as well as replacing vehicles. 
•	Land-use: Investing in a low-carbon economy will require focused effort to preserve open space and urban greenways, and end or reverse the current trend of tree canopy loss, while also ensuring improving housing access and affordability. Tradeoffs on land use can be necessary to manage competing priorities.
•	Equity: The affordability of low-carbon solutions, increasing costs of maintaining legacy systems, and power to make low-carbon choices (e.g., renters) will have disproportionate impacts on our most vulnerable communities. Energy cost burden has a disproportionate impact on vulnerable populations. Aggressive building decarbonization will shift the costs of maintaining stranded gas infrastructure to those who lack the capacity to themselves decarbonize. Underrepresentation in the decision-making process can also lead to a lack of understanding of how the consequences will fall evenly on our community. 
•	Local Economy: The impacts of a low-carbon transition don't immediately imply a just transition. Some community members work in legacy industries (e.g., oil & gas, combustion engine transit) who will feel the impacts of the transition. 
•	Supply Chain: The City of Boulder may experience the impacts of a global transition in the ability to acquire the needed technological solutions. 
•	Local Control: The city is not in control of all its systems (e.g., energy systems), making it challenging to affect the transitions needed.
•	Litigation: Those with interests in preserving the status quo will challenge regulations that are intended to support the transition. Litigation can slow and even potentially halt progress. Risk of litigation can have a chilling effect on regulators.
•	Federal Policy: Recent federal policy changes seek to preserve and even increase reliance on fossil fuel resources. Elimination of tax incentives for clean energy solutions may slow progress. Reduced federal investment in critical services places a strain on state and local investments that could otherwise be directed towards climate mitigation and adaptation.

column15: The concept of sustainability guides city policy. Santa Monica is committed to meeting its existing needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. The long-term impacts of policy choices will be considered to ensure a sustainable legacy. In 1994, the City of Santa Monica become a leader and early adopter by developing one of the first Sustainable City Plans in the nation. The comprehensive framework guides city decision makers to protect, preserve, and restore the natural environment. City decision-making will be guided by a mandate to maximize environmental benefits and reduce or eliminate negative environmental impacts. Sustainability is considered at all levels of government. The City of Santa Monica has a Council-adopted Climate Action & Adaptation Plan, EV Action Plan, Zero Waste Strategic Plan, Bike Action Plan, Pedestrian Action Plan, as well as internal policies called \'Administrative Instructions.\' Administrative Instructions include Green Building, Sustainable Fleet, Procurement, and Integrated Pest Management. This commission has an Electric Vehicle subcommittee as well. The City partners with local non-profit organizations and community based organizations to advance environmental awareness and advocacy. column15: In September 2018, the City Council established its first community-wide greenhouse gas emissions target and created a Climate Action and Adaptation Plan to develop strategies to achieve emissions reductions. In August 2019, the Council declared a Climate Crisis and approved new emissions goals in accordance with those set by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC): reduce carbon emissions by 45% from 2010 levels by 2030, then achieve net-zero carbon emissions by 2050. Community and Municipal Operations greenhouse gas inventories have been completed for the year 2015, and will be updated going forward on a regular basis to track progress of greenhouse gas emissions reductions. Additionally, a consumption-based greenhouse gas inventory has been completed for the Iowa City Community using the EcoCity Footprint Tool. Historical timeline: - Covenant of Mayors In February 2016, Mayor Throgmorton signed on to the Covenant of Mayors, formerly Compact of Mayors, the world's largest cooperative effort among mayors and city leaders to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. - In December 2016, Council approved a resolution setting a community-wide greenhouse gas reduction goal of 25-28% for the year 2025, and 80% by 2050. At the time of the commitment, this was the target the U.S. had committed to in the Paris Agreement. After the U.S. pulled out of the agreement this year, numerous cities across the country chose to uphold the commitment and targets. - In December 2017, along with over 60 other mayors, Mayor Throgmorton signed the Chicago Climate Charter specifically identifying our emissions reduction goals. - In January 2017, Council approved a resolution creating the Climate Action Steering Committee. Five of the members serve at-large and were selected by Council. The Committee is tasked with assisting the consultant selected to develop the City's first Climate Action and Adaptation Plan, which will address emissions reduction. - Sept. 2018: The completed Climate Action and Adaptation Plan was adopted by City Council. - Sept 2019: City Council declared a Climate Crisis and accelerated emissions reduction goals.

The City has awarded grants for renewable energy projects, namely rooftop solar. The City has awarded grants for zero emission transportation, including both electric vehicles and EVSE. The City has awarded grants for carbon capture, ranging from specialized equipment to capture, store and reuse carbon dioxide from the beer fermentation process, to a prairie planting project. The City has also budgeted for preparing for future severe weather events, including flooding, high winds, and tornadoes. As the City transitions the municipal fleet to electric vehicles, we expect operating costs of both the transit and general equipment fleets to decrease over time.

This will expand the job base of the local renewable energy field, bringing locally-made photovoltaic cells to local residences and businesses. As renewable energy continues to expand within Iowa City and the state of Iowa, it is expected that more workers will be attracted to this growing industry.
