The City of Flagstaff's oversight of climate-related issues is woven into the fabric of the organization. The City has a dedicated Sustainability Division comprised of 11 permanent staff and is supported by two grant-funded positions and seven AmeriCorps members. Additionally, the City has a Sustainability Commission with seven community representatives appointed by the City Council, an Equity Climate Advisory Committee, and Youth Climate Advisory Committee to inform, provide feedback, and advise on climate-related issues. 

This submittal will frequently reference multiple major plans that explicitly focus on climate-related issues or have sections within that do so, including: The Climate Action and Adaptation Plan (CAAP) from 2018 The Carbon Neutrality Plan (CNP) adopted by Council in 2021 and updated in 2022 to incorporate the goals and initiatives of Flagstaff 10-year Housing Plan and consolidate the Climate Action and Adaption Plan into the Carbon Neutrality Plan, and c) The Flagstaff Regional Plan: first ratified by voters in 2014, updated in 2022 to reflect the goals in the Carbon Neutrality Plan, and revised in 2024 to address the City's declared climate and housing emergencies. While the 2018 CAAP and 2022 CNP are Council adopted plans, the Regional Plan is a voter approved initiative and document. 

Additionally, City Council declared a Climate Emergency in June 2020. Staff provide biannual Carbon Neutrality Plan updates to Council, in addition to regular appearances for specific projects. Since 2020, the annual budget process for all departments across the City organization has incorporated fields inquiring if/how the funding requests support the Carbon Neutrality Plan. If applicable, funding requests link to specific strategies in these plans, as well as making the case that they support mitigation, adaptation, or equity.
column16: In January of 2020, the Flagstaff community brought forth a Resolution and spent hours making the case to the City Council in favor of formally declaring a Climate Emergency. In this Resolution the community sited numerous international reports (2018 IPCC 1.5 report; 2019 UN GAP report) in addition to local vulnerabilities including drought, fire, water security, etc. Indeed, after passage of the 2018 Climate Action and Adaptation Plan, Flagstaff experienced the Museum Fire (2019) which burned over 1,900 acres, leaving a scar that has resulted, and will continue to cause for years to come, severe community flooding during seasonal monsoon weather patterns. This was followed by the Rafael and Slate fires in 2021, as well as the Tunnel, Pipeline and Hayward fires in 2022 that have all had significant impacts on the community. This combination of frequent proximal wildfire and systemic community flooding has had major impacts on the emergency response, planning and development within the jurisdiction. In 2022, the City revised the Regional Plan to incorporate key elements of the Carbon Neutrality Plan, ensuring that the mitigation, resilience and equity goals of the Carbon Neutrality Plan were incorporated into the Flagstaff Regional Plan. In 2024, the City drafted an update to the Regional Plan, which provides planning out to 2045, with a prominent focus on preparing for the uncertainties and opportunities climate change presents.
column17: Large wildfires have contributed to a \'new normal\' state of systemic urban flooding during seasonal monsoon weather patterns. This flooding has required increased emergency response funding, both from the City as well as Coconino County (which manages Emergency Response and receives funding from State and Federal sources). Furthermore, in November 2022, residents approved municipal bond funding including investments of $57 million in local wildfire suppression, stormwater flood mitigation and wastewater treatment infrastructure and $20 million in general bonds to support affordable housing. Additionally, the City received directed federal funding through the American Rescue Plan Act and anticipates additional funding (Bipartisan Infrastructure, Omnibus Community Directed Funds) which are being directed to a) bolster existing programs, b) stand up new programs to help address climate-related issues. For the fiscal year 2025-2026, City Council approved $100,000 to support a pilot program for residential home hardening to increase resilience to wildfires.
column18: The main risk identified is working to ensure a just and equitable transition. One of the three overarching goals established by the Carbon Neutrality Plan (CNP) is to address climate change in a manner that prioritizes those most impacted and ensures that the costs and benefits of climate adaptation and mitigation are equitably distributed. Towards this end, the CNP identifies Targeted Universalism as well as outlines four strategies within a dedicated Equitable Systems Target Area. Still, it is acknowledged that past and current systems have contributed to the present state of deep and growing inequity, and that the transition to a low-carbon economy could either be an opportunity to address those issues or contribute to a tide that exacerbates them.

column15: The City of Asheville's City Council has adopted numerous goals and resolutions related to climate issues including: (100% renewable energy goal for municipal operations, Climate Emergency Declaration & Climate Justice Initiative, 4% Carbon reduction goal, Food Policy Action Plan and engagement with Buncombe County's 100% Community-wide renewable energy goal. In 2023 the City adopted a Municipal Climate Action Plan (MCAP) an update to the 2009 Sustainability Management Plan. This will be a guiding document to prioritize and drive climate-related activity. In 2022 the City of Asheville completed its first year utilizing Climate Justice Screening tools and data maps to inform organizational work planning activities. Following destruction from Hurricane Helene, resilience and climate adaptation considerations are being integrated in the rebuild projects to the extent possible for use of Federal funding from FEMA.
column16: Sustainability initiatives are a key component in Living Asheville, the City of Asheville's Comprehensive Plan. Climate and sustainability are woven throughout the themes of A Livable Built Environment, A Resilient Economy, Harmony with Natural Environment, a Healthy Community. Goals included in Harmony with the Natural Environment include Mitigate Flooding and Erosion, Protect land and Water Assets, Implement Green Infrastructure and Enhance the Urban Tree Canopy, Reduce Waste Production, Energy Use, Water Use and Light Pollution, Encourage Naturalized Stormwater Management Techniques, Implement Green Building Programs and Encourage the use of Alternative and Clean Energy Systems. Following Hurricane Helene, Asheville City Council approved floodplain zoning changes to ensure compliance with federally backed flood insurance programs, and to reduce future flood risks.
column17: As the City of Asheville's Sustainability Department has grown and evolved Sustainability and Resilience have become more deeply embraced and interwoven with overall city operations, decision making and resource allocation. in 2021 the Office was elevated to a full Department providing leadership staff better access to City management and decision making. One example of this is the incorporation of sustainability and climate-related issues during the Capitol Projects planning process to better allocate necessary upfront resources to budget for necessary higher up front costs and better articulate long term cost avoidance and savings through capitol investments. A second example is the utilization of Climate Justice and Climate Data Map tools for departmental and organizational work planning. The City is also pursuing Helene recovery projects that enhance resilience at multiple levels and is working to incorporate a climate relevant scoring rubric that can be used to iteratively evaluate capital and organization work plan projects to enhance climate relevant aspects of projects.
column18: Our primary risks are high upfront costs and challenges implementing interdepartmental research and planning dedicated to strategic investments in buildings and city-owned infrastructure projects.

column15: The City of Dubuque has a Sustainability Department which oversees climate-related issues. Sustainable Dubuque is a holistic approach to long-term quality of life which addresses environmental and ecological integrity, economic prosperity, and social and cultural vibrancy. The 12 key principles that guide the community's path to a more sustainable future include regional economy, smart energy use, resource management, community design, green buildings, healthy local foods, community knowledge, reasonable mobility, healthy air, clean water, and native plants and animals. Becoming a more sustainable city is one of the top priorities for the Mayor and City Council. Sustainable Dubuque strives for a more resilient and equitable community through community engagement, preparation, education, planning, partnering, and growth. The City of Dubuque has a Climate Action and Resiliency Plan that aims to reduce 50% of emissions by 2030 and a Climate Vulnerability Assessment which looks at future climate changes and vulnerabilities for the City of Dubuque. The Climate Action Plan (CAP), \'50% by 2030,\' was adopted in 2013 and updated in 2020. It is a non-binding, voluntary effort to identify opportunities to reduce Dubuque's community greenhouse gas emissions. It can be used to inform officials during goal-setting and budget decisions, inform businesses and individuals about potential emission and cost-saving options, showcase success stories, provide a roadmap that can be added to or adjusted, and expose from where Dubuque's GHG emissions really come. Additionally, Dubuque's City Council adopted the Dubuque Greenhouse Gas Inventory in 2010 which measures gases emitted by City operations and predicts future emissions if we continue our current ways. This gives the City a tool to set emission reduction targets to improve and maintain healthy air quality. Furthermore, the City of Dubuque has adopted an Environmental and Sustainability Commitment for the Municipal Services Center to evaluate operations and setting goals to lessen the negative impact on the environment in sectors such as electricity and natural gas consumption, stormwater management, small container management, de-icer materials handling, and fuel delivery and spill cleanup. The City of Dubuque also works with Green Iowa AmeriCorps in order to empower communities and school districts to make more environmental, conservation-minded decisions and improvements. Lastly, the City of Dubuque has a Resilient Community Advisory Commission which reviews research and data in order to provide input on re-identification, prevention, and plans for potential economic, environmental, and social/cultural vulnerabilities, reviews plans for long-term prevention, preparedness, and recovery efforts, reviews policy and program recommendations to the City Council in order to influence resilient outcomes for the community, provides comment to the City Council on the allocation of budgeted city funding to achieve adopted resiliency goals, educates and engages the public on commission priorities, provides input on and reviews strategies to address identified vulnerabilities in collaboration with city staff, other city commissions, and community partners, reviews and makes recommendations regarding Sustainable Dubuque Community Grant allocations, respects the policy making authority of the City Council, the City Manager's responsibilities to implement the goals and priorities the council establishes and the responsibility of city staff to report to the City Manager, and ensures coordination and communication with other commissions.
column16: In 2017, the City of Dubuque adopted a comprehensive plan, \'Imagine Dubuque 2037: A Call to Action,\' which addresses climate-related issues in terms of master/development planning. This plan serves as a policy guide for the community's physical, social, and economic development, and the goal is to create a more viable, livable, and equitable community. Sector 4 of the plan, Environmental Integrity, recognizes clean water, healthy air, and conservation of native plants and animals as the key principles. Environmental key focus areas identified include expanded, sustainable stormwater management practices, implement the Climate Action and Resiliency Plan, promote a healthy urban forest and native plantings, implement the Catfish Creek and Bee Branch Watershed Management Plans, increase eco-education programming, particularly for children, expand programs to reduce, reuse, and recycle, including composting and building materials, and strive to become a zero waste economy. Partnerships and collaboration will be key to implementing sustainable environment recommendations such as all of the key focus areas listed above in addition to supporting mobile air quality monitoring, continuing healthy homes strategies, implementing a comprehensive tree management program, increasing native plants, pollinator, and edible landscaping, and conserving natural areas . Since urban development and agricultural practices impact water quality, the City of Dubuque plans to create partnerships with private landowners, developers, citizens, and other local governments to identify and develop potential control measures, promote expanded infiltration through use of deep-rooted native plantings, and ensure that new developments meet applicable standards for water quality. Watershed projects, like the Bee Branch Watershed Stormwater Management, are underway to subdue flooding and improve water quality. Additionally, the Bee Branch Watershed Flood Mitigation Project incorporates permeable pavement, retention basins, daylighting, and resiliency efforts of storm drains. Between 2014-2017, the City of Dubuque constructed 80 green alleys that allow for ground water infiltration after storms. Because of the large swaths of rural and agricultural lands near Dubuque, protecting surface water quality is a priority. The Catfish Creek Watershed Management Authority is managing practices such as bio-retention, rain gardens, vegetated swales, soil quality restoration, rural sediment discharge, and wetland enhancements/establishments. In terms of clean air and energy, the Dubuque Energy District is an initiative in-progress which strives to implement clean energy efficiency measures and support local renewable energy. This initiative aims to reduce/eliminate methane gas emission and divert organic materials from the landfill, evaluate and implement cost-effective renewable energy sources, improve travel efficiency and enhance non-auto modes of travel such as public transit, walking, and biking, and promote efficient lighting and green building techniques. The City is working to develop a Comprehensive Tree Management Plan which will help clean air, manage stormwater, and reduce temperatures. Dubuque Trees Forever is currently hosting tree planting events and educating the community and the city has received a USDA Forestry Services grant to plant 5,280 new trees low income communities. In terms of land management, the City of Dubuque adopted an Environmental Restoration Management Plan for Eagle Point Park which will use rain gardens, infiltration basins, permeable surfaces, soil quality restoration, planting native vegetation, habitat restoration, and green infrastructure improvements. The City is also expanding composting by offering food scrap pickup which helps reduce methane emissions and landfill waste while creating natural fertilizer. The City of Dubuque will continue to implement the Climate Action Plan by focusing on waste reduction, transportation improvements, and energy efficiency of homes and businesses to achieve climate goals.
column17: According to the City of Dubuque's \'Climate Vulnerability Assessment,\' many of the strategies for increasing climate resilience can be done for little to no cost. For the projects with costs, funding for local climate adaptation and resilience will draw on a range of public and private financing. The City of Dubuque plans to fund these projects through federal grant funding, work through public/private partnerships, and/or fund project through local taxes. The Climate Vulnerability Assessment links many government entities and private foundations that offer resources to advance local adaptation and mitigation efforts including EPA Smart Growth Grants and Other Funding, Partnership for Sustainable Communities, FEMA Preparedness Grants, FEMA Hazard Mitigation Assistance (HMGP, PDM, and FMA), Clean Diesel Program, USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service (AMAP, CIG, CSP, and EQIP), Federal Funding Compendium for Urban Heat Adaptation, Tribal Climate Change Guide to Funding, Science, Programs and Adaptation Plans, Kresge Environment Program, Quadratec Cares 'Energize The Environment' Grant Program, Wildlife Conservation Society's Climate Adaptation Fund, Climate Solutions University, Open Space Institute Resilient Landscape Initiative. The City of Dubuque also utilizes many financial grants, incentives, and rebates for climate related issues such as the Clean Diesel Program which provides support for protects that protect human health and improve air quality by reducing emissions. \'Imagine Dubuque 2037: A Call to Action,\' also outlines climate-related issues in terms of financial planning. Natural disasters caused roughly $70 million in damages between 1999-2022, so the City of Dubuque has implemented and plans to implement more sustainable and green practices to mitigate climate related issues. The city is currently creating 240 green alleyways which are estimated at $57.4 million. The Comprehensive Housing Activities for Neighborhood Growth and Enrichment (CHANGE) plans to spend $19 million to revitalize older neighborhoods and improve quality of life. Dubuque's Lead Hazard Control and Healthy Homes Programs allocates $3.2 million of the US Department of Housing and Urban Development funding to households with environmental hazards. The Bee Branch Healthy Homes initiative has allotted $8.4 million in forgivable loans to flood-proof 320 flood-prone houses, mitigating mold, structural issues, and other hazards. Educational programming partners such as The National Mississippi River Museum and Aquarium, The Friends of the Mines of Spain, and The Bee Branch Beekeepers Initiative provide free days, funds, and opportunities that are cost-friendly to inform the community of climate-related risks. Additionally, Dubuque has achieved success with the Pay-As-You-Throw program which charges for additional waste pick up. This has increased recycling by 37% and decreased landfill refuse by 28%. Dubuque's Climate Action Plan (CAP) requests funding to incentivize a program for electrification of new and existing buildings which is in the works. The CAP wants to establish a policy to utilize tax increment financing to incentivize mitigation and adaptation actions and explore the creation of Community Development Finance program or institution to provide credit and financial services to underserved markets and population with focus on CAP. Some financial goals of the CAP are to develop new mechanisms for financing climate action work that account for equity and benefits, leverage existing financing pathways, develop new financing pathways, and create a local low income solar renewable energy credit market or 3rd party financing loan program. The 2021 City Council Goals and priorities include a sustainable environment which will preserve and enhance natural resources. Projects that are underway and budgeted and staff is implementing and providing updates to City Council consist of the Bee Branch pollinator celebration, emerald ash borer program, lead and copper rule compliance water sampling and testing, pollinator habitat in park system, public education on bikeable/walkable Dubuque, renew DBW solar program, sewer infrastructure asset management, and water and resource recovery center: nutrient trading. Projects that are underway and budgeted and staff is implementing and providing updates to city council include the Royal Wood Drive water tank improvement, SCADA overhaul: water, water lines extension- Southwest Arterial. Lastly, the Annual Comprehensive Financial Statement describes a master plan for Champlain Schmitt Island which will focus on environmental integrity. The landfill care is outlined with costs for environmental monitoring and cleanup, and grants from USDP and EPA for soil and water conservation, environmental quality incentives program, conservation stewardship program, and brownfield assessment and cleanup are listed.
column18: The City of Dubuque will experience many climate-related risks if we do not transition to a low-carbon economy. However, transitioning to a low-carbon economy does include some challenges. Some populations and individuals may be impeded from transitioning to a low-carbon economy because of socioeconomics, education level, physical/mental health issues, language barriers, job loss, etc. However, after the initial transition to a low-carbon economy, many of the risks will be solved. For example, job loss may happen at first, but by transitioning to a low-carbon economy, new jobs will be created. Additionally, economic losses or expenses many occur initially, too, but over time, money will be saved. According to Dubuque's CAP, the transition to renewable energy is a transition to local energy sources and infrastructure, and every dollar invested in solar will create $1.20 in local economic benefits.

column15:
Sustainability and climate action is integrated into all aspects of the City of Palo Alto. At the staff level, all Departments have sustainability goals laid out in the Sustainability and Climate Action Plan (S/CAP). The Office of Sustainability coordinates the sustainability and climate action work of the Departments, including the staff Sustainability Leadership Team, the Sustainability Steering Committee, and the Sustainability Communications Team. Committees and boards have overseen S/CAP development and implementation since 2021. Ad hoc committees in 2021-2022 oversaw the development of an updated S/CAP, followed by the Climate Protection Ad Hoc Committee formed in 2024 to accelerate the implementation of the Climate Action workplan items of the Three-Year S/CAP Workplan. The Climate Action & Sustainability Ad Hoc Committee (CASC) established in January 2025 is subject to the Brown Act, a California act that enforces standards for transparency in public committees. The three members of CASC are City Council members who to oversee and advise on implementation of the S/CAP. 

The Youth Climate Advisory Board (YCAB) established in August 2024 is an avenue for youth to provide their feedback on the City's sustainability initiatives and policies. YCAB also serves to strengthen the relationship between the City and local schools and promote the City's sustainability initiatives in local schools.

In addition, a Working Group was established in 2024 to draw on the expertise of community members. Working Group members commit to attending multiple meetings and to work on discrete projects outside of the meetings. The role of the working group is to provide feedback and discussion on proposed policies. The Working Group does not develop processes or request tasks be completed by staff or committees.
column16: Since 1991, the Palo Alto City Council, City Manager, and City of Palo Alto Departments have adopted policies, plans, ordinances, resolutions, and principles that have helped to increase the sustainability of Palo Alto and take action on climate change. The City of Palo Alto has integrated sustainability principles and climate action in the 2030 Comprehensive Plan. Annually determined City Council Priorities further reinforce the importance of addressing climate change throughout City operations as the Priorities guide how Departments allocate their resources and what they regularly report to Council. For the past 6 years, Council Priorities have includes a sustainability/climate change priority.
column17:
We must integrate climate-related risks into every aspect of our financial and capital planning because Palo Alto is located on the San Francisco Bay and has neighboring open spaces that could be vulnerable to wildfires, and because we own and operate our utilities including electricity, water supply, and wastewater treatment. It's essential that all new projects take into account critical factors such as sea level rise, drought, and increasingly severe weather events, as these elements have a direct influence on treatment volumes, operational costs, and ultimately, the rates our customers pay. 

Two examples at Palo Alto's Regional Water Quality Control Plant are illustrative of how climate change impacts planning. First, the horizontal levee pilot project is specifically designed to help combat some of the challenges posed by rising sea levels. Similarly, our advanced water purification project involves strategically elevating certain assets to account for Sea level rise and long-term resilience. These proactive adaptations not only ensure that we maintain reliable service for our community but also safeguard against the financial repercussions of climate change. By investing in these vital measures, we are committed to a sustainable future for this critical infrastructure, but climate change is one of the major driving factors that carries significant financial implications for every aspect of the plant.
column18:
Accomplishing Palo Alto's Sustainability & Climate Action Plan (S/CAP) is a top priority for the City to achieve its sustainability and climate change objectives. Electrification of services now powered by fossil fuel, including personal transportation, residential hot water, cooking and space heating, is core to S/CAP success; S/CAP outcomes needed by 2030 include: 85% of all Palo Alto new vehicle purchases are EVs, virtually all single-family gas appliances and virtually all commercial rooftop HVAC units are electrified, and significant additional multi-family and commercial building electrification. Delivering those energy services will require modernization of the City of Palo Alto Utilities (CPAU) electric distribution infrastructure: the existing infrastructure has insufficient capacity for a sufficient level of electrification of EV transportation and electrical heating to meet the S/CAP goals, and the grid has other technical shortcomings that need to be addressed. An additional challenge to meeting our climate goals is chronic staffing shortages in some programs, including transportation (which accounts for the majority of Palo Alto community emissions).

Policy-related risks affecting the City's ability to mitigate and adapt to climate change include changing federal priorities that affect funding streams, supply chains, the regulatory landscape, and staffing in federal agencies with which municipalities collaborate. Further risks occur through federal and state legislation as well as lawsuits that challenge 'reach codes' municipalities implement in order to set higher standards than state or federal regulations. 

The primary market-related risk is increasing costs for both the City and residents: bids for contractor services for City infrastructure projects are frequently higher than expected, and costs are increasing for consumers replacing gas appliances and vehicles with electric due in part to tariffs and supply chain challenges.

Technology-related risks include relatively new and at times under-regulated technologies. For example, e-mobility technologies pose a fire risk, especially if cheaper, uncertified batteries are used or if users do not properly care for the equipment. Developing, implementing, and educating about best methods for ensuring e-mobility technologies are used safely without deterring use continue are essential to the success of these transitions.

The City updated its Climate Action Plan (CAP), titled Climate Ready Fremont, which the Fremont City Council adopted on October 10, 2023.
column16: The General Plan identifies the impacts Fremont would face due to the increasing earth's temperature and policies to help reduce Fremont's GHG emissions. These policies focus on Mobility, Land Use, Public Facilities, Community Character, Housing Element, and Parks and Recreation. Mobility policies deemphasizing automobiles and emphasizing other modes Land Use policies related to Transit-Oriented Development. Public Facility policies to collaborate with the School District to reduce greenhouse gas emissions Public Facility policies related to \'greening\' the vehicle fleet Public Facility and Conservation policies on Green Buildings and energy conservation Community Character policies related to light-colored roofs and pavement Housing Element policies promoting in-fill housing development Parks and Recreation Element policies supporting linear parks The City's General Plan includes Sustainability as an element in the opening chapter and the reoccurring theme throughout the document. Within each chapter of the general plan, measures that relate to the sustainability vision are noted with the Sustainability icon. The sustainability chapter establishes a vision for Fremont to transition from an auto-oriented suburb into a sustainable, strategically urban, and modern city.
column17: We have implemented climate implementation measures that have resulted in utility bill savings that save the City money in the General Fund or annual operational costs. We have also identified capital needs for Climate implantation, such as robust electric vehicle charging infrastructure. We are now trying to identify outside funding from regional, state, and federal governments to support that implementation. We have tried to implement projects that result in financial savings for the City but also help achieve our climate goals, such as energy efficiency upgrades, lighting upgrades, and solar installations. As we identify additional capital needs that have a more significant impact on the City's budget, that's where we are looking for outside funding sources and trying to prioritize those projects as part of the City's capital improvement process. The City is starting to consider the risk that climate change may have on larger city infrastructure in our most recent planning efforts, including the Park's Masterplan, Urban Forestry Management Plan, the Housing Element update, and the Local Hazard Mitigation Plan update. Overall, we are analyzing climate issues and projects financially, and there are some savings to the City from implementing these projects. There is also a cost associated with implementing them. As we look at deeper decarbonization efforts and more comprehensive adaptation and resiliency projects, we recognize the significant capital investment that will be necessary. Nevertheless, these types of efforts will help to mitigate more significant financial risks to the City down the line.
column18: One risk is that as we transition our building stock to electric, our industrial, manufacturing, cleantech, and biotech sectors depend on natural gas for their processes. Currently, there are few technological alternatives to natural gas for these processes, and any options that do exist are prohibitively expensive. It is important to keep these industries local because the environmental impact in Silicon Valley is much lower than in other parts of the state or country, and especially internationally, due to a combination of our stringent environmental regulations as well as the emissions associated with shipping. There's also a risk that if we regulate too soon before viable alternatives exist for these companies, they may choose to relocate outside of Fremont, which would be a loss of local tax revenue.

column15: Boise has incorporated sustainability and climate action into our initiatives for many years. In 2016, to assess the impact of climate change on Boise and the surrounding region, the city developed the Boise Climate Adaptation Assessment with support from the University of Idaho. In 2021, we formally established our climate goals and actions with the development of a Climate Action Roadmap. The Roadmap serves as a foundational document across numerous City programs which relate to climate and provides direction to the community on the collective actions that need to be implemented to become a carbon neutral community. The city is working to operationalize the priorities and actions identified in our Roadmap into a broad scope of the day to day activities of City government. Boise is working to formalize reporting for the actions in our Roadmap. However, we currently use quantitative development of greenhouse gas emissions inventories and qualitative enterprise level project management and completion tracking methods to assess progress. Historically, the city developed a Livability Report to assess progress across multiple areas of city priority including climate and sustainability.
column16: Climate considerations have been coordinated between our Climate Action Roadmap with other traditional city plans like our comprehensive plan Blueprint Boise and accompanying revisions to our development related ordinances. Additionally, climate considerations are incorporated into other city plans (Water Renewal Utility Zoning Ordinance, Pathways Plan, etc.) as appropriate.
column17: Addressing climate change requires the support of numerous city departments and Boise has been proactive in preparing financially to deploy various programs to address climate mitigation and resilience. To support project and associated financial decision making in our water renewal utility wastewater programs, the city has developed a detailed business case evaluation process that incorporates the community cost of carbon as a financial proxy to monetize the benefit or risk of projects and their connection to climate change. In recent years, the city has been proactive in funding climate action initiatives. In our General Fund, there has been a near-term focus on vehicle and building electrification in municipal facilities, as well as climate resilience planning. These actions directly reduce emissions from City facilities and fleet vehicles, and help us prepare for the future impacts of climate change. Our Geothermal Fund supports the operation and maintenance of the largest direct use geothermal heating district in the United States. Our Water Renewal Fund supports innovative projects to reuse materials from the water renewal process as well as evaluate innovative approaches to water resource programs Proactively addressing water resources helps to make our community more resilient and is a critical issue in a region with limited rainfall.
column18: Boise's risks from the transition to a low carbon economy are likely limited when compared to other communities. Fossil fuel production industries are limited in Idaho and there are no fossil fuel based electricity generating facilities located in Boise. Due to Boise's geographic isolation from other large metropolitan areas and other parts of the country, our city could face challenges as the transportation system transitions to low-carbon. Range for trucking, heavy-duty vehicles, and air travel currently presents a challenge, however, it is anticipated that future technology is likely to mitigate this risk. Considering the abundance of clean energy resources in our region Boise is well positioned to benefit from the transition to a low carbon economy.

column16: The City of Reno “Reimagine Reno” Master Plan guides where and how the City will grow and develop over the next 20 years. It was adopted in December 2017 after a two-and-a-half year process to update the plan, with additional updates effective November 2021. The process was an opportunity to assess and explore trends and key issues that would influence the city's future, as well as an opportunity to articulate a shared, community-wide vision. Throughout the ReImagine Reno process, participants expressed support for the city's sustainability initiatives and a desire for the Master Plan to take a stronger stance on sustainability. As a result, Master Plan goals and policies address a range of issues key to promoting a more livable and sustainable community— infill and redevelopment, environmental protection, energy and water conservation, local food access, transit, renewable energy, access to social and human services, housing affordability, economic resilience, green buildings, sustainable development practices, and many others. The Master Plan establishes sustainable design principles and encourages sustainable development practices in both public and private development. These principles and policies build on the city's longstanding commitment to “green” and its commitment to reduce local greenhouse gas emissions and enhance resilience to climate change. Title 18 (zoning code) will be updated in 23/24 to include numerous sustainability initiatives including community gardens, EV parking, water conservation projects, and green spaces in lieu of some existing requirements.
column17: The City of Reno is rethinking how budgets are created. Sustainability is no longer being viewed as it's own budget, and the Sustainability Program Manager has been working with other departments to take into account the goals of the Sustainability & Climate Action Plan under their project and planning processes. However, this is not yet an official process.
column18: The risks to our jurisdiction are rising costs of development and housing. The creation of the low carbon economy is perceived as \'expensive\'. Even the adoption of the newest energy code (or building codes in general) are raising the costs of development which is raising housing and rental costs. The City of Reno is also running out of developable space, so the ability to affect new development is diminishing. Another risk is the resources and ability to provide adequate, updated training to building professionals.

Council endorsed our second Climate Emergency Plan in 2024 which sets the strategic direction, targets and actions for the organisation. Yarra was the first Council in Australia to endorse a second Climate Emergency Plan, and this has been extremly well received as being broad and ambitious in its intent.
Climate Emergency is a headline action in our highest level Council Plan and community-led Council Vision. 
There is an Executive Management Level - Climate Emergency Executive Oversight Committee - which ensures regular senior management level oversight of climate action. 
Council has a QBL Tool where climate, adaptation (and other TBL issues) must be considered in budget bids and capital works processes. All public Council Reports must respond to the Climate Emergency Impacts of Council Decisions. 
The Yarra Environment Advisory Committee represents interests pertaining to all aspects of urban environmental sustainability including (but not limited to) climate change; resource efficiency across water, waste and energy; urban greening and natural capital; local food systems; and the built environment, by providing advice to Council on policy, strategy and other strategic opportunities to progress the organisation's response to these issues. In addition to the appointed Councillors, the committee membership includes 16 community members who are knowledgeable in the following subject areas:
- Climate emergency
- Waste management
- Local food systems
- Biodiversity and nature
- Water
The committee provides advice to Council in respect to:- emerging and evolving environmental sustainability issues, challenges and opportunities relevant to the City of Yarra;
- the delivery of its Council Plan in relation to environmental sustainability issues;
- development and strategic implementation of environment-related council strategies, including (but not limited to) the Yarra Environment Strategy, Climate Emergency Plan, Waste Minimisation and Resource Recovery Strategy, Urban Agriculture Strategy, Urban Forest Strategy, Nature Strategy and Integrated Water Strategy (as updated from time-to-time);
- key policy development on relevant issues;- design and delivery of specific environment sustainability programs and projects by Council;
- engagement with the wider City of Yarra community to build awareness of environmental sustainability issues and activities; and- identifying strategic opportunities to collaborate with other organisations and groups to progress initiatives related to environmental sustainability issues.
column16: Climate Emergency is now a highest level action for our jurisdiction, and thus forms a key part in all that we do. Our Organisation has endorsed that from now on at Yarra \'Every Job is a Climate Job\'. All teams has developed a Climate Emergency Role Statement, and actions specific to their work. We have undertaken a climate risk assessment, and are building this across the organisation. Climate related issues are being build into the highest level strategic plans including our new 4-year Council Plan, our long term City Plan, and our Community Infrastructure Plan. In July 2024, Council endorsed our second Climate Emergency Plan. This six-year strategy and 3-year Action plan has cemented Yarra's commitment to respond strongly and urgently to the climate emergency, and significantly broadened what climate emergency action look like. The plan set out Yarra's longer term targets and laid out the path ahead for the Council's planning over the six years. Additionally Climate Risk is a highest order Strategic Risk for Yarra and we must respond to this risk regularly. We have undertaken a review of climate risk impacts for our infrastructure, and have incorporated flood mapping into our strategic planning
column17: Climate Emergency is a highest level issue for our organisation as reflected in our Council Vision, Council Plan, and our Financial Sustainability Strategy. \nAs we learn more about projected climate issues for Yarra these are incorporated into our planning and decision making. For example, we completed a \'Climate change risk and vulnerability assessment\' for multiple classes of Council assets and to identify and evaluate potential adaptation options for vulnerable building assets. This helps to inform financial planning for maintenance of these assets. Our award winning Embedding Adaptation Project developed a suite of decision-making tools and a training package which assist staff in incorporating adaptation into their working role. The resources are available for use and modification by other local councils. The outputs from this project - including the Quadruple Bottom Line (QBL) Tool, Adaptation Guidance Tools, Climate Vulnerability Screening Tool, and Adaptation Training 101 - allow projects to be financed with consideration of their environmental and adaptation outcomes. (https://www.yarracity.vic.gov.au/about-us/council-taking-climate-action/climate-adaptation#accordion-case-studies)All public Council Reports must respond to the Climate Emergency Impacts of Council Decisions. Additionally we have undertaken a Climate Risk and Vulnerability Assessment - focused predominately on our major assesses which assess the financial risks for the organisation from climate change for our assets and how we can plan for and limit this. Climate Change was a strategic factor considered in our Long Term Financial Strategy as well as our Council Plan and Budget.
column18:
The major risk to our juristiction related to the low-carbon economy is ensuring that those most in need are supported. We recognise that while the climate emergency affects everyone in our
community, it is having a disproportionate impact on some. This includes those in our community who are unable to access adequate housing
or income, have accessibility needs or chronic health conditions, work in unsafe conditions or who experience marginalisation due to culture,
language or gender identity. Additionally, the climate emergency is one of great inequity, with those least responsible - those on lower incomes, from low and middle-income countries,
and children and generations to come - facing the greatest climate and health impacts.
Other Legal Risks: Should Yarra not mitigate and adapt against the impacts of climate change, there is the risk that climate related litigation can be brought against the municipality.
Technology risk: As an innovative, leading municipality on climate action, Yarra face technology risks. This includes for example the municipality's support for innovative technologies such as all-electric tipper trucks and community batteries.
Reputation risk: Should Yarra not be perceived as responding adequately to the climate emergency, it faces a risk to its reputation.

column15: The Council (elected members) is kept updated on climate-related issues and progress on climate change work programs through regular reporting from specialist teams focusing on:- climate mitigation across council operations and the wider city- the adaptation of specific parts of Dunedin (the South Dunedin Future work programme). - DCC senior leadership and general managers are kept abreast of operational emissions through twice annual reporting. A full city-wide emissions inventory is undertaken every 2-3 years. A Zero Carbon Policy formalises -related expectations and means emissions impact is assessed for every substantive decision, and emissions considerations are built into project management and procurement processes. A risk register is maintained for both Zero Carbon and South Dunedin Future work programs, and reports to the DCC's Audit and Risk Committee on matters relating to climate change within the jurisdiction is undertaken on an as-requested or as-required base. In January 2025, council approved a two-year project to design, establish, and operate a citywide climate resilience framework, which seeks to enhance cross-council functions relating to natural hazards, risk assessment, adaptation plan, and adaptation-related actions. This work will commence 1 July 2025.
column16: Planning rules (known as the District Plan) consider risks from climate change (e.g. not allowing buildings in flood zones or requiring minimum floor heights) and assist in efforts to reduce emissions too (e.g. by considering the proximity to public transport, walking, and cycling facilities when considering new zones for housing development). This is informed by a Future Development Strategy incorporating an overarching policy to pursue a compact urban form and a climate-related master planning programme is underway for South Dunedin, a low-lying flood-affected area of the city.
column17: As set out in Dunedin's Zero Carbon Plan (an emissions reduction plan for the city), extensive change across all sectors is needed to meet Dunedin's net-zero (excluding biogenic methane) by 2030 target. Many of these changes needed are outside of the direct control of the DCC and will rely on central government institutions, businesses, and residents responding with commensurate urgency. Recent changes in central government policy have significantly reduced policy and funding supports for action to reduce emissions. This has reduced the scope of what can be achieved by local government, and resulted in delays in implementation for some projects. It has also reduced the scope and speed of action to reduce emissions elsewhere in the community. A recent update to the city's emissions modelling to account for this changed policy context, suggests that the city's net zero (excluding biogenic methane) target is unlikely to be met by 2030. Council will consider options to update the city's target, early in 2026.

column18: New Plymouth has one of the highest GDPs per capita in the country and the Taranaki energy sector represents 28% of the regional output. Taranaki Region (region around NPDC) has the second highest emissions intensities per GDP of anywhere within NZ due to its agriculture/ dairy, industrial and petrochemical industry. Within the NPDC community footprint, Methanex NZ utilises ~ 40% of all of NZ produced natural gas to create methanol exports. Taranaki is the hub of the petrochemical industry and high pressure gas transmission pipeline network that delivers fossil gas to the rest of the country.The risks of stranded assets and loss of employment and income due to a declining petrochemical industry are significant for this region of NZ. The transition to sustainable agriculture will have a major impact on sheep and beef and dairy agriculture in the region.

column18:
青岛市作为山东省的重要城市，其气候条件对低碳转型有着显著的影响。根据青岛市生态与农业气象中心发布的2023年气候影响评价，青岛市在2023年经历了创历史新高的平均气温、偏少的降水量以及多次极端天气事件，如暴雨、高温和寒潮等。这些气候特征对青岛市的水资源管理、农业生产、能源消耗和城市规划等方面都产生了一定的影响。
1.	水资源管理：降水量的减少要求青岛市在水资源管理上采取更为严格的措施，如加强水利设施建设、推广节水技术和提高水资源利用效率。
2.	农业生产：气候变暖和极端天气事件对农业生产构成挑战，需要加强农业基础设施建设，如灌溉系统的改进，以及推广适应性强的作物品种。
3.	城市规划与建设：高温和暴雨等极端天气对城市基础设施的韧性提出了更高要求，城市规划需要考虑气候适应性，加强防洪排涝系统，提高城市绿化覆盖率以缓解热岛效应。
4.	旅游业发展：青岛市作为著名的旅游城市，气候变化对其旅游业有着直接影响。需要开发更多适应不同气候条件的旅游产品和服务，同时加强旅游设施的建设和管理，以应对极端天气事件。
5.	能源需求与供应：气温的变化会影响居民和工业的能源需求，如供暖和制冷需求。青岛市需要优化能源结构，提高清洁能源比例，以应对气候变化带来的能源挑战。
6.	居民生活与健康：气候变化可能增加居民健康风险，如高温引发的中暑和呼吸系统疾病。需要加强公共卫生服务，提高居民对气候变化的健康适应能力。
2024年冬春季的气候预测显示，青岛市平均降水量可能继续偏少，气温略偏高，这将进一步影响水资源的分配和利用，以及可能对农业生产造成压力。

column15: The Rajkot Net-zero Climate Resilient City Action Plan (Towards A Net-zero future by 2070) is developed based on an urban system gap analysis; climate risk and vulnerability assessment; baseline GHG emissions inventory; future emissions scenario modelling including BAU projections and GHG emissions reduction scenarios (Progressive Action Scenario and Net-zero Pathway). Rajkot has opted for the sectoral goals and targets of the Net-zero Pathway and outlined priority adaptation and mitigation strategies and actions to help improve the city's urban climate resilience. Spearheaded by the RMC and the climate core team, the development of Net-zero CRCAP involved input from various government departments, research institutions, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and community representatives. This inclusive approach ensured that a wide range of perspectives were considered, leading to the development of a robust and comprehensive climate action plan. This plan will serve as a detailed roadmap, specifying the necessary institutional mechanisms, technical capabilities, and communication channels required to effectively integrate climate action into urban planning and infrastructure. Please refer below sections from the Rajkot's 'Climate Resilient City Action Plan (Towards A Net-zero future by 2070). 1) Annexure 1 Formation of Stakeholder Committee and Climate Core Team (Page 255 to 259); 2) Chapter 4 (section 4.1.6, 4.2.5,4.3.2, 4.4.8, 4.5.6, 4.6.2) for information on sector wise Budgetary planning for climate actions in FY 2023-24.
column16: The Second Revised Draft Development Plan, 2031 has been prepared in 2016 considering the demand of projected population for the next two decades for the entire area of 686 sq.km. under the Rajkot Urban Development Authority (RUDA), including the Rajkot city area. The implementation of the development plan is facilitated through town planning schemes that utilize the land pooling concept to enhance neighbourhood-level infrastructure. This approach involves land reconstitution, the development of road networks, and the establishment of social and physical infrastructure. RUDA has proposed a 2nd ring road around the city in 2016 which connects major highways and supports ease of traffic movement, particularly for industrial freights. To preserve the ecological balance and boost agriculture activities, the developable zone is restricted till 2nd ring road. Certain pockets between RMC and 2nd ring road are proposed as an agriculture zone. Also, along with agricultural activities, development of agro-based industries and processing units are allowed to support activities like farming, livestock etc. in conjunction with development regulations. The planned and authorized strategy aids in the local administration's ability to organize, think through, and carry out initiatives for each fiscal year by including them in the cities yearly implementation plan (municipal budget). Please refer section 3.6 of chapter 3 from Rajkot Climate Resilient City Action Plan (Towards A Net-zero future by 2070) for land use and development planning.
column17: Based on Rajkot Climate Resilient City Action Plan (Towards A Net Zero Future by 2070) and climate related issues, city has proposed various climate resilient interventions, which has increased capital allocation of Annual Municipal Budget (i.e., lake interlinking, replacing old water supply and sewerage network, RE plants, developing urban forests to increase in green cover, biomining of legacy waste etc.). A list of projects to be implemented is included in the city's Climate Resilient City Action Plan (CRCAP). The CRCAP has been given council approval, making it simpler to get funds for its implementation. Every year, the city chooses a specific area to focus on, and projects relating to low-carbon growth in that area are included in the financial budget of the city so that they may be implemented and monitored. From last 3 years, city is focusing on Transport sector and has allocated funding for deploying EV in public transportation, promoting e-auto for first and last mile connectivity and promoting use of NMT. Considering that city has establish dedicated charging station for e-buses and has announced viability gap funding of INR 30000 for the purchase of e-auto. City also provided subsidy of INR 1000 for the purchase of cycle to its citizens.Please refer below sections from the Rajkot's 'Climate Resilient City Action Plan (Towards A Net-zero future by 2070). 1) Annexure 1 Formation of Stakeholder Committee and Climate Core Team (Page 255 to 259); 2) Chapter 4 (section 4.1.6, 4.2.5,4.3.2, 4.4.8, 4.5.6, 4.6.2) for information on sector wise Budgetary planning for climate actions in FY 2023-24.

1. Pengembangan dan Revitalisasi Ruang Terbuka Hijau (RTH)
a. Penambahan dan perawatan taman kota (seperti Taman Ahmad Yani, Cadika, Gajah Mada).
b. Penanaman pohon di jalur hijau, kawasan pendidikan, dan pemukiman.
c. Rehabilitasi mangrove di kawasan pesisir Medan Utara (Belawan dan sekitarnya) untuk meredam banjir rob dan menyerap karbon.
2. Penanganan Banjir dan Adaptasi Iklim
a. Normalisasi dan pengerukan sungai seperti Sungai Deli, Babura, dan Sikambing.
b. Pembangunan kolam retensi dan sumur resapan untuk mengurangi genangan.
c. Pengembangan sistem drainase terpadu di kawasan padat penduduk.
3.Penguatan Tata Ruang Berbasis Lingkungan
a. Integrasi zona rawan bencana dan perubahan iklim dalam revisi RTRW 2022-2042.
b. Penetapan kawasan lindung, sempadan sungai, dan resapan air sebagai zona prioritas pengendalian ruang.
c. Pembatasan pembangunan di kawasan rawan banjir di lokasi RTH dan sempadan sungai.
4. Dukungan Energi Ramah Lingkungan dan Transportasi Rendah Emisi
a. Penggunaan bus listrik di koridor utama transportasi kota.
b. Penerangan jalan umum dengan lampu tenaga surya di beberapa titik.
c. Sosialisasi hemat energi dan pengurangan penggunaan plastik sekali pakai.
5. Pelaporan dan Monitoring Lingkungan
a. Pelaporan Indeks Kualitas Lingkungan Hidup (IKLH) tahunan ke KLHK.
b. Monitoring Indeks Tutupan Lahan (IKTL) sebagai bagian dari upaya menjaga cadangan karbon kota.
c. Penilaian kinerja perangkat daerah berbasis indikator lingkungan.
6. Pemberdayaan Masyarakat dan Edukasi Iklim
a. Program Kampung Iklim (Proklim) di beberapa kelurahan seperti di Medan Tuntungan dan Medan Marelan.
b. Edukasi lingkungan di sekolah (Adiwiyata), kegiatan penghijauan oleh komunitas, dan pelibatan warga dalam aksi bersih sungai dan tanam pohon.
column17: Perubahan iklim telah mempengaruhi arah perencanaan keuangan di Kota Medan, di mana alokasi anggaran secara bertahap diarahkan untuk memperkuat ketahanan lingkungan dan menghadapi risiko iklim, seperti banjir, banjir rob, dan penurunan kualitas udara. \nPemerintah Kota Medan mengalokasikan anggaran untuk mendanai program rehabilitasi dan penambahan ruang terbuka hijau, pembangunan dan revitalisasi sistem drainase serta kolam retensi, serta kegiatan normalisasi sungai di kawasan padat penduduk. Selain itu, dukungan anggaran juga disalurkan untuk program adaptasi berbasis masyarakat seperti Kampung Iklim (ProKlim) berupa sosialisasi, kegiatan edukasi lingkungan, dan insentif bagi sekolah Adiwiyata. Anggaran juga digunakan untuk kegiatan mitigasi seperti penerangan jalan tenaga surya, transportasi rendah emisi, serta penguatan sistem pengelolaan sampah dan limbah. \nPada level perencanaan strategis, Pemerintah Kota Medan juga mulai menyusun dan memperbarui dokumen-dokumen perencanaan seperti Rencana Aksi Daerah Penurunan Emisi Gas Rumah Kaca (RAD-GRK), dokumen IKLH, dan RPJMD yang terintegrasi isu iklim, yang seluruhnya memerlukan penganggaran terstruktur baik dari APBD, bantuan pusat, maupun potensi pendanaan alternatif (CSR atau donor).
column18: Kota Medan menghadapi sejumlah risiko yang perlu diantisipasi secara serius, baik dari sisi sosial, ekonomi, maupun kelembagaan. Salah satu risiko utama adalah ketergantungan terhadap sektor transportasi berbasis bahan bakar fosil, yang masih mendominasi aktivitas ekonomi dan mobilitas warga, sehingga perubahan menuju sistem transportasi rendah emisi memerlukan investasi besar dan resistensi sosial. Selain itu, jika regulasi lingkungan diperketat akan berdampak pada penurunan produktivitas sektor informal seperti industri rumahan dan UMKM. \nDari sisi fiskal, penyesuaian anggaran untuk mendukung infrastruktur hijau dan energi terbarukan berpotensi menimbulkan tekanan pada keuangan daerah, terutama jika tidak dibarengi dengan pendanaan eksternal atau insentif pusat. \nRisiko lainnya mencakup kurangnya kapasitas teknis aparatur di lingkungan Pemerintah Kota Medan dalam merancang kebijakan hijau yang efektif serta tantangan dalam mengintegrasikan data emisi karbon ke dalam sistem perencanaan dan pelaporan daerah.

column16:
Masalah terkait iklim di Kota Palembang telah mempengaruhi perencanaan pembangunan jangka menengah daerah tersebut dalam beberapa aspek:

- Perencanaan Infrastruktur: Pemerintah Kota Palembang telah melakukan normalisasi sungai dan anak sungai untuk mencegah banjir, serta merancang infrastruktur yang tahan terhadap perubahan iklim.
- Kajian Dampak Perubahan Iklim: Penelitian telah dilakukan untuk menganalisis dampak perubahan iklim dan urban sprawl di Kota Palembang, yang membantu dalam perencanaan pembangunan jangka menengah.
- Pengembangan Rencana Strategis: Rencana Strategis (Renstra) Kota Palembang tahun 2024-2026 telah disusun untuk mengakomodasi perencanaan jangka menengah yang selaras dengan Rencana Pembangunan Daerah (RPD).
- Perencanaan Pembangunan Berkelanjutan: Strategi pembangunan berkelanjutan dalam perencanaan daerah telah diintegrasikan untuk menghadapi perubahan iklim global, dengan penekanan pada adaptasi dan mitigasi iklim.
- Program Kampung Iklim: Program Kampung Iklim telah dilaksanakan untuk mengurangi dampak perubahan iklim di beberapa kelurahan di Kota Palembang.

Dalam Rencana Pembangunan Jangka Menengah Daerah (RPJMD) Kota Palembang tahun 2018-2023, perubahan iklim telah menjadi salah satu aspek yang dipertimbangkan dalam perencanaan pembangunan daerah. Begitu juga dalam Rencana Pembangunan Jangka Menengah Daerah (RPJMD) Kota Palembang Tahun 2025 - 2029 Pemerintah Kota Palembang juga telah mengintegrasikan konsep keberlanjutan lingkungan dalam perencanaan pembangunan jangka menengah untuk meningkatkan ketahanan infrastruktur daerah dan mendorong keberlanjutan lingkungan
column17:
Masalah terkait iklim di Kota Palembang berpotensi mempengaruhi perencanaan keuangan kota dalam beberapa aspek:

- Biaya Pemulihan Pasca Bencana: Kota Palembang mungkin perlu mengalokasikan anggaran untuk memulihkan infrastruktur dan layanan publik yang terdampak oleh bencana alam seperti banjir. Hal ini dapat membebani keuangan kota karena biaya pemulihan yang tidak terduga.
- Penurunan Pendapatan Asli Daerah (PAD): Perubahan iklim dapat mempengaruhi aktivitas ekonomi lokal, seperti penurunan produktivitas pertanian dan penurunan kunjungan wisatawan. Hal ini berpotensi menurunkan penerimaan asli daerah (PAD) Kota Palembang.
- Pengeluaran Darurat dan Tanggap Bencana: Kota Palembang mungkin perlu mengalokasikan anggaran untuk tanggap bencana dan pemulihan, yang dapat menghabiskan dana tak terduga dan mempengaruhi keuangan kota.
- Investasi Infrastruktur Tahan Iklim: Kota Palembang perlu melakukan investasi pada infrastruktur yang tahan terhadap perubahan iklim, seperti sistem drainase yang lebih baik dan bangunan yang tahan banjir. Hal ini memerlukan alokasi anggaran yang signifikan.
column18:
Transisi ke ekonomi rendah karbon di Kota Palembang berpotensi membawa beberapa risiko, antara lain ¹ ²:
- Risiko Transisi: Risiko kerugian akibat perubahan kebijakan demi menuju ekonomi rendah karbon, seperti penghentian penggunaan batu bara, perubahan preferensi konsumen menuju produk ramah lingkungan, yang dapat berdampak pada perubahan struktur ekonomi dan tantangan bagi dunia usaha.
- Risiko Hilangnya Pendapatan: Sektor yang bergantung pada industri karbon tinggi mungkin mengalami penurunan pendapatan dan kehilangan kesempatan kerja.
- Risiko Investasi: Investasi pada infrastruktur rendah karbon memerlukan biaya besar dan berisiko jika tidak direncanakan dengan baik.
- Risiko Ketergantungan pada Teknologi: Ketergantungan pada teknologi rendah karbon yang masih dalam tahap pengembangan dapat menimbulkan risiko jika teknologi tersebut tidak berkembang sesuai harapan.
- Risiko Ketidakpastian Kebijakan: Ketidakpastian kebijakan pemerintah terkait transisi ke ekonomi rendah karbon dapat menimbulkan risiko bagi investor dan pelaku usaha.

column15: The Bogor City Environmental Quality Indicator is one of the assessments of the extent to which the Bogor City Environment Agency (DLH) implements programs and activities, one of the objectives of which is to monitor environmental quality in the city of Bogor. Monitoring is carried out through activities such as real-time air quality monitoring, water quality monitoring, greenhouse gas inventory, and annual motor vehicle emission testing. In addition, the City of Bogor also supervises business actors' compliance with environmental permits. \nEvery year, the City of Bogor conducts greenhouse gas monitoring, evaluation, and reporting (PEP GRK) with indicators of greenhouse gas emission reduction in tons of CO2eq and greenhouse gas emission intensity reduction in tons of CO2eq/billion.
column16: The issue of climate change is one of the considerations in planning the direction of development in both the 2025-2045 Bogor City RPJPD, which was ratified in Bogor City Regulation Number 10 of 2024, and the 2025-2029 Bogor City RPJMD, which was ratified in Bogor City Regulation Number 5 of 2025. The RPJMD 2025-2029 is outlined in four missions: Healthy Bogor, Smart Bogor, Prosperous Bogor, and Smooth Bogor. The Healthy Bogor and Smooth Bogor missions include key performance indicators that must be carried out by relevant regional government agencies in an effort to reduce GHG emissions (tons of CO2eq) and GHG emission intensity (tons of CO2eq/billion) as well as sustainable development through the concepts of green economy, green building, environmentally friendly transportation, and circular economy.
column17: Climate change mitigation and adaptation activities have been budgeted for in several relevant government agencies. For example, in 2024, the city of Bogor has budgeted for 46 activities related to climate change mitigation and adaptation, with an allocation of 57.92 billion rupiah. The 2025-2029 RPJMD has formulated programs, activities, and actions in relevant regional agencies along with annual budgets and target indicators, namely GHG emission reduction (tons of CO2eq) and GHG emission intensity (tons of CO2eq/billion).
column18: In terms of budgeting, there are issues related to the reduction of transfer funds from the central government to the regions, which will result in efficiency across all regional institutions in Bogor City. This has an impact on the proportion of the budget allocated to climate change mitigation and adaptation activities. \nCircular economy-based activities have been carried out at the community level, but the obstacle faced is the lack of buyers for the products of the circular economy, which discourages the community from continuing these activities.

column15: 本市では、2008年2月に、今後の地球温暖化対策の基本的な考え方をカーボン・チャレンジ川崎エコ戦略（CCかわさき）として発表し、2010年10月に、温室効果ガス排出量を2030年までに80％削減を目指すことを目標に掲げた川崎市地球温暖化対策推進基本計画を策定、2018年3月に改定し、地球温暖化対策を総合的かつ計画的に展開してきました。2020年2月にはCO2排出実質ゼロを表明し、2050年のCO2排出量実質100％削減を達成するため同年11月に脱炭素戦略「かわさきカーボンゼロチャレンジ2050」を策定。さらに、「かわさきカーボンゼロチャレンジ2050」を踏まえ、2022年3月に基本計画を改定し、脱炭素化に向けた取組を進めています。\n
column16: 本市では、地球温暖化対策について、2010年度に、2020年度までを計画期間とした「川崎市地球温暖化対策推進基本計画」を策定し、対策を推進してきました。気候変動枠組条約第21回締約国会議（COP21）におけるパリ協定の採択や、国における「地球温暖化対策計画」の策定等の社会状況の変化を踏まえ、2018年に上記「基本計画」を改定しました。\nさらに、近年、数十年に一度と言われる規模の風水害が多発しており、令和元年東日本台風では、本市にも甚大な被害がもたらされました。気温上昇については、実際に市内の観測地点での観測結果からも上昇傾向が確認されており、熱中症や感染症リスクの増加が懸念されます。また、米国研究機関によれば、このまま気温上昇が進むと、2050年頃には川崎市臨海部の大部分が水没してしまうというデータも報告されており、気候変動の影響は差し迫った課題です。このように気候変動の影響が市民の生活に大きな影響を与える状況を踏まえ、あらゆる主体と危機感を共有し、地球温暖化対策について具体的な取組を実践し、2050年の市域の温室効果ガス排出量実質ゼロを実現するために、2020年に脱炭素戦略「かわさきカーボンゼロチャレンジ2050」を策定するとともに、2022年に「川崎市地球温暖化対策推進基本計画」を改定しました。
column17: 「脱炭素社会の実現」に向けて、川崎市地球温暖化対策推進基本計画に基づく取組を推進するための予算を確保しており、2025年度予算では、市域への再エネ普及・地産地消に向けた住宅用太陽光発電設備、蓄電池等の導入支援のための補助制度について、8億円規模での予算拡充を行っています。\nまた、国は脱炭素事業に意欲的に取り組む地方公共団体等を複数年度にわたり継続的かつ包括的に支援するスキームとして地域脱炭素推進交付金制度を設けており、本市は市民・事業者と一体となって取組を進めている「脱炭素アクションみぞのくち」などの取組が評価され、2022年度から総額50億円規模の交付金を活用しながら、市域の脱炭素化に向けた取組を推進しています。\nさらに、本市は2021年に政令市初のグリーンボンド（市債）を発行しており、グリーンボンド発行により調達した資金を「エネルギー回収率（発電能力）の向上」「エネルギー消費削減によるCO2排出量削減」「大気汚染物質の排出削減」「水災害発生時の浸水被害の緩和」「港湾・沿岸域における廃棄物削減」等のプロジェクトに充当しています。
column18: 川崎市は、製造品出荷額等、化学工業及び石油製品・石炭製品製造業の製造品出荷額等が政令市1位であり、川崎で生産・製造された製品が、日本中や世界で広く使用されている。京浜工業地帯の中核として日本経済を牽引する川崎市が、脱炭素社会の実現を目指すことの役割と重要性は非常に大きい。

column16: 令和元年10 月に発生した「令和元年東日本台風」は、本市に記録的な大雨をもたらし、中山間地域を中心に甚大な被害が発生しました。令和3年8月に策定した「さがみはら脱炭素ロードマップ」は、本市のこうした状況も受けて、2050年における脱炭素社会の実現に向けた取組の方向性を示すべく、適応策を含む施策の推進について策定しました。\nその後、令和5年4月には「さがみはら地球温暖化の防止に向けた脱炭素社会づくり条例」を施行し、この社会情勢や動向を踏まえ、令和5年11月には「第2次相模原市地球温暖化対策計画」の改定を行い、脱炭素社会の実現に向けた取組の加速化を図っています。

Pemerintah Kota Yogyakarta telah mengarusutamakan isu iklim dalam RPJPD 2025-2045 dan RPJMD 2025-2029, dengan menjadikannya sebagai isu strategis daerah yang mencakup daya dukung dan daya tampung lingkungan hidup, kualitas lingkungan, serta resiliensi terhadap bencana dan perubahan iklim. Informasi ini disampaikan kepada perangkat daerah melalui mekanisme perencanaan, rapat koordinasi, dan forum perencanaan daerah, sehingga menjadi dasar dalam penyusunan program lintas-OPD. Dalam RPJPD, visi pembangunan diarahkan untuk mewujudkan kota yang unggul, maju, dan berkelanjutan dengan memperhatikan aspek lingkungan hidup dan mitigasi risiko bencana, yang kemudian dijabarkan dalam RPJMD ke dalam strategi penguatan daya dukung lingkungan, peningkatan kualitas lingkungan hidup, dan adaptasi terhadap perubahan iklim.

RPJMD 2025-2029 juga menjadi pedoman dalam penyusunan RKPD tahunan yang memastikan alokasi anggaran untuk program-program terkait iklim, seperti pengelolaan lingkungan hidup, pengendalian tata ruang, penguatan sumber daya air, dan pembangunan infrastruktur pengendalian bencana. Pengawasan dilaksanakan melalui mekanisme pengendalian dan evaluasi RPJPD/RPJMD oleh Bappeda bersama perangkat daerah teknis, dengan menggunakan indikator seperti Indeks Risiko Bencana, Indeks Kualitas Lingkungan Hidup, serta daya dukung air dan pangan. Hasil evaluasi digunakan sebagai dasar penyesuaian kebijakan pembangunan daerah. Tujuan kinerja yang ditetapkan juga mengintegrasikan isu iklim, meliputi peningkatan kualitas lingkungan hidup, penguatan ketahanan pangan, air, dan energi, pengurangan risiko bencana iklim, serta peningkatan kapasitas adaptasi masyarakat terhadap perubahan iklim.
column16: Isu-isu iklim telah mempengaruhi perencanaan pembangunan di Kota Yogyakarta dalam RPJPD 2025-2045 dan RPJMD 2025-2029. Visi pembangunan jangka panjang menekankan keberlanjutan, perlindungan lingkungan, serta mitigasi dan adaptasi terhadap bencana iklim seperti banjir, kekeringan, dan cuaca ekstrem. Hal ini diperkuat oleh hasil kajian lingkungan yang menunjukkan keterbatasan daya dukung air, kebutuhan ruang terbuka hijau, dan meningkatnya risiko bencana hidrometeorologi yang perlu diantisipasi dalam perencanaan pembangunan.\nDalam RPJMD, isu iklim diintegrasikan melalui indikator daya dukung dan daya tampung lingkungan, kualitas lingkungan, serta resiliensi terhadap bencana dan perubahan iklim. Perubahan pola curah hujan, peningkatan suhu udara, tekanan terhadap sumber daya air, serta permasalahan pencemaran mendorong pemerintah untuk memprioritaskan program pengelolaan ruang terbuka hijau, pengendalian drainase dan banjir, konservasi air tanah, serta penguatan adaptasi masyarakat. Dengan demikian, isu iklim menjadi dasar strategi, alokasi anggaran, dan indikator kinerja dalam pembangunan daerah.\n
column17: Isu-isu iklim telah memengaruhi perencanaan keuangan di Kota Yogyakarta dengan diintegrasikan dalam RPJMD 2025-2029 yang menjadi pedoman penyusunan RKPD dan APBD tahunan. Program prioritas yang mendapatkan alokasi anggaran diarahkan pada penguatan daya dukung dan daya tampung lingkungan hidup, peningkatan kualitas ruang terbuka hijau, konservasi sumber daya air, serta pembangunan dan pemeliharaan infrastruktur pengendali banjir dan drainase. Selain itu, pengelolaan persampahan juga menjadi bagian dari strategi mitigasi emisi dan pengendalian pencemaran, sehingga masuk dalam prioritas pembiayaan daerah.\nAlokasi dana juga diarahkan pada pembangunan dan pemeliharaan ruang terbuka hijau, penghijauan kota, normalisasi sungai, peningkatan kapasitas drainase, serta pembangunan infrastruktur pengendali banjir guna mengurangi risiko genangan dan bencana hidrometeorologi. Anggaran digunakan pula untuk pemantauan kualitas lingkungan, inventarisasi emisi gas rumah kaca, serta program edukasi dan pemberdayaan masyarakat terkait ketahanan iklim. Perubahan pola curah hujan dan kejadian cuaca ekstrem mendorong pemerintah melakukan penyesuaian belanja modal serta penguatan pos pembiayaan tanggap darurat bencana, agar mampu merespons cepat terhadap dampak iklim sekaligus menjaga keberlanjutan layanan publik. Dengan demikian, pertimbangan iklim secara nyata mempengaruhi arah perencanaan keuangan daerah, baik dari sisi strategi, alokasi anggaran, maupun tujuan pembangunan berkelanjutan.\n
column18: Transisi menuju ekonomi rendah karbon di Kota Yogyakarta, sebagaimana diatur dalam Perda RPJPD 2025-2045 dan Perda RPJMD 2025-2029, berpotensi menimbulkan risiko ekonomi berupa beban adaptasi bagi usaha kecil-menengah, risiko sosial terkait kebutuhan peningkatan kapasitas tenaga kerja hijau, serta risiko teknis akibat keterbatasan infrastruktur pendukung seperti drainase, transportasi ramah lingkungan, dan pengelolaan sampah. Dari sisi keuangan, investasi besar untuk infrastruktur hijau dapat membebani APBD jika tidak diimbangi dengan pendanaan alternatif, sementara dari sisi tata kelola, keberhasilan transisi memerlukan koordinasi lintas sektor dan sinergi pemerintah, masyarakat, serta dunia usaha.\n

To enhance the management and coordination of climate change initiatives, the Greater Amman Municipality established the Sustainable Development and Amman Resilience Unit in April 2022. This unit is tasked with the following responsibilities:
1. Establishing and leading a technical committee dedicated to monitoring and addressing climate change issues.
2. Developing, updating, and overseeing the implementation of the Amman Climate Change Plan.
3. Facilitating participation and collaboration with international agencies and networks on climate-related matters.
4. Coordinating efforts with the Ministry of Environment to ensure alignment with national commitments in the field of climate change.
5. Integrating climate data with Amman Urban Observatory and the Geographical Information Systems Department.
6. Updating the city's GHG inventory and measuring emissions for Amman.
7. Conducting assessments of environmental risks associated with climate change.
8. Proposing initiatives and solutions to support climate change adaptation.
9. Collaborating with relevant sectors within the Greater Amman Municipality to support and monitor projects aimed at mitigating climate change impacts.
All climate-related activities are aligned with the overarching vision and strategy of the Greater Amman Municipality and are coordinated with national objectives.
column16: Like other cities around the globe, Amman is already experiencing the impacts of a changing climate. The country is facing irregular patterns of rainfall swinging between the extremes of drought to excessive rain over a short period of time, rising temperatures in summer and declining temperatures in winter, and a significant increase in extreme weather events. Heavy rain events are leading to flooding in lower-lying areas of the city, hazardous blizzards have closed schools, and heat waves and water shortages have directly impacted the health of the population and operation of businesses. These adverse impacts of climate change disproportionately affect the poor and most vulnerable in Amman.The Amman city administration is now acting to protect the most vulnerable, as well as improve the resilience of the city and its inhabitants. Amman's Resilience Strategy was published in 2017. It identifies a range of actions that will help city residents survive and adapt to climate shocks and grow stronger. It sets a vision for Amman and establishes specific resilience goals and actions that will help the city achieve this vision.Amman released the climate plan in 2019 followed by Amman Green City Action plan in 2021 as an action plan and supporting document, all the work related to climate change is merged within these documents, specifying the actions and initiatives needed to reach our goal. Greater Amman Municipality aligned its strategic plan 2022-2026 with the climate change commitments as a city, as part of GAM strategy 2022-2026, we released transportation strategy for 2022-2032, which tackle the transportation challenge as the second highest sector to contribute in GHG in Amman. All of GAM strategy are aligned with the national goals and commitments and the Royal Modernization vision of Jordan.
column17: GAM strategic plan is accompanied by a financial plan that relocate GAM budget to the listed projects. This is also supported by Amman Green City Action Plan which consist of a cost estimate for all actions, this includes the financial costs of capital expenditure (CapEx) and operational expenditure (OpEx) of actions, as well as other design and development costs (e.g. consultant fees). The updated Climate Action Plan for Amman that is expected to be released in September 2023 also include the costs and source of funding (i.e. Municipal budget, co-funding, government budget, donation, international financing institution, PPP).
column18:
The City of Amman fully subscribes to the philosophy that the best defence against future shocks is to transform systems now, to build resilience by addressing climate change and to reduce the vulnerability, exposure and inequality that drive disasters. This philosophy is underpinned by a thorough understanding of the risks of shocks that emerge at the intersection of hazards, and exposure and susceptibility to these hazards, within the broader socioeconomic processes taking place in the City. The City's capacity to carry out geospatially-based climate risks analysis is evolving and several development partners have recently contributed to increasing the knowledge of climate risks within the City boundary. Amman Climate Action Plan 2019 highlights the historical changes and future projections (world bank 2019) for the country.
Extreme heat: Heatwaves are increasing in intensity and duration and this trend is predicted to continue. This has led to an increase in energy requirements for air-conditioning units. It also has an effect on water requirements in the city. There is no agriculture within the Municipality boundaries, but the heat affects market supplies.
Drought: This is extremely serious, particularly with the rapidly rising population due to the influx of refugees from surrounding countries. Security of water supply is a risk for the city. Water is not always available and is pumped only at limited times during the week, so households need to store water in tanks and wells, and pay for water to be delivered if their store of water finishes. There is no agriculture within the Municipality boundaries, but the heat affects market supplies.
Urban flooding: In recent years flash floods have become a serious problem, making roads dangerous and affecting an increasing number of residential and commercial areas. There are concerns that it could also affect water supply and sanitation.
Snow and ice: Heavy snow can impact transport, hence impacting services, and preventing people from attending work and or schools. They can also have serious consequences for the sick and elderly, who are not able to get needed healthcare. Heavy snow can affect trees as many have been lost over the years due to storm, and not replaced.
