column15: The City of West Palm Beach's Office of Sustainability, established in 2008, is responsible for oversight of climate action related to city operations as well as community-wide sustainability efforts. The Office addresses climate adaptation and mitigation strategies throughout city operations and provides public programming to address various aspects of resiliency and sustainability. Numerous surveys and studies, spearheaded by the Office, have been conducted over the years to better understand the current environmental performance and future climate hazards, including but not limited to a Climate Resilience Assessment and Plan, Municipal & Community-wide Greenhouse Gas Inventories, Heat Index Study, and Tree Canopy Assessments. These studies and surveys are made available to the public as well as other city departments, Administration, and the City Commission. In March 2021, the Mayor authorized the formation of the Climate Resilience & Infrastructure Committee focused on enhancing the current resilience program while bringing more accountability and structure city-wide. The City's Sustainability Advisory Committee, a nine-member committee of residents or individuals whose principal place of employment is in West Palm Beach, provides public stakeholder input and direction as it relates to the City's sustainability and climate-related efforts. As needed, the Office of Sustainability and the Sustainability Advisory Committee bring forward important climate-related science, news, technology, and opportunities to Administration.
column16: Climate-related risks and scenarios have been addressed in the City's Strategic Plan, as well as the City's Rethink Paradise: Sustainability Action Plan, both of which inform and provide guidance for city departments. Seven of the eight pillars of the City's Strategic Plan are modeled after the USGBC's LEED for Cities and Communities framework for a sustainable and resilient community (1) Arts, Neighborhoods, & Community Engagement; (2) Built Environment; (3) Climate and Energy; (4) Education, Economy & Jobs; (5) Equity & Empowerment; (6) Natural Systems; and (7) Public Health & Public Safety. The City's Rethink Paradise: Sustainability Action Plan is the principal guiding document for the City's on how to become a resilient community, sustainable, and equitable community. The Plan's recommendations, which are organized using the nine performance measures utilized by the USGBC's LEED for Cities and Communities Program, are a product of thorough review and analysis of the City's existing and planned activities, current opportunities, and long-term goals for meeting the challenges of climate change. In consideration of the city's objective to achieve climate resilience while addressing the need for adaptation strategies, the city has incorporated sustainability components into Capital Improvement Project planning forms, which require all city departments to address adaptation and mitigation during project planning and implementation.
column17: City departments address climate resilience and adaptation strategies in planning for future projects, through the City's Capital Improvement Project planning forms, which in some cases may require more funding at the start of the project. Energy and water efficiency-related measures have the potential to provide cost savings over time, which is considered and included in life cycle planning. Some infrastructure projects may be required entirely because of climate hazards, including rebuilding of sea walls or installation of tidal valves along the city's intercoastal waterway, adding strains to the capitol improvement and operations and maintenance budgets. To potentially relieve some of that strain, the City actively and strategic identifies and seeks grant funding for climate resilience-related infrastructure projects. Sea level rise projections are addressed in project planning to ensure long-term viability of impacted infrastructure in the city's coastal neighborhoods, reducing the occurrence of asset failure and additional projects needed later as the City continues to experience the effects of climate change.
column18: Some risks to the City as we transition to a low-carbon economy include the affordability and initial capital investment needed for some of the technology until the market adjusts and reduces cost, particularly for our low-income, historically disadvantaged communities. In addition, some technologies are difficult to come by and with the supply chain issues that the nation is experiencing this may only get worse. Some other factors that can make the transition difficult is the cost of living for this area is already high and having the added cost of low-carbon (whether that is upfront investment, carbon taxes, etc.) will only make it even more difficult for our residents to afford to live in our city. Lastly, another area that will be a limitation/risk as we transition is the lack of good/extensive public transportation options for the region, we are still heavily dependent on SOVs. Without a change in our transit options (providing more options that are low carbon) our transition will rely heavily on the individual resident to make that transition.

In response to international climate change and global warming, New Taipei City has actively promoted both climate change adaptation and mitigation. In 2007, the city established the Low Carbon Community Development Center under the Environmental Protection Department—the first local government in Taiwan to set up an independent unit dedicated to implementing carbon reduction measures.
In 2016, the city government formed an interdepartmental Climate Change Mitigation and Adaptation Promotion Group, comprising 17 departments, to collaboratively develop strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. This initiative was expanded in 2020 into the New Taipei City Climate Change and Energy Countermeasures Implementation Committee, and further reorganized in 2023 into the New Taipei City Climate Change Response Steering Groups.
The Steering Groups integrate resources across government agencies to advance energy transition, improve energy efficiency, promote smart transportation and circular economy, and enhance climate resilience. Their objectives include reducing and managing greenhouse gas emissions, building a city with adaptive capacity, developing sustainable energy systems, and fostering sustainable economic development. In addition, the Groups are tasked with formulating the city's climate and energy transition vision and strategies, reviewing major policy proposals, and supporting New Taipei City's participation in national and international climate change mitigation and adaptation initiatives.

1.Medium- and Long-Term Greenhouse Gas Reduction Targets in New Taipei City
The medium-term goal is to establish a zero-carbon demonstration zone in Bali District by 2030. Additionally, by 2030, the city aims to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 30% compared to the 2005 baseline year. The long-term goal is to achieve a 100% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, relative to 2005 levels, thereby reaching net-zero emissions.

2. The New Taipei City Climate Change Response Steering Groups are divided into four working groups, each with the following implementation objectives:
(1) Energy Transition and Efficiency Enhancement Group: Guided by the principles of local energy governance and public participation, this group promotes energy transition through public-private collaboration. It also emphasizes improving the efficiency and rationality of energy use, with the aim of establishing a sustainable energy system.
(2)Smart Transportation Group: This group integrates advanced information and communication technologies into transportation infrastructure to improve traffic safety and flow, enhance public mobility, and reduce the environmental impacts of the transport sector. 
(3) Circular Economy Group: Focusing on both production and consumption processes, the group seeks to improve resource efficiency and recycling practices. It also actively promotes innovative consumption models that foster co-benefits for both the environment and the economy.
(4) Resilient Adaptation Group: Centered on the principles of strengthening adaptive capacity, enhancing resilience, and reducing vulnerability, this group aims to mitigate the risks posed by climate change. It also works to improve disaster response and build self-recovery capabilities.

3. Execution method: 
(1) The New Taipei City Climate Change Response Steering Groups convenes twice a year. During these meetings, various municipal departments report on the implementation progress of climate change mitigation and adaptation policies. Experts and scholars are invited to provide professional advice, helping to refine policy directions and foster interdepartmental collaboration.
(2) Each of the four working groups under the Steering Groups also meets biannually to present their respective progress on policy implementation, consult with experts and scholars, and determine implementation priorities for the second half of the year.
(3) A total of 80 net-zero carbon projects have been proposed and are monitored by the Steering Groups, with progress updates provided on a quarterly basis.

New Taipei City is facing multiple impacts brought by climate change, which have clearly influenced the core thinking of urban planning, land use, and disaster prevention mechanisms. Firstly, rising sea levels and increasing storm surge risks pose potential threats of flooding and infrastructure safety in coastal areas and lowland river basins, further affecting the stability of coastal industries and energy supply. Secondly, the urban heat island effect—caused by high-density development and insufficient green space—has led to higher urban temperatures, increased use of air conditioning, and greater energy consumption, negatively impacting residential comfort and public health. In addition, for areas with historical disasters or high potential risks, existing land use management and development strategies urgently need to incorporate resilience and adaptation thinking, in order to ensure land use safety and enhance the carrying capacity of the urban environment.

In response to the above challenges, New Taipei City has formulated the New Taipei City Land Plan, which mandates a comprehensive review every five years. The plan serves as a key tool to address climate change adaptation and the sustainable use and management of natural resources. Aligned with the goals of the National Spatial Plan, it integrates regional development strategies, including the spatial framework of the “Three Rings and Six Lines” MRT network, to guide coordinated urban and rural development.

Through the lens of sustainable development—encompassing life, ecology, production, and living—the plan aims to preserve environmentally sensitive areas and high-quality agricultural land. It also promotes the creation of a resilient environment for industrial growth, high-quality housing, and well-planned public infrastructure, thereby strengthening the disaster prevention and response capacity of both urban and rural areas.

Furthermore, urban planning and spatial strategies are required to incorporate climate risk assessments and disaster response measures related to flooding, sea level rise, and extreme weather events. Adaptive strategies are being developed and implemented to ensure the safety of critical facilities. A dedicated chapter in the Land Plan, titled “Principles for Land Use Planning in Response to Climate Change,” outlines the city's climate risk analysis and mandates that urban plans incorporate climate mitigation and adaptation measures. In addition, the Plan is periodically adjusted in reference to both national adaptation strategies and the New Taipei City Climate Change Adaptation Action Plan, ensuring its ongoing alignment with evolving climate priorities and resilience needs.

Implementation of the New Taipei City Land Plan:
(1) Pro-Vitality - Promoting biophilia and advancing six-level agricultural development
A. Preserve biodiversity and expand green space.
B. Inner MRT core areas: develop edible urban landscapes, cultivate特色 industries, and promote leisure agriculture.
C. Outer suburban areas: promote six-level agricultural industrialization and safeguard the total area of agricultural land.
(2) Productive Living - Fostering emerging industries and revitalizing economic activity
A. MRT core areas: facilitate clustering of knowledge-based and innovative industries, support industrial upgrading, and strengthen international connectivity.
B. Outer suburban areas: revitalize existing industrial corridors, increase industrial added value, and enhance the overall investment environment.
(3) Peaceful Living - Enabling residents to live where their hearts belong
A. Build compact, smart cities and improve resource use efficiency.
B. MRT core areas: encourage integrated and mixed-use development to support local living.
C. Outer suburban areas: reinforce rural support for urban centers and attract youth to return to their hometowns.
(4) New Ecology - Responding to extreme climate and establishing a new ecological order
A. Strengthen adaptive capacity to climate change.
B. Prevent disorderly urban sprawl.
C. Build a harmonious ecosystem and implement a low-carbon, sustainable environment.

1. Risks in the Low-Carbon Equipment Market
In the early stages of transitioning to a low-carbon economy, the market for energy-efficient equipment remains underdeveloped. As a result, significant capital investment is required, potentially crowding out budgets for other municipal policies. To address this challenge, the New Taipei City Government has adopted the Energy Service Company (ESCO) model and the Private Finance Initiative (PFI) model to reduce the city's initial financial burden and mitigate the risks associated with large-scale capital investment.
For example, in the case of LED lighting replacement, the government does not allocate upfront procurement funds. Instead, service providers carry out the replacement work first, and the government pays for the service using the cost savings from reduced electricity consumption. The ESCO model has been applied to replace lighting in community parking lots and schools, while the PFI model is used for the replacement of streetlights across the city.

2. Technological Risks and Legal Issues
To advance the low-carbon transition, the New Taipei City Government collaborates with the private sector through various emerging models. During the process of replacing conventional equipment with low-carbon alternatives, technical risks may arise, and legal disputes with vendors may occur. Therefore, appropriate risk management strategies must be developed and implemented.
For instance, municipal waste in New Taipei City is processed by three incineration plants, all constructed between 1994 and 2001, and thus have been in operation for over 20 years. To enhance incineration efficiency and electricity generation, while reducing greenhouse gas emissions, air pollutants, and fly ash output, two of the facilities have already undergone renovation. The remaining Bali Incineration Plant is scheduled for renovation between 2024 and 2028, using the ROT (Rehabilitate-Operate-Transfer) model under private participation in public infrastructure.
Throughout the renovation process, risks are categorized and managed based on different implementation phases.
(1)Construction Phase:: Risks include construction delays (due to material supply issues or other unforeseen factors), cost overruns (caused by inadequate cost control or inconsistencies between design and on-site conditions), and technical or quality issues. If sufficient funding is not secured in a timely manner, overall project progress may be affected.
(2)Operation Phase: Potential risks include revenue shortfalls (if income from waste treatment and electricity sales is lower than expected), operational interruptions (due to equipment failures), and cost overruns.
(3)Transfer Phase: There may be a decline in the quality of transferred assets due to equipment aging at the end of the concession period.
(4)Force Majeure and Other Risks:
These include natural disasters, changes in laws and regulations, civil protests, and financial instability.
To manage these risks, the city government has developed corresponding countermeasures, including enhanced project planning and monitoring, incorporation of specific risk-handling mechanisms in contract terms, and transferring risk through insurance instruments.

column15: <減緩>2010年成立「屏東低碳家園暨永續發展推動委員會」，推動屏東縣可持續發展、溫室氣體控制及氣候變化適應。 屏東縣政府每年都完成碳排放盤查，致力於在2050年實現零碳排放的目標。縣政府在2013年完成了第一次全市排放清單的第三方核查。 屏東縣政府遵循中央政府發布的清查和計算指南。 分析各排放部門的相關清單數據，作為屏東縣管理減碳策略的參考。為響應國際能源署（IEA）於2021年5月18日公佈的《淨零排放2050：全球能源產業路線圖》，屏東縣也致力落實淨零排放路線圖，2018年至2020年的成果已減少了116,000噸二氧化碳當量。屏東縣因應碳排放狀況及地方特色，提出住宅、工業、交通、能源、農業、林業五個主要減碳課題，以達至2050年淨零排放目標。<調適>屏東縣因地制宜推行相關政策，以應對氣候變化的挑戰。 該縣開展社區研討，選擇氣候災害風險高的社區舉辦“社區氣候變化研討會”。 屏東縣通過“社區適應氣候變化（Community-based adaptation to climate change, CBA）”和“參與能力與脆弱性分析（Participatory Capacity and Vulnerability Analysis, PCVA）”進行互動討論，確認居民的災害經歷和社區現有的軟硬體資源。同時參考未來社區發展方向彙整資訊，從中探討出符合社區在地調適策略與作為，引導居民對社區環境自我發想，逐漸提升社區因應氣候變遷能力，進而減少氣候變遷衝擊，自2019年本府陸續於東片社區、力里社區、興安社區等地透過CBA及PCVA協助進行如雨水監測器、降溫設施、綠能設施等相關建置，協助地方厚實氣候變遷調適能力。<Mitigation>\'Low-Carbon Homeland and Sustainable Development Promotion Committee (屏東低碳家園暨永續發展推動委員會)\' was established in 2010 to promote sustainable development, greenhouse gas control and climate change adaptation in Pingtung County. Pingtung County Government completes a carbon emission inventory every year and dedicates to achieving the goal of zero carbon emission by 2050.First, the County Government completed the first city-wide emission inventory in 2013 with third-party verification. Pingtung County Government followed the inventory and calculation guidelines issued by the central government. The relevant inventory data of various emission departments were analyzed as a reference for Pingtung County to manage the strategy of reducing carbon emissions.In response to the \'Net Zero 2050: A Roadmap for the Global Energy Sector\' announced by International Energy Agency (IEA) on May 18, 2021, Pingtung County also put efforts into the roadmap of Net Zero and the result from 2018 to 2020 has reduced 116,000 tons of CO2e. Considering about conditions of carbon emissions and local features, Pingtung County proposed five main topics to implement carbon reduction, including residential housing, industry, transportation, energy, agriculture, and forestry, to achieve the target of net-zero emissions by 2050.<Adaption>Pingtung County promoted related policies based on local conditions to face the challenges of climate change. The County conducted community-based discussions, and selected communities at risk of climate disasters to hold a \' Community-based Seminar of climate change\'. Through \'Community-based adaptation to climate change (CBA)\' and \'Participatory Capacity and Vulnerability Analysis (PCVA)\', Pingtung County conducted interactive discussions to acknowledge residents' experiences of disasters and the existing software and hardware resources of the community.At the same time, Pingtung County reviewed future development directions of the communities to gather information, and discussed the local adaptation strategies, leading the residents to think more about their environment and strengthen their ability to face climate change. Since 2019, Pingtung County has assisted Dong-pian Community, Ralekeleke Community, and Xing-an Community in the implementation of rainwater monitors, cooling facilities, green energy facilities, and other related facilities, assisting local governments to enhance their ability to face climate change.
column16: 2009年颱風莫拉克3天內為屏東帶來超過3,000毫米的降雨，嚴重破壞西部沿海城鎮的農場和漁塘，並導致停電超過15天。台電公司因電力設備維修困難 橋樑倒塌或洪水氾濫。 因此，屏東縣政府計劃以100%綠色電力滿足國內用電需求，並於2016年成立首個綠能辦公室。本府2016年成立「綠能專案推動辦公室」後，為因地制宜推動再生能源，陸續擬定綠能相關自治條例來回應中央政策，包含：1. 2016年率全國之先推動「光電農棚」2. 2018年專案專區推動「嚴重地層下陷區光電計畫」3. 2022年公告「屏東縣綠色能源開發管理自治條例」本縣實施「屏東縣綠建築自治條例」後，陸續增訂相關配套法令及補助辦法，如：太陽光電設施、屏東厝設計回饋、立體綠化補助、既有建築綠改造、聰明基地設計、建築綠亮點等相關辦法、計畫及活動，尋找屬於在地的風土建築，並以點、線、面漸進式串聯出整體鄉鎮風貌，無論新舊或公私有建物皆能參與綠建築政策，落實綠建築普及化並融入建築管理，解決既存違章、屋頂鐵皮、窳漏空間、病態建築等問題，找到屬於在地建築之認同性、識別性、自明性與未來性，成為領先各鄉鎮地方的綠建築潮流。Typhoon Morakot dumped more than 3,000 mm of rain in Pingtung within 3 days, severely damaging farms and fishery ponds in the western coastal towns and resulting in power outage for over 15 days in 2009. Tai-power company had difficulty in repairing electricity equipment because of bridge collapse or flooding. As a consequence, Pingtung County Government planned to have 100% green power to satisfy the need of domestic electricity and established the first “Green Energy Promotion Office” in 2016. The Green Energy Promotion Office aims to promote projects and policies of renewable energy. Significant results are described as below:1. The 1st solar rooftop farm was promoted in 2016.2. The \'Specific Zone for PV Projects\' and \'Severe Subsidence Area Project\' in 2018.3. Pingtung's Green Energy Management Policy is set in 2022.Pingtung County added supplementary laws and subsidy regulations, such as rules of solar photovoltaic facilities, Pingtung LOHAS Building design and feedback, subsidies for vertical planting, green renovation of existing buildings, smart base designs, green highlights constructions and other related plans. Pingtung County found styles of local buildings and connected all of them. All the buildings can join in this green building policy, whether these buildings are old or new, public or private.Pingtung County universalized green buildings with building management to solve existing problems, such as illegal constructions, iron sheets roofs, leaky buildings, and sick buildings. The County found the identity, recognition, characteristics and future of local buildings, and become the leading trend of green buildings in Taiwan.
column17: 能源治理部分，本府2016年起自空氣污染防制基金編列經費，以自籌款持續營運綠能推動事務，同時配合能源局逐年政策，提案參與「直轄市及縣（市）政府推廣再生能源補助計畫」、「地方政府推動再生能源設置專區補助」，爭取中央補助經費，惟近年相關補助申請限制條件繁瑣，使用範疇尚不符本府綠能業務實際推動需求，爰此本府後續將依「屏東縣綠色能源開發管理自治條例」，透過管理推動委員會研議「綠色能源開發管理基金(以下簡稱綠能基金)」編列綠能推動經費之可行性，彌補中央補助經費不足之處，同時作為穩定經費來源。而綠能基金收入來源，則包括依預算程序撥充之款項收入、基金孳息收入、捐贈收入以及其他收入，亦包含本府專區專案推動太陽光電案場，按行政契約事項捐贈之光電案場建置完工售電金。屏東縣於2017年啟動「嚴重沉降區（SSA）」項目，以推廣太陽能。縣政府減免改變土地類別的行政費用。土地所有者可向太陽能業者收取土地租金，而太陽能業者則可通過出售獲得收益。此外，太陽能業者還將售電收入的2%作為“綠色基金”提供給縣政府，用於開發更多的綠色能源。而綠能基金收入來源，則包括依預算程序撥充之款項收入、基金孳息收入、捐贈收入以及其他收入，亦包含本府專區專案推動太陽光電案場，按行政契約事項捐贈之光電案場建置完工售電金。Pingtung County government has designated budget from Air Pollution Prevention Fund since 2016, and operated the green energy promotion by self-financing. column15:
Çanakkale Municipality is responsible for the strategic oversight and coordination of all climate-related policies and actions within its jurisdiction. The Climate Change and Zero Waste Directorate plays a central role in implementing and coordinating initiatives aimed at reducing air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. It is also responsible for the development, execution, and alignment of relevant projects across municipal units.

The Directorate closely monitors national and international developments concerning greenhouse gas recovery, disposal, and ozone layer protection, while formulating local policies and strategies in compliance with current legislation. It leads the preparation and implementation of the Climate Change Action Plan, establishing databases and inventories to facilitate inter-departmental coordination. Progress is continuously monitored and evaluated to enhance the city's resilience against climate change.

In addition, the Directorate provides guidance for projects developed under the Climate Change Action Plan, fosters collaboration among stakeholders, and identifies potential incentives and funding opportunities. It ensures that the municipality's Strategic Plan and annual programs are aligned with climate objectives. Through participation in national and international fairs, congresses, seminars, and workshops, the Directorate promotes public awareness and engagement.

The Directorate also carries out resource and waste management activities in line with national legislation and sustainable development principles. It is responsible for the planning, establishment, and monitoring of the Zero Waste Management System, ensuring compliance with guidelines and regulations issued by the Ministry of Environment, Urbanization, and Climate Change. All activities are documented, certified, and shared with relevant institutions and the public. In accordance with the Waste Management Regulation, the municipality prioritizes material recovery and recycling processes to reduce environmental impacts and protect public health.

Oversight of climate-related initiatives is maintained by the Municipal Council and the Mayor's Office, with regular evaluation of progress toward sustainability and resilience targets. Furthermore, inter-departmental Climate Officers within the municipality, along with the Climate Ambassadors project—supported by UNDP and implemented in partnership with the Turkey-Europe Foundation—ensure that urban planning, transportation, water management, and energy efficiency policies are aligned with the Climate Action Plan.

Additionally, projects carried out during initiatives such as European Week for Waste Reduction and World Environment Day make positive contributions to climate change mitigation. The municipality collaborates with national and international institutions, local universities, and civil society organizations to collect data, implement emission reduction projects, and ensure transparency in climate-related reporting. Through public participation and awareness campaigns, community involvement in the climate management process is actively promoted, thereby strengthening accountability and fostering a shared sense of responsibility for sustainable urban development.
column16:
Climate-related issues have significantly influenced Çanakkale Municipality's master development planning and urban policy framework. The Municipality integrates climate adaptation and mitigation strategies into all key spatial and strategic planning processes to ensure a resilient, sustainable, and low-carbon urban future.

Within the framework of the Çanakkale Province Climate Change Action Plan prepared in 2023 and the Municipality's strategic plan, a foundational framework has been established to ensure that urban development projects align with emission reduction targets and the renewable energy vision. In new development areas, increasing green spaces, implementing energy-efficient building standards, and planning for low-emission transportation have become priorities. Additionally, pedestrian accessibility and energy efficiency are promoted to reduce transportation-related emissions. Collaboration with local universities and experts ensures that climate data and projections are integrated into decision-making processes.

Overall, climate considerations have become a guiding principle in Çanakkale's urban planning, ensuring that all development activities progress in alignment with the city's goals for sustainability, resilience, and climate neutrality.

column18:
The transition to a low-carbon economy presents various social, economic, and institutional risks for Çanakkale Municipality. While the main goal is to achieve environmental sustainability, the transition process also brings significant financial challenges.

1. Economic and Financial Risks:

Changes in energy prices, carbon pricing, or incentive structures may increase operational costs for municipal services and local businesses.

Limited access to financing for green projects may slow down the municipality's climate mitigation and adaptation efforts.

2. Regulatory and Policy Risks:

Compliance with national and international climate regulations may require rapid adaptation of municipal policies and planning processes.

Failure to meet emission reduction targets could result in penalties or restrictions on development projects.

3. Social and Community Risks:

Decisions made by the administration regarding climate-resilient urban development in areas such as energy efficiency, waste management, and water use may impose additional financial burdens on the public.

Challenges may arise in public acceptance and participation during the implementation of new low-carbon infrastructure or policies.

4. Operational and Technical Risks:

Renovations may be required in municipal and private building infrastructure (buildings, energy systems, etc.) to meet low-carbon standards, which could entail additional financial costs.

Limited technical capacity or expertise in implementing renewable energy and energy efficiency solutions may delay the transition process.

Overall, the transition to a low-carbon economy presents both challenges and opportunities. Although short-term financial and operational adjustments may be necessary, proactive planning, stakeholder engagement, and strategic investments enhance the city's resilience, economic sustainability, and community well-being.

column16: Høje-Taastrup Municipality is growing and creating growth while emitting less CO2. This development must continue and be strengthened by incorporating green transition into all planning of the smart city by applying new knowledge and technology. Høje-Taastrup Municipality goes all in with the Paris Agreement and the climate goals of the Danish parliament: This means that we must reduce CO2 emissions by 50% from 2017 to 2030 in order to reach the goal of 70% less CO2 emissions by 2030 compared to 1990. The long-term goal is net zero emission by 2050.This must be achieved through our climate development plan as stated:• Efficient energy consumption• Fossil free heating by 2030 at the latest• More solar power plants in Høje-Taastrup Municipality• Gradual electrification of transportClimate Plan 2030 describes the way to achieve the ambitious goals, but we cannot as a municipality succeed on our own. We therefore wish to intensify existing cooperations and invite new ones with citizens, enterprises and housing societies in the municipality and across municipal boundaries and with utility companies. In Høje-Taastrup, climate and energy are not additional aspects or a project but rather a part of a secure and modern life. It is part of everyday life in a municipality with growth, which is why we can say that we are the Municipality in Denmark with the greenest growth.

column18: Air, soil, and water pollution, along with the impacts of climate change, are disproportionately borne by communities with lower political capital and financial resources to contest these hazards, namely Black, Indigenous, people of color, working-class communities, and future generations. This pattern of unjustly displacing the costs of growth has enabled the climate crisis we face now. Addressing climate change, therefore, requires that we not only eliminate greenhouse gas emissions but also build just and equitable systems that restore and grow, rather than extract and diminish, the shared health and wealth of communities and ecosystems. However, without a deliberate focus on just and equitable strategies, the policies and programs Medford implement to address climate change could exacerbate inequity.

column15: Desde el año 2014 se cuenta con una Comisión Cantonal de Cambio Climático que ha trabajado en diferentes planes, inventarios y proyectos. El cambio climático se incluyó como un eje transversal para la planificación estratégica y territorial. Se cuenta con una Política Cantonal de Cambio Climático, 3 inventarios de GEI, plan de mitigación, plan de adaptación, plan de acción climática, hoja de ruta de economía circular, estudio de gestión de riesgo para el cantón, entre otros. Toda esta información ha sido incluida en el plan estratégico municipal, en la nueva actualización del Plan Regulador, así como en los planes anuales operativos de las unidades técnicas.
column16: Actualmente, debido a la información generada y a la estrategia con que se cuenta, se ha incluido la información en los diferentes proyectos a desarrollar año con año. Existen muchos proyectos que se han modificado o diseñado basado en la información generada. Una de las mejores y más importantes decisiones fue la implementación del diseño basado en la ciencia, infraestructura pública con blindaje climático, soluciones basadas en la naturaleza, decisión de ser ciudad esponja y los estudios y tarifas asociados al pago por servicios ambientales. Se cuenta con muchos proyectos que han sido el resultado de la investigación y la decisión oportuna, cambiando la visión cortoplacista, por una visión local pero con impacto global, con plazos en rangos para tener resultados rápidos y a mediano y largo plazo.
column17: A través de la investigación y de la mejor planificación del desarrollo municipal incluyendo el cambio climático como un eje transversal y estratégico, se ha logrado convencer a los tomadores de decisiones de la importancia de invertir en proyectos para mitigar GEI y para adaptarse al cambio climático. La Comisión Cantonal de Cambio Climático cuenta con su propio presupuesto municipal, el cual se puede invertir en investigación, divulgación y proyectos. Además de que las diferentes unidades técnicas como planificación urbana, Acueducto Municipal, Unidad Ambiental, Unidad de Saneamiento Ambiental, Obras Públicas, Comité de Movilidad Urbana Sostenible, Plan Regulador y otras, cuentan con presupuesto para invertir en proyectos basados en la ciencia, basados en datos ya generados para el cantón en temas como gestión de riesgo, blindaje climático, etc. Se ha logrado cambiar la perspectiva de que esto es un gasto y más bien se ve como una inversión, pues aún cuando en el presente los costos pueden ser más altos, tendremos proyectos asistiendo las verdaderas necesidades de la ciudad, de las personas que se encuentran en mayor vulnerabilidad y riesgo, y atendiendo los problemas de desarrollo y planificación que se tenían antes. La Comisión Cantonal de Cambio Climático es una instancia colegiada, donde además participan regidores del Concejo Municipal, por lo que los proyectos han logrado tener un verdadero impacto en todo: desde el cambio de perspectiva hasta la planificación financiera del municipio.
column18: Inicialmente se piensa que la transición debe darse en un escenario de manera gradual, progresiva, responsable y confiable. Los esfuerzos que se han realizado hasta ahora en estos temas, han sido participativos y en procesos de co- creación, pues el cantón de Belén es un cantón que cuenta con grandes desafíos, ya que es la ciudad con la mayor cantidad de recurso hídrico (nacientes para el abastecimiento de agua potable) de la Gran Área Metropolitana, y también (muy contrastante), la ciudad con la mayor cantidad de empresas transnacionales, industrias muy grandes y poderosas. El desarrollo ha ido migrando desde los años 80-90, pasando de un cantón agropecuario, a uno residencial, industrial, comercial y ahora que brinda servicios a través de call centers, etc. Los mayores riesgos en poder descarbonizar la economía en Belén están relacionados con la normativa y su aplicación en el territorio. Ni siquiera a nivel nacional hay regulación respecto a muchos de estos temas, parte de lo que se realiza es voluntario, y con el cambio de gobierno nacional, muchos de los programas nacionales se encuentran varados. Otro de los riesgos es la falta de inversión o el cierre de industrias (parte de los impuestos del municipio dependen de éstas) si se limita parte de la inversión por no transicionar a una economía baja en carbono, de ahí la importancia de incluir a todos los stakeholders en los procesos. Las políticas deben de encaminarse a esta transición, pero gradualmente. Asimismo, es necesario trabajar en la educación y sensibilización en estos temas, ya que parte de los riesgos pueden asociarse a la falta de conocimiento de los beneficios y repercusiones positivas asociadas a esta transición. Otro riesgo o reto también son el alto porcentaje de edificaciones que se tienen, que requiere modernizarse, pensar inicialmente en la eficiencia energética y luego en una transición si ésta es factible. Se requiere un papel protagónico de la Municipalidad, pero un apoyo invaluable del sector privado. Por otro lado, puede existir un incremento del precio de materias primas y del desarrollo de los cambios asociados para privados y públicos, sin contar con financiamientos apropiados o incentivos suficientes para su implementación.

column15: Oversight of climate-related issues and climate change related strategies are monitored and evaluated via several mechanisms. Progress on the Council's Climate Change Strategy which considers climate-related issues facing the city, is reported to the Executive Members for Environment and Climate Emergency. Updates are also provided to the Corporate Services, Climate Change and Scrutiny Management Committee who monitor performance of the council and city against the net-zero ambition. In addition, the Council's Climate Change and Natural Capital Programme Board provides oversight of climate related issues, monitors progress, identifies opportunities and manages risk relating to the Climate Change Programme, and ensures the Programme delivers in line with core principles. Identified risks and delays are escalated through the Directorate Management Team for Governance and the Corporate Management Team as appropriate. The York Climate Commission provides independent advice and expertise to support development and delivery of the strategy . The York Climate Commission represents and reflects public and private sector representatives from across the City of York to deliver action, strategic oversight and monitoring for the progression of the city's climate change agenda.
column16: York's Council's Local Plan Local Plan has an important role in tackling climate change and delivering wider sustainable development goals in line with the National Planning Policy Framework (2012) (NPPF). This means delivering our social, economic aspirations and legal duties without compromising the environmental limits of York for current and future generations.Key policies include: - Policy CC1 - Renewable and Low Carbon Energy Generation and Storage will be encouraged and supported in York. - Policy CC2 - Sustainable Design and Construction of New Development. On site minimum carbon reduction of 31% for all residential developments and a water consumption rate of 110 litres per person per day. All new non-residential buildings with a total internal floor area of 100m¬2 or greater should achieve a 28% emissions reduction and BREEAM 'Excellent' (or equivalent). Conversion of existing buildings to residential use should achieve BREEAM domestic refurbishment 'Very Good' and proposals for non-residential conversion of change of use will need to achieve BREEAM non-domestic refurbishment and fit out 'Excellent'. -CC3 - Decentralised Energy Networks: The council strongly supports the development of decentralised energy where the power source of such a network is non-fossil fuel based. The Council is producing a Sustainability and Climate Change Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) which addresses the requirements for new and retrofitted projects in light of climate change and the contributing factors arising from the built environment. The SPD will several areas of the jurisdiction's planning, including, but not limited to: energy, movement, land use, water, materials, waste, climate resilience, regenerative development and social value.
column17: City of York Council's Capital Budget 2024/25 to 2028/29 illustrates how climate related issues have impacted the Councils financial approach across a variety of areas including housing, transport and energy efficiency. For instance, financial planning for transport has considered climate-related issues via new proposals for EV Charging infrastructure, continued initiatives surrounding the Council's fleet replacement policy. Financial planning for housing and development also considers climate-related issues. This budget reflects the second year of delivering the Housing Investment and Energy Retrofit Plan 20232028 via Major Repairs & Modernisation of LA Homes to allow achievement of key objective that all homes will meet and retain the governments Decent Homes Standard DHS. This focuses on improving the energy efficiency of homes. The Council's Capital Budget 2024/25 to 2028/29 considers a variety of new general fund schemes comprised of external funding, including renewable heating upgrade, LED lighting conversion and EV infrastructure. The Council's Capital Budget 2025/26 to 2029/30 includes new proposals for additional funding relating to climate change including leisure facilities solar arrays, riverbank repairs (riverside path). Programmes continuing include Fleet Replacement, Park Investment and ongoing building improvements via Asset Management. Carbon Reduction is a Project assessment factor in developing and initiating all major projects.
column18: The Carbon Reduction Team keeps a Risks Log to monitor, manage and mitigate the risks associated with City of York Council's Carbon Reduction Programme, whose strategy focuses on the transition to a low-carbon economy. The risks identified thus far include:-Lack of public/political support for Climate Change Strategy-Reduced Carbon Reduction Budget limits ability to deliver-Significant infrastructure projects increasing carbon emissions-Reduced staff capacity in service delivery teams to complete work programmeThe Equalities Impact Assessment for the Climate Change Strategy also documents the potential risks/impacts associated with the Strategy in addition to mitigation actions. Risks associated with individual projects implemented to manage help York to transition towards low-carbon economy will be managed within the project management documentation by the appropriate manager and governance structure.

The Vijayawada Climate Resilient City Action Plan (CRCAP) 2047 is prepared through joint stakeholder consultation involving various departments that are implementing entities in the action plan. This action plan includes a GPC-compliant GHG emissions inventory, ward and area-level vulnerability and risk assessment, and scenario planning based on various National and State Government targets. The city has established a Climate Core Team chaired by the Municipal Commissioner and comprising heads of various departments. In addition, a Stakeholder Committee has been formed to review the CRCAP's strategies and sector-specific actions, and to prioritize projects through a participatory approach aimed at achieving net-zero emissions by 2047 through the adoption of sustainable energy and innovative solutions in city infrastructure and municipal service delivery.

Vijayawada is actively working on the National Clean Air Program, which aims to reduce air pollution through improved monitoring and control of pollutants, Swachh Bharat Mission, which focuses on solid waste management and AMRUT mission to achieve 100% coverage of water supply, sewerage, stormwater and solid waste services.

column17: Vijayawada Municipal Corporation does not have specific budget allocations dedicated solely to climate change mitigation or adaptation in its financial planning. However, provisions for such allocations are expected to be considered during future financial planning, basis the upcoming Climate Resilient Action Plan 2047. Recent flooding caused by the overflow of the Budameru rivulet has severely affected the ULB's financial stability. Extensive emergency response operations—including rescue efforts, temporary shelters, and medical assistance—have substantially increased operational expenditures. Simultaneously, infrastructure damage and disruptions to economic activities have reduced tax revenues. A significant share of capital spending has been redirected toward the repair and reconstruction of damaged infrastructure. The government has conducted loss and damage assessments and provided relief support to affected individuals and communities. To enhance resilience, the ULB has initiated several climate adaptation measures, including the removal of encroachments along the Budameru rivulet, embankment strengthening, installation of real-time water flow sensors, desilting operations, and the enhancement of early warning systems.
column18: Vijayawada will be on track to transition to a low-carbon economy following the implementation of the Climate Resilient City Action Plan, which requires coordinated efforts from all stakeholders, particularly the DISCOMs, APSRTC, and the private concessionaire. However, the city's technical capacity to access climate finance, particularly international finance, is limited. Though VMC has advanced in adopting several technological solutions across its infrastructure and service delivery, the institutional capacity to operate and maintain these interventions remains challenging.

The “Environmental Protection and Control Directorate” was officially renamed the “Climate Change and Zero Waste Directorate” on June 10, 2022, aligning our institutional structure with global climate goals and national sustainability frameworks. Despite the district's challenging demographic and geographic context, the Directorate has delivered pioneering projects, is implementing new ones, and has a pipeline of further actions that strengthen climate oversight across Beşiktaş.

Scope of responsibilities includes source-separated collection of packaging (paper, metal, plastic, glass), textiles, used vegetable oil, waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE), expired medicines, batteries and accumulators, organic waste, end-of-life tires, and mineral oils. Household, bulky and pruning waste are collected by the Cleaning Services Directorate; excavation/debris waste by the Construction Works Directorate; medical and hazardous waste by the Metropolitan Municipality. Beyond waste, the Directorate conducts compliance inspections (odor/smoke emissions, noise, asbestos, licenses and other checks) to prevent pollution and protect public health.

Beşiktaş has long been a national pioneer. In 1994, separation and collection of packaging waste at the source started here for the first time in Türkiye. In 2014, a compost pilot began and projects to restrict plastic bag use were launched. In 2017, under the Ho-Re-Ca initiative, separate glass collection from hotels, restaurants and cafes increased recovery efficiency and quality. The municipality is the first district in Türkiye to calculate, verify and neutralize its institutional carbon footprint, achieving a zero-carbon footprint status. Since 2017, the ISO 14001 Environmental Management System has been in place and a zero-waste certificate has been obtained.

Public engagement is central. The Directorate organizes hands-on trainings, workshops, awareness campaigns, social responsibility projects, social media content, festivals and fairs for students and adults, embedding recycling and climate literacy district-wide. Digital tools reinforce oversight: the “Recycle & Win” mobile app (launched 2021) makes source separation smarter; the environmental portal was renewed and made mobile-friendly in 2024 and continues to be actively used in 2025.

Governance and oversight processes, consistent with our 2024 response to Q1.3.1, are embedded across the organization: climate-related issues are integrated into performance objectives; responsibilities are assigned to management-level positions; issues are considered in plans/strategies, risk management policies and budgeting/major capital expenditures; responsibilities are assigned to committees/subcommittees; and relevant departments, committees and subcommittees are informed by management about climate-related issues. These processes provide the governance backbone for cross-departmental coordination and systematic monitoring.

International alignment: Beşiktaş Municipality voluntarily signed the Covenant of Mayors to combat climate change, fully aligned with the objectives of the Paris Agreement, signed on November 30, 2015. Through this platform, the municipality aims to intensify efforts to secure funding and develop partnerships that accelerate emission reductions, resilience and just transition measures.

Strategic planning and implementation: The Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP), launched on July 19, 2023, aims to increase energy efficiency, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, strengthen climate resilience and chart long-term climate-neutral pathways for the district. Using 2022 data, a district-wide greenhouse gas inventory was completed in June 2024; forward-looking actions are now being implemented. The SECAP sets a 41.6% emissions-reduction target by 2030, aligning the district with European and global decarbonization trajectories and providing a measurable, time-bound framework for accountability.

Looking ahead, planned and ongoing activities include establishing an integrated environmental monitoring system; creating a certification scheme that encourages establishments to adopt nature-friendly, resource-efficient practices; promoting green buildings and energy-efficient retrofits; and expanding renewable and other sustainable energy use across the district. These measures reinforce Beşiktaş Municipality's role as a proactive climate actor with robust oversight, international alignment and a clear pathway toward a resilient, low-carbon future for residents and businesses alike.
column16:
Climate change has become a defining factor in shaping Beşiktaş district's master and development planning. Rising average temperatures, intensified urban heat island effects, and the increasing frequency of floods, heavy rainfall events, and periodic droughts across Istanbul represent significant risks for the district. Beşiktaş's dense urban fabric amplifies heat stress, while stormwater flooding during intense rainfall and water scarcity during prolonged dry periods expose the district to dual climate threats. These recurring risks have fundamentally influenced the way local authorities plan infrastructure, housing, energy, and social policies.

Urban resilience and green infrastructure:
The rising number of heavy rainfall incidents has highlighted the need for improved stormwater management and climate-resilient infrastructure. Master plans now prioritize sustainable drainage systems, permeable surfaces, rainwater harvesting, and flood-resilient public spaces. To counter the urban heat island effect, development strategies focus on increasing and preserving green areas, creating ecological corridors, and promoting rooftop gardens and vertical greening. These nature-based solutions reduce heat stress while enhancing biodiversity and liveability.

Water management and drought adaptation:
Frequent droughts affecting Istanbul have directly impacted Beşiktaş's planning priorities. The district integrates water efficiency into development frameworks, including modernizing distribution systems, reducing leakages, encouraging water-saving technologies, and incorporating water reuse in public facilities. Planning policies also aim to protect natural water resources and ensure sustainable supply under changing climate conditions.

Energy transition and emissions reduction:
Energy efficiency and renewable integration are central in long-term planning. Development plans promote solar panels on municipal and residential buildings, energy retrofits, sustainable construction materials, and smart metering. These measures align with the Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP), launched in July 2023, which sets a binding target of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 41.6% by 2030. Based on the district-wide greenhouse gas inventory completed in June 2024, SECAP ensures that emission reduction targets are embedded into zoning regulations, urban renewal projects, and infrastructure investments.

Sustainable mobility and transport planning:
Master planning increasingly addresses climate risks through transport strategies. Pedestrian zones, bicycle lanes, and electrification of public transport are being prioritized to reduce fossil-fuel dependency. By decreasing local emissions, these initiatives also contribute to healthier, climate-resilient urban environments.

Social resilience and disaster preparedness:
Planning processes now emphasize inclusive adaptation measures. Public spaces are being designed as both recreational areas and emergency assembly points during disasters. Vulnerable groups—including the elderly, children, and low-income households—are considered priority beneficiaries of resilience policies. This reflects a shift from purely physical infrastructure planning to integrated socio-environmental resilience.

International alignment and long-term vision:
Beşiktaş Municipality's planning approach is shaped by international frameworks. As a signatory of the Covenant of Mayors, the district is committed to targets consistent with the Paris Agreement (signed November 30, 2015). Local master plans explicitly integrate global climate objectives and national sustainability strategies, ensuring coherence with EU and UN pathways toward climate neutrality by mid-century.

Looking ahead:
Future planning includes the establishment of an environmental monitoring and certification system, expansion of renewable energy, promotion of green building standards, and systematic inclusion of resilience criteria in new development permits. These actions demonstrate that climate-related issues—especially flooding, extreme weather, and drought risks—are not occasional concerns but frequent realities that actively shape Beşiktaş's development strategies. As a result, the district's master planning has been redefined to prioritize sustainability, resilience, and alignment with international climate commitments, securing a low-carbon and climate-resilient future for its residents.
column17:
Climate-related issues have significantly influenced Beşiktaş Municipality's financial planning by highlighting the scale and urgency of investments required for both mitigation and adaptation. The increasing likelihood of floods, extreme rainfall, droughts, and rising temperatures has made it clear that there is no upper limit to the financial resources needed to address climate risks effectively. For this reason, climate change considerations are now embedded in all financial strategies and budgetary decisions.

Under the coordination of the Climate Change and Zero Waste Directorate, comprehensive risk assessments have been conducted to evaluate the consequences of climate change. The Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP), launched in 2023 and supported by the district-wide greenhouse gas inventory completed in June 2024, provides a data-driven framework that confirms the accuracy of financial planning decisions made so far. It also ensures that financial strategies are aligned with emission reduction targets, resilience-building goals, and international climate commitments.

A significant portion of the municipal budget is now dedicated to climate-related priorities. These include investments in roadworks and transportation infrastructure designed to reduce traffic congestion, minimize noise, and cut emissions; renewal of drainage and stormwater systems to improve flood resilience; expansion and maintenance of green spaces to mitigate the urban heat island effect; and promotion of renewable energy and energy-efficient building retrofits. These expenditures are not short-term expenses but long-term investments that generate cumulative savings and reduce vulnerability to future climate shocks.

Beşiktaş's unique demographic and spatial dynamics amplify its financial challenges. The district is a cultural hub and transportation gateway, attracting hundreds of thousands of visitors daily, far exceeding the registered resident population. This fluctuating and sometimes logarithmically expanding population magnifies the environmental pressures on infrastructure and services, thereby multiplying the financial resources required for climate mitigation and adaptation. The result is an exceptionally high level of demand for resilient infrastructure, sustainable mobility, and resource-efficient urban services.

To meet these growing demands, the municipality continuously seeks external funds and develops sustainable financing policies. This includes applying for grant programs provided by international organizations, forming partnerships with private sector actors, and leveraging national and EU-level funding mechanisms. Financial planning is therefore increasingly outward-looking, ensuring that external support complements municipal resources. Such an approach reduces the municipality's exposure to financial risks, diversifies its funding base, and ensures continuity in climate projects even under fiscal constraints.

The long-term financial planning framework of Beşiktaş emphasizes sustainable returns: upfront investments in resilient infrastructure, green spaces, and energy efficiency deliver long-term cost savings and reduced exposure to damages. By embedding climate considerations into the budgeting cycle, the municipality ensures that every lira spent contributes to adaptation, mitigation, or both. This strategic orientation reflects a commitment to providing higher quality of life for residents while ensuring fiscal sustainability.

Through partnerships with national and international stakeholders, Beşiktaş Municipality aims to build a robust, widely supported financial structure that positions the district as a leader in climate resilience. By linking local financial planning with global climate goals—including those of the Paris Agreement—the municipality demonstrates that climate action is not an optional expense but a core financial responsibility, integrated into the district's overall development and governance strategies.
column18:
The transition to a low-carbon economy represents a strategic necessity for Beşiktaş Municipality, but it also carries complex risks that directly affect financial planning, infrastructure, and social stability. As a densely populated district, cultural hub, and transportation gateway that receives large numbers of daily visitors, Beşiktaş faces unique transition challenges that must be carefully managed to avoid unintended economic and social consequences.

Economic challenges
The downsizing or restructuring of sectors with a high carbon footprint may lead to job losses, reduced economic activity, and investments becoming unviable. Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which make up the backbone of Beşiktaş's local economy, may face additional costs to comply with stricter emissions regulations. For businesses in hospitality, retail, and services—sectors central to Beşiktaş's economy—the introduction of carbon pricing or new sustainability standards could increase operational expenses and potentially reduce competitiveness if not supported by incentives or capacity-building measures.

Infrastructure and investment costs
Transitioning to low-carbon processes requires substantial upgrades in infrastructure, such as renewable energy integration, district-wide energy efficiency retrofits, expansion of public transport electrification, and resilient stormwater systems. These necessary transformations place pressure on municipal budgets, which already carry high demand due to demographic fluctuations and visitor inflows. Without sufficient external financing, the cost burden may delay or limit the scope of low-carbon investments.

Social inequality and inclusivity risks
The transition may create unequal impacts across different social groups. Vulnerable populations—such as low-income households, the elderly, and those with limited digital literacy—may struggle to adapt to new technologies or bear the costs of transitioning to cleaner energy systems. If not addressed, these inequalities could deepen the social divide, reducing public support for climate action. Ensuring equitable access to clean energy, affordable housing retrofits, and sustainable mobility options is therefore critical to a just transition in Beşiktaş.

Regulatory and compliance risks
Evolving national and international regulations—including EU climate directives and carbon border adjustment mechanisms—may impose additional financial and administrative costs on local governments. Municipalities like Beşiktaş could face challenges in keeping pace with reporting obligations, emissions accounting standards, or mandatory infrastructure upgrades. While these regulations align with global goals such as the Paris Agreement (signed November 30, 2015), they also require continuous administrative capacity and financial resources to ensure compliance.

Energy supply and reliability risks
Transitioning from fossil fuels to renewable energy sources brings risks related to reliability, sustainability, and affordability. Intermittent supply from renewables, rising energy costs during market adjustments, and potential disruptions in energy imports may all impact Beşiktaş's ability to maintain stable public services. This is particularly critical for a district that hosts large daily populations whose energy demand often exceeds that of resident communities.

Integrated response
To mitigate these risks, Beşiktaş Municipality integrates transition planning into its Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP), which targets a 41.6% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030. Financial planning now prioritizes infrastructure renewal, inclusive climate policies, and active exploration of external funding, including EU programs and international grants, with the aim of reducing the fiscal burden on municipal resources. These measures are designed not only to address transition risks but also to convert them into opportunities for innovation, employment, and sustainable urban growth.

Actualmente, se encuentra formalizada a través del Decreto Alcaldicio Exento N.° 4446 del año 2024 la creación de la Mesa de Acción Climática Comunal, compuesta por todos los directores de la Municipalidad de Independencia. Su objetivo es la elaboración y actualización periódica del Plan de Acción Comunal de Cambio Climático de Independencia.
Este plan es elaborado por el Departamento de Medioambiente y presentado periódicamente a la mesa para dar cuenta de las responsabilidades que tiene cada una de las direcciones en la ejecución y planificación de las medidas establecidas, así como en el seguimiento y monitoreo de su implementación.
Asimismo, las actualizaciones del plan son presentadas para la aprobación del Concejo Municipal. Este plan se encuentra vinculado al Plan de Gestión de Riesgos y Desastres y al Plan de Desarrollo Comunal, los cuales constituyen ejes centrales de la planificación municipal.
La última versión del plan fue aprobada en julio de 2025 (Decreto Alcaldicio Exento N.° 2198 del año 2025), y la próxima actualización está programada para el año 2030. Este instrumento se encuentra estrechamente vinculado al Plan de Gestión de Riesgos y Desastres, al Plan de Desarrollo Comunal y a la Ley Marco de Cambio Climático (Ley N.° 21.455), constituyendo un eje central para la planificación municipal y el cumplimiento de los compromisos climáticos a nivel local.
column16:
El instrumento de planificación maestra de la municipalidad corresponde al Plan de Desarrollo Comunal 2023-2028 (PLADECO), el cual considera como pilar fundamental el desarrollo ambiental, avanzando hacia una conciencia de sostenibilidad mediante la ejecución de acciones en el territorio, adaptándose a los cambios que conlleva el cambio climático y comprometiéndose con la reducción de emisiones, considerando la movilidad y el desarrollo inmobiliario sostenible.

Entre sus principales lineamientos estratégicos asociados se incluyen: la consolidación y mejoramiento de áreas verdes, el mejoramiento de la gestión de residuos —con énfasis en la disminución de su generación— y el fortalecimiento de la conciencia ambiental.

Asimismo, este plan contempla la actualización periódica del Plan de Acción de Cambio Climático cada cinco años, vinculando ambos instrumentos y dando cumplimiento a lo establecido en la Ley Marco de Cambio Climático (Ley N.° 21.455).
column17: Con la construcción y aprobación, por parte del Concejo Municipal, del Plan de Acción Comunal de Cambio Climático de la comuna de Independencia, actualmente se está en proceso de formulación para la postulación a fondos gubernamentales, con el objetivo de cumplir con los compromisos y proyectos estipulados en este plan.\n\nEs importante considerar que la totalidad de los proyectos y medidas de mitigación y adaptación impulsadas a nivel municipal —con excepción de los programas de educación ambiental— han sido ejecutadas con financiamiento del Gobierno Regional de Santiago. Esto adquiere mayor relevancia si se considera que Independencia es la comuna con menor financiamiento por habitante en la Región Metropolitana, alcanzando aproximadamente 150 dólares por habitante.
column18: Los principales riesgos para transicionar hacia una economía baja en emisiones surgen, en primer lugar, de la barrera existente al intentar reducir las emisiones provenientes de las viviendas y las industrias del sector privado. En particular, aquellas asociadas a la energía estacionaria —considerando los sectores residencial y comercial—, así como las emisiones del transporte derivadas del uso de vehículos particulares.\n\nSi bien existen medidas relacionadas con programas de educación ambiental para incidir en estas emisiones, la falta de incentivos y regulaciones que impulsen la disminución tanto en empresas como en personas dificulta una verdadera reducción en estos sectores, que concentran el 87 % de las emisiones, según el Inventario de Gases de Efecto Invernadero 2022 (última actualización).

Our Official Community Plan (OCP) and our Strategic Plan are the two highest guiding policy documents for our District. They each centre sustainability and climate action. An update to the OCP was completed in May 2024, which further strengthened our climate commitments. 

OCP (2024): https://www.saanich.ca/assets/Community/Documents/Planning/Strategic~OCP~Update/OCP-adopted-2024%20May-web.pdf

The following commitments are centered in each of these high-level planning documents: 
- Land use: building compact, complete communities 
- Transportation: facilitating active and public transportation. 
- Biodiversity: protecting and enhancing ecosystems within our boundaries. 
- Adaptation: taking climate change into account in our services and infrastructure decisions.
column17:
Climate change adaptation and mitigation efforts come with huge costs for the District's operations and for the community at large. There are also savings associated with climate action such as improved efficiency and reduced waste. 

Examples of direct costs include: 
-Facilities: electrification, energy efficiency, upgrades on-site renewable energy generation, and climate adaptation upgrades for our buildings. 
-Fleet: e-bikes and electric vehicles (often considerably greater capital cost for medium/heavy duty and specialized vehicles and EV charging infrastructure. 
-Infrastructure: building out our active transportation network and transit infrastructure; installation and maintenance of bioswales, raingardens and tree planting; slope stability; and upgrading our storm water infrastructure. 

Indirect costs include: 
- Data collection, policy development, regulation, education, advocacy, and supportive programs such as incentives for community members (e.g. individuals, households, multi-unit residential buildings, businesses, and institutions) for decarbonization and resilience. 
-- Embedding climate change adaptation within the development of our Asset Management Plans utilizing the PIEVC green protocol to develop specific climate risk assessments for each asset class and identify actions to mitigate the impacts of climate change on our service delivery. This will help inform budget and funding decisions regarding our asset maintenance and replacements. 

Local government in British Columbia have limited mechanisms for accessing funds for climate action. The District has undertaken the following approaches to financial planning for climate action: 
- Establishing a dedicated Climate Action Reserve Fund which receives, among other sources, dedicated funding from the municipal tax base. 
- Accessing Provincial funding through the Local Government Climate Action Program (note that the above two are relatively small-scale funding insufficient for key infrastructure projects). 
-Accessing funding from local energy utilities to support staff climate and energy positions. 
- Applying for external grants and funding, especially from Provincial and Federal governments (often much larger funding amounts suitable to support large infrastructure projects). These are highly competitive and therefore not yet adequate to scale up municipal climate action.
 - Advocating for increased funding from other levels of government to support climate action by local governments. 
- Issuing a “Climate Accountability Letter” to 20 of the world's largest fossil fuel companies, asking the companies to pay their share of the municipality's climate costs (https://www.wcel.org/media-release/saanich-call-out-fossil-fuel-companies-local-climate-costs). 
 - Exploring the potential for a class action lawsuit against fossil fuel companies in collaboration with other local governments to help cover the costs associated with climate change (https://www.timescolonist.com/local-news/in-bc-inflation-threatens-local-governments-climate-plans-8303881).

The City of Concord faces a range of risks related to the transition to a low-carbon economy. 

Firstly, the City is working with the County and the Green Empowerment Zone to build a green workforce in the jurisdiction and regionally in order to support our low-income and historically disadvantaged communities in seeing the financial growth associated with a green transition. 

Secondly, the jurisdiction faces significant barriers, at the government, residential, and business levels, to electrifying and retrofitting existing infrastructure. These barriers are financial, and due to knowledge barriers to accessing available resources. 

Thirdly, the jurisdiction relies on coordination with other municipalities to reduce competitiveness in attracting developers. There is risk in implementing development codes that might inhibit economic growth in the jurisdiction. 

Fourth, as per the Climate Action Plan, the majority of emissions in Concord are related to transportation, as many residents must drive to access vital resources such as healthcare, food, and work. A transition to a low-carbon economy in the jurisdiction will necessitate significant investment in low-carbon transportation.

The City of Manhattan Beach has a long history of climate planning. The City's 2015 Strategic Plan includes environmental stewardship as one of the main objectives in the continued success of the community.
Community climate action was also named in the City's 2018 Environmental Work Plan.
The 2003 Manhattan Beach General Plan supports climate action through named elements in the Community Resources, Mobility, Housing, Infrastructure, and Safety sections.
The City recently unanimously approved an amendment to the Local Coastal Plan that aims to address coastal hazards and sea level rise. This amendment includes sections on adaptation strategies, assessments of current infrastructure, and more.
The City also has a Mobility Plan (2018) that aims to create a balanced, multi-modal transportation for people and goods within and in/out of the City. There is an emphasis on non-motorized transportation and creating streets that improve pedestrian, bicycle, and public transit access.
Manhattan Beach is also in the process of developing a Climate Action and Adaptation Plan and updating its Community Safety Element, which will incorporate elements of the Climate Action and Adaptation Plan, especially those related to the co-benefits of climate action and GHG reduction.
The City's 2015 and 2021 Urban Water Management Plan discusses forecasted water demand, supply, and reliability, which helps the city plan for short and long periods of drought.
The City's 2010 Water Master Plan focuses on increased water supply efficiency, economy, and reliability. This involves increasing the proportion of water from local sources as opposed to imported water, which would decrease the City's carbon footprint. There is also a discussion of the increased use of recycled water.
Manhattan Beach also has a Local Hazards Mitigation Plan from 2017 that identifies hazards and potential vulnerabilities. Some of the hazards assessed include tsunami, earthquake, landslide, flood, climate change, drought, and adverse weather. The plan also includes a list of activities that might assist the city in reducing risk from these hazards. There is a policy in place to monitor sea level rise and adjust accordingly.
2022 City is in the process of completing our dune restoration project. In addition to the ecological benefits, the project is expected to help buffer coastal infrastructure and provide important recreational and educational opportunities for the community and visitors.
2023 Our Local Coastal Plan with detailed chapters on the natural management of coastal hazards has been accepted by the Coastal Commission and expected to be certified at their August 2023 meeting.

Batangas City exercises structured oversight over climate-related issues through formal planning processes, cross-sectoral coordination, and regular monitoring mechanisms embedded in its governance systems.

1. Integration of Climate into Strategy and Planning
Climate considerations are systematically included in the review and development of major strategies and plans, such as:

The Comprehensive Land Use Plan (CLUP 2019-2028), which integrates climate vulnerability assessments and hazard maps into zoning and land allocation decisions.

The Local Climate Change Action Plan (LCCAP 2018-2028), which sets specific adaptation and mitigation targets aligned with national frameworks (e.g., NDCs, NCCAP).

The Comprehensive Development Plan (CDP) and Annual Investment Plan (AIP), which prioritize climate-resilient infrastructure and environmental programs for funding.

All development and environmental plans are reviewed by the City Development Council (CDC) and the Sangguniang Panlungsod, ensuring climate alignment before approval.

2. Oversight Structure and Monitoring Mechanisms
Oversight is led by the Office of the City Environment and Natural Resources Office (OCENRO), in collaboration with:

Batangas City Climate Core Team (BCCCT) - the main inter-office body guiding policy and implementation

Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (DRRMC) - integrating climate-related hazards into resilience planning

OCENRO coordinates with other technical departments (CPDO, Engineering, Agriculture, Health, etc.) to track progress of climate programs and ensure alignment with the LCCAP and GHG reduction goals.

3. Frequency and Process of Monitoring
Progress on climate-related goals is monitored annually through the Annual Investment Program (AIP) review and performance assessment of implementing departments.

The city conducts GHG inventories periodically, most recently aligned with the development of the GHG Management Framework Plan, providing data for adjusting mitigation priorities.

Monitoring results and updates on climate actions are reported to the City Mayor and Sangguniang Panlungsod, and also shared with national government bodies (e.g., DILG, DENR, CCC) as required.

4. Use of Data and Feedback
The city uses evidence from vulnerability assessments, emissions inventories, and stakeholder consultations to inform updates of plans and mid-term adjustments.
column16: Climate-related issues have significantly influenced Batangas City's master and development planning by driving the integration of climate adaptation and mitigation strategies into its core policies and land use frameworks. Risk assessments on flooding, sea-level rise, and geohazards have informed land zoning decisions, discouraging development in vulnerable coastal and low-lying areas.\n\nAdditionally, infrastructure planning now includes elevated housing, green open spaces, and sustainable drainage systems to reduce climate vulnerability. Urban growth is being guided by a “ridge-to-reef” approach, ensuring that upland, river, and coastal ecosystems are managed holistically. Overall, climate concerns have become central to how Batangas City shapes land use, infrastructure priorities, and investment programming, ensuring that long-term development aligns with environmental safety and resilience.
