column15: Atualmente o Governo Nacional dispõe de um Ministério de Ambiente e Energia, que define e emana as políticas, as prioridades e as orientações estratégicas a nível nacional, articulando-as ao nível local com os municípios. O Ministério do Ambiente e da Energia tem ainda sob sua tutela a Agência Portuguesa do Ambiente e o Fundo Ambiental. A Agência Portuguesa do Ambiente (APA) é uma agência do Estado Português que tem como missão a gestão integrada das políticas ambientais e de sustentabilidade, e que tem como objetivo contribuir para um elevado nível de proteção e valorização do ambiente através da prestação de serviços de qualidade aos cidadãos. A APA atua sempre em articulação, quer com outras políticas setoriais, quer com um vasto conjunto de parceiros, dos quais se destacam os municípios. Trabalhando temas como as Alterações Climáticas, Água e Litoral (bem como Resíduos, Ar, Ruído, Emergências Radiológicas, Avaliação de Impacte Ambiental, Economia Circular, ou Educação Ambiental), a APA tem competências de monitorização, planeamento e avaliação, licenciamento e fiscalização, sendo por isso o principal regulador ambiental em Portugal. Por sua vez, o Fundo Ambiental pretende apoiar financeiramente políticas ambientais com vista à prossecução dos objetivos do desenvolvimento sustentável e dos compromissos nacionais e internacionais assumidos, relativos às alterações climáticas, aos recursos hídricos, aos resíduos e à conservação da natureza e biodiversidade. Este Fundo financia assim entidades, nomeadamente os municípios, atividades ou projetos que contribuem para a mitigação e adaptação às alterações climáticas; para o sequestro de carbono e fomento da participação de entidades nos mercados de carbono; para o uso eficiente da água e proteção dos recursos hídricos; ações que visam o cumprimento dos objetivos e metas nacionais e comunitárias no que concerne a gestão de resíduos urbanos e a transição para uma economia circular ou ainda ações para a capacitação, sensibilização e investigação em matéria ambiental. O Fundo Ambiental é o principal instrumento de financiamento da política do ambiente e da ação climática em Portugal. É ainda entidade intermediária para diversas componentes do Plano de Recuperação e Resiliência em matéria de ação climática. A nível local, neste enquadramento, o Governo Local dispõe de um serviço específico para análise, revisão e orientação de Planos relacionados com a Ação Climática (Divisão de Ação Climática e Economia Circular). A Divisão de Ação Climática e Economia Circular tem como missão garantir a implementação, acompanhamento e monitorização da Estratégia Municipal de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas de Loulé (EMAAC de Loulé) e do Plano Municipal de Ação Climática de Loulé (PMAC de Loulé), assim como a sua revisão e atualização periódica, difundir o processo estratégico desenvolvido, promovendo e acrescentando conhecimento sobre alterações climáticas a nível municipal, consolidando uma base sólida para o desenvolvimento de opções e medidas concretas de adaptação e mitigação às alterações climáticas, bem como desenvolver os meios conducentes à transição para uma economia circular, assente no consumo sustentável, valorização dos recursos e na minimização dos impactos ambientais. Esta matéria encontra-se integrada também no Plano Diretor Municipal (em revisão). Também em sede de Orçamento Municipal e Plano de Investimentos Também em sede do Orçamento Municipal são anualmente estipuladas verbas destinadas a projetos no âmbito da ação climática, bem como aos serviços municipais e unidades orgânicas com competências na implementação da ação climática municipal, com destaque para a Divisão de Ação Climática e Economia Circular.
column16: Os problemas relacionados com o clima estão acautelados na Proposta de Revisão do Plano Diretor Municipal de Loulé (em curso). Neste sentido, em regulamento, o Novo Plano Diretor Municipal de Loulé enfatiza a urgência de um novo paradigma ambiental e territorial, relativamente à importância do aproveitamento racional e eficiente do solo, da garantia de desenvolvimento sustentável, e a competitividade económica e territorial, o aumento da resiliência face aos efeitos das alterações climáticas e a promoção da adaptação do território aos eventos climáticos extremos, prevenção de riscos, regeneração de áreas degradadas, através da contenção urbana e da edificação dispersa, e a valorização da identidade e do património natural, cultural e paisagístico.
column17: Tendo em conta os problemas relacionados com o Clima, o município criou um Fundo Ambiental Municipal, pela obrigatoriedade de constituir uma garantia financeira que lhe permita assumir as obrigações do Diploma de Responsabilidade Ambiental (DRA), bem como por pretender salvaguardar-se de todo o tipo de vulnerabilidades que possam ocorrer caso sejam identificadas situações de danos ambientais ou ameaças eminentes resultantes de atividades que coloquem em causa o ambiente.Assim, a constituição desta garantia financeira (Fundo Ambiental Municipal), assegura que, em caso de ocorrência de um dano ambiental, o município está preparado e tem a capacidade financeira para suportar os custos associados ao dano e a aptidão para tomar de imediato medidas de prevenção e reparação de danos ambientais causados às espécies e habitats naturais protegidos, à água e ao solo, como aludido no Decreto-lei n.º 147/2008.Também em sede do Orçamento Municipal são anualmente estipuladas verbas destinadas a projetos no âmbito da ação climática, bem como aos serviços municipais e unidades orgânicas com competências na implementação da ação climática municipal, com destaque para a Divisão de Ação Climática e Economia Circular. Neste âmbito, é ainda de referir e de destacar o trabalho que o município de Loulé tem vindo a desenvolver, desde 2023, de forte alinhamento do seu Orçamento Municipal e das Grandes Opções do Plano (GOP) 2023-2027 com os Objetivos de Desenvolvimento Sustentável (ODS) da Agenda 2030 da Assembleia Geral das Nações Unidas. O Orçamento Municipal e das Grandes Opções do Plano (GOP) são instrumentos de política orçamental e económica no serviço público, que têm como objetivo responder às necessidades das pessoas, salvaguardando o seu futuro, bem como o do meio envolvente, sem colocar em causa os equilíbrios necessários entre os recursos disponíveis e os compromissos assumidos. A estrutura do Orçamento Municipal e das Grandes Opções do Plano (GOP) 2023-2027 do município de Loulé contextualiza a intervenção municipal no atual contexto e enquadramento macroeconómico, definindo os eixos de intervenção estratégicos e prioritários do Município, cuja matriz estratégica visa projetar e promover um território mais inclusivo, mais coeso, mais competitivo e mais sustentável, concretizada através dos seguintes pilares de atuação: “Pessoas e Famílias”, “Mobilidade e Qualidade de Vida”, “Ação Climática e Eficiência Energética” e “Acesso à Cultura e ao Desporto”. A intervenção do Município está assim perfeitamente alinhada com a resolução “Transformar o nosso mundo - a Agenda 2030 para o Desenvolvimento Sustentável” (a 25 de setembro de 2015 pela Assembleia Geral das Nações Unidas), que requer o envolvimento dos municípios para que os ODS e as suas metas sejam alcançadas, constituindo uma oportunidade para que o poder local participe ativamente na definição das medidas a adotar e que, desse modo, consiga assegurar que os resultados estão o mais próximo possível das necessidades e interesses das suas populações.

Climate and wider sustainability issues are considered in decision making across key strategies and plans (including the District Plan, Council Plan, Economic Strategy, Local Plan/Spatial Plan, Transport Strategy, Climate Action Plan, Low Emissions/Air Quality planning etc).
Programme, project and service operations include a climate appraisal in a maturing approach (eg transport schemes, regeneration, infrastructure, energy and land management) 

Bradford Council is in a formal governance partnership within West Yorkshire - Mayoral Combined Authority and with Elected Mayor on regeneration, transport, infrastructure and other policy areas, with a maturing position on proactive climate-issues management and de-carbonisation. Carbon Impact Assessment approach is utilised for key investments. Critical weather/climate issues are addressed through Council risk management framework and also through collaborative emergency management and civil contingency planning. Key Central Government departments (Cabinet Office, DEFRA, DESNZ, MHCLG, OZEV etc) and arm's length government agencies undertake legal, statutory, enforcement and policy implementation roles. Local Government position in England with regard to climate-related issues remains variable with no specific statutory powers or resources ( LGA has recently undertaken consultation on need for climate related statutory obligations and associated funding for Local Government).

Continued delivery of Clean Air Zone launched in September 2022. Estimated GHG savings of 150,000 t - modelled and part of the Strategic Business case agreed with Government.
Continued progress on key Climate Action priorities and investments including Smart Street Lighting; Municipal Fleet, EV charging Infrastructure, E-bike Share Scheme, Anaerobic Digestion, Low Carbon Hydrogen, Bradford Energy Network, Biodiversity Net Gain, Sustainable regeneration) 

Focus on Growing a Sustainable Economy within Climate Action Plan, District Plan and Growth Plan, which incorporates decarbonisation, resilience, nature recovery and enviro-economics within more strategic and integrated approach. 

Climate Action Plan developed with support of Ricardo (specialist environmental consultants) and approved for district wide consultation by the Council Executive Committee. 

Foundation for the District Economic strategy/plan and approach rooted in place-shaping and creating the conditions for a sustainable and inclusive economy, that works for everyone.
column16: Current and emerging Local Plan/spatial plan features explicit climate and environmental issues within the evidence base, policy formulation, policy adoption and compliance/development management. Spatial location appraisal featuring carbon profiling and full spatial, transport and air quality modelling held on file. Air Quality work with dedicated Clean Air Zone includes de-carbonisation alongside air quality targets and has shaped investment decisions and programme design for multiple benefits. Strategic and development planning explicitly features sustainability and progress on our sustainable growth approach to a sustainable and inclusive economy. Special attention on flood risk communities - domestic and commercial properties - considered with master/development planning. Biodiversity, green space, and blue/green infrastructure are key elements of environmental management and adaptation planning (in conjunction with statutory stakeholders including the Environment Agency).\n\nRicardo's Bradford District Emissions baseline (2024) assessment and carbon emissions reduction pathway (2025) are being utilised to inform the Local Plan and Climate Action Plan development.
column17:
Jurisdiction financial planning - split between civic partners, businesses, investors and communities and government operating within national legislation, guidance and market/financial regulations/frameworks for due consideration of climate issues. 

Local authority investment in district infrastructure, regeneration, public services and communities increasingly directly and indirectly impact on financial planning and spending decisions/delivery for eg. response to flood incidents, impact on infrastructure, upstream investment in sustainable urban drainage etc

Significant impact and cost pressures for eg. flood risk interventions and increasingly inflationary cost pressures such as energy prices/energy regime and impact on goods and supplies through supply chains.

Major focus through clean growth approach to look strategically and practically at integrated proposals for regeneration that address critical challenges and opportunities (multi-solving as compared to co-benefits) and to invest in enabling schemes/interventions for place; business or community that secure social, economic and environmental outcomes - supporting the achievement of sustainable development and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). 

Draft Climate Action Plan and Growth and Regeneration Plan are allied to senior leadership/decision management to better consolidate, align and drive impact from core public funding, use of capital resources/borrowing and across to unlocking commercial, private sector, third sector or domestic investment. 
Investments across all sectors are increasingly aligned to environmental, social and governance responsibilities. 

Clean Air Zone as clean growth exemplar, recognised through LGC Climate Response Award 2021 (submission attached), c£50m investment for health improvement supporting business transitioning to low emissions including No2/CO2e especially through rapid transition support to taxis, vans, lorries etc. Targeted through dedicated 'zone' but with significant whole District and wider clean growth benefits.

Sustainable Growth approach has attracted significant commercial investment, beyond 'green finance', in infrastructure, urban renewal, transportation and clean energy production. Examples of such investment include development of Low Carbon Hydrogen production facility, potential supply of bio methane via Anaerobic Digestion, £50m Bradford Energy Network (District Heat Network), Sustainable City Centre Market (Darley Street Market) opened in 2025 which will act as catalyst for sustainable food economy and supports Sustainable Food Strategy. 

Working with WYCA to harness devolution and other significant government funding allocated for sustainable travel for Bradford District including Local Electric Vehicle Infrastructure funding, Transforming Cities Fund for cycling and pedestrianisation, and an initial £200m for West Yorkshire Mass Transit Tram System - to include significant section within Bradford District. This will connect Kirklees, Bradford and Leeds and unlock neighbourhood sustainability, decarbonisation of travel as a viable alternative to the private car and more. Design work, procurement and planning process is underway. Partners also investing heavily in core business and integrated climate action for example InCommunities (primary social housing provider for Bradford District part of the WY Housing Partnership). Investment planning to retrofit stock to Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) band C.

Significant investment being brought forward by the National Health Service, Health and Social Care Partners resulting in more sustainable health provision such as the new Airedale Hospital. https://www.airedale-trust.nhs.uk/about-us/securing-the-future-of-airedale/

Act as One collaboration investment. c£1bn. Core existing budgets and investment in estate, buildings, fleet, digital and remote health services, community support all connecting to the NHS Net Zero strategy.

City Council has an Environmental Stewardship committee that meets approximately every two months. The committee is informed by management about climate related issues and will vote and forward recommendations on environment and climate change issues to Council as a whole. Climate related issues are considered by staff when undertaking plans and strategies, according to our Energy and Emissions Plans and our Climate Change Adaptation Plan. In 2022 we started incorporating a qualitative climate lens on decision reports and our capital budget.
column16: Climate related risks were incorporated into the 2019 update of Fredericton's Municipal Plan - most notably, a growth boundary was established to concentrate growth in the urban centre and reduce urban sprawl. Additionally a minimum built environment standard was developed for new builds according to flood mapping projections. We have a special zoning called \'environmental open space\' which limits development in and near sensitive areas like riverbanks and wetlands.
column17: More operational and capital budget is being allocated for infrastructure upgrades that increase climate resilience and other climate related initiatives. We have also been able to access match funding from the federal government (and to a lesser degree the province of New Brunswick), which has allowed us to complete more projects (adaptation and mitigation) with the same number of tax payer dollars. \n\nStarting with the 2023 budget, the City runs our proposed capital projects through a climate lens to ensure operations and projects aligned with our GHG reduction targets and adaptation goals. In 2025, we introduced a \'climate budget\' and we report on the dollar value of investments in climate mitigation and adaptation annually during our capital budgeting process.

Cornwall Council is a unitary authority in the United Kingdom and provides a wide range of services to the approximately half a million people who live in Cornwall. It is responsible for a multitude of services including schools, social services, waste and recycling, roads, planning, strategy, economic growth and more. In this role Cornwall Council has a three-fold role in oversight of climate-related issues - within our operations (scope 1&2), within our influence (scope 3 - supply chain and group of companies) and wider general support for low carbon transition across key sectors across the county. Within Cornwall Council climate change sits at the heart of all decision making through our decision wheel based on doughnut economics. This emphasises the work we are already doing on emission reduction and on tackling the inequalities that exist in our society, so that everyone can live a good life in Cornwall. 

In May 2025 we welcomed the new Cornwall Council Cabinet who have now established a revised set of priorities which are:

•	Strong, safe, vibrant communities, with more decent and affordable homes 
•	A clean, green Cornwall, with healthy rivers and seas 
•	A resilient economy creating good jobs and fair opportunities 
•	A caring place for families, where every child can thrive 
•	Healthy and active people supported to live well at every stage of life 
•	Connected, reliable, safe transport that works for the people of Cornwall


We see climate action as being an overriding principle that sits across services and teams from economic, care, transport, environment and strategic services. Progress against carbon actions is included within the Corporate Performance Report to Cabinet and the Carbon Neutral Cornwall Programme Board on a quarterly basis, as well as monthly to the Council We Need Board. 

Corporate Performance Report Link: https://app.powerbi.com/view?r=eyJrIjoiNDMyYTg4MGUtN2E3OC00YWU4LWE5NjEtYjhmYmMxYzliODM2IiwidCI6ImVmYWExNmFhLWQxZGUtNGQ1OC1iYTJlLTI4MzNmZGZkZDI5ZiIsImMiOjh9

Our nationally recognised programme, including being the highest rural single-tier local authority in 2025 under the UK Climate Action Scorecard, outlines the council's multi-dimensional leadership role within a complex systems landscape. UK Climate Action Scorecard Results: https://councilclimatescorecards.uk/

Scrutiny is also provided via the Overview and Scrutiny Committee on a quarterly basis with a full report provided annually - you can read the report here: Carbon Neutral Cornwall Annual Report 2023/24 - https://letstalk.cornwall.gov.uk/20344/widgets/57754/documents/65921
column16:
The Council aligned the action plan working, with partners, to develop an integrated approach bringing together the work required to deliver our climate and ecological emergencies. An ecological emergency was declared 30 November 2021 and bespoke adaptation plans requested to respond to our changing climate. The council has three strategic responses. 1. Ecological emergency delivered through the Local Nature Recovery Strategy with a target 30 of land and seas managed by nature by 2030. 2. Climate emergency delivered via a climate action plan and, 3. Environmental Adaptation delivered via an Adaptation Plan which is in review.

Local Nature Recovery Strategy was published in March 2024 and provides a blueprint for the recovery of nature in Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly. 

Climate Change Development Planning Document DPD: A major strategic element of this is the Climate DPD which encourages better developments that use less energy developing buildings that survive future climate change and that help protect the planet. Moreover, the climate DPD ensures that all developments leave space for nature. Whilst development legislation sits with national government this document seeks to deliver a progressive development framework for Cornwall giving the council the powers it needs to deliver on its low carbon ambition. It was approved by the Inspectorate in February 2023.

The Cornwall Plan 2020-2050: The Cornwall plan is our public facing master plan which explains the direction that Cornwall is heading. Carbon neutrality is embedded into this strategy through economic social and political framing.

Local Area Energy Plan: The Council has developed a Cornwall and Isles of Scilly specific local area energy plan that has assessed the needs, and policies and provides scenarios for decarbonisation across the energy network. This plan was approved in March 2025, and the delivery phase is now in underway.

Decision making Wheel: Carbon emissions alongside wider environmental measures now features in all council decision making in the decision-making wheel. The wheel helps to show us how projects and decisions will affect the environment and people. Reviewed by carbon and equality colleague's projects can be approved or redesigned as required. 

Local Flood Risk Management Strategy: Climate Change planning resilience and adaptation form a key part of the Local Flood Risk Management Strategy which the council is required to produce as part of the Flood and Water Management Act 2010. This document outlines the responsibilities of the Risk Management Authorities in Cornwall it details how they are working in partnership to coordinate local flood risk management whilst considering the impacts of climate change.

Climate Literacy: Delivery of a bespoke service specifically 'Planning for a changing climate training' has been delivered to services to identify and embed climate mitigation and adaptation actions within service delivery plans.
column17:
The core Climate Change Programme Team is funded from the base revenue budget and the approved budget in 2025/26 is £0.807m, which continues for the current MTFP period. 
Further capacity has been built in some key services including transport and more recently housing but remains primarily derived from the Carbon Neutral Cornwall revenue/capital budget or external funding sources. 

Following an annual review of progress at Cabinet in June 2024, an additional investment of £750k revenue was approved from the Place and Green Growth Reserve. This investment is being used to secure specialist resource with expertise to develop projects, secure external funding and ensure project readiness against areas of the Carbon Neutral programme that have fallen behind or where there are particular opportunities to accelerate action. This funding is also being used to develop the business case for a strategic partner.

Since adopting the Action Plan in July 2019, the Council has seen investment of £59m committed to programmes that directly addresses the climate emergency, unlocking a further £251m of external funding. £67.3m capital is allocated in the budget approved by Cabinet in February 2025 to deliver on climate related priorities which is projected to realise carbon reductions of circa 5,700 tCO2e per year or 240,000 TCO2e lifetime savings.
column18: There are significant risks from climate change to residents and visitors to Cornwall as outlined in the Climate Change Action Plan and the Cornwall Climate Risk assessment. Addressing climate change requires our whole way of life to change presenting a number of complex or grand challenges therefore we must make careful assessments and decisions on actions to mitigate and adapt to climate change locally also considering the balance between the different timescales of potential interventions. Getting to a carbon neutral Cornwall will not be achieved through Council action alone and is a highly complex issue. Reducing greenhouse gas emissions will require systems leadership across multiple sectors, communication and behavioural change that will result in adapted lifestyles and potentially fundamentally different patterns of development and travel over a longer time horizon. Our programmes are related to the degree of control and influence the Council directly has and our overt acknowledgement that partnership working across Cornwall and the UK will be essential for us to address this challenge. Cornwall Council has recognised the impact of the changing climate has had on our communities and has updated the Corporate Risk Register to address not only carbon neutrality to also include responding to the threat posed by an already changing climate with work well underway to develop a bespoke Cornwall Adaptation Strategy. There are mixed perceptions of climate change within communities across Cornwall that manifest into a spectrum of views which the Council are expected to navigate in the development of the plan the prioritisation of resource and communication to our residents. The resourcing requirements to undertake systems leadership and the change programme required is significant. The scale of change required is unprecedented. This comes at a time of further significant financial pressures for the Council. Skills requirements to ensure a high level of skilled personnel to manage low carbon projects and initiatives as well as deliver and maintain those initiatives. Infrastructure challenges continue to be a significant risk due to the cost of replacing or upgrading current infrastructure to meet low carbon standards and is often complex and disruptive. There is a risk that the local resources available to deliver at the pace necessary is insufficient. An increased funding challenge due to the economic climate and securing funding can be competitive and require innovative financing mechanisms.

column15: The overall governance of the Climate Emergency is split between the authority's Carbon Net-Zero Board (Internal) and the borough wide Climate Emergency Board (External). The authority has a role in managing the continuity between the two Boards and this extends to the reporting of progress. Insofar as monitoring and updating the Carbon Net-Zero Action Plan, this is done on an annual basis by the authority with the support of the stakeholders who have been a central supporting factor in its development. The Carbon Net-Zero Board is the authority's internal board and governance structure which serves to oversee and steer the reduction of both its own operational carbon emissions and that of the borough as a whole. This Board is made up of 12 specific workstreams, led by senior managers and officers, and is jointly chaired by the Cabinet Member for Environment and the Director of Environment. The twelve workstreams are: WS1: Council Assets WS2: Climate Adaptation, Insetting & Nature-based Solutions WS3: Fleet WS4: Organisational Culture WS5: Travel WS6: Waste & Reuse WS7: Housing WS8: Supply Chain WS9: Green Skills WS10: Industry / Commerce / Business support WS11: Public Health WS12: Miscellaneous Projects including ICT. The Borough Climate Emergency Board brings together senior representatives from the business and public sector who wish to work together to achieve carbon net zero targets. Each representative organisation has embarked on a pathway to reduce carbon emissions and has agreed to work collaboratively where possible to: Mobilise individuals and organisations to work towards actions which will contribute to the Action Plan; Support the development of projects which will contribute to the Action Plan; Strategically monitor the progress of projects and emissions in the borough; Support the updating process of the borough Action Plan. The Board is made up of representatives from organisations which can shape the actions of others i.e., via an influencing role, provision of services or infrastructure and Board Members are representatives for organisations which: Can demonstrate commitment to the net zero vision of the borough; Have the ability to engage with other Board members and supply chains; Bring relevant experience to the Board; Take a leadership role within their organisations; Have a carbon footprint within the borough. The Borough Climate Emergency Board Membership includes a number of household names and internationally well-known organisations such as Greggs, Procter and Gamble, Suez and others. In its first year the Borough Climate Board focussed in on the following climate change related themes: Offsetting and Insetting; Renewable Energy; Developed and delivered a successful Net Zero Business Event; Climate Adaptation. Examples of Board project outputs are the Carbon Reduction Award Scheme and Climate Adaptation toolkits, which are now available from the authority. Recent Board topics include: Greening economic development; Developing and delivering low carbon themed Business Workshop Events; Transitioning the business fleet to ultra-low emissions vehicles (ULEV); The challenge of decarbonising heat; Re-visiting carbon emissions and area based insetting projects. The 2024 iteration of the Carbon Net-Zero Action Plan includes an update and outline of the adopted programme of work. The Borough Climate Board meets every 3 months. The board programme for 2024/25 was as follows: May - Waste (& the circular economy); August - Campaigning and Behaviour Change; November - Green Skills and Workforce Transition; February - Area Based Insetting; May - Procurement and Net Zero. so far, 2025/26 boards have focussed on nature based solutions and public health. https://my.northtyneside.gov.uk/sites/default/files/web-page-related-files/CNZ2030_Action%20Plan%202024.pdf

The authority routinely monitors and tracks a range of national policies which continue to shape the authority's proportionate response to the Climate Emergency via its annually updated Action Plan.

The Climate Change Act 2008 provides the framework and basis for UK climate change policy. It established long-term statutory targets for the UK to decarbonise by reducing its greenhouse gas emissions and under this Act, the UK as a whole, has a net-zero emissions target for 2050. The authority is also following closely the progress government's Ten Point Plan for a Green Industrial Revolution which will reduce UK emissions by 180 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (MtCO2e) between 2023 and 2032. The UK's Climate Change Committee's publications. The Climate Change Committee (CCC) is an independent, statutory body established under the Climate Change Act 2008. Its purpose is to advise the UK and devolved governments on emissions targets and to report to Parliament on progress made in reducing greenhouse gas emissions and preparing for and adapting to the impacts of climate change. It also provides independent advice on setting and meeting carbon budgets and preparing for climate change, monitors progress in reducing emissions and achieving carbon budgets and targets. conducts independent analysis into climate change science, economics and policy and engages with a wide range of organisations and individuals to share evidence and analysis. The council takes into account, for example, the CCC's advice on carbon budgets, mitigation, the net-zero workforce and adaptation. The Adaptation Committee of the CCC provides as Independent Assessment of UK Climate Risk which sets out the priority climate change risks and opportunities for the UK. The Third National Adaptation Programme (NAP3) was released in July 2023 and outlines the UK Government's approach to preparing for the impacts of climate change. NAP3 addresses adaptation policy for England. The programme covers the period from 2023 to 2028, after which it will be succeeded by NAP4. The council also incorporates the UK Government Climate Change Risk Assessment, which follows the CCC's advice on Climate Risk, which it is required to publish under the 2008 Climate Change Act every five years. The assessment sets out the risks and opportunities facing the UK from climate change, the most recent of which is CCRA3: https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/1047003/climate-change-risk-assessment-2022.pdf The Government released its final plan for implementing a zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate in March 2023 after a delay of several months. Although certain flexibilities in the mandate slightly reduce its strictness, it is still a reliable policy to boost electric vehicle (EV) sales up to 2030. Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG) is a rule that requires new building projects to help nature rather than harm it. Under the Environment Act 2021, most new developments in England must make sure that they leave the environment at least 10% better in terms of biodiversity than it was before they started. As part of the Civil Contingencies Act, North Tyneside Council is required to identify the risk factors for the borough and to build resilience within the borough for addressing both natural hazards and malicious threats. The National Risk Register helped to guide some of the council's local risk management strategies including the North Tyneside Surface Water Management Plan and the North Tyneside Local Flood Management Strategy: https://my.northtyneside.gov.uk/category/1135/flooding The Council has also been working with our borough partners such as public health teams, NHS trusts, neighbouring boroughs, waste and water management companies amongst others on delivering strategies and capital programmes including but not limited to: • Waste Management Strategy • Air Quality Strategy • Local Flood Management Strategy • Biodiversity Action Plan • Housing Strategy 2023 - 2028 The North Tyneside Local Plan was adopted in 2017 and sets out the Council's policies and proposals to guide planning decisions and establishes the framework for the sustainable growth and development of North Tyneside up to 2032. One of the eleven objectives set out in the Local Plan states the authority will 'ensure a sustainable future for North Tyneside with communities and infrastructure that are well placed to mitigate climate change'. North Tyneside will develop and promote approaches to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and to adapt to, and mitigate the impact of, climate change including flood risk, promoting the renewable energy sector and developments which seek to minimise energy and resource consumption, whilst improving the Borough's resilience to the effects of climate change: https://my.northtyneside.gov.uk/category/1130/local-plan
A new local plan is now in development and will include a larger emphasis on sustainability
column17: Climate related issues have put severe stress on the borough's financial planning. Extreme weather events such as 'Thunder Thursday' in 2012 and Storm Arwen in 2021 cost the council millions in damage repairs to homes and infrastructure. We would expect these financial pressures to continue as the frequency of these events increases. The Authority is clear that fairness in the transition towards a low carbon future for our businesses and residents is paramount across the borough. This will need to be considered in any financial planning to ensure climate mitigation and adaptation measures are rolled out in an equitable way which reach the most vulnerable within our communities. The Authority is also clear that meeting our net zero target requires continued societal transformations of how we live; and our businesses and residents need to be fully empowered to change. Our work towards supporting this change to a low carbon transition such as electric car charging infrastructure and the deployment and promotion of heat pumps have an important role to play, however they will not be sufficient in isolation. To enable these aspects to be developed, we are working with others to ensure there are no exclusions from opportunities. It is also recognised that there is a regional role to be undertaken and we will play a key role in this. Transitioning towards a greener economy is something that requires a coordinated and joint approach. This will be challenging in the context of a changing climate, specifically in the areas of economic development where new technologies and the associated skills supersede the tried/tested and traditional practices. It is now our ambition to create a standardised method of calculating the cost of extreme weather events, so that a financial value can be placed upon the damage/disruption caused.
column18: There are several risks in North Tyneside related to the transition to a low-carbon economy. Firstly, there is a need for economic growth in North Tyneside, to improve the quality of life for our residents, including attracting more businesses and creating more jobs. For the borough to achieve carbon neutrality, all new and existing businesses need to support this ambition and be able to make their contribution. Some businesses may have conflicting priorities, particularly during post-COVID economic recovery, the emerging cost of living crisis, and as a result of current energy cost rises, which may delay the transition to a low carbon economy. Secondly, there is a demand for road transport to be upgraded to accommodate planned population growth and the current increase in the popularity of the private car, linked partly to the impact of COVID-19. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the modal share for public transport has also fallen significantly and has not yet returned to pre-pandemic levels. Public transport is a key aspect of transitioning to a low-carbon economy, meaning its modal share therefore needs to be rebuilt. Fuel poverty is also a significant issue in North Tyneside. According to the UK Government, 9% of people in North Tyneside are in fuel poverty as of 2023. There is also a high degree of inequality within the borough, with significant differences in the quality of life between different wards in the borough with health inequalities increased during the pandemic. A transition to a low carbon economy requires the scale up of green technologies, many of which can be costly. It is important that North Tyneside takes a pragmatic approach when tackling greenhouse gas emissions particularly in relation to vulnerable and low-income households and works to ensure the well-being of residents. There are two other aspects of a Just and Fair Transition in which the Authority is working to develop, and these are the themes of; 1.\tThose of adaptation to a future physical climate change with, for example an increase trends towards events of unprecedent weather extremes 2.\tThe adaptation to a transformed economy where the demands for greener services and products will become the norm. In this is the fundamental aspects of skills and training towards that future. To enable these aspects to be developed, we are working with others to ensure there are no exclusions from opportunities. It is also recognised that there is a regional role to be undertaken and we will play a key role in this. Transitioning towards a greener economy is something that requires a coordinated and joint approach. This will be challenging in the context of a changing climate, specifically in the areas of economic development where new technologies and the associated skills supersede the tried/tested and traditional practices. For a successful and socially just transition to take place, our local workforce needs to be equipped with the right skills to adapt to this changing economic structure and the changing nature of jobs, to avoid exclusion and increased unemployment. The provision of skills and training support will ensure the workforce are equipped with the necessary expertise to fully realise future employment opportunities in the green economy. This is particularly important in the region, where skills shortages and mismatches in the context of the transition to net zero have been identified. Additionally, the transition to a low carbon economy requires a scale up of renewable energy technologies such as wind turbines and solar PV. The implementation of this infrastructure can at times take place on greenbelt land, which can reduce biodiversity. Finally, the transition to a low carbon economy is a significant challenge for any borough, particularly within limited resources. Committing to net zero comes with a substantial reputational risk, should the borough fail in meeting this ambition.

The WMCA has a number of levels of scrutiny and oversight of climate-related issues. The WMCA Board acts as the main area of governance and oversight. 
The board is the main decision-making body of the WMCA. Its membership includes the Mayor and the leaders of the constituent and non-constituent local authorities that comprise the combined authority. It has responsibility for setting the annual budget of the WMCA and Transport for West Midlands, as well as agreeing all major strategic and corporate plans and objectives and as a result provides oversight of climate-related issues in the region. The board's Terms of Reference refers to members voting on issues relating to environmental sustainability. 
The Overview & Scrutiny Committee provide a further level of accountability, through oversight of the work of the Mayor and the wider WMCA decision making processes in order to hold decision makers to account and improve the quality of these decisions.
Since 2022 the WMCA has also ran a 'Greener Together' Citizens Panel, to deliberate and provide actions for the WMCA to take on environment and energy. The panel has created participatory and deliberative processes to allow citizens to influence climate-related issues. Due to the success of the Greener Together Citizens Panel, the WMCA has decided to create a broader Citizens Panel, considering wider issues, with environment still a key priority. 
A summary of the Greener Together Citizens Panel can be found here: https://www.wmca.org.uk/media/jr0p5zxd/citizens-panel-leaflet.pdf 
Oversight for energy and emissions matters is also provided by the Energy Capital Technical Advisory Board at quarterly meetings, comprised of experts from across the energy system.

WMCA is not a planning authority but are beginning to develop regional planning strategies and guidance, working closely with local authorities to ensure that climate-related issues are factored into local development plans and supplementary planning documents. 
As outlined in the West Midlands Growth Plan, launched in July 2025, the WMCA will be working with partners to develop the West Midlands Spatial Development Strategy. This will be a land use and planning strategy, focused on delivering housing targets and transformational regional projects; these include innovation networks such as the Coventry and Warwick Gigapark, which will support EV battery development, and Wolverhampton's Green Innovation Corridor, which will support development of the circular economy and green innovation. 
The WMCA appointed as Responsible Authority for delivering the Local Nature Recovery Strategy (LNRS) for the West Midlands region in June 2023, with the final LNRS expected to be signed off by WMCA Board at the end of 2025. While not a planning document, the LNRS will provide a clear direction on the priorities for delivering nature recovery in the region, and it is hoped that the strategy will inform the planning process to help to shape emerging and new local plans and policies.
WMCA will shortly be publishing a Climate Adaptation Guidance document to support partners in embedding climate risk and adaptation considerations across project and policy life cycle stages, ensuring that climate-related issues will be addressed in future planning.
As part of the air quality work, the WMCA are developing an air quality planning guidance document, to support partners in embedding air quality as a consideration into planning.

There are two major risks related to the transition to a low-carbon economy:
1)	Ensuring there is a just transition, with the move to net zero reduce inequalities, rather than exacerbating existing inequaities. 
2)	A lack of financial resources to deliver the changes required to reach net zero. 
On the first, an important principle of WM2041 is that the move to net zero and a low-carbon economy is a just transition, that ensures that we take everyone with us on this journey and do not leave people behind. As a regional authority, the WMCA is well-placed to avoid this; he position paper on the Industrial Decarbonisation in the Trailblazing West Midlands Devolution Deal has highlighted that 'existing economic inequalities are being exacerbated by 'one-size-fits-all' infrastructure and energy policies.' The paper provides the approach that can be utilised to ensure distinctive regional activities that can effectively transition to a low-carbon economy while mitigating the risk of exacerbating inequalities. The West Midlands Growth Plan (2025), which has the transition to a low-carbon economy as a key pillar, outlines the importance of a transition that protects existing jobs, creates new green jobs and lowers energy costs for businesses. 
On the second risk, the WMCA Board has provided funding for the low-carbon economy to date. There is however an awareness that to reach net zero, private investment will be required. As a result, the WMCA has established, with Defra and DESNZ funding, the Local Investment in Natural Capital programme and the Local Net Zero Accelerator programme. Both of these programmes are creating an investable pipeline of nature and net zero projects, supporting the projects to become investment ready, and will seek to match private investors to the projects. These are innovative programmes that could support the investment required to transition to a low-carbon economy.

column15: 도봉구는 기후위기 대응을 위해 2020년 9월, 2050년까지 2005년 온실가스 배출량 1,342천톤을 감축하여 탄소중립을 실현하는 '2050 도봉구 온실가스 감축 전략'을 발표하였다. 2050년 탄소중립 목표 달성을 위해 부문별 온실가스 감축 7대 전략(Green Building: 도봉구청사 전력 자립율 50% 달성, Green Mobility: 친환경 전기차, 수소차로 100% 전환, Green Energy: 태양광 등 재생에너지 300MW 보급, Green Cycle: 생활폐기물 50% 감축, Green Forest: 1인당 도시숲 4.5제곱미터 조성, Green Life: 1인당 온실가스 4톤 줄이기 실천, Green Education: 온실가스 감축 촉진자 3만명 양성)을 수립하였으며, 효율적이고 실효성 이는 이행과제 추진을 위한 전담반을 구성 운영하고 있다. 또한, '2050 도봉구 온실가스 감축 전략'과 2022년 전문기관의 연구용역을 통해 수립한 '도봉구 기후변화대응 계획 '을 기반으로 '제1차 도봉구 탄소중립 녹색성장 기본계획(2025~2034)'을 수립하여, 2018년 온실가스 배출량 1,145천톤을 2030년까지 40%(374천톤) 감축하는 목표를 설정하고, 이를 달성하기 위해 7개부문40개 세부시행계획을 추진 중에 있다. 아울러, 사업추진 실적을 조직 내 관련 부서와 외부 전문가, 시민단체로 구성된 '온실가스 감축 T/F'를 통해 매 분기 점검, 평가하여 결과를 피드백하고 있으며, 연말 '기후변화대책위원회' 및 '도봉구의회'에 온실가스 감축 실적을 보고하고 있다. 뿐만 아니라, 2021년 6월, 유엔기후변화협약 Race To Zero 캠페인 참여를 비롯하여 국내·외 지방정부와의 네트워크 활성화 및 정보 공유를 통해 기후변화 대응을 선도해 나가고 있다. 도봉구는 기후변화 적응 분야에서도 2021년 수립한 '제2차 도봉구 기후변화 적응대책 세부시행계획'을 바탕으로 하여 건강, 재난재해, 물관리, 산림/생태계, 적응기반 등 5개 부문, 6개 세부전략, 10개 실천과제, 31개 세부사업의 기후변화 적응대책을 추진하고 있으며, 세부사업별 추진 성과를 매년 자체적으로 평가 하고 이를 환경부에 보고하여 검증 받고 있다
column16: 도봉구는 모든 지역 개발 계획에 있어 기후위기 적응과 대응을 고려하고 있다. 이는 2021년 9월, 전국 최초로 제정한 '서울특별시 도봉구 탄소중립 기본 조례'에 명문화되어 있다. (조례 제4조 제2항: 구청장은 구가 시행 주체가 되는 각종 계획 수립과 사업의 시행과정에서 그 계획과 사업이 탄소중립에 영향을 미치는 여부 등을 종합적으로 고려하고, 온실가스의 배출을 최소화하도록 노력하여야 한다.) 이에 따라, 건축물 인허가 시 일정규모 이상의 공공건물은 제로에너지빌딩으로, 민간건물은 녹색건물로 건축하는 것을 의무화 하여 건물에너지 사용량을 최소화 하기 위해 노력하고 있으며, 수송분야도 우이신설선 경전철 연장, GTX-C노선 광역 철도망 확충 등 대중교통 활성화에 주력하여 개인 승용차 이용 억제를 통해 온실가스 감축을 도모하고 있다. 또한, 공공 재활용선별장을 신축하여 생활폐기물 재활용 극대화로 소각·매립 폐기물량을 최소화 하는 등 지역 개발 계획에 온실가스 감축을 고려하고 있다. 또한, 기후변화 영향 및 취약성 분석 결과를 바탕으로 적응 중점추진 분야 선정하고, 적응대책 우선순위 도출하여, 세부시행대책의 실행 가능성 등 다양한 소요를 검토하여 건강, 재난재해, 물관리, 산림/생태계, 적응기반 등 5개 부문, 6개 세부전략, 10개 실천과제, 31개 세부사업의 기후변화 적응대책을 추진하고 있다. 이와 같은 도봉구의 기후위기 대응 및 적응은 2025년 4월에 수립된 '제1차 도봉구 탄소중립 녹색성장 기본계획(2025~2034년)' 과 2021년 12월에 수립된 '제2차 도봉구 기후변화 적응대책 세부시행계획(2022~2025년)'을 기반으로 하여 추진되고 있다
column17: 도봉구는 기후변화 적응대책으로 노약자 무더위 쉼터 운영, 감염병 대응체계 구축, 수해안전대책 강화, 산불예방및 산사태 위험지역 피해방지 등의 사업을 추진하고 있고, 완화(온실가스 감축)대책으로 노후건물 그린리모델링 추진, 재생에너지 보급 확대, 대중교통망 확충, 폐기물 감량화, 탄소흡수원 확대 등의 사업을 추진하고 있어 매년 기후변화로 인한 재정 부담이 증가하고 있다. 전문기관 연구용역에 따르며, 기후변화 적응분야에 2025년까지 약 40,266백만원, 기후변화 완화(온실가스 감축)분야에 2034년까지 548,319백만원이 소요될 것으로 전망하고 있다. 아울러, 2026년부터는 예산과 기금이 기후변화에 미치는 영향을 분석하고 이를 재정 운용에 반영하는 온실가스감축인지 예산제도를 시범 실시할 계획이다.
column18: 저탄소 경제로의 전환은 탄소기반 산업구조의 붕괴를 의미한다. 따라서 기존 탄소기반 산업이 저탄소 경제로 정의롭게 전환할 수 있도록 지방정부의 노력이 요구된다. 특히, 도봉구는 관내 많은 내연기관 자동차 정비업소가 있어, 전기· 수소자동차 등 친환경 자동차의 보급 확대로 인한 내연기관 차량 감소는 관내 정비업소에 실질적인 위험요소로 작용 할 수 있어 친환경자동차 정비로의 사업전환이나 업종 변경이 필요하며, 또한 관내 주유소나 LPG 충전소도 같은 위험에 직면하고 있어 전기차 충전소나 수소충전소로의 사업전환이 필요하다.

column15:
La jurisdicción cuenta con diversos mecanismos para la supervisión de los asuntos relacionados con el clima. Los departamentos y áreas técnicas reciben de forma periódica información de la administración sobre riesgos emergentes, eventos climatológicos extremos y oportunidades de adaptación.
Las responsabilidades vinculadas al cambio climático están asignadas a cargos dentro de la estructura administrativa para coordinar acciones entre áreas sectoriales. Además, se han conformado mesas de trabajo interjurisdiccionales e interdisciplinarias que se activan ante fenómenos específicos tales como olas de calor, viento zonda o tormentas, facilitando la toma de decisiones y la articulación interinstitucional.
El municipio ejerce la supervisión de asuntos relacionados con el clima y otras cuestiones ambientales en el territorio a través de la policia ambiental, inspectores técnicos ambientales que trabajan coordinadamente con las demás áreas de inspección con que cuenta el gobierno municipal.
column16:
Se han ejecutado obras de drenaje para mitigar el efecto de las tormentas, que consisten en 400 km de canalizaciones hidráulicas que han logrado una captación del 70% de las aguas pluviales y erradicado las inundaciones en numerosos barrios del ejido. El Plan de Drenaje ha sido el instrumento del municipio para guiar la ejecución de las obras anteriormente mencionadas, además se está realizando la planificación del drenaje de la tercera trocha de la autopista Acceso Este totalmente el municipio en una extensión de aproximadamente 16 km.

También se ha activado una mesa interjurisdiccional para prevenir los efectos de las olas y abordar sus contingencias por los próximos meses de verano, evaluando estrategias de distribución de agua, la realización de un protocolo de acción y la instalación de refugios climáticos orientados a la población más vulnerable a estos fenómenos.

Un documento importante para el abordaje de asuntos relacionados con el clima es el Plan Local de Acción Climática donde contemplan medidas como también la instalación de estaciones meteorológicas municipales que permitirán supervisar con información propia, la captación, almacenamiento y distribución de agua de lluvia por parte del municipio, la institucionalización de un comité de contingencias climáticas, 

Además, el Plan Municipal de Ordenamiento Territorial (PMOT) es un instrumento que incorpora los asuntos relacionados con el clima en su análisis y define estrategias de ordenamiento en base a ello.
column17: El cambio climático y sus efectos también son contemplados en la distribución de las partidas presupuestarias, por ejemplo en el presupuesto se han tenido en cuenta asignaciones para refugios climáticos y sistemas de alerta temprana (SAT) para eventos meteorológicos severos, programas de capacitación en tecnologías de riego eficiente, orientados a evitar el derroche de agua y amortiguar los efectos de las sequías, como también implementar estrategias de reutilización de aguas grises, especialmente en edificios públicos y desarrollos urbanos. \n
column18: Los riesgos y desafíos relevantes para la transición hacia una economía baja en carbono son, por un lado, la electrificación de flotas, mejoras en la infraestructura y servicio de transporte público y la disminución del uso de combustibles fósiles implica inversiones significativas y, por otro, la reconversión hacia fuentes renovables y la implementación de estrategias eficiencia energética. Estos riesgos se están abordando mediante estrategias progresivas de planificación y gestión.\n

column15: Actualmente, nuestra Municipalidad cuenta con una Dirección de Riesgos y Desastres, instancia en la que el clima es evaluado y considerado como un factor relevante para la toma de decisiones orientadas a la prevención de desastres naturales. Prevenir los efectos de lluvias intensas, tormentas eléctricas, granizos, heladas u otros fenómenos que puedan poner en riesgo la calidad de vida de las y los habitantes de la comuna constituye el eje principal de esta Dirección, destinándose recursos propios para fortalecer su gestión.\n\nAsimismo, se encuentra vigente el Plan de Acción de Cambio Climático Comunal, el cual establece lineamientos estratégicos que deben ser ejecutados por el municipio con el fin de adaptarse y mitigar los efectos del cambio climático en el territorio. Dichos lineamientos guardan plena concordancia con el Plan de Desarrollo Comunal y con la Política Ambiental Comunal, actualmente en proceso de elaboración, en la cual el clima se reconoce como un eje central para la correcta toma de decisiones ambientales por parte del municipio.
column16:
Nuestra comuna de Lautaro se encuentra emplazada en el valle central, con un centro urbano consolidado. No obstante, sus límites comunales colindan tanto con la precordillera como con el secano, lo que genera una diversidad territorial y climática de alta relevancia. Estas condiciones hacen que las variables climáticas sean un factor determinante al momento de planificar y ejecutar acciones por parte de la Dirección de Riesgos y Desastres de la Municipalidad.

En este sentido, resulta fundamental destacar la existencia de recursos orientados a la correcta implementación de planes de contingencia, los cuales han permitido enfrentar de manera más eficiente los eventos climáticos extremos que han afectado el territorio en los últimos años.

Paralelamente, la educación ambiental ha adquirido un rol protagónico, contribuyendo a generar conciencia en la comunidad respecto de la necesidad de prepararse y tomar acción frente a las distintas contingencias climáticas que puedan presentarse en Lautaro.

De igual manera, la Dirección de Medio Ambiente, Aseo y Ornato ha reforzado su compromiso al impulsar iniciativas de divulgación y sensibilización, difundiendo información clave sobre temáticas relacionadas con el clima y su impacto en la vida cotidiana de los habitantes de la comuna.
column17: Principalmente, estas acciones se canalizan a través de la Dirección de Riesgos y Desastres de la Municipalidad, instancia desde la cual se destinan los recursos necesarios para financiar y coordinar las medidas de respuesta frente a la contingencia climática actual. Esta unidad cumple un rol estratégico, ya que permite planificar, organizar y ejecutar los protocolos de emergencia con el fin de reducir los riesgos, resguardar la seguridad de la población y garantizar la continuidad de las actividades cotidianas en la comuna.
column18:
La principal problemática que enfrentamos se relaciona con la limitada disponibilidad de recursos para incentivar a la población en la transición hacia el uso de fuentes energéticas renovables.
Nuestra comuna es la quinta más grande de la región y presenta una alta concentración de habitantes en sectores rurales, donde, históricamente, la leña ha sido el medio de calefacción más utilizado. Sin embargo, en la mayoría de los casos, esta leña no se encuentra seca, lo que genera emisiones contaminantes que se suman a las provenientes del parque industrial existente en la comuna.
Cabe señalar que nuestra comuna se encuentra emplazada en una cuenca geográfica, lo que provoca que la acumulación de humo sea cada vez más evidente y perceptible en el ambiente.
Otra problemática relevante es la falta de conciencia ambiental en la población. La educación en esta materia resulta fundamental para fomentar un mejor uso de la energía a nivel familiar. Asimismo, es crucial incorporar contenidos relacionados con energías renovables y eficiencia energética desde los establecimientos educacionales, de manera que desde la primera infancia se promueva una nueva forma de comprender y utilizar la energía.

column15:
Our legacy comprise the municipal council, the municipal executive board, the municipal administration, committees and municipal companies. (The follow up made in the municipial companies are not mentioned in this text)

A follow-up on our climate mitigation goals and actions is made once a year in the municipal annual report. Our climate actions are reported in the organisation's quality system, as well as climate indicators.

The last two years a follow up on our carbon budget has been presented to the executive board, along with follow up on some climate actions. Climate actions are discussed reguarly by the municipal executive committee for Agenda 2030.

Since one year ago there is a central climate programme. A comprehensive follow up on our climate actions are developed at the very moment. 

When it comes to climate adaptation there is no follow up at all.
column16:
A new comprehensive plan is being formed right now, a process thats usually takes a couple of years, climate-competence are part of the process.

In the exsiting comprehensive plan energy and climate concerns are directly and indirectly addressed but the question remains whether it is sufficiently included in the plans and if it is being implemented. Climate adaptation issues will be included in the new comprehensive plan, but it is scarce in the existing plan.

The existing comprehensive plan includes nine strategies. Three of them are clearly addressing climate-related issues:
Number 2. A green and blue structure for the health and quality of life for the population
-Local stormwater management is used as an aesthetic element in city
Number 3. A traffic structure promoting an increase of pedestrians, cycling and public transport
- Prioritize walking, cycling and public transport at intersection points and the like
-Create safe and accessible hubs for public transport
Number 8. Long term resource management and reduced climate footprint
-Promote energy-efficient construction in new construction and energy efficiency in existing buildings
-Promote more buildings being built in wood
- Minimize the need for transport in urban areas through densification and nearby service of the residence
-Create and maintain conditions for the production of renewable electricity in Municipality of Trollhättan
-Promote waste minimisation based on the waste hierarchy
-In the central town, strive not to have more than 500 meters between residences and recycling stations

Energy: Wind power is a part of the comprehensive plan. There are legal requirement to designate locations. Solar power may eventually get legal requirements as well.
When it comes to energy efficiency [in buildings] and the like, Trollhättan applies national requirements.
Other climate related planning document:
-Plan for the expansion of cycle paths
-Energy plan. The current energy plan mostly focus on the municipal organization rather than the geographical area that constitutes the municipality.
-Stormwater management strategy. The buildings must be able to cope with changing climatic conditions with more intense precipitation.

The Sanliurfa Metropolitan Municipality Climate Change and Zero Waste Department's Duties and Working Regulation\' has been published to define the organizational structure. In this regulation, the duties, authorities, and responsibilities of the Head of the Climate Change and Zero Waste Department are defined as follows: a) In parallel with the 2053 zero emission and green development visions that we have set as a country within the framework of the Paris Climate Agreement, to carry out activities to create a healthy, green city that is resilient against climate hazards and risks arising from global warming by reducing the use of fossil fuels and greenhouse gas emissions at the local level, b) To carry out projects related to air, water, soil, noise, etc., aimed at the protection and development of environmental values and natural resources, and to cooperate with/recruit services from relevant public institutions and private companies for this purpose, c) To apply the necessary legal and administrative procedures within the scope of authority against individuals, institutions, and organizations causing pollution during routine inspections/controls or those based on complaints regarding the protection of the environment and environmental health, and to notify the competent authorities in matters outside the scope of authority detected during inspections/controls, d) To carry out/conduct studies, plans, projects, and laboratory work on the protection, development, improvement, and cleaning of the environment in accordance with the principle of sustainable development, e) To ensure the coordination of local climate change mitigation efforts with all relevant public institutions, and to organize/carry out capacity-building activities for the preparation and implementation of local climate change action plans, f) To monitor, control, report, and revise existing reports on greenhouse gas emissions causing climate change at the local level, g) To implement applications, develop projects, and ensure necessary coordination at the provincial level for the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions, h) To ensure the coordination of monitoring and evaluation studies on climate change adaptation policies, i) To develop and implement projects aimed at making the city resilient to the effects of climate change in cooperation with relevant institutions and organizations, j) To prepare or have prepared local reports that our country is obliged to prepare within the scope of international organizations and agreements, k) To conduct public information and awareness activities on environment and climate change issues. A total of 10 engineers (4 of them are environmental engineers), 1 architect, and 1 urban planner work on environmental issues at the Sanliurfa Metropolitan Municipality. To effectively manage climate change-related studies with city stakeholders, the \'Climate High Council and Climate Working Group Circular\' was published and came into effect on 18/07/2024. The duties and responsibilities of the Climate High Council are as follows: a) Formulate and periodically review and update the fundamental policies and strategies related to climate change. b) Approve the Climate Change Action Plans prepared by the Climate Working Group and ensure their annual review. c) Plan and implement activities envisaged in the short, medium, and long term in the Climate Change Action Plan, and ensure the provision of necessary information, human, and financial resources for this purpose. d) Establish project teams for planned actions related to climate change adaptation and greenhouse gas reduction, and determine their duties and responsibilities. e) Evaluate feedback and results of the tasks assigned to the working group and follow up on the process. f) Evaluate and decide on project proposals related to climate change from the working group.

Şanlıurfa is recognized as the central point of the Southeastern Anatolia Project (GAP) and hosts the administrative headquarters of the GAP Administration. GAP is a regional development project approached with a multi-sectoral, integrated, and sustainable development perspective. GAP envisions the construction of 22 dams, 19 hydroelectric power plants, and irrigation systems covering an area of 1.82 million hectares. However, due to drought, excessive wild irrigation poses a threat of salinization and desertification to the lands in the region. Şanlıurfa is located in the southeast of Turkey, near the Syrian border, and is grappling with a heavy influx of refugees. The city has a hot and dry desert climate, posing a threat to public health due to extreme heat waves. Sanliurfa is in a semi-arid region, making it vulnerable to drought conditions. Between 2000 and 2020, the GAP ( South-eastern Anatolia) region received less rainfall than its annual average for 12 years, and ¸Sanlıurfa has received 13% less rainfall than the average of the GAP region. Between 2008 and 2017, Sanlıurfa experienced exceptional drought conditions twice, extreme drought twice. agriculture is the most significant economic sector in Sanliurfa; for most households, seasonal agricultural work is the only source of income. Summer temperatures exceed 40°C. According to climate projections for the region between 2050 and 2060, monthly average temperatures are expected to increase by 2.1 - 2.7 °C. This will significantly affect health problems, restricted water availability, and agricultural productivity. 
The main objective of CLIMAAX is to support the implementation of preparedness and planning for climate resilience, which is the first goal of the EU Adaptation Strategy and the Horizon Europe Adaptation Mission.
The region's priorities are based on the SECAP (2022), the CLIMAAX Climate Risk Assessment (2025), and ongoing work under P2R. 
Local Level 
Key municipal goals include: 
•	Expanding green infrastructure to decrease urban heat stress, especially in low-income areas. 
•	Modernizing irrigation systems to address agricultural water stress and reduce energy use. 
•	Launching a citywide Climate Resilience Strategy and Investment Plan under P2R. 
•	Strengthening institutional capacity via cross-departmental coordination. 
Planned adaptation objectives (SECAP 2024) include increasing urban green space, reducing water network leakage, reusing treated water, implementing rainwater harvesting systems, and utilising greywater systems. 
Regional Level :
As part of the GAP Regional Action Plan (2024-2028), Şanlıurfa will benefit from: 
•	Extension of Large-scale irrigation program (from 675.000 hectares to 1.150.000 hectares) including agri-solar applications 
•	Sustainable smart-Precision transformation in Agriculture Program (from 28.000 hectares to 400,000 hectares) 
•	Socio-economic development in rural livelihoods and agricultural resilience. (Employment for 570,246 people) 

CRAS findings support climate risk awareness across neighboring provinces. 
National Level: 
Şanlıurfa aligns with: 
•	Türkiye's National Climate Change Adaptation Strategy and 2053 Net-Zero target. 
•	National programs on digital agriculture, smart irrigation, and green urban transformation. 

EU Level: 
The city contributes to the EU Mission on Adaptation and uses CLIMAAX methodology to align with EU standards. It participates in the P2R programme and engages with networks such as the Covenant of Mayors and Climate-ADAPT. Future access to Horizon Europe, Green Deal, and LIFE funding is actively pursued. 
Private Sector :
Private actors are increasingly involved in solar energy deployment, urban agriculture pilots, and irrigation technologies—often through public-private partnerships facilitated by municipal and regional initiatives.

column15: During the COP15 conference in Copenhagen on 17 December 2009, Malaysia has made a commitment to reduce carbon emissions by up to 40% of the intensity of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2020 compared to 2005. The Prime Minister of Malaysia in his speech during 2010 Malaysia Budget speech on 23 October 2009, had announced “to develop Putrajaya and Cyberjaya as Green Technology Cities as pioneers to other urban development” as one of the measures to promote green technology development activities in Malaysia. To achieve the Government's aspiration, Putrajaya Corporation (PJC) has decided to formulate a Putrajaya Green City 2025. Various national policy documents on Climate Change are in place to guide such as The National Low Carbon Cities Masterplan (NLCCM); Green Technology Master Plan Malaysia 2017-2030; Low Carbon Cities Framework etc. NLCCM has set a mitigation target for Putrajaya which is 33% absolute GHG emissions reduction by 2030. Putrajaya Corporation (PJC) must therefore adopt the target for CAP to support this national target, as well as clear goals for achieving climate adaptation by that year. Prime Minister said during the 2024 budget speech on 13 October 2023, had announced Putrajaya would be a low-carbon city model.
column16: The vision for Putrajaya is to transform itself from a Garden City into a Green City by the year 2025. In doing this, it has identified 4 Big Moves and 8 Policies in its gazette Putrajaya Structure Plan 2025. Towards achieving a Green City in Putrajaya, 12 actions are introduced here in this study. These actions are divided according to the three environmental targets. The target for “Low-carbon Putrajaya” is reducing GHG emission intensity (per economic activity) related to energy use by 60% compared to year 2007 level. This target was set in line with the National Target of 40% reduction of CO2 emission intensity by 2020 and also based on the future plan as stated in the Putrajaya Structure Plan. For “Cooler Putrajaya”, the target is reducing peak temperature 2°C from year 2005 level. Therefore, two targets were set for “3R Putrajaya”; reducing final disposal of solid waste and GHG emission from solid waste management by 50% compared to 2025 BaU level. In 2022, Putrajaya Corporation had published Putrajaya Climate Action Plan 2030 that covers both climate mitigation and adaptation. As a holistic plan, the Putrajaya CAP 2030 proposes 38 planned actions for implementation which are also in line with the Low Carbon Cities Framework (LCCF) Malaysia. The mitigation target is to reduce absolute GHG carbon emission up to 33 % by 2030, base year 2021. While the adaptation goal is to develop cooler Putrajaya City, preventing number of dengue cases and improve landscaping against severe wind.

The overall strategic approach to the climate emergency is considered and agreed by the full Council. Day to day governance of many issues concerning climate change are primarily through the Climate Change and Sustainability Committee. The Committee considers matters relating to: climate change, sustainability of the natural environment, biodiversity, and environmental well-being. The Committee monitors and oversees progress in relation to the Council's Climate Change Action Plan, while it also provides guidance to the relevant Committees in relation to: Environmental Protection and Enhancement, Countryside Management, Parks and Open Spaces, Trees and Woodlands, Flood Prevention and Waste Management.

The Climate Change and Sustainability Group (established in 2018), chaired by the Climate Change and Zero Waste Manager, leads on Climate Change within the Council and reports to the Climate Change and Sustainability Committee. The Strategic Lead for Environment and Infrastructure leads on climate change within the Council and acts as the Executive Sponsor of the Climate Change and Sustainability Group. Co-ordination and progress reporting of the Council's commitments under the Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009 is part of the remit of the Climate Change and Zero Waste Team based in Environment and Infrastructure. The Climate Change and Sustainability Group consisting of representatives from the relevant housing and environment teams allows for co-ordinated sharing of best practice across the services. The Group is divided into thematic subgroups (Energy & Buildings, Transport, Climate Resilience, Waste & Circular Economy, Education & Engagement, Governance, Business & Industry, and Land use). 

The corporate committee report template includes requirement for Sustainability and Climate Change and Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) to be considered as part of the committee reporting process. The sustainability assessment section also reflects the Council's duty under the Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009. The template also requires use of the council's Impact and Value Assessment (IVA) tool to screen reports. The IVA has been designed to screen every Council project, strategy or proposal against statutory and non-statutory environmental, social and economic requirements. The questionnaire has been designed to give a robust screening of proposals, with sections covering strategic and resource implications, and impact assessment for Climate change, Equality & Fairness, Child Rights & Wellbeing, Sustainable Procurement & Supply, and Strategic Environmental Assessment. Once the IVA form is submitted, documents are automatically emailed based on answers given in relation to: Strategic and Resource Implications, and Impact Assessments. 

Since December 2022 'Tackling Climate Change' has been one of PKC's seven corporate priorities. As such it is key theme in corporate and service level annual plans and reporting. Climate Change KPIs are embedded into the corporate performance framework and scrutinised there as well as through the annual climate change plan and update process.

 Across Perth and Kinross climate change is viewed as an area wide issue and is addressed under the remit of the Perth and Kinross Community Planning - Environment and Public Realm Outcome Delivery Group. Along with the Council, organisation members of the group include: Perth & Kinross Association of Voluntary Service (PKAVS), Scottish Environment Protection Agency (SEPA), NHS Tayside, Police Scotland, Scottish Fire and Rescue Service, Forestry Commission and NatureScot. Climate change has now become a priority within Perth & Kinross Council as reflected in the Council's Corporate Plan. 

A Perth and Kinross Climate Change Commission was also formed in 2022 .The Commission champions the delivery of the Perth and Kinross Climate Strategy and Action Plan, acting as an independent scrutiny mechanism.

In Scotland, the National Planning Framework 4 puts climate change and biodiversity as the first priority and this framework governs the Council's plans and planning decisions. The Council is currently in the process of developing the Local Development Plan 3 (local master plan). To inform the evidence base for this plan we undertook the Big Place Conversation across our communities, with climate change as one of the key themes. Climate change considerations are embedded into the plan development processes and several of the associated policies (forest and woodland strategy, heat network zoning, nature networks, blue green infrastructure, etc). 

In addition, the current Perth and Kinross Local Development Plan 2 was adopted in 2019 and guides all future development and use of land in the Perth and Kinross area. Climate Change is considered throughout the plan and more specifically, in relation to adaptation, renewable energy, sustainable/renewable heat, waste management, water and sewage, and land use. 

Perth & Kinross Council declared their support for the climate emergency through a motion in June 2019, outlining a plan of action to mitigate and adapt to the effects of Climate Change. The Interim Climate Emergency Report and Action Plan was approved by Perth & Kinross Council in December 2019 with a view to establishing a baseline from which the Council can engage with national and local elected representatives, partners, communities and citizens. The Strategy and Action Plan outline the key objectives with regards to eight thematic areas; Transport, Buildings & Energy, Waste & Circular Economy, Land Use, Climate Resilience, Education & Engagement, Governance, and Business & Industry. 
Six overarching principles have been developed that will shape Perth & Kinross Council's long-term approach to climate change. These are:- Achieving net zero aligned with with the Paris Agreement and the Scottish Government Target, with the ambition of achieving them sooner- Building a more resilient Perth and Kinross- Ensuring climate action is fair and benefits all and we deliver a green recovery to Covid-19- Enhancing biodiversity to help avoid an ecological emergency- Engaging and empowering children and young people to take action on climate change- Empowering our communities and businesses to take climate action.
column17: Climate change is becoming increasingly embedded within the Council's financial planning. Work was undertaken to identify a range of projects that would support the Council's approach to climate change. In parallel with approving the Climate Change Action Plan in December 2021, in the 2022/23 Revenue Budget £500,000 of recurring spend was approved from 2022/23 onwards. For the first time as part of the 23/24 budget setting process all pressures (additions) and cuts were screened for their climate change impact as has continued for 24/25 and 25/26 budgets. \n\nThe significant investment required to for the Council to achieve net zero are starting to appear in the Council's capital works pipeline and financial forecasting. All new builds and major refurbishments are required by council policy to meet Passivhaus standard.

Perth and Kinross Council is one of the largest geographical areas in Scotland and it consists of a very large rural population. This poses many challenges for efficient transport emission reductions. Electric vehicles have the potential to have a big impact on rural transport emissions, however, they are only part of the solution as are still unaffordable to many residents. Ensuring the availability of public charging facilities in the rural areas is also crucial to ensure that these populations are not disadvantaged in the transition to a low-carbon economy. 

The Scottish Government have set a target to reduce vehicle kms by 20% by 2030 (against a 2019 baseline). If it was all met by increased public transport usage, this would be equivalent to a 360% increase on 2019 levels. Projected population growth, especially in edge of town developments will pose additional challenge to achieving this target. 

The Perth and Kinross Local Heat and Energy Efficiency Strategy identified that homes in PKC were older, larger and had lower levels of energy performance than the national average. Decarbonising the housing stock also poses a huge challenge. 

In addition to the above, we are facing large and persistent skills gaps and skills shortages needed for the net zero transition, which may hamper the ability to meet net zero targets. To ensure the transition to a low-carbon economy requires a large behavioural shift from reactive to proactive measures by residents and businesses, as well as Perth & Kinross Council. 

The UK's Committee on Climate Change identifies that behavioural change will be required at least in part, for at least 60% of the required emission reduction. The Council is responsible for only 3% of direct emissions, but has estimated influence to varying degrees to over 80-90% of emissions. 

Financing the low-carbon transition will be a challenge - the Council has been able to resource the development of plans and strategies, but there is a looming finance gap for the implementation of these strategies. The above mentioned challenges pose a great risk to effectively reaching net zero and ensuring the transition to a low-carbon economy.
