Nowon-gu has announced the “Basic Plan for Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth” to effectively respond to the climate crisis and achieve the 2050 carbon neutrality target. The plan is designed to analyze the current status and characteristics of local greenhouse gas emissions, establish strategies for both mitigation and adaptation, and present a leading model for achieving net-zero at the municipal level.

The plan is guided by four strategic objectives: (1) implementing an urban system optimized for carbon neutrality, (2) creating comfortable and efficient living environments through Zero Energy Buildings (ZEB) and green remodeling, (3) establishing a “10-minute cycling city” to promote sustainable mobility, and (4) encouraging a 1.5℃ lifestyle that supports low-carbon practices. To achieve these objectives, Nowon-gu is undertaking 69 projects across six major sectors: energy transition, green buildings, green mobility, resource circulation, green preservation, and citizen participation.

Key measures include enhancing energy self-sufficiency with renewable energy in the energy transition sector; strengthening ZEB requirements for redevelopment projects and improving energy efficiency in non-redevelopment apartment complexes in the building sector; reducing automobile demand and improving the accessibility and convenience of cycling and public transportation in the transport sector; promoting joint campaigns and education programs to encourage citizen engagement in the resource circulation and participation sectors; and expanding carbon sinks through tree planting and transplantation management in the green preservation sector.

For the management and oversight of this plan, Nowon-gu has established a governance process. The intermediary support organization, the Carbon Neutrality Support Center, conducts monitoring, evaluation, and feedback on the implementation of carbon neutrality and incorporates the results into its reviews. The outcomes are reported to and approved by the Carbon Neutrality Committee, which performs the functions of deliberation, decision-making, and advisory on policies related to Nowon-gu's carbon neutrality and green growth. Once approved, the results are subsequently submitted to the Ministry of Environment.

In addition, Nowon-gu established its Second Climate Change Adaptation Plan in 2020, aimed at building a solid foundation for local adaptation through systematic management of climate-vulnerable groups and facilities. The plan covered five areas: the health sector (nine sub-projects, including epidemic and infectious disease response systems), the disaster/hazard sector (five sub-projects on vulnerable facility management and disaster risk reduction), the forest and ecosystem sector (five sub-projects on conservation and sustainable management), the water management sector (four sub-projects on water quality and resilient infrastructure), and the adaptation foundation sector (ten sub-projects to strengthen institutional capacity and governance).

Currently, Nowon-gu is developing its Third Climate Crisis Adaptation Plan (2026-2030), building on the outcomes of the second plan while reflecting updated climate risk assessments. This will enhance the effectiveness and forward-looking nature of adaptation policies and ensure alignment with both national and metropolitan frameworks.

Oversight and management of the Second Climate Change Adaptation Plan are carried out as follows : The Ministry of Environment provides annual guidelines for performance review, based on which Nowon-gu establishes its own self-assessment plan. A mid-term implementation review is then conducted to evaluate the status of progress and management. Subsequently, Nowon-gu performs a self-assessment and prepares an evaluation report. Each February, the self-assessment report together with the implementation plan for the following year is submitted to the Ministry of Environment for final review. If any areas require improvement, they are addressed in consultation with the Ministry of Environment.

Through this integrated approach, Nowon-gu seeks to establish strategies tailored to local conditions while aligning with national and Seoul Metropolitan Government policies, thereby positioning itself as a leading model for achieving carbon neutrality and strengthening climate resilience.
column16:
An analysis of Nowon-gu's greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by sector shows that 75% of total emissions come from the building sector, 23% from the transport sector, and 2% from the waste sector. Within the building sector, households account for 45% and the commercial/public sector accounts for 30%. This indicates that reducing emissions from buildings is critical to achieving carbon neutrality in Nowon-gu.

Based on this, the climate crisis has driven the district to take proactive measures, including the early adoption of Zero Energy Buildings (ZEB) in new construction.

The climate crisis has influenced Nowon-gu to proactively introduce Zero Energy Buildings (ZEB) in new construction. With a high proportion of aging buildings and an upcoming large-scale urban renewal project involving approximately 70,000 households, early action was deemed necessary to ensure strengthened ZEB standards are applied to redevelopment and reconstruction complexes.

In response, Nowon-gu established the Carbon Neutrality Plan for the Building Sector, guided by the vision of “No building without solar power.” Under this plan, the jurisdiction aims to move ahead of the national timeline by promoting ZEB Level 4 for new private buildings starting in 2030.

While the national government mandates ZEB Level 4 for new public buildings beginning in 2025, Nowon-gu advanced this requirement by one year and has already applied it from 2024. Similarly, although the national plan calls for ZEB Level 3 mandatory from 2030, Nowon-gu has accelerated the timeline by two years and plans to implement ZEB Level 3 or higher certification starting in 2028. Through these measures, Nowon-gu provides a roadmap for public buildings that is one to two years ahead of national policy.

Looking further ahead, Nowon-gu has set a goal that by 2050, all public and private buildings will achieve ZEB Level 1, aligning with its net-zero target year.

In addition to Zero Energy Buildings (ZEB), Nowon-gu is also planning to implement various carbon neutrality support projects in the building sector. These include the Green Campus initiative for universities, a program to support the replacement of outdated transformers, and assistance programs to improve energy efficiency for small businesses. Furthermore, to strengthen the foundation and policy framework for carbon neutrality in the building sector, the district plans to introduce demand response (DR) systems, expand the use of smart metering, and establish and operate Building Energy Management Systems (BEMS).

1. Nowon-gu has established the “Basic Plan for Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth” to implement an urban system optimized for carbon neutrality and is preparing to carry out 69 detailed projects under this plan.

To support carbon neutrality and green growth, it is projected that more than KRW 1.1 trillion will be required over the next five years (2025-2029). Estimated costs by sector include KRW 10.9 billion for buildings, KRW 4.8 billion for energy transition, KRW 60.8 billion for transport, KRW 20.4 billion for waste, KRW 2.0 billion for sinks, and KRW 0.8 billion for citizen cooperation.

The average annual fiscal growth rate for the period 2025-2029 is expected to be approximately 5.5%, which is about 3.5 times higher than the projected average annual growth rate of 1.5% in the Nowon-gu Medium-Term Local Financial Plan (2024-2028).

2. Nowon-gu has developed the Second Climate Change Adaptation Plan (2021-2025) to strengthen local adaptive capacity and reduce potential climate risks. The plan was formulated based on an assessment of local climate impacts and vulnerabilities, identifying priority adaptation areas and urgent issues, and establishing detailed implementation measures.

The plan includes 33 detailed projects with an estimated budget of KRW 80.4 billion over five years. Among these, the water management sector accounted for the largest share with KRW 36.7 billion, followed by health (KRW 14.5 billion), adaptation foundation (KRW 13.1 billion), forest/ecosystem (KRW 12.9 billion), and disaster/hazard (KRW 3.16 billion), which represented the smallest portion. Overall, the plan represents approximately 5.9% of the total district expenditure budget.

Given the worsening climate crisis since the establishment of the second plan, Nowon-gu is currently in the process of developing the Third Climate Crisis Adaptation Plan, which will introduce additional new projects and allocate a larger budget to strengthen climate resilience.

The transition to a low-carbon economy may generate additional costs and social impacts across multiple sectors in Nowon-gu.

In the building sector, the implementation of stricter Zero Energy Building (ZEB) requirements in Nowon-gu may lead to an increase in construction costs for developers, which could, in part, be reflected in higher housing expenses for residents. To proactively manage this potential risk, Nowon-gu is considering supportive measures such as floor area ratio (FAR) relaxation and tax reductions, with the aim of easing the financial impact and ensuring that the transition to low-carbon buildings remains equitable and broadly acceptable.

In the transport sector, the gradual phase-out of internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles is expected to lead to the decline of local auto repair businesses, such as Nowon-gu's “Car Center Street,” resulting in economic losses for workers and business owners in the sector. To minimize the associated economic and social costs, Nowon-gu plans to actively support training and education programs that enable industry workers to adapt to the low-carbon vehicle industry. Furthermore, the district is considering developing the existing Car Center Street into an EV-specialized street, thereby promoting a just transition and strengthening industrial adaptation capacity in the shift toward carbon neutrality.

Tepebaşı Municipality (Eskişehir) has established a structured climate governance system that operates across political, administrative, and community levels. The municipal council is regularly updated on climate and environmental issues by relevant technical departments and committees, particularly regarding the implementation of the Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP) under the Covenant of Mayors. This plan includes goals for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, increasing renewable energy use, and improving climate adaptation by 2030.

Climate responsibilities are clearly defined at both the executive and committee levels. The Sustainability and Climate Change Directorate, Environmental Protection Directorate, and Strategy Development Unit coordinate climate policies, monitor SECAP implementation, and report to senior management. Oversight is further supported by council committees and relevant departments, ensuring that climate goals are integrated into urban planning, procurement, and infrastructure projects.

Climate priorities are embedded in the municipality's programs and projects. Each proposed project is assessed not only for its technical and financial feasibility but also for its alignment with climate goals. Projects that support energy efficiency, clean transportation, and green infrastructure are prioritized. Risk management policies also take into account climate-related vulnerabilities such as extreme weather, urban flooding, and drought.
The municipality includes climate-related indicators in its performance objectives. Responsibilities for achieving climate and energy targets are assigned to senior management, ensuring accountability. Departments are informed of their roles and contributions. Internal monitoring is supported through regular emissions inventories, energy audits, and progress reports on SECAP implementation. Tepebaşı also engages in peer-learning through networks such as the Covenant of Mayors and ICLEI.

Public engagement is a key part of climate governance in Tepebaşı. The municipality organizes workshops, education programs, and public consultations to involve residents in climate action. The presence of two universities in the area supports collaboration with young people. Community-based initiatives like urban gardening and low-carbon mobility campaigns help build public ownership of climate goals.
In planning, the municipality applies sustainability principles through green infrastructure, climate-resilient urban design, and low-emission transportation systems. New projects also integrate nature-based solutions and energy-efficient technologies. Although challenges remain — particularly in accessing local climate data and securing finance — the municipality is working to improve its institutional capacity and digital tools to strengthen oversight and deliver effective, integrated climate action.
column16:
Since the year 2000, approximately 50% of maximum temperature records in Türkiye have been monitored, while this rate drops to as low as 10% for minimum temperature records. When examining Türkiye's meteorological changes over the past two decades, it is evident that the temperature regime has been significantly shifting toward milder and warmer conditions. Furthermore, there has been a noticeable increase in the frequency and intensity of heatwaves.

In Tepebaşı, the impacts of climate change are strongly felt. Increasing drought, forest fires, greenhouse gas emissions, and similar issues are becoming more prevalent. The goal of Tepebaşı Municipality is to mitigate and adapt to these challenges.

Tepebaşı Municipality is a signatory of the Covenant of Mayors (CoM), established by the European Commission to encourage and support urban mitigation plans for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and promoting the use of clean energy sources. Within this framework, the Municipality has committed to reducing greenhouse gas emissions by at least 40% by 2030 compared to the baseline year of 2019 and to implementing measures aimed at adapting to climate change.

Under the leadership of the Directorate of Climate Change and Zero Waste, and in coordination with local stakeholders, Tepebaşı Municipality has taken a significant step by preparing a Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP). The preparation process included several key phases, such as the development of greenhouse gas inventories, the formulation of emission reduction actions, risk and vulnerability assessments, and the creation of adaptation measures to better prepare the district for future climatic changes and to mitigate adverse impacts. Through the education programmes, workshops, and projects such as REMOURBAN, it has brought together citizens, NGOs, wide varairty of sector and universities within the public framework.
column17:
Climate-related issues have had a growing impact on the financial planning of Tepebaşı Municipality, particularly in shaping budget allocations, investment priorities, and project design. As the frequency and severity of extreme weather events such as droughts, floods, and heatwaves increase, the municipality has begun to integrate climate risk considerations into its long-term budgeting process. For instance, financial resources have been reallocated to support climate adaptation measures such as enhancing green infrastructure, expanding urban green spaces, and strengthening water resource management to reduce vulnerability to drought and flood risks.

Moreover, the municipality's commitment under the Covenant of Mayors to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by at least 40% by 2030 has led to the incorporation of climate mitigation targets into its fiscal frameworks. This has resulted in dedicated funds for renewable energy projects, energy efficiency upgrades in municipal buildings, and sustainable transport initiatives. Climate resilience and sustainability criteria are increasingly used in the evaluation and selection of public investment projects.

The SEAP planning process also identified the need for external funding sources, such as EU climate funds and international grants, to implement major adaptation and mitigation actions. As such, financial planning now includes mechanisms to leverage co-financing, develop bankable projects, and engage in partnerships with the private sector and academia. These shifts reflect a broader transformation towards climate-resilient budgeting and performance-based climate finance in local governance.

The transition to a low-carbon economy presents several interconnected risks for Tepebaşı Municipality, particularly in economic, social, and operational dimensions. One primary risk is financial: the upfront capital required for large-scale investments in renewable energy infrastructure, energy-efficient buildings, and sustainable mobility systems can place pressure on limited municipal budgets. Access to adequate financing and technical expertise is critical, and any delay in securing such support may hinder the transition timeline.

Another key risk is related to economic restructuring. Tepebaşı has a strong industrial base, and the decarbonization of industrial activities could result in job displacements, especially in sectors reliant on fossil fuels or high energy consumption. Without a just transition strategy that includes re-skilling, social support, and job creation in green sectors, vulnerable populations may face increased socio-economic hardship.

There is also a regulatory risk. As national and international climate policies evolve, municipalities may be required to comply with new emissions standards or sustainability reporting obligations. If not anticipated and integrated into planning, these changes could disrupt local operations or incur compliance costs.

Additionally, technological and market uncertainties—such as fluctuating costs of renewable technologies or the delayed uptake of electric vehicles and smart systems—pose operational and implementation risks for low-carbon transition projects. Resistance to behavioral change among residents and businesses, coupled with the need for institutional capacity building, may further challenge the speed and effectiveness of climate action.

Despite these risks, Tepebaşı Municipality views the transition as a necessary and strategic opportunity. Its climate action planning process includes proactive risk assessments and measures to minimize social and economic disruption while ensuring long-term environmental and financial sustainability.

column15: The Regional Municipality of Durham (Durham Region) is a regional municipality in Southern Ontario, Canada. Durham Region is comprised of eight lower tier municipalities: City of Pickering, Town of Ajax, City of Oshawa, Town of Whitby, Municipality of Clarington, Township of Scugog, Township of Brock, and the Township of Uxbridge. Durham Region's Community Climate Adaptation Plan (DCCAP) predicts a warmer, wetter and wilder future climate for the Region and its municipalities. The DCCAP is the Durham Region's response to the risks posed to the Region's infrastructure, community health and welfare, and its economy. As the Durham Region's climate is expected to get warmer in the future due to climate change, it would be essential for Durham Region to protect its forests and include measures to address climate-related issues, including the impacts of wildfires within the Region. For example, it is important to protect and adopt measures that will address climate-related issues in the Durham Regional Forest Main Tract as it encompasses over 596 hectares, and is comprised of plantation forests established over 90 years ago, as well as mixed hardwood areas. Thus, climate issues and others could be addressed during the five year renewal strategy proposed in DCCAP that identifies the inclusion of additional climate-related issues based on changing climate, extreme weather experiences, and lessons learned in program implementation.
column16: For the Durham Region, the implications of a changing climate include both local impacts which will directly affect us and national/international impacts which will affect us indirectly. Several extreme weather events have affected the Region of Durham along with its local municipalities, including:1. Summer 2008 Flooding Over the summer of 2008, Whitby and other areas in Durham Region experienced extreme rainfall. June, July, and August recorded levels at 185%, 400%, and 150% of monthly averages, with some localized intense storms exceeding the 100-year event. The extreme and constant rainfall saturated the ground and resulted in the capacity of underground storm systems being exceeded and excess stormwater flows that flooded multiple areas. Basement flooding also occurred in at least 150 homes. After this flooding event, local municipalities made upgrades to the storm system to reduce the likelihood of flood damage in the future. 2. Ice Storm of 2013The 2013 ice storm began rolling through Durham Region on Dec. 20 and by Dec. 23, thousands were without hydro after power lines were felled. Over 2,500 municipal trees, located in the boulevards, parks and open spaces, were damaged in Whitby due to the ice storm. The estimated cost of cleanup in Whitby at the time was in the order of about $795,000.3. July 2016 StormAn intense thunderstorm hit the Region in July 2016. The rainfall was estimated to be 30mm and fell very quickly, in combination with strong winds. Some businesses, like a local movie theatre, required evacuation and the estimated total cost across all of southern Ontario was $47 million.4. 2017 and 2019 Lake Ontario FloodingMany communities along Lake Ontario in both Ontario and the United States experienced record-breaking flooding in 2017. Clarington experienced significant flooding and as a result developed a comprehensive emergency response plan to be better prepared for the next flood event. Severe flooding affected households, businesses, and infrastructure in various areas of Ontario during the spring and summer of 2019. The Ontario Flooding Strategy was developed as a result of this flooding event.5. Record-breaking Snowstorm of 2022The record-breaking snowstorm on January 17, 2022, dropped up to 55 cm of snow in a 24-hour period. Whitby's Climate Emergency Response Plan Phase 1: Resilience (CERP) was being developed at this time and ISeeChange, an online climate engagement platform was being utilized to enable Whitby community members to help inform CERP by sharing their everyday experiences of climate and social vulnerability through photos and narratives. From this event, community posts mentioned increased irregularity and increased severity of winter storm events. Relatedly, public posts also discussed the prioritization of sidewalk clearing for major bus and pedestrian transit routes and around large apartment complexes where community members may rely more heavily on walking as their main form of transportation.6. Derecho In Whitby, May 2022While Whitby's Climate Emergency Response Plan Phase 1: Resilience (CERP) was being finalized in May 2022, a powerful windstorm called a derecho moved across Ontario, causing at least 11 deaths and resulted in power losses and extensive tree losses in the Town of Whitby. While it is difficult to directly correlate the derecho with climate change, the storm is a stark reminder that climate risks can take many forms. Derechos are not directly addressed in CERP, but many of the measures identified will increase resilience against windstorms and risks that are location-specific, such as flooding. In particular, this approach reduces the impact of compounding hazards when windstorms are combined with floods.While flooding and urban heat events represent the most expensive and fatal climate risks, respectively, to suburban communities like the Town of Whitby, these other year-over-year persistent risks warrant serious consideration with respect to compounding climate vulnerability, long-term costs, and planning. The feedback from the community engagement, historic extreme weather events and climate projections for Whitby under the RCP 8.5 scenario have helped to develop Phase 1: Resilience Plan of the Whitby Climate Emergency Response Plan that is being implemented across the community.
column17: Through Whitby's Climate Emergency Response Plan (CERP) Phase 1: Resilience financial modelling was completed to gain an understanding of the damages from climate change in the present day and in two future scenarios; business-as-usual future, and an adapted scenario . This has allowed for a comparison of the costs of action to adapt to climate change with the costs of inaction. The combination of the spatial, temporal, and financial analyses of Whitby today, in the business-as-usual future, and in an adapted scenario allows for a deeper understanding of the impacts of climate change on the community and helps to develop and prioritize a list of immediate actions to reduce climate risk across all sectors.The Whitby CERP Phase 1: Resilience is one of the first plans in North America to undergo a detailed financial analysis to understand the financial benefits of adapting to climate change. Annualized damages from flood and heat in Whitby are estimated to increase sevenfold by 2070 to more than $700 million per year in the absence of action using a Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) 8.5 model. Adaptation actions modelled financially include:o Restricting development from future flood zones;o Constructing flood berms in West Lynde and along Pringle Creek;o Dry-proofing and wet-proofing buildings;o Upgrading stormwater sewers for future climate conditions;o Improving culverts for future climate conditions;o Expanding green infrastructure; ando Undertaking building retrofits with heat pumps.Collectively the adaptation actions have the potential to reduce the annualized damages by 2070 to $65.8 million, representing a 27% decrease from 2020 levels and a 90% decrease over 2070 levels compared to a business-as-usual scenario. To support the achievement of the adaptation actions, a detailed five-year community-led implementation plan has been developed.
column18: The Zero Carbon Whitby Plan is a corporate mitigation strategy to achieve net zero emissions by 2045. Additionally, the Zero Carbon Whitby Costing Study (the Study), developed in 2022, is a schedule and costing analysis which provided a budgeted implementation plan for work required over the next 22 years to reduce Whitby's corporate greenhouse gas inventory to net-zero emissions. Potential risks to the implementation of Zero Carbon Whitby and related mitigation as well as contingency strategies were outlined in the study as follows:1. Labour-Related Risks - Implementation of the retrofit schedule is dependent on the availability and skill of workers.2. Electricity Risks - Changes to electricity generation sources and electricity demand will have associated risks for achieving GHG emissions reduction objectives.3. Energy Market Risks - Energy supply and costs are dependent on market forces. Changes in the energy market have inherent risks that can impact the successful implementation of several components of Zero Carbon Whitby.4. Governance Risks - Competing Town priorities and timelines could affect implementation. Strong leadership and timely and consistent implementation by departmental staff are critical for success.5. Service-Level Risks - Some changes may disrupt service levels for citizens using Whitby's facilities, such as facility closures due to implementation of energy efficiency measures.6. Supply Risk - Supply issues have the potential to delay the completion of Zero Carbon Whitby due to issues in getting the required materials and supplies.Refer Appendix A: Risk Analysis in the Zero Carbon Costing Study (pages 50 to 57 ) for risks, and related mitigation and contingency strategies. La Municipalidad de Cerro Navia cuenta con diversas instancias y estructuras orientadas a fortalecer la resiliencia climática y la capacidad de adaptación de la comuna frente a la problemática del cambio climático y sus múltiples amenazas. Este trabajo se desarrolla bajo distintas instancias formales de planificación, presentación de avances medioambientales a la Comisión Municipal de Medio Ambiente y mecanismos de articulación interdepartamental, en concordancia con los lineamientos del Gobierno Central y la normativa vigente. En particular, la comuna se alinea con lo establecido en la Ley Marco de Cambio Climático N.º 21.455, que establece la meta de carbono neutralidad y resiliencia al 2050, así como con los compromisos internacionales de Chile, tales como el Acuerdo de París y las Contribuciones Determinadas a Nivel Nacional (NDC), que obligan a implementar medidas de mitigación y adaptación a nivel local.
En este contexto, el Concejo Municipal recibe información periódica de las direcciones técnicas, especialmente de la Dirección de Medio Ambiente, Aseo y Ornato, a través de sus departamentos de Sustentabilidad y de la Dirección de Operaciones Viales y GRD, que actúan como unidades coordinadoras de las acciones ambientales, climáticas y de gestión del riesgo ante desastres. Estos reportes se orientan a la implementación del Plan de Acción Comunal de Cambio Climático (PACCC), la Estrategia Energética Local, y proyectos vinculados al Plan de Desarrollo Comunal (PLADECO) y a las metas establecidas en el Plan de Gobierno 2024-2028.
La supervisión se sustenta en una estructura organizativa con responsabilidades definidas. En ejemplo, se contempla la conformación, a más tardar a inicios de 2026, como parte de las medidas del PACCC, del Comité Ambiental Comunal, cuyo propósito será fortalecer la participación ciudadana y la fiscalización en materia climática. Este comité cumplirá funciones de seguimiento, evaluación y retroalimentación de las acciones ambientales, recibiendo información de las distintas unidades municipales y canalizando observaciones hacia el Concejo Municipal, contribuyendo al fortalecimiento de la gobernanza climática local. De manera complementaria, la Municipalidad busca actualizar su ordenanza ambiental, con el fin de incorporar de manera explícita disposiciones relativas a la mitigación y adaptación frente al cambio climático, considerando también la protección de la biodiversidad y de los servicios ecosistémicos.
En el plano operativo, las direcciones y departamentos municipales (Medio Ambiente, SECPLA, Obras, Aseo y Ornato, Educación, Salud, Operaciones Viales, GRD, entre otros) integran lineamientos climáticos en sus planes anuales de trabajo. Esto se traduce en la aplicación de criterios de eficiencia energética en edificios municipales, el diseño y mantenimiento de áreas verdes y programas de arborización urbana como sumideros de carbono, así como la gestión del riesgo climático frente a eventos extremos como olas de calor, inundaciones, sequías e incendios. La comuna está transitando hacia una gestión preventiva más que reactiva, promoviendo la mantención constante de los sumideros de carbono, la reforestación y protección de la ribera del río Mapocho (previniendo procesos de erosión del suelo), la arborización permanente en distintos barrios, y la implementación de refugios climáticos para enfrentar olas de calor extremo, entre otras medidas.
En materia de riesgos, la supervisión climática se articula con la gestión de emergencias locales, en coordinación con SENAPRED, integrando la adaptación al cambio climático en protocolos de respuesta frente a amenazas tales como inundaciones, olas de calor, sequías, incendios y episodios de contaminación atmosférica, todos fenómenos que incrementan la vulnerabilidad de la población local. Ante estos eventos, se activa el COGRID Comunal, lo que fortalece la capacidad de prevención, respuesta y recuperación ante emergencias.
En síntesis, Cerro Navia dispone de un sistema de supervisión multinivel: estratégico (planificación y Concejo Municipal), operativo (departamentos y direcciones) y participativo (comités ambientales). Este enfoque permite dar seguimiento, coordinar y alinear las acciones climáticas con los objetivos de desarrollo local, a la vez que se gestionan los riesgos climáticos, se protegen los ecosistemas y se refuerzan los servicios ecosistémicos.
column16:
La implementación de medidas, acciones y funciones permanentes orientadas a mejorar la resiliencia climática y la adaptación de la comuna frente al cambio climático ha tenido un impacto positivo en la calidad de vida de la comunidad. Cerro Navia enfrenta condiciones de alta vulnerabilidad socioambiental, derivadas de la contaminación atmosférica, el déficit de áreas verdes, la exposición a olas de calor, inundaciones y otros eventos extremos, lo que se suma a un tejido urbano con bajos índices de resiliencia climática y una creciente presión sobre los servicios ecosistémicos locales.
Frente a este contexto, el Plan de Gobierno Comunal 2024-2028 y el PLADECO han priorizado la integración de la dimensión climática en sus objetivos estratégicos. Esto se traduce en metas concretas de sustentabilidad, eficiencia energética, movilidad sostenible y mejoramiento de la infraestructura verde. Ejemplo de ello son los proyectos de arborización urbana, orientados a disminuir las islas de calor, fortalecer la biodiversidad y mejorar la calidad del aire; así como las inversiones en energías renovables comunitarias, que buscan reducir la dependencia de combustibles fósiles y la emisión de gases de efecto invernadero (GEI).
El Plan de Acción Comunal de Cambio Climático (PACCC) constituye la hoja de ruta más específica en esta materia, al definir líneas de acción en mitigación, adaptación y gestión del riesgo climático. Su implementación busca directamente incidir en la planificación urbana mediante la creación de corredores verdes, la recuperación de suelos degradados, y la incorporación de criterios de resiliencia climática en la infraestructura pública. En este ámbito, destaca también la labor del COGRID comunal, encargado de coordinar la respuesta frente a emergencias y amenazas climáticas, fortaleciendo la capacidad de adaptación de la comuna.
De igual manera, la Estrategia Energética Local ha incidido en la planificación en torno al consumo energético, estableciendo lineamientos para el uso eficiente de la energía en edificios municipales, programas de recambio tecnológico (luminarias LED, sistemas de calefacción eficiente) y la promoción de energías limpias en equipamientos comunitarios. 
En el plano social, los asuntos climáticos han incidido en las políticas de salud y educación: en salud, se han fortalecido protocolos frente a olas de calor y episodios de contaminación atmosférica, que representan un alto riesgo para la población más vulnerable, como adultos mayores, niños y mujeres, integrando un claro enfoque de género en la gestión comunal. En educación, se ha priorizado tanto la implementación de infraestructura sustentable en escuelas como la inclusión de contenidos de talleres de educación ambiental, fomentando el cuidado de los ecosistemas y la promoción de un desarrollo humano más sostenible.
En resumen, la planificación maestra de Cerro Navia ha transitado hacia un modelo más resiliente e inclusivo, en el que los asuntos climáticos ya no se abordan de forma aislada, sino como un eje transversal de la gestión comunal. Esta integración permite orientar inversiones, definir metas estratégicas y priorizar proyectos con enfoque de mitigación, adaptación, protección de la biodiversidad y fortalecimiento de los servicios ecosistémicos, contribuyendo a reducir los riesgos climáticos y a mejorar la calidad de vida de toda la población.
column17:
Los asuntos relacionados con el cambio climático han tenido un impacto directo en la planificación financiera de la Municipalidad de Cerro Navia, al generar la necesidad de asignar recursos específicos para mitigación, adaptación y fortalecimiento de la resiliencia climática. La comuna ha incorporado criterios climáticos en la formulación del presupuesto anual, considerando inversiones estratégicas que incluyen:
1.	Infraestructura verde y arborización urbana: a través de la disposición de fondos a la creación y mantención de parques, corredores verdes y sumideros de carbono, con el fin de reducir las islas de calor, mejorar la biodiversidad y fortalecer los servicios ecosistémicos.
2.	Eficiencia energética y energías renovables: se está realizando la transición en las energías limpias renovables, por lo que se está invirtiendo en la reconversión de luminarias públicas a tecnología LED, instalación de sistemas de calefacción eficiente y promoción de energías limpias en equipamientos comunitarios, contribuyendo a la reducción de emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero (GEI).
3.	Adaptación a eventos extremos: Presupuestando recursos para medidas preventivas frente a olas de calor, inundaciones y sequías, incluyendo la implementación de refugios climáticos, sistemas de alerta temprana y protocolos de emergencia a través del COGRID Comunal.
4.	Educación y sensibilización ambiental: Financiamiento de programas de educación ambiental y actividades comunitarias que fomenten la resiliencia climática, la participación ciudadana y la conciencia sobre riesgos climáticos.
5.	Planificación a largo plazo y sostenibilidad: Incorporando criterios de justicia climática y enfoque de equidad en la distribución de recursos, priorizando sectores vulnerables como niños, adultos mayores y familias de bajos ingresos.
column18:
La transición hacia una economía baja en carbono ofrece oportunidades para reducir las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero (GEI), proteger los ecosistemas y mejorar la resiliencia climática. No obstante, implica riesgos significativos para comunas con alta vulnerabilidad estructural como Cerro Navia, donde las condiciones sociales y económicas limitan la capacidad de adaptación.
De acuerdo con la Encuesta CASEN 2020, el 12,92 % de los hogares de la comuna vive en situación de pobreza por ingreso y un 2,8 % en pobreza extrema, cifras que reflejan la fragilidad de la estructura socioeconómica. A ello se suma la dependencia del Fondo Común Municipal (FCM) como principal fuente de ingresos, lo que restringe la autonomía financiera y la posibilidad de implementar proyectos de gran envergadura frente a los desafíos climáticos.
En este marco, los principales riesgos asociados a la transición se agrupan en las siguientes dimensiones:
Riesgos económicos y de financiamiento
- Las inversiones en energías renovables, eficiencia energética o infraestructura verde requieren un alto costo inicial de inversión, recursos significativos que superan la capacidad presupuestaria local actualmente. 
- Existe una sobredemanda de recursos frente a una limitada oferta de financiamiento, lo que genera una brecha entre las necesidades del territorio y los fondos disponibles a nivel central o internacional, dificultando la atención de todos los requerimientos locales

Riesgos tecnológicos e infraestructurales
- La alta densidad y condiciones de vivienda dificultan la implementación de soluciones descentralizadas como paneles solares o techos verdes.
- Ante infraestructura existente deficiente, muchas viviendas e infraestructuras no cumplirían con estándares de eficiencia energética, por lo que requerirían costosas adaptaciones.
- Equipamientos comunitarios ante la resiliencia climática pueden estar expuestos a vandalismo, particularmente en sectores de alta delincuencia o consumo problemático.

Riesgos institucionales y de gobernanza
- La implementación de políticas de descarbonización requiere alineación entre municipios, regiones y gobierno nacional, lo cual puede ser fragmentado o lento.
- Sostenibilidad política incierta, dado que las iniciativas pueden verse interrumpidas por cambios de administración o restricciones presupuestarias, afectando su continuidad y eficacia.

Riesgos asociados a la equidad climática
- Podría generarse una Inequidad en los beneficios climáticos si no se planifica con enfoque inclusivo, algunos grupos como adultos mayores o familias vulnerables pueden quedar excluidos del acceso a transporte limpio, eficiencia energética o espacios comunitarios frente a olas de calor.
- La transición puede imponer costos adicionales a quienes ya enfrentan condiciones de vulnerabilidad, incrementando las brechas en desarrollo humano.

In line with the Malaysia National Energy Roadmap.
Malaysia is committed to low-carbon development aimed at restructuring the economic landscape to a more sustainable one. In this context, the National Energy Transition Roadmap (NETR) sets the goal to accelerate energy transition and change the way energy is generated to improve climate resilience. NETR has developed the Responsible Transition (RT) Pathway 2050 to shift Malaysia's energy systems from fossil fuel-based to greener and low-carbon systems. The Total Primary Energy Source (TPES) modelling indicated that our energy demand will increase marginally at 0.2% annually from 95 Mtoe in 2023 to 102 Mtoe in 2050. The RT Pathway 2050 has also shown promising decarbonisation results as evidenced by the phasing out of coal and the reduction of fossil-fuel reliance from 96% in 2023 to 77% in 2050. Natural gas is set to be not only a transitional fuel, but also the primary contributor of TPES at 57 Mtoe (56%) followed by
renewables that include solar, hydro and bioenergy, which collectively contribute 23% of TPES in 2050 from a mere 4% in 2023.
NETR outlines 50 initiatives under the six energy transition levers and five enablers, in addition
to the 10 flagship projects and initiatives announced in July 2023. The energy transition
financing will be undertaken through a combination of grants, loans, rebates, incentives, and other investments to support the whole-of-nation approach. NETR aims to power our future by unlocking potentials in new growth areas and delivering progress and prosperity to Malaysian
households and businesses. The successful implementation of NETR will uplift GDP value from RM25 billion in 2023 to RM220 billion and generate 310,000 jobs in 2050.
NETR is not just a document about measures to meet Net-Zero GHG emissions target. NETR
represents a new way of thinking to fundamentally transform Malaysia's economy and livelihoods for a stronger and more resilient future.

Oversight of climate-related issues include the following:
• All key decisions and procurement strategies considered by Cabinet must have climate and ecology implications, verified by the council's Climate Team.
• A Low-Carbon Procurement Policy and council Sourcing Strategy require that climate considerations are taken into account in all procurement above minimum contract spend thresholds.
• A Cabinet Member for the Climate and Ecological Emergency is the lead elected member on climate-related issues.
• A Climate Change and Ecology Policy and Accountability Committee provides councillor scrutiny over progress.
• At the executive level, oversight of climate-related issues is led by the Strategic Director of Place, the Director of Climate and Transport and the Assistant Director of Climate Change and Transport.
• Responsibilities for delivery are distributed throughout council departments, with other sustainability management positions including the Strategic Lead for Net Zero Housing in council housing.
• Climate risks are included in the council's risk register.
• Climate-related key performance indicators are included in the council's corporate performance monitoring.
• Annual progress reports and carbon audits, and bi-annual performance indicator updates, are shared with responsible officers and cabinet members by the Climate team.

Our Local Plan is linked to the London Plan, which covers the metropolitan area and has a range of policies covering heat risks, water use, flood risk/SuDS, biodiversity and urban greening. Adapting to climate change is referenced in the spatial vision of our Local Plan (our highest level of planning document) and managed through a number of policies within this document: 
• CC1: Reducing carbon dioxide emissions
• CC2 on Sustainable Design and Construction: that developments “allow adaptation to the potential impacts of climate change during its lifetime such as heatwaves and droughts in summer months and potentially wetter winters.”
• CC3 and CC4 on flood risk, sustainable drainage and water efficiency.
• O5 'Greening the Borough' covers enhancing biodiversity and green infrastructure. 

Depending on a range of factors, planning applications are required to include a number of supporting documents to comply with policies relating to climate adaptation. Examples include: 
• Energy Assessment including Overheating Assessment
• Sustainability Statement
• Flood Risk Assessment including SuDS Strategy
• Circular Economy Statement
• Whole Lifecycle Carbon Assessment
• Urban Greening Factor calculation. 

In October 2023 H&F Council adopted a Climate Change Supplementary Planning Document (SPD). The purpose of the SPD is to provide supplementary guidance for the climate-related planning policies in the council's Local Plan and to help implement the actions contained in the council's climate change strategy. This includes topics encompassing (but not limited to) sustainable design and construction, flooding, energy, ecology, waste and transport and travel.
column17: H&F Council is investing in decarbonising. For example, we have allocated 106m to council housing retrofit as part of its 12-year asset management capital program. In late 2023, H&F Council launched the H&F Green Investment - a £5 million investment offer to support local climate and ecological projects: https://www.lbhf.gov.uk/environment/climate-and-ecological-emergency/hf-green-investment-make-impact-and-some-money-along-way. The fund raised £1.7 million in 2024. We are also decarbonising our pension fund; H&F's pension fund ESG approach was formalized in its first Investment Strategy Statement, published in 2017. This led to an investigation into the risks of holding fossil fuel companies, and the fund has since committed to reducing its carbon emissions. The weighted average carbon to value invested of the Fund has fallen by circa 77% since then, and is considered one of the most divested pension funds in the UK by divest.org: https://divest.platformlondon.org/fund/hammersmith-&-fulham-pension-fund. The fund has published an online ESG dashboard presenting the council's performance over recent years: https://www.lbhfpensionfund.org/your-pension/investment-performance-esg.
column18:
Key regulatory and policy risks include:
1) Reputational risk of insufficiently rapid decarbonisation leading to missed targets.
2) Rising regulatory standards leading to stranded assets e.g. minimum energy efficiency standards for homes and commercial premises leased out by the council.
3) Legal and regulatory barriers to transition, including: constraints on the freedom to set local planning policy that exceeds national policy requirements; constraints on the ability to impose measures and costs on domestic and commercial leaseholders of our freehold assets for decarbonisation and adaptation Technology and implementation.
4) High costs and complexity of building decarbonization, particularly the transition to clean heat. Upfront capital costs for heat pumps are high; energy savings accrue to occupants rather than the council; payback from energy savings may be insufficient to make a case based on return on investment; costs may not be possible to pass on to leaseholders under current regulations.
5) Investing in changing technology: there is some risk that technologies invested in today will be improved on or superseded by future technological advancements, such as clean heat technology. However, the risk of continued investment in fossil fuel technology is higher given this is incompatible with net zero and is likely to be regulated against in time.
6) Higher costs from replacement of fossil fuel equipment before its end of life.

Key social and economic risks include:
1) Withdrawal of popular support for transition actions, or perception of this risk influencing decision-making
2) Failure to rebalance financial incentives at the national level (such as the higher cost of electricity than gas) leading to low uptake of transition technologies, and posing a risk of exacerbating poverty and inequality through transition to alternative technologies such as low-carbon heating.

column15: In 2016, Burlington City Council approved a long term (25 year) versus Council term (3 - 4 year) strategic plan called Vision 2040. This plan is a framework for critical decision-making. It guides how the City manages its resources today to position Burlington for the future. The Plan helps Burlington prepare for challenging issues and current and future opportunities. The plan is also supported by the Official Plan (community planning), Integrated Mobility Plan, Asset Management Plan, and Burlington Economic Development Strategic Plan to name a few. Climate goals include an increase in tree canopy to 35 percent and our City operations will be net carbon neutral. \nFrom Vision to Focus (2022 - 2026) is Council's work plan and includes four focus areas: 1) Designing and delivering complete communities - Create all-inclusive, thriving, vibrant, healthy, connected, and safe communities; 2) Providing the best services and experiences - Deliver quality services to meet the diverse needs of our customers and foster the highest quality of life; 3) Protecting and improving the natural environment and taking action on climate change - Establish sustainable, healthy and low-carbon climate resilient communities; and, 4) Driving organizational performance - Attract and retain high-performing employees to deliver the best services and experiences. There are a number of objectives and key performance indicators in the plan that are related to climate action. In addition, City Council and staff are guided by five enabling behaviours to reach the plan's objectives, one of which is 'taking action on climate change.'\n
column16: In April 2019, Burlington City Council declared a climate emergency “for the purposes of deepening our commitment to protecting our economy, environment and community from climate change” and to “apply a climate lens to the plans and actions of the City of Burlington including the Council strategic workplan and future budgets.” However, even before the climate emergency declaration, the 2014 Community Energy Plan set the stage for staff to understand the linkages between city planning, building and development and transportation - essentially how we plan our communities affects how we use energy, the type of energy, and the resulting greenhouse gas emissions. The new Official Plan (approved by Halton Region in 2020 but under appeal) which sets out applicable policies for growth and development in the community includes a section on Climate Change and Air Quality. Complete communities are achieved through sustainable, effective and efficient land use and transportation policies, reducing the community impact on climate change. The Climate Action Plan (CAP), approved in April 2020, had seven program areas to help the community reach carbon neutrality by 2050. With emissions from transportation and buildings being the predominant source of GHGs in Burlington, priority areas included the Integrated Mobility Plan, Electric Mobility and Green Fleet Strategies, Better Homes Burlington program and the Sustainable Development and Building Guideline. Progress reports on the Climate Action Plan were presented to Council annually in 2021-2024. In October 2025, City Council will receive the update to the 2020 Climate Action Plan, titled Burlington Climate Plan: Taking Action to Reduce Community Greenhouse Gas Emissions. This updated plan contains 17 actions over three themes - Buildings and Energy, Integrated Mobility, and Local Economy - to help the community move toward the net zero carbon goal. The City also has a Corporate Energy and Emissions Management Plan (CEEMP) which lays out a plan to reach carbon neutrality by 2040 for City operations. Our first net zero building (operations) was completed in 2022, and the Robert Bateman Community Centre and Skyway Arena redevelopments will result in low carbon facilities. The City rents out roof space for solar PV but the City has completed a capital plan for its own solar projects, with the two installations completed and a third in the planning stages. In addition, the City continues to expand its network of EV charging stations (burlington.ca/ev), is planning to add hybrid buses to its transit fleet and has completed a deep energy retrofit feasibility study of four city buildings, with four more underway. An updated CEEMP was completed and presented to Council in July 2024. In 2021, the City updated its Asset Management Plan (AMP) to incorporate the urban forest (inventoried street trees) with a commitment to include more green assets and acknowledged climate as a risk. The AMP was updated again and approved by City Council in July 2025, and incorporated data gathered while developing the Urban Forest Master Plan and Woodland Management Strategy, both approved in 2024. In 2022-2023 City staff from Engineering (asset management), Finance and Sustainability were part of a Canadian Network of Asset Managers Applied Climate Action Cohort (one of 13 municipalities in Canada) to operationalize climate change through asset management. In 2020, the Stormwater Management Design Guidelines were updated to incorporate new IDF curves taking into account our changing climate with a commitment to revisit the guidelines every five years. This review is currently underway. In 2021, a climate projections report for Burlington was presented to City Council. In May 2022, the draft Climate Resilient Burlington plan was also presented and in July, the final plan was endorsed by Council. There are 32 actions under five themes aligned with Canada's National Adaptation Strategy. The plan was developed with extensive stakeholder consultation (12 city departments and 17 community groups) and incorporates actions for current (Asset Management Plan) or upcoming (Biodiversity Strategy, Agricultural Action Plan) plans. Three annual updates have been presented to council since the plan was approved. To help advance momentum, City staff are currently part of two communities of practice (Climate-Ready Plans and Processes, and Adaptation in Action) and ICLEI Canada's Advancing Adaptation Training Initiative.
column17: After the 2014 flood resulting in $90M in insured claims, an additional $20M was added to the stormwater capital budget. The City experienced another flood in 2024. The approved 2025 budget included substantial resources to enhance stormwater systems and bolster emergency preparedness including $5.2 million for stormwater management infrastructure projects to reduce flood risk in high-priority areas. https://burlingtonpublishing.escribemeetings.com/filestream.ashx?DocumentId=82447\nThe City, Halton Region and Conservation Halton have completed several projects related to flooding and continue work on this front spending millions of dollars to reduce flood risk. The City continues to provide a Home Flood Protection Program to reduce the risk of basement flooding (since 2017) and a Plumbing Permit Grant Program (since 2014). In 2024, the City also introduced a temporary Flood Recovery Grant to help cover the cost of the insurance deductible for those impacted by the July 2024 flood. Parts of the City also qualified for Disaster Recovery Assistance for Ontarians program. With increasing heat, there is a growing demand for water features such as splash pads, outdoor water fountains, etc. Such features incur not only capital costs but also operational costs. There are several ways in which climate change can impact the budget. For example, increasing extreme weather events such as wind, freezing rain, extreme heat and cold can result in operational expenditures due to clean-up costs potentially requiring a review of the Severe Weather Reserve Fund and impacts to infrastructure resulting in unbudgeted expenses to repair and/or replace. A severe wind storm in May 2022 resulted in almost $500K in forestry related costs. Similarly, efforts to mitigate climate change can have a budgetary impact. Investments in renewable energy and electric vehicle charging infrastructure to help reduce greenhouse gas emissions require higher upfront investments but save the City on operating costs in the longer-term. Two of seven drivers and priorities in the 2025 approved budget were mitigating flood risk (additional investments in ditch, culvert, and creek maintenance to reduce future flooding risk) and emergency management (more resources to respond to floods, windstorms and other extreme events).
column18: Increased costs of electricity will impact the local economy due to the necessary upgrades required to support a low carbon and resilient electricity grid. In addition, there is a risk that the Ontario provincial government will not support a future low carbon electricity grid as it continues to invest in natural gas generation plants as some of the nuclear plants are decommissioned, which will negate our efforts to reduce emissions at a local level through electrification. The energy sector is highly regulated by senior levels of government reducing the authority of the municipality to lead on reducing the reliance of the use of fossil fuels for buildings and industry production. For instance, the municipality does not have the authority to restrict connections or expansion of the natural gas distribution system which is the main source of fuel for thermal (heating) energy in the community. Another risk is the limited supply chain of electric vehicles and charging infrastructure to support the local community, especially for heavy duty vehicles. The provincial government has not implemented a mandate for electric vehicles (EVs), where suppliers are targeting those provinces that do have mandates such as Quebec and British Columbia. Dealerships continue to promote gas powered vehicles to customers over EVs. Fast charging infrastructure for heavy duty vehicles (trucks and buses) is very expensive. We are also finding that there is a lack of skilled labour to implement measures to reduce the carbon footprint of buildings. As an example, finding suppliers and contractors to install air source heat pumps is proving to be challenging in the region. Contractors continue to encourage homeowners to use traditional methods to heat and cool buildings (furnaces and air conditioners) instead of more efficient air source heat pumps. There is also a lack of knowledge by homeowners on what air source heat pumps are and the benefits of making the switch. The local municipality also lacks the authority to require net carbon zero standards for new development as the building code requirements are again regulated by the provincial government. The municipality can only incentivize and encourage.

Sakarya Metropolitan Municipality (SBB) is one of the local government units authorized and responsible for combating and adapting to climate change, within the scope of Turkish Republic legislation. Monitoring activities are tailored to align with national policies and strategies, as well as local needs.

The national legal framework is established by Municipality Law No. 5393, Metropolitan Municipality Law No. 5216, Environmental Law No. 2872, and the Law on Combating Climate Change, which entered into force in 2023. Within this framework, municipalities are obligated to monitor climate change-related risks and develop mitigation and adaptation measures. Furthermore, Sakarya province complies with Turkey's commitments under the Paris Agreement and the EU Green Deal. In this regard, Sakarya Metropolitan Municipality signed the European Union Covenant of Mayors in 2018, voluntarily committing to reducing greenhouse gas emissions, increasing climate change adaptation, and promoting energy efficiency by 2030.

Within our municipality's institutional structure, monitoring of climate issues is carried out by the Climate Change Branch Directorate, which reports to the Department of Climate Change and Zero Waste. The monitoring system encompasses data collection, analysis, planning, implementation, and reporting.

Our core monitoring activities are conducted under the following headings:

Monitoring greenhouse gas emissions: Specifically for Sakarya province, emission data originating from the energy, transportation, waste, building, and agriculture sectors are collected and analyzed. Emission calculations are made in accordance with IPCC methodologies.

Climate risk analyses: Physical risks such as floods, inundations, heat waves, and droughts are analyzed, and these risks are integrated with the Sakarya Province Disaster Risk Reduction Plan (İRAP) and urban planning processes.

Planning and integration: Our municipality integrates climate change mitigation and adaptation objectives into its institutional plans. High-level plans such as the Strategic Plan, Climate Action Plan, Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SEEP), Adaptation Action Plan, and Sustainable Urban Mobility Plan (SUMP) clearly define climate change-related goals, priorities, and concrete actions. These plans are periodically updated with monitoring and performance indicators, guiding urban decision-making processes.

Data reporting: Regular reporting is made to international platforms such as the CDP, and transparency and accountability principles are adopted. Indicators such as emissions (tCO₂e), energy consumption (kWh), recovery rate (%), and green space increase (m²) are used.

Monitoring and capacity building through projects: Our municipality implements EU-funded projects (e.g., EU4ETTR, ENPED) in the areas of climate change adaptation and mitigation. Through these projects, both technical infrastructure is improved and monitoring capacity is enhanced.

Stakeholder engagement: Developments in climate issues are regularly evaluated in collaboration with district municipalities, universities, public institutions, and NGOs, and data and analysis are shared.

These climate-related monitoring efforts directly inform municipal planning. Infrastructure projects, transportation investments, green space development, and energy efficiency policies are shaped by this monitoring system. This enables our municipality to adopt a scientific and strategic approach to transform Sakarya into a climate-resilient, sustainable, and environmentally sound city.
column16:
Sakarya Metropolitan Municipality considers climate-related issues a key determining factor in all urban development, investment, and service planning processes. The impacts of climate change challenge existing systems and directly impact future projections in many sectors, particularly water management, disaster risk, transportation, energy, infrastructure, and public health. Therefore, our municipality is reshaping its planning by integrating climate-related risks and opportunities into its strategic and development plans.

1. Integration with Strategic Plans and Performance Programs:
In our municipality's Strategic Plan, 'combatting climate change' and 'adaptation' are defined as separate target areas. In line with these goals, priority activities are identified in themes such as energy efficiency, green infrastructure, waste management, and sustainable transportation and are monitored with performance indicators.

2. Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SEEP):
In its SEEP plan, prepared with the goal of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 2030, Sakarya Metropolitan Municipality has integrated areas such as energy efficiency measures, renewable energy investments, and low-carbon transportation systems into its development plans. The Plan is also used as a systematic tool to assess the climate impacts of projects.

3. Climate Change Adaptation Action Plan:
The Adaptation Action Plan, prepared to transform Sakarya into a city resilient to climate risks, identifies measures to be taken against climate risks in sectors such as urban planning, water resources management, agriculture, healthcare, and disaster management. In line with this plan, infrastructure investments to combat floods, green space planning to combat the urban heat island effect, and improvements to irrigation systems to mitigate drought risks are being implemented.

4. Integration with the Disaster Risk Reduction Plan (DRP):
Climate-related disaster risks (floods, inundations, storms, heat waves) are identified within the DRP, and these findings are taken into account in urban planning and infrastructure projects. New zoning decisions are being reviewed, particularly in high-risk areas, and infrastructure investments to prevent floods are prioritized.

5. Urban Mobility and Infrastructure Planning:
As part of the Sustainable Urban Mobility Plan (SUMP), carbon emissions are being reduced by developing climate-friendly transportation systems (bike paths, electric transportation infrastructure, etc.). Public transportation systems are being improved while also meeting air quality and energy consumption targets.

6. Planning Monitoring Mechanism with Climate Indicators:
Our municipality monitors the activities defined in its development plans using indicators such as energy consumption (kWh), per capita emissions (tCO₂e/capita), green space ratio (%), and recycled waste volume (tons). This allows us to monitor the achievement of climate-related targets at every stage of the planning cycle, and necessary revisions are made.

7. Project Prioritization and Financing:

Investments in areas with high climate impacts (e.g., infrastructure renovations in high-flood-prone neighborhoods, green roofs, and rain gardens) have been prioritized, and externally funded and EU-supported projects have been directed to these strategic areas.

As a result, Sakarya Metropolitan Municipality's core planning documents address climate change not only as an environmental issue but also as a multidimensional determinant of economic sustainability, social well-being, and infrastructure security. The municipality views planning as a dynamic process and continues to update it in line with climate data and scientific analyses.
column17:
Sakarya Metropolitan Municipality conducts its financial planning with a long-term, sustainability-focused approach, taking into account the current and future impacts of climate change. Climate-related threats such as increasing extreme weather events, heat waves, and flood and inundation risks create additional financial burdens on both the municipality's infrastructure investments and disaster management capacity. Therefore, climate-related risks and opportunities directly impact investment priorities and resource allocations.

Due to its geographical location, particularly vulnerable to flood and inundation risk, Sakarya province integrates projects aimed at improving the resilience of urban infrastructure into its financial planning. Accordingly, budgets allocated to areas such as water management, green infrastructure implementations, early warning systems, and nature-based solutions are being increased.

Furthermore, Sakarya Metropolitan Municipality prioritizes access to national and international funding to support climate-friendly investments. In this context, financial instruments provided by European Union IPA projects, grant programs, development agency support, and institutions such as the Iller Bank play a crucial role in the implementation of climate-compatible projects. Furthermore, priorities identified through strategic documents such as the Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP) and the Adaptation Action Plan are integrated into annual investment programs and reflected in budgeting processes.

These plans are critical for both reducing greenhouse gas emissions and increasing resilience to climate change. Thus, climate-related issues have become not only an environmental agenda but also a strategic planning issue aimed at mitigating economic risks and utilizing resources more efficiently.
column18:
Sakarya Metropolitan Municipality supports Turkey's transition to a low-carbon economy in line with its commitments under the Paris Agreement and the EU Green Deal. However, this transformation also poses certain socio-economic and structural risks for the municipality.

Firstly, the infrastructure transformations required by the transition to low-carbon technologies (e.g., renewable energy systems, energy-efficient buildings, green transportation systems, etc.) entail high initial costs. This creates financial pressure on local governments with limited budgets and necessitates the reprioritization of resources.

Furthermore, if local businesses operating in carbon-intensive sectors (e.g., construction, transportation, agriculture, and industry) struggle to adapt to the transformation process, this could have temporary negative impacts on employment. This risks exacerbating economic and social inequalities and necessitates the retraining and support of the local workforce.

New regulations introduced as part of the alignment with low-carbon policies (e.g., emission limits, green purchasing criteria, energy efficiency requirements in buildings, etc.) may create administrative and technical capacity challenges for public and private sector stakeholders. This could lead to delays or resistance in implementation.

Furthermore, mechanisms such as carbon pricing or border carbon adjustments, which will be implemented at the national level during the green transformation process, could impact economic activities and costs at the local level. This increases the pressure on the municipality to replace carbon-intensive inputs with low-carbon alternatives in its supply chain.

Given all these risks, the Sakarya Metropolitan Municipality is adopting a multi-stakeholder approach to achieve a just and gradual transition to a low-carbon economy, working in coordination with local businesses, citizens, and public institutions. Furthermore, strategic documents such as SECAP and the Adaptation Action Plan plan the management of these risks, and the adaptation process is supported through training, awareness-raising, financial support mechanisms, and capacity-building activities.

As the regional planning authority, the Metropolitan Council sets guidance and requirements for local government comprehensive planning through the regional development guide. In Thrive MSP 2040, sustainability was one of five desired outcomes for the region. Sustainability was defined to include “providing leadership to support climate change mitigation, adaptation, and resilience'. Local governments were required to plan for protection and development of solar energy systems and were encouraged to do broader climate mitigation and adaptation planning. In early 2025 the Metropolitan Council adopted the next region development guide, Imagine 2050, with a core regional goal for 2050 being “We lead on addressing climate change: We have mitigated greenhouse gas emissions and have adapted to ensure our communities and systems are resilient to climate impacts”. Imagine 2050 includes requirements for local governments to make climate action commitments across all policy areas in their comprehensive plans. 

 Climate minimum requirements include: 

- Include a greenhouse gas emissions inventory that includes transportation, energy use, solid waste, and livestock and agriculture. 
- Include at least one strategy to reduce greenhouse gas emissions per emissions sector. 
- Detail the emissions impact of reduction strategies through 2050 for each emissions sector using the Met Council Strategy Planning Tool. 
- Include a policy or policies relating to the protection and development of access to direct sunlight for solar energy systems. 
- Include strategies needed to implement the policy or policies. 
- Identify social, built, and natural systems vulnerabilities to extreme heat and localized flooding  
- Include strategies to address social, built, and natural systems vulnerabilities for extreme heat, and localized flooding.  
- Include strategies that support local food systems to increase access to healthy food, food security, and community resilience.
