La ciudad de Ushuaia, a través de sus principales órganos, tiene un rol activo en la supervisión de los asuntos climáticos. La Secretaría de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sustentable y el Concejo Deliberante de la ciudad trabajan de manera coordinada, cada uno con funciones específicas.
Secretaría de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sustentable de Ushuaia: Esta secretaría es el órgano ejecutivo que se encarga de implementar y fiscalizar las políticas ambientales en el ámbito del territorio de Ushuaia. Sus responsabilidades incluyen:
Fiscalización y control: Supervisa y controla todas las formas de impacto negativo provenientes de proyectos tanto públicos como privados a través de su cuerpo de inspectores de vía pública y de los equipos de inspección de la obra privada.
Gestión de residuos: Optimiza la gestión de residuos sólidos urbanos y se encarga de la recolección selectiva puerta a puerta de materiales reciclables en barrios piloto de la ciudad (Barrio Malvinas, Casas del Sur). 
En paralelo el pliego licitatorio actual de GIRSU incorpora el avance del piloto de separación definiendo año a año mayor superficie territorial. 
Planificación estratégica: Participa activamente en la elaboración e implementación de planes de acción climática, como el Plan Local de Acción Climática Ushuaia 2030.
Se han realizado en la actualidad dos IGEI y dos PLAC. se encuentran adjuntos a la página web oficial de la Municipalidad de Ushuaia.
Innovación y sostenibilidad: Promueve el uso de tecnologías más limpias y sostenibles, y fomenta iniciativas como el uso de energías renovables (solar y eólica) en el ejido urbano. En el caso de Ushuaia, la ciudad se encuentra trabajando en el proyecto GEF 7 Inversiones Integradas Bajas en Carbono y Conservación en Ciudades Argentinas.
Conservación: Se encarga de la conservación de las reservas naturales urbanas y la protección de los ecosistemas terrestres.
Concejo Deliberante de Ushuaia
El Concejo Deliberante es el órgano legislativo que crea las ordenanzas que rigen la política ambiental de la ciudad. Sus funciones clave en materia climática son:
Creación de normativas: Aprueba y sanciona ordenanzas que buscan mitigar los efectos del cambio climático, afectando a sectores clave como la energía, la construcción, el transporte y la gestión de residuos.
Presupuesto: Analiza y aprueba el presupuesto asignado a la Secretaría de Ambiente, asegurando que se destinen los recursos necesarios para llevar a cabo los programas y proyectos ambientales.
Control y seguimiento: A través de sus comisiones, realiza el seguimiento de las políticas y acciones del Poder Ejecutivo, evaluando si los programas municipales cumplen con sus objetivos de cuidado ambiental.
column16:
El municipio de Ushuaia ha integrado activamente la cuestión climática en su planificación maestra y de desarrollos, considerándola un pilar fundamental de su gestión pública. Esta integración se detalla en el Plan Local de Acción Climática (PLAC), que sirve como una hoja de ruta para la ciudad.

Integración Transversal y Marco Legal

El compromiso de Ushuaia con la sostenibilidad ambiental no es solo una declaración, sino que está respaldado por su Carta Orgánica Municipal de 2022, un instrumento legal que eleva la protección del medio ambiente a una prioridad transversal. Esto garantiza que cada decisión municipal, desde la planificación urbana hasta la gestión de residuos y la conservación de ecosistemas, considere el impacto ambiental.

Proyectos y Políticas de Mitigación y Adaptación
El Plan Local de Acción Climática aborda la planificación urbana y de desarrollo a través de estrategias específicas en diferentes sectores para mitigar las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero y adaptarse a los riesgos climáticos.
Movilidad y Transporte:Para reducir las emisiones y el uso masivo de automóviles, la ciudad promueve la movilidad sostenible a través de proyectos como la instalación de bicicleteros.Además, se ha manifestado interés en la adquisición de buses con energías alternativas. Existen actualmente diferentes ciclovías y bicisendas desarrolladas en el marco de la acción climática.
Infraestructura y Riesgos:Se han realizado obras de repavimentación y bacheo en calles clave para mitigar los daños causados por nevadas y lluvias. También se han ejecutado proyectos de reemplazo y conexión de la red cloacal y pluvial, así como alcantarillado, con el fin de reducir la vulnerabilidad a las inundaciones urbanas.
Uso del Suelo y Biodiversidad: El municipio ha implementado acciones de reforestación como parte de las Soluciones Basadas en la Naturaleza (SbN), destinadas a proteger y gestionar los ecosistemas del ámbito urbano de Ushuaia.
Vivienda y Emergencias: Para abordar la vulnerabilidad social, se ha llevado a cabo la reubicación de familias del municipio hacia zonas aptas para uso habitacional. Además, se ha establecido un plan de comunicación llamado “Ushuaia Segura” para proveer información clara y oportuna a la comunidad durante eventos de desastres climáticos.
column17:
Los asuntos relacionados con el clima han tenido un impacto directo en la planificación financiera del municipio de Ushuaia, reflejado en la asignación de recursos dentro de su presupuesto. La Ordenanza Municipal N° 6444 para el Ejercicio 2025 detalla cómo la jurisdicción destina fondos para abordar estas cuestiones.

Asignación Presupuestaria Específica: La Secretaría de Medio Ambiente y Desarrollo Sustentable cuenta con una asignación presupuestaria específica, lo que indica que se le han asignado recursos financieros dedicados para llevar a cabo sus funciones y proyectos.
Estos fondos son cruciales para la ejecución de obras públicas plurianuales, que pueden incluir proyectos de infraestructura resiliente, como la mejora de sistemas de drenaje o la reubicación de viviendas, que son clave para la adaptación al cambio climático.

En resumen, la planificación financiera de Ushuaia se alinea con sus objetivos climáticos a través de la asignación de fondos a la secretaría ambiental y a proyectos de capital que buscan fortalecer la infraestructura y la capacidad de la ciudad para enfrentar los desafíos del clima.
column18:
La transición hacia una economía baja en carbono presenta riesgos y desafíos para Ushuaia, principalmente debido a su alta dependencia de sectores que generan una gran cantidad de emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero (GEI).
Se describen a continuación los Riesgos Sectoriales implicados en la planificación climática de Ushuaia asociados a la transición:

Dependencia de la Energía Estacionaria y el Gas Natural: El sector de Energía Estacionaria es el mayor emisor de GEI en el municipio, representando el 68.5% del total de emisiones en 2021. La ciudad utiliza grandes volúmenes de gas natural para alimentar la usina local. Esto significa que cualquier transición a energías más limpias requeriría una inversión considerable para cambiar la infraestructura energética y podría afectar la estabilidad económica de la Dirección Provincial de Energía.
Impacto en el Transporte: El sector de Transporte representa el 26.4% de las emisiones de Ushuaia. Dentro de este sector, el transporte por navegación y la aviación son subsectores significativos según se define en el PLAC. La economía de Ushuaia, al ser una puerta de entrada a la Antártida, tiene una fuerte dependencia de la navegación y el turismo. Una transición a una economía baja en carbono podría implicar la necesidad de adaptar o reemplazar flotas de transporte, lo cual podría generar un impacto económico significativo en el sector turístico y de servicios asociados.

Desafíos Financieros y de Implementación
Aunque la Ordenanza Municipal 6444 y el Plan Local de Acción Climática (PLAC) demuestran un compromiso con la acción climática, también exponen los desafíos para financiar esta transición:

Necesidad de financiamiento para Proyectos clave para la transición, como la instalación de cargadores solares y la energía eólica experimental, tienen su viabilidad técnica completa, pero no cuentan con financiamiento garantizado al igual que variadas obras públicas de impacto en la resiliencia de la ciudad. La implementación de estas acciones depende de la obtención de un presupuesto necesario para su continuidad. Esto representa un riesgo para la capacidad de la ciudad de cumplir con sus metas de reducción de emisiones.

The City Government recognizes that climate and disaster risk management is a shared responsibility, and therefore promotes multi-stakeholder, risk-informed planning as the standard practice in development. At present, the Climate and Disaster Risk Assessment (CDRA) is being updated to serve as a science-based decision support tool, providing local policymakers with comprehensive information on risks, hazards, exposures, and vulnerabilities. This enables the city to identify appropriate actions to reduce disaster impacts and strengthen community resilience.

Oversight of climate-related issues is carried out through the City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management (DRRM) Council, which is composed of representatives from various government agencies, civil society organizations, and other stakeholders. The Council meets quarterly, and convenes more frequently in anticipation of major hazard events such as strong typhoons or earthquakes.

The Council is also tasked with reviewing and endorsing climate- and disaster-related interventions, including the city's long-term DRRM Plan and the annual Local DRRM Fund utilization plan. Its resolutions are forwarded to the City Development Council (CDC), which integrates these measures into the Annual Investment Program (AIP). The AIP then serves as the primary basis for budget allocation, ensuring that climate resilience and risk reduction are embedded in the city's overall development agenda.
column16:
Climate-related issues, as highlighted by the CDRA, have significantly influenced Ormoc City's development planning. The assessment results have guided land use zoning, mainstreamed climate adaptation into sectoral programs, and prioritized investments in risk reduction and ecosystem management. A key outcome of this process is the completion of the Master Plan for Flood Control and Drainage Improvement, which directly addresses the city's recurring flooding problems identified in the CDRA. The plan combines structural measures—such as upgraded drainage networks, riverbank protection, and floodways—with non-structural approaches like maintenance, monitoring, and early warning systems.

Building on this, the city is also exploring funding opportunities from the People's Survival Fund (PSF) to implement nature-based solutions in 35 flood-prone barangays. These interventions will focus on ecosystem-based approaches such as watershed rehabilitation, mangrove and riparian reforestation, and green infrastructure, which complement the structural measures under the Master Plan. Together, these strategies are expected to reduce urban flooding, protect lives and property, and strengthen the city's long-term climate resilience.

CDRA has shifted Ormoc's planning approach toward a risk-informed, resilience-oriented, and sustainable development framework, ensuring that economic growth goes hand in hand with community safety and ecosystem protection.
column17:
Climate-related issues have transformed Ormoc City's financial planning from being purely growth-driven to becoming risk-informed and resilience-focused. Budgets now prioritize structural and nature-based adaptation measures, institutionalize DRRM allocations, and actively pursue external financing to protect communities and ensure sustainable development.

Ormoc City's financial planning has increasingly prioritized climate-resilient investments, with budget allocations directed toward projects identified in the Climate and Disaster Risk Assessment (CDRA), such as flood control, drainage improvement, and ecosystem rehabilitation. A centerpiece of this effort is the Master Plan for Flood Control and Drainage Improvement, which has been integrated into the city's medium- and long-term investment programming to ensure that capital outlays reduce disaster risks while supporting growth. In line with the DRRM Act, at least 5% of the annual city budget is earmarked for the Local DRRM Fund, with a significant portion devoted to preparedness, prevention, and adaptation programs—reflecting a shift from reactive spending to proactive, resilience-building measures. Resolutions from the City DRRM Council are also embedded into the Annual Investment Program (AIP), mainstreaming climate adaptation and risk reduction across sectors rather than treating them as standalone projects. Recognizing the limitations of local resources, the city actively pursues external financing through mechanisms such as the People's Survival Fund (PSF), particularly to support nature-based solutions in 35 flood-prone barangays, while participation in initiatives like the EU Green Economy Programme in the Philippines (EU-GEPP) helps diversify funding streams for climate-smart initiatives. Finally, climate risks have highlighted the importance of contingency funds and fiscal flexibility, prompting the city to embed buffers in its financial framework to better withstand the economic shocks of extreme events.
column18: Ormoc City faces several risks as it transitions to a low-carbon economy, particularly in relation to the national government's push for sustainable energy, the Public Utility Vehicle (PUV) Modernization Program, and circular economy initiatives. Economically, transport operators and workers are vulnerable to displacement as traditional jeepneys and tricycles are phased out, since many lack the capital to shift to modern, low-emission vehicles. Financially, the city may encounter challenges in meeting the high investment requirements for renewable energy integration, cleaner transport, and waste reduction infrastructure, while existing systems risk becoming obsolete or stranded if they fail to meet stricter standards. Small businesses and low-income households may also face higher costs of compliance, creating potential social inequities if the transition is not supported with subsidies or inclusive programs. Moreover, aligning with circular economy principles will require behavioral shifts, institutional capacity, and market readiness that could strain local resources in the short term. These challenges underscore the need for Ormoc to pursue a phased and inclusive transition strategy, ensuring that national low-carbon policies translate into both environmental gains and equitable socio-economic benefits for its communities.

column15:
La supervisión de asuntos relacionados con el clima por parte de la jurisdicción es un componente esencial dentro de la planificación urbana y territorial, ya que permite identificar, evaluar y gestionar los riesgos y oportunidades derivados del cambio climático, garantizando un desarrollo sostenible y resiliente. Esta supervisión se enfoca en monitorear los impactos ambientales, sociales y económicos, y en asegurar que las políticas y planes locales cumplan con los objetivos nacionales e internacionales de adaptación y mitigación climática.

En primer lugar, la jurisdicción realiza un monitoreo constante de indicadores climáticos y ambientales que incluyen la temperatura, precipitación, calidad del aire, niveles de contaminación, disponibilidad de agua y la ocurrencia de eventos climáticos extremos. Este monitoreo se realiza mediante sistemas automáticos y pasivos de registro de datos, así como inspecciones periódicas, lo que permite generar información confiable sobre la evolución del clima y sus efectos en los ecosistemas y la población. Los datos recopilados constituyen la base para la toma de decisiones estratégicas, priorizando las áreas de mayor riesgo y determinando medidas de prevención y mitigación.

Asimismo, la supervisión incluye evaluaciones de riesgo climático que identifican zonas vulnerables y sectores socioeconómicos que pueden verse más afectados por fenómenos como inundaciones, sequías, olas de calor, tormentas o erosión costera. Estas evaluaciones permiten a la jurisdicción desarrollar planes de adaptación específicos, orientados a fortalecer la resiliencia de la comunidad, proteger los recursos naturales y reducir impactos sobre la salud pública y la infraestructura crítica.

La coordinación interinstitucional y la participación comunitaria son componentes clave de la supervisión. La jurisdicción trabaja conjuntamente con entidades nacionales, regionales y locales, así como con organizaciones de la sociedad civil, instituciones académicas y el sector privado. Esta colaboración asegura que las acciones sean coherentes con las políticas ambientales vigentes y promueve la sensibilización ciudadana sobre la importancia de la adaptación y mitigación climática. La participación activa de la comunidad permite mejorar la eficiencia de las estrategias implementadas y fortalecer la capacidad local de respuesta ante eventos climáticos.

Otro aspecto central es la implementación de sistemas de alerta temprana y protocolos de respuesta frente a emergencias climáticas, que garantizan la rápida reacción ante fenómenos extremos, minimizando daños a la población y a la infraestructura. De manera complementaria, la jurisdicción realiza un seguimiento continuo y evalúa la efectividad de las políticas y medidas adoptadas, ajustando estrategias según los resultados obtenidos y las lecciones aprendidas.

Finalmente, los asuntos climáticos tienen un impacto directo en la planificación territorial y en la gestión del desarrollo urbano, ya que las decisiones sobre uso de suelo, construcción de infraestructura y conservación de recursos naturales deben considerar escenarios climáticos futuros. La supervisión permite anticiparse a los riesgos, aprovechar oportunidades de desarrollo sostenible y garantizar que las acciones locales contribuyan a la reducción de emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero, fomentando un territorio resiliente y preparado para los desafíos del cambio climático.

En síntesis, la supervisión por parte de la jurisdicción abarca monitoreo ambiental, evaluación de riesgos, coordinación interinstitucional, participación comunitaria, sistemas de alerta y ajuste de políticas, integrándose con la planificación territorial para proteger a la población, los ecosistemas y promover un desarrollo urbano sostenible frente al cambio climático.
column16:
Los asuntos relacionados con el clima han tenido un impacto significativo en la planificación maestra de desarrollo de la jurisdicción, ya que obligan a integrar criterios de sostenibilidad, resiliencia y adaptación frente a los riesgos climáticos dentro de todas las decisiones de planificación territorial y urbana. El cambio climático, los fenómenos extremos y las variaciones en los patrones climáticos requieren que la planificación no solo considere el crecimiento económico y poblacional, sino también la capacidad del territorio y las comunidades para responder a estos desafíos.

En la práctica, este impacto se refleja en la priorización de áreas más seguras y menos vulnerables para la expansión urbana, evitando zonas propensas a inundaciones, deslizamientos de tierra o erosión costera. Asimismo, la planificación maestra incorpora medidas de conservación de ecosistemas estratégicos, como humedales, ríos y bosques, que funcionan como barreras naturales frente a fenómenos extremos y ayudan a regular el microclima local.

Los planes de infraestructura también se han visto influenciados. La construcción de carreteras, sistemas de drenaje, puentes y edificaciones considera ahora estándares que permiten resistir eventos climáticos severos, reduciendo riesgos para la población y los bienes públicos. La planificación urbana incorpora además espacios verdes, áreas de captación de agua y corredores ecológicos que contribuyen a la mitigación de efectos climáticos, como la reducción de la temperatura urbana y el control de inundaciones.

Otro efecto importante se observa en la gestión de recursos hídricos y energéticos. La planificación maestra integra estrategias para asegurar la disponibilidad de agua potable, controlar la calidad de los cuerpos de agua y fomentar el uso de fuentes de energía renovable, anticipando posibles impactos del cambio climático en la oferta y demanda de estos recursos.

La adaptación climática también se refleja en la planificación de servicios públicos y sistemas de emergencia. Se diseñan rutas de evacuación, planes de contingencia y sistemas de alerta temprana para proteger a la población frente a tormentas, sequías u olas de calor, integrando estos criterios desde la etapa de diseño de la ciudad hasta la gestión operativa.

Por último, los asuntos climáticos han impulsado la participación ciudadana y la coordinación interinstitucional como parte de la planificación maestra. La jurisdicción involucra a la comunidad, a organismos ambientales y a expertos técnicos en la definición de políticas de desarrollo, garantizando que las decisiones sean inclusivas, informadas y alineadas con los objetivos de sostenibilidad.

En resumen, el impacto de los asuntos climáticos en la planificación maestra se manifiesta en la selección estratégica de áreas de desarrollo, la integración de infraestructura resiliente, la conservación de ecosistemas, la gestión de recursos y la participación comunitaria, asegurando un crecimiento urbano y territorial más sostenible, seguro y adaptado a los desafíos del cambio climático.
column17:
Los asuntos relacionados con el clima han influido de manera creciente en la planificación financiera de la jurisdicción, ya que los riesgos y oportunidades derivados del cambio climático requieren asignaciones presupuestarias estratégicas que permitan tanto la adaptación como la mitigación de sus efectos. Los fenómenos climáticos extremos, como inundaciones, sequías, olas de calor o deslizamientos de tierra, generan necesidades financieras adicionales, tanto para prevenir daños como para atender emergencias, lo que obliga a la jurisdicción a planificar y priorizar el uso de los recursos económicos de manera más eficiente y proactiva.

En primer lugar, la planificación financiera ahora incluye presupuestos específicos para proyectos de resiliencia climática, como infraestructura resistente a eventos extremos, sistemas de drenaje pluvial, protección de riberas y conservación de ecosistemas estratégicos. Estos proyectos requieren inversiones anticipadas, pero reducen costos futuros asociados a daños en infraestructura y pérdida de servicios públicos. Además, se contemplan fondos de contingencia y reservas de emergencia, que permiten a la jurisdicción responder rápidamente ante desastres climáticos, garantizando continuidad en servicios esenciales como agua potable, energía y transporte.

Otro impacto importante se observa en la priorización de inversiones sostenibles, donde la jurisdicción asigna recursos a programas de eficiencia energética, energías renovables, gestión de residuos y mejora de la calidad del aire. Estas acciones, además de mitigar emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero, generan ahorros a largo plazo al reducir costos operativos y aumentar la eficiencia de los servicios públicos.

La planificación financiera también ha incorporado evaluaciones de riesgo económico asociadas al clima, identificando sectores vulnerables y proyectando posibles pérdidas derivadas de eventos extremos. Esto permite ajustar presupuestos, definir seguros y diseñar instrumentos financieros que protejan los recursos públicos frente a impactos climáticos.

Finalmente, los asuntos climáticos han fomentado la coordinación con organismos nacionales e internacionales para acceder a financiamiento climático, subvenciones y préstamos blandos destinados a proyectos de adaptación y mitigación. Esto permite a la jurisdicción complementar sus recursos propios, acelerar la implementación de proyectos estratégicos y fortalecer la resiliencia financiera frente a cambios ambientales.

En resumen, los asuntos climáticos han transformado la planificación financiera de la jurisdicción al introducir presupuestos específicos para resiliencia, fondos de contingencia, priorización de inversiones sostenibles, evaluaciones de riesgo económico y acceso a financiamiento externo, garantizando que los recursos públicos se utilicen de manera estratégica para proteger a la población, los ecosistemas y la infraestructura frente a los desafíos del cambio climático.
column18:
La transición hacia una economía baja en carbono implica cambios profundos en los sistemas energéticos, productivos y sociales, y aunque representa oportunidades para el desarrollo sostenible, también genera una serie de riesgos que pueden afectar a la jurisdicción. Entre los principales riesgos se destacan los económicos, sociales, técnicos y regulatorios, los cuales deben ser gestionados dentro de la planificación y la política local.

En términos económicos, la transición puede generar riesgos financieros derivados de la desvalorización de activos ligados a sectores intensivos en carbono, como industrias extractivas, producción de combustibles fósiles o transporte convencional. La reducción en la demanda de estos sectores puede afectar los ingresos fiscales, la inversión privada y los empleos relacionados, generando desafíos para la estabilidad económica local. Además, la necesidad de invertir en tecnologías limpias, infraestructura verde y energías renovables puede implicar un alto costo inicial, especialmente si los recursos financieros de la jurisdicción son limitados.

En el ámbito social, la transición a una economía baja en carbono puede generar impactos en la fuerza laboral. La reconversión de empleos en sectores tradicionales hacia empleos verdes requiere capacitación, formación técnica y políticas de inclusión laboral. Sin una adecuada planificación, existe el riesgo de desempleo temporal, desigualdad social o resistencia de ciertos sectores productivos a los cambios.

Desde el punto de vista técnico, la jurisdicción enfrenta riesgos asociados a la adopción de nuevas tecnologías, como la integración de energías renovables, eficiencia energética y transporte limpio. La falta de infraestructura adecuada, estándares técnicos o experiencia local puede retrasar la implementación de proyectos y aumentar los costos de transición.

Finalmente, en el ámbito regulatorio y político, la jurisdicción puede enfrentar riesgos relacionados con cambios en normativas nacionales e internacionales sobre emisiones, metas de reducción de carbono o incentivos financieros. La adaptación a estas regulaciones requiere coordinación interinstitucional, capacidad administrativa y seguimiento constante de los compromisos climáticos, para evitar sanciones o pérdida de acceso a financiamiento internacional.

column15: Westminster City Council has a dedicated Climate Emergency team, responsible for delivering the council's Climate Emergency Action Plan and embedding climate considerations across all functions in the council. The council's Climate Emergency programme has several key objectives:-To become a net zero council by 2030-To become a net zero city by 2040 -To ensure that Westminster, its residents and workers are protected from the impacts of climate change now and in the future
column16: The council continues to review how the climate considerations can be factored into all key decisions. An initial example of this is the Carbon Impact Evaluation Toolkit which was created in 2022 and used to determine the carbon impact of all the projects within the council's capital programme. Action is currently underway to see how this toolkit can be enhanced and identify opportunities to go further in incorporating climate in council decisions and planning. The council is also taking action to strengthen the environmental considerations within our planning documents. This includes:-Reviewing the Environment Supplementary Planning Document (ESPD) to see where there are opportunities to be more ambitious - the document currently requires all major new developments to be built to net zero standards if a development can't meet the standards directly they then are required to pay an offset fee.-Introducing a new Planning Obligations SPD and guidance on offsetting payments and raising the local cost of carbon to incentivise emission savings.-Updating key planning policies in our City Plan to strengthen requirements for new developments and prioritising whole-life carbon
column17: On an immediate level, the council has incorporated budget for a permanent Climate Emergency team within its Medium Term Financial Plan, reflecting the commitment to tackling the Climate Emergency. The council is still undergoing assessments to understand the true cost of delivering net zero - whilst an exact figure is not yet known, it has already been identified that considerable additional funding will be required, especially to deliver the large-scale infrastructure projects which will produce significant carbon reductions. As such, planning to identify suitable external sources of funding is underway - an example of this is the recent Westminster Green Investment scheme which has raised £1m to fund a range of green projects within the borough. A review is currently underway to understand how best to incorporate climate considerations / impact into decision making across the council, including financial decisions. An initial example of this is the Carbon Impact Evaluation Toolkit which was used for the first time in 2022 to establish the carbon impact of the council's capital programme. Early investigations in to the use of green budgeting is also underway.
column18: We are undertaking research to identify the scope of the low carbon technology business sector in our borough and from that identifying what our Business Unit and Inward Investment offer can do to support it grow.We are identifying the skills gaps we have around the green economy and exploring the options to help close those gaps. Working with colleges and training providers to identify the routes that connect residents to emerging sectors as well as help influence training provision where upskilling is required.We are working closely with our in-house Adult Education provider who have strong referral routes across our borough and putting in place signposting so that the transition to a lower-carbon economy is accessible and inclusive.

column15: In April 2019, recognizing the global concern raised by the International Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) to limit global warming to 1.5°C, Nanaimo's City Council declared a Climate Emergency and set new community-wide emission reduction targets to be set to between 50% and 58% below 2010 levels by 2030, and between 94% and 107% below 2010 levels by 2050. Staff have and will continue to work with Council in developing plans and programs to lower GHG emission in the community and adapt to a changing climate. Most policies are developed by Staff through Council direction and in consultation with relevant stakeholders and the public and ultimately adopted by Council. Climate issues are integrated into a number of City policy documents including the City Plan Nanaimo ReImagined (City Plan). City Plan was adopted on 2022-JUL-04. When developing City Plan Nanaimo Council adopted the Doughnut Economics framework; a guiding model designed \'to build a city and community that operates within the planetary boundaries.\' The framework was used to guide the development of City Plan and all future policy and decision-making going forward. Nanaimo was the first city in Canada to adopt the doughnut economic model. City plan includes an accompanying Action Plan (endorsed June 26, 2023) used to prioritize future city projects as well several targets and indicators related to the doughnut model which staff will use to monitor the City's progress in working within the doughnut economic framework. Phase one of the monitoring strategy is now complete and was endorsed by Council. Future indicators are under development. Both the current and future indicators include several indicators related to climate mitigation, resiliency and environmental protection. Indicators will be monitored and reported on yearly, with more detailed reporting every 4 years. The monitoring strategy uses an innovative Multiple Capital Scorecard (MCS) method to develop context-based sustainability performance indicators and connect actions with goals in a meaningful way. To the best of our knowledge, the City of Nanaimo will be the first community in North America to implement the MCS framework at a community wide scale. In January, 2022 the City established a new Sustainability Section within the Community Development Department. Sustainability section staff are responsible for supporting the City's GHG reduction targets and climate resiliency plans. They work with staff in a number of other sections including Transportation (the City has an active transportation coordinator), Planning, Engineering and Environmental Protection, Infrastructure Planning and Energy, Emergency Management, Waste Reduction and Parks Staff dedicated to climate mitigation and resiliency. The City has both a qualified community (Manager, Sustainability) and corporate energy manager (Manager, Infrastructure Planning and Energy) on Staff; both of these positions are partially funded by the Provincial electric energy utility (BC Hydro) and along with other Staff such as the Environmental Planner participate in Provincial networking opportunities related to sustainable energy. On the corporate side the City has a Corporate Strategic Energy Management Plan 2020-2024. Within the last 10 years the City has completed 189 energy and emission saving initiatives (includes studies, renewals, new construction) which has reduced 1,171 tones of carbon dioxide (equivalent) (tCO2e). In 2022, the City entered into a voluntary energy bench marking program with Building Benchmarking BC, and benchmarked 21 key City owned facilities in order to publicly disclose there energy use and emissions. The City also a green fleet program. Whenever the City adds or replaces a vehicle or piece of equipment, an operational review is completed. This will determine vehicle size, operational need, efficiencies and alternative fuel source options, and we see it all through a green lens.
column16:
Climate issues are integrated throughout the City's policy and master planning documents. City Plan recommends the City set and actively work towards interim targets for greenhouse gas emission reductions for 2025, 2030, 2035, and 2040; as well as sets sectoral targets for buildings, transportation and waste. Local climate-related impacts such as the June 2021 heat dome, flooding, and wildfires (including the ongoing 2025 Wesley Ridge wildfire within the Nanaimo Regional District) have further stressed the impact and urgency of the climate emergency. 
Following the June 2021 heat dome, the City has developed an Extreme Weather Response Strategy and completed an Extreme Heat Mapping Assessment. That assessment included solutions for extreme heat response and mapped neighbourhoods disproportionately at risk of extreme heat. Based on the strategy the City has established daytime extreme heat and cold shelters for people experiencing homelessness and others in need a cool/warm place during these extreme events. 
City Plan Nanaimo ReImagined (City Plan), adopted on July 4, 2022, includes dedicated policy sections on greenhouse gas emission reduction, climate adaptation and hazard mitigation, solid waste management, urban tree canopy and greenways, watersheds and a blue and green network that includes information and policy about climate resiliency. Following the adoption of City Plan, 2023, Council endorsed the Integrated Action Plan, which includes a list of climate mitigation and resiliency actions required for the City to implement City Plan policies. 

City Plan includes a new development permit area (DPA) established to avoid and mitigate the impacts of sea level rise. The Sea Level Rise DPA was informed by the City of Nanaimo's 2019 Sea Level Rise Study completed by Associated Engineering and the 2020 Climate Change Resiliency Strategy. The objective of the DPA is to protect property and development from the impacts of sea level rise on lands at risk of flooding, erosion, and slope failure due to sea level rise and storm surge. All lands within the mapped DPA area will require further localized study by a professional engineer and may be subject to setbacks from the ocean boundary and an increased minimum flood construction level. The City received funding to complete a detailed sea level rise management plan which is currently under development. 

The City with the Snuneymuxw First Nation recently completed a revised Climate Hazard Assessment and Mapping. This project identified the location and probability of climate-driven hazards that may impact the infrastructure or communities of the Snuneymuxw First Nation or the City of Nanaimo. 

Since 2018, the City has required bicycle storage and EV charging for new developments. The City's Off-street Parking Bylaw was updated in 2021 (amendment 7266.02) to increase the % of spaces required to have access to EV charging facilities in new developments, these rates are currently under review as part of a parking bylaw study. 

In 2021 the City adopted the BC Step Code Rezoning policy which requires new development to exceed Provincial building code energy efficiency standards or include a low carbon energy system that does not exceed a greenhouse gas intensity limit of 3kg/m2/year. In 2024, Nanaimo became just the third municipality in British Columbia to adopt the top level of the Zero Carbon Step Code and the first to accelerate both the top level of the Zero Carbon Step Code and the upper step of the Energy Step Code in the same bylaw. The BC Zero Carbon Step Code is a provincial BC Building Code standard that local governments can choose to implement in their jurisdiction, starting May 1, 2023. The Zero Carbon Step Code sets a maximum annual amount of greenhouse gas emissions that each new building is allowed to emit. All development applications are reviewed by Planning and Sustainability Staff to ensure they meet the City's climate related policies.
column17:
In 2021, the City established the Climate Action Reserve Fund. This new fund replaces the Emission Reduction Reserve Fund and Sustainability Reserve Fund and will support community and corporate initiatives, plans or projects that reduce the City's greenhouse gas emissions. Funds are used to support the City in becoming carbon neutral; and/or support the reduction of energy consumption of City owned and operated facilities. The City of Nanaimo Council allocated $165,000 per year in the 2022 - 2026 Financial Plan to the Climate Action Reserve Fund. These funds supplement the Local Government Climate Action Plan (LGCAP) funds the City receives from the Provincial Government. 
In 2016, the City of Nanaimo was chosen as one of five communities across Canada to participate in the Municipal Natural Capital Initiative Study. This program studied the importance of a local wetland as a stormwater retention asset and identified ways to apply measurement and management methods used in asset and financial management practices to conserve and enhance natural capital. The study identified the storage benefit of the wetland was valued at approximately $4,694,295. Under climate change scenarios (increased rainfall) this value increases to between $6,559,676 and $8,207,305. Based on the findings of the pilot project the City is working towards including natural assets in the City's asset management and financial planning. More recently the City has participated in a similar natural capital study in partnership with the Regional District of Nanaimo through the Ecological Accounting Process (EAP) program to study the natural capital value of the Millstone River in Nanaimo. The EAP report was completed in 2021. The report concluded the portion of the river within the City boundary has a natural asset value of $68.2 million. The City is currently undertaking another EAP study for Departure Creek, another important salmon supporting watercourse in the City, in which a large amount of funding and paid and volunteer time has been invested on restoration work within the last 10 years. 
Climate change is a key consideration within the City's infrastructure and capital planning. For example all new stormwater management designs must account for climate change. As such pipe sizes need to account for increased rainfall. Before installing and when maintaining City infrastructure near the ocean Staff are required to review and accommodate sea level rise in their planning and design work. 

In 2024, the city received funding to complete a sea level rise management plan (SLRMP). The SLRMP is now underway and will build on the work completed during the 2018 Sea Level Rise study. The SLRMP will include a economic analysis to help the City better understand the economic risk posed by sea level rise and evaluate mitigation options.

In 2021 the City implemented a Sustainable Purchasing Policy to align City purchasing with environmental, social and ethical objectives within the City's Strategic Plan. The City has also invested a significant amount to help mitigate climate change by reducing our own corporate emissions and supporting reduced community emissions. Strategic energy management planning for the organization, including meeting energy saving targets and the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions, and a 19-year partnership with BC Hydro, who has provided $1.8M in funding for studies, grants, incentives, etc. since partnership inception.
column18: With respect to transitioning to low carbon housing, the City of Nanaimo needs to consider the impact of low carbon and energy efficiency building policy on housing affordability. Like protecting the environment and mitigating climate change, affordability and equity are critical components of the City's adopted Doughnut Economic Model. During the Nanaimo Reimagine City Plan consultation, 45% of participants identified affordability of housing as a top concern for the future of the City. The City will need to consider what if any impacts increased housing performance or low carbon energy system requirements may have on future housing costs. Equity and affordability are key considerations in all sustainability actions. Prior to implementing the Zero Carbon Step Code, the City consulted with serval affordable and low barrier housing providers to understand the impacts of the policy on their housing programs. On April 2025. the City launched a property-assessed clean energy (PACE) home energy retrofit financing program in order to provide zero interest property tied loans for home energy retrofits. The pilot program includes a scoring and eligibility criteria design to integrate affordability and equity into the program. The pilot program funds are limited due to Provincial restrictions, as such we are working towards implementing a complimentary third party funding program using funds from a partnering financial institution. This program will also allow residents such as those living in manufactured home parks, who are not able to apply for the property tied financing program, to access low interest loans for home retrofits.\n\nAs we continue to support a transition to low carbon transportation including electric vehicles (EVs) we need to ensure EV charging capacity is sufficient to support new EV's. The City is working to minimize this risk by requiring EV charges and rough-in wiring in new development and recently launched a EV charger rebate program to supplement an existing Provincial program. As we look to add new public chargers to also need to consider the risk and costs of maintaining the chargers that may be damaged due to wire theft and vandalism. The City will continue to work closely with the Provincial energy utility to ensure they have the capacity both locally and Provincially to support more EV chargers and vehicles. Electrical grid capacity also been raised as an issue as the City continues to promote switching to electric home systems and vehicles. The City continues to work with BC Hydro, the Provincial electric power utility, to ensure local grid capacity sufficiency supports electrification requirements and programs. As we continue to invest in active transportation options, such as cycling and walking, we need to ensure that we provide infrastructure to support safe and accessible active transportation opportunities for as many residents and visitors as possible. The City has a dedicated Active Transportation Project Specialist and will continue to make active transportation a priority. The City needs to also continue to assess the budget implications, including Staff Capacity, of all projects designed to support a transition to a low carbon economy. The cost and Staff time required for these projects will continue to be evaluated against other City priorities. Conversely, the City acknowledges the risk of NOT acting to transition to a low carbon economy or preparing the City to be resilient to Climate Change. By not supporting the transition to a low carbon economy the City will not only fail to meet our GHG reduction targets but will not do our part of lessening the global impact of climate change. By not preparing for the ongoing impacts of climate change now, the City may be forced to react to climate change impacts later with less time, resources and options. The City may face significant consequences including human health impacts, and damage to property, infrastructure and the environment if we failure to properly plan for climate change impacts

Cardiff Capital Region (CCR) is a regional body made up of 10 Local Authority areas across South East Wales including; Blaenau Gwent; Bridgend; Caerphilly; Cardiff; Merthyr Tydfil; Monmouthshire; Newport; Rhondda Cynon Taf; Torfaen; and Vale of Glamorgan. It's a diverse region comprising two cities; Cardiff and Newport, a range of market towns, the industrial heartland of the South Wales Valleys, rural communities and a coastal belt. The area has a population of around 1.6 million which equates to almost half the total population of Wales. 

From April 1, 2024, Cardiff Capital Region became part of the Southeast Wales Corporate Joint Committee (CJC), a regional, statutory public body that has wider responsibilities for transport and planning which will enhance the opportunity for delivery to improve residents' quality of life through investment in jobs, transport, homes and communities. 

The Southeast Wales CJC will still be known as Cardiff Capital Region (CCR) with elected members who meet every six weeks made up of the elected council leaders of the 10 Local Authorities within the region together with a nominated representative from the Bannau Brycheiniog National Park Authority. 

A dedicated member lead for the Climate Response portfolio is in place, including board oversight for CCR Energy Ltd, a vehicle to support delivery of CCR energy and decarbonization and delivery of the Energy Strategy and Energy Investment Funds. 

CCR Governance is organised into four sections; Finance; Legal and Governance; Direct Regional Growth; Policy, Impact and Partnerships (PIP). In FY25, significant progress has been made to develop core principles and embed policy processes that underpin CCR objectives to improve lives across the region. 
PIP support delivery of the fundamental values of CCR (stronger, fairer, greener) in line with the principles of the Well Being of Future Generations Act. Capacity to deliver growth and prosperity in line with sustainable development and Net Zero goals are growing within the organisation with an increasing team and initiatives including an ESG scorecard for assessing investment decisions and outcome, output and impact framework to asses programme delivery impact.

The principles upon which CCR operates and which are embedded across all sections can be summarised as; 
•	Sustainability, with examples such as the Energy Vision and Strategy (more details below), Local Area Energy Plans, CCR Energy, ESG frameworks, sustainable housing and development and adaptation planning. 
•	Productivity, with examples off CCR core functionality to support sustainable growth across the region, growing industrial clusters and supporting innovative investment to delivery GVA goals 
•	Inclusivity, for example, CCR has just published a Regional Transport Plan, a statutory strategy to develop a sustainable transport network across the region enhancing access to jobs and delivering net zero commitments; skills development to establish a pipeline of skills and talent for the sustainable transition of the region and the bespoke Northen Valleys Initiative which aims to bring investment and opportunity to the less developed areas in the region. 

In December 2020, the Region published an Energy Vision and Strategy which sets out ambitious targets to achieve the regions vision of 'creating the conditions for a shift to a carbon neutral economy and society in the CCR'. The Energy Strategy behind the vision sets out decarbonization targets to 2035 for key sectors including domestic, commercial and industrial, transport and renewable energy generation. The regional energy vision and strategy is focused on the GHG emissions associated with the energy system, covering: • power • heat • transport equating to around 67% of the region's total GHG emissions. 

The energy system modelling does not include emissions or sequestration from: • non-energy activity such as agriculture and land use; • aviation and shipping, where emissions are treated nationally / internationally rather than regionally; • very large industrial energy users, due to data limitations. 

Targets set out in the Energy Vision contribute to Welsh Government's Net Zero statutory 2050 target and reflect the Climate Change Committee's 6th carbon budget projection. CCR need to reduce emissions from energy system by 80% by 2035. Sectoral Targets to meet this objective are 88% emissions reduction from Transport, 74% emissions reduction from Domestic Heat and Power and 78% emissions reduction from Commercial and Industrial. Target for increasing renewable energy generation capacity is 2.2GW by 2035. 

Energy Vision targets are energy sector specific to support CCR's remit to economically grow the region in a sustainable way, complimented by a of metrics and policy interventions that consider regional wellbeing and underpin delivery of the CJC principles and to consider wider socio-economic, climate mitigation and adaptation impact.
column16:
The Cardiff Capital Region is a unique programme of collaborative working, passionately committed to being the catalyst for regional growth, sustainability and improving people's lives in the region. Now CCR has evolved into a CJC with statutory powers, there is even more opportunity to impact on sustainably advancing the region with development of a Regional Transport Plan and Strategic Regional Development Plan. 

1.	A Regional 5 year Transport Plan has been finalised in June 2025 setting policy and planning that facilitates the transition to a decarbonized transport system. The strategy facilitates the roll out of charging infrastructure, ULEV and a connected, sustainable transport system for the region in line with a wellbeing assessment. 
2.	A Regional Strategic Development Plan is being developed over the coming seven years and will be in line with Welsh Government guidance to compliment individual Local Authorities Local Development Plans at a strategic, regional level.
The Strategic Development Plan will facilitate a regional, decarbonized transformation for homes, businesses, and all stakeholders across the region. 

Below are some of the most substantial strategic decisions within the CCR delivery programme that have been influenced by climate-related risks and opportunities; Master planning/Development of the Region 

1. South Wales Metro In 2025 has delivered the Metro Plus and Metro central programme, a £50 million programme of schemes to improve transport connectivity across the region. Project Hub - Cardiff Capital Region and South Wales Metro Project delivered by Transport for Wales (tfw.wales) including electrification of the Valley railway lines, over 260 ULEV chargers have been installed and work is ongoing to deliver at scale with the private sector. A ULEV taxi trial has been handed over to the Local Authorities and a raft of support to transition the bus and public sector fleet to ULEV is ongoing. 

2. CCR has coordinated development of Local Area Energy Plans (LAEP) to set out a transition pathway to affordable and decarbonized energy system for each of the 10 Local Authorities across the region. The LAEP will deliver a new, decarbonised energy system across Cardiff Capital Region These have been signed off by all Local Authorities and include regional strategic targets that collectively, facilitate a regional (CCR) and national (Wales) aggregated approach.
 
CCR will coordinate delivery of the plans for the region, facilitating collaboration, at scale delivery packages and attracting investment to accelerate a just transition. 

3. In 2022, CCR Energy Ltd was established as a partnership between the 10 local authority areas with the CJC as the sole shareholder. CCR purchased the decommissioned Aberthaw Power Station to develop and reposition it as an exemplar for green energy production and zero-carbon business in the region. https://ccrenergy.com/ 

4. CCR coordinate Housing and Property programmes to improve quality of housing across the region to a high energy standard or Net Zero homes. Ecoflex is an obligation on energy companies to invest in low income homes in the region, raising the EPC rating by at least two (so for example a D - B). The programme runs until 2026 and delivery is ongoing with EDF and EON. Homes for the Region is a 35m targeted funding programme to unlock allocated residential sites across the region. The fund is intended to deliver 2,800 new homes across the 10 local authority areas to a minimum EPC B rating with around 800 social housing EPC A rated homes and no fossil fuel. Strategic Premises Fund is a 10 year programme (2021 - 2031) offering a £50m evergreen loan fund to support development of commercial property with ESG and BREAAM conditions attached to enhance the efficiency and sustainability of buildings. Since 2024, £28m loans have been drawn down with a pipeline of £52m committed from this circular fund. 

6. CCR have an innovation and challenge portfolio that supports sector and technology development. The https://www.challengefund.wales/ has a remit to accelerate decarbonisation projects such as Infuse, battery storage projects, Spaceforge, https://www.transcendpackaging.com/ and tidal power demonstration projects. CCR are stakeholders in HyBont which has achieved planning permission and begins construction in 2025, CCR are facilitating collaborative hydrogen infrastructure and deployment opportunities funded by the Whole Systems Research and Innovation for Decarbonisation (WSRID) Programme ). 'Solar Together' is a group buying scheme for domestic customers to install solar PV, batteries and charging infrastructure on homes at lower cost through group purchasing. 

7. CCR are also a stakeholder investor in https://media.cymru/about/our-vision/green/ run by a Cardiff University subsidiary, media Cymru, working across the media sector in Wales to enhance the competitiveness of Wales as a sustainable media destination.
column17:
In terms of financial planning, climate change mitigation is built into all projects and supplier requirements across all CCR activities via a output, outcomes and impact assessment framework. An Environmental, Social and Governance 'ESG' scorecard is being used to assess all outward investment to ensure partner organisations can deliver on CCR core principles. Crucially, all activities of the CCR are underpinned by CCR priorities' to deliver growth based on the principles of sustainability, productivity and inclusivity and based on the requirements of the Wellbeing of Future Generations Act 2015. Climate change and driving towards Net Zero is at the core of all delivery, and funded programmes. For example, low carbon options are built into transport infrastructure, buildings, energy and economic development targets in line with the energy vision, and across all wider funding and investment programmes such as innovation initiatives, the Northern Valleys Initiative, and industrial zone development, decarbonisation of infrastructure, products and services is key to delivery.

CCR also continue to directly invest in infrastructure to strengthen the energy resilience of the region, for example Home - CCR Energy Limited at Aberthaw development of the Regional Transport Plan prioritising public and active travel infrastructure and delivery of the metro scheme which is not being extended to deliver a cross-rail train- tram link in Cardiff CCR Metro Extension are great examples of investment in low carbon infrastructure.

CCR are also hoping to be successful in their bid for UK Government funding to deliver one of four investment zones around the UK, potentially, a £160m programme over 10 years focused on growing the compound semi-conductor industry hub in Wales. 

The Investment Zone has to pass through 4 UK Government gateways, currently working through gateway three which is a requirement to demonstrate programme Governance, stage 4 will be designing interventions around themes such as skills, R&D etc which is expected to take place over the summer 2025 and section 5 will be high-level delivery models before gaining approval.

In addition, CCR have established private sector joint ventures to accelerate the production of hydrogen in the region and are working to overcome policy and perception barriers with the public sector that will unlock delivery at scale of low carbon infrastructure, for example, roll out of ULEV charging infrastructure and delivery of renewable energy schemes. 

CCR's aim is to develop a low carbon region to attract investment and innovative business by providing resilient and low carbon energy infrastructure, as well as attracting clean tech business to boost economic growth and support the full transition to a low carbon economy. Newport Waferfab is one such innovative company. Examples of access to capital provided or facilitated by CCR include; CCR Challenge fund has enabled Local Authority fleet operators to work with the private sector to provide innovative solutions to accelerate transition to ULEV, from management to fuel and storage options. CCR is managing Ecoflex funding available via the energy companies for retrofitting housing, funding streams available from Welsh Government and UK government CCR has managed delivery of the 50m metro-plus infrastructure projects and a ULEV programmes to install charging infrastructure and support the roll out ULEV to the public and private sector. Homes for the region 35m fund to unlock development of modern, low carbon homes across the region. CCR Strategic premises fund is a 50m evergreen loan fund to support development of commercial property with ESG/BREAAM conditions attached. Procurement and development of the Aberthaw site and establishing of CCR Energy is and initial 38.4 million investment to procure and remediate the site and develop the full masterplan for a net zero carbon hub for the region.


As a statutory body, CCR CJC is also required (voluntarily) to annually report its own operational Carbon Footprint to Welsh Government as part of voluntary public sector reporting in line with Welsh Governments ambitious target for the Welsh Public Sector to be Carbon Neutral by 2030.

 This includes 'Scope 3' supply chain emissions which will require development of an emissions reduction programme and further influence procurement decisions moving forward. CCR have already established an internal Net Zero working group and implemented agile working practices to reduce the need for staff to travel as well as mitigating the need to operate permanent, fixed desk large office spaces. Public transport is always prioritised for business travel.
column18:
There are many risks associated with the decarbonization delivery plan, not least of which is having the confidence to choose a decarbonization pathway when there are so many options and unknowns about future power markets. For instance what will be the power source for heat in the future or will hydrogen be available at a competitive price. At a programme level the risk of failure is significant. Wales is home to many of the UK's carbon intense industries, for instance 19 major emitters under the Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS), (meaning that they emit more than 25k tonnes of carbon a year) paying 49.9m/year to HMT, according to statistics from the South Wales Industrial Cluster, (SWIC) September 2021. There are also many more smaller emitters. These companies are facing a double hit at present - with these industries having to pay the ETS fine to UK Government, how can they marshal the resources to make an investment in to energy efficiency measures or low carbon fuel switching? Furthermore, managing the efficient and prudent use of capital in global markets means that CCR has a real risk of losing its economic power base of manufacturing if businesses cannot find economical viable low carbon solutions. Quite simply the investment capital might go to greener economies. According to research by Bolton and Kacperczyk, featured in the Journal of Financial Economics in May this year “investors are already demanding compensation for their exposure to carbon emission risk.” As a CJC, CCR is now a political body with statutory obligations and the additional possibility of failure to deliver on the decarbonization plan also presents a huge risk of reputational damage to Elected Members and Programme Officers. There is a genuine appetite in CCR's Regional Cabinet to tackle this agenda, not least to address the wide spread concern about Climate Change and energy prices.. This is obviously a huge, multi stakeholder transformation programme, the success of which will be significantly influenced by future power markets. A strategic assessment of some of the most pertinent risks which could affect delivery of the Energy Vision Programme has been undertaken following best practice approaches set out by Management of Risk Foundation and the Association of Project Management Body of Knowledge. This is also the accepted approach for the Welsh Government. 

Now CCR is a statutory body, with obligations to produce a regional transport plan and regional development plan, there are risks associated with the efficiency and speed with which these plans are developed ready for delivery. However, there are also significant opportunities in influencing regional public sector policy to facilitate an energy transition and increase appetite for longer term contracts and commitments to facilitate private sector investment. 

Access to funding and resources to deliver at scale and pace is also a high risk, both human resources including skilled and trained labour and material availability. Supply chain risks have been highlighted by the COVID-19 pandemic alongside the impact on import and export of materials caused by Brexit. Geopolitical influences are still significant, resulting in inflation and significantly increased cost of materials for delivery. Public sector budgets are still under severe pressure and there are always competing pressures, however, CCR are fundamentally committed to delivering sustainable and inclusive growth for the region and have the opportunity to use their position to drive best practice.

column17:
1. Impacto en la operación y mantenimiento de infraestructura y transporte
Se observa un presupuesto considerable destinado a combustible, mantenimiento y seguro de vehículos oficiales (Pick-up 4x4, motor diésel).

Estos gastos reflejan la necesidad de movilidad constante para el monitoreo de áreas naturales y seguimiento de proyectos ambientales, los cuales están directamente relacionados con fenómenos climáticos, como sequías o lluvias, que afectan el acceso a sitios remotos.

Por ejemplo, caminos rurales pueden verse afectados por lluvias intensas, lo que incrementa los costos de mantenimiento, verificación y llantas de vehículos.

2. Costos asociados a la conservación de la biodiversidad
El monitoreo de águila real (Aquila chrysaetos).

Los fenómenos climáticos, como cambios en la temperatura, sequías o eventos extremos, influyen directamente en la disponibilidad de presas y la seguridad de los nidos, lo que hace necesario un seguimiento más frecuente y profesionalizado.

Esto refleja que la planificación financiera incluye recursos para adaptarse a la variabilidad climática, asegurando que los programas de conservación no se vean interrumpidos.

3. Inversiones en educación y cultura ambiental
Se incluyen partidas para foros de cultura ambiental y materiales de difusión.

Esto muestra que la JIAN considera que los asuntos climáticos requieren sensibilización y educación continua, lo que implica planificación de gastos en actividades de comunicación, talleres y campañas de concientización sobre la gestión del agua y otros recursos afectados por el clima.

4. Gestión integral del territorio
Se destina presupuesto a capacitación jurídica ambiental para servidores públicos municipales 

Esto refleja que los efectos del clima sobre el territorio (sequías, inundaciones, degradación de suelos) requieren actualización normativa y capacitación, lo que impacta la planificación financiera al asignar recursos para fortalecer capacidades institucionales.
column18:
1. Riesgos financieros
Aumento de costos operativos iniciales: La adopción de tecnologías bajas en carbono (vehículos eléctricos, energía solar, eficiencia energética en oficinas) puede implicar inversiones iniciales significativas.

Dependencia de subsidios o incentivos externos: Programas de transición energética muchas veces requieren apoyo gubernamental; cambios en políticas pueden afectar presupuestos.

Reducción de recursos para otras áreas: Al destinar parte del presupuesto a energías limpias o transporte sostenible, se puede reducir la inversión en conservación de biodiversidad, educación ambiental o mantenimiento de infraestructura.

2. Riesgos tecnológicos
Necesidad de actualización de infraestructura y sistemas: Por ejemplo, el reemplazo de vehículos diésel por eléctricos o híbridos requiere instalación de estaciones de carga, capacitación del personal y mantenimiento especializado.

Obsolescencia tecnológica: Equipos actuales (como vehículos o generadores) podrían quedar fuera de norma o regulaciones, afectando operaciones y generando costos adicionales.

3. Riesgos regulatorios y legales
Cumplimiento normativo: La transición a bajo carbono implica cumplir nuevas regulaciones ambientales y fiscales, lo que puede exigir auditorías, reportes y ajustes operativos.

Riesgos legales por incumplimiento: Si la JIAN mantiene prácticas de alto carbono en sus operaciones (vehículos, consumo energético), podría enfrentar sanciones o pérdida de credibilidad institucional.

4. Riesgos reputacionales
Expectativas de sostenibilidad: Como organismo ambiental, la JIAN tiene visibilidad pública; mantener prácticas no sostenibles puede afectar su imagen frente a gobiernos locales, ciudadanía y organismos internacionales.

Percepción sobre liderazgo ambiental: La falta de acciones concretas hacia una economía baja en carbono podría debilitar su autoridad y capacidad de influencia en proyectos regionales.

5. Riesgos operativos
Interrupciones en programas por transición tecnológica: Implementar nuevas fuentes de energía o transporte sostenible puede generar ajustes logísticos y retrasos en actividades como monitoreo de biodiversidad o campañas educativas.

Capacitación del personal: Se requiere formación en nuevas tecnologías y prácticas sostenibles, lo que implica tiempo y recursos.

En resumen, la transición a una economía baja en carbono para la JIAN implica riesgos financieros, tecnológicos, regulatorios, reputacionales y operativos, pero también representa oportunidades de innovación, eficiencia y liderazgo ambiental si se planifica estratégicamente.

column15: In February 2023, Järfälla municipality accepted a new Environmental plan in which the council agreed on climate neutrality at 2030. The plan also includes a goal to decrease the emissions of CO2e with 15 % every year, for the geographical area of Järfälla. The Environmental plan includes sector targets and suggested mitigation actions. Since 2017, Järfälla has a carbon budget in line with the Paris agreement, showing geographical emissions of CO2 from different sectors. In 2023, the council stated that the department for sustainability will implement the carbon budget, to work towards climate neutrality 2030. The implementation will include coordination of climate work through all departments of the municipality. Furthermore, Järfälla has a climate adaptation plan to prevent severe damage during climate change. The municipality also have a new climate and energy plan that provides targets and actions to lower the emissions in the municipality and develop energy efficiency. Since 1997, the municipality have been working with an environmental management system, which is a tool to implement and follow up on the adopted targets and actions.\nFurthermore, Järfälla has been a part of Viable Cities since 2019, with a climate contract stating a commitment to work towards climate neutrality, through specific projects for e.g. energy efficiency and sustainable construction within Järfälla.
column16:
Employees with expertise in climate issues is found in several places in the municipality. Järfälla has a number of environmental planners who work closely with development and planning to ensure that environmental issues are taken into account at an early stage. The department of urban planning also has ecologists, water strategists and traffic planners who participate in public planning and work actively on climate issues.

At a strategic level, the Department for Sustainable Development is responsible for steering and driving sustainability work at a municipal-wide level. The department of sustainability has a broad knowledge in climate, energy, chemicals, sustainable procurement and social sustainability. Their expertise is used in various projects, for example as support for monitoring energy requirements or for the development of new plans as well as urban development projects. 

The work with implementing climate actions in the different departments is accelerating. Järfälla has started to develop a new system for sustainable planning, where environmental and climate issues will be planned on the same level as the economic budget. Through this the municipality can implement the carbon budget more efficient in all departments. In 2023, the work with a new comprehensive plan has started, and has a clear focus on how Järfälla can accelerate climate mitigation and be circular and robust during climate change. The implementation of the carbon budget also includes a new form of coorporation within the municipality organisation that goes across all of its departments. The department of sustainability coordinates the municipal climate work, partly through the established environmental management system and partly through climate meetings with all larger departments of the organisation. Through both the environmental management system and the climate meetings the organisation can develop actions for lower emissions. This process is planned to be joined with the yearly operation plans for each department.
column17:
Together with the participants in Viable Cities, climate investment plans are developed. A climate investment plan strategically mobilizes and organizes public resources and addresses how to attract private capital to finance cities' paths towards climate neutrality.

Within our Viable Cities-project we have a work package on combining the municipality's budget with climate impact to make visible which climate investments are necessary and how this affects the municipality's finances in the long term. By examining the costs and savings of climate investments, it is easier to make a long-term budget for the municipality's climate work and ensure that the right investments are prioritized.

In the Environmental plan and other policy documents, there is a great focus on working towards a circular economy, in both the municipality organization and for the citizens and companies in Järfälla. When discussing issues of circular economy, reuse in construction and environmental friendly consumption, the development of procurement requirements is a hot topic. There is an ongoing work within the municipality for sustainable growth, without an increase of emissions.
column18: It is a challenge to establish a stable economy and working life for the citizens of Järfälla during a transition in transports, material flow and energy consumption. We want to have companies and citizens that can thrive in a market that is characterized by reuse and circularity. There are risks to lose strong companies and markets in the transition towards a low-carbon economy. There are challenges for building companies in the development towards circular construction, with reusing materials and higher demands on low emissions. The municipality is working on solutions for planning, procurement and logistics to make the transition towards a climate neutral construction industry possible. The municipality needs to provide an atractive city, for the people and businesses living in Järfälla, otherwise the credability towards the municipality will be to low. In the transition towards a climate neutral transport system for example, the municipality needs to develop solutions for mobility that are as efficient and easy to use as the private car.

column16: In response to the rising concern over the urgent need for action, in July 2019, Wokingham Borough Council members unanimously declared a climate emergency. The declaration set out the commitment to play as full a role as possible, leading by example as well as by exhortation, in achieving a carbon neutral Wokingham Borough by 2030. Subsequently, in January 2020, the council published its first Climate Emergency Action Plan (CEAP), establishing the key priority areas to focus on for reducing CO2, all of which influence the long-term planning of the councils actions and direction. The action plan specifically focuses the councils current and future efforts on tackling emissions from transport, energy usage, generating renewable energy, planting more trees and other green foliage, encourage more recycling and encouraging behavioural change. This includes local planning, with targets focused around a local plan update, which seeks to incorporate sustainability measures and utilising renewable energy wherever possible, combined with support for active and sustainable travel infrastructure and green spaces. This is a live report which is continually reviewed and an updated progress report is published each year, documenting the progress on actions and changes within, which determines the long-term plan for many key areas of the council.
column17: In order to prepare for potential climate related risks and minimise our own emissions to reduce the chances of such, significant resources have needed to be utilised in order to help achieve the targets set out in the action plan.
