column16:
Isu-isu terkait dengan Perubahan Iklim menjadi target dalam dokumen Perencanaan Daerah di Kabupaten Sumbawa NTB. 
Isu-isu terkait iklim telah memberikan pengaruh yang sangat besar terhadap perencanaan induk dan perencanaan pembangunan di Kabupaten Sumbawa dalam beberapa tahun terakhir. Tekanan iklim yang terus berulang—seperti musim kemarau yang semakin panjang, kekurangan air, degradasi daerah aliran sungai (DAS), abrasi pesisir, curah hujan ekstrem, serta meningkatnya frekuensi bencana—telah membuat pemerintah daerah perlu menggeser pendekatan pembangunan menjadi lebih responsif terhadap iklim dan berbasis pengurangan risiko.
Pertama, dampak iklim tersebut telah diintegrasikan ke dalam perencanaan tata ruang (RTRW) dan perencanaan pembangunan jangka menengah daerah (RPJMD). Wilayah-wilayah yang diidentifikasi rentan terhadap kekeringan dan banjir—terutama zona pertanian di daerah tengah, kawasan DAS, dan beberapa desa pesisir—telah ditetapkan untuk pengaturan pemanfaatan ruang yang lebih ketat, perlindungan ekosistem, dan pembangunan infrastruktur adaptif. Hal ini mencakup penetapan kawasan lindung DAS, pembatasan pembangunan di dataran banjir berisiko tinggi, serta prioritas rehabilitasi lahan terdegradasi di daerah hulu yang menjadi sumber air bagi sungai dan jaringan irigasi utama.
Kedua, perencanaan pembangunan Kabupaten Sumbawa kini memasukkan strategi adaptasi iklim pada sektor-sektor teknis. Sektor pertanian menyesuaikan pola tanam dan jadwal irigasi untuk merespon variabilitas curah hujan. Dinas Pekerjaan Umum dan Sumber Daya Air memperkuat program pemanenan air hujan, pemeliharaan embung dan waduk, serta pembangunan infrastruktur mitigasi kekeringan. Kawasan pesisir—terutama yang terdampak abrasi—diintegrasikan dalam perencanaan perlindungan pesisir, rehabilitasi mangrove, dan sistem peringatan dini berbasis masyarakat. Pengurangan risiko bencana juga menjadi komponen utama dalam perencanaan tahunan BPBD, sehingga memengaruhi arah pembangunan permukiman dan perencanaan desa.
Ketiga, pertimbangan perubahan iklim kini menjadi dasar dalam penentuan prioritas program dan penganggaran. Pemerintah Kabupaten mengalokasikan sumber daya untuk perlindungan DAS, pengelolaan lahan berkelanjutan, pembangunan infrastruktur tahan iklim, serta mendukung inisiatif adaptasi di tingkat desa. Keselarasan dengan kebijakan iklim Provinsi NTB dan kebijakan nasional—seperti RAD API NTB dan kerangka nasional penanggulangan bencana—juga menjadi penting untuk mendapatkan dukungan pendanaan dari luar.
Secara keseluruhan, isu-isu iklim telah menggeser perencanaan pembangunan Kabupaten Sumbawa dari pendekatan yang berorientasi pertumbuhan konvensional menuju kerangka yang lebih menekankan ketahanan, keberlanjutan ekologis, dan pengurangan risiko jangka panjang. Pendekatan ini bertujuan memastikan pembangunan ekonomi dapat berjalan sambil tetap melindungi masyarakat, sistem pertanian, dan ekosistem penting dari risiko iklim yang semakin meningkat.
column17:
Dampak Isu Iklim terhadap Perencanaan Keuangan Kabupaten Sumbawa

Isu-isu terkait iklim telah memberikan pengaruh yang signifikan terhadap perencanaan keuangan Kabupaten Sumbawa. Perubahan pola curah hujan, meningkatnya kejadian kekeringan, banjir, abrasi pesisir, serta kerentanan sektor pertanian dan wilayah pesisir telah memaksa pemerintah daerah mengalokasikan anggaran secara lebih strategis dan responsif terhadap risiko iklim.

Pertama, perubahan iklim telah menyebabkan peningkatan kebutuhan anggaran untuk program adaptasi dan penanggulangan bencana. Pemerintah Kabupaten harus menambah alokasi pada kegiatan seperti penyediaan air bersih saat musim kemarau, pemeliharaan embung dan waduk, rehabilitasi daerah aliran sungai, penguatan infrastruktur irigasi, serta penanganan banjir dan longsor pada musim penghujan. BPBD, DPUPR, dan dinas teknis lainnya semakin sering mengajukan anggaran mendesak (contingency budget) untuk respon kejadian iklim ekstrem.

Kedua, perencanaan keuangan daerah kini mengintegrasikan kriteria ketahanan iklim dalam proses penyusunan RKPD dan APBD. Program fisik yang sebelumnya hanya menekankan pertumbuhan ekonomi kini harus memenuhi aspek keberlanjutan, seperti penggunaan material tahan iklim, desain bangunan adaptif, konservasi air, serta perlindungan kawasan rawan bencana. Hal ini memengaruhi besarnya investasi daerah, prioritas belanja modal, dan penyesuaian pada proyek-proyek infrastruktur strategis.

Ketiga, isu iklim mendorong Kabupaten Sumbawa untuk mengoptimalkan sumber-sumber pendanaan eksternal. Pemerintah daerah semakin aktif menyesuaikan programnya dengan kebijakan iklim provinsi dan nasional guna memperoleh Dana Alokasi Khusus (DAK) tematik lingkungan, pendanaan rehabilitasi DAS, bantuan penanggulangan bencana, serta peluang pendanaan dari lembaga donor atau program kemitraan pembangunan. Upaya ini penting untuk menutup kesenjangan pendanaan dalam membiayai infrastruktur adaptasi jangka panjang.

Keempat, isu iklim juga berdampak pada penganggaran desa, terutama di wilayah rawan kekeringan dan banjir. Desa-desa diarahkan untuk mengalokasikan Dana Desa bagi program adaptasi seperti pipanisasi air bersih, penghijauan, pengelolaan lahan berkelanjutan, serta kesiapsiagaan bencana. Ini membuat perencanaan keuangan daerah menjadi lebih terintegrasi antara tingkat kabupaten dan desa.

Secara keseluruhan, perubahan iklim telah mengubah perencanaan keuangan Kabupaten Sumbawa dari sekadar perencanaan pengeluaran rutin menjadi perencanaan yang berbasis risiko, berorientasi ketahanan jangka panjang, dan terhubung dengan prioritas adaptasi serta mitigasi. Pendekatan ini penting untuk memastikan keberlanjutan pembangunan dan perlindungan masyarakat dari dampak iklim yang semakin meningkat.
column18:
Penilaian Peluang dan Manfaat Lingkungan, Sosial, dan Ekonomi dari Aksi Iklim di Kabupaten Sumbawa
Kabupaten Sumbawa menilai peluang serta manfaat lingkungan, sosial, dan ekonomi dari aksi iklim melalui pendekatan terpadu yang melibatkan analisis teknis perangkat daerah, perencanaan jangka menengah, serta kajian risiko dan potensi pembangunan daerah. Penilaian ini dilakukan untuk memastikan bahwa program adaptasi dan mitigasi tidak hanya mengurangi kerentanan, tetapi juga memberikan nilai tambah bagi masyarakat dan perekonomian lokal.
Pertama, dari sisi lingkungan, pemerintah daerah menilai manfaat aksi iklim melalui pemantauan kondisi daerah aliran sungai (DAS), tutupan vegetasi, kualitas air, dan kesehatan ekosistem pesisir. Program seperti rehabilitasi mangrove, penghijauan lahan kritis, dan perlindungan kawasan hulu dipandang memberikan manfaat ekologis jangka panjang, termasuk peningkatan kualitas air, pengurangan risiko banjir dan abrasi, serta stabilitas ekosistem yang mendukung perikanan dan pertanian. Indikator-indikator tersebut dinilai melalui data yang dihimpun oleh DLH, Dinas Pertanian, Dinas Kelautan dan Perikanan, serta BPBD.
Kedua, manfaat sosial dievaluasi melalui dampaknya terhadap ketahanan masyarakat, pengurangan risiko bencana, dan peningkatan akses terhadap layanan dasar. Aksi iklim seperti penyediaan air bersih saat musim kemarau, pembangunan infrastruktur tahan iklim, sistem peringatan dini, dan program desa tangguh iklim memberikan manfaat berupa meningkatnya keamanan dan kenyamanan hidup masyarakat, berkurangnya gangguan terhadap aktivitas pendidikan dan kesehatan, serta meningkatnya kapasitas desa untuk merespon kejadian ekstrem. Pemerintah Kabupaten memantau indikator sosial ini melalui laporan rutin desa, data BPBD, dan evaluasi program tingkat kecamatan.
Ketiga, dari sisi ekonomi, Kabupaten Sumbawa menilai manfaat aksi iklim melalui peningkatan produktivitas sektor pertanian dan perikanan, stabilitas pendapatan masyarakat, serta efisiensi biaya penanggulangan bencana. Investasi pada infrastruktur irigasi yang adaptif, perlindungan wilayah pesisir, dan pengembangan pertanian berkelanjutan dianggap sebagai langkah yang mampu menjaga stabilitas produksi pangan, mengurangi kerugian akibat kekeringan atau banjir, serta menciptakan peluang usaha baru seperti ekowisata, perikanan berkelanjutan, dan jasa lingkungan. Analisis manfaat ekonomi ini dilakukan melalui perencanaan Bappeda, Dinas Pertanian, dan Dinas Perikanan.
Keempat, Kabupaten Sumbawa juga melakukan kajian manfaat lintas sektor melalui integrasi aksi iklim dalam RPJMD, RKPD, dan perencanaan desa. Proses ini memastikan bahwa setiap program adaptasi atau mitigasi dipertimbangkan tidak hanya dari sisi biaya, tetapi juga dari potensi manfaat lebih luas, termasuk kesempatan kerja hijau, peningkatan kualitas hidup, dan keberlanjutan pemanfaatan sumber daya alam.
Secara keseluruhan, Kabupaten Sumbawa menilai manfaat aksi iklim melalui gabungan pendekatan teknis, sosial, dan ekonomi yang terintegrasi dalam perencanaan pembangunan daerah. Pendekatan ini memastikan bahwa aksi iklim tidak hanya mengurangi risiko, tetapi juga menciptakan peluang baru untuk pertumbuhan berkelanjutan dan peningkatan kesejahteraan masyarakat

Selkirk has the following By-laws which are approved by Council and are to be reviewed at least every five (5) years:

- Greenhouse Gas Accountability By-law #5630 (2021) 

- Capital Asset Management By-law #5300 (2017) which ensures that municipal infrastructure is constructed, maintained, and decommissioned in a manner that facilitates the social, environmental, and economic sustainability of the City. 

- Capital Levy By-law #5349 (2021) which establishes a system for the assessment and allocation of capital levies on development to support the sustainability of city infrastructure. It incentivizes density and infill by reducing development fees for sustainable design.

- Economic Incentive By-law #5317 (2018) which establishes an Economic Incentive Program to promote and facilitate sustainable economic growth, encourages higher density residential development and mixed uses of existing buildings in the downtown, and supports the remediation of contaminated properties.

Selkirk has the following plans and strategies which are reviewed and approved by City Council:

- Strategic Plan (2014) which identifies a number of important priorities for the City that focus on continuing to build a vibrant and efficient community and economy while also practicing environmental stewardship and development of safe and sustainable infrastructure. 

- Climate Change Adaptation Strategy (2019-2029) that identifies some of the likely impacts climate change will have on municipal service delivery for the City of Selkirk, and identifies adaptation actions. It also outlines the need for continuous improvement and review of the strategy. 

 - Capital Asset Management Strategy (2016-2020). City Administration has outlined a high-level legislative framework for the Capital Asset Management program. This framework identified the key policy, procedures and tools that it will develop over the next few years to meet the objectives and requirements as set out in the associated by-law. 

- West End Concept Plan (2020), which establishes an overarching vision and set of core principles to guide the long-term development of Selkirk's West End. Aligned with the City's broader strategic planning objectives, the purpose of the Plan is to provide the City of Selkirk with a progressive planning framework to direct the West End's long-term development consistent with its pursuit of a sustainable future. 

- Active Transportation Strategy (2021-2025) 

Selkirk has the following policies: 

- Street Tree Policy (2021)

- Capital Asset Management Program Policies (2019 - 2021). 

The polices include: Asset Registry Policy, Asset Evaluation Policy, Capital Asset Life Cycle Management Policy, Capital Asset Level of Service Policy, and Capital Asset Risk Management Policy. 

The City of Selkirk launched an internal planning department in May 2022. This will provide Selkirk with additional opportunity to influence development in a way that supports climate action.
column16:
All land use planning in the province of Manitoba, including Selkirk, is governed by the Provincial Planning Act. This means that although Development Plans are written by municipalities or planning districts, all Development Plans must be approved by the provincial government and adhere to the Act. 

Selkirk currently operates under the Red River Planning District, but recently created a separate planning department that will be preparing a Selkirk-specific Development Plan.

The RRPD Development Plan addresses implementing the three pillars of sustainable development in a regional context, where the three pillars focus on environmental stewardship (minimizing negative impacts on natural resources), economic development, and social equity (including topics like affordable housing and inclusivity). Objectives of the plan include facilitating measures that are adaptive to climate change. 

The plan includes standards for wastewater treatment and water master planning, as well as the following specifics to Selkirk : 

- Municipalities should consider implementing climate change reduction, adaptation and/or resiliency measures in their community (e.g. infrastructure, drought resistant landscaping, tree retention and planting, etc.). As previously shown, Selkirk has meet this recommendation. 

- Promote the City of Selkirk as a regional urban centre with appropriate services, development, and redevelopment of existing neighbourhoods. This puts additional regional expectations on Selkirk's services. 

- Encourage the development of an efficient public transit corridor between Selkirk and Winnipeg- secure a long-term sustainable water supply for the City of Selkirk.

- Densification of residential development in the City of Selkirk, Settlement Centres, and General Development Areas where appropriate services can be provided will be encouraged to make the provision of municipal piped sewer and water services increasingly fiscally feasible.

- Protect the Urban Forest in the City of Selkirk

- Designation of a Downtown Mixed Use area, which allows for an urban central business district where commercial, office, retail and residential uses are encouraged to locate within proximity to each other or in the same building, to facilitate a walkable urban environment. 

- Designation of a Regional Recreation and Open Space area, which allows for large areas and facilities that provide private or public, active or passive, recreational facilities that service both residents within and outside of the community. These facilities can be used as cooling areas during times of intense heat. 

- Reserve resource and Agriculture areas in the City of Selkirk for future orderly and sustainable urban expansion- A general housing strategy for the City of Selkirk should be established to ensure that new residential development projects include an affordable housing component and provide opportunities for home ownership. The strategy may consider alternative ownership models such as cooperatives.

- Encourage downtown (denser) living by supporting the creation of a pedestrian friendly downtown, supporting the creation of a visually attractive downtown, promoting a safe downtown, etc. 

Looking ahead, the Winnipeg Metropolitan Region was mandated by the Provincial Government to assemble a 30-year regional vision and plan for Manitoba's capital region, which includes Selkirk. The plan is called Plan20-50. This new plan will cover five policy areas: integrated communities and infrastructure, One Environment, Resource Management, Investment and Employment, and Collaborative Governance. The One Environment policy area will clarify that we must plan for climate change and build regional resiliency. The plan will provide effective and consistent approaches to protect, restore and enhance ecosystems, watersheds and environmentally sensitive areas across the region, while recognizing the social and economic importance of traditional lifestyles, recreation, and tourism for future generations.

- Selkirk's Greenhouse Gas Accountability By-law #5630 (2021) establishes a financial framework which clearly and transparently ensures GHG targets can be met. It establishes a reserve fund, which puts a price on carbon emissions and sets aside funds for future climate change adaptation projects. It also requires regular reporting on GHGs, like CDP reporting. 

The CDP reporting includes adhering to the TCFD framework, which will further advance the consideration of climate change in financial planning activities. Reporting to the public is also required, which will increase public awareness and support for budget items that advance climate action. 

- Selkirk has been proactive in accessing government funding for climate action-related activities. The following historical actions highlight this: 

-In 2018, Selkirk received funding support from the Federation of Canadian Municipalities' Municipal Asset Management Program (MAMP) which enabled Selkirk to establish key policies for core assets and service levels.

-Selkirk has applied the Infrastructure Canada Climate Lens when applying for federal funding. 

-Funding support from the Federation of Canadian Municipalities' Municipal Asset Management Program (MAMP) enabled Selkirk to establish key policies for core assets and service levels. Selkirk leveraged this foundation to completed a new, state of the art, $39M wastewater treatment plant in 2021, which exceeds Provincial performance requirements and has capacity for a doubling of Selkirk's population. Selkirk obtained funding support of $750,000 and a $5 million loan from The Green Municipal Fund, delivered by the Federation of Canadian Municipalities and funded by the Government of Canada. The Manitoba Water Services Board, a provincial agency, partnered with the city as the project manager and will contributed just under $250,000.

The city has also received significant funding through the Investing in Canada Infrastructure program to enhance it's urban forest and mitigate and adapt to the negative affects of climate change through afforestation and urban tree management by planting over 900 trees since 2021.

Current and emerging regulation: 

- Selkirk currently has a supportive City Council that understands the urgency and importance of climate action. This political will has been translated into by-law, long-term strategy, and policy; however, more are required. There is a risk associated with changes in Council and the loss of political will for bold and rapid climate action. 

- Provincial and/or Federal regulations and incentive programs will not be sufficient to spur meaningful climate action. 

- Electricity Grid Regulation and Policy 

- Manitoba Hydro regulation and policy for micro-generation and financial reimbursement, smart grid investment, and ensuring capacity and reliability to support electrification are not adequate to facilitate change. 

Technology: 

- Selkirk is blessed with a hydro-electric power grid, however, aging transmission and distribution infrastructure may limit electrification efforts, particularly for transportation. 

- Cold temperatures reduce electric vehicle range. Market: 

- Elevated costs of basic commodities increase the cost of living and reduce funding available for bold climate action. 

- Availability of electric vehicles is limited 

- A lack of skilled change agents (eg: energy auditors, electric vehicle repair, geothermal, heat pump, and solar installation) slows the ability to change). 

- Community engagement and education is not sufficient to stoke consumer awareness and behaviour change. 

Reputation: 

- Selkirk's, like Manitoba's, culture is focused on vehicles and driving. Challenges exist in seeking to adjust the status quo in the direction of meaningful climate action, such as removing paved areas and switching transportation modes.

- Being a smaller community, it is harder for Selkirk to get the attention and support of the larger government for innovation and investment support.

Este departamento no sólo monitorea las toneladas de residuos que se generan si no que contabilizan el % que corresponden a material reciclable y se está planeando el crear un sistema de gestión de basura orgánica en el mediano plazo.\nDentro de la Dirección de Asesoría Urbana y Espacio Público se encuentra la oficina de SmartCity la cual monitorea diferentes elementos de la calidad ambiental de la comuna, a través de la instalación de sensores, la gestión y visualización de datos. column16:
La comuna ha vivido varios eventos de riesgo para su población y espacios naturales, los cuales están vinculados al cambio climático. Por ejemplo, la comuna ha sufrido comuna aluviones durante el invierno de 2021 y 2023 el sector de El Arrayán. Esto ha significado la movilización de personal municipal y la necesidad de invertir en limpiezas de cauces así como en apoyo a familias afectadas. A lo anterior se suma el riesgo de remoción en masa, el cual se ha visto incrementado por las precipitaciones intensa que se han vivido durante los años 2023 y 2024.

La comuna es altamente vulnerable al riesgo de sequía y con el aumento de las temperaturas promedio durante los últimos años, esta situación se ha visto intensificada. Al respecto, la comuna ha visto una baja en la disponibilidad de agua por la sequía lo que se agrava si se tiene en consideración que es una de las comunas con mayor demanda de agua en el sector residencial del país y tiene presencia de empresa con alto consumo hídrica como lo son minería, centros de ski, clubes de golf, entre otros. La comuna ha sido declarada zona de escasez hídrica en múltiples ocasiones, siendo la última durante el año 2019. 

Sumado a lo anterior, mediante los estudios de 'Piloto de Monitoreo de Glaciares' y 'Estudio de Dinámica Glacial”, se logró observar un retroceso de la cobertura glaciar (glaciares descubiertos) de un 30% en los últimos 30 años y un acelerado retroceso en los últimos 10. Lo anterior se debe, en gran medida, al aumento de la temperatura promedio y tiene un impacto negativo en la disponibilidad de agua en la cuenca. 

Por último, en 2023 se registró un incendio que abarcó más de 900 Ha. Ambos fenómenos están conectados al cambio climático (aumento en volumen de precipitaciones y fenómenos climáticos y aumento de probabilidad de incendio). Esto ha obligado a la Municipalidad a abordar el tema climático y considerarlo al momento de planificar la comuna. por ejemplo, mediante la generación de planes de emergencia y respuesta ante posibles desastres naturales.
column17: Los eventos climáticos ocurridos en los últimos años (por ejemplo: aluvión del año 2021, precipitaciones intensas con isoterma 0 en zonas altas del año 2023) traen consigo arrastre de materiales, los cuales deben ser recogidos y despejados para poder mantener la seguridad y conectividad dentro de la comuna. Esto último repercute directamente en un aumento de los costos operativos en materia de aseo y seguridad a nivel comunal. Asimismo, se despliegan recursos para atender a los damnificados por los eventos, por ejemplo mediante la implementación de albergues. Debido al río atmosférico que afecto la RM en invierno de 2024, muchas familias se vieron afectadas por los fuertes vientos, lo que obligó al Municipio a desplegar funcionarios para ayudar a la emergencia así como fondos para ayudar a las familias afectadas. \n\nJunto a lo anterior, se destaca el efecto que ha tenido la sequía sobre las actividades productivas de la comuna. Si bien no existe una cuantificación como tal de las pérdidas económicas, la sequía prolongada que ha vivido la comuna ha obligado a los dueños de derechos de aguas a no hacer uso de ellos o disponibilizar parte del caudal del río para mantener el caudal ecológico o para agua potable y servicios de saneamiento. Lo anterior ha generado pérdidas económicas y productivas en la comuna e implica la coordinación efectiva de diferentes organizaciones, lo cual requiere tiempo e inversión tanto de privados como de entes públicos como la Municipalidad.
column18: Los riesgos asociados a una transición a una economía baja en carbono están relacionados con la tecnología, el mercado y desigualdad social. En relación a la tecnología, existe el riesgo de que los valores de las nuevas tecnologías sean muy elevados, lo que repercuta en que solo un sector de la población pueda adquirirlos, generándose una desventaja para los sectores más vulnerables y ampliando las desigualdades existentes en el territorio.\nPor su parte, en relación a los riesgos del mercado se puede dar que el aumento de interés por determinados productos o servicios, genere una falta de stock y esto repercuta en un aumento de los precios. En ambos casos, la dificultad de acceso a bienes y servicios asociados a una economía baja en carbono, puede afectar a parte de la población de menos recursos. Esto puede generar desigualdades de acceso a bienes y servicios, así como malestar social.

column16:
En la Municipalidad de Renca, el cambio climático ha comenzado a integrarse de forma activa en la planificación urbana y territorial. Durante 2024, esta preocupación se reflejó en varias iniciativas estratégicas:

Actualización del Plan Regulador Comunal (PRC): Se elaboró un informe fundado para su modificación parcial, justificando la necesidad de ajustar las normas urbanas debido a su bajo impacto en la promoción de un desarrollo más sostenible y resiliente. Este proceso incluyó evaluaciones técnicas con enfoque ambiental, considerando los desafíos climáticos del territorio.

Diseño de infraestructura verde y soluciones basadas en la naturaleza: Se desarrolló el anteproyecto del Corredor Verde Urbano Condell, financiado por el programa Cities Forward, con criterios de resiliencia climática. Además, se avanzó en el Plan Maestro del Agua para los Cerros de Renca, que considera abastecimiento hídrico, reducción de riesgos de incendio y restauración ecológica.

Instrumentos como la Estrategia Hídrica Local y la participación en redes internacionales (Cities Forward, Urban Transitions Mission, Reinventing Cities C40) han influido directamente en la priorización de inversiones, como el Parque Costanera, que recupera la relación con el río desde una perspectiva de justicia ambiental y adaptación al cambio climático.

En conjunto, estas acciones muestran cómo el cambio climático ha comenzado a incidir en la planificación maestra de Renca, orientando decisiones normativas, inversiones urbanas y diseño de espacios públicos hacia un desarrollo urbano más sostenible y resiliente.
column17:
Durante 2024, el cambio climático influyó de manera creciente en la planificación financiera de la Municipalidad de Renca. Esto se reflejó en la priorización de proyectos vinculados a adaptación, eficiencia energética, gestión hídrica y recuperación de espacios públicos resilientes. Ejemplos concretos incluyen:

- La asignación de recursos para el diseño del Plan Maestro del Agua en los Cerros de Renca (USD 50.000), orientado a reducir riesgos climáticos e incendios forestales.

- La inversión pública de 175.000 UF para el Parque Costanera, con enfoque en recuperación ecológica y acceso equitativo a áreas verdes.

- El fortalecimiento del programa Renca 100% LED, que permitió completar la transición del alumbrado público, reduciendo el consumo energético y gastos operativos.

- La implementación del Centro de Inteligencia Hídrica, financiado con aportes privados, para monitorear el uso eficiente del agua en infraestructura municipal.

Además, se postularon proyectos a programas de financiamiento climático nacional e internacional, como el Youth Climate Action Fund (YCAF) y el Reinventing Cities (C40), orientando parte de la planificación presupuestaria hacia la acción climática. Estas decisiones evidencian un cambio progresivo en los criterios de priorización presupuestaria, incorporando variables ambientales y de riesgo climático en la planificación financiera de Renca.
column18:
La transición hacia una economía baja en carbono representa oportunidades, pero también riesgos relevantes para la comuna de Renca, especialmente por su perfil industrial y logístico.

Uno de los principales riesgos identificados es el impacto en pequeñas y medianas empresas (pymes), especialmente aquellas vinculadas al transporte, manufactura y logística, sectores con alta presencia en la comuna. La adopción de tecnologías limpias o medidas de compensación de emisiones puede representar costos financieros difíciles de asumir sin apoyo público o privado, afectando su competitividad.

Además, existe un riesgo de exclusión en el acceso a financiamiento climático por parte de actores locales, debido a las altas barreras técnicas y administrativas de los mecanismos disponibles. Esto podría profundizar brechas territoriales si no se garantiza una distribución equitativa de recursos para la descarbonización.

También se observa un riesgo de pérdida de empleos en sectores con baja preparación para la transición energética, como el transporte de carga o actividades altamente intensivas en energía, si no se implementan planes de capacitación laboral y reconversión productiva.

Por último, la transición acelerada sin planificación adecuada podría generar conflictos de uso del suelo urbano, entre industrias contaminantes y proyectos de infraestructura verde o vivienda sustentable, afectando la cohesión territorial y social.

Ante este escenario, el municipio ha comenzado a desarrollar estrategias como el Centro de Innovación y Emprendimiento Circular (CIE) y la Agencia Local de Inversiones, que buscan promover una reconversión productiva justa e inclusiva.

Low-Carbon Economic Potentials that have been implemented in Langsa City include:

1. Carbon Utilization and Mangrove Environmental Services

On February 21, 2024, the Langsa City Government signed an MoU with PT PEMA, focusing on carbon utilization and environmental services from mangrove forests. This collaboration includes a framework, legalization, program synchronization, and a two-year carbon mitigation action plan.

Through this partnership, Langsa City seeks to develop an environmental services-based economy while unlocking the potential for carbon financing (such as carbon credits) as a source of local green economy.

2. Establishment of the Pentahelix Technical Team

In July 2024, a technical team for carbon utilization was established, involving various stakeholders (government, regionally-owned enterprises, communities, and the environmental sector). This team focuses on MRV (Measurement, Reporting, Verification), legality, and the preparation of Mitigation Action Plan Documents (DRAM) for emission certification (SPEI).

Local community involvement—especially around mangrove forests—is key to creating a participatory and sustainable low-carbon economic system.

3. Carbon Trading Literacy at the Village Level
There is also a community service initiative in Sungai Lueng Village, where carbon trading literacy has been introduced to residents and the government for a year through a Training of Trainers (TOT) program.

The community has shown high enthusiasm and understanding of the economic opportunities of the mangrove ecosystem—marking the potential for establishing low-carbon villages as part of the local economy.

column15: As a council of governments and lead for the East Central Florida Regional Resilience Collaborative (R2C), we have developed, alongside an established Technical Advisory Committee, a regional-scale greenhouse gas inventory, science-based target, and high impact actions analysis providing a framework for action to accelerate emissions reduction across the region. As GCoM members, the Council agreed to complete an inventory every three years establishing structure and momentum, then requested the development of the region's first climate action plan laying out pathways to increase collective impact and achieve the SBT. Due to CPRG federal funding, the R2C has expanded the 2019 and 2022 inventories to include additional sectors like agriculture and land use/land cover, providing additional sector engagement for emissions reduction action. Currently, the R2C is in the process of redoing the 2019 high impact actions with updated strategies as we develop a climate action plan for the region. Already completed under the EPA CPRG program is a Priority Climate Action Plan, with the Comprehensive Climate Action Plan due to the EPA by the end of 2025. \nThe regional integrated Climate Action Plan will include emission-reducing actions, a mitigation and adaptation strategy, as well as a climate-informed conservation strategy, and upon completion will be considered for adoption by the East Central Florida Regional Planning Council (ECFRPC) Board and operationalized by our partners across east central Florida.
column16:
The impacts our local jurisdictions experience from shocks and stressors are exacerbated by climate change. This acknowledgment has yielded the establishment of the Regional Resilience Collaborative and its advisory committees, the development of a Strategic Resilience Action Plan (SRAP), the development of the first East Central Florida region-wide greenhouse gas inventory (2019), the establishment of a regional absolute Science-Based Target (SBT) of 54.3% emissions reduction by 2030, and a high impact action analysis to identify region-specific actions to work toward the SBT. The culmination of this work has led to the acknowledgment and acceptance of a Regional Climate Action Plan development in the following year. 
Because of the volatility of climate-related discussion, the R2C has engaged local jurisdictions through a number of departments in each of our 8 counties to spur action from various vernaculars. We worked with emergency management directors to produce a new definition of risk in the region that takes into account not only social vulnerabilities but climate sensitivities. In this expansion, we incorporated Department of Health data that considered human impacts to hazards like heat in a new way. Subsequently, heat as a hazard ranked #2 and cooling centers were deployed upon the discussion of results. The baseline data for the spatial organization of the regional risk assessment is being worked into government required plans like the Comprehensive Emergency Management Plan, Local Mitigation Strategy, as well as informing planning and development decisions with empirically organized data.
As another example, the R2C is leading efforts in each county to develop and/or update conservation strategies through the use of the Marxan model which allows local participants to prioritize natural layers and identify pathways to conserve or preserve the environment. Common themes across the region have led to conversation and the development of a biodiversity framework that remains in progress to this day. 
As a result, all of this work will serve the R2C to build resilience through a 'people, places, and prosperity' lens by reducing risks, vulnerabilities, and the region's carbon footprint and increasing sustainability goals across the region.
column17: The changing climate is certainly having an impact on every jurisdiction and resident in the State of Florida. Insurance in the state is quickly becoming the \'income tax\' replacement burden as insurance rates are ever rising for governments and the public. \nRecognizing these concerns, the State of Florida passed \'resilient Florida\' legislation that provides a funding mechanism to conduct vulnerability assessments on defined critical assets in relevance to flooding related impacts. Funding is also available for implementation efforts to mitigate the identified vulnerabilities. This funding is aimed to spur flood adaptation and mitigation planning and action (emissions reduction may be a co-benefit) . \nThe funding available at the federal level for emissions reducing related work has also increased the region's ability to focus climate efforts and projects across the region. Providing a framework for action and the appropriate discussion around activities like reducing VMT, alternative fuels and electric vehicles, as well as redundancy around energy and solar deployment is spurring additional action from multiple sectors within the region and economy.
column18: Jurisdictions in the East Central Florida Region have been working to incorporate low-carbon energy and transportation alternatives into their practices and operations. Moreover, fossil fuel industries do not drive our regional economy; in fact, our region's innovation clusters include wind turbines and other opportunities for greener manufacturing growth in our metro areas. \nOur port is incorporating infrastructure to support LNG demands alongside the space industry which has an ever increasing demand for natural gas equivalents to propel rockets into space. As the private space businesses continue to adapt new technologies and reuse rocket parts, our policy requires continual refinement.

Climate-related issues are beginning to shape New Glasgow's land-use and development planning, mainly through the Town's climate plans and related provincial funding:

Council has adopted a Corporate Climate Action Plan (2020-2025) and a Community Climate Action Plan (2022-2030) with sectors that include “Policy, Planning & Procedures” and “Collaboration, Adaptation & Resilience,” which are used to guide staff advice on development and infrastructure decisions. 

Provincial funding awarded in 2025 explicitly supports New Glasgow to “integrate policy and land-use planning into a new community climate action plan” and to support equity-focused resilience measures, formalizing the link between climate action and planning practice. 


In partnership with neighbouring municipalities, source-water protection (e.g., development limits and buffers in the Forbes Lake watershed, which supplies New Glasgow's drinking water) is being addressed through land-use controls, reflecting climate- and water-security concerns in planning policy.
column17:
Climate change influences New Glasgow's financial planning mainly through targeted capital projects and external climate funding:

The corporate and community climate action plans set formal GHG reduction targets (15% below 2018 levels by 2025 and 30% by 2030 corporately; 50% below 2018 levels by 2030 community-wide), which require investment in building efficiency, fleet transition, renewable energy and policy changes. These needs are now part of multi-year capital and operating discussions. 


The Town accesses provincial and federal climate funding (e.g., recent Nova Scotia funding to implement the corporate climate action plan and integrate land-use planning with the community climate plan), so project timing and scope are partially shaped by grant opportunities and reporting requirements. 

Emerging projects such as district energy and deep building retrofits (through programs like FCM/GMF, CEF, etc., which you've referenced in your work) require lifecycle costing, risk assessment and staff time that are now explicitly recognized in financial planning and budget submissions.
column18:
New Glasgow has identified several potential transition risks as Nova Scotia and Canada move toward a low-carbon economy:

Capital and fiscal risk: Significant upfront investment is required to meet our corporate and community GHG targets (building retrofits, fleet decarbonization, potential district energy). Without sustained external funding, these costs could strain a small-town tax base. 


Policy and regulatory risk: Changes to provincial energy policy, carbon pricing, and building/vehicle standards could increase short-term costs for municipal operations and local businesses before low-carbon options are fully deployed.

Social and equity risk: Energy-price changes and fuel-switching may disproportionately impact low-income and energy-insecure residents; New Glasgow's participation in equity-focused climate programs reflects awareness of this risk. 

Capacity and supply-chain risk: As a smaller municipality, New Glasgow has limited internal staff capacity and depends on external consultants and contractors; workforce or supply constraints in low-carbon technologies could delay implementation and increase costs.

Sector-specific risk (e.g., biomass/forestry, transportation): Transition pathways such as bioenergy or expanded transit must be managed carefully to avoid exposure to fuel-supply volatility or operating-funding risk.

column16: En la comuna de San Bernardo, los asuntos vinculados al cambio climático han generado un impacto profundo en la planificación comunal, obligando a replantear prioridades y estrategias. La Ley Marco de Cambio Climático (Ley 21.455) estableció como mandato que cada municipio elaborara su Plan de Acción Comunal de Cambio Climático (PACCC), el cual se transformó en un instrumento clave de gestión local. El PACCC de San Bernardo (2025) identifica vulnerabilidades críticas asociadas a la disminución de precipitaciones, olas de calor, riesgos de inundación y pérdida de biodiversidad, y define medidas de adaptación y mitigación.\n\nEste instrumento, además, se articula con la actualización del PLADECO 2024, que integra la sostenibilidad y la resiliencia territorial como ejes transversales de desarrollo, y con la Estrategia Hídrica Local 2024-2034, que aborda la seguridad hídrica como desafío prioritario. Gracias a estos instrumentos, San Bernardo avanza hacia una planificación comunal que no se limita al ordenamiento territorial o al crecimiento económico, sino que incorpora la gestión climática como eje estructurante, vinculando proyectos de reforestación con especies nativas, eficiencia hídrica en áreas verdes, rehabilitación de acequias patrimoniales, programas de educación ambiental

Regulatory and policy risks include the possibility for regional, state, or federal requirements outpacing local capacity, requiring accelerated timelines for implementation. column16: Flooding: Dhaka is vulnerable to severe flooding due to its low-lying geography, inadequate drainage systems, and heavy monsoon rains. Flooding disrupts transportation, damages infrastructure, and affects livelihoods. In response, the city's master development plans have had to incorporate measures for improved urban drainage and flood management systems, such as building resilient infrastructure, elevating roads, and creating water retention areas. Major affected areas are ward number 52,53,60,61,62,65,66,67,68,75Water Scarcity: Despite being prone to flooding, Dhaka also faces water scarcity issues during dry periods. This has necessitated the implementation of water conservation measures, improved water supply systems, and the promotion of rainwater harvesting in the city's development planning.Heat Island Effect: The urban heat island effect in Dhaka is exacerbated by rapid urbanization, deforestation, and increased concrete and asphalt surfaces. As a result, the city experiences higher temperatures than surrounding rural areas. To combat this, Dhaka's master planning has started incorporating green spaces, parks, and tree planting initiatives to mitigate the heat island effect and enhance the city's climate resilience. Major infected wards are 1,3,14,15,19,20,55,56,57,63,64,67,68,69,70,74,75 Although Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakkha (RAJUK) is the responsible government entity for developing the Master Plan for the entire Dhaka city and regulating development control, DSCC plays a significant role in implementing the master plans. Recently, DSCC has recognized the importance of incorporating climate impacts into sector-wise development strategies. The following climate-related considerations have been identified:•The increasing risks of flooding, storm surges, and heatwaves due to climate change necessitate infrastructure upgrades and modifications for enhanced resilience and adaptability.•Rapid urbanization and extensive concrete surfaces in dense areas contribute to the urban heat island effect, resulting in higher temperatures. To combat this, DSCC is actively working on initiatives to increase green spaces and promote tree planting.•RAJUK's master plan has taken into account changes in rainfall patterns, and local policies have been developed to address sustainable drainage systems, rainwater harvesting, and flood management.•Proper regulation of designated land use is crucial to avoid vulnerable areas and protect sensitive ecosystems from potential climate impacts.•DSCC recognizes the importance of measuring social equity and building resilience among marginalized populations. Collaborative efforts involving DSCC and I/NGOs are underway in this sector to ensure inclusive and equitable development.

The Council will set policy direction in climate change mitigation and adaptation strategies and actions, driving green economic growth and catalyzing green technology and low-carbon growth at all levels. National Policy on Climate Change is also being drafted. Various other policy documents are in place to guide such as National Low Carbon Cities Masterplan; Green Technology Master Plan Malaysia 2017-2030; Low Carbon Cities Framework etc.Low Carbon has been embedded in Johor State and Local Authority policy. The Johor State government is committed to promoting sustainable development with the launching of the Johor Sustainable Development Plan (PPMJ) 2030. Low Carbon elements were incorporated in the plan where specifically mentioned sustainable and low carbon mobility. The Johor Structure Plan (RSN) 2030 is to mainstream State Sustainability through low-carbon communities and disaster resistance. The State Government through Johor State Council Meeting in 2016 has endorsed the implementation of LCSBPIM and LCS Action Plan implementation. In pursuing this vision, Segamat City needs to focus on a balance of economic growth, social progress, and environmental protection, as well as reducing the impact of climate change. Presently, Segamat City is also very exposed and vulnerable to climate risks such as floods, extreme precipitation, and dengue. Tackling these issues without a strategic planning document designed to address them would potentially result in the waste of valuable resources. As such, Segamat City started out by producing the Segamat Low Carbon Society Action Plan 2030 (SLCSAP2030) in 2018, a document that focuses on climate mitigation through the involvement of government agencies, the commercial and corporate sectors, as well as the people who reside within the municipality. Prior to the completion of the document, projects and programs undertaken by Segamat Municipal Council did not take climate issues into consideration. The SLCSAP2030 guides departments within the municipality as well as those within the municipality to take climate issues into account when planning their projects. Global warming is one aspect that was given the most attention, as agencies within the municipality have embraced the idea that reducing energy consumption can help tackle climate change issues. En nuestro territorio, los efectos del cambio climático, como las recientes olas de calor e inundaciones, han convertido la gestión climática en una prioridad municipal. Para enfrentar este desafío, tanto el Concejo Municipal como las diversas direcciones están activamente involucradas, tomando decisiones basadas en datos e información que se gestionan internamente y se comparten con la comunidad.

La municipalidad juega un rol crucial en esta materia, no solo informando a los vecinos a través de distintos medios, sino también proporcionando datos esenciales al gobierno central para el desarrollo de políticas públicas. Esta colaboración es fundamental para construir una respuesta integral y efectiva a nivel local y nacional.

Para potenciar esta labor, es clave enfocar los esfuerzos en tres áreas principales:

Mejorar la comunicación con la comunidad: Utilizar plataformas digitales, campañas informativas y talleres comunitarios para que los ciudadanos comprendan los datos y participen activamente en las iniciativas de mitigación y adaptación.

Fortalecer la toma de decisiones: Implementar sistemas de información geográfica (SIG) y herramientas de análisis de datos para identificar zonas de riesgo y planificar intervenciones estratégicas de infraestructura resiliente.

Optimizar la colaboración con el gobierno central: Establecer canales formales para el envío de reportes detallados y propuestas que reflejen las necesidades específicas de nuestro territorio, asegurando que la voz local sea considerada en la formulación de políticas climáticas a gran escala.
column16:
En la comuna de Quilicura, el impacto del cambio climático ha transformado significativamente la planificación municipal, impulsando una revisión profunda de sus políticas y proyectos. Las problemáticas ambientales derivadas de las variaciones climáticas han obligado a la municipalidad a replantear su desarrollo territorial, adoptando un enfoque más sólido en la sustentabilidad y la resiliencia ambiental.

Uno de los hitos más relevantes en esta nueva dirección es la actualización del Plan Regulador Comunal (PRC). Este proceso ha destacado por una activa participación ciudadana, que ha incorporado una perspectiva ambiental robusta. Tanto las autoridades como la comunidad comprenden la urgencia de conservar zonas de alto valor ecológico, como los humedales y cerros, considerándolos pilares fundamentales para mitigar los efectos del cambio climático.

En este contexto, la protección de áreas como el Humedal de Quilicura y los cerros de San Ignacio y Renca, se ha vuelto una prioridad. La evidencia científica demuestra que los humedales actúan como esponjas naturales, absorbiendo el exceso de agua durante las lluvias intensas y liberándola lentamente en periodos de sequía, lo que ayuda a prevenir inundaciones y a mantener el equilibrio hídrico. Además, la planificación urbana se está enfocando en la creación de nuevas áreas verdes con vegetación nativa y de bajo consumo hídrico, lo que fomenta la biodiversidad local y reduce la presión sobre los recursos hídricos.

El cambio climático también ha generado retrasos en diversos proyectos del territorio, ya que han tenido que ser modificados para integrar soluciones que aborden estas nuevas problemáticas. Para complementar estas medidas, se ha desarrollado un plan de fiscalización más robusto, especialmente dirigido al sector industrial, uno de los más grandes del país.

La concentración de industrias en Quilicura significa que una parte significativa de la contaminación y los problemas ambientales se originan en sus procesos productivos. Según datos del Ministerio del Medio Ambiente de Chile, la industria es uno de los principales emisores de gases de efecto invernadero y contaminantes atmosféricos. Ante este escenario, es crucial controlar y regular los procesos industriales para reducir su huella ecológica y mitigar sus impactos negativos en la calidad del aire y el agua de la comuna. La municipalidad está colaborando con las autoridades competentes para asegurar el cumplimiento de la normativa ambiental y promover la adopción de tecnologías más limpias y sostenibles por parte de las empresas.

En resumen, Quilicura está tomando medidas proactivas para enfrentar el cambio climático. A través de la actualización de su Plan Regulador Comunal, la conservación de sus ecosistemas clave y una fiscalización más estricta del sector industrial, la comuna busca no solo adaptarse a las nuevas condiciones climáticas, sino también convertirse en un modelo de desarrollo urbano sostenible y resiliente en la Región Metropolitana.
column17:
El cambio climático ha generado un aumento significativo en el presupuesto municipal de Quilicura, redefiniendo la planificación financiera con un enfoque en la sostenibilidad y la resiliencia. La municipalidad ha tenido que destinar considerables recursos a la mitigación y adaptación a los efectos climáticos, lo que ha modificado sustancialmente la distribución de sus fondos.

Este incremento de gastos se debe a varias necesidades urgentes:

Adquisición de Equipamiento y Tecnología: La municipalidad ha invertido en tecnologías avanzadas, como sistemas de monitoreo de la calidad del aire y del agua, y equipamiento para la gestión de residuos y la respuesta a emergencias climáticas, como inundaciones o sequías.

Contratación de Profesionales Especializados: Se ha requerido la incorporación de expertos en gestión ambiental, hidrología urbana y energías renovables, cuyos conocimientos son cruciales para la formulación e implementación de políticas y proyectos ambientales.

Desarrollo de Estudios y Proyectos: Se han destinado fondos para la realización de estudios de vulnerabilidad climática y para el diseño de proyectos de infraestructura verde, como la restauración de humedales y la creación de parques con especies nativas, que son más resistentes a las variaciones climáticas.

Redistribución Presupuestaria y Proyecciones a Futuro
Para cubrir estos nuevos gastos, la municipalidad ha tenido que redirigir recursos de otras áreas, priorizando las acciones climáticas. Este cambio en la asignación presupuestaria refleja la urgencia de proteger a la comunidad y el entorno natural.

Además de reajustar los presupuestos existentes, la comuna ha debido considerar un aumento en la asignación de recursos para futuras actividades. Esto incluye el financiamiento de programas de educación ambiental y la entrega de apoyo directo a las comunidades más afectadas por fenómenos como las olas de calor o las inundaciones.

En conclusión, la planificación financiera de Quilicura ha evolucionado para enfrentar los desafíos del cambio climático, demostrando un compromiso con la protección del medio ambiente y el bienestar de sus habitantes. Estos ajustes presupuestarios no son solo un gasto, sino una inversión estratégica a largo plazo para asegurar un futuro más sostenible y seguro para la comuna.
column18:
Quilicura, según estudios del gobierno central, presenta un alto índice de vulnerabilidad económica dentro de la Región Metropolitana. Esta realidad financiera implica que gran parte del presupuesto municipal se destina a cubrir servicios de primera necesidad para sus habitantes, lo que a menudo ralentiza el desarrollo de proyectos ambientales a gran escala. A pesar de estas limitaciones, la transición hacia una comuna más sostenible avanza, impulsada por políticas de Estado y colaboraciones estratégicas.

Un claro ejemplo de este avance es la reciente integración de la electromovilidad en el transporte público local. El pasado mes de agosto de 2025, se anunció la llegada de 100 buses eléctricos para el servicio de transporte en Quilicura. Esta medida representa un paso significativo hacia la reducción de la huella de carbono de la comuna, al disminuir considerablemente la emisión de CO2 y otros contaminantes atmosféricos.

Esta iniciativa no solo beneficia el medio ambiente, sino que también mejora la calidad de vida de los residentes al ofrecer un transporte más limpio y silencioso. La incorporación de estos vehículos eléctricos es parte de un esfuerzo mayor a nivel nacional para modernizar el sistema de transporte público, demostrando que, incluso con desafíos económicos, es posible implementar políticas ambientales de gran impacto con el apoyo del gobierno central y otras instituciones.

Since November 2022, climate change has been the top risk on the Council's Corporate Risk Register. The Register highlights the consequences of failing to meet key targets: carbon neutrality for Council operations by 2030, for the region by 2034, and net negative emissions by 2040. Risks include increased extreme weather impacts, unmet public expectations, and missed energy-saving opportunities.
To address this, all formal decisions must undergo a Climate Change Impact Assessment (CCIA), to evaluate environmental impacts and support the Council's climate change goals.

The elected Executive Member for Managing our Environment, oversees services related to natural capital, carbon reduction, biodiversity, waste, and environmental health, and represents these areas at full Council.

The Transport, Economy, Environment and Enterprise Overview and Scrutiny Committee reviews climate strategy, sustainable development, and environmental management. It monitors Strategy progress biannually and reports annually to the Executive.

The Strategy is refreshed every two years to reflect new data and technologies .

The Beyond Carbon Board, comprising senior officers, oversees operational carbon reduction and the Climate Change Strategy. It also allocates funding for net zero projects. Operational Groups may be formed to drive delivery in key sectors like transport and housing, often in partnership with external bodies to avoid duplication.

Public, private, and voluntary sector stakeholders are regularly engaged to support progress on climate action.
column16:
The Local Development Scheme (LDS), adopted in February 2024, outlines the planning policy documents North Yorkshire Council will produce over the next four years. It supports the development of the new Local Plan, currently in early stages, with an Issues and Options consultation currently underway. The LDS is aligned with updates to the National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF).

Local Planning Authorities are legally required to address climate change through emissions reduction and resilience measures. Climate change is a key focus in the emerging Local Plan, and in the ongoing Selby Local Plan, and the Harrogate New Settlement DPD, which includes ambitious climate policies.

Until the new Local Plan is adopted, planning decisions rely on legacy Development Plans, unless significant material considerations - such as NPPF changes -apply. Annual Authority Monitoring Reports track progress and policy effectiveness.

The Local Plan is a major opportunity to embed climate action across the county. Climate change, alongside health and well-being, is a core theme. The Council is exploring how to integrate mitigation, adaptation, and nature resilience into planning, supported by evidence such as Local Area Energy Plans and landscape assessments for renewable energy. 

Key areas under review include reducing travel demand, promoting sustainable transport, energy-efficient building, water conservation, and retrofitting. Nature-based solutions will be supported through strategies like Biodiversity Net Gain, Local Nature Recovery, and a new Strategic Flood Risk Assessment, all contributing to a Green and Blue Infrastructure Strategy.
column17:
Amid ongoing budget pressures, the Council is focused on securing external funding to support climate initiatives. Current projects include those funded by the Mayoral Combined Authority's Net Zero Fund and Renewables Fund, with Council match funding.

A key area of focus is the decarbonisation of the Council's vehicle fleet. Whilst a number of electric vehicles have been introduced, a broader fleet decarbonisation strategy is being developed to guide future investment, balancing climate and financial considerations. EV charging infrastructure rollout is being delivered via the LEVI-funded project.
column18:
To oversee changes in regulation the Beyond Carbon Board, senior officers from the Council, ensure to keep abreast of climate change policy developments and work closely in partnership with regional bodies to continue developing crosscutting adaptation approaches. North Yorkshire Council will work with local suppliers through the developed procurement strategy framework to support businesses in their transition to a low carbon economy. The Council will also continue working with the Combined Authority to support new innovations in technology. This may include innovations such as the production of green hydrogen for transportation to ensure breakthroughs in sustainable technologies are explored.
North Yorkshire Council's Delivery Pathway, which is currently being developed, will ensure to support embedding low carbon initiatives into placemaking and regeneration programmes. It will also support businesses to adopt low carbon and circular economy practices, develop local supply chains to maximise the economic multiplier of our investment in climate change activities, and support local climate change skills development. This will include action through the Adult Education service and partnerships with the Combined Authority and colleges.

The Public Services Board (PSB) is a statutory strategic partnership established under the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015. The Act requires key local organisations in Powys to work together and take a more co-ordinated and long-term approach to the issues that really matter to the people of the county.

The Wellbeing Plan for Powys is a strategic document developed by the Powys Public Services Board (PSB) aimed at improving the wellbeing of residents across the county. It aligns with the Wellbeing of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015, which emphasizes the need for public bodies to work collaboratively towards long-term goals for social, economic, environmental, and cultural wellbeing.

Key Aspects of the Wellbeing Plan:
Vision and Objectives: The plan outlines a vision for a sustainable future, focusing on enhancing the quality of life for all residents. It includes objectives related to health, education, the economy, and the environment.

Collaboration and Partnerships: The PSB emphasizes collaborative efforts among various stakeholders, including local authorities, health boards, community organizations, and residents. This partnership approach is crucial for addressing complex challenges and implementing effective solutions.

Community Engagement: The Wellbeing Plan incorporates feedback and insights from local communities to ensure that the strategies reflect the needs and priorities of residents. This engagement is essential for fostering a sense of ownership and accountability within the community.

Monitoring and Evaluation: The plan includes mechanisms for monitoring progress and evaluating the effectiveness of the initiatives undertaken. Regular assessments help identify areas for improvement and ensure that the objectives are being met.

Focus on Climate and Sustainability: Recognizing the impact of climate change, the Wellbeing Plan integrates environmental considerations into all aspects of planning and decision-making. This includes promoting sustainable practices, enhancing biodiversity, and reducing carbon emissions.

In 2020, the Powys Public Services Board (PSB) declared a climate emergency in response to growing concerns about the impacts of climate change on local communities and ecosystems. This declaration underscored the urgency of addressing climate-related challenges and prompted the board to take decisive action towards sustainability and resilience.

Key Components of the Climate Action Plan for Powys:
Assessment of Emissions: The climate action plan involves a comprehensive assessment of the current greenhouse gas emissions in Powys. This includes identifying key sectors contributing to emissions and establishing baseline figures to track progress over time.

Climate Risk and Vulnerability Assessment: Understanding the key risks to people and nature for a changing climate across the region - using the CCRA3 risk categories. 

Setting Targets: The PSB aims to set ambitious yet achievable targets for reducing carbon emissions across various sectors, including transport, energy, and waste management. The goal aligns with the Welsh Government's commitment to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050.

Community Engagement: The development of the climate action plan emphasizes engaging with local communities, businesses, and stakeholders. This collaborative approach aims to gather insights, foster community ownership, and ensure that initiatives reflect the needs and priorities of residents.

Sustainable Practices: The plan promotes sustainable practices across all sectors, focusing on renewable energy, energy efficiency, sustainable land use, and high emitting sectors. This holistic approach not only addresses climate change but also enhances the overall well-being of Powys.

Monitoring and Reporting: An essential aspect of the climate action plan is the establishment of monitoring mechanisms to assess progress and report outcomes. Regular updates help track the effectiveness of initiatives and facilitate adaptive management. Part of this will include reporting to CDP annually.

Transitioning to a low-carbon economy presents several risks to Powys, which need to be carefully managed to ensure a sustainable future. These risks include:

Economic Disruption: As industries shift away from fossil fuels and high carbon industries, there may be short-term job losses or disruption in traditional sectors, such as farming. This transition could lead to economic challenges, particularly in areas heavily reliant on these industries.

Social Inequality: The transition may disproportionately affect vulnerable communities that lack the resources to adapt. If not managed carefully, this could exacerbate social inequalities, leading to increased energy poverty and access issues.

Public Resistance and Change Management: There may be resistance from the public and local businesses to adopt low-carbon practices, particularly if these changes are perceived as disruptive or costly. Effective communication and engagement strategies will be essential to foster acceptance and collaboration.

Investment Risks: The public sector is increasingly embedding sustainability and low-carbon initiatives into its practices. Yet the constrained land-scape of the public sector means long-term financial funding for these projects puts them at risk.

Using renewable energy sources (RES), such as solar, wind, hydroelectric power, and biofuels.

Developing and deploying clean energy technologies that replace fossil fuels.

Electrification of transportation and replacing fossil fuels with electrical energy.

Improving industrial processes to reduce emissions.

Implementing regulatory measures and financial tools such as carbon taxes and emissions trading systems to reflect the social cost of emissions.

Gradually phasing out fossil fuels and replacing them with non-fossil energy sources, ensuring supply security and technological progress.

a) Fluctuations of external energy prices (natural gas, oil) that affect electricity prices regardless of the transition and possible increases in production costs, thus undermining competitiveness of private sector and leading to price increases of products and services in the short and medium term.

b) Possible lack or scarcity of the huge financial resources needed to fund the green transition due to changing political priorities at EU and national level.

c) diminishing public support and lower acceptance rates to green transition due to the extensive adjustments needed in consumption patterns and everyday lives of citizens and households.

Riesgos para la jurisdicción en la transición a una economía baja en carbono

1. Normativos

 * Adaptación a nuevas normativas nacionales y regionales que promuevan la descarbonización (p. ej., estándares de eficiencia energética, restricciones de emisiones, obligaciones de gestión de residuos).
 * Posible aumento de costos para cumplir con regulaciones más estrictas, especialmente en infraestructura municipal, transporte y alumbrado público.

2. Tecnológicos

 * Necesidad de renovar o adaptar infraestructura y equipamiento municipal para tecnologías más limpias (vehículos eléctricos, eficiencia energética en edificios públicos, sistemas de energías renovables).
 * Riesgo de rezago si la comuna no logra acceder a financiamiento o capacitación para adoptar nuevas tecnologías.

3. Legales

 * Eventual exposición a litigios o sanciones si no se cumplen futuras obligaciones climáticas o de sostenibilidad establecidas por ley.

4. De mercado

 * Cambios en la demanda de bienes y servicios (p. ej., mayor preferencia por proveedores con certificaciones ambientales, exigencias de compras públicas sostenibles).
 * Posibles incrementos en el precio de insumos (energía, combustibles fósiles) a medida que se apliquen impuestos verdes o restricciones.

5. Reputacionales

 * Pérdida de confianza ciudadana o de acceso a financiamiento si la comuna no demuestra avances en la transición a una economía baja en carbono.
 * Impacto negativo en el posicionamiento turístico si Frutillar no mantiene estándares ambientales alineados con sus atributos de ciudad cultural y natural.

Policy and Regulatory Risks: The Compliance challenges for local businesses in meeting stricter low-carbon regulations and Potential resistance from stakeholders affected by new policies or stricter enforcement measures. 

*Citizen
In the transition to a low-carbon economy, there is a significant risk that less fortunate citizens may be left behind, particularly those who rely on traditional livelihoods and lack access to new opportunities.

*Transportation
The transition to electric vehicles in public transportation may lead to fare increases due to high upfront costs of e-vehicles, charging infrastructure, and maintenance. While this move supports emission reduction goals, it risks making transportation less affordable, especially for low-income commuters who are most dependent on public transit.

*Political
There is a political risk that some stakeholders may resist or disagree with policy shifts, potentially leading to conflicts, delays, or weakened implementation. Competing interests—such as those of industries reliant on fossil fuels, transport operators, or communities concerned about economic impacts—may create opposition.

*Financial
The City Government of Butuan may face financial stress due to the significant costs of adopting green technologies, upgrading infrastructure, and implementing climate-resilient programs.

Despite these challenges, the City is addressing these risks through capacity-building programs, stakeholder engagement, and the gradual integration of low-carbon strategies in its Comprehensive Development Plan (CDP) and investment programming.
