column15: En el PDOT 2023 - 2027 del Cantón Otavalo, tiene como eje transversal la adopción de medidas de mitigación y adopción frente al cambio climático, para lo cual se establecen acciones concretas como la resiliencia social y económica, sostenibilidad a largo plazo, el cumplimiento de compromisos internacionales. El PDOT es de cumplimiento para la administración y a su vez este se alinea con el POA institucional, lo que garantiza la asignación presupuetaria para planes y/o proyectos que se ejecuten en esta línea.\nA partir de ellos se considera dentro de todas aquellas obras, consultorías o demás acciones que involucren la adhesión de recursos económicos el análisis de sostenibilidad ambiental, esto con la finalidad de que se incorporen acciones que permitan a las obras de infraestructura u otras, presentar medidas de adaptación y mitigación al cambio climático.
column16:
A partir del Plan de Gobierno 'Otavalo para todos, Otavalo para el Mundo', se ha buscado la alineación con los Objetivos de Desarrollo Sostenible (ODS), así como con el PDOT 2023-2027; con ello se ha logrado incluir el concepto de cambio climático como una meta de gobierno local, de manera específica el eje 5 del Plan de Gobierno denominado 'Otavalo Verde, Limpio y Sano', cuya meta es: 'Crear mecanismos para una ciudad verde, con la promoción del uso de tecnologías limpias, acciones para descontaminar nuestros ríos, quebradas y vertientes, construir colectores de aguas servidas, plantas de tratamiento, mejorar el alcantarillado, construir centros de reciclaje y generar campañas de sensibilización con la acción juvenil'.

En coherencia con este eje, se han establecido actividades concretas orientadas a fortalecer la resiliencia climática y reducir la huella ecológica del cantón, entre ellas: 'control de la contaminación, como la promoción del uso de tecnologías limpias e implementación de prácticas de producción y consumo; mitigar los efectos del cambio climático, impulsando procesos de reforestación; impulso a la transición energética en Otavalo con la promoción de energías verdes, como la energía eólica y/o energía solar, buscando la articulación estratégica necesarias para implementar los mecanismos de captación de estas energías; y, la implementación de un modelo de gestión de residuos sólidos y tratamiento eficiente, basado en la reducción, reutilización y reciclaje'.

De manera complementaria, el PDOT vigente incorpora dentro de su modelo deseado la agenda ambiental y de control del cambio climático del cantón Otavalo, en estrecha vinculación con la gestión de riesgos. Este enfoque reconoce la importancia de la participación activa de comunidades, barrios y actores sociales en el diseño e implementación de acciones climáticas, promoviendo procesos de corresponsabilidad ciudadana.

Para garantizar la efectividad de estas metas, resulta indispensable que el gobierno local consolide políticas públicas claras, medibles y evaluables, que permitan normar y regular la gestión ambiental de manera integral. Esto implica no solo establecer marcos normativos, sino también generar instrumentos de monitoreo, indicadores de impacto y mecanismos de financiamiento que aseguren la sostenibilidad de las acciones en el tiempo. Asimismo, se requiere la articulación interinstitucional con organismos provinciales, nacionales e internacionales, a fin de aprovechar experiencias, recursos y cooperación técnica orientada al cumplimiento de los compromisos globales en materia de cambio climático.
column17:
En el cantón Otavalo, los efectos del cambio climático han incidido directamente en la planificación financiera institucional, obligando a redirigir recursos y diseñar mecanismos de gestión que garanticen respuestas oportunas y sostenibles. En este marco, se destinó un presupuesto de $18.332,00 para la contratación de servicios profesionales locales, priorizando tanto la optimización del gasto público como el fortalecimiento de las capacidades técnicas del territorio. Esta inversión busca garantizar que la planificación presupuestaria esté en concordancia con los objetivos de mitigación y adaptación al cambio climático, incorporando criterios de eficiencia y sostenibilidad en el uso de los recursos públicos.

El impacto climático ha motivado la elaboración e implementación del Plan de Educación Ambiental Cantonal, orientado a generar conciencia y participación ciudadana frente a los retos ambientales. Asimismo, se financia la construcción de un proyecto de ordenanza sobre descontaminación de ríos, quebradas y vertientes, concebido como un instrumento de política pública que responde a la necesidad de proteger los ecosistemas hídricos, cada vez más vulnerables por variaciones climáticas y presiones antrópicas.

De manera complementaria, se ha considerado la realización de un diagnóstico de buenas prácticas ambientales que permitirá establecer una línea base para evaluar la gestión institucional en temas como manejo de residuos, eficiencia energética, uso sostenible de recursos naturales y cumplimiento de la normativa ambiental. A partir de este diagnóstico, se prevé un cronograma de implementación y un plan de capacitaciones para el personal administrativo y operativo, lo que permitirá institucionalizar una cultura ambiental y fortalecer la resiliencia de la administración pública local.

Estas acciones reflejan cómo el cambio climático no solo constituye un desafío ambiental, sino también financiero y administrativo, en tanto demanda la priorización de partidas presupuestarias específicas, la optimización de recursos disponibles y la incorporación de nuevos enfoques de gestión que aseguren la sostenibilidad a largo plazo. Con ello, se busca garantizar que cada inversión pública tenga un efecto multiplicador en la protección del ambiente, la calidad de vida de la ciudadanía y la adaptación de Otavalo frente a los riesgos climáticos.
column18: El GAD Municipal del Cantón Otavalo enfrenta un alto riesgo financiero asociado principalmente a sus activos vinculados a combustibles fósiles, como maquinaria, equipos y vehículos utilizados en la prestación de servicios municipales. La transición de estos activos hacia tecnologías más limpias y energías renovables representa un desafío complejo, que no solo es político sino también financiero. Aunque el GAD cuenta con fondos propios para operar, su capacidad de inversión se encuentra limitada por una dependencia significativa de los desembolsos estatales, los cuales no siempre son suficientes para cubrir la totalidad de los servicios públicos, obras de infraestructura y programas requeridos por la ciudadanía otavaleña. Esta situación genera tensión entre la necesidad de modernizar y descarbonizar los recursos del municipio y las restricciones presupuestarias que podrían limitar la ejecución de proyectos estratégicos para la mitigación del cambio climático.\n\nParalelamente, el GAD se enfrenta a un riesgo normativo y social, ya que, si bien tiene competencia para desarrollar regulaciones locales orientadas a la sostenibilidad y a la reducción de emisiones, la población mantiene prácticas arraigadas en sectores como la construcción, la agricultura, el transporte y otras actividades económicas tradicionales. Esta resistencia al cambio puede traducirse en impactos políticos, generando dificultades para implementar políticas ambientales, mantener la legitimidad institucional y garantizar la continuidad de medidas de mitigación a largo plazo. En este sentido, la gestión municipal requiere no solo diseñar normas técnicamente sólidas, sino también fortalecer la educación ambiental, la sensibilización ciudadana y la participación comunitaria, de modo que las iniciativas de transición hacia una economía baja en carbono sean percibidas como beneficiosas y no como una imposición.

The City of Balanga has institutionalized oversight of climate-related issues through a governance framework that integrates its Climate and Disaster Risk Assessment (CDRA), Comprehensive Land Use Plan (CLUP), Local Climate Change Action Plan (LCCAP), and Disaster Risk Reduction and Management (DRRM) Plan. Oversight is led by the City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (CDRRMC), with technical and policy support from the City Planning and Development Office (CPDO). In line with RA 10121, the City earmarks at least five percent of its annual income for the DRRM Fund (DRRMF), which finances risk reduction, preparedness, response, and rehabilitation initiatives. Fiscal planning systematically applies hazard maps, vulnerability assessments, and climate impact analyses to guide investment programming, thereby ensuring that allocations for infrastructure, housing, agriculture, fisheries, and health services are climate-informed and resilient.

This oversight framework is directly aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). For instance, SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) and SDG 13 (Climate Action) are advanced through resilient infrastructure investments and mainstreaming of climate adaptation in urban planning. SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) and SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being) are supported through climate-responsive agriculture, fisheries, and health systems, while SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation) and SDG 14 (Life Below Water) are addressed through watershed protection, flood control, and coastal management. Tracking of climate-tagged expenditures and DRRMF utilization strengthens accountability and aligns with SDG 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions).

Moreover, these oversight mechanisms are consistent with the City of Balanga's Vision 2030, which aspires to transform the locality into a “University Town” and a model of sustainable urban development. By embedding climate resilience and disaster preparedness into governance and fiscal management, the City safeguards its human capital, infrastructure, and economic drivers, ensuring that its long-term development goals are not derailed by climate risks. In this way, the City's oversight of climate-related issues serves as both a regulatory safeguard and a strategic enabler for achieving inclusive, knowledge-driven, and sustainable growth toward 2030.
column16:
The impact of climate change is evident in a perennial manner through extreme weather conditions, flooding, erosion, and the degradation of environmental structures. These phenomena disrupt the natural replenishment of resources and threaten biodiversity, ultimately affecting the foundational, economic, and social development sectors.

The availability of the Climate Disaster Risk Assessment (CDRA) has become an essential regulatory and measuring tool in guiding the City's development plans, particularly the Comprehensive Land Use Plan (CLUP), to ensure climate-responsive growth. This instrument provides a deeper understanding of the City's current landscape, generating science- and data-based solutions through Programs, Projects, and Activities (PPAs), as well as relevant policies tailored to community needs. These interventions strengthen the City's capacity to withstand climate impacts while establishing resilient and efficient platforms that serve the public.

Moreover, the CDRA raises awareness among various sectoral groups by presenting the realities of existing conditions and highlighting the impacts of climate-related events on their daily lives and engagements.
column17: Climate-related issues have significantly influenced the City of Balanga's financial planning. Intensifying hazards such as flooding, sea level rise, and stronger typhoons have required the City to allocate an increasing portion of its revenues to disaster risk reduction and management, with the DRRM Fund rising from ₱29.8 million in 2017 to ₱43.2 million in 2021. These climate pressures necessitate the realignment of funds toward relocation of vulnerable households, emergency response, and social protection measures, thereby reducing budgetary flexibility for other development initiatives. At the same time, projected impacts on agriculture, fisheries, and tourism pose risks to local revenue streams, requiring fiscal adjustments to compensate for potential losses. To address these challenges, the City has mainstreamed adaptation and resilience-building measures into its financial planning, ensuring that both annual appropriations and multi-year investment programs are risk-sensitive and responsive to the long-term effects of climate change.
column18:
The transition to a low-carbon economy presents several risks for the City of Balanga, particularly in terms of economic adjustment, fiscal stability, and social impacts. First, stricter national and global climate policies may increase compliance costs for industries, transport operators, and energy users within the City, potentially leading to higher operating expenses and reduced competitiveness. This can affect sectors such as manufacturing, construction, and transport, which remain dependent on fossil fuel-based energy. Second, the gradual shift toward renewable energy and energy-efficient technologies requires significant capital investments, which may strain both local businesses and household budgets. Without adequate financial support mechanisms, small enterprises and low-income households could face affordability challenges, creating equity concerns.

The City's revenue streams are also at risk, as carbon-intensive activities such as quarrying, transport services, and traditional energy consumption contribute to local income. Transitioning away from these sources may temporarily reduce tax collections and business permit revenues, necessitating fiscal realignment. In addition, workforce displacement is a concern, particularly for workers employed in energy-dependent and extractive industries. Skills upgrading, retraining, and social protection measures will be required to mitigate potential job losses and support livelihood transitions.

From a governance perspective, the need to upgrade infrastructure for renewable energy, expand public transport systems, and implement stricter environmental regulations places additional demands on local fiscal resources. These adjustments may divert funds from other development priorities if not matched with external financing and public-private partnerships.

Despite these risks, the transition is also an opportunity to align with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy), SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth), and SDG 13 (Climate Action). For the City of Balanga, managing these transition risks is crucial to achieving its Vision 2030 of becoming a knowledge-based, sustainable “University Town,” where economic competitiveness is balanced with environmental stewardship and social equity.

In the Philippines, climate governance is shaped by a blend of national policies and local responsibilities. The legal and institutional framework recognizes that while climate change is a global concern, its impacts are felt most acutely at the community level. For this reason, local government units (LGUs)—provinces, cities, municipalities, and barangays—are placed at the frontline of climate action, with their mandates anchored on both the Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160) and the Climate Change Act of 2009 (RA 9729, as amended).

The Local Government Code grants LGUs local autonomy in addressing environmental concerns, while still placing them under the general supervision of the President to ensure that actions remain within their prescribed powers. It also requires national agencies to coordinate with LGUs when implementing projects with environmental or ecological implications, emphasizing shared accountability. This creates an early framework for LGU participation in environmental governance that later became central to climate change planning.

With the passage of the Climate Change Act, oversight was further strengthened through the creation of the Climate Change Commission (CCC), the lead policy-making and coordinating body on climate issues. The law designates LGUs as frontline agencies for climate planning and implementation, requiring them to prepare Local Climate Change Action Plans (LCCAPs) that align with the National Climate Change Action Plan (NCCAP). LGUs must not only draft but also update these plans to reflect new vulnerabilities and risks, ensuring that adaptation and mitigation measures remain responsive to changing conditions. To institutionalize these commitments, LGUs are obligated to mobilize personnel, finances, and other resources—often sourced from their Internal Revenue Allotment—to carry out local climate actions.

National oversight does not stop at policy alignment. Agencies such as the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) provide technical guidance and training, while the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) enforces financial accountability through Climate Change Expenditure Tagging (CCET), requiring LGUs to tag climate programs in their Annual Investment Plans. This mechanism ensures that climate-related projects are properly funded and visible in budget allocations. At the same time, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) provides scientific data, risk assessments, and environmental enforcement, helping LGUs ground their climate planning in evidence.

Beyond these national-local linkages, legislative oversight is exercised through the Joint Congressional Oversight Committee on climate change, which monitors the implementation of the Climate Change Act and related programs. At the local level, barangays are required to be directly engaged in planning and implementing adaptation strategies, ensuring grassroots participation. Community involvement is reinforced by mandatory public consultations and sanggunian (council) approval for projects with environmental impacts, strengthening democratic accountability.

Oversight also takes the form of performance evaluation. Through the Seal of Good Local Governance (SGLG), LGUs are assessed on their compliance with governance and environmental criteria, including climate-related safeguards such as solid waste management, wetlands protection, and green spaces. This creates both incentives and pressure for LGUs to meet higher standards in climate resilience.

Despite the well-designed oversight framework, challenges persist. Many LGUs lack the technical expertise to conduct vulnerability assessments or update climate action plans regularly. Financing, though mandated, remains uneven—some LGUs face difficulties in allocating sufficient resources for climate programs due to competing local priorities. Coordination gaps between LGUs and national agencies, as well as among LGUs themselves, further complicate implementation. Most importantly, the effectiveness of climate action often depends on the political will of local leaders, which varies significantly across jurisdictions.

At present, national agencies such as the CCC and DILG are pushing for stronger mainstreaming of climate considerations into all aspects of local governance—from land use and development planning to budgeting and disaster risk management. With climate change increasingly visible through extreme weather, flooding, and ecosystem loss, the oversight role of both national and local institutions is evolving from mere compliance to proactive risk management. LGUs are expected not only to follow regulations but also to innovate and integrate climate resilience into their development agendas.
column16:
The City of Carmona, like many urbanizing areas in the Philippines, faces the dual challenge of sustaining rapid development while addressing the growing threats of climate change. Once a municipality and now a city, Carmona has been experiencing steady economic growth, driven by industrial estates, housing projects, and commercial establishments. But with this growth comes increased pressure on land, water, and other natural resources—pressures made even more complex by the effects of a changing climate.

Climate-related issues such as flooding, heat stress, and waste management have already influenced how Carmona exercises its jurisdiction in development planning. As a local government unit (LGU), Carmona is legally mandated under the Climate Change Act of 2009 (RA 9729) and the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010 (RA 10121) to mainstream climate considerations into its local plans. This means its Comprehensive Land Use Plan (CLUP), Comprehensive Development Plan (CDP), and Annual Investment Plan (AIP) must all integrate climate change adaptation and disaster risk reduction measures.

One practical example is land use zoning. Carmona's planning authorities cannot simply designate land for housing or industrial use without considering flood risks. Areas identified as vulnerable to inundation or soil erosion, based on hazard maps and geoscience data, must be restricted from settlement or subject to stricter building codes. In this way, climate concerns directly reshape zoning decisions and, therefore, the city's physical development trajectory.

Budgeting has also been affected. Through Climate Change Expenditure Tagging (CCET), Carmona is required to identify and prioritize climate-related programs in its Annual Investment Plan. Instead of allocating all resources to conventional infrastructure, the city must now dedicate funds for projects such as flood control systems, renewable energy installations, tree planting programs, and ecological solid waste management. This reflects a jurisdictional shift: development planning is no longer only about economic expansion, but about building resilience against climate risks.

Carmona's solid waste management initiatives provide another illustration. The city has invested in composting technologies such as the Happy Soil Composter and DOST-assisted bioreactors. These initiatives not only address waste disposal issues but also reduce methane emissions, a potent greenhouse gas. Integrating waste management into the city's climate action framework demonstrates how environmental services now fall squarely within the broader scope of climate-sensitive development planning.

Community participation has likewise expanded. Barangays in Carmona are directly involved in identifying vulnerabilities—such as drainage problems, localized flooding, or lack of green spaces—that must be addressed in the Local Climate Change Action Plan (LCCAP). This participatory approach ensures that climate action is grounded in the lived experiences of residents, while also reinforcing the city's accountability to its constituents.

National oversight further shapes Carmona's jurisdiction. Agencies such as the Climate Change Commission (CCC) and the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) require submission of updated LCCAPs and evaluate performance under programs like the Seal of Good Local Governance (SGLG). For Carmona, compliance with these oversight mechanisms not only ensures access to technical and financial assistance but also strengthens its reputation as a progressive city that integrates climate resilience into its governance agenda.

Yet, challenges remain. As an emerging city, Carmona faces the tension of balancing industrial growth with environmental protection. Rapid urbanization increases energy demand, traffic congestion, and pollution—all of which intersect with climate concerns. Financing is also a constant hurdle, since climate-resilient infrastructure and adaptive programs often require significant investments. The political will of local leaders and the engagement of communities will continue to determine how effectively Carmona can translate its climate-related mandates into concrete development outcomes.

In essence, climate-related issues have expanded Carmona City's jurisdiction in development planning. From zoning to budgeting, infrastructure to waste management, and community participation to national oversight, the city must now plan its growth with a climate lens. Development decisions can no longer be detached from environmental realities; instead, climate resilience has become the guiding principle of local planning. Carmona's case illustrates how LGUs in the Philippines are evolving—not only as engines of growth but also as guardians of sustainability in an era of climate uncertainty.
column17:
Climate change has reshaped not only the development priorities of local government units (LGUs) in the Philippines but also their financial planning and allocation processes. For the City of Carmona, this shift is evident in how climate-related issues now directly influence budget decisions, investment priorities, and fiscal strategies.

Traditionally, LGU financial planning was driven by basic service delivery and infrastructure development. Budgets largely revolved around education, health, roads, and community facilities. However, with the legal mandates of the Climate Change Act of 2009 (RA 9729) and the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010 (RA 10121), Carmona, like all LGUs, is now required to mainstream climate change adaptation (CCA) and disaster risk reduction and management (DRRM) into its Annual Investment Plan (AIP). This institutional mandate expands Carmona's financial jurisdiction, obligating it to allocate resources for climate resilience alongside traditional expenditures.

A key mechanism shaping this is Climate Change Expenditure Tagging (CCET). Under this system, Carmona must identify which programs in its budget are climate-related and ensure that a share of its Internal Revenue Allotment (IRA, now the National Tax Allotment or NTA) supports adaptation and mitigation efforts. This means that financial planning can no longer ignore environmental risks. For example, instead of dedicating all infrastructure funds to road expansion or commercial development, Carmona has to earmark part of its budget for flood control projects, improved drainage systems, and sustainable urban greening.

Waste management provides a concrete illustration. Carmona's investments in technologies such as the Happy Soil Composter and DOST-assisted bioreactors required financial prioritization. While composting and biodegradable processing may not generate large revenues, the city allocates funds for them because they mitigate methane emissions and reduce landfill waste—an investment in long-term climate and environmental health. This redefines financial planning, making environmental value as important as economic return.

The city's budget is also shaped by climate-induced vulnerabilities. Recurrent flooding and the risk of heat stress have compelled Carmona to allocate more resources for disaster preparedness, health services, and climate-resilient infrastructure. Emergency response funds, previously seen as contingency allocations, are now integrated as regular budget items because climate impacts are no longer exceptional—they are recurring realities.

Moreover, performance-based incentives affect financial planning. The Seal of Good Local Governance (SGLG) includes environmental and climate-related criteria. For Carmona, aligning its budget to meet these standards is both a compliance requirement and a strategic move to access national recognition, grants, and technical assistance. Thus, financial planning is not only about internal allocation but also about leveraging external resources linked to climate-responsive governance.

However, challenges remain. Allocating sufficient funds for climate action often competes with the immediate demands of a growing city. Carmona's rapid urbanization drives demand for housing, roads, and utilities, which absorb significant budgetary resources. Balancing these with climate-oriented programs requires careful financial management and, above all, political will. Additionally, while CCET improves accountability, it can be complex for smaller LGU departments to implement, especially when technical expertise in climate finance is limited.

In summary, climate-related issues have significantly expanded Carmona City's jurisdiction in financial planning. From compulsory budget tagging to investment in climate-smart technologies, from recurrent allocations for disaster preparedness to the pursuit of performance-based incentives, climate change now directly shapes how the city prioritizes and spends its resources. Carmona's case demonstrates how LGU financial planning is evolving—shifting from a narrow focus on economic development to a broader agenda of resilience, sustainability, and adaptive capacity in the face of climate uncertainty.

The transition to a low-carbon economy presents both opportunities and risks for local government units (LGUs) in the Philippines, and Carmona City illustrates these challenges. As a growing urban-industrial hub in Cavite, Carmona derives much of its fiscal strength from manufacturing and other energy-intensive sectors. National and global climate commitments now require LGUs to pursue cleaner development, which creates pressure on cities like Carmona to balance environmental responsibility with economic stability.

One major risk lies in revenue generation. Carmona relies heavily on taxes and fees from industries that may face higher costs due to stricter energy efficiency and environmental standards. Businesses could reduce operations or relocate, leading to fiscal shortfalls that threaten the city's capacity to fund services and programs. At the same time, transitioning to a low-carbon pathway requires large capital investments in renewable energy systems, sustainable transport, waste management, and resilient infrastructure. Without sufficient access to climate finance, Carmona risks falling behind in meeting climate goals.

The social dimension also poses challenges. Carmona's workforce is tied to industries that may be disrupted by low-carbon policies. If workers lose jobs or need new skill sets, resistance to reforms could arise. The city will need to support retraining and livelihood programs to ensure a just transition. Institutional risks add another layer: Carmona's planning and budget offices must acquire technical expertise in climate finance and sustainable development, but capacity limitations could slow progress.

Political risks are equally pressing. Policies such as stricter zoning, higher compliance costs for businesses, or shifting funds from traditional projects to green initiatives may face opposition. Since Carmona's growth has long depended on industrial expansion, leaders must strike a balance between economic interests and climate commitments. Timing is also critical—moving too slowly risks locking the city into high-carbon infrastructure, while moving too quickly without preparation could strain finances and disrupt the local economy.

Despite these risks, Carmona has taken steps toward sustainability through ecological solid waste management, composting, and greening initiatives such as solar electrification, transition to LED lights, and utilization of electric vehicles. These efforts show its ability to integrate low-carbon practices into local governance. The challenge lies in scaling them while managing fiscal and social pressures. Carmona's case reflects the broader reality for Philippine LGUs: the transition to a low-carbon economy requires careful financial planning, strong political will, and institutional capacity. While the risks are significant, the long-term costs of inaction—climate vulnerability, economic stagnation, and social inequities—would be far greater.

The Island Garden City of Samal (IGaCoS) has established multiple layers of oversight to ensure that climate-related issues are addressed systematically in governance, planning, and implementation.

1. Policy and Planning Oversight

Climate considerations are embedded in the Comprehensive Land Use Plan (CLUP) and Comprehensive Development Plan (CDP) and mainstreamed into the Local Climate Change Action Plan (LCCAP 2022-2027 and other local development plans. These policy instruments provide the framework for incorporating mitigation and adaptation measures in sectors such as agriculture, fisheries, energy, infrastructure, and social services

Oversight also extends to alignment with national frameworks, such as the Climate Change Act of 2009 (RA 9729), the Philippine DRRM Act of 2010 (RA 10121), and the People's Survival Fund (RA 10174), ensuring that the LGU's climate actions are legally anchored and financially supported.

2. Institutional Oversight

The City Environment and Natural Resources Office (CENRO) serves as the lead agency in implementing climate programs, particularly those related to greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction, waste management, enforcing environmental ordinances, and ecosystem rehabilitation. 

The City Planning and Development Office (CPDO) ensures that climate change actions are integrated into development planning and land-use management.
The City Agriculture's office oversees the implementation of organic farming and establishment and monitoring of Marine Protected Areas (MPAs).

The City Public Order and Safety Office (CPOSO) oversees risk assessments, preparedness, and disaster response, ensuring climate adaptation is addressed at both city and barangay levels. 

Oversight is further supported by the City DRRM Council and Barangay DRRM Councils, which facilitate community-level monitoring and action.

3. Risk Management Oversight

The LCCAP identifies key hazards, such as sea level rise, storm surge, flooding, drought, and landslides, and outlines strategies for minimizing risks. Oversight mechanisms include multi-hazard early warning systems, end-to-end monitoring, and community-based disaster risk reduction approaches, ensuring active involvement of vulnerable groups.

4. Performance and Monitoring Oversight

The GHG Inventory (2022) serves as the primary baseline for monitoring emissions and setting performance targets. With 137,588.78 tCO2e recorded emissions and net emissions of 110,782 tCO2e, oversight mechanisms include tracking reductions through reforestation programs, tree planting targets (738,547 trees), and monitoring of energy consumption and waste management. 

5. Stakeholder and Community Oversight

IGaCoS adopts participatory oversight by involving civil society organizations (CSOs), people's organizations, NGOs, and private sector partners in planning, implementation, and monitoring.

Barangay-level enumerators and functionaries are mobilized during surveys and monitoring activities, building grassroots ownership of climate action

6. Financial Oversight

Budget allocations for climate programs are monitored through the Local Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Fund (LDRRMF), and the city is positioned to access external financing mechanisms like the People's Survival Fund for long-term adaptation projects.

Oversight includes ensuring that capital expenditures (e.g., climate-resilient infrastructure, renewable energy facilities, and resettlement sites) are screened for climate responsiveness.

In conclusion, the Island Garden City of Samal's oversight of climate-related issues is multi-tiered, integrating policies, institutions, risk management tools, performance monitoring, stakeholder engagement, and financial mechanisms to ensure that climate action is mainstreamed in governance.

Climate-related issues have significantly shaped the Island Garden City of Samal's (IGaCoS) Comprehensive Land Use Plan (CLUP), Comprehensive Development Plan (CDP), Local Climate Change Adaptation Plan (LCCAP), and other development priorities. 

Hazard mapping (sea level rise, storm surge, flooding, drought, landslides, and earthquake susceptibility) has influenced master/development planning. The city implements the following mitigation and adaptation measures to address different climate-related issues.

1. Land Use and Zoning Adjustments

Various hazards had influenced the city's zoning regulations. For example, coastal barangays like Villarica and Balet face restrictions or additional safeguards due to high exposure to sea level rise and storm surges.

Relocation and resettlement sites are being prioritized in safe zones, with operational utilities and facilities, to reduce risks for populations in danger-prone areas.

2. Infrastructure and Public Safety Planning

In compliance with Batas Pambansa 1096 or the 'Building Standard Code of the Philippines' and Green Building Code, the City Engineering Office strictly implements the law in the development planning that requires climate-resilient infrastructure standards (e.g., buildings designed to withstand a magnitude 7.2 earthquake and withstand climate hazards).

Further, designs for roads, drainage, and public facilities are future-proofed to accommodate the anticipated larger volume of stormwater, reducing vulnerability to flooding and coastal erosion.

3. Resource Management

Implementation of climate pressures on water supply and agriculture that integrate water sufficiency programs (rainwater catchment, watershed rehabilitation) and climate-resilient agriculture practices (distribution of drought-resistant crops, organic fertilizer, and aquaculture inputs) into its development strategy.

4. Ecosystem and Ecological-Based Planning

The LCCAP, Forest Land Use Plan (FLUP), Solid Waste Management Plan (SWMP), Integrated Coastal Resource Management Plan (ICRMP), Local Shelter Plan, Fisheries Code, and Tourism Plan include conservation and expansion of mangroves, seagrass beds, and coral reefs as natural buffers against climate hazards.

5. Governance and Financing

The LGU mainstream DRRM and CCA in local plans and access financing mechanisms such as the Local Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Fund (LDRRMF) and potentially the People's Survival Fund for long-term adaptation investments.

column18:
1. Economic Risks

The transition to a low-carbon economy may impose short-term economic adjustments for sectors heavily reliant on conventional energy and resource use. Tourism and fisheries, two of the city's main economic drivers, may face increased operational costs from the adoption of renewable energy, stricter environmental standards, and the phase-out of fossil fuel-dependent practices. Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) could encounter financial strain in meeting compliance requirements, particularly in waste management and energy efficiency upgrades. 

2. Infrastructure and Technology Risks

A shift to low-carbon systems requires new infrastructure and technologies, such as renewable energy facilities, sustainable transport systems, and improved solid waste management facilities. The upfront capital investments for these projects pose risks to the city's financial planning, especially if internal and external financing is insufficient. Limited technical capacity within the LGU and among local operators may also slow adoption of low-carbon technologies due to high cost of low-carbon technologies.

3. Social Risks

The transition may lead to social and livelihood disruptions. Households and communities dependent on fuel-based income activities, such as small-scale transport operators and traditional energy users, could experience challenges in adapting to renewable energy or low-emission technologies. Without adequate social safety nets or retraining programs, these groups risk being marginalized in the transition process.

4. Governance and Institutional Risks

Managing a transition to a low-carbon economy requires institutional strengthening and inter-agency coordination. The city must ensure that its policies are harmonized with national frameworks, including the Philippine Energy Plan and Climate Change Act mandates. Inadequate enforcement of ordinances or fragmented oversight could undermine the effectiveness of low-carbon strategies. Moreover, the lack of climate finance readiness could hinder access to funds intended for supporting low-carbon transitions.

5. Reputational Risks

As a tourism-oriented city, IGaCoS's reputation depends on being perceived as a clean, sustainable, and climate-resilient destination. Failure to effectively transition to low-carbon practices could affect investor confidence, tourism competitiveness, and partnerships with development organizations, potentially reducing revenue streams that support climate programs.


Despite the risks and challenges, the city has taken valuable steps for the transition to the low-carbon economy through the installation of 466 KW solar-powered energy at the new city hall site, formulation of policy on circular economy, implementation of Green Procurement through RA 12009 or the 'New Government Procurement Act', digitalization of government transactions, and enforcement of the Banning on single-use plastics.

column15: Karatay signed the Global Covenant of Mayors / GCoM (EU Climate & Energy Mayors' Covenant), signalling a formal municipal commitment to follow international climate goals and report on climate work. The municipality adopted a Sustainable Energy & Climate Action Plan (SECAP / Sürdürülebilir Enerji ve İklim Eylem Planı) — prepared with partners — which sets mitigation and adaptation measures and timeframe targets. The plan was put to the municipal council and adopted in mid-2025. Main instruments / oversight mechanisms. SECAP as the central oversight tool. The SECAP contains: a local greenhouse-gas inventory, climate risk & vulnerability analysis, prioritized mitigation and adaptation measures (short/medium/long term), cost and responsibility assignments, and monitoring indicators. The plan explicitly names responsible institutions (Karatay Municipality together with Konya Metropolitan Municipality and KOSKİ for many actions). The plan and related commitments were considered and approved at the municipal council level, which provides political oversight and formal adoption. Local departments (environment/energy/park & gardens/technical units) are identified as implementation leads for specific measures. Partnerships and external support. Karatay works with metropolitan bodies (Konya Büyükşehir, KOSKİ) and international programs / networks (EU-supported projects and MLGP4Climate-type initiatives) to obtain technical support, funding models, and monitoring tools. The municipality has taken part in stakeholder/SECAP workshops and international cooperation activities. Mitigation (cutting emissions): rooftop/solar energy promotion, energy efficiency measures for municipal buildings and street lighting, and planning measures to support low-carbon technologies. Karatay has publicly stated a target of moving toward a climate-neutral and climate-resilient district by 2050. Adaptation (reducing climate risk): measures include water management (rainwater harvesting, greywater reuse, use of treated wastewater for green spaces), urban greening, zoning rules to preserve wind paths/airflow, and heat-wave / drought resilience actions. These adaptation measures and their timeframes appear in the SECAP. Karatay runs zero-waste projects and waste collection/bring-center initiatives as part of local environmental policy, which complements mitigation by reducing emissions from waste. SECAP includes indicators and assigns responsible institutions for each measure; the GCoM and SECAP framework also implies periodic monitoring and reporting obligations (local GHG inventory updates, progress on measures). The municipality has also discussed digital tools for plan monitoring in the SECAP project descriptions. The SECAP ranks actions by cost and impact and lists potential responsible partners (local utilities, metropolitan institutions). Karatay has sought funding and technical models through national and EU-linked programs to finance solar, energy efficiency, and adaptation projects.

column17: The 2025 budget of Karatay Municipality is set at about 7 billion TL, with 73% of the budget allocated to investment-producing directorates (i.e., capital projects) — one of which is the Environmental Protection & Control Directorate. Key transition-risk categories for Karatay: 
1. Regulatory & policy risk: As European Commission mechanisms such as the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) come into effect, Turkish exporters—including those in Konya region—are exposed to additional costs if their production remains carbon-intensive. National policy may tighten: Turkey has pledged a net-zero target for 2053 and is reformulating its climate agenda. If municipal or regional sectors (industry, buildings, transport) do not keep pace, Karatay may face retrospective compliance costs or “stranded” assets.
2. Market & technology risk: If Karatay's economy (or its constituent firms) remains invested in carbon-intensive technologies or infrastructure (e.g., fossil‐fuel reliant) these could lose competitiveness or become non-viable. For example, the Turkey-wide risk analysis of coal/gas assets shows these can become uneconomical. 
3. Rapid technological change: If renewable energy, energy-efficiency or low-carbon technologies advance quickly, older investments may become obsolete (“stranded”). Karatay's municipal investments need to anticipate this.
4. Demand shift: If industries or households in the district shift demand (e.g., favour low-carbon construction, mobility, appliances), then businesses or real-estate in Karatay that rely on old models may suffer lower value.
5. Financial & investment risk: Municipal or private investments that do not account for transition risks may face higher costs or shorter lifespans. The national financial-sector study warns of uncertainties translating into economic/financial impacts. 
6. Social & employment risk: The transition can lead to job losses or economic dislocation in sectors bound to older, carbon-intensive activities. The literature notes that a “just transition” is needed to avoid negative socio-economic outcomes. In Karatay's region (agriculture, manufacturing, construction), if workers or firms are not prepared for low-carbon modes (e.g., energy-efficient building, renewable installations), there may be lag-effects, unemployment or skills mismatches.
7. Reputation & viability risk: If Karatay fails to align with broader climate/low-carbon goals, there may be reputational damage (for example, investment attractiveness may drop) or missed opportunities (green investment flows bypass the district). Businesses and municipal services in Karatay will increasingly be evaluated for their climate credentials; lagging behind could reduce access to finance, partnerships or grants.

A more focused overview of Ca Mau Province's oversight and actions regarding climate-related issues, which typically cover governance, policy frameworks, risk management, adaptation, and community engagement, is shown below:
1. Institutional Oversight & Governance Structures
•	The Department of Agriculture & Rural Development (DARD) and the Department of Natural Resources & Environment (DONRE) are key provincial agencies involved in climate policy implementation and coordination 
•	There is also a dedicated Office of Climate Change within DONRE supporting initiatives and policy formulation 
•	These institutions coordinate data collection, classification, and execution of local climate-related programs, often with involvement at the commune level 
2. Provincial Policies, Projects, and Adaptation Measures
•	Through Open Development Mekong data (collected and managed by DARD, DONRE, and the Office of Climate Change), the province catalogs policies on climate resilience—targeting coastal/marine communities with details on objectives, budgets, implementers, and administrative levels 
•	Key initiatives under projects such as the World Bank-funded Mekong Delta Integrated Climate Resilience and Sustainable Livelihoods (ICRSL) subproject include construction of infrastructure for:
o	Preventing coastal erosion
o	Supplying freshwater to reduce harmful groundwater extraction
o	Mangrove ecosystem restoration coupled with sustainable livelihoods (e.g., ecologically-certified shrimp farming under forest canopy) 
3. Climate Risks & Scientific Collaborations
•	Cà Mau faces severe climate threats—particularly sea level rise (SLR) and land subsidence. Scientific studies warn that by 2030, up to 43% of the province could be submerged; by 2050, this risk could reach 75% 
•	Groundwater extraction—mainly for shrimp aquaculture—is a significant driver of subsidence, compounding climate risks 
•	International collaborations—through institutions such as Can Tho University's DRAGON-Mekong Institute—are helping build a “Monitoring and Adaptation Community” in Cà Mau to enhance climate risk management and work toward net-zero emission strategies by 2050 
4. Nature-Based Solutions & Ecosystem Services
•	Mũi Cà Mau National Park is a crucial biodiversity and ecological buffer zone. Plans for 2025 include replanting ~150 hectares of mangroves to bolster natural defense against disasters 
•	Earlier WWF and SIWRP studies emphasized integrating both hard infrastructure (like dikes and sluices) and soft solutions (like mangrove restoration and wetland creation), alongside regional cooperation, to sustain sediment flow and land elevation 
5. Livelihoods, Vulnerabilities & Community Resilience
•	Research shows that coastal communities in Cà Mau face diverse livelihood losses—especially in physical and ecological capital—due to high tides, droughts, heatwaves, floods, and sea level variability 
•	Climate shocks disproportionately impact sectors like fishing, farming, tourism, and shipping 
•	Enhancing sustainable livelihood frameworks, assembling community-based vulnerability assessments, and strengthening adaptive capacities have been flagged as urgent priorities
column16:
Climate-related issues have become a central pillar of Ca Mau Province's master and development planning. From identifying climate change as a fundamental constraint to embedding climate-resilient infrastructure, renewable energy, and ecosystem-based solutions into its long-term development vision, Ca Mau has mainstreamed adaptation across its planning framework. Scientific research and scenario modeling provide the evidence base, while large-scale investment programs ensure practical implementation.
1. Climate Change as a Central Planning Consideration
Ca Mau's Provincial Master Plan for 2021-2030, with a vision to 2050 (approved by Decision No. 1386/QĐ-TTg, November 2023), explicitly identifies climate change, land subsidence, saline intrusion, and erosion as critical constraints to development. The plan's vision is that by 2050 Ca Mau will be a modern, climate-resilient province, where ecosystems are conserved and economic growth goes hand in hand with climate adaptation. This demonstrates that climate change is not treated as an add-on, but as a core determinant of development direction.
2. Infrastructure and Adaptation Measures in the Plan
The province has integrated multiple climate adaptation projects and measures into its planning framework, including:
•	Disaster prevention and climate adaptation infrastructure, such as upgraded irrigation and flood control systems, modern hydro-meteorological stations, and seawater intrusion barriers.
•	Forest conservation and mangrove restoration, serving both as a natural buffer against disasters and a carbon sink.
•	Promotion of renewable energy and the marine economy, including the Hon Khoai deep-sea port, Nam Can Economic Zone, and large-scale renewable power projects.
•	Water supply security, with projects to expand freshwater systems and reduce reliance on groundwater extraction.
Notably, in 2020 Ca Mau also announced a climate adaptation investment program worth ~USD 820 million (19 trillion VND), funded mainly through ODA. This program included advanced shrimp aquaculture systems, dike construction, mangrove reforestation, and real-time weather monitoring—initiatives that were subsequently incorporated into the official master plan.
3. Scientific Foundations Guiding Planning
The province's planning integrates climate science and scenario modeling:
•	Studies by Can Tho University's DRAGON-Mekong Institute and DONRE modeled groundwater reserves under climate change and socio-economic development scenarios for 2030, 2050, and 2070, guiding water management in provincial planning.
•	Research has highlighted that Ca Mau faces severe land subsidence and sea-level rise risks, with projections that 43% of the province may be inundated by 2030 and up to 75% by 2050. Such findings have reinforced the urgency of embedding adaptation and disaster risk reduction into all development pathways.
column17:
Climate-related issues have significantly impacted Cà Mau Province's financial planning, creating both the need for substantial investment and a shift in how the province allocates its budget. The financial impact can be summarized in the following ways:
1. Allocation of a large budget for climate change adaptation projects:
•	Cà Mau has allocated a large portion of its financial resources to address the immediate and long-term impacts of climate change. For the period 2021-2030, the province planned to spend over VND 19 trillion (approximately 820 million USD) on 55 'priority' projects related to climate change and disaster prevention.
•	These funds are primarily used for 'hard' infrastructure projects, such as building and upgrading sea and river dykes, sluice gates, and irrigation systems to prevent saline intrusion and coastal erosion.
•	The budget also covers the construction of storm shelters for fishing vessels and embankments to protect residential areas.
2. Dependence on central government and international funding:
•	Given the immense financial burden, Cà Mau's financial planning is heavily dependent on external sources. A significant portion of the planned budget, about VND 18.178 trillion, is expected to come from the central government's budget and Official Development Assistance (ODA) from international partners like the World Bank, UNDP, and the Green Climate Fund (GCF).
•	This dependence means that the province's ability to implement large-scale projects is tied to the availability and conditions of this external funding, which can be a complex and lengthy process.
3. Shift in resource allocation priorities:
•	Climate change has forced the province to re-prioritize its financial planning, shifting funds from other development areas towards climate change resilience. This includes not only building physical infrastructure but also investing in monitoring systems (hydro-meteorological stations), research on climate-resilient livelihoods, and community awareness programs.
•	Recently, the province has also started exploring new financial mechanisms like 'green carbon credits' to attract more funding for forest protection and carbon sequestration projects.
4. Indirect economic and fiscal impacts:
•	Beyond direct project costs, climate change impacts the provincial budget through reduced tax revenue and increased spending on disaster relief.
•	Saline intrusion and drought severely damage agricultural production (especially rice), impacting the incomes of farmers and the overall provincial economy. This reduces the tax base and can lead to a need for more social welfare spending to support affected communities.
•	The loss of coastal land and forests due to erosion also represents a significant economic loss, which strains the province's long-term financial stability.

The transition to a low-carbon economy presents a unique set of risks for Cà Mau Province, primarily due to its economic structure and its vulnerability to climate change itself. While the province has significant opportunities in this transition, the following risks must be carefully managed:
1. Economic and Social Transition Risks:
•	Impact on key economic sectors: Cà Mau's economy is heavily dependent on agriculture, particularly rice and aquaculture. The shift to a low-carbon economy requires a fundamental change in production methods, such as low-emission rice farming and sustainable shrimp-forest models. Failure to effectively implement these changes could lead to reduced productivity and income for local farmers and fishers, potentially impacting a large portion of the rural population.
•	Job market disruption: While the green transition is expected to create new 'green jobs' in renewable energy and sustainable agriculture, there is a risk of job displacement in traditional sectors if workers are not adequately retrained. The transition may require new skills that the current workforce does not possess, creating a skills gap and potential unemployment.
•	Access to technology and finance: The high initial investment required for low-carbon technologies (e.g., solar panels, wind turbines) can be a significant barrier for local businesses and households. Cà Mau's financial capacity is limited, making it highly reliant on national and international support. Delays or insufficient funding could slow down the transition and put the province at a disadvantage.
2. Policy and Market Risks:
•	Inconsistent or unclear regulations: The transition to a low-carbon economy is still in its early stages in Vietnam. Risks exist from a lack of clear and consistent national policies and legal frameworks, particularly concerning carbon markets, green financing, and renewable energy development. This regulatory uncertainty can deter private sector investment and create obstacles for the province's planning and implementation efforts.
•	Market volatility: Cà Mau is exploring a carbon credit market, leveraging its extensive mangrove forests. However, this market is subject to price volatility and strict international standards. If carbon prices drop or if the province's projects fail to meet international certification requirements, the anticipated revenue stream from these credits may not materialize, impacting the province's ability to fund its climate resilience projects.
•	Competition: The potential for renewable energy development is high in Cà Mau, particularly for wind and solar power. However, as more provinces and private companies enter this market, competition for land, grid connection capacity, and financing could increase, posing a risk to the viability of future projects.
3. Environmental and Biophysical Risks:
•	Continued physical risks from climate change: Even with a low-carbon transition, Cà Mau will continue to face severe physical risks from climate change, such as sea-level rise, coastal erosion, and saltwater intrusion. If mitigation efforts are not fully effective or if the pace of climate change accelerates, these physical risks could undermine the very economic and social benefits the low-carbon transition is meant to bring.
•	Potential for unintended consequences: The rapid conversion of land for large-scale solar or wind farms could lead to unintended environmental consequences, such as changes in local ecosystems or water management issues, if not managed properly. The shift to more sustainable practices in one sector must be balanced to avoid creating new environmental problems in another.

En la comuna de Cochrane, la transición hacia una economía baja en carbono implica enfrenar diversos riesgos:
La implementación de nuevas regulaciones nacionales o regionales sobre emisiones, uso de combustibles fósiles y gestión de residuos puede generar mayores exigencias de cumplimiento para el municipio. Esto implicaría destinar recursos adicionales para adecuar la infraestructura, los sistemas de transporte municipal y los servicios comunitarios a estándares más estrictos de sostenibilidad.
La adopción de tecnologías limpias y eficientes, como calefacción distrital renovable, electro movilidad o sistemas de energías renovables, requiere inversiones significativas. La limitada capacidad financiera del municipio y de los hogares de Cochrane puede retrasar esta transición, generando desigualdad en el acceso a soluciones tecnológicas y aumentando la brecha con otras comunas mas grandes.
A medida que aumenten las exigencias normativas ambientales, existe el riesgo de que a nivel municipal se enfrenten reclamos o presiones legales por no implementar medidas de reducción de emisiones o adaptación energética en plazos adecuados.
La economía local depende en parte del uso de combustibles fósiles para suministro eléctrico, calefacción y transporte. El aumento de costos derivados de impuestos verdes o restricciones en el acceso a combustibles podría encarecer la vida en la localidad y afectar la competitividad de sectores productivos.
La transición energética y hacia una economía baja en carbono implica riesgos financieros, sociales, y operativos, pero también abre oportunidades para acceder a fondos, mejorar la resiliencia y posicionar a la comuna como referente en sostenibilidad en la región de aysén.

En Rapa Nui, la supervisión de los asuntos relacionados con el clima se complementa con la información proveniente de las estaciones de monitoreo de la Armada de Chile y la Dirección Meteorológica de Chile (DMC). Estas estaciones entregan datos sobre precipitaciones, temperatura, mareas y condiciones oceánicas, fundamentales para evaluar la variabilidad climática, el riesgo de sequías, las olas de calor, y los eventos extremos que afectan directamente a la isla.

El PACCC utiliza esta información técnica como línea base para proyectar escenarios de vulnerabilidad, priorizar medidas de adaptación (gestión hídrica, prevención de incendios, protección marina) y fortalecer la capacidad de respuesta local.

De esta forma, los procesos de supervisión climática combinan la información de organismos nacionales (Armada y DMC), el análisis científico con universidades, y la gobernanza local a través de comités y mesas territoriales.
column16: El cambio climático ha impactado la planificación comunal de Rapa Nui al integrar criterios de adaptación y sostenibilidad en la planificación maestra. Se priorizan proyectos de gestión hídrica, energías renovables, residuos, agroecología y protección de biodiversidad. El PACCC orienta la inversión y el ordenamiento territorial, reconociendo al clima como condicionante estructural del desarrollo local.
column17:
En Rapa Nui, los asuntos relacionados con el clima han tenido un efecto directo en la forma en que se planifica y prioriza la inversión pública comunal. El Plan de Acción Comunal de Cambio Climático (PACCC), elaborado en coordinación con la comunidad y en coherencia con la Ley Marco de Cambio Climático de Chile, se ha transformado en un instrumento orientador de la planificación financiera municipal.

El PACCC identifica riesgos como la escasez hídrica, la degradación de ecosistemas, los incendios forestales, el impacto sobre la seguridad alimentaria y los efectos del cambio climático en el mar. Estos diagnósticos han llevado a que la Municipalidad de Rapa Nui oriente sus recursos a proyectos de adaptación y mitigación climática, así como a la búsqueda de financiamiento externo para complementar las limitadas capacidades locales.

Principales impactos en la planificación financiera:

Gestión hídrica: la amenaza de sequías ha impulsado la priorización de proyectos de captación de aguas lluvias, mejoras en la infraestructura de almacenamiento y protección de acuíferos. Estos proyectos han sido incluidos en los presupuestos comunales y en postulaciones a fondos sectoriales y externos.

Residuos y energía: la planificación financiera considera la implementación progresiva de una gestión integral de residuos sólidos y el impulso de energías renovables que reduzcan la dependencia del diésel importado, lo que representa una oportunidad de ahorro a largo plazo y de reducción de emisiones.

Soberanía alimentaria: el financiamiento municipal se ha orientado hacia programas de agroecología y apoyo a productores locales, como medida de adaptación frente a la variabilidad climática y la dependencia de productos importados.

Protección de biodiversidad y prevención de riesgos: se han asignado recursos y buscado alianzas para proyectos de conservación de ecosistemas marinos y terrestres, y para programas de prevención de incendios forestales.

Alianzas y fondos externos: la gestión financiera se ha ampliado mediante convenios con universidades y organismos internacionalescon el fin de acceder a investigación aplicada, asistencia técnica y financiamiento complementario..

En la práctica, esto significa que toda planificación financiera comunal incorpora criterios climáticos de manera transversal: los proyectos priorizados por la Secretaría Comunal de Planificación (SECPLAC) deben demostrar coherencia con los objetivos del PACCC y su contribución a la resiliencia del territorio.

Asimismo, la presión climática sobre los recursos ha impulsado una mayor disciplina en la búsqueda de eficiencia financiera, promoviendo soluciones basadas en la naturaleza y esquemas de economía circular que no solo responden al cambio climático, sino que generan beneficios económicos y sociales.
column18:
Para Rapa Nui, la transición hacia una economía baja en carbono es una oportunidad estratégica, pero también conlleva riesgos específicos derivados de nuestra condición insular, la dependencia de recursos externos y la fragilidad de nuestro patrimonio cultural y natural. Estos riesgos son considerados en la planificación local y en el Plan de Acción Comunal de Cambio Climático (PACCC).

Principales riesgos identificados que hemo identificado:

Dependencia energética del diésel: la isla depende casi en su totalidad de la importación de combustibles fósiles para generar electricidad. La transición a renovables exige inversiones iniciales muy altas y enfrenta barreras técnicas, como el almacenamiento de energía y la estabilidad del sistema eléctrico insular.

Costos financieros y de infraestructura: la implementación de sistemas solares, eólicos, de electromovilidad o gestión circular de residuos requiere inversiones que superan las capacidades financieras municipales. Existe riesgo de endeudamiento o de dependencia excesiva de financiamiento externo.

Capacidades técnicas limitadas: la falta de especialistas locales en energías renovables, electromovilidad o reciclaje avanzado puede retrasar la transición y generar dependencia de consultores externos, encareciendo la implementación y el mantenimiento.

Vulnerabilidad de sectores económicos dependientes de importaciones: la mayor parte de los bienes de consumo y alimentos llegan a la isla en barco o avión, ambos con alta huella de carbono. En un escenario de transición global, podrían aumentar los costos logísticos o imponerse nuevas regulaciones externas que afecten la seguridad alimentaria y económica de la isla.

Aceptación social y cultural: los cambios en patrones de consumo, movilidad o manejo de residuos requieren educación y participación comunitaria. Si la transición se percibe como impuesta, puede generar resistencias sociales, sobre todo si los costos iniciales recaen en las familias.

Riesgo de inequidad social: si los costos de tecnologías limpias no se acompañan de subsidios o apoyos, pueden afectar de manera desproporcionada a hogares de menores ingresos.

Riesgo patrimonial y cultural: la instalación de infraestructura energética (paneles solares, aerogeneradores) puede entrar en conflicto con sitios arqueológicos y paisajes culturales protegidos. Asimismo, existe el riesgo de que se implementen soluciones tecnológicas que no respeten el derecho consuetudinario ni la cosmovisión del pueblo Rapa Nui, generando tensiones comunitarias.

Dependencia tecnológica externa: la isla puede quedar atrapada en soluciones importadas que no tienen soporte local de reparación o recambio, lo que aumenta los costos y reduce la autonomía tecnológica.

Turismo y carbono: como destino remoto, el turismo a Rapa Nui depende casi exclusivamente de vuelos de largo alcance, con alta huella de carbono. En un contexto de transición global, podrían surgir regulaciones o percepciones que reduzcan la llegada de visitantes, afectando la principal actividad económica local.

Riesgo reputacional y de financiamiento: como Patrimonio Mundial y destino turístico de relevancia internacional, Rapa Nui enfrenta presión global para demostrar sostenibilidad. No avanzar de manera clara en la transición baja en carbono podría dificultar el acceso a fondos internacionales o disminuir su atractivo turístico.

Pemerintah Kabupaten Gunungkidul memantau kerentanan dan kapasitas adaptasi masyarakat terhadap dampak perubahan iklim. Pendekatan ini berfokus pada:
1. Pemetaan Risiko: Dokumen tersebut mengidentifikasi desa-desa yang memiliki risiko tinggi terhadap kekeringan. Pengawasan ini melibatkan analisis kerentanan berdasarkan data historis, proyeksi iklim, dan data sosial-ekonomi masyarakat.

2. Pengukuran Kapasitas Adaptasi: Pengawasan tidak hanya terbatas pada ancaman, tetapi juga mengukur kemampuan masyarakat untuk beradaptasi. Ini termasuk mengevaluasi ketersediaan air (melalui embung dan mata air), praktik pertanian, dan sistem sanitasi.

3. Menyusun Tindakan Prioritas: Hasil dari kajian ini digunakan untuk menyusun Rencana Aksi Adaptasi Perubahan Iklim (RAD-API), yang berisi daftar langkah-langkah prioritas untuk meningkatkan ketahanan masyarakat. Pengawasan terus dilakukan untuk memastikan implementasi rencana ini berjalan efektif di tingkat lokal.

Berdasarkan dokumen Rencana Pembangunan Jangka Menengah Daerah (RPJMD) Kabupaten Gunungkidul Tahun 2025-2029, isu-isu terkait iklim telah berdampak signifikan pada perencanaan pembangunan daerah. Dokumen tersebut mengidentifikasi masalah lingkungan dan kebencanaan sebagai isu strategis yang harus ditangani dalam periode perencanaan.

Berikut adalah dampak isu-isu iklim pada perencanaan pembangunan di Kabupaten Gunungkidul:
1. Peningkatan Kualitas Lingkungan dan Adaptasi Perubahan Iklim: Perencanaan pembangunan menempatkan peningkatan kualitas lingkungan hidup, mitigasi bencana, dan adaptasi perubahan iklim sebagai isu strategis yang penting. Hal ini sejalan dengan agenda global, yaitu tujuan ke-13 yang berfokus pada penanganan perubahan iklim dan dampaknya.

2. Mitigasi Bencana dan Penanganan Kekeringan: Dokumen ini menyoroti perlunya penanganan bencana, terutama terkait dengan masalah kekeringan dan penyediaan air bersih. Hal ini menjadi masalah utama dalam aspek geografi, yang ditunjukkan dengan belum optimalnya mitigasi bencana.

3. Perencanaan Tata Ruang Berbasis Risiko Bencana: Perencanaan tata ruang di Kabupaten Gunungkidul kini harus mempertimbangkan risiko bencana, daya dukung dan daya tampung lingkungan, serta perubahan iklim, khususnya di wilayah perkotaan dan pesisir. Selain itu, kawasan budidaya diatur dengan memperhatikan risiko bencana.

4. Dampak Perubahan Cuaca Ekstrem pada Kualitas Udara: Dampak cuaca ekstrem, seperti kemarau panjang, turut memengaruhi kualitas udara. Dokumen ini menyebutkan bahwa rentang waktu kemarau panjang menjadi salah satu penyebab peningkatan zat pencemar di udara pada tahun 2023.

5. Kecenderungan Penurunan Kualitas Tutupan Lahan: Indeks Kualitas Tutupan Lahan (IKTL) Kabupaten Gunungkidul menunjukkan fluktuasi dengan kecenderungan menurun dalam lima tahun terakhir. Hal ini mengindikasikan adanya masalah dalam pengelolaan kualitas lahan yang menjadi bagian dari isu lingkungan.

Prioritas Strategis: Dokumen ini menempatkan 'peningkatan kualitas lingkungan hidup, mitigasi bencana, dan adaptasi perubahan iklim' sebagai salah satu isu strategis utama yang harus ditangani dalam periode perencanaan.
